2026-10-02.title: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
2026-10-02.authors: Yen-Jen Wang , Haozhe Jiang , Shuying Deng , Haoru Xue , Weirui Ye , Rocky Duan , Nika Haghtalab , S. Shankar Sastry , Pieter Abbeel , Haozhi Qi
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Building reliable robot capabilities across diverse tasks requires substantial human effort to develop and maintain skills, design rewards, and integrate perception with control.
We present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework for autonomous improvement of robot execution systems without updating model weights.
RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset and constructs related practice tasks in simulation.
During practice, RPG uses execution feedback, privileged simulator state, and available dataset videos to diagnose failures.
It develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt based on these diagnoses.
Cross-task evaluation tests individual candidate changes and merged revisions before they are retained for reuse.
At test time, a multimodal LLM uses the resulting system prompt and skill library to coordinate perception and robot control.
On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, outperforming all evaluated baselines, including ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%).
After a common calibration and hardware-adaptation procedure, the frozen system succeeds in all 30 physical trials, with ten trials on each of three tasks.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled agents to perceive environments and reason about tasks [ 1 ] . Language-model agents can also generate and execute code [ 2 ] and improve through feedback [ 3 ] . These capabilities offer a way to expand robot behavior with less task-specific human engineering. In particular, multimodal coding agents can use visual observations and execution feedback to construct, refine, and compose executable skills that robots can retain and reuse across tasks [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

Language-model-based robot control involves a tradeoff between program execution and online reasoning. Code-as-Policy combines perception and control primitives into executable programs [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . These programs can execute efficiently and incorporate feedback loops, but their responses depend on explicit program logic and perception interfaces. For example, a robust symbolic check for grasp success can be difficult to specify, while an MLLM can assess the outcome from images. In Agent-as-Policy , the MLLM remains in the control loop, providing flexible visual and semantic reasoning [ 1 , 5 ] . However, frequent model calls can make low-level decisions slow. A scalable system should combine these strengths by delegating repeatable execution to reusable code and reserving multimodal reasoning for decisions that benefit from visual or semantic judgment.

We introduce Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework that develops and refines reusable robot skills through autonomous practice without updating model weights (Fig. ). RPG improves both the shared skill library and the system prompt that guides a multimodal agent in using it. Changes to these shared components persist across episodes and can benefit other tasks that reuse them.

Given an offline dataset, Reconstruct selects source tasks that expose useful manipulation capabilities and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. The resulting practice suite can be expanded by processing additional tasks from the dataset. A practice task may cover part of a source task or an analogous manipulation. It need not reproduce the original trajectory or scene. We use ABC [ 10 ] in this work because it covers 193 diverse tasks. During Practice , RPG compares executions from the Runtime Agent and the Privileged Agent, which uses the same model and skill library but additionally receives simulator state. The Video Analyzer uses these execution records and available dataset videos to diagnose failures. RPG then develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt. It evaluates candidate changes across the practice tasks and retests merged changes before retaining them. Finally, Go Real calibrates and freezes the resulting system for physical deployment, where the Runtime Agent coordinates perception and control through the shared skill library.

On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, outperforming ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%). Through comprehensive ablation experiments, we demonstrate the benefits of the Privileged Agent, Video Analyzer, and skill revisions. After a hardware calibration procedure, the frozen RPG system successfully completes all 30 physical trials, with 10 trials for each of the three evaluated tasks. These results show that autonomous practice can develop and refine shared robot skills that support physical deployment. Our contributions are:

We introduce RPG, a framework that autonomously selects manipulation capabilities from an offline dataset and constructs an expandable suite of simulation practice tasks for developing reusable robot skills.

We develop an autonomous practice procedure that uses privileged execution and video-based failure diagnosis to revise shared skills and the system prompt, validating both individual and merged changes across tasks.

We demonstrate 95.0% success on held-out initializations of 22 simulated manipulation tasks and 100% success over 30 trials across three physical tasks.

1. We introduce RPG, a framework that autonomously selects manipulation capabilities from an offline dataset and constructs an expandable suite of simulation practice tasks for developing reusable robot skills.

2. We develop an autonomous practice procedure that uses privileged execution and video-based failure diagnosis to revise shared skills and the system prompt, validating both individual and merged changes across tasks.

3. We demonstrate 95.0% success on held-out initializations of 22 simulated manipulation tasks and 100% success over 30 trials across three physical tasks.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Robot Programs and Skill Improvement

Code as Policies [ 7 ] , ProgPrompt [ 8 ] ,
and CaP-X [ 9 ] use language models to generate executable
robot programs, while Prompt2Walk [ 11 ] generates
low-level locomotion commands. SayCan [ 12 ] grounds skill
selection in learned affordances, while VoxPoser [ 13 ] generates 3D value maps for motion planning. Execution feedback also supports
closed-loop reasoning: Inner Monologue [ 14 ] uses
success detection and scene descriptions to revise plans, and
REFLECT [ 15 ] summarizes multisensory execution records to
explain failures and propose corrections.

Agents can retain execution experience for use beyond the current task.
Voyager [ 16 ] accumulates executable skills in Minecraft.
Lifelong Robot Library Learning (LRLL) [ 4 ] grows a robot skill
library through simulation exploration and code abstraction with human
guidance. ASPIRE [ 5 ] diagnoses failures from multimodal traces
and stores validated strategies as in-context skills. RATs [ 6 ] uses self-directed play to build reusable skills and failure memories.
RHO [ 17 ] searches over multi-file robot policy repositories using
execution feedback, paired candidate tests, and validation.
ENPIRE [ 18 ] improves robot policies through autonomous
experimentation with physical feedback.
SHAPER [ 19 ] evolves reusable skills and a context-code harness from embodied rollouts without updating model parameters. HERO [ 20 ] autonomously accumulates and consolidates reusable manipulation behaviors. Outside robotics, GRASP [ 21 ] studies regression-gated updates to persistent agent skill libraries.
RPG combines dataset-guided
simulation practice with failure diagnosis that compares executions from the Runtime Agent and Privileged Agent, using source videos when available. It revises
shared skill code and the system prompt, then tests both individual
candidates and merged revisions across a fixed practice suite before
retaining them. RPG performs all self-improvement in simulation and freezes the execution system before physical deployment.

## II-B Offline Data and Simulation Practice

Demo2Code [ 22 ] summarizes
state-based demonstrations into task specifications and synthesizes
executable code. Uni-Skill [ 23 ] trains a multimodal planner
and retrieves skill-level video
examples to implement missing skills. RPG uses videos and textual
descriptions from an offline dataset, here ABC [ 10 ] ,
to identify manipulation capabilities worth practicing. It constructs
related simulation tasks rather than directly reproducing the source
trajectories or their scene geometry. Simulation can also expand the data and objectives available for robot
learning. MimicGen [ 24 ] transforms demonstrations to generate
additional training trajectories, while Re 3 Sim [ 25 ] reconstructs real scenes to generate simulation data for imitation
learning. Eureka [ 26 ] generates reward code for reinforcement
learning. GenSim [ 27 ] and GenSim2 [ 28 ] generate
simulation tasks and demonstrations for policy training, with GenSim2
using multimodal reasoning to construct task solvers. RPG uses
simulation to develop and refine executable skills and the system
prompt rather than to train a neural policy. Model weights, task
definitions, and evaluation criteria remain fixed during practice.

2026-10-02.title: InterEvolve: Test-Time Evolution of Reward Programs for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Zhuo Lin , Sirui Xu , Liuyu Bian , Yu-Xiong Wang , Liang-Yan Gui
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR)
2026-10-02.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: We study test-time evolution for humanoid loco-manipulation: solving tasks that a controller was never trained for by repurposing its existing skills, improving from its own attempts, and retaining what it learns, without retraining. Our key insight is that a broad controller already holds much of the competence a new task needs , and that this competence becomes accessible through an interface between planning and control that is expressive enough to specify contact-rich, multi-stage interactions, yet executable and measurable enough that execution feedback can guide planning from experience. InterEvolve realizes this interface with two components. First, we develop an object-aware forward-backward (FB) behavioral foundation model, whose object residuals on a frozen body prior turn a new reward about the body or objects into loco-manipulation behavior at test time. Second, we specify tasks as reward programs : staged rewards with completion conditions and tunable constants. A large language model (LLM) agent revises the program structure in context, drawing on execution feedback and a skill library of verified programs, while a numerical optimizer tunes its constants. With every candidate verified across parallel simulation scenarios, the program explores new ways to induce, repurpose, and compose the controller’s existing motor competence for the task at hand, and thus improves over iterations. Experiments show that human-designed rewards leave much of the FB model’s loco-manipulation competence untapped, whereas the programs InterEvolve evolves release it, sometimes through novel strategies. It further produces behaviors for diverse tasks, complex scenes, and long-horizon compositions in simulation, and evolved skills run autonomously on a physical Unitree G1 from egocentric onboard perception.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Learned humanoid controllers now provide broad whole-body motion for real-robot control ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , as well as contact-rich loco-manipulation ( He et al., 2024 ) , trained from human data. Yet a humanoid in an open-ended environment will meet tasks and scenes that were not enumerated during training. Consider a controller that has learned to push, lift, and carry boxes from human demonstrations. When asked to tip a box onto another face, it does not have a demonstration of this behavior, although the motions it needs lie within what it can already do. We study test-time evolution , in which a humanoid finds such uses of its existing skills, improves from its own attempts within a budget of trials, and keeps what it learns, so that a later long-horizon composite task, such as carrying a box, placing it, and then kicking it, or a novel box tip, can build on earlier experience. What evolves is the task strategies, meaning which objectives to use or what stages to decompose, together with the experience retained across tasks, while the controller stays fixed.

Achieving this capability requires a way to state a new task that is expressive enough for contact-rich, multi-stage interaction, yet cheap to revise after each attempt. Common task interfaces for humanoid control, such as motion references ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , goal states ( He et al., 2026 ) , and skill labels ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , request desired motions, target states, or predefined behaviors. An objective such as tipping an object must therefore be translated into a reference goal or a new skill, either of which can be difficult to design for nuanced interactions. Rewards offer a more expressive alternative: they can specify contact-rich objectives and indicate where an attempt fell short, as their role in shaping such behavior during training demonstrates ( Andrychowicz et al., 2020 ) . Conventionally, however, each reward revision requires training a new policy, making it slow to iterate over many candidates ( Ma et al., 2024a ) .

We introduce InterEvolve , which builds this interface from reward programs and a behavioral foundation model that executes them without retraining (Fig. 1 ). A reward program is a sequence of stages, each with a reward and a completion condition, plus tunable weights and thresholds. To execute a program, we use a forward-backward (FB) behavioral foundation model ( Touati and Ollivier, 2021 ; Tirinzoni et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , which maps a reward to a latent that elicits the corresponding behavior from one fixed policy. Existing humanoid FB models, however, observe only the body, so rewards that differ only in the object’s goal can collapse into one behavior. We extend the model in two ways: we attach trainable object residuals that read object features to its frozen body networks, and we train these residuals on large-scale human-object interaction (HOI) data.

With execution in place, the central challenge becomes reward formulation itself. It is especially pronounced in loco-manipulation, where a naively handcrafted reward underperforms even if the controller contains the relevant motor capabilities. InterEvolve therefore lets a large language model (LLM) agent iterates reward programs in context : with its weights fixed, the agent combines task intent and execution feedback from simulation to refine the rewards and their composition. Instead of collecting references and training a policy for each new behavior, InterEvolve spends compute proposing, tuning, and verifying reward programs. This mirrors test-time scaling in language models, where more inference compute yields better solutions ( Snell et al., 2025 ; Brown et al., 2024 ) .

We organize this evolution around two complementary objectives: improving the reward program for the current task and retaining what is learned to guide future tasks. ( i ) Two parts of a program must be searched together: its structure , meaning which rewards and stages it uses, and its constants , meaning the weights and thresholds. A promising structure can still fail under poor weights, so the agent revises the structure while an inner search with the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) ( Hansen and Ostermeier, 2001 ) tunes the constants of each proposal. Parallel simulation supplies batches of execution evidence, so each revision is guided by a comparison over many rollouts. ( ii ) For future tasks, InterEvolve summarizes successful reward programs as a skill library . Later tasks can retrieve these experiences without rediscovering them from scratch.

Our contributions are threefold. First, a framework for self-evolving humanoid loco-manipulation that shifts task-specific compute from training to test-time evolution: an LLM agent learns in context to write and adapt reward programs that a fixed, reusable controller executes for new tasks and scenes. Second, an object-aware FB behavioral foundation model that translates reward objectives into whole-body interaction. Third, an evaluation of how reward design and accumulated experience affect reference tracking and goal-conditioned tasks, showing that success grows with evolution. We further show unseen tasks and long-horizon compositions in simulation and fully autonomous deployment on a physical Unitree G1 from onboard perception.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Humanoid loco-manipulation and task interfaces. Humanoid control has grown reusable, from simulated characters ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2022 ) to real-robot whole-body policies learned from teleoperation and human motion ( Fu et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2026 ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Ze et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Loco-manipulation policies learn grasping and contact-rich interaction from references ( Luo et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Tessler et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Xu et al., 2026b ) and transfer to real robots ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2026 ) . Others condition control on multimodal prompts ( Kareer et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Kalaria et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , sequences existing skills with planners ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2024 ; Tevet et al., 2025 ) , or imitates video-imagined interactions ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . InterEvolve instead states the task as a reward program, which says which contacts and stage transitions matter, and revises it after each attempt.

Behavioral foundation models and reward inference. Successor features decouple occupancy from reward ( Dayan, 1993 ; Barreto et al., 2017 ) , and FB representations factorize the successor measure so a backward map projects any reward into a latent prompt ( Touati and Ollivier, 2021 ; Touati et al., 2023 ) . Humanoid behavioral foundation models thus run one policy for new rewards, goals, or references without task-specific training ( Tirinzoni et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Follow-ups refines the representation ( Cetin et al., 2025 ; Bagatella et al., 2026 ) , searches the latent space ( Sikchi et al., 2025b ) , infers tasks online ( Rupf et al., 2025 ; Bagot et al., 2026 ) , grounds language ( Sikchi et al., 2025a ) . These models observe only the body, so rewards that differ only in what happens to an object collapse into one behavior. Our object-aware FB model removes this limit.

Reward design and agents that learn from execution. Language models write reward functions from task descriptions ( Xie et al., 2024 ) , refine them from simulator feedback ( Ma et al., 2024a ; Ma et al., 2024b ) , and search over reward designs ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , including for humanoid locomotion ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , but each candidate reward is realized by training a policy. Language to Rewards optimizes LLM-written rewards with model predictive control instead ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) . MotionDisco evolves humanoid motions with an LLM and trajectory optimization before training trackers for them ( Taouil et al., 2026 ) , and ROSETTA builds multi-stage reward programs from language preferences ( Srivastava et al., 2026 ) . Coding agents likewise refine executable plans from feedback and retain reusable experience ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Zha et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . In InterEvolve, each candidate reward costs a batch of rollouts on a fixed controller rather than an RL run, and verified programs form a skill library for later tasks.

Test-time compute and search. Language models improve with more inference compute through repeated sampling, step-level search, and long reasoning ( Snell et al., 2025 ; Brown et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , and program-search systems evolve code against an automatic evaluator ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ) . In control, test-time search usually plans actions with a dynamics model ( Hansen et al., 2024 ) or steers a pretrained humanoid policy ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Seo et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) . InterEvolve searches over task specifications instead, keeping the controller fixed and verifying proposed reward programs in parallel rollouts.

2026-10-02.title: Watch, Infer, Coordinate: Inferring Robot Partner Constraints for Zero-Shot Coordination
2026-10-02.authors: Suyu Ye , Zheyuan Zhang , Vaishnav Tadiparthi , Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub , Ehsan Moradi Pari , Tianmin Shu , Homanga Bharadhwaj , Nakul Agarwal
2026-10-02.abstract: Robots operating in the physical world will increasingly need to coordinate with other robots, particularly in manipulation tasks where an object may be too large or heavy for a single robot to carry alone. Physical limitations caused by hardware degradation or actuator faults can restrict the actions a robot can reliably execute, yet these limitations may be unknown to its partner. We study whether a helper can infer a robot partner’s physical constraints from observing it coordinate with another robot, then use the inferred capability to coordinate with the same partner on a new task. This is difficult because a demonstration shows what the constrained robot did, but not what it could have done. In physically coupled tasks, the other robot may also compensate for its limitations, making those limitations difficult to identify from the constrained robot’s behavior alone. Our key insight is that these constraints shape the joint behavior of the team, making the actions of both robots informative about the constrained partner’s capability. We introduce Watch, Infer, Coordinate, a benchmark spanning three physically coupled manipulation settings, together with an inference approach that scores candidate constraints using observed joint behavior. Across all three settings, our method substantially improves constraint inference and zero-shot coordination, approaching an oracle with access to the true constraints.
2026-10-02.introduction:
As robots move from controlled laboratories into the physical world, they will increasingly need to not only adapt to their environment, but also to learn to coordinate with one another. Some manipulation tasks naturally require multiple robots, for example when transporting objects that are too large or heavy for a single robot to handle alone ( Farivarnejad and Berman, 2022 ) . In such physically coupled tasks, the robots’ actions jointly determine the motion of the shared object, requiring closely coordinated movements, often in decentralized settings in which robots cannot access one another’s plans ( Pandit et al., 2025b ; Doshi et al., 2026 ; Yang and Mavrogiannis, 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . In practice, a robot’s physical capabilities may also change over time due to hardware degradation or actuator faults. Such failures can reduce actuator effectiveness or restrict the motion of individual joints, changing the set of actions the robot can reliably execute ( Lewis and Maciejewski, 1997 ; Tinós et al., 2007 ) . In this work, we consider a helper that must coordinate with a robot, which we call the constrained agent , subject to unknown constraints on its low-level physical actions, such as position or velocity limits on individual joints.

Existing methods do not directly address how a helper could learn these constraints from observing prior coordination. Partner-aware assistance approaches have inferred properties such as goals or task-level capabilities ( Puig et al., 2021 ; Cao et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ) , while methods for physically coupled coordination typically adapt to a partner’s behavior without explicitly inferring persistent constraints on the actions that partner can execute ( Yang and Mavrogiannis, 2025 ; Pandit et al., 2025b ; Doshi et al., 2026 ) . We therefore ask whether a helper can infer a partner’s physical constraints by observing it coordinate with another robot, and then use that knowledge to coordinate with the same partner on a new task. As illustrated in Figure 1 , the helper first observes a demonstrator coordinate with the constrained agent, then takes the demonstrator’s place on a different task. Because the helper has not observed how the constrained agent coordinates on this new task before deployment, we refer to this as zero-shot coordination .

Inferring these constraints from watching prior coordination is difficult because a demonstration shows what the constrained agent did, but not what it could have done. If the constrained agent does not take a particular action, that action may be physically infeasible or simply unnecessary for the task. Physical coupling makes this ambiguity more subtle, as the demonstrator may compensate for the constrained agent’s limitations. This can make the constraint difficult to identify from the task outcome or the constrained agent’s actions alone. Our key insight is that a partner’s physical constraints shape the joint behavior of the team, so the actions of both agents can be used to reason about them. Because these low-level constraints belong to the agent rather than a particular task, they can also provide a capability model that remains useful when the task changes. We study these ideas in simulation settings with varying levels of complexity, allowing us to systematically vary physical constraints across different coordination problems.

We introduce Watch, Infer, Coordinate , a framework for studying coordination under unknown partner constraints. As shown in Figure 2 , Watch, Infer, Coordinate includes a benchmark spanning three joint-carrying settings of increasing physical complexity, with obstacle-free demonstrations followed by a new task at test time in which obstacles block the direct path to the goal and require different coordinated motions. The benchmark includes 2D rod carrying, fixed-base dual-UR5 carrying, and mobile dual-UR5 carrying, spanning a low-dimensional abstraction to increasingly complex robotic manipulation. We also propose an inference approach that uses the observed actions of both agents to determine which candidate constraints are most consistent with their coordination. We use the resulting capability estimate to support zero-shot coordination with the constrained agent on the new task.

To summarize, our main contributions are fourfold. (1) We formulate the problem of inferring a robot partner’s persistent low-level physical constraints from prior multi-agent coordination and using them for zero-shot coordination on a new task. (2) We introduce the Watch, Infer, Coordinate benchmark, spanning three joint-carrying settings of increasing physical complexity. (3) We propose an inference approach that uses the actions of both agents to infer the constrained agent’s physical constraints from observed coordination. (4) We show that our approach improves both constraint inference and downstream task success across all three settings, approaching the performance of an oracle that is given the true constraints.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Physically Coupled Robot Collaboration. Prior work has studied physically coupled robot collaboration in both human-robot and robot-robot teams. Human-robot methods adapt to the partner’s current behavior, for example by inferring intent from joint motion ( Yang and Mavrogiannis, 2025 ) , using language to revise motion plans ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , or learning cooperative policies from human-human demonstrations ( Ng et al., 2023 ) . Multi-robot methods learn decentralized controllers using shared ( Pandit et al., 2025a ; Pandit et al., 2025b ; Doshi et al., 2026 ) , or agent-specific policies ( He et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . These methods span model-based planning ( Stouraitis et al., 2020 ; Kennel-Maushart and Coros, 2024 ; Jaafar et al., 2024 ; Yang and Mavrogiannis, 2025 ) , reinforcement learning ( Nachum et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Shibata et al., 2023 ; Aljalbout et al., 2023 ; Pandit et al., 2025a ; Pandit et al., 2025b ) , diffusion policies ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Ng et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and VLM/VLA-based policies ( Song et al., 2025 ; Doshi et al., 2026 ) . However, they do not explicitly infer a persistent physical constraint on the actions that a particular partner can execute. Ability-aware controllers can account for differences in robots’ actuation limits, but assume those limits are known ( Yan et al., 2021 ) . Our work instead infers the constrained agent’s feasible action set from prior physically coupled demonstrations and uses the inferred model to coordinate with the same agent in a new environment.

Partner-Aware Assistance. The watch-and-help challenge proposed the problem of observing an agent, inferring its goal, and then helping it achieve that goal ( Puig et al., 2021 ) . Subsequent work has developed methods for inferring and updating the agent’s goal online ( Puig et al., 2023 ; Zhi-Xuan et al., 2020 ) . More broadly, partner-aware assistance methods has modeled other properties that shape an agent’s behavior, including its beliefs about environment dynamics ( Reddy et al., 2018 ) , and its latent strategy across repeated interactions ( Xie et al., 2021 ) . Capability-aware methods instead reason about what the partner can do, but often represent capability through task-level properties or high-level actions. TICC-POMDP models capability through action success probabilities ( Lee et al., 2020 ) . Smart Help estimates semantic capabilities such as reachable height and liftable weight ( Cao et al., 2024 ) , while CHAIC uses VLM and LLM based helpers to infer a partner’s goals and physical limitations online and reasons about these limitations through task-level actions and assistance plans ( Du et al., 2024 ) . CE-CM-Div infers domain-specific capabilities defined over symbolic and macro actions ( Tisnikar et al., 2026 ) . Our work instead infers a partner’s low-level physical action constraints, such as joint and velocity limits, from demonstrations of the partner collaborating with another agent. A new helper then uses this capability model to plan joint motion with the partner, zero-shot, on a new task.

Constraint Inference from Demonstrations. The goal of constraint inference from demonstrations is to recover unknown constraints on an agent or its environment from observed behavior ( Chou et al., 2018 ; Scobee and Sastry, 2019 ; Malik et al., 2021 ) . Optimization-based methods search for lower-cost alternatives to the demonstrated trajectory, relying on the idea that if the demonstration is optimal, these alternatives must violate an unknown constraint ( Chou et al., 2018 ; Chou et al., 2020 ) . Other methods infer constraints by finding those that make the observed demonstrations most likely ( Scobee and Sastry, 2019 ; Malik et al., 2021 ) . However, much of this work focuses on environmental constraints, such as hidden obstacles and forbidden regions, that are directly reflected in a single agent’s trajectory. Prior work on agent centric constraint inference either observes the agent acting on its own ( Tisnikar et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) or models capability as domain-specific restrictions on which tools or task-level actions the agent can use ( Tisnikar et al., 2026 ) . Recent work has also inferred constraints from multi-agent demonstrations, but focuses on interaction constraints between agents rather than the physical limits of a particular partner ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Our work instead infers a partner’s low-level physical limits from cooperative, physically coupled team demonstrations, where the helper may compensate for the constrained partner, and the resulting team motion can hide the partner’s limitations.

2026-10-02.title: DuoMind: Enabling Distributed Multi-Robot Coordination with Semantic Communication
2026-10-02.authors: Hanchu Zhou , Dechen Gao , Hang Wang , Brendan Lynch , Boqi Zhao , Qiyao Ma , Raman Goyal , Junshan Zhang
2026-10-02.abstract: Vision–language models (VLMs) and vision–language–action models (VLAs) have recently driven rapid progress in general-purpose robots, yet most progress has focused on single-robot settings. Extending these capabilities to multi-robot systems remains challenging because robots must coordinate long-horizon behaviors while maintaining reliable, fine-grained execution. We introduce DuoMind , a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination through semantic communication. Each robot uses a VLA-based action model for low-level execution and a VLM-based orchestrator for high-level reasoning and inter-agent coordination. At each planning step, the orchestrator at each robot reasons over the task instruction, local observations, and messages received from other robots. It then generates low-level instructions for the action model and semantic messages for peer robots. This architecture exploits the complementary strengths of pretrained models by combining the semantic reasoning capabilities of VLMs with the precise action-generation capabilities of VLAs. To address the scarcity of benchmarks for multi-robot coordination, we further develop RoboPoly , a benchmark comprising long-horizon manipulation tasks that require coordinated, closed-loop execution under distributed control. Experiments on RoboPoly and RoboTwin demonstrate that DuoMind improves multi-robot task performance, while ablation studies confirm the contributions of hierarchical orchestration and semantic communication. More details are available on our project page .

Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have substantially expanded the capabilities of general-purpose robots. VLMs ( Beyer et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) provide strong visual understanding and high-level reasoning, while VLAs translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into robot actions ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Team et al., 2025 ) . Building on these complementary capabilities, recent design of robot agents ( Song et al., 2025a ; Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Team et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025a ) combines a high-level embodied reasoning model with a low-level VLA policy. In this design, the reasoning model aims to understand the environment and then decompose complex tasks into more specific instructions, while the VLA executes these instructions through fine-grained robot actions. Such a separation of functionalities allows the high-level model to focus on semantic understanding and long-horizon planning, while the VLA specializes in executing detailed instructions with precise low-level control.

Notably, most of the above progress has focused on a single robot acting in isolation, but many practical tasks are infeasible for a single agent and inherently require multi-robot collaboration, and others can benefit from multiple robots working together to improve efficiency. Effective multi-robot coordination requires each robot to construct appropriate subgoals and continuously adapt its behavior as the shared workspace evolves. For many practical settings, distributed execution ( Amirkhani and Barshooi, 2022 ; Lo et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024a ) is particularly desirable, where each robot makes decisions primarily from its own observations rather than relying on a centralized controller, making the system more scalable as the number of robots increases ( Nayak et al., 2023 ) . Yet combining distributed multi-agent decision making with complex robotic manipulation creates a particularly challenging coordination problem, requiring robots to reason about both team-level cooperation and precise low-level task execution.

Conventional multi-agent learning and planning methods are often studied in relatively simple environments ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Wong et al., 2023 ; Liang et al., 2025a ) , with limited physical interaction and shorter task horizons. More recently, language-model-based robotic systems have leveraged the high-level reasoning capabilities of LLMs to decompose complex objectives and schedule robot behaviors ( Chen et al., 2024b ; He et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Mandi et al., 2024 ) . However, most of these systems focus primarily on high-level planning, while low-level control is executed through simply predefined action primitives or rule-based skills. An important gap remains between high-level multi-agent reasoning and end-to-end robot control. In addition, existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematic evaluation of multi-robot coordination, leaving the field without a comprehensive testbed for measuring such capabilities.

To address the above challenges, we introduce DuoMind , a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-agent robotic coordination, together with RoboPoly , a benchmark designed specifically for long-horizon multi-robot coordination. Each robot in DuoMind operates with a VLM as its orchestrator for high-level reasoning and a VLA as its action model for low-level control. At each planning step, each orchestrator reasons over the high-level instruction, its local observation, and the shared message from other robots. It then generates both a low-level instruction for the action model and a structured message for other robots. These two outputs serve complementary roles. The low-level instruction guides the action model to produce fine-grained robot actions, while the message communicates the robot’s intention, subgoal, and task belief, allowing each agent to remain aware of its peers despite partial observability ( Liang et al., 2025b ) in the distributed setting. In this way, DuoMind provides an agentic harness around the action model: the orchestrator dynamically reasons and invokes the action model to realize long-horizon coordinated behavior at a relatively low frequency, while the action model focuses on high-frequency execution. Importantly, this decoupled design allows DuoMind to capitalize on the strong pretrained capabilities of existing VLM and VLA backbones. Rather than heavily fine-tuning models specifically for multi-robot coordination, high-level coordination and low-level manipulation can be largely handled by off-the-shelf VLM models, requiring only limited adaptation to the multi-robot setting. To systematically evaluate the coordination capabilities, we introduce RoboPoly , which provides challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks in which multiple robots must coordinate and complete the task through closed-loop physical execution rather than high-level planning alone. We further evaluate DuoMind across diverse cooperative scenarios and systematically study the contributions of hierarchical design and inter-agent communication.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We introduce DuoMind , a distributed hierarchical framework for end-to-end multi-agent robotic coordination. DuoMind utilizes a VLM as the orchestrator at each robot for high-level reasoning and a VLA as the action model for low-level control, enabling inter-agent semantic communication with natural language. This design harnesses the strong reasoning and control capabilities of existing foundation models to enable effective coordination in complex multi-robot tasks.

We develop RoboPoly , a benchmark for long-horizon multi-robot coordination under distributed observations and control. The benchmark emphasizes closed-loop physical execution and includes tasks that are challenging for a single agent, requiring multiple agents to coordinate and schedule their behaviors throughout task execution.

We conduct extensive experiments and ablation studies to evaluate DuoMind across challenging cooperative manipulation tasks on both RoboPoly and RoboTwin. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical design in multi-robot coordination and further quantify the contributions of integrating orchestrator and inter-agent communication.

# 2 DuoMind : Distributed Hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework

## 2.1 Multi-Agent Coordination via Embodied Reasoning

Existing studies on hierarchical robotic architectures have shown that action models are effective at low-level control and instruction following when provided with specific commands ( Team et al., 2025 ) . To extend this capability toward more general and long-horizon tasks, a promising approach is to introduce a reasoning model as an orchestrator, leveraging its strong visual understanding, semantic grounding, and planning capabilities to generate appropriate instructions for the action model. In distributed multi-agent settings, where task coordination are substantially more complex, we extend this hierarchical paradigm to distributed multi-robot coordination in DuoMind .

Specifically, DuoMind decomposes multi-agent coordination into two complementary levels: high-level multi-agent reasoning and low-level execution. Each robot employs a VLM as an orchestrator that reasons over the task-level instruction, its local visual observation, and message shared by other agents. The orchestrator determines the robot’s current subtask and translates it into a single-agent, short-horizon instruction for low-level control. The VLA, serving as the action model, then follows the low-level instruction using local observations to generate fine-grained robot actions. This division of responsibility allows each module to focus on the capability for which it is best suited: the orchestrator handles high-level understanding and inter-agent coordination in multi-agent setting, while the action model performs reliable low-level control.

Importantly, this decomposition avoids requiring the action model to directly interpret complex multi-agent state that includes the joint behavior of multiple robots and environment, which can be extremely challenging since action models are primarily trained with single-agent demonstrations. It therefore decouples multi-agent reasoning from low-level control, reducing the need for the action model itself to possess strong reasoning capabilities for multi-agent coordination. Moreover, DuoMind does not require the orchestrator, the action model, or the interface between them to be extensively redesigned for multi-agent settings. These foundation models developed for single-agent systems can be reused largely off the shelf, with only lightweight adaptation when necessary. This greatly extends the possibility of deploying DuoMind to diverse multi-robot tasks and offers strong compatibility to future upgrades on components.

The design of DuoMind naturally supports coordination among multiple robots. However, the complexity of task design, data collection, and evaluation increases substantially as the number of agents grows. Considering the high computational cost when the number of robots scales up, we focus on two-agent settings in this work and leave coordination at larger team scales for future study.

## 2.2 Bridging High-Level Reasoning and Low-Level Control via Natural Language Based Semantic Communication

Hierarchical robotic architectures bridge high-level reasoning and low-level control through different intermediate representations, including natural-language subgoals or motion descriptions ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Belkhale et al., 2024 ) , spatial representations such as trajectories or visual subgoals ( Li et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) , and learned latent representations in tightly coupled dual-system models ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) . Among these approaches, natural language offers interpretability and broad compatibility with language-conditioned models, whereas other representations can convey compact information but typically require stronger coupling between the two modules, making them harder to replace or adapt across architectures and embodiments.

Our framework adopts natural language as a unified interface between the high-level orchestrator and the low-level action model. The orchestrator harnesses the action model by generating low-level instructions in natural language, thereby decoupling high-level reasoning from low-level control. This design allows existing VLMs and VLAs to be incorporated as off-the-shelf components with minimal adaptation, without requiring them to be jointly trained through a specialized interface. It also enables either component to be independently replaced as stronger reasoning or action models become available.

Natural language further provides a common interface for inter-agent semantic communication. Each orchestrator can interpret messages from other agents even when they use different reasoning models, facilitating coordination across heterogeneous agents. The same interface also supports human participation by allowing users to inspect or revise instructions using ordinary language. More broadly, this shared linguistic interface provides a scalable foundation for future multi-robot systems, where heterogeneous robots and multiple human users can coordinate through a common communication protocol.

## 2.3 Inter-Agent Information Sharing

Distributed multi-agent systems face the challenges of partial observability and non-stationarity: each agent has only partial knowledge of the global task state, while the environment continues to evolve as other agents act. Insufficient awareness of such information can lead to conflicting actions or ineffective collaboration. To address these challenges, DuoMind enables agents to share and integrate structured natural-language messages during high-level reasoning. These messages convey key information about other agents’ decisions and task-relevant changes in the environment, providing additional context for more precise high-level reasoning. To support effective decision-making, we structure each shared message using four fields:

Intention. It is identical to the low-level instruction sent to the action model and describes the next subtask that the ego agent intends to execute. Sharing this intention makes other agents aware of the ego agent’s next action, helping them avoid behaviors that may interfere with its execution.

Subgoals. This field specifies the expected task state after the ego agent completes its current subtask. It explicitly communicates the future state that the ego agent aims to achieve, allowing other agents to act proactively to facilitate task completion or avoid undesirable outcomes.

Belief of task. This part describes task-relevant information observed or inferred by the ego agent, such as the location of a key object or whether a particular subtask has been completed. For example, in a kitchen task, a robot operating near the cabinets may inform another robot preparing to cook that “the pot is in the third cabinet.” Sharing such information reduces the impact of partial observability by propagating locally available knowledge across agents.

Uncertainty of belief. This optional field communicates the uncertainty associated with the ego agent’s task belief. It is particularly useful in complex tasks, where information inferred through reasoning may not always be reliable. This uncertainty provides an additional confidence signal that allows the orchestrator to appropriately weigh different beliefs during high-level reasoning, especially when agents hold inconsistent beliefs or when the available information is ambiguous.

Through this structured information sharing, DuoMind provides each agent with compact contextual information about the intentions, subgoals, beliefs, and associated uncertainty of other agents. This additional context enables the orchestrator to generate more precise low-level instructions, thereby improving the safety and efficiency of multi-robot coordination.

2026-10-02.title: SkeleWAM: Skeleton World-Action Modeling for Efficient Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Juyi Sheng , Hua Wang , Mengyuan Liu
2026-10-02.abstract: World action models (WAMs) combine robot action generation with future state prediction. Existing WAMs typically predict videos or learned visual latents, which represent interaction geometry only implicitly and may retain appearance information unrelated to control. We introduce SkeleWAM , a compact WAM that represents a manipulation scene as a sparse 3D skeleton composed of robot joints, object centers, and interaction points. Constructed online from current RGB-D observations and robot proprioception, the skeleton provides a unified geometric state for action generation and future skeleton prediction. Future skeleton prediction provides additional geometric supervision for action learning without requiring visual reconstruction. At inference, SkeleWAM generates actions directly from the current skeleton and language instruction, while Medoid Action Consensus (MAC) serves as an auxiliary consensus strategy for stochastic action samples. On LIBERO-Plus, SkeleWAM achieves an overall success rate of 85.9% with 57.1M parameters, outperforming Cosmos-Policy by 3.7 percentage points. These results demonstrate that sparse 3D robot–object structure provides an effective state space for robust and parameter-efficient world action learning. The project is available at https://skelewam-project.github.io/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Learning-based robotic manipulation has rapidly evolved from task-specific visuomotor policies to general-purpose robot foundation models. ACT learns action chunks from visual observations, while Diffusion Policy and DP3 model expressive action distributions using 2D and 3D visual representations, respectively [ 22 , 5 , 21 ] . As model pretraining and robot datasets continue to scale, generalist policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models, including RT-2, Octo, OpenVLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , have demonstrated increasingly broad capabilities across diverse manipulation tasks and environments [ 2 , 15 , 11 , 1 , 8 ] . World action models (WAMs) jointly model robot action generation and future state prediction, where the latter provides additional supervision for learning how manipulation scenes evolve under robot actions [ 19 , 12 , 20 , 10 ] . Many existing WAMs represent future states as generated videos or learned visual latents [ 19 , 4 , 14 ] . Although latent prediction reduces the computational cost of explicit video generation, the information retained by visual latents is largely shaped by the underlying visual encoder and its pretraining objective. More importantly, compressing visual observations does not by itself isolate the geometric variables that govern robot–object interactions, such as their spatial configurations and relative motions. This raises a fundamental question: can a sparse representation of robot–object structure support effective world action learning while substantially reducing model complexity?

Our key observation is that the aspects of a manipulation scene most relevant to control can be represented as a skeleton consisting of a sparse set of 3D landmarks on the robot and manipulated objects. The robot is represented by the 3D positions of its joints, while each object is represented by its center and a set of interaction points connected to that center. The object center captures its overall spatial location, whereas the interaction points identify locations relevant to robot contact and manipulation. Together, these landmarks provide a compact and explicit representation of the robot configuration and object interaction geometry. We use this unified skeleton as the state representation and jointly learn robot action generation and future skeleton prediction without reconstructing visual appearance.

Building on this representation, we introduce SkeleWAM , a compact world action model that operates on sparse skeleton states. Given current RGB-D observations and robot proprioception, SkeleWAM constructs the skeleton online and encodes it as a set of geometric tokens. During training, the model jointly learns robot action generation and future skeleton prediction, allowing future prediction to supervise the shared geometric representation. At inference, the future prediction branch is omitted, and actions are generated directly from the current skeleton and language instruction. To reduce sensitivity to stochastic sampling, SkeleWAM additionally uses Medoid Action Consensus (MAC) as an auxiliary inference strategy. MAC selects the trajectory with the smallest average distance to other independently sampled candidates, without requiring a reward model or averaging multiple trajectories.

We evaluate SkeleWAM on the full LIBERO-Plus benchmark in a primary observation-based setting, where object landmarks are estimated from RGB-D observations. We additionally report SkeleWAM (sim-state), which replaces these estimates with privileged simulator coordinates solely as a diagnostic reference. In the primary setting, SkeleWAM achieves an overall success rate of 85.9% with 57.1M parameters, outperforming the strongest compared observation-based baseline, Cosmos-Policy, by 3.7 percentage points. Under camera perturbations, it achieves 93.4% success, exceeding Cosmos-Policy by 17.6 percentage points. The sim-state variant achieves 87.7% overall success, leaving a gap of only 1.8 percentage points from the primary setting. These results support our central hypothesis that sparse and explicit robot–object geometry provides an effective state representation for robust manipulation with a compact world action model.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We formulate world action modeling in a unified, sparse 3D skeleton state space composed of robot joints, object centers, and interaction points, providing an explicit representation of geometry relevant to manipulation.

We introduce SkeleWAM, a compact model that jointly learns robot action generation and future skeleton prediction, with the latter serving as auxiliary supervision during training. SkeleWAM also employs MAC as an auxiliary inference strategy to improve sampling robustness without requiring a reward model.

We conduct extensive evaluations on the full LIBERO-Plus benchmark, demonstrating the zero-shot robustness and parameter efficiency of SkeleWAM. Systematic ablations examine the effects of skeleton composition, future skeleton supervision, visual skeleton estimation, and MAC.

2. We introduce SkeleWAM, a compact model that jointly learns robot action generation and future skeleton prediction, with the latter serving as auxiliary supervision during training. SkeleWAM also employs MAC as an auxiliary inference strategy to improve sampling robustness without requiring a reward model.

3. We conduct extensive evaluations on the full LIBERO-Plus benchmark, demonstrating the zero-shot robustness and parameter efficiency of SkeleWAM. Systematic ablations examine the effects of skeleton composition, future skeleton supervision, visual skeleton estimation, and MAC.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Visuomotor and Vision-Language-Action Models

Visuomotor policies learn direct mappings from observations to robot actions. ACT predicts temporally coherent action chunks [ 22 ] , while Diffusion Policy and DP3 model multimodal action distributions using image and 3D point-cloud observations, respectively [ 5 , 21 ] . Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend this paradigm by incorporating pretrained vision-language representations for language-conditioned multitask control. RT-2 and OpenVLA adapt vision-language representations to action generation [ 2 , 11 ] , while π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} improve continuous control and generalization through flow matching and heterogeneous co-training [ 1 , 8 ] . More recent methods improve policy adaptation, action encoding, and model compactness through OpenVLA-OFT, π 0 \pi_{0} -FAST, and NORA, respectively [ 9 , 16 , 7 ] . Despite these advances, such policies primarily optimize action prediction and do not explicitly model how manipulation scenes evolve under robot actions.

## 2.2 World Action Models

To capture how manipulation scenes evolve under robot actions, world action models augment action learning with future state prediction. WorldVLA and UniVLA jointly model action generation and visual world evolution [ 3 , 18 ] , while DreamZero, GE-Act, and Cosmos-Policy leverage pretrained video models for robot control and planning [ 19 , 13 , 10 ] . VLA-JEPA replaces pixel reconstruction with the prediction of future latent target representations [ 17 ] , whereas Fast-WAM retains future video prediction as a co-training objective but removes future generation at inference [ 20 ] . Although latent objectives reduce the computational cost and dependence on pixel reconstruction, both videos and visual latents represent interaction geometry only implicitly rather than parameterizing it as explicit state variables. In contrast, SkeleWAM defines both current and future states directly in a sparse 3D skeleton space composed of robot joints, object centers, and interaction points. It jointly learns action generation and future skeleton prediction, allowing future geometric prediction to supervise representation learning during training without being required for action generation at inference.

2026-10-02.title: GlassGuard: Verified Glass Plane Mapping for Robot Navigation
2026-10-02.authors: Hanwen Guo , Zhengzhi Lin , Yusen Xie , Ji Zhang
2026-10-02.comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
2026-10-02.abstract: Transparent and specular surfaces pose a serious challenge to LiDAR-based SLAM and navigation because laser returns may pass through glass, leaving collision boundaries absent from the map. Prior work attempts to reconstruct the missing surfaces, but inaccurate obstacle placement can create the opposite failure: contamination of traversable free space. Recognizing this dual requirement, we present GlassGuard, a navigation-oriented framework for reconstructing planar architectural glass from complementary visual and LiDAR evidence. We formulate success in terms of both glass coverage and free-space contamination and apply this principle throughout proposal verification and global map construction. A foundation vision model provides glass-instance masks, structural 3D cues generate metric plane hypotheses, and depth-free 2D projective geometry checks their orientations before they enter a consolidated global map. We evaluate GlassGuard in nine building-scale scenes spanning diverse glass structures, spatial scales, and lighting conditions, with more than one hour and 2.1 km of real-world robot traversal. GlassGuard achieves 85% of total glass coverage for its panoramic version. Under identical pinhole inputs, GlassGuard achieves 82% total coverage, compared with at most 61% for the evaluated baselines, while producing 5–17 × \times fewer false voxels per frame. Qualitative examples with a navigation planner illustrate the reconstructed planes blocking paths through glass while leaving traversable routes open. The project page is available at https://glassguardproject.github.io/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Mobile robots commonly rely on LiDAR-based SLAM for autonomous movement.
However, transparent surfaces remain a fundamental challenge for light-based
sensing: laser energy may be transmitted through glass, specularly reflected,
or only weakly returned, causing ghost points or missed detections. This problem
is particularly relevant to widely used compact LiDARs, which operate at
905 nm [ 1 ] . Returns from glass
are highly variable and unreliable [ 2 , 3 ] ,
potentially producing incomplete or corrupted maps that compromise scene
reconstruction, exploration, and safe navigation.

One way to address this is to exploit physical cues such as return intensity,
reflection patterns, or additional sonar.
Although effective, this route depends on the returns, viewing
geometry, and sensor measurements that happen to be observable, or on
additional hardware. A more broadly accessible alternative is to combine visual glass
detection with surrounding 3D geometry.

Current efforts can already localize
glass in an image, but converting that detection into a correctly
placed 3D surface remains challenging. This step can be accomplished with a learning-based or a
pipeline-based strategy. A learning-based strategy directly infers glass depth or
plane parameters from observed RGB, and sometimes depth. However,
architectural glass offers almost no features of its own: what a camera sees at
a pane is predominantly the scene behind or reflected in it, which makes the
mapping from image appearance to metric depth ambiguous. Errors in the predicted depth or orientation can
therefore place obstacles in traversable space.

A pipeline-based strategy instead anchors image evidence, such as detections or
learned depth priors, to nearby metric RGB-D or LiDAR measurements. But,
placement requires associating glass with the correct structure: an apparent
frame or edge may belong to an occluder, or structure behind the glass
(Fig. 1 ). Both strategies can therefore produce plausible but
incorrectly placed planes in complex scenes. We therefore introduce GlassGuard, an onboard, VRAM-efficient framework that jointly
addresses the metric placement of architectural glass while checking each
proposed plane against the evidence obtained from the image. Rather than relying on an
end-to-end model to generalize directly to 3D glass geometry, GlassGuard shifts
the learned component to the more reliable task of 2D glass detection using the
foundation model SAM3. It then constructs metric 3D candidates from structural
line features extracted from surrounding LiDAR points, reducing the influence of
noisy or spurious returns, and verifies their orientations using depth-free
projective geometry before admitting them to the map. Accepted observations are
consolidated into persistent world-frame planes that can be reinforced, trimmed,
or removed.
The resulting map is designed to cover physical glass while limiting false
occupancy in traversable space.

We evaluate GlassGuard on a Mecanum-wheeled robot across nine building-scale
scenes, six indoor and outdoor environments, and 2.1 km of robot
traversal. Under matched pinhole inputs, GlassGuard achieves higher glass
coverage and substantially less false occupancy than the evaluated
learning-based and pipeline-based baselines, while its panoramic variant further
improves early coverage.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

Physical-Cue-Based Glass Perception. Early robotic systems addressed laser-scanner failures around mirrors and
windows or adapted localization to glass-walled environments [ 4 , 5 ] . Subsequent methods exploit
glass-specific physical cues such as return intensity, reflection patterns,
anomalous or multipath measurements, and view-dependent reflectance [ 2 , 6 , 3 , 7 ] .
Several systems further incorporate detected glass or reflective planes into
local and global SLAM maps [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Other
approaches confirm suspected glass through physical contact [ 11 ] or fusion of time-of-flight and ultrasonic sensing [ 12 ] . These methods depend on observable sensor cues,
surface interaction, or additional sensing hardware. Our work considers the
complementary setting in which reliable measurement and additional sensing
hardware cannot be assumed available.

2D Glass Detection. Visual glass perception has advanced substantially over the past decade.
Representative works include monocular mirror and glass segmentation [ 13 , 14 ] , reflection- and semantic-context modeling [ 15 , 16 ] , polarization-based perception [ 17 , 18 ] , and boundary-aware or
progressive refinement [ 19 , 20 ] . More recent
methods exploit reciprocal feature evolution, ghosting cues, and
foundation-model or diffusion priors [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . These
advances make image-space glass localization increasingly reliable, but 2D
segmentation alone does not provide the metric 3D location at which a detected
surface should be inserted into a navigation map.

Visual-to-3D Glass Reconstruction. Methods that reconstruct glass from visual input are the closest to our
setting and serve as our baselines. GW-Depth is a supervised monocular estimator that combines glass-structure and
reflection contexts [ 25 ] ; MonoGlass3D, which we evaluate as
the representative learned baseline, jointly predicts glass masks and plane
parameters [ 26 ] . As the representative pipeline-based baseline,
GlassRecon [ 27 ] (Zheng et al. ) aligns a
foundation-model depth prior with metric RGB-D measurements using local
RANSAC; for brevity we refer to this pipeline as GlassRecon, the name of its
released dataset. These methods place each surface from a single frame without
checking its orientation or depth, and never revise it afterwards. GlassGuard instead uses 2D image geometry and persistent plane
management to verify and update the reconstructed glass.

2026-10-02.title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution
2026-10-02.authors: Kyochul Jang , Seohyeon Park , Ohchul Kwon , Sangjun Park , Junhyeok Choi , Seungyeop Yi , Chaeyun Kim , Sangkyu Lee , Idan Szpektor , Avi Caciularu , Jongmin Park , Youngjae Yu
2026-10-02.abstract: As robotic hardware and learning methods advance, humanoids need tools to perform tasks beyond their inherent physical limits. Successful tool use requires selecting a suitable tool and coordinating manipulation and, when needed, locomotion to complete the task. Existing benchmarks do not jointly evaluate these capabilities on a humanoid. We introduce HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark spanning three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes, together with ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1. Evaluation of seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot reveals substantial gaps between selecting a suitable tool and completing the task. Focused GR00T N1.7 probes show reduced selection accuracy on unseen tools and continued task execution under unrelated instructions. Code and data are available at https://snu-pi.github.io/HumanoidToolBench/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Recent advances in robot hardware and learning have accelerated research on humanoids that can perform diverse tasks in human environments [ nvidiaGR00TN1Open2025 , sferrazzaHumanoidBenchSimulatedHumanoid2024 ] . Humans overcome physical limitations by using tools to extend the reach and capabilities of their bodies [ maravitaToolsBodySchema2004 , cardinaliToolUseInduces2009 ] . Humanoids intended to work in the same environments must likewise be able to use tools when their bodies alone cannot accomplish a task. This requires selecting a tool whose properties suit the goal and coordinating grasping, manipulation, and, when needed, locomotion to use it effectively. The grasp determines how much of a tool’s reach is available and how its working end is oriented for pushing, pulling, or striking. Body motion must then preserve the spatial relationship needed for contact with the target object. Evaluating humanoid tool use therefore requires testing the full process from selection to task completion.

Existing benchmarks address parts of this problem ( Table I ). HumanoidBench [ sferrazzaHumanoidBenchSimulatedHumanoid2024 ] includes spoon and window-wiping tasks, but does not evaluate the choice among tools with contrasting functional properties. Dedicated tool-use benchmarks are limited to visual question answering (VQA) [ zhangPhysToolBenchBenchmarkingPhysical2025 ] or fixed-base arms [ yuanGraspsDexterityLargeScale2026 , linRoboWitsUnexpectedChallenges2026 ] . A benchmark is therefore needed that jointly evaluates functional tool selection and task completion on a humanoid in both stationary and mobile settings.

To address these limitations, we introduce HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark, and ToolBook, 3.1k human demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 ( HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution ). The design separates selection from execution. Three scenarios, BallMove , BallRetrieve , and IceBreak , require sufficient reach, a shape that can engage and pull, and physical properties that support striking, respectively. Three execution levels distinguish selection and pickup (L0), stationary tool use (L1), and mobile tool use (L2), separating acquisition from task completion. Standard (S) and decoy (D) modes vary the alternatives under the same instruction: standard mode presents the suitable tool among unrelated objects, while decoy mode adds a competing tool that lacks a required property. Combining levels and modes exposes cases where a suitable choice is followed by failed execution, as well as behavior changes induced by competing candidates. ToolBook spans this structure to support policy training and real-robot adaptation.

Our central question is how reliably humanoid policies select and use suitable tools, and how these behaviors respond to changes in tool appearance and task instructions. We examine task completion, selection and execution failures, and responses to changes in tools and instructions. We evaluate seven policies in simulation and three on the real G1, comparing task success across scenarios, execution levels, and modes. Recorded interaction events distinguish contacting a candidate, lifting the suitable tool, and applying it to the target object. They reveal whether low completion accompanies limited pickup or persists despite frequent tool interaction, and capture changes in initial choice that final success can conceal. Focused probes of a separately trained standard-mode GR00T N1.7 policy examine representations and initial contact for unseen suitable tools, and success and motion under instruction changes in a fixed IceBreak scene. The results reveal gaps between acquisition and completion, with further declines when tasks combine locomotion and manipulation. Our contributions are as follows:

To the best of our knowledge, HumanoidToolBench is the first benchmark of humanoid tool use that spans selection and pickup, stationary tool use, and mobile tool use, with ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k human demonstrations in simulation and on a Unitree G1.

HumanoidToolBench combines execution levels, decoy tool sets, and recorded interaction events to distinguish limitations of selection and task execution.

We evaluate seven policies in simulation and three on the real G1 and probes to examine behavior beyond final success.

2. HumanoidToolBench combines execution levels, decoy tool sets, and recorded interaction events to distinguish limitations of selection and task execution.

3. We evaluate seven policies in simulation and three on the real G1 and probes to examine behavior beyond final success.

# II Related Work

Humanoid Benchmarks. Manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO [ liuLIBEROBenchmarkingKnowledge2023 ] and RoboTwin 2.0 [ chenRoboTwin20Scalable2026 ] evaluate vision-language-action models (VLAs) on single- and dual-arm manipulators. Meanwhile, humanoid policies such as GR00T N1.7 [ nvidiaGR00TN1Open2025 ] and Ψ 0 \Psi_{0} [ weiPs0OpenFoundation2026 ] require evaluation on a humanoid, and several benchmarks have been proposed: HumanoidBench [ sferrazzaHumanoidBenchSimulatedHumanoid2024 ] evaluates whole-body control, including spoon and window-wiping tasks, and SIMPLE [ weiSIMPLESimulationBasedPolicy2026 ] and WOLF-VLA [ boukheddimiWOLFVLAWholeBodyHumanoid2026 ] extend evaluation to humanoid VLAs. SIMPLE stages its tasks to report where a policy fails but does not vary the decision a task requires, and WOLF-VLA releases no human demonstrations for training. These benchmarks do not jointly evaluate functional selection, stationary and mobile use, and controlled tool-set variations ( Table I ). Our HumanoidToolBench fills this gap: a humanoid selects a tool from 55 assets, with or without a decoy, and uses it while stationary and while moving, with 3,003 simulation and 91 real-robot demonstrations for training.

Tool Use Benchmarks in Robotics. Tool use extends the limits of the body [ maravitaToolsBodySchema2004 , irikiCodingModifiedBody1996 ] and is also studied for AI systems [ schickToolformerLanguageModels2023 , jangDICEBENCHEvaluatingToolUse2025 ] , but physical tool use additionally requires a body that grasps, carries, and applies the tool. Three benchmarks target robotic tool use ( Table I ): PhysToolBench [ zhangPhysToolBenchBenchmarkingPhysical2025 ] evaluates tool understanding through visual question answering without acting on it, DexCraft [ yuanGraspsDexterityLargeScale2026 ] collects tool-use grasps on a single arm with the tool provided, and RoboWits [ linRoboWitsUnexpectedChallenges2026 ] asks a dual-arm robot to select a tool in unexpected situations. None evaluates tool use on a humanoid or combines execution levels with controlled tool-set variations: PhysToolBench tiers understanding but not execution, DexCraft and RoboWits do not divide their tasks into progressive levels, and only RoboWits varies the decision a task requires. Our HumanoidToolBench evaluates tool use on a humanoid that selects, carries, and applies the tool, and structures every scenario along two axes: execution levels increase the demands of task completion, while standard and decoy modes vary the tool choice under the same instruction. Pairing these axes supports comparisons among policies facing the same alternatives and within a policy as execution demands change. This links a tool’s functional suitability to the physical demands of grasping it, contacting the target, and coordinating body motion.
