2026-10-02.title: Completion Aware Guidance for World Action Models
2026-10-02.authors: Seungyeon Kim , Junhoo Lee , Baekseung Kim , Minkyu Kim , Nojun Kwak
2026-10-02.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) predict visual futures and robot actions, yet they remain susceptible to task-incomplete imagination , where plausible, action-consistent predictions omit the transition needed for task completion. In this paper, we show that this failure is not inherent to the world model backbone, but emerges when adapted for short-chunk control, which can repeatedly favor plausible local continuations over task-completing transitions. To address this, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method that guides generation toward task completion. Across representative WAMs, CAG improves success from 64% to 70% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation, while reducing task-incomplete imagination from 79% to 40%.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Robot tasks unfold through changes in the world state, and therefore require temporal understanding of what is likely to happen after an action is executed. Vision–language–action policies [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] predict actions from the current observation, yet the resulting future changes are difficult to infer from observed images alone. World Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by using video generative models to jointly predict a visual future and the actions that realize it [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . However, generating visual futures with aligned actions does not guarantee task success.

Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 1 , we find that WAMs exhibit task-incomplete imagination , generating visually coherent, instruction-relevant futures while omitting the state transitions required for task completion. For example, given a pick-and-place instruction, the imagined video may move an object above its target but continue holding it instead of releasing it, and the predicted actions follow this future, resulting in task failure. This differs from a corrupted video or video–action misalignment in that both modalities agree on a plausible continuation that does not complete the task.

In this paper, we ask why WAMs exhibit task-incomplete imagination and how this failure can be addressed. We argue that it arises from an objective mismatch between the fixed-horizon video-generation objective for video-backbone pretraining and the short-horizon video-action prediction objective for WAM fine-tuning . Under the former objective, video diffusion models jointly predict an instruction-following trajectory over a fixed horizon, whereas WAMs predict video-action chunks that are executed and regenerated from the observation . Because the WAM objective does not require the current phase to be completed within each horizon, the state transition required for task completion can be repeatedly deferred. As a result, although the video backbone can generate instruction-following trajectories, this capability is not reliably elicited when needed .

To address this mismatch, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG) , a training-free sampling method for WAMs. CAG strengthens the conditioning of instruction tokens most relevant to the current video–action prediction, steering the current chunk toward the required state transition without retraining the WAM. Across DreamZero and Fast-WAM [ 6 , 7 ] , CAG improves the average task success rate from 64.4% to 70.0% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation. More importantly, in a representative manipulation setting exhibiting task-incomplete imagination, CAG further reduces the incidence of this failure from 79% to 40%.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action Models. Generalist robot policies have largely been developed as vision–language–action models, which map visual observations and language instructions directly to actions or action chunks [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . For temporally extended tasks, however, a global instruction may not specify the next semantic subtask or desired near-future state. Recent approaches [ 9 ] therefore provide language subtask instructions or visual subgoal images to make task progress explicit [ 10 , 11 ] . Yet specifying an intermediate target and reaching it are distinct problems: external guidance does not ensure that the policy produces the state transition required to complete the subtask.

World Models and World Action Models. Video generative models capture temporal dynamics in observations, making them natural backbones for predictive world models in robot planning and control [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . WAMs extend this idea by coupling the imagined visual trajectory with actions , allowing a generated future to act as an implicit temporal plan [ 6 , 7 , 21 , 22 , 8 ] . Prior works [ 6 , 7 , 23 , 24 ] do not isolate the case in which the imagined video and predicted actions remain mutually consistent and locally plausible while omitting a phase-completing transition. We characterize this failure as task-incomplete imagination and mitigate it with training-free sampling guidance.

2026-10-02.title: OpenSpace Lab Solution to the IROS 2026 Indoor Exploration Competition
2026-10-02.authors: Yuxuan Zhang , Dong Li , Zezhou Sun , Yuxuan Xu , Siyu Teng , Yuchen Li , Jianjian Yang , Long Chen
2026-10-02.comment: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
This report presents the OpenSpace Lab ’s solution to the Competition on Intelligent Information Gathering for Single and Multi-Robot Systems Workshops, organized as part of the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026. Our team reached 1st place in the Single-Robot Public Track and 3rd place in both the Single- and Multi-Robot Private Tracks.
The single-robot framework utilizes pre-trained map completion predictions for global planning to prioritize unexplored areas. To reconcile map coverage with limited operation time, we introduce a remaining-time-based exploration strategy that integrates homing constraints into the decision-making process.
For multi-robot exploration, we utilize a utility-driven target selection strategy that balances observation gains, movement costs, and budget constraints, leveraging shared map and intent data to eliminate redundant search and maximize coordination efficiency.
Our solution reached a 61.04% coverage rate in the Single-Robot Public Track, while reaching 39.53% and 39.91% coverage in the Single- and Multi-Robot Private Tracks, respectively.
An extended full-length paper based on this report is currently being prepared for submission, and the source code will be released upon acceptance of the full manuscript at https://github.com/OpenSpace-Lab/Indoor-Exploration-IROS2026 .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Robotics exploration is a fundamental capability for autonomous robots, aiming to guide robotic actions through the real-time evaluation of information gain to maximize environmental information collection within minimal temporal budgets [ 8 ] . This capability underpins a wide spectrum of applications, ranging from indoor search and wild rescue to underwater surveying and planetary exploration [ 6 ] . Progressively, the target of quantified information extends beyond conventional geometric representations, such as point clouds and signal sources, to high-level spatial semantic representations and field-based environmental resources [ 7 , 2 ] .

Despite extensive research in autonomous robotic exploration, existing methods predominantly treat execution time or path length as a passive evaluation metric after mission completion, rather than an active constraint governing real-time decision-making. In many critical real-world scenarios, such as battery-constrained rovers exploring the lunar south pole or search-and-rescue agents operating in hazardous environments, time-bounded exploration is paramount. Under these strict temporal budgets, robots must not only maximize information gathering within a finite horizon, but also continuously evaluate the time cost of returning to a base station or communications hub to deliver collected data. However, incorporating explicit, hard time constraints into real-time frontier evaluation and path planning remains largely unaddressed in current exploration frameworks [ 1 , 3 ] .

The Indoor Exploration Competition 1 1 1 https://github.com/BYU-FROST-Lab/indoor-exploration-competition , hosted by Seungchan Kim and Brady Moon at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Intelligent Information Gathering for Single and Multi-Robot Systems 2 2 2 https://frostlab.byu.edu/IIG-workshop/ , evaluates autonomous agents under realistic operational constraints. The competition provides scale-dependent step budgets and strictly requires robots to return to the base station range to upload gathered map data.

To address these challenges, our team, OpenSpace Lab, developed specialized solutions for both single- and multi-robot tracks. The single-robot strategy generates candidate goals based on immediate observations and leverages pre-trained map completion to prioritize exploration sequences. Adapting to varying step budgets, it dynamically adjusts goal selection and pathing rules. The multi-robot extension reduces redundant search by initializing dispersed exploration directions and incorporating shared teammate goals alongside historical trajectories. Both strategies monitor remaining steps against estimated homing costs to guarantee timely return and data delivery. Detailed formulations of these methods are presented in Section 2 .

2026-10-02.title: ALFRED: Requirement-driven development of an open-source mobile manipulator for long-term plant monitoring
2026-10-02.authors: Ciarán Miceal Johnson , Christopher Quail , Garry Ellard , Alistair McConnell , Steve Tonneau , Fernando Auat Cheein
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-02.abstract: Tracking seasonal change in crops and forests requires observing the same plants repeatedly. Ground robots can do this at close range, and a manipulator gives their sensors more viewpoints. Yet the robots behind long-term field datasets are rarely released with their design files, and how a robot’s own structure limits arm reach and occludes its sensors is seldom compared between builds. We present ALFRED, an open-source mobile manipulator built from commercially available components. It carries a six-degree-of-freedom arm, LiDAR, RGB-D cameras, RTK GNSS and an IMU on an Ackermann-steered base, all mounted on a reconfigurable aluminium strut frame, and runs containerised ROS software. It was developed through four builds against six requirements for repeated outdoor deployment: durability, modularity, repairability, sensing reach, endurance and reproducibility. Model-based analysis of the last three builds shows the usable share of the arm’s reachable poses rising from 34.0% to 60.0% and then 66.1%, and ray casting shows that only the final build keeps the frame-mounted LiDAR’s horizontal view clear both forwards and backwards. ALFRED completed a year of monthly forest surveys (528 traversals) without missing a scheduled collection. This was despite battery degradation, reconfiguration for another researcher’s study, and the parallel development of ALFRED 2.0 for autonomous crop-row operation, with each switch between builds taking about six hours. The deployment also showed that mechanical modularity is only as dependable as the robot description that tracks it. Design files, bill of materials, robot descriptions, containers and build documentation are openly released.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Crop growth models simulate crop development from weather, soil and management practices, but numerous uncertainties compromise their performance ( Dlamini et al., 2023 ) . Data assimilation can reduce this uncertainty using in-season measurements of crop traits ( Huang et al., 2016 ) . Acquiring those measurements conventionally requires manual and often destructive sampling, which is slow, labour-intensive and costly ( Atefi et al., 2021 ) . Destructive sampling is also unsuitable for monitoring a crop continuously through its growth cycle: the plant is removed or damaged, and the gap it leaves alters the plants either side of it, which partially compensate for its loss ( Pavek and Thornton, 2006 ) . Non-destructive measurement, by contrast, allows the same plants to be measured repeatedly and their growth tracked over time ( Poorter et al., 2023 ) .

Satellites and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) both provide in-season observations for crop model data assimilation, and each makes a different trade-off between coverage and detail ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Satellites cover whole regions, but their resolution is coarse and cloud cover can leave long gaps between usable images during the growing season ( Matese et al., 2015 ; Whitcraft et al., 2015 ) .UAVs offer finer spatial resolution and more flexible revisits than satellites, at the cost of coverage ( Bazrafkan et al., 2025 ) . However, they view the crop from above or at an oblique angle, so lower leaves, stems and internal canopy structure are often occluded in dense or tall crops ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Low-altitude multi-rotor flight adds a further problem, since rotor downwash can deform flexible plants and alter the canopy geometry being measured Shi et al. (2021) . Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) do not suffer from the same issue and can sense plants at close range, where more information can be acquired about individual organs, and adding a manipulator allows cameras to be positioned and oriented at the best viewpoints ( Atefi et al., 2021 ) . Because the end effector can be swapped, a single mobile manipulator can be reconfigured for different tasks ( Guri et al., 2024 ) , allowing several kinds of data to be collected from the same plants. This article focuses on mobile manipulators of this kind.

Long-term experiments and data collection place additional demands on the platform. The platform must be able to operate outdoors all year round, be reconfigurable as sensing requirements change, and maintainable and repairable. Further demands arise when the platform is needed for other experiments, as happens when it is shared between projects, or during planned upgrades, which must be built and validated without missing scheduled data collections. Existing research shows that long-term deployment of agricultural robots is achievable ( Bender et al., 2020 ; Polvara et al., 2024 ) , as are modular platforms ( Grimstad and From, 2017 ; Guri et al., 2024 ) . However, these studies rarely discuss the rapid prototyping required before and during sustained, repeated deployment, or compare successive prototype builds against desirable characteristics to quantify their improvements. Additionally, reachability analysis ( Zacharias et al., 2007 ; Vahrenkamp et al., 2013 ) and LiDAR placement ( Kim and Park, 2020 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) are common tools in manipulation and autonomous driving, but are rarely used as development tools to compare agricultural robot prototypes.

This paper presents the Autonomous Leaf and Forestry Research Exploration Device (ALFRED), a mobile manipulator assembled from commercially available components for repeated close-range sensing of crops and forests. It was developed through four builds, each motivated by a requirement its predecessor failed to meet, against six design requirements: outdoor durability, modularity and reconfigurability, repairability, sensing reach and coverage, endurance, and reproducibility by others. The last two builds are ALFRED, an aluminium strut-frame robot that collected a year of monthly forest surveys, and ALFRED 2.0, which adds a second frame layer, a second computer and real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning for autonomous crop-row operation. Since the authors had no access to farmland, forestry served as a proxy, testing the platform’s ability to capture seasonal and structural change in living plants over a full annual cycle. For the same reason, ALFRED 2.0’s crop-row operation used artificial plants set out in rows in a field.

The contributions of this article are:

the presentation of a modular platform used in three experiments in the course of a year all requiring significantly different builds while not missing scheduled data collection in a year long experiment

a requirement-traced account of the four builds, recording the failure behind each design change

a model-based comparison of the last three builds, in which the usable share of the arm’s reachable workspace rises from 34.0% to 60.0% and 66.1%, and the visibility of the frame-mounted LiDAR is compared across build, task, and arm posture

an open release of the design files, robot description, and containerised software

The remainder of this article is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews data assimilation into crop models, mobile manipulators for repeated crop sensing, and the use of reachability and visibility analysis as design tools. Section 3 introduces ALFRED and ALFRED 2.0 together with the ForestYear3D and ROWCAST experiments they were built for, and Section 4 describes the hardware and software shared by both builds and the differences between them. Section 5 states the six design requirements and Section 6 introduces the four prototypes. Sections 7 to 10.4 then assess every build against each requirement in turn, including the model-based comparison of manipulator reach and sensor visibility in Section 10 . Section 11 sets out the limitations and future work, and Section 12 concludes.

1. the presentation of a modular platform used in three experiments in the course of a year all requiring significantly different builds while not missing scheduled data collection in a year long experiment

2. a requirement-traced account of the four builds, recording the failure behind each design change

3. a model-based comparison of the last three builds, in which the usable share of the arm’s reachable workspace rises from 34.0% to 60.0% and 66.1%, and the visibility of the frame-mounted LiDAR is compared across build, task, and arm posture

4. an open release of the design files, robot description, and containerised software
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Background

## 2.1 Data assimilation into crop models

Assimilating in-season observations can reduce the error between crop model estimates and in-field observations ( Dlamini et al., 2023 ) . Assimilating leaf area index into WOFOST, Curnel et al. (2011) found that accurate weekly observations throughout the season are required to halve yield error. Their experiments used synthetic data, because assessing an assimilation scheme against real observations requires more observations than can be collected. However, the weight of each observation is not uniform throughout the season. Assimilating a single Sentinel-2 leaf area index estimate from tillering, or from booting to flowering, matched or bettered the biomass simulated from assimilating several estimates taken during stem elongation ( Tewes et al., 2020 ) . These phenological windows are short, and their dates are unknown in advance. On calibrated data, Wallach et al. (2021) tested the ability of 27 modelling groups to predict phenology in wheat, the best model had a mean absolute error of around three days. An error of a few days in the date of a window that is itself only days wide means the informative observation cannot be scheduled reliably in advance. Capturing it requires sampling densely enough around the expected stage to bracket that uncertainty, rather than relying on a single well-timed acquisition. Satellite records cannot guarantee this, because revisit is fixed and acquisitions are lost to cloud ( Whitcraft et al., 2015 ) , and the accuracy requirement compounds the difficulty. A ground robot answers both: it can be sent out on the days that matter rather than when an orbit allows, and it observes the canopy at close range and from viewpoints that platforms above the crop cannot reach.

## 2.2 Mobile manipulators for long-term crop sensing

Ground robots can carry heavier sensors and provide more viewing angles than aerial platforms when measuring traits at the plant and organ level ( Xu and Li, 2022 ) . These measurements are non-destructively and repeatable at several time points through a growing season ( Atefi et al., 2021 ) . Xu and Li (2022) state that a challenge for phenotyping robots is they are often designed for one crop and field layout and do not generalise to other crops or layouts. Even within the same crop and layout perception systems can suffer. Burusa et al. (2024) claim that perception systems in greenhouses generalise poorly to variation and struggle with issues such as occlusion. They address this issue through the use of a manipulator and an end-effector mounted RGB-D camera deployed upon a cart which could be manoeuvred around the greenhouse.

Repeated observation of the same vegetation has been demonstrated over many months, with sensors carried by hand ( Knights et al., 2022 ) , backpack ( Malladi et al., 2025 ) and on ground robots carrying fixed sensors ( Bender et al., 2020 ; Polvara et al., 2024 ; Boxan et al., 2026 ) . The demands placed on these robots range from battery problems cutting deployments short ( Boxan et al., 2026 ) to map reuse degradation in vineyards as the crop grows ( Polvara et al., 2024 ) . To the best of the authors’ knowledge, however, no in-field campaign has monitored the same plants across a full growing season using a mobile manipulator, and none reports the design requirements the platform was built against or releases the information needed to rebuild it.

## 2.3 Reachability and visibility as design tools

When designing a mobile manipulator for in-field plant monitoring it is useful to quantify the sensor coverage a build provides. Coverage here has two components: the set of poses at which the manipulator can place a sensor, which is a question of reachability, and what the frame-mounted sensors can see from the vehicle, which is a question of visibility. Both can be computed from a model of the robot before it is built, and the tools for doing so are established elsewhere.

Reachability is commonly represented as a capability map, which records where and in which orientations an arm can reach ( Zacharias et al., 2007 ) , and inverting such a map yields the base positions from which a target is reachable ( Vahrenkamp et al., 2013 ) . Agriculture applies this at the design stage with Van Henten et al. (2009) selecting a manipulator’s kinematic structure by evaluating candidate configurations against the collision-free workspace the crop demands, and Bloch et al. (2018) co-designed orchard architecture together with the robot. In both cases the analysis was performed to test the ability of the arm to interact with the environment, rather than evaluate sensor coverage.

Visibility is treated in the same spirit in autonomous driving, where the placement of one or more LiDAR units is optimised against sensing coverage ( Kim and Park, 2020 ) and against downstream object detection ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Since the carrier is a rigid body, self-occlusion is identical in every scan. This however does not hold for the mobile manipulator where the largest occluder is the arm that moves independently of the vehicle. Therefore the field of view depends on posture as well as on mounting position. The two components are also coupled, because the structure mounted around the arm that limits its reach is largely the same structure that blocks the vehicle’s own LiDAR, so a change intended to improve one alters the other.

This paper reports one mobile manipulator developed through four builds against six requirements, deployed monthly for a year and rebuilt for autonomous crop-row operation while that year was still running. Reachability and visibility are computed on the robot descriptions to compare successive builds before anything is manufactured, and the design files, robot descriptions and containerised software are released.

2026-10-02.title: Continue, Abort, or Fall: Viability-Aware Policy Selection (VAPS) for Safe Humanoid Acrobatics
2026-10-02.authors: Siwei Ju , Lu Liu , Jan Peters , Oleg Arenz
2026-10-02.abstract:
Dynamic humanoid motions such as flips risk hardware damage due to suboptimal policies, disturbances or sim-to-real gaps. A motion tracking policy offers no way out once the maneuver leaves its reference, and a backup policy needs to take over to protect the hardware for a minimum-damage landing.
Which backup to use matters as much as when to switch.
We present Viability-Aware Policy Selection ( VAPS ), which treats safety as a policy-conditioned, receding-horizon decision.
Besides a protective fall policy, we also train an abort policy which can abort the motion at any time, landing on its feet.
At every control step, learned predictors estimate whether the nominal tracking policy and the abort policy remain viable over a short horizon, and a least-sacrificial hierarchy keeps the most task-ambitious behavior that remains viable.
In simulation with randomized disturbances, VAPS sharply reduces head contact and hand contact, which are the dominant sources of hardware damage, with both a Unitree G1 and a LimX Oli; on the LimX Oli, we validate the viability predictors and the full VAPS controller for side-flip motions. VAPS Pareto-dominates the strongest single-network alternatives we could train, including an end-to-end safe-tracking policy and students distilled from VAPS ’s own oracle-routed decisions, in both task success and head impact.
We also show that VAPS is a powerful framework to supervise undertrained policies and protect the hardware.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Humanoid robots are increasingly capable of highly dynamic whole-body behaviors, including running, jumping, and acrobatics [ 1 , 2 ] , but deploying such maneuvers safely remains difficult. Sim-to-real gaps, disturbances or suboptimal policies are common reasons for deployment failure and cause significant hardware damage, especially for highly dynamic acrobatic motions.

Humanoid acrobatics are typically learned as reference-tracking policies [ 2 ] . A tracking policy is rewarded for staying close to its reference, and its training episodes terminate as soon as it strays from it; at deployment, once the maneuver has left the reference, a backup must take over. Most existing safety mechanisms nonetheless cast this intervention as a binary choice between continuing the nominal controller and activating a single backup policy or safety shield, which either steers the robot back to a safe region [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] or executes a safe fall [ 6 ] . Highly dynamic acrobatics are fast and short, lasting only one to two seconds. When something goes wrong, there is little time left to correct or recover, only to abort safely.
Depending on the severity of the deviation, a robot that has left its reference may still be able to abort the motion with a controlled landing on its feet rather than a fall, whereas even a learned safe fall can cause serious damage at these speeds.
A single switch is therefore too coarse, particularly in the intermediate regime where the maneuver is already lost but a controlled landing is not.
Folding execution and recovery into one policy [ 7 , 8 ] does not restore the missing granularity either.

We address these challenges with policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability : whether a state is safe depends on which closed-loop behavior runs next, and should be judged over a short, continuously re-evaluated window rather than by a single guess for the end of the episode. We instantiate this as Viability-Aware Policy Selection ( VAPS ), which selects among the nominal tracking policy and backups ordered by decreasing task ambition: an abort policy that seeks a controlled feet-first landing, and a protective-fall policy that minimizes harm once upright recovery is no longer viable. A policy-dependent predictor, which encodes a short observation history, re-estimates each behavior’s short-horizon viability at every control step, and VAPS preserves the most ambitious behavior that remains viable. As the predictor judges the state and the candidate behavior rather than the cause of risk, the same mechanism recovers a mature policy from disturbances, supervises a new and unproven one, and handles a stop request issued by an operator or a workspace monitor. As hardware failures are expensive to collect, all failure cases are generated in simulation, and each state is reloaded under every candidate behavior.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

Least-sacrificial safety. VAPS formulates intervention during a dynamic maneuver as a selection over an ordered hierarchy of behaviors: continue, abort, and protective fall, committing to the smallest sacrifice of task ambition that remains viable.

Policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability. We learn viability predictors for the nominal policy and the abort policy from counterfactual rollouts and evaluate them continuously from proprioceptive history.

Analysis of single-policy alternatives. We investigate monolithic alternatives, including end-to-end RL policies and students distilled from VAPS with DAgger, and show that VAPS dominates all of them.

Hardware validation. We develop and test VAPS in simulation on Unitree G1 and LimX Oli, deploy it and validate the sim-to-real transfer on LimX Oli.

2. Policy-conditioned, receding-horizon viability. We learn viability predictors for the nominal policy and the abort policy from counterfactual rollouts and evaluate them continuously from proprioceptive history.

3. Analysis of single-policy alternatives. We investigate monolithic alternatives, including end-to-end RL policies and students distilled from VAPS with DAgger, and show that VAPS dominates all of them.

4. Hardware validation. We develop and test VAPS in simulation on Unitree G1 and LimX Oli, deploy it and validate the sim-to-real transfer on LimX Oli.

# II Related Work

A safety architecture for a dynamic maneuver must supply four things: a controller that executes the motion, behaviors that protect the robot when it fails, a signal that says when to intervene, and a structure that organizes the intervention. We review the literature on each in turn and then position VAPS against all four.

Humanoid motion tracking and acrobatics. Reference-conditioned reinforcement learning lets humanoids reproduce complex motions from human demonstrations, from phase-conditioned tracking [ 9 ] to large-scale retargeting, privileged learning, and sim-to-real transfer [ 10 , 1 , 2 ] , and now covers jumping, spinning, cartwheels, and parkour [ 2 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . These methods enable the motion, but don’t tell what the robot should do once the reference is infeasible at deployment.

Protective and recovery behaviors. Fall protection spans model-based contact selection that minimizes impact impulse [ 14 ] , learned protective policies triggered by a continuously running fall predictor [ 6 ] , curriculum-discovered protective postures [ 15 ] , and robot-agnostic stylized falling [ 16 ] . These supply the behavior a robot needs once the maneuver is lost, and supply it well. What none of them does is a controlled landing while nominal motion is not possible any more, but a fall is still avoidable.

Deciding when to intervene. The trigger has been cast as a learned shield or constraint critic [ 3 , 4 ] , as control barrier functions and reachability [ 17 , 18 ] , as a model-predictive safety filter [ 19 ] , as Hamilton–Jacobi values scaled to humanoids by a geometrically distributed receding horizon [ 20 ] , and, closest to humanoid falls, as a continuously running fall predictor [ 6 ] . Each computes one safety value for one policy. A quantity of that form cannot identify the severity of the lost maneuver and whether a controlled abort is still possible.

Organizing the intervention. Given a signal, the common structure is binary handover from the task policy to a recovery policy, whether triggered by a constraint critic [ 3 ] , by predicted violations on a legged robot [ 5 ] , or by a reach-avoid backup in a hierarchical controller [ 21 ] ; these designs assume one nominal objective, one generic recovery behavior, and a mature nominal policy [ 22 ] . Closest to our setting, concurrent work on humanoid locomotion learns a task-agnostic stoppability value and, on a commanded stop, chooses between holding upright and a damping fall [ 23 ] , while the controlled abort is more challenging to train for aerobatic motions than locomotion. A growing line removes the structure instead, blending execution and recovery in one policy: martial-arts motions, flips included, that recover from disturbed or fallen states [ 7 ] ; fall prevention, impact mitigation, and standing recovery unified [ 8 ] and distilled into a vision-based student [ 24 ] ; or locomotion learned jointly with recovery [ 25 , 26 ] .

Positioning. VAPS takes the motion tracking policy as given and fixed. It is whichever tracking controller that is deployed, mature or not. For backup behaviors, it trains two backup specialists rather than one: an abort policy that aims for a controlled landing, and a protective-fall policy as the last resort. In terms of the predictive trigger, where prior work computes one safety value for one policy, a per-policy predictor re-estimates each candidate behavior’s finite-horizon viability at every control step. Last but not least, for the intervention, prior work uses a switch which hands one policy over to one backup, VAPS keeps several named behaviors (continue, abort, fall) and retains the most ambitious one that is still viable. We also investigate the single-policy alternatives to VAPS .

2026-10-02.title: Is Success All You Need? Investigating the Impact of Input Perturbations on VLA Behaviour in Tabletop Manipulation Tasks
2026-10-02.authors: Sophie Higham , Riccardo Andrea Izzo , Matteo Matteucci , Alessandro Suglia
2026-10-02.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 1 ] have emerged as a prominent paradigm in robotics, with the ability to map visual observations, natural language instructions and proprioceptive states directly to motor commands. Building upon large-scale pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), VLAs have progressed rapidly in recent years, demonstrating generalisation to unseen objects and language instructions [ 2 , 3 ] . Such models have shown strong performance across robotic tasks, including tabletop manipulation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . More recently, increasing attention has been given to the robustness of VLA models, which have shown brittleness to environmental variations such as altered scene lighting and visual distractors [ 7 , 8 ] . A number of works investigate this by introducing perturbations to the evaluation data, along dimensions including scene lighting and language instruction [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . However, this robustness is typically measured by binary task success rate (TSR). Focussing primarily on TSR enables straightforward comparison; however, it may obscure other critical failures which aren’t captured by this binary outcome alone [ 11 , 12 ] .

In their work on AI agent reliability, Rabanser et al. argue that once agents are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably face environmental perturbations, but that ”robust agents should maintain comparable performance despite such perturbations” [ 11 ] . We argue that, for embodied AI systems, the notion of comparable performance should account for the fundamentally embodied nature of the application. The decisions and control outputs of embodied AI agents translate into physical actions , which can have significant real-world consequences [ 13 ] . Beyond binary TSR alone, behavioural metrics may more suitably reflect the deployability of VLA models. We consider a number of such metrics. The jerkiness of the trajectory may be important, as large acceleration changes can lead to higher mechanical stress and manipulator wear [ 14 , 15 ] . Behavioural metrics also matter from a human acceptability perspective. Sheidlower et al. [ 16 ] found that task completion speed data, a marker of efficiency, was requested by users. Additionally, perceived reliability and predictability are central factors affecting trust [ 17 ] , and unexpected behaviour from robots can degrade the trust that users may have in the technology [ 18 ] . In addition to TSR, we argue for the inclusion of behavioural metrics , which we find can offer greater insight into the comparative robustness of VLA models.

We identify a gap in the evaluation of VLA and embodied AI models. Work exists which either (i) evaluates the trajectory behaviour beyond binary task success, or (ii) measures robustness to perturbations using task success as the primary metric. To our knowledge, these two practices have not yet been combined. As a result, current robustness evaluation cannot determine whether a policy’s behaviour has meaningfully degraded when it continues to complete a task successfully. Two policies may achieve identical success rates under perturbation, while exhibiting substantially different trajectory quality . A demonstrative example is given in Figure 1 . Motivated by this gap, we propose a framework for evaluating the behavioural robustness of VLA models under perturbation by calculating metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour, to complement TSR. With this evaluation framework, we aim to answer the following research questions:

RQ1: How does the typical behaviour of successful trajectories change under input perturbation?

RQ1: How does the typical behaviour of successful trajectories change under input perturbation?

RQ2: Are perturbation-induced behavioural changes reflected by changes in the TSR?

RQ3: Do perturbations alter the behavioural consistency of successful trajectories?

We implement this framework by extending the LIBERO [ 19 ] and LIBERO-Plus [ 7 ] benchmarks. While we use these benchmarks as an experimental testbed given their wide adoption [ 6 , 7 ] , the proposed behavioural evaluation is benchmark-agnostic and could be applied to other benchmarks, as long as trajectory-level state and action information can be retrieved (e.g. MetaWorld) [ 20 ] .

Thus, through this work, we:

Propose a benchmark-agnostic behavioural evaluation methodology that complements task success rate with trajectory-level behaviour metrics, enabling practitioners to derive a more complete performance assessment of the robustness of VLA models, and implement it on the popular LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. The metrics comprise the duration , total gripper movement , Cartesian jerk , joint jerk , Cartesian path length , and joint path length observed for the trajectories.

Characterise perturbation effects in terms of the change in typical behaviour and consistency of behaviour.

Demonstrate that for state-of-the-art VLA models, robustness of task success does not necessarily equate to robustness of successful execution behaviour. Under perturbations, successful trajectories can change substantially even when task success is preserved.

1. RQ1: How does the typical behaviour of successful trajectories change under input perturbation?

2. RQ2: Are perturbation-induced behavioural changes reflected by changes in the TSR?

3. RQ3: Do perturbations alter the behavioural consistency of successful trajectories?

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Vision-Language-Action models

Building on advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend multimodal language modelling by predicting robot control actions from visual observations and language instructions [ 2 , 21 ] . Early VLA approaches represented robot control actions as discrete tokens alongside natural language tokens [ 2 ] . OpenVLA is an open-source model which adopted token-based action representation, and used large-scale robot demonstration data for pre-training [ 22 ] . More recent approaches have used continuous action representation and action chunking. OpenVLA-OFT [ 6 ] replaces OpenVLA’s discrete action representation with continuous action prediction, training using an L1 regression objective. Models in the π 0 \pi_{0} family use flow matching for continuous action generation [ 3 , 4 ] . The VLANeXt open-source model similarly uses a dedicated policy module with action chunking and flow matching, conditioned on learned representations from a VLM backbone [ 5 ] . These developments have enabled increasingly capable models, which has motivated efforts to more rigorously evaluate their behaviour and robustness.

## II-B Evaluation of VLA models

We observe that the majority of widely used benchmarks for evaluating the performance of embodied AI models emphasise the overall task success rate (TSR). See Table I for a breakdown of this. Benchmarks include those in the LIBERO family (including LIBERO-Plus [ 7 ] and LIBERO-PRO [ 8 ] ). The primary reported metric is the percentage of successful episodes, measured using task-specific goal logic. Other relevant robotic manipulation benchmarks include RLBench [ 23 ] , CALVIN [ 24 ] , RoboCasa [ 25 ] , MetaWorld [ 20 ] and MolmoSpaces-Bench [ 26 ] . These benchmarks vary in terms of which skills are being evaluated and task complexity, however a commonality is that binary task success rates are reported. A number of works propose behaviour quality metrics beyond TSR, which can largely be grouped into metrics focussing on safety and metrics focussing on efficiency .

Safety In their RoboEval work, Wang et al. [ 12 ] propose computing and reporting on joint jerk , Cartesian jerk , self-collisions , environment collisions and object slips , arguing that evaluating TSR alone may conceal critical failures.

Efficiency Wang et al. [ 12 ] also propose the metrics of trajectory length , completion time , joint path length and Cartesian path length . In their BEHAVIOR benchmark [ 27 ] , Srivastava et al. incorporate a number of efficiency metrics, citing deployment infeasibility of policies which are overly inefficient. Specifically, they report on time taken , kinematic displacement (i.e., the displacement caused by an agent in the environment), logical disarrangement (i.e., the number of changes caused by the agent to the logical state of the environment), distance navigated (i.e., the accumulated distance travelled by the agent) and the displacement of hands (i.e., the accumulated displacement of each hand while manipulating objects).

A number of works introduce perturbations to modify the evaluation data, and evaluate model robustness to distribution shift. Rather than evaluating models on tasks which are nearly identical to the training tasks, the LIBERO-Plus [ 7 ] benchmark introduces controlled perturbations along seven dimensions. These are the object layout , camera viewpoints , robot initial state , language instruction , lighting conditions , background textures and sensor noise . The authors find that, while several SOTA VLA models perform very well on the original LIBERO benchmark, under perturbations the performance of the models dropped substantially. Similarly, the LIBERO-PRO benchmark from Zhou et al. [ 8 ] introduces variations along four dimensions: object attributes (e.g. colour, textures), initial configuration, task instruction, and environment (e.g. background, lighting). Constraints ensure the tasks remain feasible despite the perturbations introduced, yet the authors find that models fail under simple perturbations.

Beyond the LIBERO benchmark family, the Colosseum V2 benchmark [ 9 ] specifically targets the evaluation of VLA models, expanding and creating visual, language and action perturbation categories. In their RobustVLA work, Guo et al. [ 10 ] implement four perturbation dimensions: observation, environment, language, and action . However, these benchmarks investigate the effect of the perturbation in terms of the reduction in TSR. To the best of our knowledge, there is no work yet addressing whether successful trajectories change as a result of the perturbations.

2026-10-02.title: Cross-entropy optimization with prioritized constraints
2026-10-02.authors: Francisco Roldan Sanchez , Pau de las Heras Molins , David Fridovich-Keil , Georgios Bakirtzis
2026-10-02.abstract: When constraints conflict, an optimizer must determine which requirements to preserve and which to relax. On the one hand, a priority ordering specifies which requirements take precedence. On the other hand, penalty-based formulations encode their relative importance through numerical weights. Depending on these weights, a solution can improve its weighted score while violating intended priorities. We introduce TierCEM, a variant of the cross-entropy method that incorporates strict constraint priorities directly into elite selection without requiring per-constraint importance weights. TierCEM works by sequentially filtering sampled candidates, from highest- to lowest-priority constraint. If and when a constraint eliminates all remaining candidates, TierCEM returns to the last nonempty set and selects elites with the smallest violations of that blocking constraint, recursively preserving satisfaction of all higher-priority constraints. We evaluate TierCEM on 2D navigation and contact-rich pushing tasks in proprioceptive and learned world-model settings. Experiments show that reversing the constraint ordering changes which constraints are violated under conflict. Prioritizing progress toward the task objective also enables TierCEM to relax lower-priority constraints when they would otherwise prevent further progress.
2026-10-02.introduction:
When constraints have different priorities, optimizing a scalarized objective turns the priority order into a weighted trade-off and the optimizer can sacrifice a higher-priority constraint to reduce lower-priority violations. In autonomous driving, for example, better lane keeping must not compensate for a collision when collision avoidance takes precedence ( Censi et al., 2019 ) . A priority ordering among possibly conflicting constraints makes that distinction explicit. Satisfying a lower-priority requirement must not sacrifice a higher-priority requirement that could otherwise be preserved.

Incorporating multiple constraints into a single optimization problem is often achieved by combining the task objective and constraint penalties into a scalar score, making constraint priorities dependent on numerical trade-offs between the competing terms ( Ma et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Kushwaha et al., 2025 ) . Under that task objective, an improvement in objective value or lower-priority penalties can compensate for a higher-priority violation. Preventing such compensation requires weights calibrated to both the prescribed ordering and the scales and attainable values of the competing terms, making constraint satisfaction sensitive to that calibration ( Imanov et al., 2026 ) .

Sampling-based optimizers such as the cross-entropy method (CEM) ( Botev et al., 2013 ) and model-predictive path integral (MPPI) ( Williams et al., 2017 ) provide a natural setting for candidate-wise constraint evaluation. In standard CEM, the top ℓ \ell candidates according to a ranking metric are called elites and are used to update the sampling distribution in an iterative fashion. We propose the tiered CEM (TierCEM), which implements ordered constraint relaxation directly in CEM’s elite selection logic through a priority-relaxation cascade (cf. Figure 1 ). At each iteration, TierCEM filters sampled candidate solutions from highest- to lowest-priority constraint. If a filter eliminates every remaining candidate, the cascade returns to the preceding nonempty elite set and selects samples with the smallest violations of the blocking constraint. If all filters retain candidates, those that maximize the distance to the boundary of the lowest-priority constraint are selected as elites.

The selected elites then determine the next sampling distribution through the standard CEM update. The constraint ordering thus governs which requirements are preserved and which violation guides relaxation when the current sample batch contains no jointly satisfying candidate, without per-constraint importance weights.

We evaluate TierCEM in the context of trajectory optimization, where different constraint orderings lead to distinct behavioral tradeoffs.
In a controlled two-dimensional navigation problem with explicit dynamics, geometric conflicts prevent simultaneous satisfaction of all spatial constraints while also reaching the goal. Reversing the constraint ordering changes which spatial constraint is violated.
We then evaluate contact-rich manipulation in the Push-T environment ( Chi et al., 2024 ) , optimizing action sequences through a frozen latent-space world model and evaluating constraints with learned decoder heads that predict constraint violation.
World model-based experiments reproduce the priority-dependent relaxation observed in the controlled setting: changing the ordering changes which constraint is violated, even when future states and constraint satisfaction are evaluated using imperfect learned predictions.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2. Related work

Constrained CEM can separate constraint satisfaction from task reward when selecting the candidates that update the sampling distribution ( Wen and Topcu, 2021 ) . Extensions incorporate differentiable optimization ( Mottahedi and Pavlak, 2022 ) , while related constrained optimization methods adjust feasibility tolerances through adaptive ϵ \epsilon -constraint handling ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Within model-based optimization, Liu et al. (2020) use ensemble predictions to evaluate safety, selecting feasible candidates by reward and falling back to the lowest-cost candidates when no feasible sample remains. Their fallback ranks violating candidates by an accumulated constraint cost. TierCEM instead uses an ordering over individual constraints to determine which violation guides elite selection and which higher-priority requirements the selected candidates must preserve. The distinction is therefore not the existence of an infeasibility fallback, but how the prescribed priorities govern that fallback and the resulting distribution update.

Lexicographic optimization specifies precedence among objectives or constraints without requiring their priorities to be expressed as weighted trade-offs ( Lesser and Abate, 2017 ; Quan et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) . Hierarchical quadratic programming applies ordered equality and inequality constraints to humanoid motion generation ( Escande et al., 2014 ) , while Rulebooks encode priorities among traffic rules for comparing driving behaviors ( Censi et al., 2019 ) . More recently, Jia and How (2026) combine gradient-based dynamic barriers with lexicographic selection to steer trajectories output by pretrained generative robot policies. TierCEM applies the same priority principle to the finite candidate set used in each CEM update, but incorporates it directly into the CEM optimization process to determine which candidates are retained and how the sampling distribution is updated.

Learned models supply predictions of future state given potential action sequences.
CEM is commonly used for reward-based planning with learned dynamics models ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2020 ; Kotb et al., 2023 ) and safety-aware planning ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Knuth et al., 2021 ) . Dreamer learns policies from imagined latent rollouts ( Hafner et al., 2020 ) , while SafeDreamer incorporates safety costs and Lagrangian-based planning into world-model control ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . MUARL combines predicted safety costs and model uncertainty in sampling-based candidate selection through adaptive Lagrange multipliers ( Kolling et al., 2026 ) . Within this literature, TierCEM targets planning problems with lexicographically-ordered constraints.
In our learned-model experiments, a frozen world model and learned constraint heads provide candidate evaluations, while TierCEM determines which requirements to preserve when no predicted candidate satisfies every constraint.

2026-10-02.title: Ex vivo breach detection using electrical conductivity during robotic pedicle drilling in the spine
2026-10-02.authors: Jorge Andrés Pérez Velásquez , François Teyssere , Thibault Chandanson , Quentin Grimal , Brahim Tamadazte
2026-10-02.abstract: Purpose: Pedicle screw placement is technically demanding in scoliosis treatment. High precision is required due to limited visibility, anatomical variability, and the risk of complications. Although robotic systems assist CT-based planning and execution, they still rely on ionizing intraoperative imaging and complex registration. This study proposes robotic pedicle drilling with real-time preventive breach detection using electrical bioimpedance sensing.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Pedicle Screw Placement (PSP) is a surgical procedure used to treat various spinal pathologies, such as scoliosis, spinal trauma, or spinal instability. Drilling the pedicles for screw positioning is a challenging procedure. Failure can lead to injuries, such as major vessels (aorta, vena cava) or the spinal cord Esses et al. (1993) . The literature reports a complication rate in the case of screw mispositioning of up to 18% Tang et al. (2014) . Indeed, the main risk arises during the pedicle preparation phase, when the surgeon defines a drilling trajectory that is considered optimal and safe for the patient. The surgeon has no means of real-time, in-depth visualization of the vertebra and therefore relies primarily on skill and experience. For example, in scoliosis (Fig. 1 left), which is characterized by severe three-dimensional deformities of the spinal column, identifying the entry point for each pedicle screw is particularly challenging. This often leads to high rates of pedicle screw misplacement, and approximately 7% of these mispositioned screws may result in medial or lateral breaches (Fig. 1 , right). Lateral breaches can damage vascular structures, causing significant bleeding and potentially life-threatening complications Lopera et al. (2010) . When medial breaches occur into the spinal canal, they can expose the spinal cord to risk and lead to neurological consequences ranging from paraparesis to complete paralysis Mac-Thiong et al. (2013) . The literature reports that most breaches are classified as ”A” or ”B” under the Gertzbein and Robbins classification Gertzbein and others (1990) . In this well-established classification, the position of a transpedicular screw is graded from ”A” to ”E” based on the extent of pedicle cortex breach: grade ”A” corresponds to a fully intrapedicular position without cortical violation, grade ”B” to a breach of less than 2 mm, grade ”C” to a breach of 2–4 mm, grade ”D” to a breach of 4–6 mm, and grade ”E” to a breach greater than 6 mm or a screw located outside the pedicle.

To improve the accuracy of pedicle screw placement and prevent breaches, various techniques have been proposed in the literature. First, patient-specific 3D-printed guides generated from preoperative imaging have been introduced as templates to assist PSP procedures Sheha et al. (2019) . Several studies also report the use of different non-visual exteroceptive or proprioceptive sensors, including vibroacoustic, accelerometric, torque, and force sensors Seibold et al. (2021) ; Massalimova et al. (2023) ; Saghbiny et al. (2024) . However, most solutions rely on image-based navigation, using fluoroscopy or CT scans.

Furthermore, robotic assistance in spinal surgery was first introduced in 2004, marking a major advancement in the field, which primarily uses navigation systems to optimize pedicle screw placement Bozic et al. (2003) . Most of the available robotic systems are integrated with stereotactic navigation systems Kia and Esmende (2021) . The SpineAssist system, developed by Mazor Robotics, was the first robotic system for spinal surgery to receive FDA (Food and Drug Administration) approval. Over the years, significant advances have been achieved, with the latest generation, Mazor X ® , incorporating a camera to assess the surgical environment and improve accuracy Ringel et al. (2012) . Another widely used robotic system is ROSA Spine ® , which operates according to similar shared-control principles Lefranc and Peltier (2016) . The most recent system, ExcelsiusGPS ® , integrates real-time intraoperative imaging and enables screw placement without the use of guidewires Zygourakis et al. (2018) .

Although navigation and robotic systems have improved spinal surgery, they remain limited by usability, cost, and accuracy. Respiratory motion and small patient movements during pedicle preparation can introduce substantial registration errors Shuman et al. (2022) . Moreover, these systems improve trajectory planning but do not fully prevent pedicle breaches. To address this limitation, we developed a robotic platform for pedicle screw placement that integrates a SpineGuard ® bioelectrical conductivity sensor, hereafter referred to as the DSG sensor, which is already used clinically Bai et al. (2013) ; Yurube et al. (2022) . A threaded drill bit with a pyramidal sensorised tip operating at 25 Hz was mounted on a custom motorized drilling system attached to Kurobot’s end effector.

A real-time algorithm uses adaptive conductivity thresholds and a dual-alert mechanism to stop drilling before a breach occurs. The system was evaluated ex vivo on fresh pig vertebrae through 51 drillings, achieving preventive detection in all trials. The mean error remained within [-1, +1.4] mm, and 100% of drillings were graded ”A” or ”B” according to the Gertzbein and Robbins classification.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Materials and Methods

## 2.1 Experimental Setup

The SpineGuard ® -derived drill bit (Fig. 2 (a)) has a 3 mm diameter and a pyramidal tip with bipolar electrodes that provide a real-time electrical signal dependent on the tissue traversed. Its threaded profile maintains contact with the bone and limits slipping along the drilling axis (Fig. 2 (b)). The drill is driven by a custom unit delivering 1.5 Nm nominal torque and up to 922 rpm, and is mounted on the robot end-effector at 30 ∘ to improve surgical access. DSG technology measures local tissue conductivity using the bipolar electrodes Bolger et al. (2007) : conductivity is low in cortical bone, higher in cancellous bone, and highest in blood and soft tissue (Fig. 2 (c)).

Figure 3 shows a representative DSG signal acquired during drilling in a fresh pig vertebra. Tissue-dependent conductivity variations enable detection of both lateral and medial breaches. Micro-fractures in the cortical bone allow fluid to reach the pyramidal tip, producing a detectable signal change before the drill fully enters the spinal canal.

## 2.2 Drilling Workflow

To mimic the conditions of a typical drilling procedure on a patient, fresh pig vertebrae were immersed in a saline solution that reproduces the electrical conductivity of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). This solution contains sodium chloride (NaCl), chosen to replicate the ionic composition of CSF, particularly the sodium (Na + ) and chloride (Cl - ) ions, which play a crucial role in its conductivity. The concentrations of these ions in CSF are approximately 130–150 mEq/L for sodium and 120–125 mEq/L for chloride Maeda and others (2016) . To replicate this ionic environment, which reflects a near 1:1 ratio of sodium and chloride ions, we prepared a solution with a NaCl concentration of approximately 120–130 mmol/L.

## 2.3 Vertebrae Collection and Preparation

Pig vertebrae exhibit a pedicle morphology similar to that of humans, making them a suitable model. A limitation is the presence of growth cartilage at the vertebral ends, which may affect conductivity signals. To minimize these artifacts, we selected a drilling trajectory from the pedicle towards the spinal canal, simulating a misjudged surgical path while avoiding the cartilage.

Compared with spinous process drilling Gautschi et al. (2011) , pedicle trajectories may approach the spinal canal tangentially, reducing electrode contact with cerebrospinal fluid. Conductivity changes are therefore weaker and more gradual, requiring robust signal processing to reliably detect early breaches.

In this study, 51 fresh porcine lumbar vertebrae were prepared by a surgeon to simulate operating room conditions. Each vertebra was clamped in a transparent box facing a camera for continuous inspection of the spinal canal. An orthopedic surgeon created the entry point with an awl, after which the robot was hand-guided into position. Drilling was performed at 10 N and 30 rpm, with a maximum descent rate of 50 mm/s. The real-time breach-detection method is summarised in Algorithm 1 .

## 2.4 Methodology

To verify result accuracy and detect potential breaches, several approaches were applied both during and following the drilling experiments:

Palpation with a ball-tip feeler: this method (usually used by surgeons during surgery) was used to assess the integrity of the cortical bone and rule out the existence of grade ”C” breaches.

Visual inspection: following the experiments, the spinal canal was visually examined to identify any deformation caused by the drill bit tip.

Imaging and video analysis: a combination of CT scans and video recordings obtained during drilling was used to confirm the absence of false positives and false negatives and to validate the experimental results.

These methods ensured a comprehensive analysis of both the mechanical and structural impacts of the drilling process.

2026-10-02.title: Continual Learning for 6-DoF Grasp Synthesis via Experience and Demonstrations
2026-10-02.authors: Giulio Schiavi , Andrei Cramariuc , Michael Pantic , Roland Siegwart
2026-10-02.comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026
2026-10-02.abstract:
Most current grasp synthesis systems are trained offline and remain fixed during deployment. While this works well when deployment conditions resemble the training data, performance can degrade when robots encounter conditions they have not seen before, such as unfamiliar objects. In this work, we present a continual-learning framework for single-view 6-DoF grasp synthesis for a parallel-jaw gripper in cluttered scenes. Rather than finetuning a large parametric model, our method adapts through memory in a learned embedding space: grasp outcomes update future grasp scores, while optional user demonstrations are recalled and transferred to new scenes as additional candidate grasps. We evaluate our method in simulation and in extensive real-world experiments comprising over 1500 grasp trials. We show that our method matches the performance of existing 6-DoF grasping baselines even before adaptation, improves online on unseen objects from categories absent or underrepresented during training, and supports long-horizon continual learning with limited forgetting. In real-world experiments, our method reaches over 90% success rates on several challenging object categories after only 50 online grasp attempts.
Videos and code at https://giuschio.github.io/cl_grasping/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Current 6-DoF grasp synthesis systems can generate grasps in cluttered scenes with impressive reliability. Most do so by training parametric models on large offline datasets of synthetic or real-world grasp examples [ 6 , 1 , 10 , 3 , 29 ] . Once trained, however, these models are typically frozen during deployment, and can still fail when the robot encounters conditions that are poorly covered by the training distribution, such as unfamiliar object geometries that were absent or underrepresented during training. One promising direction is to let grasping systems continue learning on site from the feedback available to them, such as grasp outcomes and occasional user demonstrations.

In this work, we present a continual-learning framework for 6-DoF grasp synthesis. As in many prior works [ 10 , 30 ] , our system (Figure 1 ) has two main components: a proposal module that generates candidate grasps and a scoring module that ranks them for execution. Unlike standard learned grasping systems, however, both modules can change during deployment through memory. Instead of using a parametric grasp scorer that remains fixed after training, we use a memory-based scorer in a learned embedding space, so new grasp outcomes immediately influence future scores. We also augment heuristic grasp proposals with lightweight recall from user demonstrations, transferring previously shown grasps to geometrically similar regions in new scenes. Together, these mechanisms let the system combine offline experience, deployment trials, and demonstrations into a single adaptive system. In addition, because adaptation only requires adding entries to memory, each update is simple and practical to apply on site, without requiring gradient-based retraining.

We evaluate our method in simulation and on a real robot and compare it with common 6-DoF grasping baselines. Our method achieves strong offline performance, improves online through deployment experience on unfamiliar objects, and supports long-horizon continual learning with limited forgetting. In real-world experiments comprising over 1500 grasp trials, online adaptation improves performance across challenging object categories and reaches over 90% success on several of them.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 RELATED WORK

## 2.1 Deep Grasp Synthesis

6-DoF grasp synthesis aims to predict feasible SE(3) grasp poses from scene observations. A common strategy is a proposal-and-score pipeline: generate a set of candidate grasps, then rank them according to predicted grasp success. Some methods sample candidates with geometric heuristics, such as GPD [ 30 ] and EdgeGraspNet [ 10 ] . Others evaluate dense anchors over points or voxels, as in VGN [ 3 ] , ICGNet [ 36 ] , ContactGraspNet [ 29 ] , GraspNet [ 6 ] , and AnyGrasp [ 5 ] . Recent progress has come from larger datasets and stronger priors, such as adversarial sim-to-real alignment [ 35 ] , antipodal constraints [ 17 ] , and center-of-gravity priors [ 5 ] . Other methods learn the proposal distribution with VAEs [ 19 ] or diffusion models [ 20 , 28 , 2 ] . Despite this progress, current systems remain tied to the coverage of their training data, and can still fail when deployment scenes differ from the examples seen offline.

## 2.2 Adaptation and Continual Learning for Grasping

Prior work has addressed the problem of how grasping models should be adapted during deployment. Existing approaches use self-training signals [ 8 , 15 ] , continual-learning regularizers [ 23 ] , reinforcement learning [ 27 , 14 ] , or retraining with deployment data [ 12 ] . Other works exploit structural invariances in 2D top-down grasping to adapt from few examples [ 33 ] . These methods show that deployment data is valuable, but often consider settings with simplifying assumptions, such as top-down grasping or access to test-time CAD models. We instead consider single-view 6-DoF grasping in scenes with multiple objects. Our approach also differs in how adaptation is performed: rather than updating the parameters of the grasping model, we incorporate deployment experience non-parametrically by adding entries to memory. In our experiments, we compare our approach against parametric finetuning using the protocol of Julian et al. [12] .

## 2.3 Registration- and Retrieval-Based Grasping

Retrieval-based methods store grasps and transfer them to new scenes through registration or correspondences. Early work transfers grasps geometrically [ 13 ] . Later methods integrate category templates [ 32 ] , semantic correspondences [ 11 ] , or continual retrieval from successful grasps [ 21 ] . These frameworks can often incorporate new demonstrations without retraining, but they depend on database coverage and can be sensitive to registration errors. Our method differs in three main ways. First, recall adds to geometric sampling instead of replacing it; the system can still propose grasps for unfamiliar objects. Second, whereas retrieval methods learn from successful grasps or demonstrations only, our method can learn from both successful and failed grasp attempts. Third, registration is used only to generate candidates, not to determine their scores. This allows us to reject a well-registered recall when the accumulated outcome evidence indicates that the transferred grasp is unlikely to succeed. In our experiments, we isolate these differences by comparing against a recall-only pipeline that disables geometric sampling and adaptive scoring.

## 2.4 Exploratory and Trial-Based Grasp Learning

Exploratory and trial-based grasp learning methods are closely related to our work. Dex-Net [ 18 ] , BORGES [ 4 ] , and LEGS [ 7 ] maintain probabilistic grasp success estimates and update them from heuristic evaluations or real-world trials. These works primarily target efficient grasp dataset generation [ 18 ] or exploratory grasping for a single isolated object [ 7 ] . They also tend to treat grasps independently, maintaining separate success estimates for each candidate grasp or object pose. We build on the same trial-based idea, but use it for 6-DoF grasping from partial observations in cluttered scenes. Rather than maintaining independent beliefs over individual grasps, we operate in a learned embedding space, so evidence from one grasp attempt can generalize to similar grasps.

2026-10-02.title: Interaction-Stiffness-Guided Basis Allocation in Dynamic Movement Primitives for Efficient Skill Transfer
2026-10-02.authors: Chan Xu , Silu Chen , Dehao Wang , Xiyu Chen , Dexin Jiang , Chi Zhang , Guilin Yang , Chenguang Yang , Zaojun Fang
2026-10-02.abstract: Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) provide a compact and stable formulation for trajectory representation and generalization in robot skill learning. However, their predefined basis layout limits the allocation of approximation capacity according to stage-dependent precision requirements. To address this issue, this article proposes Stage-Criticality-Guided Dynamic Movement Primitives (SC-DMPs) with adaptive basis allocation for precision-critical skill learning. Operator-robot interaction stiffness and a trajectory-consistency cue derived from cross-demonstration task-space variability are integrated to construct a stage-criticality index. Guided by this index, basis centers are redistributed in normalized time through inverse cumulative criticality and mapped to the canonical phase domain, while their bandwidths are refined to adjust local approximation support. This enables denser and more flexible representation at high-criticality stages while retaining sparser allocation elsewhere. Experiments on handwriting trajectories and three real-robot tasks show that the inferred criticality is concentrated in geometrically demanding and task-constrained regions. Comparisons with DMPs, ProMPs, ProDMP, GP-MP, and KMP demonstrate improved trajectory reproduction, endpoint generalization, and task-critical accuracy while retaining a compact model and the stable structure of classical DMPs.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) has emerged as an effective paradigm for transferring dexterous human motion skills to robots, especially in settings where explicit programming is difficult or costly [ 1 ] . Representative applications include fine insertion, tight-clearance assembly, and other operations with stringent precision requirements [ 2 ] . In such tasks, the robot must not only reproduce the overall shape of the demonstrated trajectory, but also maintain high geometric accuracy at critical local stages, which are often less tolerant to error than other segments [ 3 ] . Accordingly, achieving global fidelity and local accuracy at task-critical stages is central to precision-oriented trajectory learning [ 4 ] .

Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) are one of the most representative trajectory-encoding frameworks in LfD, owing to their compact dynamical formulation, stability guarantees, and convenient spatiotemporal modulation [ 5 ] . Classical DMPs represent demonstrated motions through stable dynamical systems, where nonlinear forcing terms encode task-specific trajectory profiles [ 6 ] . In particular, the forcing term is approximated by basis functions preset along the canonical phase variable, where the basis layout is associated with the resulting reproduction performance [ 7 ] . Although this design is generally effective, it provides limited stage-wise adaptability for precision-critical skill representation [ 8 ] . Trajectory adaptability and tracking accuracy can be improved by integrating DMPs with model predictive control, reinforcement learning, and adaptive or neural feedback [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . However, such approaches may require additional environmental information or interaction, online computation, or specialized controller design, while local approximation errors introduced during trajectory encoding are not directly addressed [ 12 ] .

By contrast, representation-level methods modify movement primitives to improve trajectory reproduction and generalization, primarily through probabilistic or kernel-based formulations and parameter refinement. The former represents demonstrated trajectories and their uncertainty through probability distributions or kernel mappings, as in ProMPs [ 13 ] , ProDMP [ 14 ] , GP-MP [ 15 ] , and KMP [ 16 ] . However, local reproduction fidelity is typically regulated through covariance structures, kernel design, or hyperparameter settings, without explicitly allocating approximation support according to stage-dependent precision requirements. The latter refines movement-primitive parameterization by adjusting the number, locations, widths, or forms of basis functions, providing more explicit control over local approximation support [ 17 , 18 ] . Among these refinements, basis-center redistribution relocates approximation support without increasing the basis number or altering the stable DMP dynamics, making it an efficient strategy for precision-critical skill learning [ 19 ] . Existing methods refine trajectory representations based on curvature, variance, recovered temporal structure, or mutual-information-based timestep weights [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . These criteria characterize trajectory structure or informativeness but do not necessarily indicate task-imposed motion tolerances. For example, peg-in-hole insertion may follow a geometrically simple path yet require high positioning accuracy under tight clearances [ 23 ] .

In precision-oriented physical interaction, increased stiffness may accompany stronger regulation of positional deviations, providing task information that is not evident from trajectory geometry alone [ 24 , 25 ] . Robot-environment contact stiffness can reveal such constraints during sustained contact, but its force-displacement-based estimation may be unreliable in noncontact, weak-contact, or contact-transition stages [ 26 , 27 ] . Operator-robot interaction stiffness can instead be estimated from muscle activation and upper-limb configuration without requiring robot-environment contact-force measurements, making it available across different stages of kinesthetic teaching [ 28 , 29 ] . Existing stiffness-aware skill learning methods primarily incorporate stiffness or compliance into task execution through variable-impedance profiles, compliant dynamical systems, or programmed interaction behaviors [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] . Alternatively, operator-robot interaction stiffness can serve as a task-informed cue for trajectory representation. Although informative, it may not fully characterize task criticality on its own, since some dynamic or periodic manipulation tasks may instead depend on compliant behavior [ 33 , 34 ] . Accordingly, operator-robot interaction stiffness and cross-demonstration trajectory consistency may offer complementary cues for characterizing stage-dependent reproduction requirements.

In this work, operator-robot interaction stiffness and a trajectory-consistency cue derived from cross-demonstration variability are integrated to construct a stage-criticality index. Based on this index, Stage-Criticality-Guided Dynamic Movement Primitives (SC-DMPs) redistribute basis centers and adapt their bandwidths to allocate approximation support according to stage-dependent reproduction requirements. The main contributions are as follows.

A physically motivated stage-criticality index is formulated by integrating operator-robot interaction stiffness and cross-demonstration task-space variability, providing an interpretable estimate of stage-wise reproduction-fidelity requirements.

A criticality-guided basis allocation strategy is developed by redistributing centers through inverse cumulative criticality and adapting bandwidths to refine local support in high-criticality stages.

Comprehensive experiments on handwriting trajectories and real-robot tasks compare SC-DMPs with DMPs, ProMPs, ProDMP, GP-MP, and KMP, demonstrating improved trajectory reproduction, generalization, and task-critical accuracy while retaining a compact model.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II formulates a probabilistic model of multiple demonstrations. Section III develops the stage-criticality index and SC-DMPs method. Section IV validates the effectiveness of the proposed method. Finally, Section V concludes this article.
