2026-10-02.title: Admissibility-Preserving Control for Multi-Input Systems with Joint Capacity Constraints
2026-10-02.authors: Saurabh Kumar , Lohitvel Gopikannan , Shashi Ranjan Kumar , Abhinav Sinha
2026-10-02.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Dynamical Systems (math.DS); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-02.abstract: This paper addresses the control of multi-input strict-feedback nonlinear systems subject to a joint capacity constraint , in which the admissible input set is a coupled subset of the individual actuator limits. Unlike existing constraint-handling methods that enforce actuator bounds channel by channel and may unnecessarily suppress admissible control directions, we develop an Anisotropic Joint-Admissibility-Preserving Input Realization (AJ-APIR) framework that explicitly exploits the geometry of the joint constraint. The proposed realization constructs a state-dependent gain matrix whose spectral decomposition separates the commanded input into normal and tangential directions relative to the constraint boundary. The normal component is attenuated as the boundary is approached, while the tangential component is preserved, which allows the admissible control effort to be redistributed without loss of tracking authority. Integrated with a backstepping controller, the AJ-APIR framework guarantees forward invariance of the joint admissible set for all time. We establish exponential convergence of the tracking error to zero together with uniform boundedness of all closed-loop signals, and characterize the resulting command-demand behavior under the joint constraint. Simulation results for a representative second-order, two-input nonlinear system subject to a power-budget constraint demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method to enforce the joint input constraint.
2026-10-02.introduction:
In many practical multi-actuator systems, actuator channels share a common physical resource, such as the electrical bus shared by control surfaces and propulsion in fixed-wing UAVs, the thermal path shared by joint motors in redundantly actuated manipulators, or the prime mover shared by azimuth thrusters in marine surface vessels. This physical coupling gives rise to a joint constraint on the collective input that independent per-channel bounds fail to capture. In practice, the aggregate demand may breach the shared operating limit even when every individual channel remains within its own admissible range. Consequently, to maintain the collective input within the jointly admissible set at all times while ensuring that the system output tracks a prescribed reference trajectory remains an open challenge concerning safety-critical control.

The problem of designing feedback controllers for nonlinear systems subject to actuator constraints has attracted sustained research attention for more than three decades. Nevertheless, the systematic treatment of coupled actuator constraints, particularly without unnecessarily sacrificing admissible control authority, remains an open problem. A foundational body of work addresses this problem through anti-windup augmentation of pre-designed linear controllers, in which a secondary compensator is introduced to recover closed-loop performance when the primary loop saturates [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Although systematic and amenable to convex synthesis, anti-windup methods are generally developed for linear nominal plants and do not readily accommodate the state-dependent gain structure of nonlinear strict-feedback systems. A parallel stream exploits the recursive structure of strict-feedback dynamics through backstepping [ 4 ] , with constraint handling achieved by confining each virtual control to a bounded feasible set. The authors in [ 5 ] showed that augmenting a standard backstepping design with auxiliary dynamics whose equilibrium tracks the saturated channel yields a complete Lyapunov analysis for tracking under asymmetric saturation, and the construction was subsequently extended to uncertain multi-input systems in [ 6 ] . It is worth noting that these treatments bound each channel separately, so that the feasible set they enforce is, by construction, a Cartesian product.

Barrier Lyapunov functions (BLFs) provide an alternative mechanism for enforcing constraints in strict-feedback systems by introducing a potential that grows without bound as a constrained variable approaches its prescribed limit, thereby preventing the trajectory from reaching the boundary. The authors in [ 7 ] established asymptotic tracking for single-output systems subject to output constraints using BLFs. In [ 8 ] , this framework was discussed for full-state constraints, while [ 9 ] combined BLFs with adaptive neural networks to address uncertain strict-feedback systems. However, standard BLF constructions assign an independent barrier potential to each constrained channel, resulting in a Lyapunov function composed of decoupled terms. Consequently, they do not directly capture the inter-channel coupling induced by a joint capacity constraint.

Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) [ 10 ] provide a unified framework for barrier-certificate and Lyapunov-based stability analysis, with a quadratic program (QP)-based safety filter applicable to a broad class of nonlinear systems. The safety-critical control framework in [ 11 ] accommodates general smooth constraint sets, including joint constraints, by incorporating barrier-function gradients into a pointwise QP. The authors in [ 12 ] demonstrated the compatibility of such constraint-handling mechanisms with backstepping for relative-degree-one input constraints. Nevertheless, the QP formulation modifies the nominal control according to the Euclidean minimum-norm criterion, which is effectively direction-blind with respect to the geometry of the joint constraint. Near a joint constraint boundary, this may unnecessarily attenuate components of the commanded input that are tangent to the boundary and therefore do not contribute to constraint violation. Thus, constraint enforcement need not be isotropic, yet this geometric structure does not appear to be explicitly exploited in the existing CBF-based formulations.

A further class of methods relies on control allocation to map a scalar or low-dimensional virtual control into a higher-dimensional actuator command subject to box and joint constraints, typically by solving a weighted least-squares problem or quadratic program at each instant [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . The relationship between control allocation and optimal control was discussed in [ 17 ] , while a dynamic counterpart was developed in [ 18 ] . Control allocation decouples the outer-loop control design from the constraint-satisfaction problem, making it attractive for redundant platforms. However, the feasibility of the allocation problem depends on the actuator authority available at each instant and is therefore not guaranteed during large-signal transients. Moreover, the stability of the interconnected outer-loop and allocator dynamics generally requires a separate analysis. Governor and predictive architectures [ 19 , 20 ] , in contrast, address feasibility at the planning or reference-generation level by reshaping the reference or optimizing over a finite horizon, respectively, but at a potentially high computational cost for fast actuation loops.

The Admissibility-Preserving Input Realization (APIR) framework, introduced for strict-feedback systems with asymmetric single-channel actuator constraints [ 21 ] , adopts a dynamical-systems perspective on constraint satisfaction. Rather than modifying a nominal controller through a pointwise optimization or treating constraint enforcement as a separate allocation layer, APIR embeds admissibility directly into the physical input dynamics through a differential realization whose gain vanishes at the constraint boundary. A distributed extension to networked systems with directed communication graphs was subsequently developed in [ 22 ] . These works establish an intrinsic alternative to optimization-based safety filters [ 10 , 11 ] and allocation-based constraint handling [ 16 ] , in which admissibility is enforced through the dynamics of the realized input itself.

However, the existing APIR construction [ 21 ] is fundamentally channel-wise, that is, its realization is formed from independent scalar admissibility factors and therefore applies to admissible sets that are Cartesian products of individual actuator ranges. This indicates that it may not directly address a coupled input envelope whose boundary depends on the collective actuator state. This may appear as a limitation, which is nonetheless shared by standard channel-wise saturation and backstepping- based controllers [ 5 , 6 ] and by BLF formulations that impose separate barrier terms on individual constrained variables [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . CBF-based formulations can represent general smooth joint constraint sets [ 10 , 11 ] . However, their standard optimization-based realization modifies the nominal command through a pointwise safety filter rather than embedding the joint admissibility mechanism directly into the input dynamics. Likewise, control-allocation methods explicitly account for coupled actuator limitations, but do so by introducing a separate allocation layer between the outer-loop controller and the physical actuators [ 16 ] . It must be noted that this scheme may be effective for distributing control effort among constrained actuators, but the architecture separates constraint satisfaction from the closed-loop analysis. However, the feasibility must be maintained by the allocation problem, and the effect of the allocation on the stability and tracking properties of the overall closed-loop system warrants a separate analysis. To the best of our knowledge, the existing literature does not provide a dynamic realization that simultaneously enforces a non-Cartesian joint input envelope and preserves admissible control authority in directions tangent to its boundary.

The current work extends the notion of the admissibility-preserving control framework [ 21 ] from individual actuator constraints to coupled multi-input constraints. We replace the channel-wise scalar realization with a matrix-valued, geometry-aware realization that differentiates between control directions that may risk joint admissibility and those that remain feasible. In particular, the proposed AJ-APIR selectively suppresses the component normal to the joint constraint boundary as it is approached, while preserving the tangential component. Thus, the proposed realization enforces the shared input envelope inherently while avoiding the unnecessary attenuation of admissible control redistribution that arises from direction-independent constraint handling. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose an anisotropic joint-admissibility-preserving input realization (AJ-APIR) for multi-input strict-feedback nonlinear systems subject to coupled joint capacity constraints. This is unlike the channel-wise methods [ 5 , 6 ] , which cannot express a coupled set.

The proposed realization employs a matrix-valued gain that splits spectrally into normal and tangential components relative to the joint constraint boundary. This allows the normal component of the commanded input to be attenuated near the boundary while retaining the tangential component. Thus, the proposed strategy extends the admissibility-preserving control of [ 21 ] from channel-wise constraints to a non-Cartesian joint admissible set.

We integrate AJ-APIR with recursive backstepping and establish the corresponding closed-loop guarantees. In particular, we derive a compact forward-invariant subset of the joint admissible set on which the realization channel remains uniformly nondegenerate.

An AJ-APC compatibility condition is then introduced to relate the available actuator authority to the tracking demand, under which the tracking and input realization errors converge exponentially, and all closed-loop signals remain uniformly bounded.

2026-10-02.title: EgoRefine: Ego-Referenced Predictive Alignment and Trajectory-Conditioned Reliability-Aware Fusion for Asynchronous Collaborative Perception
2026-10-02.authors: Lingzhao Kong , Yongsheng Zang , Yu Kang , Kailun Yang , Jie Fu , Yukun Zuo , Zhiyong Li

2026-10-02.abstract: Collaborative perception enables connected agents to share complementary observations for 3D object detection, extending sensing range and mitigating occlusion. Under asynchronous communication, however, cooperative features arrive with temporal delay. Existing prediction-based methods compensate for these features mainly from the transmitting agent’s own history, leaving residual misalignment with the ego agent’s current observation; subsequent fusion also often overlooks spatial variations in alignment quality. We propose EgoRefine, an ego-referenced predictive alignment and reliability-aware fusion framework for asynchronous collaborative perception. Its Ego-referenced Predictive Alignment module uses the current ego feature to guide cooperative trajectory-field prediction and refines the sampling offsets along an ego-referenced trajectory direction. Its Trajectory-conditioned Reliability-aware Fusion module treats the trajectory discrepancy between the ego and cooperative streams and the directional refinement magnitude as alignment cues, using them to condition the relation between aligned features and adaptively reweight the two streams before convolutional fusion. Experiments on V2V4Real and DAIR-V2X-Seq show that EgoRefine outperforms TraF-Align by 1.6 1.6 and 2.9 2.9 points on average in AP@0.5 and AP@0.7, respectively. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/godk0509/EgoRefine .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Collaborative perception has emerged as a promising paradigm for autonomous driving, where connected vehicles and infrastructure agents share complementary perceptual information to extend the sensing range and mitigate occlusion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . In this work, we focus on collaborative 3D object detection, where an ego agent fuses observations from multiple connected agents to localize objects in dynamic traffic scenes. Existing systems commonly transmit intermediate Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) features from cooperative agents to the ego agent, which then aggregates them with its own feature for detection. However, such collaboration relies on wireless links that inevitably introduce latency in real-world vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure scenarios [ 6 , 7 ] , so that cooperative features received by the ego agent correspond to past timestamps. This is particularly harmful for moving objects, since their responses in a delayed feature are spatially displaced from the ego agent’s current observation, and directly fusing them produces mislocalized boxes and duplicate detections. Asynchronous collaborative perception, which aims to exploit delayed cooperative features while maintaining consistency with the ego agent’s current view, is therefore a practical and important problem.

Compared with synchronous collaboration, temporal latency changes the spatial correspondence between agents. Throughout this paper, CAV denotes a cooperative agent, either a connected and automated vehicle or roadside infrastructure. Although a delayed CAV feature retains complementary cues, its object responses are shifted from their current positions by spatially varying amounts, making different regions differently reliable after alignment. Asynchronous collaboration therefore requires both predictive alignment and careful feature selection. Existing latency-compensation methods, including feature forecasting in SyncNet [ 8 ] and FFNet [ 9 ] , flow-based warping in CoBEVFlow [ 10 ] , and trajectory-field prediction in TraF-Align [ 11 ] , predict the current-time cooperative feature mainly from the CAV’s own history, without using the current ego representation to condition prediction. Such extrapolation cannot fully capture motion changes during the delay, leaving residual misalignment. Moreover, the concatenation-and-convolution fusion of TraF-Align and the attention-based [ 12 ] fusion of V2X-ViT [ 13 ] and CoBEVT [ 14 ] do not directly use alignment-stage cues to assess local reliability. Consequently, residually misaligned regions can contaminate the fused representation.

To address these issues, the key insight of this work is that the current ego feature should serve as a temporal and spatial reference for both predictive alignment and feature fusion, as shown in Fig. 1 . For delayed CAV features, ego information should not simply be added as another feature source; instead, it should guide the prediction of how the delayed feature evolves toward the ego agent’s current timestamp, since the ego feature provides direct current-time cues for co-visible objects. Furthermore, any correction to the predicted offset should follow the predicted motion direction rather than be learned as an independent, unconstrained offset, so that the refinement stays consistent with the underlying object motion. For feature fusion, the contributions of ego and aligned CAV features should be adaptively adjusted according to their local alignment status, rather than treating the compensated representation as uniformly reliable. Notably, the cross-agent discrepancy between the ego and ego-guided CAV trajectory fields and the magnitude of directional offset refinement provide complementary cues about local alignment status and can be reused for fusion without additional supervision.

Based on this insight, we propose EgoRefine, an ego-referenced predictive alignment and reliability-aware fusion framework for asynchronous collaborative perception. It comprises two modules: Ego-referenced Predictive Alignment (EPA) and Trajectory-conditioned Reliability-aware Fusion (TRF). EPA selectively injects the current ego feature into the delayed CAV feature before trajectory-field prediction, anchoring the predicted field to the current ego timestamp rather than the CAV’s history alone. It then applies a scalar refinement along the predicted orientation field to the base offsets, preserving the trajectory-induced motion structure while limiting the correction degrees of freedom. TRF reuses the ego-CAV trajectory discrepancy and directional refinement magnitude as alignment cues. These cues condition the semantic relation between the aligned features, which is mapped to a spatial gate that adaptively reweights the ego and CAV representations before convolutional fusion. In this way, the current ego observation informs both where the delayed feature is reconstructed and how strongly it contributes to the final representation.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We introduce an ego-referenced view for asynchronous collaborative perception, where the current ego feature serves as a temporal-spatial reference to guide both delayed CAV feature alignment and fusion, rather than relying primarily on the cooperative agent’s own history for temporal compensation.

We propose EgoRefine, which consists of Ego-referenced Predictive Alignment that anchors prediction to the ego timestamp and refines offsets only along the predicted motion direction, and Trajectory-conditioned Reliability-aware Fusion that reuses ego-CAV trajectory discrepancy and directional refinement magnitude to condition reliability-aware feature fusion.

Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, V2V4Real and DAIR-V2X-Seq, show that EgoRefine outperforms TraF-Align under every latency from 0 0 to 400 400 ms, with average gains of 1.6 / 2.9 1.6/2.9 points in AP@0.5/AP@0.7 and the largest margins under the stricter AP@0.7 criterion, while adding no extra supervision, annotation, or communication overhead.

2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Collaborative Perception for 3D Object Detection

Collaborative perception aims to improve autonomous driving perception by allowing connected vehicles and infrastructure agents to share complementary observations for 3D object detection [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Existing methods can be broadly divided into early fusion, late fusion, and intermediate feature fusion [ 15 ] , among which feature-level collaboration has become dominant due to its balance between accuracy and communication cost. V2VNet [ 20 ] aggregates multi-agent features with graph neural networks, while DiscoNet [ 21 ] learns a distilled collaboration graph to improve communication efficiency. Transformer-based methods further enhance multi-agent interaction, where V2X-ViT [ 13 ] models V2X collaboration with spatial-aware attention and CoBEVT [ 14 ] performs cooperative BEV fusion with sparse transformer blocks. Other methods focus on practical constraints in collaborative perception: CoAlign [ 22 ] addresses pose errors, Where2comm [ 23 ] selects spatially critical regions for communication, and HEAL [ 24 ] studies open heterogeneous collaborative perception. Recent works such as STAMP [ 25 ] and CoBEVMoE [ 26 ] further improve scalability and heterogeneity modeling in multi-agent BEV perception. However, these methods mainly improve feature aggregation, communication efficiency, or heterogeneity under synchronized or near-synchronized settings, while temporal inconsistency caused by communication latency is not their primary focus. In contrast, our work focuses on asynchronous feature-level collaborative 3D detection, where delayed CAV features are aligned toward the ego agent’s current timestamp and subsequently fused with reliability-aware adaptive weighting.

## II-B Asynchronous Collaborative Perception

Asynchronous collaborative perception studies how to exploit cooperative messages that arrive with temporal latency, so that delayed information can still benefit perception at the ego agent’s current timestamp [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] . Existing approaches mainly investigate feature forecasting, motion-based compensation, and trajectory-aware alignment under latency. SyncNet [ 8 ] synchronizes asynchronous features through feature-attention estimation and time modulation, while FFNet [ 9 ] predicts future features for vehicle-infrastructure cooperative detection. CoBEVFlow [ 10 ] explicitly estimates BEV flow to warp asynchronous cooperative features; How2comm [ 27 ] adopts flow-guided delay compensation within a communication-efficient framework, and LRCP [ 28 ] improves latency robustness by leveraging cached BEV features. These methods alleviate temporal misalignment through forecasting or warping, but their compensation is mainly driven by the transmitting agent’s historical context. More recently, TraF-Align [ 11 ] predicts trajectory fields to guide deformable sampling offsets for temporal feature alignment, providing a strong trajectory-based solution for asynchronous multi-agent perception.
These methods perform temporal compensation and subsequent fusion as separate stages: compensation relies mainly on historical observations, while fusion does not directly use cues generated during alignment. EgoRefine instead couples alignment and fusion by using the current ego representation to guide CAV prediction and reusing the resulting ego-CAV trajectory discrepancy and directional refinement magnitude as alignment cues for feature fusion.

2026-10-02.title: Decentralized Safe Path Following for Multiple Quadrotors on Intersecting Paths with Theoretical Guarantees
2026-10-02.authors: Hamza Tariq , Adeel Akhtar
2026-10-02.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-02.abstract: This paper studies decentralized safe path following for multiple quadrotors on intersecting paths, where safety requires both collision avoidance and strict adherence to pre-assigned routes. The proposed controller reformulates transverse feedback linearization as a constrained quadratic program with four equality constraints: two enforce convergence to and strict adherence to the path, and two prescribe the desired speed and heading. Safety is achieved by relaxing only the along-path speed constraint, while the path and heading constraints remain hard. Under the stated assumptions, and for admissible initial conditions, the controller guarantees that all agents converge to and thereafter follow their assigned paths, avoid collisions, and avoid attitude singularities. We evaluate the controller in the Drake physics engine on non-planar intersecting paths and compare it against two nominal-plus-safety-filter cascades. Code and additional results are available at https://gradslab.github.io/safe_multiquad_pf/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Multi-quadrotor systems are increasingly deployed in applications that require multiple vehicles to follow prescribed routes within a shared airspace, such as warehouse inventory and cooperative inspection of power lines and bridges. A vehicle that deviates from its route is both a collision hazard and a worse sensor, because what it records depends on where it flies [ 1 , 2 ] . We study safe path following , which requires simultaneously enforcing collision avoidance and strict adherence to assigned routes, i.e., path invariance .

Path invariance means that once the state of a vehicle reaches its path-following manifold [ 3 ] , formalized in Section II , its deviation from that path remains zero. Path invariance matters most in settings where lateral deviations are not acceptable, for example flight through narrow corridors and tunnels, or inspection at close range. There, the vehicle must also hold a prescribed heading so that an onboard camera stays pointed at the structure [ 4 ] .

Prior work on safe path following for multi-quadrotor systems handles collision avoidance indirectly through nonintersecting path design or timing coordination [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . These strategies are not suitable in confined environments, where nonintersecting paths might not exist and agents repeatedly pass through shared intersections. An alternative is to use control barrier functions (CBFs) or exponential CBFs (ECBFs) to design safety filters for collision avoidance [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , but these filters generally do not preserve path invariance. For example, [ 11 ] applies a safety filter to a multi-agent guiding-vector-field controller, but the resulting closed-loop system does not guarantee path invariance when paths intersect. Consequently, most work on safe multi-quadrotor systems has focused on trajectory tracking, where deviation from a given route is allowed [ 12 , 13 ] . A virtual reference governor has achieved safe path following with obstacle avoidance, but only for a single agent [ 14 ] . To the best of our knowledge, no decentralized safe path-following controller has been developed that guarantees both collision avoidance and path invariance for multiple quadrotors on intersecting paths.

Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) provides a natural framework for the safe path-following problem [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Specifically, TFL splits the control task into a primary objective, which drives the quadrotor to the desired path and keeps it there, and a secondary objective, which determines its speed and heading along the path [ 18 ] . For the dynamically extended quadrotor model, this separation gives four decoupled integrator chains. Stabilizing two of them stabilizes the path-following manifold, on which the quadrotor stays on its path, and stabilizing the other two stabilizes the secondary-objective manifold, where it maintains the desired speed and heading (Fig. 1 ).
We first reformulate the TFL controller in [ 17 ] as an equivalent parametric quadratic program (QP) with four equality constraints: two transversal constraints that stabilize the path-following manifold and two tangential constraints that stabilize the secondary-objective manifold.
We then augment the QP with higher-order ECBF constraints [ 9 ] to ensure that each quadrotor avoids attitude singularities and collisions with other agents, extending the decentralization approach in [ 10 ] to safe path following. This four-constraint structure is the central strength of the framework. Each equality constraint realizes exactly one control objective, so a designer may relax any subset of the four, including all four, by attaching a slack variable to the chosen constraints. Relaxing all four, while minimizing the deviation from the nominal input, recovers the standard nominal-plus-safety-filter cascade (Remark 2 ). The choice sets a tradeoff between guarantees and feasibility, because every constraint kept hard is an objective enforced exactly, yet each hard constraint also shrinks the feasible set of the QP. Here we treat three constraints as hard and relax only the speed, so the speed channel is the only nominal objective allowed to deviate, while the nominal transverse and heading-error dynamics are preserved exactly. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

We propose the first decentralized path-following controller for multiple quadrotors on intersecting paths that guarantees path invariance, collision avoidance, and singularity avoidance under the stated assumptions.

We reformulate the TFL controller as a QP that relaxes only the speed constraint, preserves the transverse and heading dynamics, and admits a closed-form solution (Remark 1 ).

We validate the controller in the Drake physics engine [ 19 ] on non-planar intersecting paths against two safety-filtered cascade baselines.

2026-10-02.title: The Geometry of Time: Horizon-Independent Feasibility and Repair for STL
2026-10-02.authors: Avinash Malik
2026-10-02.abstract:
Signal Temporal Logic control synthesis frequently encounters
physical infeasibility due to actuator limits or flawed task
deadlines. Standard optimization methods model time by discretizing
the horizon, which leads to exponential computational growth and
prevents the extraction of continuous temporal adjustments. This paper
presents a geometric decision procedure that evaluates physical
feasibility completely independently of the temporal horizon length.
The method operates by transforming explicit temporal logic
constraints into continuous spatial backward reachable sets evaluated
at time zero. It analytically inverts the Bhat–Bernstein settling-time
integral to map temporal windows into continuous spatial boundaries,
reducing the feasibility check to a local matrix and vector inclusion
evaluation When a specification is infeasible. The procedure extracts
a Farkas dual certificate to isolate conflicting constraints and
identifies the maximum geometric spatial gap. It then analytically
inverts the system’s dynamic expansion to map this largest geometric
gap into an exact, closed-form temporal delay, precisely fixing the
boundary deficit to restore physical realizability. We formally prove
the strict soundness, mathematically bounded completeness, and
horizon-independent scalability of this procedure. Experimental
evaluations on six-dimensional drone kinematics demonstrate
sub-millisecond execution times, massive speedups over
state-of-the-art optimization encodings, and computational immunity to
deeply nested logical formulas.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Signal Temporal Logic (STL) Maler and Nickovic (2004) is a formal
language used to specify continuous real-time behavior, such as
reach-avoid requirements, deadline constraints, and spatial bounds over
continuous physical states. In formal methods and automated control, STL control synthesis is the problem of automatically
constructing a feedback control policy or state-input trajectory that
guarantees a physical system satisfies a given temporal logic
specification over time Raman et al. (2014) ; Belta and Sadraddini (2019) . STL
synthesis has become a foundational building block in autonomous
systems, serving as the temporal logic layer for real-time Control
Barrier Function Quadratic Program (CBF-QP)
controllers Raman et al. (2014) , Large Language Model (LLM) task
translation from natural language to formal
specifications He et al. (2022) ; Chen et al. (2023) , autoregressive task
and motion planning Chen et al. (2024) , and data-driven
specification mining and inference Bartocci et al. (2022) .

A central challenge across these domains is handling infeasibility . In physical controller synthesis, infeasibility
occurs when a specification cannot be satisfied due to system dynamics,
actuator limits, or conflicting temporal
constraints Ghosh et al. (2016) ; Belta and Sadraddini (2019) . In modern
automated planning pipelines, it frequently arises from LLMs generating
logically incorrect or physically impossible temporal
deadlines Chen et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2023) . For both automated
verification tools and LLM-in-the-loop agents, simply returning a binary
failure signal is insufficient; the synthesis framework must provide
actionable diagnostic feedback to explain why a task failed and how to
correct it Kress-Gazit et al. (2018) ; Ghosh et al. (2016) . In discrete
reactive synthesis, such feedback is typically delivered as
counterexample trajectories on symbolic
abstractions Kress-Gazit et al. (2018) . In continuous STL synthesis, the
standard decision procedure encodes both the temporal logic formula and
the system dynamics into a Mixed-Integer Linear Program
(MILP) Raman et al. (2014) ; Belta and Sadraddini (2019) . When the
specification is infeasible, existing approaches extract an Irreducible
Infeasible Set (IIS) from the optimization solver to isolate the subset
of conflicting constraints Ghosh et al. (2016) .

However, MILP-based synthesis suffers from a fundamental structural
limitation. Standard encodings model time by discretizing the horizon
into explicit temporal steps, introducing binary decision variables for
every predicate at every time step, with nested temporal operators
compounding this variable count multiplicatively Kurtz and Lin (2022) .
For flat, short-horizon specifications, modern solvers terminate quickly
and the extracted infeasible set offers useful qualitative insight. For
long-horizon or deeply nested specifications, the variable structure
grows beyond the capacity of branch-and-bound solvers. Furthermore, even
when an infeasible set is successfully isolated, it identifies which spatial constraints conflict but cannot determine how
to repair the temporal structure , because time windows are encoded as
fixed structural dimensions of the mathematical model rather than
adjustable continuous parameters.

Our primary contribution is a geometric decision procedure for
STL synthesis feasibility that addresses this structural bottleneck.
Rather than constructing a trajectory optimization problem over
discretized time, our procedure evaluates synthesis feasibility via a
single matrix-vector inequality check executed in polynomial time
completely independent of the temporal horizon length and formula
nesting depth. When a specification is infeasible, the procedure returns
a Farkas dual certificate identifying the minimal conflicting subset, a
spatial deficit metric quantifying the physical violation, and a
closed-form temporal repair value that restores feasibility. This repair
value provides an exact scalar delay that a task planner or
specification author can apply directly to broaden temporal deadlines.

decision procedures and motivate our geometric framework, we examine a
usual robotic task execution scenario.

2026-10-02.title: STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets
2026-10-02.authors: Animesh Varma
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.comment: . Preprint
2026-10-02.abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark , comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Inferring physical properties from visual data remains a challenge for contemporary foundation models. While progress has been achieved in tasks predicated on static image features, performance degrades when systems are tasked with deducing internal states from observed motion. Current approaches excel at recognizing objects and classifying scenes, yet struggle to generalize to Newtonian mechanics, particularly when evaluating opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies undergoing multi-axis rotation. This limitation stems from a reliance on spatial Euclidean metrics, which fail to capture the temporal dynamics governing rigid-body motion.

The primary challenge is localizing the Center of Mass (CoM) of an object with an uneven internal mass distribution, absent direct visual indicators (see Figure 1 ). Standard object-detection pipelines and spatial foundation models (such as DINOv2 [ 23 ] ) predictably suffer from visual-kinematic aliasing, actively tracking spurious visual features rather than recovering the true hidden mass. While defaulting to the geometric centroid is a valid heuristic for uniformly dense objects, it fails for asymmetric payloads. Contemporary dense point-tracking architectures (e.g., CoTracker [ 13 ] , TAPIR [ 5 ] ) attempt to map surface motion. While surface point-trackers are mathematically ill-posed for internal volumetric tracking, we include them to empirically highlight the fundamental failure mode of applying surface-tracking pipelines to hidden mass estimation. Because the CoM is a hidden internal coordinate, and surfaces undergo self-occlusion during tumbling, point trackers fundamentally cannot solve internal kinematics. Intuitively, standard spatial models track the visible, wobbly exterior of a thrown hammer, whereas our temporal model aims to track the smooth, invisible parabolic trajectory of its heavy iron head. By optimizing for static pixel reconstruction or visible surface tracking rather than continuous momentum, these models conflate visual appearance with physical mass.

STATERA (Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Tensor Embeddings for Rigid-body Asymmetry) takes a preliminary step toward addressing this by evaluating motion across a temporal sequence rather than isolated spatial frames. By processing video through a partially-frozen V-JEPA backbone [ 22 ] (utilizing two adapted transformer blocks), the model observes the rotational torque and momentum transfer that occurs during freefall and impact. Instead of memorizing surface appearances, the model infers internal mass distribution directly from the object’s rigid-body kinematics. We operate on the hypothesis that models pre-trained on video encode physical priors—such as inertia and momentum—which can be extracted by optimizing for continuous motion tracking rather than static point localization. Our ablation studies support this: isolating the spatial layers without temporal mixing causes the predictions to collapse to the geometric center, failing to preserve physical momentum.

The contributions of this work are as follows:

We present STATERA, an architecture that tracks the unobservable CoM of asymmetric rigid bodies from raw video by extracting temporal features from a partially-frozen V-JEPA backbone.

We expose the settling-state dataset bias, demonstrating that complex phase-aware targets cause visual-kinematic aliasing, and we resolve this via curriculum label smoothing [ 27 , 3 ] .

We demonstrate zero-shot object transfer under calibrated camera conditions on real-world trajectories. Evaluated via a Normalized Center of Mass Error (N-CoME), STATERA isolates inertial mechanics from visual geometry, outperforming spatial foundation models, standard 3D-CNNs, and point trackers.

2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Recent advances in self-supervised learning have established spatial foundation models as the standard for visual feature extraction. These architectures excel at semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and geometric reasoning by optimizing for spatial similarities and patch-level reconstruction. However, because they evaluate isolated frames, they lack the temporal derivatives required to encode Newtonian mechanics like momentum and rotational inertia. Conversely, Video Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (V-JEPA) optimize for predicting missing temporal segments within an abstract latent space. This approach forces the network to learn the underlying transition dynamics of a scene. STATERA builds upon this by utilizing a partially-frozen V-JEPA backbone, leveraging its pre-trained temporal representations to track kinematic properties that are invisible in static spatial embeddings.

The capacity to infer physical properties from visual stimuli draws heavily on early cognitive models of intuitive physics [ 2 , 28 ] . Early computational frameworks and benchmarks, such as PHYRE [ 1 ] , explicitly tested forward prediction of mechanical events. However, these systems largely relied on simplified 2D physics engines or explicit state access. Our work transitions this objective to unconstrained real-world video, demanding that the network independently extracts hidden mass values from raw pixel spatiotemporal derivatives without engineered state abstractions.

Tracking objects through space has evolved via Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) [ 21 ] , 3D Gaussian Splatting [ 14 ] , and Slot Attention mechanisms [ 18 ] , which excel at disentangling independent entities and reconstructing complex surface geometries. Despite their spatial fidelity, these methods struggle to deduce hidden internal physical properties (e.g., density or asymmetric CoM), as their optimization targets remain strictly bounded by visible surface rendering or segmentation accuracy, rather than continuous Newtonian momentum constraints.

Estimating physical properties from visual data is an established problem in embodied AI. Classical System Identification [ 17 ] in robotics often employs Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) [ 12 ] to estimate inertial parameters. However, these classical approaches typically require explicit, noise-free state observations (e.g., bounding box dimensions or IMU data). STATERA transitions this objective directly to raw, unconstrained visual pixels. A common modern approach is a two-step pipeline: extracting surface coordinates using point-tracking models (e.g., CoTracker [ 13 ] , TAPIR [ 5 ] ), and feeding those tracks into a classical rigid-body solver. However, optical point trackers fail on opaque, tumbling bodies due to severe motion blur and self-occlusion. The true Center of Mass is an internal mathematical coordinate that is visually inaccessible from the exterior surface. STATERA’s latent end-to-end temporal approach bypasses surface correspondences entirely.

2026-10-05.title: EyeRobot 2.0: Active Gaze for Precise Manipulation without Wrist Cameras
2026-10-05.authors: Kush Hari , Justin Kerr , Nidhya Shivakumar , Samarth Mahapatra , Carmelo Sferrazza , Jiahui Lei , Jitendra Malik , C. Karen Liu , Ken Goldberg , Angjoo Kanazawa
2026-10-05.comment: Project Page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Inspired by human vision, we introduce a framework using active gaze to enable fine-grained bimanual manipulation with only a single stereo camera. EyeRobot 2.0 physically attends to a 3D fixation point in the scene by swiveling two eye viewpoints to center their gaze on it. The resulting images are processed foveally by allocating more visual tokens to the image centers, focusing computation on task-relevant features. Such Active Visual Fixation (AVF) requires carefully coordinated gaze during task execution, which we accomplish hierarchically by first training a low-level gaze servoing policy conditioned on a goal object, then training a target selector which emits fixation goals based on task progress. Both modules are trained with RL on real-world data: the first is trained with a dense geometric reward and the second co-trains with the BC gripper policy which allows it to discover fixation sequences that can resemble a human’s fixation sequence while performing the task (Fig. 1 ). EyeRobot 2.0 further takes advantage of fixation by canonicalizing gripper proprioception and actions into a rotating fixation-relative SE ​ ( 3 ) \text{SE}(3) frame, which compacts the size of the action distribution to learn.
We collect teleoperation data for 7 real-world and 6 simulated tasks, and conduct over 1000 physical and 1800 simulated robot trials comparing EyeRobot 2.0 against passive stereo and ego + + wrist camera policies trained on the same data. Removing wrist cameras is costly for standard policies: with only passive stereo, real-world success drops from 52 % 52\% to 27 % 27\% . EyeRobot 2.0 closes this gap without any wrist cameras, outperforming passive stereo by 40 % 40\% in real and 20 % 20\% in sim. It matches ego + + wrist policies when their wrist views are clear ( 69 % 69\% vs. 64 % 64\% ), and more than doubles their success when grasped objects occlude the wrist cameras ( 48 % 48\% vs. 22 % 22\% ). These results suggest active gaze as a single-camera alternative to wrist cameras for fine-grained manipulation.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Consider the task of picking up a cup with a lid, grasping a straw, and inserting the straw into a small opening in the lid (Fig. 1 ). As humans carry out this task, our eyes flit around the scene, filtering information with coordinated look-ahead movements that anticipate hand motion [ 1 ] . This task-relevant visual sampling, called fixation , directs high-resolution foveal vision to relevant parts of the visual field. Fixation also provides 3D anchor points for manipulation, simplifying the challenge of spatially reasoning about the scene [ 2 ] and implicitly breaking larger tasks into concrete sub-goals as gaze switches between targets.

We hypothesize that this behavior could also benefit robot manipulation.
Fixating on a dynamic task-relevant 3D point acts as a form of physical attention which
centers input observations, compacts the data distribution, filters irrelevant visual regions, and allocates additional resolution where it matters for fine-grained tasks without the cost of processing the full panorama at high resolution.
Some of these benefits can be offered by wrist-mounted cameras, which are used by nearly all existing bimanual manipulation systems [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, colocating vision with the gripper ties precise visual input to the manipulator, which is limiting in tool use, whole-body manipulation, or when grasped objects occlude the camera.
In addition, these systems constrain manipulator design because of their direct mounting to the gripper, which adds complexity, often occludes the ego camera, introduces motion blur, and prevents sleeker gripper designs. A purely ego-centric behavior cloning approach has the potential to ease constraints on end effector design, make better use of ego-centric human data, and improve tasks which benefit from vision-manipulator decoupling like fast motion, reaching into tight spaces, or searching large spaces [ 7 ] .

We present EyeRobot 2.0, a robot learning framework which introduces Active Visual Fixation (AVF). Using input only from one fixed stereo camera, EyeRobot 2.0 can carry out precise manipulation tasks like inserting a straw, capping a marker, zipping a bag, or extracting a wrench from a toolkit, and multi-stage tasks like opening a toaster oven, pulling the tray out, extracting a pan, pushing the tray back, and closing the door again.

EyeRobot 2.0 couples a fixation policy with a fixation-centric gripper policy. The fixation policy has two modules: a low-level gaze policy that coordinates two eye viewpoints to rapidly find and track 3D objects in the scene, and a high-level target selector to choose what object to look at and when to look at it during the task. Visual inputs are represented as foveated stereo multi-crops centered at the fixation point, which allocate more resolution towards the direction of interest. This physical attention not only increases visual acuity, but also reduces computation allocated to distractors.
In addition, EyeRobot 2.0 trains a fixation-centric gripper policy via behavior cloning, by representing SE(3) proprioception and action chunks canonicalized into the rotated fixation frame. This effectively constrains the input and output space for the gripper model with respect to task-relevant local regions. The gripper policy additionally receives the distance of the 3D fixation point as an observation, which acts as an anchor point for the policy to understand depth.
Both the gaze policy and target selector are trained with reinforcement learning (RL), with gaze emerging from a BC-RL loop as in Kerr et al. [7] .

We evaluate EyeRobot 2.0 on 7 physical tasks and 6 simulated MuJoCo tasks, collecting data and training single-task policies from scratch. Across over 1000 physical trials , it outperforms static stereo baselines by 40%, and by 20% on simulated pick-place tasks, with a larger performance improvement on fine-precision tasks. Compared to the widely adopted SOTA ego + wrist setup, EyeRobot 2.0 without wrist cameras matches task performance in physical trials, and on tasks with heavy occlusion of wrist cameras maintains strong performance while wrist baselines regress to static stereo performance. In ablations we find that fixation-centric actions account for a significant portion of EyeRobot 2.0’s improvement, causing a 20% performance boost across sim tasks, and foveation contributes strongly to real-world success on fine-grained tasks, boosting by 20% overall.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Learning manipulation from human demonstrations

Behavior Cloning (BC) allows robots to learn complex behaviors from teleoperated demonstrations without requiring handcrafted motion primitives and reward functions [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . BC has been extended to work in complex settings including mobile manipulation [ 12 , 6 ] and bimanual manipulation [ 3 , 4 ] , and several recent efforts have been directed towards scaling teleoperation datasets [ 13 , 14 , 5 , 15 , 16 ] . Another enticing direction for scaling is learning from ego-centric human data, either by instrumenting humans or scraping internet videos [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . However, learning from human videos presents a significant domain gap between ego-centric sensors in first-person datasets and the wrist cameras that our robot policies so frequently rely on for fine-grained performance. EyeRobot 2.0 aims to provide a route towards lessening this gap by leveraging human-like fixation for precise bimanual manipulation. We are also inspired by task conditioning approaches in BC which condition a low-level policy on the output of a higher-level task sequencer [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Similarly, EyeRobot 2.0 learns a target selector to control gaze, but does not require human gaze supervision and instead trains gaze with RL via a BC accuracy reward.

## 2.2 Active vision for manipulation

Active vision deliberately moves sensors to improve observability, filter information, and reduce occlusions for better environment understanding [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] .
Previous systems have used active vision to help with tasks such as visual search [ 34 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] , object detection and tracking [ 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 ] , and 3D reconstruction [ 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 ] .
Similarly, active vision has proven beneficial for robot manipulation with a “robot neck” moving the camera based on VR headset movement during task teleoperation to reveal better viewpoints [ 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 ] . Active visual search can also benefit from training on ego-centric human data [ 53 , 54 , 55 ] . EyeRobot 2.0 in contrast does not attempt to address viewpoint selection which has been explored in prior works, but rather investigates how coordinated fine-grained eye movements can boost performance even with a well-positioned viewpoint .

Related to learning more precise gaze, some papers collect human eye tracking data during teleoperation to predict a gaze point as an intermediate output to condition a gripper policy with [ 56 , 57 ] or crop a high-resolution finger-tip image [ 58 ] . Others [ 59 ] learn gaze in simulation through on-policy task-based rewards; however, these methods struggle with sim-to-real transfer. EyeRobot [ 7 ] overcomes the need for gaze demonstrations by training a gaze policy on top of real-world behavior cloning data from 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} video by co-training the eye and arm policies with an action feedback loop for reward. Building on this, EyeRobot 2.0 uses a similar co-training loop but tackles much more fine-grained manipulation tasks by utilizing active stereo fixation, a fixation-centric action representation, and a hierarchical target selector to precisely coordinate gaze throughout execution.

2026-10-05.title: CORNAV: Construction-Aware Reasoning for Robot Navigation on Active Worksites
2026-10-05.authors: Parastoo Ali Pour , Deepak Prakash Kumar , Tommy Zhou , Pramod Khargonekar , Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque
2026-10-05.abstract: The construction industry faces persistent labor shortages, low productivity that costs the global economy over $1.6 trillion annually, and one of the highest injury rates among major industries. These factors motivate the use of autonomous robots to improve efficiency and worker safety. Existing language-grounded navigation systems, however, rely on semantic scene understanding alone and lack access to construction-specific context such as architectural plans, evolving work schedules, and safety constraints. As a result, they localize permanent building features unreliably and cannot safely navigate active jobsites. We present CORNAV, a blueprint-grounded, schedule-aware navigation framework that operates from 2D CAD drawings and project schedules without requiring a Building Information Model. CORNAV aligns architectural blueprints against hierarchical open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs to ground object queries, converts project schedules into time-varying navigation constraints, and validates requests through an LLM-based safety module that escalates hazardous zones before planning. An A* planner then enforces mandatory exclusion zones while preferentially avoiding higher-risk areas. Across an indoor office and a real construction site, blueprint grounding raises task success from 13.0% to 72.2% over semantic retrieval alone, schedule awareness eliminates all hard-zone violations, and the safety module correctly rejects hazardous requests arising from mislabeled project schedules. Project website: https://cornav.github.io/CORNAV/ .
2026-10-05.introduction:
The construction industry continues to face persistent workforce shortages [ 1 ] . In the United States alone, more than 80% of contractors report shortages of experienced skilled workers [ 2 ] , and two-thirds of firms are actively seeking to hire despite ongoing recruitment challenges [ 3 ] . Construction remains one of the most hazardous industries, with more than 1,000 worker fatalities reported annually since 2016 [ 4 ] . This industry has also experienced a prolonged decline in productivity relative to other sectors [ 1 , 5 ] . In the United States, construction value added per worker was roughly 40% lower in 2020 than in 1970, while manufacturing labor productivity increased more than nine-fold over the same period [ 5 ] . The economic cost of this gap is substantial and closing it could raise the sector’s value added by roughly $1.6 trillion per year globally, about one-third of that in the United States [ 6 ] .

These challenges, together with the growing need to build and renew aging infrastructure, have accelerated interest in construction robotics. Applications include site inspection and quality control, material handling and transport, assembly and installation, and operation in hazardous environments [ 1 ] . By automating repetitive and dangerous tasks, robotic systems can improve worker safety, increase operational efficiency, and support more consistent project execution.

Construction sites present a demanding environment for autonomous robots. Unlike structured manufacturing settings, where robots operate within fixed work cells and standardized workflows, construction environments change continuously. Partially completed structures, dynamic equipment, and shifting work zones alter the site as the project progresses [ 7 , 8 ] . Activities such as concrete placement, material staging, and structural installation can change traversable regions and render previously generated maps outdated, making robust localization and frequent map updates essential. To protect workers, construction managers routinely establish temporary work zones, exclusion areas, and task-specific safety procedures that may change throughout the day [ 1 ] . Autonomous robots must, therefore, reason beyond geometric obstacle avoidance, incorporating semantic understanding, operational context, and evolving safety constraints to navigate active jobsites safely.

Recent work addresses these requirements independently: (i) 3D scene graphs organize objects and spaces into structured semantic representations [ 9 , 10 ] , (ii) open-vocabulary methods add natural-language querying over them [ 11 , 12 ] , (iii) architectural floor plans and Building Information Models (BIMs) supply geometric and semantic priors for localization and mapping [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , and (iv) large language models (LLMs) enable task planning and safety reasoning [ 16 ] .

These capabilities, however, have developed largely in isolation. First, scene graph methods offer rich semantic understanding but derive room-level structure from geometric heuristics or vision-language labeling, which varies across scenes and sensing conditions [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Second, blueprint- and BIM-based approaches supply stable geometric priors [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] but, as commonly deployed, keep schedule information separate from the geometric model and treat the workspace as static. Third, safety-aware planning methods enforce constraints specified by the robot designer rather than incorporating constraints from the operational documents construction managers already maintain [ 16 ] . Robots therefore lack a unified representation of what exists in the environment, where it is located, when hazards are active, and which safety constraints apply.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions. First , we present a unified construction-aware navigation framework that integrates architectural CAD drawings, open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs, construction schedules, and predefined safety rules into a single planning pipeline for autonomous mobile robots (Fig. 1 ). Second , we introduce a hybrid semantic grounding strategy that combines object retrieval [ 11 ] with deterministic blueprint-based room resolution. This enables reasoning over observed objects and architectural fixtures in the CAD while maintaining stable room identities for downstream schedule reasoning. Third , we incorporate construction look-ahead project schedules (refer to the project page for an example) directly into navigation. An LLM interprets hazard descriptions and site safety rules to augment hazard labels specified in the project schedule, allowing constraints to adapt as work progresses. Finally , we evaluate the framework on robot-collected sensor data (RGB, depth, and pose) from a Unitree Go2 quadruped in an indoor environment and an active construction site, and demonstrate live deployment on both the Go2 and a Unitree G1 humanoid.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Architectural Drawings for Robot Localization

Architectural drawings have long supplied geometric priors for robot localization and navigation. A range of methods localize against them, using LiDAR [ 13 , 14 ] , RGB-D imagery, or learned room-layout features [ 17 ] to improve robustness in indoor environments with relatively stable layouts. Recent work extends architectural plans to construction-site localization through situational graphs and semantic building representations [ 15 ] . Collectively, these approaches use architectural information primarily for spatial localization and mapping, without accounting for the temporal and safety constraints introduced by ongoing construction activities.

We use architectural drawings differently. Rather than treating the blueprint solely as a localization prior, we use CAD drawings as the authoritative spatial representation for room identities, spatial hierarchy, and safety constraint grounding. This yields stable room assignments robust to errors in perception-based room classification, and provides the backbone for integrating project schedules and safety information.

## II-B 3D Scene Graphs for Semantic Environment

Recent advances in 3D scene understanding allow robots to build semantic representations of the environment. Hydra introduced real-time hierarchical 3D scene graphs for spatial structure and semantic entities [ 10 ] . Building on advances in open-vocabulary 3D perception [ 18 ] , open-vocabulary scene graphs such as OVSG and ConceptGraphs enable language-based grounding and retrieval of objects and regions [ 19 , 12 ] . HOV-SG organizes them hierarchically across floors, rooms, and objects for language-grounded navigation [ 11 ] . These representations offer far richer environmental understanding than occupancy maps.

Our framework builds the open-vocabulary 3D scene graph using HOV-SG [ 11 ] , while recognizing that such graphs alone are insufficient for construction environments, as they do not reliably ground room identity. A region such as a kitchen or living area may be mislabeled in the scene graph, making it hard to associate operational knowledge, such as scheduled hazardous work zones, with the correct region. We therefore combine 3D scene graphs with blueprint-derived spatial information and construction-specific operational knowledge.

## II-C BIMs for Robot Navigation

BIMs support robotic inspection, localization, and task planning by providing detailed semantic representations of buildings [ 15 ] , and can be linked to project schedules through 4D BIM workflows. However, they require significant modeling effort and ongoing maintenance [ 20 ] , and adoption remains slow and uneven [ 21 ] , particularly among the small and medium-sized firms that make up most of the industry [ 22 , 23 ] . Limited budgets, training costs, and the perceived adequacy of established 2D architectural drawings sustain the reliance on traditional CAD drawings [ 24 , 21 ] . 4D BIM in particular sees limited uptake [ 25 ] , and schedule information is typically maintained separately from the geometric model.

Closest to our setting, several systems generate schedule-aware navigation maps from BIM. Follini et al. [ 26 ] incorporate construction schedules into Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) geometry to produce a schedule-aware obstacle map, and Gopee et al. [ 27 ] block spaces containing active work while generating schedule-dependent waypoints. Others use BIM semantics for routing and task planning. Karimi et al. [ 28 ] build an IFC-derived hypergraph where room attributes (such as wall material
and construction hazards) determine per-room costs, and routing minimizes total path cost. Kim and Peavy [ 29 ] convert IFC into a queryable building world for element-level task planning. In parallel, recent work combines BIM with natural-language risk cues to shape navigation behavior. Amani et al. [ 30 ] use Bayesian inference over building data and prompt sentiment to adjust potential fields during planning, biasing the robot away from obstacles when a command signals elevated risk.

These systems demonstrate the value of schedule- and safety-aware navigation, but each presupposes a BIM or IFC model and treats declared hazards as static exclusion zones. They also resolve queried entities through structured lookup over model classes rather than open-vocabulary grounding, so they cannot interpret instructions referring to objects observed on site but absent from the model. Methods that infer risk from prompt tone [ 30 ] face a further limitation. They adjust behavior from the phrasing of a command rather than validating declared hazards against predefined safety rules.

Our framework addresses these gaps in the following ways. We draw operational knowledge directly from the 2D CAD drawings and project schedules already maintained on site, rather than from a BIM or IFC model. Instead of treating scheduled zones as static obstacles, we distinguish mandatory exclusion zones (hard constraints) from cautionary regions (soft constraints). We use an LLM-based validation module to escalate hazardous activity zones to hard constraints, guarding against mislabeled annotations in the project schedules. Finally, an open-vocabulary 3D scene graph lets us ground natural-language queries to both blueprint-defined fixtures and movable objects observed on site, extending beyond the structured lookups of BIM-based systems.

2026-10-05.title: LLA-MPC on Embedded Hardware: Rapid Adaptive Control with Thousands of Parallel Models
2026-10-05.authors: Henry Z. Liao , Maitham F. AL-Sunni , John M. Dolan
2026-10-05.comment: This work has been accepted in the Sim2Real and Classical Control: From Rigorous Theory to Data-Driven Robotics Workshop at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026), Pittsburgh, PA, USA
2026-10-05.abstract:
We present a generalized implementation of Look-Back and Look-Ahead Adaptive
Model Predictive Control (LLA-MPC) , a learning-free framework for real-time,
rapid adaptive system identification and control. The original formulation
was demonstrated only in simulation, for autonomous racing with a fixed model
structure. Our implementation has modular dynamics and integrators, and we
validate it on the F1TENTH platform under constrained computation and noisy
state estimation. The system identifies tire parameters online by evaluating
thousands of candidate models in real time on an embedded computer.
Experiments with low-friction tires across changing surfaces show that LLA-MPC completes high-speed tracking tasks where a fixed nominal model
fails. Code, videos, and our related work are available at lla-control.github.io . This work has been accepted in the Sim2Real and Classical Control: From Rigorous Theory to Data-Driven Robotics Workshop at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). Link: https://sim2realgap.github.io/sim2real-and-control-workshop-iros2026/
2026-10-05.introduction:
Model-based control for robots degrades when dynamics change rapidly during operation. Car tires wear, surfaces change, and payloads shift. Recovering performance requires identification that reacts within a fraction of a second. Look-back and Look-ahead Adaptive Model Predictive Control ( LLA-MPC ) addresses this without learning [ 3 ] . The framework holds a large bank of candidate models with varied parameter values and evaluates their one-step predictions in a single batched computation. At every step, the candidate with the best performance over a short look-back window becomes the prediction model of a receding-horizon controller.

LLA-MPC runs an ensemble of physics simulators onboard, and the look-back selection
re-aligns it with reality. The original paper demonstrated the
framework only in simulation, and its vehicle model did not survive the
transfer to hardware. This paper presents a generalized implementation that
bridges this gap. We deploy it on the F1TENTH platform [ 18 ] ,
with a new single-track dynamics module and Fiala brush tire forces, on
embedded computation, with onboard state estimation in
extreme driving conditions.

Adaptive control with multiple models is a classical idea. Multiple-model adaptive control switches among pre-designed controllers paired with parallel identification models [ 16 ] , multiple-model predictive control blends a bank of linear models by residual weights [ 4 ] , and adaptive MPC estimates parameters continuously inside the controller [ 2 ] . LLA-MPC instead keeps a single receding-horizon optimizer and selects among thousands of nonlinear physics models by batched prediction error [ 3 ] . A recent method also selects models online from residual errors, but its library spans models of different fidelity and cost to balance accuracy against computation [ 8 ] , whereas the LLA-MPC bank varies one model’s parameters to follow changing dynamics.

Online adaptation methods for racing usually learn a model or a correction, either beforehand or during operation. They update a Gaussian process residual
during the race [ 10 ] , learn tire residuals after a warm-up lap [ 11 ] , calibrate a tire model from seconds of driving [ 9 ] , or pair online estimation with offline-trained components [ 17 ] . Meta-learned and pretrained models adapt online only after offline training [ 13 , 12 , 24 , 15 ] . Robust formulations skip identification and hedge against a fixed model set [ 1 , 14 ] , and domain randomization trains one policy across randomized simulation parameters [ 20 , 19 ] . LLA-MPC holds the same kind of
ensemble as a bank of simulators and identifies at run time which one
matches reality. It requires no training, no warm-up data, and no fitting
step, so it adapts within a look-back window of a change rather than after
a data collection phase, and its identified parameters remain physical
quantities.

The contributions of this work are threefold.

A generalized, open-source implementation of LLA-MPC with modular dynamics, integrators, and parallelization backends.

Hardware validation of LLA-MPC under constrained computation and noisy state estimation, showing improved performance over a fixed nominal model.

Demonstrations that show the robustness of LLA-MPC across tasks, noise levels, and environmental conditions.

2026-10-05.title: Bridging Frontier Reasoning and Robot Execution: From Autonomous Demonstration Generation to Dense Language Supervision
2026-10-05.authors: Bosung Kim , Alexander Trevithick , Ruiyi Wang , Prithviraj Ammanabrolu
2026-10-05.abstract: Recent advances in frontier models enable robot manipulation from only a few demonstrations, but high inference latency limits their use for real-time robot control. To bridge this gap, we study two complementary approaches that connect frontier reasoning with low-latency local execution. First, we use a frontier model to autonomously generate demonstrations that supplement human demonstrations for training a fast local policy. We augment its in-context examples with corrective demonstration segments that show how to recover from physical errors, improving generation reliability. Generation time and cost decrease as successful examples accumulate in context, suggesting a path toward more efficient data collection. At deployment, a harness combines frontier-generated instructions with a fast local policy, enabling efficient execution while preserving the frontier model’s ability to guide and correct actions.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Robot learning has explored several approaches to translating frontier-level intelligence into physical robot actions. These approaches differ in how frontier models guide execution: they can issue instructions to a trained local policy ( Shi et al., 2025 ) , generate executable programs over control primitives ( Liang et al., 2022 ) , provide spatial guidance such as trajectories ( Li et al., 2025 ) , or produce robot commands directly ( Menon et al., 2026 ) . Recent advances in frontier models enable robot manipulation from only a few demonstrations through in-context learning, without task-specific fine-tuning. However, frontier-model inference and API latency limit the responsiveness of direct robot control, whereas practical manipulation requires high-frequency sensory feedback and timely action adjustments for reliable physical interaction ( Berman et al., 2026 ) . This motivates our central question: how can we retain the benefits of frontier-model reasoning while delegating motor execution to a fast local policy?

The ability to manipulate objects from a few examples makes frontier models a potential source of additional robot demonstrations, complementing teleoperation-based data collection. Our first bridge explores this capability by generating manipulation trajectories and incorporating them into local-policy training. Successful demonstrations alone do not reliably support autonomous generation, particularly during precise contact operations. We augment the in-context examples with corrective demonstration segments: short demonstrations of adjustments at moments when execution encounters physical errors. As successful trajectories accumulate, we retain useful segments for reuse in subsequent episodes and examine how generation time and API cost evolve. At deployment, a harness combines frontier-generated plans with the policy’s low-latency execution, allowing the frontier model to provide high-level direction while the policy generates motor actions within each execution segment.

Delegating motor execution reduces the need for frontier inference to generate actions, but makes the policy’s instruction-following capabilities a central constraint. We propose dense language supervision as the next bridge, enabling the policy to interpret and execute diverse, fine-grained instructions generated by the frontier model. We annotate the same demonstrations at three nested granularities—primitive, atomic, and composite—and pair these annotations with multi-aspect descriptions to broaden instruction diversity.

We study two complementary bridges between frontier reasoning and robot execution: generating demonstrations for local-policy training and expanding the policy’s language interface through dense supervision. Across four manipulation tasks, mixed human and generated demonstrations achieve the same aggregate policy success as an equally sized human-only corpus, supporting generated trajectories as a supplementary training source. Hierarchical and multi-aspect supervision together achieve the strongest results across both simulation benchmarks and instructor conditions. Finally, the crossword task demonstrates their integration, with dense supervision improving performance under dynamic spatial instructions. Together, these results support autonomous demonstration generation and dense language supervision as complementary bridges between frontier reasoning and low-latency local execution.

# 2 Related Work

Foundation Models for Robot Control. Foundation models guide robot execution through several interfaces, summarized in Figure 8 in Appendix B . Direct-control evaluations of frontier models demonstrate manipulation capabilities alongside limitations in execution speed and precision ( Menon et al., 2026 ; Berman et al., 2026 ) . Hierarchical and dual-system architectures couple vision-language processing with low-level control ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Cheng et al., 2025 ) , while other approaches provide spatial guidance ( Li et al., 2025 ; Shridhar et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) or synthesized goal images ( Black et al., 2024 ) . Hi Robot fine-tunes a high-level VLM using labeled demonstrations and synthetic language interactions, and a low-level VLA using robot demonstrations ( Shi et al., 2025 ) . Harness frameworks such as Thea support feedback-driven task execution ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Our study retains a frontier model without task-specific fine-tuning and examines how to train a local policy that executes its instructions.

Autonomous Data Generation and Policy Learning. MimicGen adapts human demonstrations to new scene configurations and embodiments ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) . Manipulate-Anything uses VLM-generated actions and visual verification to collect physical demonstrations for policy learning ( Duan et al., 2024 ) . Show-Harness collects human and frontier-generated demonstrations through predefined semantic actions mapped to robot commands by an embodiment-specific interpreter, and uses the resulting trajectories for policy training ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Program-synthesis approaches generate executable programs over perception and control primitives ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) , with ASPIRE accumulating reusable skills ( Lu et al., 2026 ) and ENPIRE extending agent-driven improvement to neural policies, training infrastructure, and algorithms ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Our first bridge studies autonomous demonstration generation through direct, low-level robot control by frontier models. Using successful demonstrations and corrective demonstration segments as in-context references, a frontier model executes tasks with visual feedback and produces new training trajectories. We examine generation reliability, track how generation time and cost evolve as successful examples accumulate, and evaluate the resulting demonstrations as a supplementary source for local-policy training.

Language Supervision and Instruction Following. RT-H learns language-motion prediction and action generation within a single VLM, enabling corrections through language ( Belkhale et al., 2024 ) . Hu et al. (2026) show that a controller’s responsiveness to varied instructions affects hierarchical execution. DeMiAn provides multi-aspect segment annotations and a learned instructor, including evaluation on composite tasks with changing atomic instructions ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Building on multi-aspect supervision, our second bridge jointly annotates shared trajectories at three nested granularities—primitive, atomic, and composite—and adds alternative descriptions and rephrasings. We examine how temporal granularity and linguistic diversity affect instruction following under oracle and frontier-model instructors, with additional robustness evaluations across planners and instruction phrasings.
