2026-10-05.title: On Representational Alignment among Embodied Agents
2026-10-05.authors: Fulvio Mastrogiovanni
2026-10-05.abstract:
Embodied agents interacting with the same physical process may maintain heterogeneous, asynchronous, and observer-relative representations.
Rather than assuming that such representations should always be globally aligned, we investigate which distinctions among them must actually be resolved for coherent interaction.
We formalize this question through relational sufficiency : an interaction-specific relational-evidence map defines the representational ambiguity left unresolved by comparison, and sufficiency holds when each residual ambiguity fiber lies within an interaction-equivalence class.
When this condition fails, additional sensorimotor anchors must separate precisely the ambiguities that can change the interaction-relevant outcome.
For smooth systems, we derive a local first-order lower bound on the number of independent scalar anchors required, given by the dimension of directions that are invisible to relational evidence but visible to the interaction-relevant map.
We instantiate the theory in two variants of an asynchronous hand-off scenario that share the same observer agents, representations, transports, and relational evidence.
Relative synchronization requires no additional anchor, whereas hand-off at an absolute time requires exactly one.
The analysis therefore provides a task-relative stopping condition for representational alignment: residual disagreement need not be eliminated when it is invariant with respect to the interaction.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Embodied, cognitive agents do not observe and act in the world from a common viewpoint.
Their access to an environment is mediated by their body morphologies, sensors, action capabilities, interaction histories, and internal
representational processes.
Even when two agents cooperate by interacting with the same physical process, the representations available to them may differ in reference frame, time, content, abstraction level, or semantic form.
Partial and asynchronous observations further amplify these differences.
From the perspective of embodied cognitive systems, this raises a basic question: what kind of representational compatibility is actually required for coherent interaction between two or more embodied agents?

A common approach is to seek some form of representational alignment .
Different methods have been pursued toward this aim.
Distributed estimation methods aim at deriving mutually compatible estimates of a shared state;
multi-agent systems exchange information to coordinate private beliefs;
multimodal and cross-agent representation-learning methods construct mappings between heterogeneous latent spaces;
recent work has shown that local comparison spaces can support alignment even when a single global latent space is absent ( Robinson, 2017 ; Moschella et al., 2023 ; Ghalkha et al., 2026 ; D’Acunto et al., 2026 ) .
Similarly, recent embodied multi-agent architectures explicitly study the alignment of private world models through communication ( Dongre and Hakkani-Tür, 2026 ) .
These developments substantially weaken the requirement that different agents should maintain identical internal representations.
They nevertheless retain, in different forms, an objective of making the representations relevant to coordination mutually compatible.

This paper investigates a different possibility.
We ask whether some representational disagreements can remain unresolved because they are irrelevant to the interaction task.
More precisely, we consider embodied observer agents whose local representations may be heterogeneous and not directly comparable;
when required, observer-specific representations are transported into an interaction-dependent comparison context;
the resulting joint relational configuration may still be compatible with multiple underlying representational configurations.
We refer to this residual indeterminacy as relational ambiguity .
Our central hypothesis is that such ambiguity need not be eliminated in general .
It only needs to be resolved along those representational degrees of freedom that can change the task-relevant outcome.

This small shift changes the question from how two representations should be globally aligned to which relations between them must be determined.
The distinction is especially important in the case of embodied agents.
For such agents, representations are not detached descriptions, as they participate in a closed sensorimotor loop in which sensing produces observer-relative information, representations support action, actions modify subsequent interaction conditions, and new observations constrain what the agents can continue to represent.
Therefore, the environment may constrain local representations through the consequences of sensorimotor interaction without providing the agents with a
privileged, globally accessible representation of itself.

A minimal example illustrates the issue.
Let us consider two embodied observers coordinating around the future occurrence of an event, for example, to determine when such an event will occur.
The first observer represents the event through an estimated distance and velocity, while the second represents it directly through an estimated time-to-event.
Their native representations differ, but both can be transported into estimates of event time.
Let us suppose that the only relational evidence available after transport is the difference between the two estimates.
This evidence is invariant to a common temporal shift of both estimates.
If the interaction requires only relative synchronization, the common shift is therefore irrelevant, and every representation pair related by that shift supports the same task response.
If, instead, the interaction requires both agents to act relative to an external physical event, the same ambiguity becomes consequential.
Relative agreement is then insufficient, and some additional sensorimotor relation to the environment is required.
It is noteworthy that the observers, their representations, their transport mechanisms, and their relational evidence can remain unchanged across the two cases, since only the task determines whether the unresolved ambiguity matters.

We use this contrast to develop a theory of relational sufficiency among embodied observer agents .
Let a joint configuration of transported representations be denoted by q q , and let C I ​ ( q ) C_{I}(q) denote the relational evidence available for an interaction I I .
The configurations that cannot be distinguished through this evidence form an ambiguity class Ω C ​ ( q ) \Omega_{C}(q) .
Independently, the interaction induces an equivalence relation over representational configurations, such that two configurations are equivalent when they cannot be distinguished by the task-relevant response.
The resulting class is denoted by [ q ] Θ [q]_{\Theta} .
Therefore, the basic sufficiency condition studied in this paper is

It can be noted that this relation expresses a deliberately weaker requirement than representational identification or global alignment.
Relational evidence is sufficient whenever all configurations that remain epistemically indistinguishable are also indistinguishable to the
interaction.
The interacting agents do not have to determine which member of the equivalence class is the “correct” representation.

However, when this inclusion relation fails, relational evidence leaves unresolved a distinction that the interaction can detect.
We introduce sensorimotor anchors to characterize the additional information required in this case.
An anchor is not a global world representation or an oracle supplying ground truth.
On the contrary, it is an interaction-derived constraint that is available through the agents’ admissible sensorimotor coupling.
For example, it could be an environmental cue, a contact event, a landmark observation, or other locally obtainable consequence of interaction.
Anchors are sufficient when they separate those relational ambiguities that correspond to different task-relevant outcomes.
This leads to a principle that guides our model, that is, an embodied agent should resolve only those relational ambiguities that the interaction itself can distinguish.

In this paper, we develop this principle formally and examine its consequences in two analytically solvable variants of the same hand-off scenario.
The two variants share the same observer agents, local representations, representational transports, and relational evidence, but differ in their task invariances.
The first introduces an observer-relative synchronization task, in which the ambiguity preserved by relational evidence is entirely task-invariant and no additional anchor is required.
In the second, we discuss an absolute hand-off task, for which the same ambiguity is task-relevant and exactly one independent scalar
anchor is required.
The comparison therefore isolates task structure, rather than representational accuracy or sensing capability, as the factor that determines how much relational alignment is necessary.

The main contributions of the paper are as follows.

We formulate relational sufficiency for two embodied observer agents with heterogeneous local representations, and we explicitly distinguish relational epistemic evidence, task response, and interaction adequacy.

We formulate relational sufficiency for two embodied observer agents with heterogeneous local representations, and we explicitly distinguish relational epistemic evidence, task response, and interaction adequacy.

We establish a mismatch result showing that relational evidence is insufficient whenever it preserves ambiguities that the task can distinguish, and we characterize sufficient sensorimotor anchoring as the separation of such task-conflicting ambiguities.

We derive a local first-order lower bound on the number of independent scalar anchors required for relational sufficiency; the bound is given by the dimensional mismatch between directions that are invisible to relational evidence and directions that are invariant to the task.

We instantiate the theory in two asynchronous hand-off toy scenarios and show analytically that the same relational ambiguity requires no anchors for relative synchronization but one anchor for absolute interaction; we further show that adequacy can require less information than exact task-response reconstruction.

We characterize representational alignment as task-over-refined whenever it distinguishes configurations lying within the same interaction-equivalence class; this provides a precise sense in which global alignment may be sufficient while being stronger than necessary for embodied interaction.

The remainder of the paper first positions the problem with respect to existing work on representation alignment, sufficient representations, decentralized information, and task-relevant observability, while introducing the hand-off scenarios that serve as a running example.
Then, we define the sensorimotor and representational model of embodied observer agents, develop the relational sufficiency and anchoring results, and instantiate them analytically in the two hand-off scenarios.
Finally, we discuss implications for representation alignment, learning for embodied agents, the degenerate single-observer case, and extensions to interactions involving more than two observer agents.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Background and Motivating Scenario

## 2.1 Shared representations and relational sufficiency

The problem addressed in this paper lies at the intersection of several well-established research directions.
Distributed estimation and sensor fusion have long considered systems in which multiple sensing units access different, noisy, and possibly delayed observations of a common dynamical process.
Such methods provide mature mechanisms for combining heterogeneous measurements and handling partial or asynchronous information ( Capitán et al., 2011 ) .
In robotics, problems like multi-robot simultaneous localisation and mapping similarly demonstrate that consistency can often be assessed through relative constraints rather than through direct access to an external ground truth.
Pairwise consistency methods and their higher-order extensions, for example, identify mutually compatible inter-robot measurements through graphs or hypergraphs of relative constraints ( Mangelson et al., 2018 ; Forsgren et al., 2024 ) .
Estimation and SLAM also make explicit the role of unobservable directions: some transformations of the estimated state can leave the available relative measurements unchanged, and consistent estimation must avoid acquiring spurious information along those directions.
Our setting shares this concern with unresolved degrees of freedom, but asks an additional question: whether a direction that is invisible to the available relational evidence is also invisible to the interaction.

These approaches already establish an important principle for the work discussed here, that is, useful consistency relations can be defined locally and relationally.
However, their usual objective remains the recovery of a mutually compatible description, typically expressed in a geometric, dynamical, or symbolic form.
The latent object to be estimated or aligned may be decentralized, partially observed, or represented in multiple coordinate systems, but the different information sources are ultimately
interpreted with respect to a common estimation problem.

Recent representation-learning methods weaken this requirement further.
Observer-relative representations allow independently learned latent spaces to be compared through relations to shared reference samples, which enables communication across otherwise incompatible latent coordinates ( Moschella et al., 2023 ) .
Sheaf-theoretic approaches provide a more general ontology for heterogeneous information sources.
Local data may remain in different spaces, while restriction or transport maps specify how information
is compared on overlaps ( Robinson, 2017 ) .
Recent decentralized representation-learning methods extend this idea to multiple local comparison spaces and learned mappings, thus relaxing the requirement for a single shared latent space ( Ghalkha et al., 2026 ; D’Acunto et al., 2026 ) .

A related strand of work appears in multi-agent world modelling.
Embodied agents may maintain private and evolving internal descriptions of their environment, communicate selectively, and reason about what other agents know.
Recent work has explicitly investigated the suitability of dialogues as a mechanism for aligning such private world models under partial observability ( Dongre and Hakkani-Tür, 2026 ) .
These approaches are particularly relevant because they hypothesise that representational disagreement is no longer merely a mismatch grounded in geometric, dynamical, or symbolic information.
On the contrary, it can involve different observation modalities, beliefs, semantic structures, and histories of interaction.

A second set of antecedents concerns sufficiency rather than global alignment.
Decentralized stochastic control has long studied how agents with asymmetric information can act optimally from limited private and common information.
The common-information approach reformulates certain decentralized problems through information shared by the controllers ( Nayyar et al., 2013 ) , while the sufficient-information approach explicitly seeks mutually consistent
compressions that preserve decision quality ( Tavafoghi et al., 2018 ) .
These results are close in principle to our work because they show that decision making need not necessarily retain all available information.
Their starting point, however, is a common stochastic decision model coupled with agent-specific information structures.
Our object of study is different, in that we ask which task-relevant discrepancies between heterogeneous observer-relative representations must become distinguishable at all.

Related ideas appear in state abstraction and representation learning for decision making.
Bisimulation-based abstractions and approximate state abstractions identify states that can be merged without materially changing optimal behaviour ( Ferns et al., 2004 ; Abel et al., 2016 ) .
Learned latent-state models make a similar distinction between high-dimensional observations and compact representations sufficient for reward prediction and dynamics ( Gelada et al., 2019 ) .
These works establish that task-relevant quotienting , that is, collapsing distinctions that do not matter for decision making, is not itself new.
In our work, the quotient is instead defined over a joint relational configuration assembled from representations that may originate in different observers, times, or representational spaces.

A particularly important related field of inquiry is functional observability.
Functional observers seek to reconstruct only a target function or a subset of a system state when reconstructing the complete state is unnecessary ( Montanari et al., 2022a ; Montanari et al., 2022b ) .
Recent work also studies minimum sensor placement for functional observability ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
The distinction pursued in this work with respect to this literature is that the unobservable object is not simply a part of a single underlying state.
Instead, it is a degree of freedom in the relation among heterogeneous representations, and the additional measurements are constrained to arise as admissible sensorimotor anchors.

Finally, goal- and task-oriented communication explicitly prioritizes the information that matters to shared objectives rather than maximizing message fidelity ( Charalambous et al., 2026 ) .
Also in this case, our question is adjacent but not identical.
We do not optimize what agents communicate.
We characterize which inter-agent ambiguities must be eliminated, regardless of whether the relevant evidence is obtained through communication, sensing, or physical interaction.

In a general sense, the present work starts from these developments but poses a different question.
We do not investigate how heterogeneous representations maintained by different observer agents can always be made globally consistent, nor do we propose another mechanism for mapping them into a common latent space.
Instead, we ask whether representational consistency should itself be treated as a task-dependent requirement.

This distinction is relevant because an embodied agent does not acquire, maintain, or use a representation in isolation.
Representations participate in sensorimotor loops.
Observations are conditioned by the agent’s embodiment and sensing capabilities;
internal representations support action;
actions modify the subsequent interaction with the environment;
the environment produces new observations and constraints.
Classical active-perception accounts already emphasize that perception is inseparable from the actions through which information is acquired ( Bajcsy, 1988 ) .
More recent embodiment-oriented accounts of cognition similarly stress that predictive internal models acquire their meaning through their role in
closed-loop sensorimotor interaction ( Pezzulo et al., 2024 ) .

Therefore, we deliberately adopt a relational perspective.
Two embodied observer agents may maintain different internal representations and may even remain globally incompatible, while still possessing enough relational structure to interact successfully.
We posit that what matters is not necessarily whether their representations can be fully reconciled, but whether the distinctions that remain unresolved can alter the interaction.

This leads to three levels that we keep separate throughout the paper.
First, agreement describes a relation between already comparable representational quantities, such as whether two estimates differ by less than
a specified tolerance.
Second, epistemic congruity refers more generally to whether the available relational evidence satisfies the constraints relevant to a particular interaction.
Third, interaction adequacy concerns the physical or operational outcome generated when those representations are used for action.
Agreement can contribute to congruity, and congruity can contribute to successful interaction, but none of these notions is identified with the others.
This separation also distinguishes the problem we address from approaches whose goal is to maximize alignment.
A residual disagreement may be harmless if the task is invariant to it.
Conversely, even perfect agreement may be insufficient if both agents share an error along a factor that matters to the interaction.
The theoretical problem is therefore not to minimize representational discrepancy indiscriminately, but to determine which relational ambiguities are consequential.

## 2.2 An example scenario

Its purpose at this stage is not to establish any result, but to make the distinction between agreement, relational sufficiency, and physical adequacy concrete.

Thus R A ∈ ℛ A R_{A}\in\mathcal{R}_{A} and R B ∈ ℛ B R_{B}\in\mathcal{R}_{B} , with no requirement that ℛ A = ℛ B \mathcal{R}_{A}=\mathcal{R}_{B} .

The contrast between S1-R and S1-A is deliberately minimal.
The physical process, observer agents, sensing models, native representations, representational transports, and pairwise evidence can remain identical.
Only the invariance structure of the interaction changes.

This pair of scenarios isolates the central theoretical issue of the paper: Does the ambiguity left unresolved by relational evidence contain distinctions that the interaction can detect? If the answer is negative, further representational alignment is unnecessary.
Otherwise, some additional relation to the environment must remove the interaction-relevant part of that ambiguity.

2026-10-05.title: From Language Priors to Field Adaptation: Preference Learning for Traversability Estimation
2026-10-05.authors: Simon Schwaiger , David Seyser , Alessandro Scherl , Zlatan Ajanović , Wilfried Wöber , Gerald Steinbauer-Wagner
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-05.abstract:
Image-based traversability estimation is inherently dependent on the robot platform, deployment domain, and mission preferences, which limits the applicability of purpose-trained models.
To facilitate domain adaptation, this work aims to reduce the number of required annotations in the target domain using sample-efficient preference learning.
Our method represents traversability through von Mises-Fisher mixture prototypes in a frozen vision-language feature space.
Relative natural-language rules provide a commonsense prior, while sparse relative image annotations adapt the prototype directions and utilities to a target domain through computationally and sample-efficient fine-tuning.
Experiments on WayFAST demonstrate accuracy competitive with end-to-end trained estimators while enabling sample-efficient image-based adaptation.
Qualitative experiments further demonstrate the language prior’s zero shot applicability and the fine-tuned estimator’s improved dense prediction on semantic maps.
Evaluation is complemented via semantic interpretation of learned prototypes by dissecting semantically close natural language prompts.
Code and trained estimators available at https://resireg.github.io .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Image-based traversability estimation (TE) is important for autonomous outdoor navigation since it incorporates semantic differences between surfaces that might be geometrically similar but have different traversability properties.
However, TE is challenging due to the lack of platform- and domain-agnostic ground truth data.
Furthermore, the same terrain may have different traversability costs for different robots and application domains [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Existing methods have tackled TE by i) learning physical capability from robot-specific field experience [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , ii) learning from absolute or relative human supervision [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , and iii) using language and foundation models as broad priors [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 2 ] .
However, these methods either require i) physical robot experience, limiting zero-shot domain-adaptation, ii) platform-specific annotations, or iii) expensive computational power to provide semantically broad predictions, not suitable for targeted domain adaptation from experience.

We hypothesise that traversability does not need to be relearned from scratch as a dense visual prediction problem for each domain transfer.
We leverage terrain structure encoded in a frozen vision language model (VLM) [ 19 ] .
The VLM feature space, aligned across frozen image and language encoders, is reused across application domains.
This allows our method to be used zero-shot on out-of-distribution domains using a generic language prior, while enabling subsequent fine-tuning on image-based field data.
Instead of training a prediction head on top of a frozen foundation model, our method models traversability using von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture [ 20 ] responsibilities over a set of prototypes with learned utility in vision-language feature space.
These prototypes are learned from relative annotations, both in language and vision, allowing a platform-agnostic language prior to bootstrap image-based fine-tuning.

Our method (see Fig. 1 ) is competitive in terms of prediction accuracy with end-to-end trained models [ 11 ] , given the same amount of annotations, while offering language-based initialisation and sample-efficient learning from human annotations.
To this end, we combine the principle of visual prototypes in robotics [ 21 ] with recent VLM-based architectures [ 19 ] , and extend this architecture with alternative mixture modes to extend the state of the art and outperform alternative approaches.
To our knowledge, this combination of language-based prior and sample-efficient adaptation has not previously been demonstrated for traversability estimation.
The sole reliance on relative labels also allows us to incorporate new information sources, such as human-in-the-loop, self-labelling, or large language model (LLM) and large vision language model (LVLM)-generated relative image labels [ 22 ] .
Our experiments evaluate zero-shot and data-efficient adaptation, competitive fine-tuning accuracy, as well as downstream language-alignment of learned prototypes.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Background

For mobile robots, TE provides terrain-dependent cost information for path and motion planning.
Estimated traversability cost can differ for surfaces that are of identical geometry, for different robotic embodiments, and across application domains with different risk tolerances [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Traversability is thus a function of terrain, platform, and mission, and no single label can be correct for every robot or every task.
Therefore, even though multiple regimes have been established to collect traversability data, no TE training data source can be used as ground truth across domains.

Traversability Annotations. Three main annotation types for TE have been established in literature.
First, self-supervised labels are generated through robot experience, either as proprioceptive signals such as velocity-tracking error, torque, slip, and collisions [ 6 , 4 , 10 , 7 , 8 ] or as hindsight labels that mark successfully traversed terrain as traversable and leave the rest unlabeled [ 5 , 9 ] .
Secondly, an alternative source is human-generated labels, either as absolute labels (classes, scores) [ 10 , 14 , 13 , 15 ] or as relative labels for different image regions [ 11 , 12 ] .
Finally, the most recent option is to generate labels using large language models (LLMs), which either generate cost labels [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] or select navigation goals [ 22 ] .

Within these regimes, relative annotations have the advantage of being retrievable from absolute supervision signals.
Furthermore, the scale of absolute labels is tied to the platform they were estimated on, whereas ordering is invariant to the arbitrary numerical scaling of traversability. Therefore, relative labels offer increased flexibility for downstream estimator training w.r.t. training data for supervision.
However, this flexibility comes at the cost of information: an ordering says which region is easier, not by how much, which makes it harder to learn from, especially if the annotations are sparse.
Existing TE methods balance this trade-off either with end-to-end training, which reaches high accuracy at the cost of many labels [ 11 ] , or with few-shot adaptation on frozen features, which needs few labels but reaches lower accuracy [ 12 ] .
This accuracy-adaptability trade-off is further complicated by both regimes’ inability to initialise from generic open-world knowledge, e.g., provided by LLMs.
This is detrimental to open-world robots exploring environments whose conditions constantly change.
These robots simultaneously require short onboarding time as well as the ability to adapt to domain-specific TE preferences.

Preference Learning. Preference learning [ 23 ] , whose goal is to learn from relative feedback in evaluative space, uniquely fits TE due to the absence of objective traversability scale.
A scalar score s ⁡ ( x ) s(x) is assigned to each item, and pairs are supervised only through their difference Δ = s ⁡ ( x B ) − s ⁡ ( x A ) \Delta=s(x_{B})-s(x_{A}) with the goal of matching teacher preferences.
This is consistent with existing relative supervision in TE, where a ranking loss pushes Δ \Delta past a margin in the labelled direction and toward zero for ties [ 11 ] .
We therefore introduce a preference learning method that builds upon this established training objective, while, contrary to the state of the art, simultaneously enabling initialisation from a commonsense natural language prior and sample-efficient fine-tuning to adapt to new domains.

2026-10-05.title: MixVLA: Adaptive Mixing of Non-Invariant Information for Generalizable Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-05.authors: Pingrui Zhang , Yu Zhang , Pengyuan Wu , Bin Wang , Haoming Song , Xianqiang Gao , ZhaxiZhuoma , Zhigang Wang , Dong Wang , Bin Zhao , Xuelong Li
2026-10-05.abstract: This supplementary material expands upon our main paper by providing additional theoretical analysis, implementation details, experimental results, and discussions to further support the proposed method MixVLA. ⊳ \triangleright Sec. A : We provide theoretical analyses of MixVLA, including the information-compression effect of IB, the statistical properties of adaptive mixing, and an illustrative regression analysis that characterizes when regularizing complementary information can improve OOD robustness. ⊳ \triangleright Sec. B : We provide additional implementation details, including model architectures, optimization settings, and training configurations. ⊳ \triangleright Sec. C : We report additional experiments and qualitative results, including ablations on mixing strategies, more visualizations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and real-world demonstration videos. ⊳ \triangleright Sec. D : We discuss the limitations of the current framework and outline several possible directions for future research.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2023 ) have advanced rapidly in recent years and are increasingly applied to robotic manipulation.
This trend has led to the emergence of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Brohan et al., 2022 ) that map multimodal observations and language instructions into low-level control actions.
Benefiting from rich cross-modal representations learned by VLMs, these models achieve competitive task success rates across both simulated ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) and real-world ( Walke et al., 2023 ) manipulation benchmarks.

Despite strong performance on in-distribution benchmarks, VLA models still struggle to achieve robust zero-shot generalization under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts ( Li et al., 2025a ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
Recent studies ( Fei et al., 2025b ) show that even mild variations in lighting, appearance, or camera viewpoint can cause substantial performance degradation.
Some prior works ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Team, 2025 ) attempt to improve robustness through large-scale and diverse data collection, but they incur substantial labor and financial costs.
Other approaches ( Abouzeid et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) enhance specific aspects of generalization by introducing model-specific modifications, which often limit their general applicability.
In this work, we instead focus on improving zero-shot generalization through a model-agnostic training strategy that does not rely on additional out-of-distribution data.
As illustrated in figure 1 , our key idea is to explicitly regularize the variability of non-invariant signals in the latent representation space.

To better understand this intuition, we analyze the problem from a representation learning perspective.
Policies trained with empirical risk minimization (ERM) ( Vapnik, 1999 ) tend to capture both task-relevant invariant correlations and environment-specific non-invariant signals.
While invariant features provide stable cues for action prediction, non-invariant factors such as lighting, texture, and viewpoint often contain both nuisance variations and complementary predictive information.
Under ERM training, directly relying on raw non-invariant features can introduce spurious dependencies under distribution shifts.
Conversely, enforcing strict invariance may be overly conservative, as it can discard informative signals that remain useful for action prediction.
This observation motivates explicitly regularizing the variability of non-invariant signals rather than relying on invariant features alone.

Building on the above insights, we propose MixVLA , a model-agnostic training framework that improves zero-shot generalization of Vision-Language-Action models, without modifying model architectures or requiring additional data.
The core of MixVLA is A daptive M ixing of Non- I nvariant Information ( AMI ).
Specifically, we first disentangle invariant and non-invariant representations using an information-theoretic objective.
We then perform stochastic mixing within the non-invariant feature space to regularize environment-specific variability while preserving complementary predictive cues.
The resulting mixed non-invariant representation is subsequently fused with invariant features for final action prediction, enabling a more favorable balance between robustness and policy expressiveness.
We evaluate MixVLA across a range of challenging manipulation settings, including the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks, the RoboTwin perturbation suite, and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.
The results show that MixVLA substantially improves the robustness of VLA policies under diverse observation shifts without requiring additional data collection.

Our key contributions are three-fold:

A model-agnostic framework for generalized VLA models. We present MixVLA , a model-agnostic training framework that improves the zero-shot generalization of Vision-Language-Action models under out-of-distribution (OOD) data without additional data collection or architectural redesign.

Adaptive mixing of non-invariant information (AMI). We propose AMI , which adaptively mixes non-invariant representations and fuses them with invariant features to improve robustness under distribution shifts.

Consistent zero-shot gains on challenging manipulation benchmarks. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MixVLA consistently improves zero-shot task success rates under diverse perturbations.

1. A model-agnostic framework for generalized VLA models. We present MixVLA , a model-agnostic training framework that improves the zero-shot generalization of Vision-Language-Action models under out-of-distribution (OOD) data without additional data collection or architectural redesign.

2. Adaptive mixing of non-invariant information (AMI). We propose AMI , which adaptively mixes non-invariant representations and fuses them with invariant features to improve robustness under distribution shifts.

3. Consistent zero-shot gains on challenging manipulation benchmarks. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MixVLA consistently improves zero-shot task success rates under diverse perturbations.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Model

Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models build upon large-scale Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ( Bai et al., 2023 ; Team and others, 2025 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ; Comanici et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) and are fine-tuned on diverse robot trajectory datasets to learn language-conditioned visuomotor policies ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Ebert et al., 2021 ; O’Neill et al., 2024 ) .
RT-1 and RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) demonstrate that scaling cross-modal pretraining together with large robot datasets can substantially improve manipulation performance and semantic grounding.
Following this paradigm, OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) discretizes robot actions into rarely used vocabulary tokens and performs autoregressive action generation on top of the Prismatic-7B backbone ( Karamcheti et al., 2024 ) .
The π 0 \pi_{0} family ( Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) further introduces a dual-system design that augments a VLM backbone with a dedicated action expert to jointly model high-level reasoning and low-level control.
Beyond architectural scaling, recent efforts explore richer spatial representations ( Zhen et al., 2024 ; Bhat et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) , intermediate supervision such as subtask decomposition and trajectory prediction ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , and post-training optimization via planning or reinforcement learning ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025d ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Fei et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2025 ) to enhance VLA capability.
Despite these advances in scaling and architectural design, improving robustness to observation variations in unseen environments remains an open challenge for VLA policies. This motivates our focus on enhancing the intrinsic generalization ability of VLA models through a model-agnostic training strategy.

## 2.2 Generalization in Robotic Manipulation

Recent work has explored multiple directions to improve generalization in robotic manipulation.
One common line of work ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Driess et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Zhaxizhuoma et al., 2025 ; Team, 2025 ) seeks to enhance robustness through large-scale and diverse data collection.
By expanding the coverage of training distributions, these approaches aim to improve policy generalization across varied environments.
However, such strategies often incur substantial human and financial costs, and the practical boundary of data-driven generalization for embodied models remains insufficiently understood ( Team, 2025 ) .
Complementary to data scaling, another line of research improves robustness by introducing additional architectural modules or auxiliary components.
For example, GeoAware-VLA ( Abouzeid et al., 2025 ) incorporates VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) to improve robustness to camera viewpoint changes.
AffordDP ( Wu et al., 2025 ) enhances cross-scene manipulation through affordance retrieval and transfer, while 3DS-VLA ( Li et al., 2025b ) improves robustness to appearance and viewpoint variations by introducing a 3D point cloud perception module.
While these designs can improve robustness under specific perturbations, they often introduce additional system complexity and may not generalize well to diverse out-of-distribution scenarios, where realistic shifts are typically multifaceted rather than isolated.
A separate line of work ( Yang et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Seo et al., 2024 ; Ryu et al., 2023 ) seeks to improve policy generalization by learning robust visual representations or incorporating structured equivariant priors.
These approaches typically integrate mechanisms such as associative memory or geometric equivariance to maintain policy consistency under object-level transformations, including scaling, rotation, and translation.
However, such methods primarily focus on object-centric variations and do not explicitly address variability arising from environment-level nuisance factors, such as lighting changes, background appearance, or camera viewpoint shifts.

In contrast to these directions, our work improves VLA robustness through a model-agnostic training strategy that explicitly regularizes non-invariant environmental variability without requiring additional data or specialized architectural modules.

2026-10-05.title: SceneFactory-3D: Lifting 2D Traffic Scenes into 3D Physical Counterfactuals for Scalable Physically Grounded Safety Evaluation
2026-10-05.authors: Yicheng Zhu , Linfeng Tian , Tianmu Zhao , Yang Chen , Fan Zuo , Tao Li , Zilin Bian
2026-10-05.abstract: Scalable driving simulators typically execute vehicle commands using prescribed behavioral or kinematic rules, overlooking the physics of tire-road interfaces, thereby limiting their ability to capture how adverse road and environmental conditions alter vehicle execution and propagate through traffic. To address this limitation, we present SceneFactory-3D, a GPU-batched, physics-grounded multi-agent driving simulator. Vehicles execute acceleration and steering commands via suspension- and friction-limited forces evaluated at each wheel-contact point. Spatially varying friction, per-world 3D heightfields, gravity, and rigid contact consistently govern wheel motion and chassis collisions. Per-world terrain isolation and GPU batching enable SceneFactory-3D to run matched physical counterfactuals in parallel: traffic scenario setup and vehicle controllers remain fixed while only the road condition changes, enabling the resulting closed-loop effects to be evaluated across parallel worlds. To demonstrate the advantage of the SceneFactory-3D-enabled counterfactual evaluation, we conduct an empirical study on vehicle controllers’ sensitivity to road conditions. We study three learned-policy families on 1,024 matched 12-vehicle worlds per condition, and two classical planners on a shared 32-world subset, across 21 friction and grade conditions. When friction drops from 1.0 to 0.18, the share of vehicles that clear the work zone safely falls by 6 to 90 percentage points across learned policies (18–19 for classical planners), and near-collision situations become more frequent for every learned policy.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Traffic simulation makes large interactive experiments tractable by skipping some physics-grounded modeling. For example, a car-following law or a prescribed kinematic rule scales thousands of
vehicle interactions at low cost ( Lopez et al., 2018 ; Treiber et al., 2000 ; Gulino et al., 2023 ; Kazemkhani et al., 2025 ) . However, such rules also
fix how vehicle control execution responds to the physical environment: once a vehicle has decided to brake or
merge, the motion it realizes follows exactly the prescribed rule, which is detached from the underlying physics when the adverse road conditions affect vehicle control execution, resulting in a widening sim2real gap.

To motivate the integration of vehicle-environment interacting physics with driving and traffic simulations, consider a temporary
lane closure planned for winter in a city such as Rochester. Although the proposed merge path may remain geometrically feasible on a low-friction road, vehicles’ ability to follow that path, e.g., to brake safely for one another, depends on the physical conditions at the tire–road interface. If one vehicle cannot complete the merge as intended, it may alter the behavior and trajectory of every vehicle behind it, potentially changing the traffic outcome. A credible evaluation, whether for self-driving testing or traffic management and planning, must therefore capture how the same scenario and controllers perform under different road conditions. Without this physical modeling, the simulation may substantially overestimate safety and traffic efficiency when adverse conditions affect vehicle dynamics.

While existing work accounts for physical friction in 2D planar driving simulations, comprehensive physics-grounded vehicle–environment interactions go beyond what these two-dimensional models can faithfully represent. Planar single-track models can enforce friction limits through tire-force constraints and friction-circle checks ( Althoff et al., 2017 ; CommonRoad, n.d. ) , but they do not explicitly capture how three-dimensional road geometry and gravity affect wheel-level contact. Road grade, banking, and elevation change the normal force at each wheel and, consequently, the friction available to the vehicle. These effects become especially important when friction varies across the wheels of a vehicle or between lanes across diverse terrains.

To support efficient and scalable simulation of many interacting vehicles across parallel 3D worlds with underlying physics, we present SceneFactory-3D, a GPU-batched simulator that extends SceneFactory ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , a GPU-vectorized Isaac Lab platform
whose articulated vehicles drive on flat roads with only a planar friction mechanism. SceneFactory-3D replaces the default vehicle model with a custom tire-force model evaluated at each wheel–road contact. It supports spatially varying friction patches and a separate terrain heightfield for each parallel world. Wheel-contact queries, terrain preview, and chassis collisions all reference the same heightfield, ensuring a consistent representation of the physical environment. Finally, a canonical-route interface provides classical and learned controllers with the same geometric route reference.

As a physics-grounded and GPU-batched 3D platform, SceneFactory-3D makes matched physical environment counterfactuals practical at scale. From the same traffic scene, initial state, routes, and controller population, it instantiates parallel counterfactual worlds that differ only in their physical road conditions. This design makes three factors directly controllable: where a physical condition occurs relative to a planned maneuver, whether the controller observes that condition, and how its effect on one vehicle propagates through interacting traffic. We demonstrate this capability using route-conditioned policies trained with PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . We compare a policy trained on nominal roads with two continued-training variants exposed to diverse terrain as well as two classical planners, across 21 physical conditions. Although terrain randomization and privileged physical context are established techniques ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Kumar et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2017 ) , SceneFactory-3D enables their separation and evaluation via matched counterfactual worlds. Across 1,024 matched worlds per learned policy and condition, reduced friction degraded task completion for every controller, propagated to vehicles traveling in the unchanged lane, and was not anticipated by the preview-enabled policy. The magnitude of these effects varied more across training seeds than across training regimes, while the tested grades affected only a few policies.

In summary, our contributions are as follows. Section 2 highlights our unique contributions by comparing SceneFactory-3D with prior efforts on driving simulation, co-simulation frameworks, and learning-based driving and vehicle controls using simulations.

SceneFactory-3D: a GPU-batched physics-grounded multi-agent driving simulator where Per-wheel forces and rigid contact couple vehicle motion to spatially varying friction and 3D terrain. Per-world terrain ownership keeps wheel queries, observations, and collisions physically consistent.

A matched physical-counterfactual evaluation framework. SceneFactory-3D creates matched counterfactual worlds that differ only in road conditions and 2D-to-3D geometry differences, enabling controlled comparisons across classical and learned vehicle controllers in terms of physical behaviors and safety risks.

An empirical study of vehicle controller sensitivity to road physics . Across 21 friction and grade conditions, we evaluate two classical planners and three learned-policy families that separate terrain-diverse training from explicit terrain preview. When friction drops from 1.0 to 0.18, the share of vehicles that clear the work zone safely falls by 6 to 90 percentage points across learned policies (18–19 for classical planners), and near-collision situations become more frequent for every learned policy.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Traffic and driving simulators differ less in whether they recognize road
conditions than in which transition law executes a vehicle’s commands.
Microscopic traffic simulators such as SUMO move vehicles with behavioral models
of car-following and lane changing ( Lopez et al., 2018 ) ; the original Intelligent Driver
Model study represents road inhomogeneities such as uphill gradients through
modified driver parameters ( Treiber et al., 2000 ) . Accelerator-based simulators extend this
trade to learning at scale: Waymax advances agents with kinematic bicycle or
position-delta dynamics, and GPUDrive by default with a kinematic bicycle model,
over compact state ( Gulino et al., 2023 ; Kazemkhani et al., 2025 ) ; neither has tire forces or a friction
limit. Planar dynamic models occupy the middle ground. CommonRoad provides
point-mass, kinematic and dynamic single-track and multi-body vehicle models, and
checks trajectories against a friction circle ( Althoff et al., 2017 ; CommonRoad, n.d. ) .
Every simulator takes friction as an input; the relevant distinction is between
prescribing a behavioral response to the road and computing execution through an
explicit force and contact model.

Driving environments built on physics engines compute execution in this way,
with different arrangements of the surrounding traffic. CARLA simulates vehicles
in a game-engine physics model with localized friction triggers and an optional
hybrid mode, off by default, that teleports distant background
vehicles ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; CARLA, n.d.a ; CARLA, n.d.b ) ; SUMMIT extends it with a
velocity-space model of massive mixed traffic ( Cai et al., 2020 ) ; SMARTS combines
Bullet-simulated vehicles of interest with SUMO background traffic ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) ;
and MetaDrive composes diverse scenarios on a physics simulator ( Li et al., 2023b ) .
Chrono::Vehicle offers detailed subsystems, several tire models and deformable
terrain ( Project Chrono Development Team, n.d. ; Tasora et al., 2016 ) , and SynChrono distributes interacting agents across
compute nodes ( Project Chrono, n.d. ) , an architecture different from batching many
worlds in one accelerator process. Figure 1 A and
Appendix A compare the capabilities we could verify.

Several recent systems are closer to our motivation. SceneFactory batches
articulated PhysX vehicles on flattened roads converted from the Waymo Open
Motion Dataset, maps weather to one friction coefficient per world, and compares
policies with and without a weather-context input ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) ; its own
limitations name flat geometry and spatially uniform friction. Its two policies
differed both in wet-road training exposure and in the context input, whereas
our learned arms separate these factors. SceneFactory-3D
inherits its GPU-batched, Isaac Lab-based design and replaces the vehicle, road
and evaluation layers (Appendix Table 3 ). μ \mu Sync-GS couples friction and road-elevation edits to the response of a
single ego vehicle, modeled as a half-car with a Burckhardt tire curve, to
synthesize consistent driving video ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ; it involves no traffic
interaction, and SceneFactory-3D shares neither its vehicle model nor its rendering.
MultiDrive co-simulates CommonRoad scenarios in the BeamNG.tech simulator and
reports discrepancies between a motion planner’s intended and executed
behavior ( Kaufeld et al., 2025 ) . Converting scenarios between simulators, executing
them with richer physics, and comparing intended with realized motion are thus
established. ScenarioNet likewise converts real-world driving logs into
interactive simulation scenarios ( Li et al., 2023a ) . Our emphasis is a batched
workflow in which physical interventions are authored, matched and repeated
across many interacting vehicles and learned controllers.

On the learning side, training under randomized dynamics ( Peng et al., 2018 ) and
conditioning a policy on physical parameters, either given or
inferred ( Yu et al., 2017 ; Kumar et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2023c ) , are established tools; contextual reinforcement
learning formalizes when such context must be observed ( Benjamins et al., 2023 ; Martinez et al., 2026 ) . Friction
preview has also been used explicitly in model-predictive trajectory
tracking ( Gao et al., 2022 ) . Our terrain-trained arm without preview corresponds to
randomization with latent context, and our preview arm to privileged explicit
context, both for a feed-forward policy. What the simulator adds is control over
the spatial placement of the physical context, over the interacting population
that experiences it, and over matched execution of the same scenario. Closed-loop
planning benchmarks such as nuPlan evaluate a planner by the traffic outcomes its
decisions produce ( Caesar et al., 2021 ) ; our experiments hold the scenario and controller
population fixed while the physical world changes.

2026-10-05.title: Permutation Robustness Is Not Enough: Action Collapse in Multi-Agent Transformer Policies
2026-10-05.authors: Amit Thakur , Mukesh Singhal
2026-10-05.abstract: Transformer policies are attractive for multi-agent robot learning because self-attention can model interactions among agents. However, multi-agent teams are unordered, while transformers typically process agents as ordered token sequences. We study how this mismatch affects cooperative navigation policies under agent-order permutations. Our results show that low permutation error alone can be misleading: policies may appear robust simply because all agents choose the same action. We therefore evaluate policies using both permutation-consistency metrics and action-collapse diagnostics, including action diversity, same-action fraction, and maximum action frequency. A PPO-ID baseline yields non-collapsed behavior but remains order-sensitive, while strong equivariance regularization can still induce homogeneous behavior. A weak equivariance penalty improves the robustness while preserving more diverse actions for teams with N = 3 N=3 agents, whereas teams with N = 4 N=4 agents require substantially smaller regularization weights. These findings suggest that multi-agent transformer policies should be evaluated not only by return and permutation robustness, but also by whether they maintain non-collapsed, differentiated multi-agent behavior.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Multi-robot systems are naturally composed of exchangeable entities. A team of ground robots, drones, or manipulation agents should not fail because the observations of two robots are listed in a different order. Yet transformer policies, now common as interaction models, operate on ordered token sequences [ 18 ] . A typical multi-agent transformer forms tokens

Practical policies often add learned agent identity or sequence-position embeddings to the tokens. Such embeddings can improve nominal performance because agents may specialize, but they can also create an ordering shortcut: the policy attaches behavior to token slots rather than to physical context. This is problematic because robot ordering may change due to communication, batching, logging, dynamic team membership, or a deployment interface.

In this paper, we address the following question: do transformer-based multi-agent policies learn coordination or agent ordering? A natural test is to measure Eq. ( 2 ). However, our experiments reveal that low equivariance error can be misleading. A policy can satisfy permutation tests almost perfectly by outputting the same action for every agent. Such a policy can appear permutation-consistent for the wrong reason: not because it coordinates robustly, but because all agents behave nearly identically. We therefore evaluate task return, permutation consistency, and non-collapsed action behavior jointly.

Our contributions are as follows. (i) We formalize permutation sensitivity for transformer-based multi-agent policies with logit, policy-distribution, action, and return metrics. (ii) We introduce action-collapse diagnostics, including normalized action diversity, same-action fraction, and maximum action frequency. (iii) We show empirically that PPO-style training [ 13 , 19 ] produces a strong non-collapsed baseline, but equivariance regularization still creates a measurable robustness-diversity tradeoff. (iv) We add a four-agent stress test showing that useful regularization strength is team-size dependent.

The practical message is deliberately conservative: a low permutation error should not be interpreted in isolation. A good multi-agent policy should satisfy three requirements simultaneously. It should solve the task, remain stable under benign relabelings of the same physical team, and avoid degenerate homogeneous behavior. The experiments below are organized around these three requirements.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Cooperative MARL studies how a team of agents can optimize a shared objective under coupled dynamics and partial observations [ 14 , 16 ] . Centralized-training methods such as MADDPG [ 8 ] , COMA [ 4 ] , VDN [ 15 ] , and QMIX [ 11 ] address credit assignment and coordination by using centralized information during learning. PPO-based multi-agent training has also emerged as a strong practical baseline in cooperative games [ 19 ] . Our work uses this PPO/MAPPO-style training regime, but focuses on a different question: whether a transformer policy’s representation of agents is stable to arbitrary ordering.

Transformers [ 18 , 3 ] process inputs as token sequences. Without position-dependent information, self-attention is permutation-equivariant over tokens; learned position or agent-ID embeddings generally break that property. Set architectures such as Deep Sets [ 20 ] and Set Transformer [ 7 ] explicitly enforce permutation symmetry, and geometric deep learning emphasizes matching neural architectures to the symmetries of the domain [ 2 ] . Robot teams have a natural exchangeability symmetry: changing the list order of identical agents should not change the physical command assigned to each robot.

Attention has been used for communication, critic design, and interaction modeling in MARL [ 6 , 5 ] . Emergent cooperative behavior and role differentiation have also been studied in multi-agent populations [ 10 , 1 , 9 ] . These works motivate attention as a useful inductive bias for interaction, but most evaluations emphasize return. Our results show that return can hide order sensitivity, while equivariance error can hide same-action collapse. The proposed diagnostics are meant to complement rather than replace standard task performance.

The core methodological point of this paper is that robustness metrics can be gamed by degenerate policies. In our setting, a policy that emits the same logits for every agent is perfectly permutation-consistent, yet it may not represent meaningful coordination. This failure mode is analogous to shortcut solutions in representation learning: the metric is optimized, but the intended behavior is not obtained. We therefore evaluate distributional consistency, executed-action consistency, and action diversity together.

2026-10-05.title: PointWAM: 3D World Action Modeling for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Chunghyun Park , Beomjun Kim , Seungcheol Park , Heeseung Kwon , Yashu Shukla , Seunghoon Sim , Jinwoo Shin , Minsu Cho
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-05.comment: Preprint. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
World action models jointly learn to forecast world dynamics and predict robot actions, such that the learned internal world dynamics guide accurate actions.
Existing approaches typically represent the world as RGB frames or latent counterparts while predicting actions as end-effector poses or joint angles, but they often struggle to capture the 3D spatial structure and contact geometry central to dexterous manipulation.
We introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene ( i.e. , environment) and hands ( i.e. , actor), and jointly forecasts both as 3D point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame.
This explicit, disentangled representation enables effective pre-training on large-scale human demonstration videos without requiring any task-specific object or keypoint selection.
Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, PointWAM predicts how the scene and hands co-evolve in 3D space over time, then retargets the forecast hand motion to robot actions.
Pre-training on human videos improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points, and scene-trajectory supervision adds 10.9 points over forecasting the hands alone.
With both, PointWAM surpasses the prior state of the art on ten DexJoCo tasks by 11.7 points and outperforms strong VLAs on a real robot.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Dexterous robotic manipulation requires multiple fingers to precisely coordinate their 3D motion relative to object surfaces ( Salisbury & Craig, 1982 ; Okamura et al., 2000 ) , enabling robots to perform a wide range of tasks from grasping objects of varied shapes to tool use ( Bicchi, 2000 ; An et al., 2026 ) . Conventional Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) ( Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) map observations to motor commands without explicitly forecasting how the scene evolves. World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative by treating world and action modeling as deeply intertwined: they jointly learn to forecast how the world will change and what actions cause those changes ( Li et al., 2025a ) .

Many existing WAMs build on video generation backbones and represent the world as RGB frames ( Du et al., 2023 ) or their latent counterparts ( Li et al., 2025a ; Liao et al., 2026 ) . These representations are limited in their ability to capture key aspects of physical interaction, including 3D spatial structure and causal relations between the actor and the environment. Point-based policies ( Haldar & Pinto, 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026a ) address the 3D action prediction problem by forecasting trajectories of 3D points, but do not model how the environment evolves. They also rely on humans or external perception models to select task-relevant objects for their scene inputs. Conversely, action-conditioned 3D world models forecast dense 3D scene trajectories, yet treat robot actions as inputs rather than quantities to be predicted ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .

In this work, we introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene ( i.e. , environment) and hands ( i.e. , actor), and represents both as three-dimensional point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame (Fig. 1 ). This explicit, disentangled world representation enables effective learning of cause-and-effect relations between the environment and the actor by modeling how their points co-evolve in 3D space over time. Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, PointWAM forecasts trajectories for every observed scene point and hand keypoint in a common coordinate frame. Its action retargeter then converts the forecast hand trajectories into the corresponding robot actions.

The proposed approach offers three additional advantages. First, modeling both the scene and hands in a shared 3D space enables effective pre-training on human demonstration videos from EgoDex ( Hoque et al., 2026 ) and VITRA ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Second, no task-specific objects or scene keypoints need to be selected in advance, so scene forecasting is not restricted to a predefined set of target objects. Third, by decoupling hand-point trajectories from the scene, the forecast hand motion is amenable to effective retargeting onto robot hands for action prediction.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows.

We introduce PointWAM, which jointly forecasts the 3D trajectories of scene points and hand keypoints in a shared space-time coordinate frame, unifying world and action modeling.

We demonstrate that 3D world modeling benefits dexterous manipulation. Scene-trajectory supervision improves average DexJoCo success by 10.9 percentage points over the same model without it, and our 3D encoder outperforms lifted image features by 5.4 percentage points.

We show that pre-training on human demonstrations from EgoDex and VITRA improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points over training from scratch. With this pre-training, PointWAM surpasses the prior best multi-task success rate on DexJoCo by 11.7 percentage points and outperforms robot-pre-trained VLAs on a real robot by up to 25 percentage points.

1. We introduce PointWAM, which jointly forecasts the 3D trajectories of scene points and hand keypoints in a shared space-time coordinate frame, unifying world and action modeling.

2. We demonstrate that 3D world modeling benefits dexterous manipulation. Scene-trajectory supervision improves average DexJoCo success by 10.9 percentage points over the same model without it, and our 3D encoder outperforms lifted image features by 5.4 percentage points.

3. We show that pre-training on human demonstrations from EgoDex and VITRA improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points over training from scratch. With this pre-training, PointWAM surpasses the prior best multi-task success rate on DexJoCo by 11.7 percentage points and outperforms robot-pre-trained VLAs on a real robot by up to 25 percentage points.

# 2 Related Work

We discuss the closest work here and provide a broader review in Appendix A .

WAMs unify predictive world modeling with action prediction; unlike conventional VLAs, which map a visual observation straight to a motor command, a WAM is trained to forecast how the world will change and predict what actions the robot must perform ( Du et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026d ; Li et al., 2025a ) . Existing WAMs
typically forecast future visual representations in the latent space of pretrained video models
while predicting robot actions as end-effector poses.
These models must therefore learn how changes in latent visual features correspond to robot
motion, rather than explicitly modeling both scene and hand motion as 3D trajectories. Closest to ours,
EgoWAM ( Li et al., 2026a ) , PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and PointZero ( Duisterhof et al., 2026 ) forecast dense 3D scene motion.
EgoWAM jointly learns scene forecasting and action prediction but maps human hand motion to the
actions of parallel-jaw grippers, a 6-DoF pose and a gripper state per hand, which lacks
individual finger motions. Pri4R ( Kim et al., 2026c ) likewise
targets grippers, adding a training-only 3D point-trajectory head to a VLA fine-tuned on robot
demonstrations. PointWorld forecasts scene motion with a
3D point-cloud network ( Wu et al., 2024 ) conditioned on future robot trajectories, so it needs a
separate planner that selects them with a task cost. PointZero pre-trains a similar
world model without robot data and, like PointWorld, predicts no actions. PointWAM instead pre-trains on human demonstration videos for dexterous
hands, jointly forecasts scene and hand trajectories in a shared space-time coordinate frame, and
retargets the hand trajectories to robot actions without a separate planner.

Human demonstration videos show hand and scene motion from which trajectory supervision can be
extracted without recorded robot actions. Point-based policies can learn to forecast hand keypoint
trajectories from these videos and retarget the forecasts to robot actions. Point
Policy ( Haldar & Pinto, 2025 ) and Dexterous Point Policy ( Kim et al., 2026a ) , however, rely
on humans or external perception models to select the objects in the policy’s scene input, object
keypoints specified by a human for Point Policy and object point clouds segmented by external models
for Dexterous Point Policy. Neither performs explicit world modeling through scene-motion
forecasting. 3PoinTr ( Hung et al., 2026 ) does forecast dense 3D scene trajectories from human
demonstration videos. Extracted
video tracks supervise its forecasts, and a separate policy trained on robot demonstrations predicts
actions from the forecast tracks. PointWAM instead forecasts trajectories for every observed scene
point and hand keypoint with one backbone, and a retargeter converts the hand trajectories into
robot actions without a separate policy.

2026-10-05.title: FastOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Lightweight VLA Deployment
2026-10-05.authors: Yoojin Oh , Jeongsol Kim , Yeonwoo Seo , Jangho Park , Seonghyun Jin , Sunwoo Park , Youngmin Kim , Youngjun Jun , Kyumin Choi , Jong Chul Ye
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-05.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging.
Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies.
In this work, we propose FastOPD , a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation.
Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics.
Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model.
We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments.
On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84% of the performance of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1% while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Recent progress in robot learning has moved toward large-scale foundation policies, ranging from Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Collaboration, 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026a ) to emerging World Action Models (WAMs) ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . In particular, recent methods such as DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026 ) and Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) leverage pretrained video generation models to capture rich visual dynamics and achieve strong generalization and manipulation performance.
However, these powerful foundation priors also lead to increasingly large policy backbones and high computational cost, creating a tension between model capability and deployment efficiency on physical robots.
Lightweight VLA models such as SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) address the efficiency side of this trade-off by directly designing smaller policies with less than 0.5B parameters.

A complementary direction is to transfer the capability of a powerful foundation policy into a compact student through knowledge distillation.
Knowledge Distillation (KD) ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Mansourian et al., 2025 ) has been widely studied for transferring the capability of a large teacher model into a smaller student. Specifically, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) supervises the student using teacher predictions on its own generated trajectories, reducing distribution mismatch and compounding errors from offline distillation. OPD also provides dense supervision along the student trajectory, in contrast to the sparse rewards commonly used in reinforcement learning. While OPD has been actively explored in LLM post-training, recent works have extended it to diffusion and flow models ( Li et al., 2026a ; Fang et al., 2026b ) .
However, directly applying OPD to flow-based policies is computationally inefficient. It requires rolling out the student’s denoising trajectory and repeatedly evaluating the teacher at the visited timesteps, resulting in high training cost for large foundation teachers.

In this work, we revisit few-step flow-map models through the lens of
on-policy distillation (OPD) and introduce FastOPD , a
foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework for efficient policy distillation.
Our goal is to transfer the capabilities of a large-scale VLA into a
compact student while substantially reducing both training and inference
costs, without sacrificing policy performance
(see Fig. 1 ).
To reduce the training cost of conventional OPD, FastOPD combines
on-policy teacher supervision of the student’s velocity field with a
self-consistency objective ( Frans et al., 2025 ) .
Rather than querying teacher supervision throughout an entire
generation trajectory, the self-consistency objective propagates local
velocity supervision to finite-interval shortcut transitions, as
illustrated in Fig. 2 .
This allows the student to approximate the teacher dynamics without
explicitly constructing or evaluating a teacher flow map over each
shortcut transition.
We further show theoretically that FastOPD implicitly recovers the
distribution induced by the teacher’s ideal shortcut model, providing a
distributional justification for few-step distillation.

Importantly, the same self-consistency formulation naturally induces an
any-step flow map ( Boffi et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) ,
allowing the distilled student to operate with substantially fewer
sampling steps at inference.
FastOPD therefore compresses the foundation VLA along two complementary
dimensions: model capacity and sampling complexity, enabling deployment
on resource-constrained, consumer-grade hardware.
The proposed formulation also enables stable training in the challenging
few-step regime without adversarial objectives or costly higher-order
derivative computations.
A concurrent work, VLA-OPD ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) , also studies on-policy
distillation for VLA models, but primarily uses expert supervision to
improve policy performance.
In contrast, FastOPD focuses on transferring a foundation policy into a
lightweight few-step student.

We evaluate FastOPD on two simulation benchmarks and one real-world
manipulation task, using diverse foundation teachers with 3B–6B
parameters ( Black et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026a ) .
To maximize both architectural and inference efficiency, we adopt
SmolVLA as the lightweight student policy.
We compare against representative few-step distillation methods,
including CTM, DMD, and iMF.
Across these settings, FastOPD enables the compact student to recover up
to 84% of the performance of teacher models that are more than 7.3 × 7.3\times larger, using only one or two sampling steps.
This substantially reduces inference cost while retaining a large
fraction of the foundation policy’s performance.
To the best of our knowledge, FastOPD is the first OPD framework for
VLAs that jointly reduces both model size and the number of sampling
steps while retaining the capabilities of a large-scale foundation
policy.
