2026-10-05.title: Register-Routed Delayed Fusion: Rewiring Shortcut-Prone Observation Fusion in Visuomotor Imitation
2026-10-05.authors: Jieting Long , Weidong Cai , Weiming Zhi
2026-10-05.abstract: Visuomotor imitation policies combine high-dimensional visual observations with compact signals such as proprioception, and their fusion topology determines when and through which tokens these streams interact. In dense token fusion, visual tokens may attend directly to compact tokens from the first encoder layer, allowing action-predictive compact cues to influence spatial visual representations early in their formation. We ask whether controlling this route improves visual responsiveness and policy behavior. We introduce Register-Routed Delayed Fusion ( RRDF ), which masks direct compact–visual attention and stages cross-modal interaction through a learned register workspace. Its isolate–collect–route schedule protects an early stream-separated prefix and later permits only register-mediated exchange, while compact conditioning remains available to the native action generator. Across five simulation tasks and three real-robot tasks, RRDF matches or improves dense ACT under nominal conditions. Appearance-shift evaluations on four simulation tasks and held-out-position evaluations on three real-robot tasks also favor RRDF. Phase-matched input probes show lower measured state-to-image sensitivity, while ablations indicate that adding registers alone does not reproduce the full performance gain. These results support controlling cross-modal propagation while retaining compact action conditioning.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Visuomotor imitation policies predict future robot actions from heterogeneous observation histories, typically combining high-dimensional visual inputs with compact signals such as robot proprioception and policy-internal context. Recent work focused more on action generation, including action chunking [ 1 , 2 ] , diffusion [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , and flow matching [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . We examine how layer-wise observation-fusion routes affect visual representations and closed-loop policy behavior.

We study this fusion stage through its layer-wise communication topology. Under dense token fusion, spatial visual and compact tokens participate in unrestricted self-attention from the first encoder layer, creating a direct compact-to-visual route, 𝒞 → 𝒱 \mathcal{C}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{V} . Compact signals are often strongly correlated with task phase and future actions, so this one-hop route allows action-predictive compact cues to influence spatial visual representations from the beginning of encoder computation. More broadly, imitation policies are known to exploit nuisance signals correlated with expert actions, leading to causal confusion and brittle behavior under distribution shift [ 10 , 11 ] . Recent work further shows that proprioceptive signals can dominate vision–proprioception policies and suppress visual utilization [ 12 ] . We hypothesize that unrestricted early compact-to-visual attention can encourage overreliance on action-correlated compact cues at the expense of task-relevant visual evidence. Consistent with this hypothesis, our intervention analysis later reveals greater sensitivity to state relative to image interventions under dense fusion, at both the representation and action-output levels.

Our focus is therefore not whether compact conditioning should be available, but when and through which routes it enters spatial visual representations. Proprioceptive feedback provides useful control information and remains directly accessible to the action generator. We ask whether controlling early compact-to-visual propagation can improve policy behavior without removing this conditioning. To address this issue, we introduce Register-Routed Delayed Fusion ( RRDF , illustrated in Figure 2 ), which masks direct compact–visual attention throughout the fusion encoder and delays cross-modal influence on the primary streams through a learned register workspace. Its isolate–collect–route schedule protects an early stream-separated prefix, collects cross-modal context in registers, and later exposes it only through register-mediated paths. Compact conditioning remains directly available to the native action generator.

Across five simulation tasks, RRDF matches or improves the reported nominal performance of dense fusion. Appearance-shift tests and real-robot held-out-position evaluations also favor RRDF, with task-dependent gains. Figure 1 illustrates a representative difference in trajectory adaptation. We examine these results through phase-matched input-sensitivity probes and fusion-topology ablations.

Concretely, this paper makes the following contributions:

We introduce a source-partitioned isolate–collect–route schedule that blocks direct compact–visual attention, jointly collects information before primary-stream readback, and preserves compact action conditioning.

We evaluate nominal performance on five simulation and three real-robot tasks, appearance shifts on four simulation tasks, and held-out-position configurations on three real-robot tasks.

We characterize the permitted encoder dependencies, show that register capacity alone does not explain the gains, and reveal reduced state-to-image sensitivity through phase-matched probes.

1. We introduce a source-partitioned isolate–collect–route schedule that blocks direct compact–visual attention, jointly collects information before primary-stream readback, and preserves compact action conditioning.

2. We evaluate nominal performance on five simulation and three real-robot tasks, appearance shifts on four simulation tasks, and held-out-position configurations on three real-robot tasks.

3. We characterize the permitted encoder dependencies, show that register capacity alone does not explain the gains, and reveal reduced state-to-image sensitivity through phase-matched probes.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

Multimodal observation fusion in visuomotor policies. Visuomotor policies also differ in how heterogeneous observations are combined before action generation. Feature-level approaches , such as Diffusion Policy [ 3 ] , encode observations into a shared conditioning representation, whereas token-based fusions retain explicit modality tokens within a shared Transformer. ACT [ 1 ] , HPT [ 13 ] , and sensorimotor pre-training [ 14 ] process heterogeneous robot inputs in shared Transformer token spaces, while broader systems incorporate visual, linguistic, and additional sensory inputs [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Structured token fusions further constrain inter-group communication: Octo [ 19 ] employs blockwise attention over task, observation, and readout tokens. RRDF targets explicit token fusion and treats the layer-wise routes between separately addressable modality groups as an architectural design variable.

Shortcut learning and proprioceptive dominance. Behavioral cloning is susceptible to causal confusion , where features correlated with expert actions become predictive shortcuts that fail under distribution shift [ 10 , 20 ] , and to copycat effects , where strongly action-correlated history becomes an easier predictor than task-relevant observations [ 21 , 22 ] . More recently, shortcut learning has been identified as a limiting factor in large robot-policy generalization [ 23 ] . Closest to our motivation, Lu et al. [ 12 ] show that proprioception can dominate vision-proprioception learning and suppress visual utilization, degrading generalization. Existing remedies modify data or invariance objectives [ 10 , 20 ] , state or observation design [ 24 , 25 ] , regularization [ 11 ] , priming [ 26 ] , or optimization dynamics [ 12 ] . Complementary work studies visual representation learning and pretraining [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] . Recent VLA studies [ 31 ] examine state representation, history length, and injection location; RRDF retains compact action conditioning while controlling layer-wise communication within the observation encoder.

Register and bottleneck tokens. Learned latent tokens provide compact computational interfaces in Transformers. Perceiver [ 32 ] uses latent bottlenecks for general perception, while Perceiver-Actor [ 33 ] adapts this paradigm to robotic manipulation. Outside robotics, Multimodal Bottleneck Transformers constrain audio-visual fusion through shared bottleneck tokens and introduce fusion at a configurable depth [ 34 ] . InterACT [ 2 ] combines segment-wise encoding with cross-segment attention over CLS summaries while retaining original visual features at its output. ViT registers [ 35 ] provide learned computational slots for visual representation learning under unrestricted self-attention. RRDF uses a source-partitioned register workspace with an explicit read/write schedule. Source-specific accumulation without primary-stream readback is followed by joint collection and only then register-mediated feedback into the primary streams. Direct compact–visual attention remains masked throughout. This directed, depth-dependent schedule controls when information enters, mixes within, and leaves the workspace.

2026-10-05.title: Learning Reflexive Behavior for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Quan Nguyen , Yunho Kim , Joonho Lee
2026-10-05.abstract:
During contact-rich manipulation, interactions between a robot and its environment carry information about local geometry: a surface prevents penetration, a bore guides a peg. A controller that exploits these interactions can can comply with environmental constraints while preserving task intent.
Robot-learning systems commonly use position, hybrid force–position, or Cartesian impedance control. Their prescribed tracking objectives, stiffness, or force-control directions may not match local constraints and may degrade performance.
We learn a proprioceptive reflex policy in simulation on three simple interaction primitives: a spring, a plane, and a rail.
The policy maps task-space commands to joint-position targets using state history, without direct force or geometrical measurements.
Once trained, it serves as a frozen execution layer beneath higher-level controllers.
We evaluate it in dual-arm box lifting, peg insertion, and surface following.
In box lifting, the reflex kept the force below the threshold while the baseline failed. In rough-surface following it stayed below the 10 N reference, on par with tuned hybrid force-position control. In 0.02 mm peg insertion It reduced mean estimated contact force to less than half that of the baseline while increasing hardware success rates from at most 22 % to 36–58 %. By separating contact response from command generation, the reflex policy provides motion planners, learned policies, and teleoperators with robust contact-rich execution.
2026-10-05.introduction:
In contact-rich manipulation, environmental geometry shapes how a robot or its tools can move and provides guidance for completing a task. A surface supports sliding while restricting penetration, and a groove guides motion along a path. By maintaining contact while yielding in constrained directions, a robot can exploit this geometry to guide execution despite errors in perception, grasping, or nominal motion.

High-level commands from a motion planner, a learned policy, or a human operator may specify the intended behavior without matching the exact geometry of the current task instance [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
For example, a surface-search command is useful only if execution maintains contact while moving over the actual surface. Li and Brock [ 1 ] separate task structure from instance-specific geometry and recover the latter through interaction with environmental constraints. Compliant execution beneath high-level policies similarly supports adaptation to local contact [ 2 ] . These observations motivate an execution capability that makes environmental constraints useful to a broad range of command sources.

We present a method for training a proprioceptive reflex policy through RL ( RL ) using three primitive interaction scenarios shown in Fig. 1 (bottom).
The proposed a control hierarchy is shown in Fig. 1 C with high level controller supplies contact intent and nominal motion while the reflex policy adjusts joint-space targets using a history proprioceptive measurements, and a compliant joint controller executes them. A single training environment samples virtual spring, plane, and rail constraints alongside free-space motion. The objective encourages progress toward a compliant reference and command-derived interaction force while penalizing excessive loading. This formulation builds directly on three prior designs: the force-threshold penalty of FORGE ( FORGE ) [ 4 ] , through which an RL policy learns to respect a maximum allowable force; the force-compensated position reward of Zhi et al. [ 5 ] ; and the interaction-mode command of Lee et al. [ 6 ] , which tells a controller whether contact is permitted.

We evaluate our approach across the two robot embodiments shown in Fig. 1 . We apply the learned reflex controller to improve performance on dual-arm box lifting (A) and high-precision peg insertion (B) tasks. The results show that the learned reflex supports stable lifting under imperfect motion commands, enables insertion under hole-position uncertainty, and follows rough surfaces while limiting contact loading. Our contribution is a reusable reflex-training paradigm that uses simple interaction primitives to train policies that adapt task-level motion commands to local contact.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Environmental Constraints and Compliant Manipulation

Li and Brock [ 1 ] represent manipulation with environmental constraint (EC) primitives, recover instance geometry through exploratory interaction, and execute through compliant contact; their plane primitive, for example, maintains surface contact during motion and search. Minimalist Compliance Control [ 2 ] places actuator-based wrench estimation and task-space admittance beneath visual, imitation, and model-based policies. Both separate task intent from the response to local contact, the division our reflex adopts. Impedance control specifies a mechanical relationship between motion error and interaction force [ 7 ] , and admittance control turns measured force into reference motion for an inner position loop [ 8 ] ; these classical schemes are the reference points against which we position a learned reflex. We ask whether learning from structured interactions improves on them when the nominal geometry is imperfect.

## II-B Learned Interaction Control

FORGE [ 4 ] conditions assembly policies on a maximum allowable contact force and penalizes simulated force above that threshold during RL .The policy learns to modulate its actions so that the threshold is respected regardless of controller gains.
This force-thresholded RL formulation is the central insight our training objective shares: the excess-force cost in Sec. III-B plays the role of the FORGE penalty, and the peg-insertion study (Sec. IV-C ) builds on its assembly setup. Portela et al. [ 9 ] and Zhi et al. [ 5 ] learn force or position–force control for legged manipulators from robot-state history without force sensors. Zhi et al. reward tracking of a target position that is offset from the command by the net force through a static impedance relation, so that position tracking, force application, and compliance follow from one reward. Our compliant reference reward is based on this reward design. Direction Matters [ 10 ] predicts a contact-force direction for admittance control. Lee et al. [ 6 ] supply a collision-avoidance controller with a binary interaction-mode command that determines whether tool contact is permitted. Inspired by this design, we use a compliance-mode input to tell the policy whether to prioritize following the commanded motion or yielding to contact forces. Unlike these systems, the reflex policy adapts joint-space references beneath an independently supplied task command.

## II-C Proprioceptive Control and Local Reflexes

Proprioceptive control and local reflexes have been studied as mechanisms for adapting robot motion during physical interaction. Hyun et al. [ 11 ] combine high-level gait commands with proprioceptive impedance control on the MIT Cheetah, while Wensing et al. [ 12 ] connect effective physical interaction to backdrivable actuation and low mechanical impedance. In manipulation, SaLoutos et al. [ 13 ] use local anti-slip and regrasping reflexes to correct imperfect teleoperator grasps. Their reflexes use fingertip force/contact sensing; our reflex policy observes joint and kinematic history. These results motivate learning proprioceptive reflexes from environmental interaction and evaluating their reuse across manipulation conditions.

2026-10-05.title: SARI: Phase-Split Sim-Real Co-Training for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Xingxin He , Yuxuan Jiang , Haonan Zhang , Chuhan Cui , Kaile Li , Zhongxing Zheng , Caihao Xu , Ziqi Wang
2026-10-05.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often require costly real-world demonstrations to adapt to contact-rich manipulation tasks, particularly when generalization across object placements is needed. We propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split sim-and-real co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them. Specifically, free-space approaches require spatial diversity but tolerate modest simulation gaps, making them ideal for synthetic generation; conversely, contact interactions demand accurate physics but vary little across object placements, allowing a few real demonstrations to generalize across the workspace. SARI generates diverse simulated approaches in a photorealistic digital twin while collecting real contact interactions at only a few placements. Post-trained on these phase-segmented demonstrations, a single policy seamlessly stitches simulated approaches with real contact interactions using visual appearance alignment and a shared camera-relative action representation—without explicit phase labels or hand-coded switches. Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3% and achieves 27.5% success at unseen placements, where all full-task sim-real baselines fail completely (0%).
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong and
increasingly general manipulation capabilities, but this progress
has been enabled by human-collected robot data at a formidable scale.
Recent VLAs, including π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 1 ] , GR00T N1.7 [ 2 ] ,
and GEN-1.5 [ 3 ] , are trained on large and diverse
collections of robot, human, and synthetic data. Yet adapting these models
to a new, contact-rich task still commonly requires many task demonstrations,
and long-horizon tasks amplify this demand because errors and distribution
shifts accumulate over time.

An important cause is the limited spatial generalization of VLA policies.
Although visual encoders are pretrained on broad data, post-trained policies
can still overfit an action sequence to the specific object placements observed in
their demonstrations, rather than reliably extrapolating across the
workspace [ 4 , 5 ] . Consequently, achieving workspace-wide coverage requires the redundant repetition of near-identical free-space approaches, rather than focusing effort on contact-rich supervision.

Simulation offers an effective route to alleviate this human collection burden.
Recent advances, including MimicGen [ 6 ] ,
DemoGen [ 4 ] , Real2Render2Real [ 7 ] , and
others [ 8 , 9 ] , synthesize additional demonstrations by transforming a small set of
source demonstrations, generating trajectories in reconstructed scenes or combining simulated
and real data for policy training.
These methods can efficiently expand workspace coverage, diversify trajectories, and
eliminate redundant teleoperation of identical free-space approaches.

However, existing synthetic-data pipelines commonly assume that simulation is reliable throughout an entire task or require accurate modeling of contact
dynamics [ 10 , 4 , 8 , 9 ] .
In contact-rich manipulation, unmodeled friction, compliance, object resistance,
and visual sim-to-real discrepancies can make synthetic contact data unreliable.
To bridge this gap, straightforward sim-and-real co-training mixes full-task simulated and real demonstrations; yet, this still wastes costly real-world effort on free-space approaches and allows the spatially narrow real-data distribution to override and dilute the broad spatial coverage provided by simulation.

To address these challenges, we propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them.
Simulation can cheaply provide broad spatial coverage for free-space approaches, while a few real demonstrations suffice to teach contact interactions that generalize across placements.
Specifically, the approach phase requires broad spatial diversity but tolerates modest simulation gaps, making it ideal for synthetic generation. Conversely, the interaction phase demands accurate contact dynamics but varies little across object placements, allowing a modest number of real demonstrations at a few placements to generalize across the workspace.
Figure contrasts this phase-split allocation with full-task sim-real co-training.

We instantiate this phase-specific allocation using a Gaussian-Splatting [ 11 ] digital twin that generates simulated approaches across all placements, while collecting real contact interactions near the pre-contact boundary at only a subset. To enable a single policy to learn seamlessly from both sources without phase labels or a hand-coded switch, we align visual appearances and express actions in a shared camera-relative representation.
Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3% and achieves 27.5% unseen task completion, whereas all baselines achieve 0%.

Our core contributions are:

We introduce SARI , a phase-split sim-and-real co-training
framework that decouples workspace-wide spatial reaching from contact interactions, allocating data collection to the domain best suited for each phase.

We present a sim-to-real alignment pipeline, enabling a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approaches with real contact interactions without explicit phase labels or switching heuristics.

We evaluate SARI on a Franka robot across five contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating that our camera-relative action representation serves as the key mechanism to unlock zero-shot spatial generalization to unseen placements while reducing real-world collection time.

1. We introduce SARI , a phase-split sim-and-real co-training
framework that decouples workspace-wide spatial reaching from contact interactions, allocating data collection to the domain best suited for each phase.

2. We present a sim-to-real alignment pipeline, enabling a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approaches with real contact interactions without explicit phase labels or switching heuristics.

3. We evaluate SARI on a Franka robot across five contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating that our camera-relative action representation serves as the key mechanism to unlock zero-shot spatial generalization to unseen placements while reducing real-world collection time.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II RELATED WORKS

Synthetic data generation. Reconstructed scenes and digital twins are increasingly used to reduce
robot-data collection cost. Gaussian Splatting enables photorealistic
robot-workspace rendering and has recently supported simulation, memory,
and reactive control [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] ;
related systems synthesize demonstrations from few real examples or
reconstructed workspaces [ 6 , 10 , 4 , 7 , 8 , 14 , 15 ] .
However, these pipelines often require full-task demonstrations
or assume that synthetic rollouts are reliable throughout the task,
including contact regimes where friction, compliance, and object
resistance are hard to model. We therefore restrict reconstruction-based synthesis to the phase where geometric fidelity is sufficient: generating appearance-aligned free-space approaches across placements, while reserving contact-rich interaction for real data.

Sim-and-real co-training. Sim-to-real and mixed-domain training combine simulation scalability with real-world deployment fidelity. Existing methods typically co-train policies on full-task simulated and real data [ 9 , 16 ] , introduce online corrections or real-world residuals for contact-rich transfer [ 17 , 18 ] , or study robust assembly in simulation prior to deployment [ 19 , 20 ] . However, these approaches generally assume full-task trajectory in both domains or require extra adaptation machinery when simulated physics fails. In contrast, SARI exploits a fundamental task-phase asymmetry: simulation provides workspace-wide coverage for free-space approaches, while real demonstrations supply accurate contact dynamics at a sparse subset of placements. A single policy is post-trained on their union without phase labels, residual controllers, or phase-specific losses.

VLA post-training. Large robot datasets and VLA policies have
made post-training a practical mechanism for adapting pretrained robot
models to new tasks [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 1 , 27 ] .
Recent work improves VLA action generation, pretraining sources,
obstacle-aware imitation, and world-model conditioning [ 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] ,
while contact-rich variants introduce force-aware modules or
curricula [ 32 , 33 ] . Yet adapting VLAs to a new workspace
usually still requires full task demonstrations covering both approach
and interaction, and specialized contact signals add assumptions beyond
standard behavior cloning. We keep the recipe plain: a pretrained VLA, a shared camera-relative action representation, and phase-specific sim-real data. Together, these ingredients enable a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approach trajectories with real contact interactions, supporting spatial generalization to placements without real interaction demonstrations using only standard behavior cloning.

2026-10-05.title: LOCUS: Landmark-Oriented Container Discrimination Using Spatial Graphs
2026-10-05.authors: Taylor Bergeron , Shibani Senthilbabu , Kevin Leahy
2026-10-05.abstract: As robots are increasingly deployed in unstructured, real-world environments, the ability to reason about complex spatial and semantic relationships among objects remains a fundamental challenge in enabling robust and generalizable manipulation and navigation. For example, deciding where to search for an object that is not in plain sight depends on where it is physically plausible as well as semantically likely. Popular methods such as cosine similarity with CLIP struggle to disambiguate between spatially and semantically similar objects that could contain a target object. We propose Landmark-Oriented Container Discrimination Using Spatial Graphs (LOCUS). To jointly reason about spatial information and semantics, we train a GNN to update CLIP embeddings on a full environment scene graph by passing embedding information between nodes based on proximity. CLIP embeddings, augmented by semantic knowledge from a fusion of household ontologies provide a robust semantic signal. We evaluate in simulation on a noiseless scene graph from simulator metadata, making the approach detection-agnostic. Our approach outperforms random, CLIP, Tidybot, and an LLM planner in the majority of room classes and configurations in simulation. To show our approach is robust to scene graph node placement and label noise, we demonstrate a physical mobile manipulator running in an exploration pipeline start-to-finish including scene graph labels from Detic.
2026-10-05.introduction:
To accomplish many complex tasks in the real world, robots must understand physical and semantic relationships between objects in their environment. For example, to find occluded objects in household or search-and-rescue tasks, a robot needs both general and domain-specific knowledge of object relationships to hypothesize where an object may be hidden, including inside other containers.
The robot may also be provided with a general floor plan which it can use to inform its search, but have no knowledge about the items within each room. In many cases, there are multiple instances of the same container object which could contain the target object, such as multiple drawers that could contain a fork, and the robot must find a way to discriminate between the containers to generate a container search order. We posit that the correct approach requires both the generality of Large Language Models (LLMs) or Vision Language Models (VLMs) and the structured knowledge of an ontology.

We introduce a novel approach, Landmark-Oriented Container discrimination Using Spatial Graphs (LOCUS), the first reasoning pipeline for concealed objects that makes instance-level decisions between containers of the same class. Locus is Latin for place — reflecting our hypothesis that where a container is matters as much as what it looks like. LOCUS combines domain specific formal ontologies and general semantic knowledge. It accounts for cases not explicitly covered in the ontologies with the spatial relationship between objects in the environment in order to find an occluded object and is generalizable sim-to-sim and sim-to-real. We pretrain a GNN over scene graphs and use ontologies to learn typical spatial relationships and augment each scene graph node’s CLIP [ 1 ] embedding.

Our contributions include:
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Background and Problem Formulation

To reason over object search and retrieval solutions, many approaches [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] use CLIP for retrieval, comparing search locations by cosine similarity with the query; however, same-class containers receive nearly identical embeddings, whether from a bounding-box crop or a wider frame containing context (e.g., a drawer with the sink visible). Methods exist for semantic object search [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] and container reasoning [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , but none produce a principled pipeline to search for an occluded object in a realistic environment with multiple containers of the same class to choose between during exploration given a floor plan and an ontology for the domain. Scene-graph GNNs. rank navigation goals in observable space [ 15 , 16 ] ; HOLM [ 17 ] and VLMaps [ 18 ] resolve only viewpoint occlusion, where the target becomes visible once the agent looks in the right direction; semantic mechanical search [ 19 ] reasons over occupancy rather than which of several identical containers to open.

Semantic World Knowledge for Object Search Decisions Many approaches investigate commonsense reasoning while exploring for not completely occluded objects, with LLMs as a popular solution. The approaches that reason over room-object navigation decisions for unknown environments either combine preexisting pretrained models for image parsing and an LLM to reason over objects in the image to inform the search [ 5 , 6 ] , use LLM chain-of-thought prompting for commonsense context [ 7 ] , or build multi-layer VLM value maps from LLM-inferred semantic priors [ 8 , 9 ] . An approach to incorporating environment understanding into the reasoning pipeline is using a scene graph of the current environment to aid in decision making. For partially known environments with a floor plan, [ 10 ] and [ 11 ] use a scene graph to inform their neural network based approaches. [ 10 ] use LLMs to generate training data for their network which can lead to hallucinations and [ 11 ] manually craft the semantic categories governing where objects are placed, which makes the vocabulary sparse and unable to accurately reflect or scale to real-world distributions. These approaches lack principled semantic grounding through ontologies or human placement data, which would impact performance for occluded object search.

Container Reasoning Approaches for object-container reasoning don’t consider instances of containers but rather consider object to container class relationship (e.g. a fork goes in a drawer, and all drawers are treated as the same since they belong to the same class) [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Approaches that consider finding entirely occluded objects rely on simulation metadata at runtime and abstract away manipulation task choices, as if the agent is within range of a fully occluded object, then it is found [ 12 , 13 ] , while the approach that considers sensor data for labels using d-DETR [ 20 ] rather than the ground truth labels from simulation metadata at run time only considers fully visible objects [ 14 ] . TidyBot [ 21 ] likewise selects a receptacle type from LLM preferences, so it cannot order same-class instances. To our knowledge, no prior work discriminates same-class container instances under full occlusion. Notably, all of these approaches are in simulation and do not generalize cross-simulation. There is a gap for real world robotics deployment when the robot needs to choose between containers, some of which are of the same class, to search to physically retrieve an occluded object.
Therefore, our goal is to answer, Given a room level floor plan of an environment and task/environment relevant ontologies, can a robot distinguish between instances of the same object class with different semantic and spatial information and generalize to unseen environment configurations and domains?

Our work focuses on bridging the gap between semantic world knowledge for object search decisions and instance container reasoning for realistic object retrieval. CLIP provides strong semantic understanding. Rather than training an entirely new network, we update CLIP with spatial context for instance-level container discrimination via a GNN that learns over an environment’s scene graph.

To showcase LOCUS’s ability to provide detailed distinctions between nodes of the same class, at run time we score nodes by cosine similarity between the updated container embedding and the query text, retaining CLIP’s comparability while adding spatial and semantic reasoning.

2026-10-05.title: ManiPhysicsBench: Physics-Based Assessment of Object Preservation in VLA Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Sangwu Park , Yeonjun In , Wonjoong Kim , Sungwon Kim , Sein Kim , Chanyoung Park
2026-10-05.comment: Preprint
2026-10-05.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform diverse manipulation tasks, but task success in existing rigid-body benchmarks does not indicate whether they preserve objects. We introduce ManiPhysicsZoo , which consolidates literature-supported material properties, 3D meshes, and supporting references into reusable object assets. Using these assets, a solver-based assessment computes grasp-specific damage thresholds from object geometry, material properties, and recorded grasp conditions and compares them with recorded contact forces to assess potential deformation and fracture. Building on these components, ManiPhysicsBench evaluates object preservation in LIBERO and SimplerEnv across three physics axes and three difficulty levels. Public VLA checkpoints show a substantial gap between task success and safe success, defined as task completion while preserving the object. Their gripper commands concentrate near full opening and closure, with largely similar aggregate distributions across objects, consistent with binary gripper supervision. We examine how object-specific continuous gripper labels change model behavior by retraining a VLA model. The retrained model shows more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success, but lower task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform a wide range of manipulation tasks from visual observations and language instructions. Their recent performance and generality across tasks and embodiments have made them a major paradigm in robot learning ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) . This capability has been evaluated through manipulation tasks in simulation and in the real world, which serve as a standard protocol for VLA evaluation ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024b ) .

However, task completion alone does not establish whether a policy handles objects without damaging them. In real-world deployment, VLAs may need to grasp and move objects with diverse physical properties, such as fragile eggs and rigid wooden boxes. Humans take these properties into account by holding fragile objects firmly enough to prevent slipping but gently enough to avoid damage, while using a stronger grip when handling rigid objects. In this sense, physical properties determine which actions are appropriate, and a genuinely generalist policy should be able to complete a task while preserving the object. We therefore ask: Can current VLAs account for objects’ physical properties to complete manipulation tasks without causing damage?

The direct way to evaluate this ability is to conduct real-world experiments. However, fractured or permanently deformed objects cannot be reused under the same conditions, so repeated trials incur object replacement costs. Moreover, damaged objects and fragments may pose safety risks to the robot and its surroundings. Therefore, a simulation-based framework is needed to assess object preservation under repeatable conditions. Yet widely used simulation benchmarks do not account for object damage when evaluating task success ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024b ) . Because objects are modeled as rigid bodies, a policy can receive the same success score regardless of whether it handles the object carefully or uses gripping that would damage it in the real world. Adjacent lines of work, including physical understanding benchmarks, robot safety benchmarks, and tactile and force-aware VLAs, leave this gap open, as none of them judges a policy’s actions against a physically grounded criterion for object preservation ( Chow et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Balaji et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . These limitations highlight the need for a common evaluation protocol that assesses whether policies complete tasks while respecting each object’s physical constraints.

Developing such an evaluation protocol requires defining preservation criteria for each object and reliably assessing how policy-applied forces affect its state during a rollout. This entails two challenges. First, defining physically grounded preservation criteria requires object-specific material properties, geometric meshes, and supporting references, but these resources are not readily available in a unified, verifiable form. Second, evaluating object preservation requires translating the forces applied during a rollout into predictions of deformation or fracture, but the rigid-body simulators used in standard manipulation benchmarks do not model these outcomes.

To address the first challenge, we propose ManiPhysicsZoo , an object library that consolidates object-specific material properties, 3D meshes, supporting references, structural information, and validation status into reusable assets. These assets can be reused for evaluating new policies, robots, and objects across simulation environments. The supporting references justify the material properties and preservation criteria, making their physical basis traceable and verifiable.

To address the second challenge, we introduce an assessment method that uses physics solvers to determine whether contact forces recorded during a manipulation rollout could cause object deformation or fracture under the corresponding grasp conditions.
After each rollout is completed, the physics solver combines the recorded grasp information with the material properties and 3D mesh from ManiPhysicsZoo to compute a damage threshold for each grasp. We compare the recorded contact forces with the corresponding thresholds and judge an interaction to be potentially damaging if its force exceeds the threshold. We justify each threshold using material properties and damage criteria supported by the literature, and document the modeling assumptions to make the resulting evaluation traceable and verifiable.

Building on these two components, we construct ManiPhysicsBench , a physics-based benchmark for evaluating object preservation during manipulation. ManiPhysicsBench constructs manipulation tasks in LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and SimplerEnv ( Li et al., 2024b ) using objects selected from our ManiPhysicsZoo .

Solver-based assessment enables object-preservation evaluation on these platforms, even though their simulators model objects as rigid bodies. The benchmark is organized into three physics axes: brittle fracture, soft object deformation, and thin-walled container deformation. Each axis includes high, medium, and low difficulty levels, with higher difficulty corresponding to a narrower range of gripping forces that allow the object to be lifted without damage.

We evaluate public VLA checkpoints ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Black et al., 2025a ; Fang et al., 2026 ) on ManiPhysicsBench and observe a substantial gap between task success and safe success, defined as task completion while preserving the object. To investigate this gap, we analyze the policies’ gripper commands to examine whether they adapt their gripping behavior to objects’ physical properties. We find that these commands concentrate near fully open and fully closed states, with largely similar aggregate distributions across objects.

This pattern motivates examining the role of gripper supervision. Standard VLA pipelines often binarize gripper labels into open and close, which may limit the learning of object-dependent gripper control ( Walke et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . We therefore replace binary labels with continuous labels derived from object-specific physical constraints and evaluate how retraining with these labels affects gripper behavior and safe success. Retraining yields more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success. However, task success decreases, and the resulting object-preserving behavior shows limited generalization.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

ManiPhysicsZoo . An object library that consolidates object-specific meshes, properties, and supporting references into reusable assets for physically grounded preservation assessment.

Physics solver-based assessment. A solver-based pipeline that computes damage thresholds for each grasp from object geometry, material properties, and grasp conditions.

ManiPhysicsBench . A benchmark that evaluates across three physics axes and three difficulty levels whether VLA models manipulate objects while respecting their physical constraints.

Evaluation and behavioral analysis. An evaluation of public VLA checkpoints, reporting the gap between task success and safe success. We analyze gripper behavior and examine the effects of object-specific continuous gripper supervision, identifying improvements in safe success alongside reduced task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior.

1. ManiPhysicsZoo . An object library that consolidates object-specific meshes, properties, and supporting references into reusable assets for physically grounded preservation assessment.

2. Physics solver-based assessment. A solver-based pipeline that computes damage thresholds for each grasp from object geometry, material properties, and grasp conditions.

3. ManiPhysicsBench . A benchmark that evaluates across three physics axes and three difficulty levels whether VLA models manipulate objects while respecting their physical constraints.

4. Evaluation and behavioral analysis. An evaluation of public VLA checkpoints, reporting the gap between task success and safe success. We analyze gripper behavior and examine the effects of object-specific continuous gripper supervision, identifying improvements in safe success alongside reduced task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Manipulation Benchmarks. Manipulation benchmarks evaluate policies across diverse tasks, objects, and environments. LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) studies knowledge transfer across manipulation tasks, while SimplerEnv ( Li et al., 2024b ) provides simulation-based evaluation of real world robot policies. CALVIN ( Mees et al., 2022 ) evaluates language-conditioned task sequences, and RLBench ( James et al., 2020 ) provides a diverse task suite with demonstrations. Because these benchmarks model objects as rigid bodies and do not track whether an object is damaged, task success alone does not indicate object preservation.

Physical Understanding and Interaction. Physical understanding benchmarks evaluate VLMs’ knowledge of physical properties and interactions through question answering. PhysBench ( Chow et al., 2025 ) assesses understanding of object properties and physical dynamics, while ManipBench ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) evaluates low-level manipulation reasoning through multiple-choice questions on interaction keypoints and action trajectories. We share their interest in connecting physical knowledge to manipulation. However, in these benchmarks’ question-answering evaluations, models answer questions without executing manipulation actions, so object preservation during task execution is not directly assessed. Even PhysBench’s force test relies on VLM-specified gripping forces, while its simulator treats all objects as rigid bodies and does not simulate grasp-induced damage. Our work complements these evaluations by assessing whether contact forces recorded during policy rollouts exceed physically grounded damage thresholds for each grasp.

Deformable manipulation environments aim to simulate objects that change shape. SoftGym ( Lin et al., 2021 ) provides tasks with cloth, rope, and fluids, while PlasticineLab ( Huang et al., 2021 ) focuses on shaping elastoplastic materials. However, deformation is the goal of these tasks, so object preservation is neglected and the damage criterion is absent. DefGraspSim ( Huang et al., 2022 ) computes the stress and deformation of an object under a grasp with the finite element method (FEM). However, its material parameters are assigned from a fixed set rather than sourced from the object’s own material, so the computed response is hypothetical. Moreover, in DefGraspSim a gripper is placed at candidate poses produced by a sampler and closes on the object, without an arm and a manipulation task. Therefore, grasping as part of manipulation falls outside its concern.

Robot Safety Benchmarks. Robot safety benchmarks assess hazards and harmful interactions during policy execution. SafeVLA-Bench ( Fan et al., 2026 ) scores rollouts on existing benchmarks against safety constraints specified for the robot, the scene, and how the object is carried. OopsieVerse ( Balaji et al., 2026 ) accumulates mechanical, thermal, and fluid damage as a health value that the authors define for each object. Both share our premise that task completion should be separate from safe completion when evaluating VLAs. However, SafeVLA-Bench centers on the safety of the scenario and does not evaluate object preservation. OopsieVerse evaluates object damage, including preservation, but from damage criteria that are annotated manually rather than derived from the object’s properties. The authors describe this model as an approximation adopted in place of accurate physical computation, and it judges preservation regardless of where the object is grasped. The physical rigor of these verdicts therefore cannot be ensured.

Force and Tactile-Aware Manipulation. Force and tactile-aware methods such as Tactile-VLA, TaF-VLA, and DeliGrasp adapt contact behavior to object properties and feedback during execution, and demonstrate this capability through real robot experiments ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . These methods share our view that appropriate manipulation requires adapting actions to objects’ physical properties and contact conditions. However, their focus is on improving models, and evaluation is conducted on dedicated task protocols and real robot setups, where object preservation is judged by visual inspection after each trial. Because each evaluation runs on real hardware, it is subject to cost and safety constraints, and a common criterion under which existing models could be compared remains outside their scope.

Summary. As summarized in Table 1 , ManiPhysicsBench brings together reusable object assets, grasp-specific damage assessment using physics solvers, and evaluation of public VLA checkpoints on existing manipulation platforms. Using the object geometry and material properties documented in ManiPhysicsZoo , physics solvers compute damage thresholds for the grasp conditions recorded during each rollout. We compare these thresholds with recorded contact forces to assess whether task completion also satisfies the object’s preservation criteria. Each judgment therefore depends on both the object’s physical properties and how the policy interacts with it. This post-rollout assessment supports a common evaluation protocol while retaining the platforms’ existing observation and action interfaces and rigid-body simulators.

Sim-to-real learning commonly adapts policies or representations to domain
variation, often directing the learning budget toward task-agnostic low-level
representations at the expense of task-level knowledge. Skill2Real builds on
cross-domain grounding from foundation vision-language models (VLMs) to
acquire validated, reusable skills in simulation through a shared
code-based policy interface. In its
asymmetric Proposer–Verifier–Governor (PVG) loop, the Proposer acts
from public observations and API returns, the Verifier diagnoses outcomes with
privileged simulation evidence, and the Governor admits updates supported by
validation rollouts. A Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills; a
Brain then composes the frozen library into long-horizon programs with planning
and recovery. At deployment, this hierarchy is grounded in real observations
through the same interface. On unseen LIBERO-Pro Long, frozen LIBERO-90
skills raise success from 2.0% to 56.3% with Astra and from 0.5% to 49.0%
with Opus 5. Robosuite success reaches 85.1–89.4% across seven tasks. On a
real UR5e, the same agent’s mean completion rises from 27.50% to 78.75% across
four tasks with Skill2Real, a controlled gain that, with cross-model
improvements, shows Skill2Real adds a capability orthogonal to the foundation
model by learning transferable task knowledge in simulation. Project page: skill2real.github.io .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Zero-shot sim-to-real robot manipulation aims to convert experience acquired
in simulation into behavior that can be executed by a physical robot without
real-world task training. Simulation provides a scalable environment for
learning such behavior, but discrepancies in appearance, dynamics, contact,
and embodiment can prevent policies learned in simulation from transferring
reliably to reality ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Chebotar et al., 2019 ) . For long-horizon manipulation,
the challenge extends beyond transferring individual actions: a robot must
reliably execute local manipulation skills, compose them into task-level
behavior ( Gupta et al., 2020 ; Shi et al., 2025b ) , and recover when
intermediate actions fail.

Existing methods leave a central bottleneck unresolved: learning reusable,
composable task knowledge from privileged simulation evidence without spending
the learning budget on task-agnostic low-level representations. Randomization
and asymmetric actor–critic methods improve transfer by adapting neural
policies or representations ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Pinto et al., 2018 ) . Appearance-heavy
domain randomization can therefore spend much of the learning budget modeling
task-irrelevant variation in lighting and texture rather than acquiring
reusable manipulation knowledge. Code-generation
methods make behavior composable, but assemble supplied primitives rather than
acquire local skills and task strategies from experience ( Liang et al., 2022 ) .
Representative skill-library systems accumulate programs through human guidance
or real-world execution feedback ( Tziafas & Kasaei, 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) .
Skill2Real instead relies on foundation VLMs for cross-domain grounding and
directs simulation learning toward validated, hierarchical executable
knowledge.

We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns executable
robot skills through a shared code-based policy interface. The key idea is to separate the
information used to supervise skill learning from the information required to
execute learned skills: simulator privilege can evaluate and improve behavior,
while persistent skill knowledge is expressed entirely through public
observations and API semantics. The shared interface defines the transfer boundary:
programs invoke operations with common semantics, while each backend provides
its own perception, calibration, and low-level execution. This separation lets
task knowledge be reused across simulation and reality without incorporating
simulator-only state into the deployed policy.

Skill2Real realizes this idea with an asymmetric
Proposer–Verifier–Governor (PVG) loop that learns a two-level skill
hierarchy. The Proposer executes programs from public observations and proposes
reusable updates; the Verifier turns privileged simulation outcomes into
publicly grounded diagnoses; and the Governor aggregates evidence across
validation rollouts to admit supported updates into memory. Stage I learns
Cerebellum skills for reusable local manipulation. Stage II freezes this
library and learns Brain skills that compose it into long-horizon task programs
with planning and recovery. At deployment, the Proposer grounds both frozen
memories in current observations through the real code-based policy
interface.

Our experiments test whether frozen hierarchical knowledge generalizes across
task suites, Proposers, and the real robot. As frozen LIBERO-90
libraries ( Liu et al., 2023 ) progress from no memory through the
Cerebellum to the full hierarchy, success on unseen LIBERO-Pro Long
tasks ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) rises from 2.0% to 35.3% to 56.3% with
Astra and from 0.5% to 29.3% to 49.0% with Opus 5, showing that both skill
levels transfer across Proposers beyond the source tasks. Across seven single-arm and bimanual
Robosuite tasks ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) , independently learned libraries raise
mean success from 16.6% to 85.1% with Sol and from 19.4% to 89.4% with
Opus 5, demonstrating consistent gains across Proposers. On the real UR5e, the
full Brain–Cerebellum hierarchy reaches 78.75% mean task completion versus
56.25% with local skills alone, confirming the value of task-level composition
for long-horizon behavior.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns
executable robot programs in simulation and transfers frozen skill
knowledge through a shared code-based policy interface using only public observations at
deployment, without real-world task-policy adaptation.

knowledge through a shared code-based policy interface using only public observations at
deployment, without real-world task-policy adaptation.

We develop an asymmetric Proposer–Verifier–Governor scheme: the
Proposer acts on public observations, the Verifier translates privileged
execution evidence into public feedback, and the Governor admits updates
supported by validation rollouts.

We develop a hierarchical policy learning strategy in which the
Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills and the Brain learns
long-horizon compositions conditioned on the frozen Cerebellum library,
enabling task-level planning and recovery.

knowledge through a shared code-based policy interface using only public observations at
deployment, without real-world task-policy adaptation.

Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills and the Brain learns
long-horizon compositions conditioned on the frozen Cerebellum library,
enabling task-level planning and recovery.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Classical sim-to-real methods
primarily bridge visual, dynamics, and execution gaps by learning policies or
representations that are invariant to domain shift. Domain
randomization ( Tobin et al., 2017 ) and dynamics
randomization ( Peng et al., 2018 ) expose the learner to controlled variation,
while privileged critics ( Pinto et al., 2018 ) , real-world
adaptation ( Chebotar et al., 2019 ) , and active
randomization ( Mehta et al., 2020 ) provide additional training signals
or target-domain experience when the gap is difficult to model. Foundation
vision-language-action models instead bring broadly pretrained
representations that can reason across heterogeneous observations, tasks, and
embodiments: RT-2 ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) and
Open X ( Collaboration, 2024 ) scale such learning, while
Octo ( Ghosh et al., 2024 ) and OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025 ) make generalist
policies more accessible. Building on the cross-domain reasoning capability
of foundation VLMs, Skill2Real learns transferable task-level knowledge in
the form of validated, executable skills and task programs, without learning
a new representation from scratch. The frozen skills are deployed through a
shared code-based policy interface:
privileged state and evaluation are used only during simulation training,
while the real backend supplies perception, calibration, and low-level
execution.

Language-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for composing robot
behavior. Code as Policies ( Liang et al., 2022 ) and
ProgPrompt ( Singh et al., 2023 ) generate executable programs, while
SayCan ( Ichter et al., 2023 ) grounds language plans in physically feasible
affordances. Recent agentic systems expand beyond fixed skill sets: Agentic
Skill Discovery ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) bootstraps skills and success criteria,
CaP-X ( Fu et al., 2026 ) studies feedback-driven coding-agent improvement,
and ASPIRE ( Lu et al., 2026 ) executes, diagnoses, repairs, and validates
robot programs. Playful Agentic Robot Learning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and
ENPIRE ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) further investigate autonomous
exploration and real-world policy evolution. Zetta ( Ding et al., 2026 ) evolves code-based runtime critics and recovery skills around frozen base
policies, combining action-level monitoring with validation-gated harness
updates. It also demonstrates zero-shot transfer of learned recovery skills.
Skill2Real is a multi-agent decision-making system in which the Proposer
generates executable robot programs, the Verifier diagnoses their outcomes
using privileged simulation evidence, and the Governor decides which validated
updates enter persistent skill memory. Together, the agents learn a two-level
hierarchy of local skills and task programs that is deployed as frozen,
publicly grounded knowledge through the shared interface.

Hierarchical reinforcement learning separates short-horizon control from
long-horizon decisions. Options ( Sutton et al., 1999 ) ,
MAXQ ( Dietterich, 2000 ) , and
HIRO ( Nachum et al., 2018 ) establish temporal abstraction through subpolicies, value decompositions, and
subgoal-conditioned control. Relay Policy Learning ( Gupta et al., 2020 ) and SPiRL ( Pertsch et al., 2021 ) show that reusable stages or skill
priors can improve long-horizon manipulation. More recent systems build
semantic or persistent skill libraries, including Lifelong Robot Library
Learning ( Tziafas & Kasaei, 2024 ) ,
AtomSkill ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and Hi Robot ( Shi et al., 2025b ) ;
MemoryVLA ( Shi et al., 2025a ) , MemoryVAM ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) ,
RoboHarness ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , RoboHiMan ( Chen et al., 2025 ) ,
RoboPARA ( Duan et al., 2026 ) , and
RigPI ( He et al., 2026 ) study memory, policy routing,
hierarchical evaluation, task planning, or dynamics identification for manipulation. Their
transfer units are typically policies, latent skills, fixed stages, or
episodic records. Skill2Real instead learns a two-level hierarchy of reusable
skills. The Cerebellum acquires and freezes validated local manipulation
skills, while the Brain learns task-level skills that compositionally
recombine the local library into long-horizon programs. Reuse and composition
at both levels support generalization across tasks, scenes, and deployment
domains through the shared interface.

2026-10-05.title: SimpleTouch: Can Vision-Language-Action Models Master Contact-Rich Manipulation Without Tactile Policy Pretraining?
2026-10-05.authors: Chen Yang , Linzhe Shi , Changjie Wu , Hang Zhang , Ronghan Chen , Lingjun Zhang , Xu Hu , Mu Xu , Jiansheng Fan , Chen Wang
2026-10-05.abstract:
Tactile sensing provides essential contact information for robotic manipulation, yet incorporating it into pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging.
A common concern is that simply introducing touch during task-specific fine-tuning may fail to bridge the cross-modal gap, yielding limited gains or even reduced success.
Consequently, existing methods often rely on large-scale tactile policy pretraining or separate visuotactile alignment, adding data requirements and training stages.
We introduce \simpletouchfont SimpleTouch, a simple VLA extension that augments π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with a tactile expert, to test whether these additional stages are necessary.
Leveraging all tokens from a frozen pretrained tactile encoder, the expert learns from action supervision and multi-horizon prediction of future tactile latents.
This single-stage training uses only task demonstrations, without additional tactile policy pretraining or separate alignment.
With 50 demonstrations per task, \simpletouchfont SimpleTouch achieves the highest success rate among evaluated methods on all six UniVTAC tasks.
Its average success rate reaches 77.5%, compared with 45.2% for FTP- π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 66.7% for FTP-1, corresponding to gains of 32.3 and 10.8 percentage points, respectively.
Across four real-world tasks, it averages 71.3%, exceeding FTP-1 by 8.8 percentage points.
These results demonstrate that, given pretrained VLA and tactile representations, additional tactile policy pretraining is not a prerequisite for strong performance on these tasks, offering a simpler route to contact-rich manipulation.
Project page: https://simpletouch-robot.github.io/
2026-10-05.introduction:
Robot manipulation has made substantial progress through learned policies ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) and pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2024 ) . Much of this progress has relied on visual perception as the primary interface for scene understanding. However, visual observations do not fully determine contact-rich interaction: two manipulation states can appear visually similar while requiring different actions because their contact geometry, deformation, or slip state differs ( Li et al., 2014 ; Yuan et al., 2017 ) . Tactile sensing supplies local feedback about these otherwise hidden contact states, motivating policies that learn from touch and use it during manipulation ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Lou et al., 2026 ) .

However, adding touch to a pretrained policy does not automatically make it useful. Tactile observations lie outside the pretraining modalities of many VLA backbones, and directly incorporating them during fine-tuning can yield limited gains or even reduce success ( Niu et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . The central challenge is therefore not merely obtaining tactile features, but presenting them to a pretrained VLA in a form that preserves contact information while allowing the policy to learn their task-specific use from limited demonstrations. Representative responses include large-scale tactile policy pretraining, as in FTP-1 ( Yuan et al., 2026a ) , and separate visuotactile representation alignment, as in VITaL ( George et al., 2025 ) . These routes provide useful priors but introduce additional data requirements and training stages. Meanwhile, pretrained tactile encoders already offer reusable contact representations ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . This distinction between acquiring tactile representations and learning a tactile policy motivates our question: given a pretrained VLA and tactile encoder, can a policy learn strong contact-rich manipulation from task-specific tactile demonstrations without additional tactile policy pretraining or a separate alignment stage?

We introduce \simpletouchfont SimpleTouch, a simple recipe that augments π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) with one tactile expert, without additional tactile policy pretraining or a separate alignment stage. Its design follows two principles. First, it preserves the pretrained tactile representation: we freeze the tactile encoder and retain all current tokens, including global and spatial features, as a stable source of contact information. Second, it learns the task-specific use of that representation through a tactile expert. The tactile expert processes current tactile features separately from the visual-language backbone, and the action expert reads them through layerwise attention. During joint training, the expert learns from both action supervision and multi-horizon prediction of future tactile latents through latent flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . This task-trained pathway gives action generation direct access to high-fidelity tactile features. During task-level training, we jointly optimize the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, including its visual-language backbone and action expert, together with the tactile expert, while keeping the tactile encoder frozen.

With 50 demonstrations per task, \simpletouchfont SimpleTouch achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated methods on all six UniVTAC ( Chen et al., 2026a ) tasks. Its mean success rate of 77.5% exceeds those of FTP- π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and the pretrained FTP-1 policy by 32.3 and 10.8 percentage points, respectively. Across four real-world tasks, \simpletouchfont SimpleTouch averages 71.3%, surpassing FTP-1 by 8.8 points and showing improvements in real-world experiments as well. At deployment, the tactile expert processes the current observation once, and its layerwise cache is reused throughout action-flow integration; future tactile prediction is used only as training supervision. Together, these results show that, given strong pretrained VLA and tactile representations, a frozen tactile representation and task-trained tactile expert can achieve strong performance without additional tactile policy pretraining or explicit alignment.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Generalist policy learning converts broad visual and language priors into continuous robot control across diverse tasks. The π \pi series couples pretrained vision-language backbones with flow-matching action experts ( Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Other VLA systems investigate large-scale data, efficient fine-tuning, execution, generalization, and modular policy development ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2023 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Cai et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; StarVLA Community, 2026 ) . Complementary world-action models incorporate predictive visual or feature dynamics into action learning, including Video Prediction Policy, LingBot-VA, Motus, DreamZero, LaWAM, and Fast-WAM ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Bi et al., 2025a ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Yuan et al., 2026b ) . These directions establish strong reusable architectures and priors for action generation, but their observation interfaces are primarily built around vision, language, and proprioception rather than local tactile contact feedback.

Tactile policy learning can be organized by where contact-sensitive priors are acquired. One route first learns how tactile observations participate in control through large-scale tactile policy pretraining or tactile-grounded mid-training, as in FTP-1, the N 0 N_{0} -TWAM/ N 0 N_{0} -VTLA family, and T-Rex ( Yuan et al., 2026a ; NeoteAI Team and Fudan TEAI Team, 2026a ; NeoteAI Team and Fudan TEAI Team, 2026b ; Niu et al., 2026a ) . A second route aligns tactile and visual representations before policy learning, including VITaL, UniTouch, and VT-MUSE ( George et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Both front-load resources beyond task-level learning. Other methods explore task-level tactile reasoning, adaptive fusion, or reactive feedback ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Heng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026c ; Xue et al., 2025 ) , while predictive approaches model future contact or multimodal dynamics ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Niu et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Across these settings, simply adding tactile input during fine-tuning does not consistently improve success ( Yuan et al., 2026a ; Niu et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026c ) . An open question is whether strong contact-rich control instead requires an additional tactile policy-learning or alignment stage once pretrained VLA and tactile representations are available.

Pretrained tactile encoders address representation acquisition rather than action generation. Early work such as T-Dex learns self-supervised tactile embeddings from robotic play for downstream dexterous control ( Guzey et al., 2023 ) . Sparsh and Sparsh-X learn general-purpose representations from self-supervised vision-based and multisensory touch data, respectively ( Higuera et al., 2024 ; Higuera et al., 2025 ) ; the AnyTouch series models static and dynamic tactile signals across sensors and downstream tasks ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . T3 combines sensor-specific encoders with a shared Transformer trained across sensors and tasks ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Such encoders provide reusable contact-sensitive features across tasks and sensing configurations. This differs from tactile policy pretraining: encoders supply sensory representations, whereas policy pretraining also learns how touch influences action generation. Existing encoder work does not prescribe the downstream action interface or establish whether a separate tactile policy-training stage remains necessary. A detailed review of related work is provided in Appendix B .

2026-10-05.authors: Luís Marques , Rong Fang , Disha Kamale , Dmitry Berenson

2026-10-05.abstract:
Monitoring planned driving trajectories requires accurately estimating the collision likelihood
with actors whose motion is itself impacted by the ego motion.
Existing classical approaches are often limited by the quality of their forecasting model.
Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise in reasoning about the consequences of high-level actions, yet their approximate
predictions are unsuitable for safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving.
Conformal prediction (CP) has emerged as a data-driven framework for quantifying the uncertainty of black-box model predictions.
We propose Split Label-Localized Conformal Prediction (SLLCP),
a post-hoc calibration layer over frozen VLMs that transforms their unreliable predictions into probabilistically calibrated safety prediction sets.
We consider how the ability to estimate safety can depend on the observed driving scene and introduce a localized procedure that upweights
relevant past experience when calculating uncertainty thresholds. We provide label-conditional finite-sample distribution-free coverage under exchangeability.
Evaluated over 15k CARLA trajectories from unseen scenarios, SLLCP correctly flags 89.6 % 89.6\% of collision-causing trajectories with a Qwen backbone and 88.4 % 88.4\% with a
Cosmos backbone, while the base VLMs only flagged 4.6 % 4.6\% and 39.1 % 39.1\% of the collision-causing trajectories,
respectively. These results indicate that local, label-conditional
calibration can reduce missed unsafe trajectories.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Before self-driving cars execute planned trajectories, they must
assess whether the intended motion can be safely executed, considering the surrounding scene.
This is nontrivial: pedestrians and other vehicles move in response to the ego vehicle.
For example, a trajectory passing a pedestrian near the curb may be
collision-free if the pedestrian waits, but unsafe if they step into the
vehicle’s path.
Further, the information available at planning time might miss occluded actors and not provide sufficient signal to enable accurate forecasting of the scene’s evolution.
Even seemingly robust driving policies can demonstrate degraded performance when operating in unfamiliar
scenarios — Fail2Drive reports substantial drops in closed-loop success under
controlled scenario shifts [ 5 ] .

We study the problem of designing a
safety monitor that examines each
candidate trajectory before execution, independently of the quality of the underlying planning module.
That monitor should flag trajectories that would collide within a fixed
time horizon, while avoiding unnecessary alarms hindering task progress.
In general, a safety monitor might need to reason about the candidate
motion and the scene jointly, while considering uncertainty in the true unknown
outcome.
While vision-language driving systems, such as SimLingo, incorporate scene
understanding with action-taking [ 17 ] , we aim to construct a monitor that can be applied post-hoc over any base planner.
We seek a theoretically-informed way to probabilistically limit the number of missed unsafe trajectories.

Safety monitors. Driving pipelines often forecast the motion of nearby actors
before checking a planned trajectory for collision [ 16 ] .
Model-based safety checks can account for uncertain actor motion and
dynamics [ 9 ] , but their assurances
depend on assumed scene knowledge. When an actor is missed entirely or its response to the
ego vehicle is incorrectly predicted, using a collision check may fail.
We thus investigate the complementary problem of assessing candidate trajectories using
front-facing images, so that a vision-language model (VLM) can assess hard to model risks.
A VLM’s raw safe / unsafe prediction provides no
assurances of low-rate missed collisions, since VLM spatial reasoning can be
unreliable [ 18 ] . Hence, we aim to augment VLMs’ common-sense reasoning with a post-hoc calibration layer providing probabilistic
guarantees on their prediction performance.

Conformal prediction in robotics. Conformal prediction
(CP) transforms approximate predictions into prediction sets with finite-sample guarantees under
exchangeability [ 19 , 1 ] . In
robotics, CP has calibrated: forecasts in dynamic scenes for social navigation [ 9 , 3 ] ; how dynamics uncertainty varies over a system’s
state–action space [ 11 ] ; action uncertainty for Lie-algebraic systems [ 12 ] ; and motion uncertainty across
contact modes [ 13 ] .

In this extended abstract, we propose a monitor calibrating a base VLM safety prediction in a scene-adaptive manner.
Our key contributions are:

We develop Split Label-Localized Conformal Prediction (SLLCP), a post-hoc method over a planner-agnostic generated trajectory image and a frozen VLM backbone, that
provides probabilistic guarantees on a low probability of missing unsafe trajectories.

provides probabilistic guarantees on a low probability of missing unsafe trajectories.

We empirically validate the tradeoff between missed unsafe trajectories and
false alarms on edge-case CARLA scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in the calibration of two open-weight VLMs, using the same hyperparameter set.
