2026-10-05.title: Proprioceptive Sketches as Long-Horizon Intent for Generative Action Policies
2026-10-05.authors: Fangyuan Wang , Songhao Huang , Haoxiang Sun , Shipeng Lyu , Chengyang He , Anqing Duan , Peng Zhou , David Navarro-Alarcon
2026-10-05.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: Generative robot policies predict short action chunks but lack explicit long-horizon intent. Recent methods expose longer-horizon structure through language plans, subgoal images, or video forecasts, which are costly to generate and still need to be translated into robot motion. Predicting future robot motions avoids this translation, but a dense, time-indexed trajectory requires numerous parameters to cover the full remaining task, and over a short horizon it largely repeats the action chunk and adds little guidance for action generation. We propose Proprioceptive Action Models (PAM), which jointly generate a compact, timing-free sketch of the robot’s remaining joint-space path and a dense executable action chunk within a single transformer denoiser. The sketch parameterizes the path by arc length rather than time, capturing geometric intent invariant to execution timing. Block-causal attention and a staggered denoising schedule maintain directed sketch-to-action dependence, ensuring the action tokens condition on a progressively cleaner sketch throughout sampling. In simulation, PAM improves over its action-only counterparts on Push-T and LIBERO-Long; on four real-world bimanual tasks, it raises success from 47.5% to 75.0%. Project page: https://nicehiro.github.io/pam_dp/ .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Generative action policies have become a dominant paradigm for visuomotor robot control, producing temporally coherent commands through action chunking ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Reuss et al., 2025 ) . Despite strong performance on short-horizon tasks, these policies remain less effective on long-horizon manipulation ( Fan et al., 2025 ) . One approach to this challenge is to guide action prediction with visual forecasts ( Black et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) , predictive scene latents ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , or language-based plans and reasoning ( Wen et al., 2025 ; Zawalski et al., 2025 ) . These representations capture anticipated scene evolution or semantic task structure, but can be costly to generate or require additional learned mappings to continuous control. This motivates a compact representation of long-horizon intent closely tied to the robot’s own motion.

Future robot configurations provide a natural representation of the robot’s intended motion. Demonstrations contain synchronized proprioceptive measurements, providing supervision without additional annotation in a space directly related to robot control. Prior work has used robot-motion representations to guide action prediction, including image-plane trajectories ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Niu et al., 2025 ) and predicted end-effector paths ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . However, a dense, time-indexed configuration trajectory over the full remaining task is long and varies in length across demonstrations, making it difficult to represent with a limited number of parameters. Restricting the prediction to a short horizon instead makes it largely redundant with the executable action chunk, so it provides little additional guidance for action generation. An effective intent representation should therefore cover the full remaining motion with a fixed number of parameters while providing information beyond the action chunk.

We introduce the proprioceptive sketch , a compact representation of the robot’s remaining configuration-space path to task completion. The sketch uses arc-length parameterization to remove execution timing and a small number of B-spline coefficients to limit geometric details. In the handoff task in Figure 1 , the sketch describes the arm paths toward the transfer region and around the barrier without specifying motion speed or the duration of the exchange. It provides long-horizon geometric context for predicting a separate, short-horizon action chunk. Only the action chunk is executed, determining the immediate motion and gripper commands.

Proprioceptive Action Models (PAM) jointly generate the sketch and an action chunk within a single transformer denoiser. As illustrated in Figure 1 , both outputs are initialized with Gaussian noise and refined through iterative denoising. A block-causal attention mask allows action tokens to attend to the sketch while preventing sketch tokens from reading the action stream. Following Diffusion Forcing ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , we train the denoiser with varying corruption levels across the two streams and use a staggered denoising schedule that denoises the sketch ahead of the actions, providing cleaner geometric context for action generation.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate the proprioceptive sketch, a compact, timing-free representation of the remaining configuration-space path that serves as an explicit intermediate variable for action generation and is, by construction, invariant to temporal reparameterization of the demonstrated path. Second, we develop a joint generator with directed attention and staggered denoising to guide action prediction with the sketch. Third, we apply PAM to a diffusion transformer trained from scratch (PAM-DP), and a pretrained vision-language-action model (PAM-VLA). We evaluate PAM-DP on Push-T and four real-world bimanual tasks, and PAM-VLA on LIBERO-Long.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Predictive intermediate representations. Intermediate predictions provide action policies with information about intended behavior. Language-based approaches express task structure through subtask descriptions or reasoning traces ( Wen et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025a ; Zawalski et al., 2025 ) . Visual approaches use future images or video to represent goal configurations and scene evolution ( Black et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) . Other methods learn predictive representations of scene dynamics or visuomotor behavior in latent space ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . These representations describe the task rather than the robot’s own motion, and they are either expensive to generate or require a learned decoder to reach continuous control. PAM instead predicts intended motion as a configuration-space path, which requires no annotation beyond recorded proprioception.

Robot-motion representations. Robot motion provides an intermediate representation for planning and control. Hierarchical reinforcement learning uses state-space subgoals to guide lower-level policies ( Nachum et al., 2018 ) . RT-Trajectory conditions action prediction on image-plane trajectory sketches ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , while TraceVLA supplies visual traces of past motion ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Predictive approaches use future motion in different ways. GeoPredict supervises future keypoint prediction during training ( Qian et al., 2026 ) , whereas OASIS predicts end-effector trajectories that condition a separate action decoder ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Recent spline policies similarly parameterize executable action trajectories with spline coefficients ( Tian et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . PAM likewise predicts future robot motion but differs in three respects: the sketch spans the remaining path to task completion, it removes execution timing through arc-length parameterization, and it is generated jointly with actions in a single denoiser.

Joint generation and denoising schedules. Joint world-action models generate actions together with predicted images, video, or scene representations ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026a ) . Trajectory-diffusion methods instead generate state-action plans ( Janner et al., 2022 ) from which actions are recovered through inverse dynamics ( Ajay et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion Forcing introduces independent token-level corruption during training, enabling flexible denoising schedules at inference ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . PAM draws on these joint-generation and scheduling principles to couple a non-executable motion sketch with an executable action chunk. Directed attention allows actions to depend on the sketch without feeding action information back into sketch generation, while staggered denoising lets the sketch become cleaner ahead of the actions.

2026-10-05.title: CSIR: Contextually and Socially Informed Robots for Efficient Person Goal Navigation
2026-10-05.authors: Tyler Chung , Nahl Farhan , Hao Zhang , Mingfeng Yuan , Jinjun Shan , Amy Wu , Yue Hu
2026-10-05.abstract:
We address the Person Goal Navigation (PersonNav) problem, enabling robots to search for people under realistic constraints on information accessibility and language uncertainty. This tackles the current solutions revolving around rigid person finding systems requiring exact knowledge of the individual for item-delivery in indoor settings. While the focus in literature is on learned methods using unavailable public or sparse data due to human privacy. We propose a planning framework that combines distance and semantic information about the recipient (habits and intent) weighted by the trust of the user-provided information. A synthetic benchmark of scenarios is also developed including actors, items, and requests to evaluate performance before real-world deployment aiming to simulate natural language human-robot interactions.
Results show our informed search outperforms classical distance-based graph baselines, while semantics alone lead to ungrounded, sporadic search. Our method achieves strong gains over baselines, with an LLM-based variant performing comparably, and its explicit belief representation naturally supports future Bayesian filtering. Hardware tests demonstrate our method supports real-world embodiment able to leverage between semantic and distance information in a real setting. This work moves toward more intelligent mobile service agents capable of human-like, informed search in realistic environments to be leveraged in day-to-day use. https://anonymous.4open.science/r/personnav-site-4ED2/index.html .
2026-10-05.introduction:
About one in three physicians experience burnout interfering with not only their well being but ability to provide quality care for others [ 1 ] . As result of the working conditions, this has led to an increase in burnout, health issues, and errors in medical practice [ 2 ] . To alleviate staffing pressure, nursing robots are used to automate item-delivery tasks [ 3 ] , with platforms such as MOXI or TUG use voice or graphical interfaces to schedule and design routes for transportation in hospitals [ 3 ] . One limitation is that current tools require fixed location scheduling to deliver items, but people are dynamic, not bounded to locations as they are goal driven. This realizes the problem that these solutions lack the capability to perform its tasked when the assumption that people are static fail. Moving away from fixed location settings and towards dynamic goal-driven people raises the question of “How can robots find people given partial observations of their behaviours and the environment”, we define this problem space as Person Goal Navigation (PersonNav). While this is motivated by the healthcare landscape, this problem expands to other tasks ranging from food delivery, office supply transportation, to nursing home monitoring.

This paper proposes the development of a travel efficient PersonNav framework for indoor item-delivery tasks under limited and uncertain information about the recipient (whom we want to deliver to). Our proposed task space for PersonNav is catered to real-world feasibility in indoor item-delivery scenarios, where a user requests the agent to deliver an item to a recipient (consented information to the robot). Current methods in literature require critical pieces of information from human-activity logs [ 4 ] or daily schedules [ 5 ] , but are partially or fully unavailable in the real-world due to privacy reasons. The current gap is that existing methods leverage critical and sensitive information without consideration of realistic information availability. To address this problem, our work aimed to investigate methods to extrapolate a person’s location from natural language requests and handle information uncertainty (e.g. Low: “They might be at …” vs High: “They’re definitely at …”). We hypothesized that by using several weaker/indirect signals of the person’s whereabouts, we can improve search under uncertain information gains for efficient indoor item-delivery tasks while abiding by real-world constraints in human privacy. The contributions of this paper are:

Contextually and Socially Informed Robots (CSIR) , that addresses the PersonNav problem aimed to perform efficiency item-delivery tasks under varying linguistic uncertainty.

2026-10-05.related_work:
# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav)

The PersonNav problem space is inspired by the Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) field where an agent navigates in an unseen environment to find a requested object [ 6 ] . The methods deployed can range from end-to-end methods for navigating the environment to zero-shot methods that leverage pre-trained semantic models to inform search such as Large Language Models (LLMs) [ 6 ] . LLMs are trained on a massive corpus of human text information and hence developed a causal understanding of the human world semantically [ 7 ] . This helps informing search by leveraging priors using zero-shot methods to infer object locations (e.g. food can normally be found in the kitchen). The difference between ObjectNav and PersonNav is that the former focuses on static object search while the latter on goal-driven people search requiring a different set of observations to inform search.

## II-B Probabilistic and Semantic-Based Person Finding

Literature on person finding tasks exploits information such as activity logs or schedules and fall under the categories of behaviour-based search, spatio-temporal search, and semantic-based exploration. Behavioural search uses a human activity schedule (probabilities of being in different locations at a given time). This frames the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [ 8 ] and uses a learned policy leveraging activity, last known location, distance, and field-of-view to explore optimal frontiers [ 9 ] . For spatio-temporal search, [ 4 ] uses spatial affordance maps to learn where a person is using a Poisson distribution which maps human activity during the day to optimize encounters to the person in an office environment. Semantic-based exploration is similar to ObjectNav methods, using the person’s behaviour and schedule through natural language prompts to explore a set of waypoints on a map to search for a recipient [ 5 ] . In general these methods requires information such as human-activity logs or daily schedules that are not fully or at all available in the real-world for privacy concerns, making real-world deployment in public settings challenging. Therefore, further methods are required to extrapolate indirect observations of a person’s behaviour to inform person search while under ethical constraints.

2026-10-05.title: Around the World: Unified Learned Locomotion on a 270 g Continuous-Rotation Quadruped
2026-10-05.authors: Arturo Flores Alvarez , Nathan Lintu , Dennis Hong
2026-10-05.comment: including appendices. Project website: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Closed-loop learned locomotion is established on commercial quadrupeds
but remains uncommon at the sub-kilogram scale. Continuous-rotation
legs give MiNI-Q, a 270 g 270\text{\,}\mathrm{g} quadruped, access to supporting
configurations on either side of the body. We exploit this range with
a single posture-conditioned reinforcement-learning policy that runs
entirely onboard. A continuous joint-space reference on the torus T 8 T^{8} and its gravity-conditioned transformation connect upright
walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery without state machines
or phase switching. Coordinated posture and release curricula train
this behavior family; identified actuation, cross-engine validation,
and embedded execution support hardware transfer. The same
sub-100k-parameter network tracks forward velocity with RMSE of 0.037 m s − 1 0.037\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} upright and 0.050 m s − 1 0.050\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} inverted, resumes walking in 24 of 30
release trials, and operates with four interchangeable foot geometries
across four indoor surfaces. Hardware experiments and simulation
ablations connect these capabilities to the representation,
conditioning, and training choices that exploit the platform’s motion
range. Demonstration videos and supplementary material are available
on the project website: https://submissionreview.github.io/around-the-world/ .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion and diverse
behaviors on quadruped robots [ 13 , 34 , 27 ] .
At the sub-kilogram scale, learned locomotion remains less
established [ 15 , 1 ] . Small, low-cost
quadrupeds are widely available for educational and research use, but
closed-loop learned control with sim-to-real transfer at this mass is
comparatively rare. The closest sibling platforms in this class,
MiNI-Q [ 20 ] and Q8bot [ 41 ] , have been
reported as hardware introductions or under open-loop control.
MiNI-Q is a 270 g 270\text{\,}\mathrm{g} quadruped whose eight belt-driven joints
rotate without mechanical stops. This range permits supporting leg
configurations on either side of the body and continuous changes of
stance.

That topology has two consequences for control. First, each joint
lives on the circle S 1 S^{1} rather than a bounded interval, so the joint
space is the torus T 8 = ( S 1 ) 8 T^{8}=(S^{1})^{8} . One policy can therefore represent
inverted gaits, mid-flight repositioning, and interpolated postures
that joint limits would exclude. Second, the platform is modular
enough that reprinting lower links, swapping foot geometries, and
reflashing compute are part of ordinary laboratory iteration. These
properties also introduce specific challenges. Unbounded joints break
standard observation pipelines at ± π \pm\pi . The 270 g 270\text{\,}\mathrm{g} mass
sits near simulator integration regimes where effort-mode and
position-mode actuation diverge, and the lower links weigh only 1 g 1\text{\,}\mathrm{g} each. The belt drive introduces measurable backlash, the
onboard compute is a pair of microcontrollers linked over
I 2 C rather than a single processor, and printed foot
geometry varies with manufacturing tolerance and wear.

On this miniature platform, learning must turn the continuous-rotation
range into a controller that follows posture and velocity commands,
repositions its legs during a fall, and resumes walking after contact.
Periodic joint representations and training across postures and
release conditions connect these behaviors. Hardware deployment
further requires transfer to the dynamics of the geared servos,
lightweight links, and interchangeable feet within the robot’s onboard
sensing and compute budget.

The published MiNI-Q platform demonstrates inverted mobility using
precomputed trajectories [ 20 ] . We exploit its leg
symmetry to connect these behaviors in one closed-loop policy. To our
knowledge, this is the first demonstration on a sub-kilogram quadruped
of a single learned policy, executed entirely on onboard
microcontrollers, that unifies upright and inverted locomotion,
continuous posture conditioning, and landing recovery.
Our contributions are:

Unified locomotion and recovery across body orientations. A gravity-conditioned reference exploits the leg symmetry to connect
upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery in one
policy, with periodic observations and a release curriculum. No
state machines or phase switching are used; a compact network runs
entirely onboard at 50 Hz 50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} .

Continuous posture conditioning during locomotion. A continuous joint-space command on T 8 T^{8} represents stance, body
attitude, and interpolated references, including their inverted
counterparts, while the same policy follows a velocity command. An
interpolation curriculum reaches intermediate postures that are
never presented as discrete training targets.

Onboard transfer across foot geometries. Foot-shape randomization, identified actuation, and embedded execution
support the same trained policy across tested foot variants and
surfaces without retraining, connecting the formulation to a modular
miniature robot.

Each contribution is evaluated in Section VI and
ablated in Section VI-G . The supporting identification,
validation, and onboard inference pipeline is detailed in
Sections III – IV and
Appendix A .
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

MiNI-Q [ 20 ] and Q8bot [ 41 ] explore
miniature quadruped mechanisms and electronics. Stanford
Doggo [ 18 ] and Pupper [ 19 ] provide accessible platforms for dynamic locomotion and benchmarking.
Jabbour et al. [ 15 ] deploy learned walking on
Petoi Bittle using an onboard Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. TinyRL studies
compressed Bittle policies in simulation [ 1 ] ;
learned source seeking has been
executed on a nano-drone microcontroller [ 7 ] .
RLtools [ 8 ] , ARM-oriented
CMSIS-NN [ 22 ] , and related onboard inference
tooling [ 32 ] address efficient learning and neural
inference under embedded resource limits. Closed-loop learned control
on sub-kilogram quadrupeds remains uncommon; most published results
report open-loop motion replay or off-board policy execution. We study
continuous-rotation behaviors with the entire policy running on a
dual-microcontroller stack and no off-board compute in the loop.

Massively parallel simulation and proximal policy
optimization [ 35 , 26 , 31 , 40 , 34 ] have made data-efficient training of locomotion policies routine.
Learning and optimization have enabled quadruped locomotion over
challenging terrain [ 17 , 11 ] .
Actuator and contact modeling [ 38 , 13 , 14 ] support sim-to-real reinforcement learning [ 24 ] ,
with demonstrations on bipeds as well as
quadrupeds [ 42 , 37 ] .
Energy-based reward shaping [ 10 ] and concurrent state
estimation [ 16 ] address gait emergence and
imperfect observations. Rapid motor adaptation [ 21 ] and domain randomization [ 39 , 33 ] also support transfer in dexterous
manipulation [ 2 , 12 ] .
Perception-aware locomotion [ 30 , 25 ] and recent surveys [ 9 ] cover the heavier mass class.
We reuse standard learning components and apply identified servo
dynamics and randomized feet to transfer the posture and recovery
formulation at sub-kilogram scale.

Walk These Ways [ 27 ] and
AllGaits [ 3 ] encode families of locomotion
behaviors, while ManyQuadrupeds [ 36 ] studies one policy across robot morphologies. Learned locomotion also
supports rapid running [ 29 ] , agility
benchmarks [ 5 ] , and
parkour [ 6 ] . Perceptive systems extend the motion
repertoire through terrain-aware walking [ 30 ] and
visually guided jumping [ 28 ] . Hierarchical or
recovery-specific controllers such as ANYmal
recovery [ 23 ] target the fall–recover–walk regime
with separate behavior policies. We study one posture-conditioned
policy that resumes walking in either body orientation after landing,
without a separate recovery controller.

Those behavior-family methods operate on bounded-joint quadrupeds and
constrain the command set to the kinematically reachable subspace.
Conditioning on T 8 T^{8} is a natural fit for a platform whose joints are
unbounded. Wheeled-legged robots exploit continuous actuator rotation
for hybrid locomotion [ 4 ] , and the
published MiNI-Q platform demonstrates inverted mobility using
precomputed trajectories [ 20 ] . Closely related
miniature quadrupeds such as Q8bot [ 41 ] and Stanford
Pupper [ 19 ] retain conventional bounded revolute
joints. Here, an eight-joint posture reference specifies stance and
body attitude on a fixed robot. Its periodic representation and
gravity-conditioned transformation let the same command interface
describe upright and inverted configurations. Continuous rotation
admits references that joint limits can exclude, while conditioning
represents them within one policy. The foot-swap study then tests the
controller under physical changes to contact geometry.

2026-10-05.title: RoboBridge: A Self-Evolving Embodied Agent Framework for Sim-to-Real Transfer
2026-10-05.authors: Chenxi Li , Zhangrui Zhao , Rui Li , Yuan Gao , Kehui Liu , Jiarui Li , Dong Wang , Tong Si , Minting Pan , Wanli Ouyang , Dongzhan Zhou
2026-10-05.abstract: A key challenge in bringing embodied intelligence into the real world is transferring capabilities from simulation to reality and enabling agents to continually adapt after deployment. End-to-end vision-language-action policies provide strong manipulation capabilities, but their transfer to physical environments typically relies on calibrating simulated visual and dynamical conditions, collecting additional target-domain demonstrations, and optimizing the policy through further training. Tool-using embodied agents offer flexible task orchestration, yet existing systems primarily emphasize task execution and experience reuse within a given environment, with limited support for transferring procedural knowledge and continuously adapting it across simulation and reality. We propose RoboBridge, a framework that treats sim-to-real transfer as the continued adaptation of executable task skills. The agent represents task knowledge as procedures connecting task intent, observations, tool operations, and outcome verification. Interaction feedback is used to generate candidate skill revisions, which are evaluated before being persisted or rejected. A pretrained vision-language-action policy is exposed as a reusable action tool and enhanced with inference-time guidance, enabling fine-grained execution without retraining the underlying policy. RoboBridge grounds transferable skills in task semantics and interaction interfaces shared across simulation and reality. This representation preserves reusable task structure while allowing environment-dependent operations to be selectively revised through real-world execution feedback. We evaluate the framework on LIBERO-PRO and corresponding physical tasks, studying both skill evolution and post-transfer adaptation. Our framework provides a route from one-shot policy deployment to continual procedural learning across environments.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Reliable sim-to-real transfer requires robotic systems to preserve task performance across differences in visual observations and physical dynamics ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) .
End-to-end vision-language-action models provide fine-grained manipulation capabilities by mapping visual observations and language instructions to action sequences ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . The policy-centered pathway illustrated in Figure 1 includes adapting simulation conditions using real-world experience ( Chebotar et al., 2018 ) . For pretrained VLA models, adaptation to new robotic settings commonly involves target-domain demonstrations and policy fine-tuning ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . In this formulation, task knowledge is largely embedded in model parameters and learned action distributions. This makes it difficult to isolate a reusable task procedure and selectively revise it when execution conditions change, tying procedural adaptation closely to policy optimization.

Tool-using embodied agents offer a way to make task procedures explicit ( Singh et al., 2022 ; Rana et al., 2023 ) . An agent harness provides the observation and tool interfaces through which the agent organizes subtasks, invokes operations, and verifies their outcomes ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . Successful procedures can then be retained as skills for subsequent execution ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . Feedback-based memory updates and skill refinement extend this reuse across interactions ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , and recent robotic systems further incorporate repair validation and validation-gated skill updates ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) . Sim-to-real deployment requires these mechanisms to govern which parts of a transferred procedure remain applicable and how the others should be refined using target-environment feedback. Meanwhile, task decomposition and tool selection still require an underlying capability to execute continuous, fine-grained manipulation ( Yu et al., 2023 ) . Recent harnesses address this execution requirement by exposing frozen VLA policies as reusable manipulation primitives ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . This perspective motivates a framework that combines revisable task knowledge with the manipulation capabilities of pretrained policies.

We propose RoboBridge, a self-evolving embodied agent framework for sim-to-real transfer of procedural skills. RoboBridge incorporates a pretrained VLA policy as a reusable action tool within an agent harness. The policy supplies short manipulation segments, while the agent determines how these operations are organized, when they should be invoked, and whether their outcomes satisfy the task. Task knowledge is stored as procedural skills connecting intent, observations, tool operations, and outcome verification. This organization preserves pretrained execution capabilities while exposing task procedures for revision through interaction. As illustrated in Figure 1 , skills evolved in simulation are reused in reality through aligned task semantics and interaction interfaces, with action tools instantiated for each environment. Real-world execution feedback then supports continued skill adaptation. Effective transfer requires both reliable revision of the transferred procedures and accurate execution of their local operations.

Reliable execution presents a complementary challenge: even a suitable task procedure can fail when a frozen policy produces actions that do not meet the current subtask requirements ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . Prior work has explored adapting pretrained policy behavior during inference through external guidance or verification ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . RoboBridge therefore augments the policy tool with inference-time guidance. The agent determines whether guidance is needed and configures a reward specification from the subtask objective, execution constraints, and observed feedback. This reward steers action generation toward the intended operation while keeping the policy parameters fixed. Skill evolution thus adjusts the procedure across episodes, while inference-time guidance adapts action generation within an invocation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A self-evolving framework for procedural sim-to-real transfer. We integrate pretrained action capabilities with explicit task skills, enabling procedures evolved in simulation to be reused through aligned interaction interfaces and further adapted from real-world feedback.

Controlled skill evolution. We develop a feedback-driven process for adding, revising, and deleting procedural knowledge, with validation governing which updates are persisted and which are rejected or rolled back.

Adaptive policy-tool orchestration. We enable the agent to determine when to invoke the pretrained policy, when to activate inference-time guidance, and how to configure subtask rewards, supporting context-dependent execution with frozen policy parameters.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 End-to-End Embodied Models

End-to-end embodied models learn to map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions. Early systems such as RT-1 ( Brohan et al., 2022 ) and RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) established this paradigm, while later models expanded its scope through embodied multimodal reasoning, multi-robot datasets, and generalist policies, including PaLM-E ( Driess et al., 2023 ) , Open X-Embodiment ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) , Octo ( Team et al., 2024 ) , OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) . These models improve generalization by increasing the diversity of training tasks, observations, robot embodiments, and demonstrations, but their behavior remains primarily encoded in a fixed policy. To address the gap between simulation and physical deployment, existing approaches increase the diversity of simulated observations ( Tobin et al., 2017 ) , perturb simulated dynamics ( Peng et al., 2018 ) , or adapt the simulator distribution using informative variations and posterior estimation ( Mehta et al., 2020 ; Muratore et al., 2022 ) . Recent data-centric methods further scale simulated experiences and adaptation data to improve transfer across tasks and robot embodiments ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , while inference-time steering adjusts a frozen policy during execution ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . These approaches use a single end-to-end policy to map observations and instructions to actions, leaving adaptation coupled to the policy itself. Our framework instead uses an agent to organize reusable skills and invoke action tools, so the transferred procedure can be revised in the target environment without retraining the entire policy.

## 2.2 Embodied Agents

Embodied-agent research introduces explicit reasoning, tool use, and feedback into robotic execution. Early systems grounded language in executable affordances and used environment feedback for closed-loop planning ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2022 ) , while program-based approaches synthesized control logic or composed spatial value functions for manipulation ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent work explored skill bootstrapping, lifelong skill libraries, and open-vocabulary adaptation through interaction and memory ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Tziafas and Kasaei, 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Recent systems have further studied workflow reasoning, self-directed skill acquisition, feedback-based repair, and continual adaptation in simulated or physical environments ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Nie et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Lei et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . These studies show that explicit procedures, persistent memory, and execution feedback can extend embodied reasoning beyond direct policy execution. Their primary focus, however, varies between workflow planning, skill discovery, memory expansion, and runtime self-improvement. Our work focuses on the migration process itself: a skill is treated as a revisable task hypothesis, and feedback from the target environment determines which parts of the transferred procedure should be retained, modified, or removed.

2026-10-05.title: RoboChemGym: A Protocol-Driven Generative Simulation Framework for Long-Horizon Chemical Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Chenxi Li , Haiyuan Wan , Rui Li , Jingyuan Li , Sha Zhang , Bohan Feng , Jianbao Cao , Zhangrui Zhao , Di Hu , Wangmeng Zuo , Shixiang Tang , Minting Pan , Dongzhan Zhou
2026-10-05.abstract: Wet-lab experimentation serves as the gold standard for hypothesis verification in scientific discovery; yet it is inherently labor-intensive, costly, and safety-critical. Embodied agents hold the promise of automating these tedious workflows, but their development is hindered by the scarcity of real-world training data. While simulation offers a scalable alternative for producing demonstrations, current methods primarily target relatively short-horizon tasks with loosely structured interactions, failing to meet the strict procedural constraints and fine-grained manipulation demands of chemical experiments. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboChemGym , a framework that autonomously generates high-fidelity manipulation demonstrations aligned with real-world experiment protocols, featuring a self-improving task synthesis mechanism to iteratively refine task execution and scene configurations, enabling the reliable generation of expert trajectories for complex, multi-object protocols exceeding 10 interaction steps. Furthermore, we introduce a hierarchical benchmark that systematically assesses performance across varying granularities, spanning from atomic operations to full-cycle experimental workflows. RoboChemGym sets a scalable paradigm for the automated data synthesis and capability evaluation of embodied agents in intricate chemical tasks, serving as a critical stepping stone toward fully intelligent laboratories.

2026-10-05.title: AdaTempo: Learning Shared Relative Tempo from Demonstrations for Faster Robot Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Jiale Cao , Yike Niu , Zhengrong Xue , Huazhe Xu
2026-10-05.abstract:
Visuomotor policies trained via imitation learning
often inherit the unnecessarily slow timing of teleoperated
demonstrations. Yet uniform speedup is unreliable because
different phases of a manipulation task tolerate acceleration
differently. In this work, we introduce AdaTempo, a self-supervised method that accelerates visuomotor policies by exploiting shared relative-tempo structure in demonstrations. AdaTempo establishes phase correspondence, aggregates the aligned relative tempo into a consensus, and maps it to a continuous speedup profile used to resample demonstrations into accelerated training trajectories. Training
standard policies such as ACT or Diffusion Policy on these
resampled trajectories directly embeds the desired tempo in the
learned behavior, without runtime tempo selection or online
retiming. Extensive evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves
up to a 3.57 × 3.57\times speedup and yields a stronger success–speed trade-off than the original policies and representative acceleration baselines.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Visuomotor imitation learning has become a practical paradigm for acquiring
complex manipulation skills from teleoperated
demonstrations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Recent
large-scale policies have further improved generalization across tasks and
robot embodiments [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Yet standard imitation
objectives optimize what actions to reproduce, not how quickly they should be
executed. Since teleoperated demonstrations are often slow and cautious, the
resulting policies tend to inherit this conservative execution
timing [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

Removing this inefficiency is not as simple as downsampling the demonstrated
trajectories by a constant rate. Different phases of a manipulation task
tolerate acceleration differently. Uniform acceleration can skip important
intermediate states, alter the closed-loop state distribution, or request
motions that the controller cannot track over the shortened time
horizon [ 8 , 10 , 11 ] . Effective
speedup therefore requires determining both how much to accelerate a task and
how to distribute that acceleration over its progress.

Recent work has made substantial progress in accelerating learned manipulation
policies beyond demonstration
speed [ 7 , 9 , 8 , 10 , 11 ] . However, existing methods typically determine
how acceleration should vary using policy-derived proxies,
interaction-based optimization, or additional runtime mechanisms, requiring auxiliary machinery during training or deployment. This motivates a
central question: can demonstrations themselves provide a direct and
fine-grained supervisory signal for phase-dependent speedup?

As illustrated in Fig. , our key observation is that
demonstrations may differ in absolute speed yet
tend to exhibit similar relative-tempo patterns over task progress, consistent
with prior observations of approximate relative-timing invariance in skilled
movement [ 12 ] . Rather than absolute speed, we focus on
relative tempo: within each demonstration, which phases are executed relatively
faster or slower? When corresponding phases exhibit similar relative tempo
across demonstrations, this consistency suggests phase-specific task
characteristics. Phases consistently executed more cautiously, such as
grasping or insertion, may tolerate less temporal compression, while relatively
fast phases such as free-space transport offer greater acceleration potential.

Based on this insight, we introduce AdaTempo , a self-supervised method
for learning cross-demonstration relative tempo to accelerate visuomotor policies. AdaTempo aligns demonstrations with different durations, constructs
episode-relative tempo profiles at corresponding task phases, and aggregates
them into a cross-demonstration consensus while downweighting phases with high
disagreement. It maps this consensus to a continuous speedup profile used
for smooth virtual-time resampling of the original trajectories. A standard visuomotor policy, such as ACT or Diffusion Policy (DP), is then trained on the
accelerated trajectories. The desired tempo is thus embedded directly in the
learned behavior, requiring no runtime tempo-selection module, online retiming,
or changes to the control interface at deployment.

Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves
up to a 3.57 × 3.57\times speedup over demonstrations and yields a stronger
success–speed trade-off than the original policies and representative
acceleration baselines. Our contributions are:

We identify shared relative tempo across demonstrations as a self-supervised cue for phase-dependent speedup, revealing recurring phase-wise timing structure beyond demonstrator-specific absolute speed.

We develop AdaTempo, which phase-aligns demonstrations, converts their relative-tempo consensus into a continuous speedup profile for offline virtual-time resampling, without auxiliary models or additional mechanisms at deployment.

We validate AdaTempo across 11 simulated and real-world manipulation tasks with ACT or DP, achieving up to a 3.57 × 3.57\times speedup and a stronger success–speed trade-off than representative acceleration baselines.

1. We identify shared relative tempo across demonstrations as a self-supervised cue for phase-dependent speedup, revealing recurring phase-wise timing structure beyond demonstrator-specific absolute speed.

2. We develop AdaTempo, which phase-aligns demonstrations, converts their relative-tempo consensus into a continuous speedup profile for offline virtual-time resampling, without auxiliary models or additional mechanisms at deployment.

3. We validate AdaTempo across 11 simulated and real-world manipulation tasks with ACT or DP, achieving up to a 3.57 × 3.57\times speedup and a stronger success–speed trade-off than representative acceleration baselines.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Visuomotor Imitation Learning

Modern visuomotor policies learn temporally coherent manipulation behaviors
through action chunking, generative sequence modeling, and increasingly
large-scale multi-task training [ 13 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 14 , 15 , 4 , 5 , 16 , 6 , 17 , 18 ] . These methods typically train on the temporal sampling
provided by demonstrations and can therefore reproduce not only demonstrated
motions but also their execution tempo [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Orthogonal work reduces
policy inference latency through distillation, efficient generative modeling,
or asynchronous action generation [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . AdaTempo instead targets physical task execution time by temporally resampling demonstrations before policy training.

## II-B Acceleration of Imitation Learning Execution

Existing approaches accelerate manipulation policies either by modifying policy execution at runtime or by altering demonstrations and training targets before deployment.

Runtime methods advance within action chunks, select speed multipliers, or
retime commands based on motion complexity, tracking error, latency, or
physical reachability [ 23 , 9 , 8 , 10 , 24 ] . Related approaches expose
speed explicitly through variable-frequency conditioning or continuous action
parameterizations that can be adjusted at
deployment [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . While
effective for adapting frozen policies or enabling on-demand speed control,
these approaches require additional mechanisms to select execution
speed at runtime. Some, such as SpeedTuning, further learn speed selection
through reinforcement learning and environment
interaction [ 9 ] .

Another family of methods accelerates policy execution by modifying the temporal structure of demonstrations or training targets before deployment. DemoSpeedup estimates conditional action entropy with a proxy generative policy
and assigns different downsampling factors to the resulting trajectory
segments [ 7 ] . Semantic approaches instead use
vision–language reasoning, gripper–object relations, or propagated stage
labels to identify regions that can be accelerated, while motion-frequency
cues have been used to remove temporally redundant
frames [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] . AutoSpeed optimizes
over smoothly speed-transformed action targets using a prediction-error and
horizon criterion, whereas SpeedAug combines variable-tempo augmentation with
reinforcement-learning refinement [ 31 , 11 ] . However, these methods typically rely on auxiliary signals or objectives to
determine where and how much to accelerate. In contrast, AdaTempo derives a
continuous speedup signal directly from relative-tempo structure
shared across demonstrations and incorporates it through temporally resampled training data.

## II-C Temporal Correspondence and Relative Tempo

Temporal alignment enables comparison between demonstrations that follow
similar task progress with different durations. Dynamic time warping (DTW)
constructs a monotone correspondence between sequences [ 32 ] and has been used to align demonstrations before extracting or transferring
skill structure [ 33 ] . In acceleration work, ESPADA uses
DTW to propagate semantic stage labels from an annotated trajectory to other
demonstrations [ 28 ] . Complementary evidence from motor-control
studies indicates that skilled movements can retain relative timing and
normalized velocity structure under changes in execution
speed [ 12 , 34 , 35 , 36 ] . This observation motivates comparing demonstrations in
a normalized temporal coordinate rather than by their absolute execution
speeds. AdaTempo uses DTW not to propagate predefined labels, but to establish
correspondences across demonstrations, enabling relative tempo to be compared
at matched task progress. Recurring cross-demonstration relative-tempo
structure is then used to derive a continuous speedup profile.

2026-10-05.title: GeoScaffold: Learning Compact Geometric Latents via Reconstruction for Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
2026-10-05.authors: Yixuan Jiang , Wentong Li , An Liu , Zihao Xin , Fulin Tang , Cong Leng , Yang Gao , Jian Cheng
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-05.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adopt streaming Video-LLM policies that map egocentric RGB observations and instructions directly to low-level actions. Yet these policies inherit weak 3D geometric priors from 2D pretraining. Existing geometry-aware extensions charge a persistent inference-time price: depth sensors, 3D encoders, or per-step perception tool calls. We propose GeoScaffold, a geometric supervision framework that pays this price once, at training time, by internalizing geometry into the policy itself. It first learns a compact depth tokenizer on depth maps from the training trajectories and freezes it. It then fine-tunes the policy with a handful of learnable geometry query tokens, training their hidden states to reconstruct navigation-critical geometry such as depth, connectivity, and traversability. This supervision turns the query states into compact geometric latents for action decoding, and through the shared weights also internalizes geometry into the backbone’s own representations. Like a scaffold, the tokenizer, target generators, and reconstruction heads are discarded after training, leaving the backbone and action interface unchanged. Extensive experiments show that GeoScaffold consistently outperforms leading vision-only navigators on continuous VLN benchmarks, offering a practical paradigm for lightweight edge deployment of spatially aware embodied navigation models.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions while moving through a previously unseen environment ( Anderson et al., 2018 ; Ku et al., 2020 ; Krantz et al., 2020 ) . Recent progress has increasingly moved VLN toward an end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm, in which a Video-LLM policy maps egocentric RGB observations and the instruction to navigation actions step by step ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Xin et al., 2026b ) . However, the backbones underlying these policies are pretrained almost entirely on internet-scale 2D data, which makes them strong at semantic recognition yet weak at metric and topological reasoning ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Navigation demands exactly these abilities. Beyond recognizing objects and matching them to linguistic landmarks, an agent must reason about free space, relative scale, doorway structure, and route connectivity. These policies therefore struggle with depth-sensitive decisions, such as judging whether a landmark is nearby, whether a passage is traversable, or whether to continue exploring rather than stop prematurely.

Existing methods compensate for this weakness with additional machinery at inference time. Geometry-enhanced methods give the policy explicit spatial support, running a frozen 3D encoder alongside the backbone ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) or lifting RGB-D observations into geometry-aware BEV maps ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . As shown in Figure 1 (b), these components remain active at deployment, with depth sensors adding hardware requirements and 3D encoders increasing GPU memory usage and inference latency. Other methods restructure the system, adopting dual-system designs in which a slow reasoning module guides a fast controller ( Wei et al., 2026 ; Intern Robotics, 2025 ; Xue et al., 2026 ) or zero-shot pipelines of LLM planners, perception, and path-planning components ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Long et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Such designs require coordination among multiple modules, complicating system integration and deployment.

By contrast, humans act with rich spatial awareness from visual experience alone, without explicit depth sensing at every step. For navigation, such spatial awareness should help the agent judge distances, identify traversable regions, and recognize passages that connect spaces. We therefore ask whether geometric supervision can equip an end-to-end VLA navigator with these abilities during training, while requiring only RGB observations and language instructions at deployment.

To this end, we propose GeoScaffold , a training-only geometric enhancement framework for streaming VLN. GeoScaffold supervises the policy with three geometric targets. Depth captures metric scale, while connectivity and traversability mark route-relevant passages and free space, respectively. The supervision enters through a small set of learnable geometry query tokens ( Carion et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Mu et al., 2023 ; Lai et al., 2024 ) , inserted before each action block, one dedicated group per target. Each group learns to reconstruct its own target from its hidden states. Training proceeds in two stages. Stage I learns a compact depth tokenizer offline. Stage II then fine-tunes the policy with the navigation objective unchanged plus the auxiliary reconstruction losses. This pressure compresses scene geometry into the query hidden states, which act as compact geometric latents for action decoding. After training, all auxiliary modules are discarded. The deployed policy runs on RGB and text alone, with only the learned geometry tokens remaining in the prompt.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce GeoScaffold , a lightweight, removable geometric enhancement framework for efficient end-to-end streaming VLN that requires no depth sensors, 3D encoders, or reconstruction modules at inference time and deploys on edge hardware.

We design a query-token reconstruction objective whose dedicated depth, connectivity, and traversability groups shape their hidden states into compact geometric latents.

We present an empirical study of training-only geometric supervision for VLN, showing consistent success-rate gains across different backbones and in real-world deployment, with only the learned geometry tokens retained at inference.

1. We introduce GeoScaffold , a lightweight, removable geometric enhancement framework for efficient end-to-end streaming VLN that requires no depth sensors, 3D encoders, or reconstruction modules at inference time and deploys on edge hardware.

2. We design a query-token reconstruction objective whose dedicated depth, connectivity, and traversability groups shape their hidden states into compact geometric latents.

3. We present an empirical study of training-only geometric supervision for VLN, showing consistent success-rate gains across different backbones and in real-world deployment, with only the learned geometry tokens retained at inference.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 VLA Model for Navigation

Recent VLN research has increasingly reformulated navigation as an end-to-end vision-language-action problem. Navigators of this kind fine-tune a multimodal language model to map visual observations and the instruction to navigation decisions ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) , inheriting rich visual priors and the commonsense knowledge of the backbone. To run over long trajectories, other work turned the interaction into a streaming multi-turn dialogue whose cached context and compact memory keep the cost of each step bounded ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Xin et al., 2026b ) . Building on these policies, dual-system designs add a slow reasoning module above a fast controller ( Wei et al., 2026 ; Intern Robotics, 2025 ; Xue et al., 2026 ) . However, their backbones are pretrained almost exclusively on 2D web images and videos, so the resulting policies inherit little sense of metric scale or 3D structure, precisely the abilities that navigation requires.

## 2.2 Geometry-Enhanced VLN

A broad line of VLN research addresses this spatial weakness by injecting depth or 3D structure into the agent. These methods make geometry an input to the policy at deployment time, whether through RGB-D or stereo observations ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , 3D-language feature fields and tokens ( Wang & Lee, 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) , map-like memories ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , frozen 3D foundation models ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) such as VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , or agentic perception tools that query occupancy, LiDAR, or depth on demand ( Xin et al., 2026a ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . These designs improve spatial understanding, but the sensors, encoders, maps, or tool calls that supply geometry must stay active at deployment and add latency, memory, or hardware to the robot. GeoScaffold instead uses geometry only as a training-time supervision signal, so the policy learns geometric representations from RGB alone and carries them into deployment as compact latents, with no geometry module on the inference path.

## 2.3 Auxiliary Perception Supervision and Query Tokens

Auxiliary perception supervision enriches visual representations through prediction and reconstruction tasks. Early navigation methods explore depth prediction ( Mirowski et al., 2017 ) and self-supervised reasoning ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) . Recent approaches extend this idea to multimodal LLMs and VLAs: ROSS ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , 3DRS ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , and Spatial Forcing ( Li et al., 2026a ) use visual reconstruction or 3D feature alignment, while DreamVLA ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) predicts future world knowledge for manipulation. Query-based aggregation and special-token readouts, as in DETR ( Carion et al., 2020 ) , BLIP-2 ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and LISA ( Lai et al., 2024 ) , provide compact interfaces for visual prediction. Perception Tokens ( Bigverdi et al., 2025 ) and Perceptio ( Li et al., 2026b ) also explore autoregressive perception-token generation. GeoScaffold uses dedicated query states to reconstruct current-frame depth, connectivity, and traversability during training, learning compact geometric latents for RGB-only streaming navigation.

2026-10-05.title: Who Went Where When on the Lunar Surface: Forensic Trajectory Analysis to Identify Byzantine Rovers
2026-10-05.authors: Lachlan Holden , Feras Dayoub , Melissa de Zwart , David Harvey , Tat-Jun Chin
2026-10-05.comment: accepted to iSpaRo 2026
2026-10-05.abstract: Future planetary surface missions are likely to involve multiple independently operated rovers sharing the same deployment region, raising the need to verify compliance with operational constraints such as Lunar Safety Zones. Because continuous in-situ observability is rarely available, such verification requires post-hoc reconstruction of rover trajectories from sparse telemetry, including odometry, pose priors, and relative inter-rover detections. We introduce the problem of forensic trajectory analysis for non-cooperative planetary rovers in the presence of Byzantine agents: rovers that provide miscalibrated or deliberately falsified measurements to support an incorrect trajectory. We show that standard outlier-robust pose graph optimisation methods are vulnerable in this setting, because Byzantine rovers can generate measurements that are internally consistent and numerous enough to make truthful incriminating measurements appear as outliers. To address this, we propose an attribution-aware trajectory estimation method that reasons over rover credibility rather than individual measurement validity. The method evaluates candidate credible rover subsets by comparing the statistical consistency of their internal and boundary relative detections against provided priors, and then estimates trajectories using only measurements attributed to credible agents. Across synthetic simulations and real planetary-analogue trajectory data, the proposed method identifies Byzantine rovers and produces significantly more accurate trajectory estimates than existing robust pose graph optimisation baselines.
2026-10-05.introduction:
One of the key characteristics of the New Space era of the 21st century is the rise of space missions driven by private companies [ 1 ] . With lunar landings no longer solely the domain of individual nation-states, current and future missions involve the rovers and landers of multiple companies and countries working together in close proximity. This is exemplified by missions like IM-2, which involved multiple US and Japan-based companies [ 12 ] . For successful co-located operation of this kind, efforts like the Artemis Accords [ 21 ] and the Chinese-led International Lunar Research Station [ 23 ] are attempting to establish norms. One relevant provision of the Artemis Accords is that of Lunar Safety Zones, where stakeholders can establish areas where only certain parties may enter.

To be able to determine the compliance of different rovers with protocols like Lunar Safety Zones under the situational awareness constraints typical of planetary missions, a method for post-hoc determining the trajectories that rovers have taken based on relatively low-fidelity downlinked data is essential. This data includes metrics like odometry, map localisation estimates, and relative detections from infrequent images. For the real-world application of these trajectories, it is crucial to design a method that is Byzantine-resilient, which is to say capable of handling agents that are providing poorly calibrated or deliberately misleading data. This work introduces this problem of “forensic trajectory analysis”: post-hoc determination of multi-rover trajectories in the presence of adversarial measurements.

This paper makes three contributions:

We formulate forensic trajectory analysis for non-cooperative planetary rovers as a post-hoc state-estimation problem with Byzantine measurement sources;

We propose an attribution-aware credibility inference method that scores candidate rover subsets using internal consistency and boundary inconsistency of relative detections; and

We demonstrate, using synthetic and planetary-analogue trajectories, that conventional robust pose graph optimisation (PGO) methods can be systematically misled by Byzantine agents, while the proposed method identifies non-credible rovers and improves trajectory reconstruction.

1. We formulate forensic trajectory analysis for non-cooperative planetary rovers as a post-hoc state-estimation problem with Byzantine measurement sources;

2. We propose an attribution-aware credibility inference method that scores candidate rover subsets using internal consistency and boundary inconsistency of relative detections; and

3. We demonstrate, using synthetic and planetary-analogue trajectories, that conventional robust pose graph optimisation (PGO) methods can be systematically misled by Byzantine agents, while the proposed method identifies non-credible rovers and improves trajectory reconstruction.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related work

## II-A Multi-Robot Localisation

One of the key problems in multi-agent robotic systems is that of localisation. While methods for accurate localisation of individual rovers over time exist [ verma.etal.2024_enabling , 13 ] , there has also been considerable investigation into how the relative detections between multiple rovers can be leveraged for even better estimation [ 4 ] .

These kinds of approaches are used as the basis for multi-rover collaborative localisation and mapping (C-SLAM), with key implementations DOOR-SLAM [ 15 ] , Kimera-Multi [ 3 ] , and Swarm-SLAM [ 14 ] . Approaches for especially challenging environments like caves, mines, and planetary surfaces have been developed [ 8 , 2 , 16 ] .

These systems generally assume that robots are cooperative participants in a shared estimation problem, whereas forensic trajectory analysis treats rovers as independently operated sources of evidence whose measurements may not be credible.

## II-B Robust Pose Graph Optimisation

Pose graph optimisation is a form of Bayesian state estimation that is commonly used for SLAM back-ends, especially for state-of-the-art multi-agent SLAM [ 15 , 3 , 8 , 14 ] , with well-known forms for factors representing pose priors, odometry, relative measurements, and loop closures [ 7 ] .

Perceptual aliasing causing loop closure outliers is a key challenge of SLAM. Two primary underlying approaches for outlier-robust PGO are Pairwise Consistency Maximisation (PCM) [ 19 ] , which underpins [ 15 , 8 ] , and Graduated Non-Convexity (GNC) [ 24 ] , which underpins [ 3 , 14 , 2 ] . These are the two methods that we compare against in this paper.

PCM [ 19 ] and variations [ 22 , 9 ] robustly merge two maps with loop closures between them by leveraging graph theory to efficiently find the maximum clique of pairwise-consistent measurements. GNC [ 24 ] is a more general method for robust optimisation of any kind of factor graph, which uses robust cost functions with an iterative solver.

These robust PGO methods are very effective at handling perceptual aliasing and allowing successful SLAM back-end optimisation, but as we discuss further in Sec. III-C , they are insufficient for identifying and rejecting actively misleading information from Byzantine agents.

## II-C Byzantine Robotics

While much of the literature focuses on the cases of cooperative agents working together to solve problems, there is also investigation into resilience against Byzantine agents – those who are adversarial or misleading when participating in multi-agent systems. While Byzantine resilience is relevant to all manner of distributed and networked systems, within robotics it is frequently considered in the context of multi-agent consensus [ 18 , 25 ] or distributed learning [ 5 , 17 ] .

At the specific intersection of Byzantine resilience for robotic localisation, problems like Byzantine detection by comparing against GNSS signals in UAV swarms [ 11 ] , and target and formation tracking [ 6 , 10 ] have been investigated. These works address challenges in an online filtering context and with local, constrained communication and connectivity. This contrasts against our post-hoc, forensic trajectory analysis focus in this paper, which motivates using PGO as our underlying method and hence the comparisons to PCM and GNC.

The closest work we are aware of is by [ 20 ] , which also explicitly considers the problem of Byzantine agents in a SLAM or PGO-based setting. Our work contrasts against theirs in a few key ways: we consider more advanced Byzantine behaviour including groups of consistent, collaborative agents; we use a statistically-motivated criteria for identifying Byzantine agents; we explain and demonstrate the vulnerability of robust PGO to Byzantine attacks; and we include the attribution of measurements and the identification of Byzantine agents as a first-class output of our system.

Taken together, there is a clear gap in the literature: existing multi-robot localisation methods provide the estimation machinery, and robust PGO methods provide measurement-level outlier rejection, but neither addresses adversarial measurement sources that can generate coherent false trajectories. In contrast, Byzantine robotics studies unreliable agents, but rarely in a post-hoc pose-graph reconstruction setting with attributed odometry, pose priors, and relative detections. Our work addresses this gap by treating credibility as a property of rovers rather than individual measurements.

2026-10-05.title: DeltaWorld: Physically Consistent Interactive World Simulators via Action-Conditioned Latent Increment Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Boyuan Hou , Xiaoge Cao , Chaofan Zhang , Shuo Wang , Shaowei Cui
2026-10-05.abstract: Interactive world simulators can provide scalable environments for robot planning, policy training, and evaluation by predicting action consequences while reducing reliance on repeated physical rollouts. To serve these applications, they must generate future image sequences that respond faithfully to robot actions and preserve the dynamics of robot-object interactions over long horizons. However, existing world models typically predict the entire next latent state and often fail to capture subtle changes induced by robot actions. Such omissions can produce physically implausible outcomes, including object interpenetration and excessive deformation. To address this limitation, we propose DeltaWorld, a physically consistent interactive world simulator for robotic manipulation. Our method introduces the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which predicts action-induced latent feature changes and adds them to the current latent state to obtain the next state, rather than predicting the next latent state directly. To mitigate object interpenetration and excessive deformation in predicted future frames, Interaction-aware Latent Alignment is introduced to construct counterfactual interaction regions and supervise interaction-related latent changes. DeltaWorld is evaluated on the IWS manipulation benchmark and a self-collected cross-robot dataset covering multiple robot embodiments and manipulation tasks. On the cross-robot dataset, DeltaWorld reduces FVD by 46.6% and LPIPS by 31.1% relative to the IWS baseline. These results highlight the potential of DeltaWorld for long-horizon action-conditioned video prediction in robotic manipulation.
2026-10-05.introduction:
With the increasing adoption of data-driven approaches in robotic manipulation, real-world robot interaction data have become a fundamental resource for learning complex manipulation behaviors [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . However, policy training, action exploration, and performance evaluation often require repeated physical robot rollouts. These rollouts consume time and hardware resources, limiting the scale and reproducibility of experiments [ 1 , 6 ] . World models offer a promising way to reduce reliance on physical rollouts by learning action-conditioned environment dynamics from existing robot interaction data. Such models can simulate the outcomes of robot actions, thereby supporting planning [ 7 , 8 ] , policy learning, and evaluation [ 9 , 6 , 10 ] . Unlike conventional image prediction models that primarily focus on visual appearance changes, world models for robotic manipulation place greater emphasis on action-conditioned environment evolution, including object motion, robot–object interactions, and long-horizon action consequences [ 11 ] .

To realize action-conditioned prediction, recent work has explored different representations of future robot observations. JEPA-style models forecast learned visual features without directly reconstructing pixels [ 12 , 13 ] . The Interactive World Simulator (IWS) learns action-conditioned dynamics in a compact image latent space and decodes predicted states into video [ 6 ] . In parallel, video-generative world models support interactive evaluation by conditioning future frames on policy-derived latent actions [ 14 ] or on frame-level controls with pose-conditioned memory [ 10 ] . More recently, dWorldEval has modeled observations and actions jointly as discrete tokens, with sparse keyframes to support long-horizon prediction [ 15 ] .

Despite these advances, predicting robot manipulation videos remains difficult when an action changes only a small part of the scene. Most of the image may stay the same between adjacent frames, while a robot action can move an object or alter its shape. Models that directly predict future frames or their latent representations may capture the largely unchanged scene while missing small changes to manipulated objects. The resulting errors can grow during autoregressive rollout and cause object drift or implausible deformation. Therefore, the key challenge is to predict the changes caused by robot actions, especially in regions where the robot interacts with objects.

To address this challenge, we propose DeltaWorld, a physically consistent interactive world simulator that predicts action-induced latent changes instead of the entire next latent state. Our method introduces the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which estimates these changes and adds them to the current latent state to obtain the next state. Interaction-aware Latent Alignment uses counterfactual interaction regions to emphasize changes around robot–object interactions during training. Experiments on the IWS benchmark and a self-collected cross-robot dataset show improved action-conditioned video prediction quality and long-horizon consistency across multiple manipulation tasks and robot embodiments. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose DeltaWorld, an interactive world simulator built on the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which predicts action-conditioned latent increments to update the current state, promoting stable long-horizon prediction and physically plausible interaction dynamics.

We propose DeltaWorld, an interactive world simulator built on the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which predicts action-conditioned latent increments to update the current state, promoting stable long-horizon prediction and physically plausible interaction dynamics.

We introduce Interaction-aware Latent Alignment, which provides structured supervision over task-relevant regions and encourages the simulator to capture the physical regularities underlying object changes rather than appearance-dominated latent transitions.

We conduct systematic evaluations on the IWS manipulation benchmark and a self-collected dataset covering multiple robot embodiments. Experimental results show that DeltaWorld outperforms existing world model baselines across image- and video-level metrics for action-conditioned video prediction, while ablation studies further verify the complementary roles of Delta-LTM and Interaction-aware Latent Alignment.

# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A World Models for Robotic Manipulation

World models have recently emerged as an important research direction in robot learning. By learning predictive models of how the environment evolves under robot actions, robots can internally simulate possible future outcomes, enabling applications such as planning, control, policy steering, and policy evaluation [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 6 , 10 ] . Early and classical world-modeling approaches typically learn environment dynamics in compact state spaces and use the learned models for model-based decision making and control [ 16 , 17 ] . More recently, advances in visual generative modeling have motivated world models that learn action-conditioned environment dynamics directly from high-dimensional visual observations, often through compact latent representations [ 18 , 7 , 6 ] .

Existing visual world models have mainly developed along two representative directions. One line of work leverages visual priors learned by large-scale video generation models to support robotic planning and interaction through future video or visual trajectory generation [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 8 ] . Another line builds action-conditioned predictive models directly from robot interaction data, allowing generated observations to explicitly respond to robot actions and further support interactive rollouts, policy steering, and policy evaluation [ 6 , 10 , 22 ] . These studies indicate that robotic world models are gradually evolving from open-ended visual generation toward interactive environment models that can capture action consequences and interaction outcomes. Nevertheless, effectively modeling action-driven environment state changes in a compact representation space remains a key challenge for achieving stable long-horizon prediction and physically consistent interaction.

## II-B Action-conditioned Latent Dynamics

To avoid long-horizon prediction directly in high-dimensional pixel space, an increasing number of recent studies have explored action-conditioned dynamics in compact latent spaces. These methods typically map visual observations into latent states using pretrained visual encoders, autoencoders, or joint-embedding models, and predict future states from historical latent representations and robot actions [ 7 , 6 , 23 , 24 ] . For example, DINO-WM [ 7 ] directly predicts future patch-level representations based on pretrained visual features, thereby avoiding explicit pixel reconstruction. IWS [ 6 ] adopts a two-stage framework, where an action-conditioned latent dynamics model is learned after freezing the visual autoencoder.

Recent studies have further investigated whether latent dynamics representations truly preserve information relevant to control and interaction. One line of work employs joint-embedding prediction [ 25 ] or task-relevant representation learning [ 12 ] to encourage future latent representations to focus more on state information useful for planning [ 26 ] . Another line of work further leverages predicted latent states, latent subgoals, or action-relevant representations for action generation and policy learning [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] . These studies suggest that, compared with directly generating future observations at the pixel level, modeling action-conditioned environment evolution in latent space [ 32 ] can provide more compact and decision-relevant dynamics representations. However, most existing methods still take future latent states or future visual representations as their primary prediction targets, while explicitly modeling latent state transitions induced by robot actions has received comparatively less attention. In contrast, we focus on the action-conditioned latent transition itself and explicitly model this transition in interaction-relevant regions.

## II-C World Models for Policy Training and Evaluation

Beyond predicting future environment evolution, world models can also serve as interactive surrogate environments that provide scalable data sources for robot policy training. Imitation learning and vision-language-action policies typically rely on large amounts of high-quality real-robot demonstrations, while collecting such data is costly, hardware-dependent, and difficult to scale rapidly. To alleviate this bottleneck, recent studies have begun to use world models as interactive environments for data generation and policy optimization, supporting synthetic interaction trajectory generation, data augmentation, and world-model-based policy training and post-training [ 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 ] . IWS further demonstrates that demonstrations can be collected directly within a learned interactive world model to support the training of multiple imitation learning policies without requiring additional real-robot interaction [ 6 ] .

Another important application of world models is robot policy evaluation. Real-world evaluation often requires repeated environment resets, human supervision, and substantial hardware runtime, while strictly controlling initial conditions across experiments is difficult. These factors make large-scale checkpoint selection and policy comparison challenging. To address this issue, an increasing number of studies have explored action-conditioned video world models as surrogates for the real environment, estimating policy performance through closed-loop interaction between the policy and the generated environment [ 14 , 40 , 41 , 42 , 15 ] . Works such as WorldEval [ 14 ] , WorldGym [ 40 ] , and dWorldEval [ 15 ] suggest that world-model-based evaluation can, to some extent, preserve the relative performance ordering among different policies or model checkpoints, while providing a scalable and reproducible environment for screening policies before real-world deployment.
