2026-10-05.title: SocialVLA: A Social Perception Gateway for Human-Reaction-Based Failure Detection and Recovery in VLA Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Sofya Konstantinova , Miguel Altamirano Cabrera , Artem Lykov , Dzmitry Tsetserukou
2026-10-05.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies enable diverse robotic manipulation but remain susceptible to execution failures that may not be recognized by the policy itself. An observing human provides complementary information: unexpected robot behavior can elicit rapid vocal, facial, or explicit verbal reactions before an undesirable manipulation outcome is completed. We introduce SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts spontaneous human reactions into runtime intervention signals for VLA manipulation. SocialVLA combines causal paralinguistic audio detection, visual reaction recognition, explicit stop phrases, and robot-relevance estimation. An asynchronous first-event fusion mechanism allows the earliest sufficiently confident signal to request a VLA hold without waiting for complete multimodal agreement. After intervention, a separate speech channel records the participant’s verbal correction and associates it with the interrupted VLA action, enabling participant-directed continuation, restart, or instruction revision. We evaluate SocialVLA during physical Unitree G1 manipulation using recordings from 15 participants, comprising 238 annotated intervention-worthy reaction episodes and 1.038 h of annotated non-intervention behavior. Frozen offline replay of the multimodal cascade achieves 54.6% event recall and 69.5% precision, while unfiltered first-event audio–video fusion reaches 64.3% recall. The relevance module reduces false-stop episodes from 100 to 57 and increases precision from 60.5% to 69.8%. In a prospective deployment on a 16th unseen participant, the frozen system achieves 59.5% recall and 91.7% precision. Median detector-to-fusion delivery is 47.9 ms, median VLA-gate-to-physical-hold latency is 336 ms, and matched reaction-onset-to-physical-hold latency is 1.021 s. These results demonstrate a complete local pathway from spontaneous social reaction to physical VLA interruption and a participant-directed recovery interface.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, enabling policies to generalize across objects, tasks, and semantic commands [ 1 , 2 ] . Their generality, however, does not eliminate execution failures. During pick-and-place manipulation, a policy can select the wrong object, generate an unsuitable approach, fail to establish a grasp, drop an object, or place it at an incorrect location. These failures may occur even when individual actions appear locally plausible.

Recent methods detect failures from robot observations, trajectories, uncertainty estimates, or internal VLA representations. SAFE learns a failure score from VLA features and successful and failed rollouts [ 3 ] . FAIL-Detect frames runtime monitoring as sequential out-of-distribution detection [ 4 ] . AHA uses a vision-language model to identify and explain manipulation failures [ 5 ] . These approaches provide direct task evidence, but they may require access to policy internals, compatible observations, representative training data, or an explicit model of task progress.

An observing person provides a different source of information. Humans can discriminate complex visual scenes within a fraction of a second [ 6 ] , while nonverbal vocalizations can communicate recognizable affect within several hundred milliseconds [ 7 ] . When a robot acts unexpectedly, a person may use an explicit stop phrase, alter vocal prosody, display a negative facial reaction, shake their head, or redirect attention. These responses reflect the person’s appraisal of the interaction [ 8 ] and may reveal discrepancies that were not enumerated during policy training. Moreover, an observer need not wait until a failure is physically complete. From the evolving scene, motion direction, and task context, a person may recognize that a grasp or placement is developing incorrectly and react before the object is dropped, displaced, or released at the wrong location. Recent HRI benchmarks explicitly distinguish such anticipatory responses from reactions observed after failure completion [ 9 ] .

Prior human-robot interaction (HRI) studies have established that human reactions correlate with robot errors [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . However, retrospective reaction classification is not equivalent to an operational gate for a continuously executing VLA. In manipulation, detection time is part of the task: a correct decision made after an object has already been dropped or incorrectly placed cannot prevent the consequence. A runtime system must therefore process the earliest reliable signal with low delay, handle missing or uncertain modalities, and avoid waiting for unnecessary multimodal agreement. It should run locally without dependence on an Internet service, remain independent of the internal VLA architecture, and connect as an external layer to any policy that exposes a pause, hold, or stop interface. Repeated evidence must reinforce an intervention rather than reverse an already issued stop. The key challenge is therefore to convert spontaneous social behavior into a sufficiently fast and reliable runtime intervention signal for a continuously executing VLA, while avoiding unnecessary stops caused by unrelated human behavior.

We address this challenge with SocialVLA, a modular social perception gateway between a human observer and an executing VLA. Rather than attempting to infer physical failure solely from the robot state, SocialVLA detects human-perceived discrepancies from continuous audio-visual behavior and converts them into structured runtime intervention events. The framework is local and does not require access to VLA activations, action probabilities, or internal uncertainty estimates. In this work, failure detection refers to detecting human-perceived intervention need during robot execution rather than exhaustively identifying all physical robot failures.

The main contributions are:

SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts
spontaneous human audio-visual reactions and explicit stop commands into
runtime interventions during VLA-controlled humanoid manipulation;

spontaneous human audio-visual reactions and explicit stop commands into
runtime interventions during VLA-controlled humanoid manipulation;

a causal multimodal intervention architecture that combines fast and
extended-context paralinguistic detection, visual reaction recognition,
explicit stop phrases, separately estimated robot relevance, and
asynchronous first-event fusion, allowing the earliest sufficiently
confident signal to request a hold without waiting for complete multimodal
agreement; and

a real-robot evaluation on the Unitree G1 using a 15-participant annotated
corpus and a prospective frozen-system deployment on a 16th, previously
unseen participant, measuring reaction detection, false interventions,
timely recall, and end-to-end physical stopping latency.

Together, these contributions establish spontaneous social behavior as an operational input to VLA execution rather than only an offline observation signal. SocialVLA complements robot-internal failure monitors by contributing the observer’s task-level assessment while remaining independent of the internal architecture of the underlying VLA.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Failure Detection for Robot Policies

VLA policies extend vision-language representations to robotic action generation [ 1 , 2 ] . SAFE estimates task failure using internal VLA features and studies the trade-off between detection accuracy and timeliness [ 3 ] . FAIL-Detect extracts uncertainty-related signals from policy inputs and outputs and applies conformal sequential detection [ 4 ] . AHA instead observes robot trajectories and produces semantic failure judgments and explanations [ 5 ] .

SocialVLA is complementary to these methods. It does not require VLA activations, action probabilities, uncertainty estimates, or a task-specific success predicate. The same external reaction channel can therefore be attached to different policies. The cost of this independence is that SocialVLA cannot verify whether the observer’s interpretation is physically correct. A practical robot should combine human-centered and robot-internal evidence rather than treating either source as universally reliable.

## II-B Human Reactions to Robot Errors

Stiber et al. showed that multimodal human responses can support timely robot-error detection [ 10 ] . The BAD dataset subsequently captured bystander reactions to recorded robot failures [ 11 ] , while REFLEX studied multimodal reactions to robot failures and subsequent explanations [ 13 ] . ERR@HRI introduced standardized multimodal benchmarks and time-sensitive evaluation of error-related human behavior [ 14 , 9 ] . Recent observations further show that human reactions remain informative in less controlled environments, although unrelated stimuli, groups, and repeated failures introduce substantial noise [ 15 ] .

Most closely related to SocialVLA, Stiber et al. implemented a proactive system that combines facial behavior, speech, explicit feedback, and robot-error context during live interaction [ 12 ] . SocialVLA differs in its intended role as an external gateway around a continuously executing VLA: it does not require access to VLA internals, explicitly separates reaction recognition from robot-relevance estimation, and prioritizes causal first-event intervention so that a sufficiently strong unimodal signal need not wait for multimodal agreement. The objective is therefore not only to recognize a human response retrospectively, but to convert that response into a actionable hold request during physical VLA execution.

## II-C Human Reactions as Temporal Supervision

Beyond triggering intervention, a detected human response indicates that the recent execution has become inconsistent with the observer’s expected task outcome. SocialVLA records this evidence without requiring the observer to operate a dedicated control device. The synchronized stop record identifies the active VLA action or chunk and associates it with the subsequent verbal correction. Such synchronized reaction and correction records may provide temporal supervision for future failure-aware or preference-based policy learning.

2026-10-05.title: Filter-Aware Fine-Tuning for Safe Humanoid Whole-Body Tracking
2026-10-05.authors: Pranit Mohnot , Christian Helten , Daniele Gammelli , Marco Pavone
2026-10-05.abstract: Safe whole-body motion is essential for deploying humanoid robots in unstructured environments. Modern humanoid control commonly separates reference specification from execution, with a planner, teleoperator, or motion generator providing a reference that a reinforcement-learning policy tracks through dynamically feasible whole-body control. Runtime safety filters, such as control barrier functions (CBFs), offer a promising approach for enforcing newly introduced constraints via interventions on the tracker’s outputs. We show, however, that treating the tracking policy and safety filter independently induces fundamental mismatches, as filtering alters both the executed actions and the induced state distribution. We study this policy–filter interface through case studies that isolate dynamics, objective, and information mismatches, highlight their root causes, and use these insights to develop CoFiT ( Co nstrained Fi lter-aware T uning), a filter-aware fine-tuning method for pretrained trackers. Across diverse constraint scenes, CoFiT reduces violation time relative to filter-only training by 91% on TWIST2 and 21% on SONIC, while requiring smaller safety filter corrections. On Unitree G1 hardware, CoFiT reduces violation time by 83% for TWIST2 and completes every trial without operator intervention, whereas 50% of baseline trials require an operator stop. Together, these results provide actionable insights into policy–filter interactions and establish design principles for integrating learned trackers with runtime safety filters.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Humanoid robots are rapidly moving toward deployment in homes, warehouses, hospitals, and other human-centered environments, where safe operation requires coordinating the full body under task- and environment-dependent constraints.
Whole-body control increasingly relies on learning-based motion tracking, in which a motion source, such as a teleoperator, recorded demonstration, or kinematic motion generator, provides a reference trajectory that a reinforcement-learning (RL) tracking policy translates into joint commands consistent with the robot’s dynamics [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
While this control architecture enables expressive whole-body motion, ensuring its safety in real-world environments remains challenging.
A reference trajectory specifies the intended motion but does not, in general, encode every constraint of the environment in which that motion will be executed.
Obstacles, workspace limits, and other safety requirements may be absent from the motion source, emerge only at runtime, or change after the tracking policy has been trained.

Two broad strategies have emerged for enforcing safety in whole-body control.
The first internalizes safety within the learned tracking policy, for example by training with penalties on constraint violations or barrier-based rewards that encourage avoidance of unsafe states [ 4 ] .
This approach tightly couples safety to training, as accommodating a new constraint generally requires retraining, and the resulting policy does not by itself provide a runtime guarantee.
The second strategy places a safety filter downstream of the tracking policy to correct its actions at runtime [ 5 , 6 ] .
This modular approach leaves the nominal policy unchanged and can enforce constraints that were not present during training.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) are widely used to construct such safety filters.
A CBF expresses a constraint as a condition on the control input, and the filter modifies the tracker’s proposed command only as much as needed to satisfy that condition [ 5 ] .
Whole-body formulations can additionally account for contact constraints and task priorities when selecting the correction [ 7 ] .
This modularity is appealing, as the tracker can be treated as a fixed nominal controller, while the filter supplies policy-agnostic corrections, seemingly allowing the two components to be designed independently.

In this work, we show that treating the tracking policy and safety filter independently induces fundamental mismatches in closed-loop execution (Fig. 1 ).
The safety filter changes the tracker’s outputs even though the tracker was trained under an unfiltered closed loop.
As a result, both the actions executed by the robot and the states induced by those actions differ from those encountered during training.
Through systematic case studies, we identify three key sources of incompatibility at the policy–filter interface: dynamics mismatch , objective mismatch , and information mismatch .
Guided by these findings and their underlying causes, we develop CoFiT ( Co nstrained Fi lter-aware T uning), a method that adapts a pretrained tracker to an existing CBF filter.
CoFiT fine-tunes the tracker with filters active and supplies it with compact constraint information, temporal feedback, and constraint-aware penalties.
This allows the tracker to anticipate filter interventions and respond with coordinated, constraint-compatible motion while retaining its original tracking objective where possible.

Our contributions are as follows:

We provide a systematic analysis of the policy–filter interface, identifying dynamics, objective, and information mismatches between pretrained tracking policies and runtime CBF filters and relating them to specific training and interface design choices.

We introduce CoFiT , a filter-aware fine-tuning method that adapts pretrained whole-body tracking policies to an existing CBF filter using action-space constraint observations, temporal feedback, and constraint-aware rewards.

We validate CoFiT through extensive ablations and experiments across multiple base trackers in simulation and on hardware, demonstrating fewer constraint violations, smaller filter corrections, and smoother motion.

1. We provide a systematic analysis of the policy–filter interface, identifying dynamics, objective, and information mismatches between pretrained tracking policies and runtime CBF filters and relating them to specific training and interface design choices.

2. We introduce CoFiT , a filter-aware fine-tuning method that adapts pretrained whole-body tracking policies to an existing CBF filter using action-space constraint observations, temporal feedback, and constraint-aware rewards.

3. We validate CoFiT through extensive ablations and experiments across multiple base trackers in simulation and on hardware, demonstrating fewer constraint violations, smaller filter corrections, and smoother motion.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learning with safety filters

Safety filters separate nominal task execution from explicit safety enforcement by admitting or modifying a policy’s proposed actions according to safety constraints.
CBF-based methods enforce local model-based inequality constraints on proposed controls, while predictive safety filters evaluate candidate inputs through backup trajectories and terminal safe sets [ 8 , 6 ] .
Several works train policies directly on the resulting filtered system so that they can adapt to these interventions.
CBF-RL combines training-time filtering with rewards based on barrier conditions and filter corrections [ 9 ] , while Safety Filtering While Training learns from filtered transitions and penalizes corrective interventions with a predictive filter retained during evaluation [ 10 ] .
Related approaches differentiate through CBF layers [ 11 ] or expose barrier and Lie-derivative quantities to the policy when selecting CBF-related parameters [ 12 ] .
These methods show that policies can benefit from being trained with knowledge of the safety mechanism, but they do not address how a pretrained whole-body tracker should be adapted to an already deployed runtime filter, nor which constraint representations and feedback signals are most useful for doing so.
Our work targets this setting by conditioning the nominal whole-body tracker on a compact action-space representation of constraint information and systematically studying how this constraint information, along with temporal feedback and training objectives, affects behavior under the inherited filter.

## II-B Constraints across the control hierarchy

Safety constraints can be incorporated at multiple levels of a legged or humanoid control stack, including motion planning, reference generation, and whole-body command execution.
Planning and tracking layers can share CBF constraints, while filters above learned locomotion controllers can modify high-level references [ 13 , 14 ] .
At the command level, humanoid controllers combine barrier constraints with full dynamics and contact variables [ 15 , 16 ] .
Task-consistent formulations further account for how safety corrections affect the primary motion and posture, as in OSCBF for manipulation and ConstrainedMimic for pretrained humanoid tracking [ 7 , 17 ] .
Other works study the role of safety-related perception. For example, PAC-MAN combines depth with barrier-based rewards for reactive humanoid dodgeball [ 4 ] .
Collectively, these works establish effective mechanisms for injecting safety constraints at different levels of the control hierarchy, but largely treat the nominal tracking policy and downstream whole-body filter as separately designed components.
Our work focuses on this interface: we retain the existing whole-body safety filter and study how the tracking policy that supplies its nominal commands should be adapted to account for the filter’s constraints and interventions.

2026-10-05.title: NEEDLEWORK: Offline Rewriting of Robot Data with Verified Local Stitches
2026-10-05.authors: Juntao Ren , Yifan Hou , Shuran Song
2026-10-05.comment: Submitted to ICLR 2027. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: Robot demonstrations may contain useful behavior even when individual episodes are inefficient or unsuccessful. Trajectory stitching offers a way to compose these behaviors into improved training data, but identifying useful connections and verifying their feasibility is difficult in high-dimensional robot data, where many prior methods rely on low-dimensional state representations. We introduce Needle , an offline dataset-augmentation algorithm that addresses these challenges by adding short, verified action bridges between recorded observations in high-dimensional robot demonstrations. First, Needle identifies and creates connections that bypass suboptimal detours, broaden action coverage, and augment the original dataset with failed trajectories, using only RGB images, proprioception, and episode-level outcomes, without new environment interaction or privileged object state. Next, we present a sampling technique that incorporates accepted bridges into policy training without synthesizing intermediate images or discarding the original demonstrations, allowing policies to learn alternative actions while retaining the original dataset’s coverage. On real-robot tasks, Needle improves success rate over the strongest baseline on each task by an average of 21 percentage points. Videos and supplementary materials are on needle-work.github.io .
2026-10-05.introduction:
The best robot behavior may not exist in any single trajectory of a dataset. Consider a bimanual laundry-folding task. One demonstration may fold the sleeves reliably but require several corrective grasps to complete the bottom fold; another may fold the sleeves poorly but fold the bottom cleanly. Neither demonstration alone completes the task well, but synthesizing a connection between the two good segments would produce a demonstration better than either individually.

This example illustrates one of three opportunities offered by trajectory stitching (Fig. 1 ). Within a trajectory , it can bypass inefficient detours within a demonstration, allowing a policy to learn shorter routes to success. Across successful trajectories , it can combine complementary behaviors and expose continuations that were never recorded together. From failure trajectories , it can recover useful behavior from failed episodes by connecting states along an unsuccessful execution to a successful continuation.

Despite this promise, realizing this in real-world robot manipulation is difficult. A stitch must be both useful , offering a better continuation, and feasible , with actions that physically reach its target. Most prior methods that stitch trajectories typically assume access to low-dimensional or privileged state ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Lee and Choi, 2025 ; Hepburn and Montana, 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Char et al., 2021 ) , while methods designed to improve mixed-quality robot data typically filter or reweight recorded behavior without supplying the actions needed to connect desirable segments ( Du et al., 2023 ; Hejna et al., 2025 ; Agia et al., 2025 ; Dass et al., 2026 ) . We ask if we can get the best of both.

We introduce N ew E dges from E xisting D emonstrations through L ocal E diting ( Needle ), which identifies valuable segments with no existing connection, and proposes verified action bridges to connect them. Our key insight is that rather than learning a globally accurate dynamics model or task-specific value function and asking either to reason over long horizons, we can reduce stitching in high-dimensional spaces to a series of locally supervised reachability problems.

Specifically, the feasibility and duration of a local connection can be learned directly from recorded action sequences. Across any episode, successful, suboptimal, or failed, each short segment is an example of which two observations can be connected, the specific action sequence that connects them, and the exact number of steps it takes. We use this insight to train two modules. Given source and target observations, a goal-conditioned diffusion Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) generates action sequences that attempt to reach from source to target. In parallel, we supervise an action-conditioned verifier that receives the same source and target observations and predicts whether, and after how many steps, the proposed actions reach the target.

To make these connections useful for policy learning, Needle turns accepted bridges into action sequences at recorded observations. Pairing each bridge with the originally-recorded actions leading up to its source exposes the synthesized actions from multiple preceding observations, without needing to generate intermediate images. Original training examples remain available, including those the bridge bypasses, so the policy receives new ways to make progress without losing supervision for the situations and behaviors covered by the original demonstrations.

Our contributions are threefold:

(1) An offline stitching method that finds useful connections and verifies bridges with an action-conditioned reachability model.

(2) A training formulation that adds bridge actions while preserving recorded supervision, without synthesizing observations or requiring a shared coordinate frame.

(3) Evaluations on a real robot and in simulation of success, completion efficiency, recovery, and key design decisions.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Explicit Stitching of Offline Datasets. Explicit dataset stitching materializes a connection between recorded segments of a trajectory as new training data. Existing methods select connections using signals such as task value, return, temporal structure, or coverage ( Char et al., 2021 ; Hepburn and Montana, 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Lee and Choi, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . They assess connectivity through learned dynamics, successor likelihoods, or proximity in a learned temporal metric ( Char et al., 2021 ; Hepburn and Montana, 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Lee and Choi, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Generative approaches additionally synthesize states or longer trajectories for policy training ( Li et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Lee and Choi, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Needle instead formulates multistep connectivity as action-conditioned reachability between recorded observations, adding action supervision without reconstructing intermediate images. Connection utility depends on continuation lengths and success rather than a learned value function.

Curation via Filtering, Retrieval, and Reweighting. Filtering, retrieval, and reweighting methods determine which recorded behavior should influence policy learning ( Du et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025a ; Hejna et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Agia et al., 2025 ; Dass et al., 2026 ) . They vary in granularity, from complete demonstrations to subtrajectories or individual transitions, and use signals such as relevance, progress, graph-based value, or backward reachability to identify useful behavior ( Memmel et al., 2025 ; Yin and Abbeel, 2024 ; Yue et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . These approaches can recover useful supervision from heterogeneous data while leaving the recorded action targets unchanged. More broadly, reusing recorded trajectories to construct corrective supervision has been explored in learned models ( Venkatraman et al., 2015 ) and
policies ( Ke et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Needle similarly creates supervision from existing trajectories, but constructs alternative action sequences connecting recorded observations, rather than corrections for predicted states.

Implicit Stitching and Compositional Planning. Offline RL can improve on recorded behavior by propagating value across transitions and composing favorable continuations through policy learning ( Kumar et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2021 ; Chebotar et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Goal-conditioned formulations also relate action selection to learned estimates of future reachability ( Eysenbach et al., 2022 ; Kaelbling, 1993 ) . Generative planners construct trajectories or subgoals at inference ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , while graph-based approaches search over recorded states using learned goal-reaching relationships ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ; Emmons et al., 2020 ) . Related policy-steering methods search over or evaluate action proposals using predicted outcomes at deployment ( Jain et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Ren et al., 2024 ) . In these approaches, composition is expressed through learned values and policies, or inference-time planning and steering. Needle materializes its connections offline as explicit action supervision, so the resulting imitation policy requires neither connection search nor verification at deployment. We select baselines from each category to evaluate against in Section 4 .

2026-10-05.title: SoTa: Soft Tactile Skins for Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Jingyun Yang , Baiyu Shi , Timothy Yu , Haitian Liu , Alberta Longhini , Weichen Wang , Rika Antonova , Zhenan Bao , Jeannette Bohg
2026-10-05.comment: The first three authors contributed equally. Project website: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
A growing body of work suggests that tactile sensing gives robot policies contact information that complements vision in dexterous manipulation. However, visuo-tactile robot data remains scarce: dexterous demonstrations require teleoperating robots, which limits dataset scale. Human demonstrations are far cheaper to collect and offer a path to scale this data, but only if human and robot hands carry tactile sensors with corresponding signals. This requires sensors that conform to different hand geometries, cover the full hand, and share a common layout across embodiments.
We present SoTa, a low-cost capacitive tactile skin that provides full-hand coverage on humans and robots while preserving a shared layout of 202 taxels across corresponding finger and palm regions. Our multilayer design with fabric electrodes enables in-house fabrication of thin, soft skins with customizable geometry for under $10 in materials per skin.
The sensor retains over 97% of its initial response span after 10,000 loading-unloading cycles with traces retaining continuity through 1,280 tight-fist folding cycles.
The shared taxel layout supports human-robot co-training with a common tactile encoder and no learned cross-sensor mapping.
Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, tactile observations improve in-distribution success over vision-only policies.
With a fixed robot demonstration budget, adding human demonstrations more than doubles mean success across eight evaluation conditions, from 22.8% to 45.9%, improving success in all five out-of-distribution conditions.
We plan to open-source the resources needed to fabricate and operate these skins.
Project website: https://sota-skin.github.io
2026-10-05.introduction:
Many dexterous manipulation tasks, such as lifting a fragile cup, wiping dirt from a table, or inserting a charger into a power strip, require carefully controlled contact between objects and different parts of the hand.
Vision-based policies can perform a wide range of manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , but they observe contact only indirectly, and a growing body of work suggests that tactile or force observations improve performance on contact-rich tasks [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] .

Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning, however, is limited by data. Dexterous robot demonstrations require teleoperation [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] , which is slow and depends on costly hardware. Human demonstrations are much cheaper to collect and could supplement robot data, but only if human hands carry tactile sensors whose signals correspond to the robot’s. Existing visuo-tactile systems rarely meet this requirement. Most sense contact only at the fingertips [ 7 , 19 , 9 , 11 ] , so they miss contacts on the phalanges and palm in tasks such as table wiping and plug insertion, and most are built for a single embodiment. A sensor that supports learning from both humans and robots must therefore cover the full hand, conform to different hand geometries, withstand repeated contact and flexing, and present the same tactile structure on both embodiments.

We present SoTa, a low-cost capacitive tactile skin that meets these requirements.
Our laser-patterned, multilayer fabric-electrode design
produces thin, soft skins whose geometry is fitted to each hand while preserving a shared layout of 202 taxels, with corresponding indices assigned to the same semantic hand regions. Each skin costs under $10 in materials, responds to forces from 20mN to 10N, retains over 97% of its initial response span after 10,000 loading–unloading cycles, and keeps trace continuity through 1,280 tight-fist folding cycles.
Because both embodiments share the same layout, human and robot observations use a common tactile encoder without a learned cross-sensor mapping. Human demonstrations contain no action labels (as robot demonstrations do), so we incorporate human demonstrations through an auxiliary objective that predicts task phases from human and robot visuo-tactile observations, while action supervision comes only from robot data.

We evaluate the system on three dexterous manipulation tasks involving contact with different parts of the hand: box reorientation, cup picking, and plug insertion. Tactile observations improve in-distribution success on all three tasks, although these benefits do not consistently extend to out-of-distribution conditions.
With a fixed robot-demonstration budget, adding human visuo-tactile demonstrations improves every evaluated condition relative to robot-only visuo-tactile training, raising average success from 22.8% to 45.9%.

Our contributions are:
(1) a soft, flexible, low-cost, and customizable capacitive tactile skin with coverage across the fingers and palm and a shared 202-taxel layout for human and robot hands; (2) characterization of the sensor’s response, cyclic stability, flexing durability, and motion-induced artifacts; and (3) a language-supervised training pipeline that incorporates human visuo-tactile demonstrations into robot policy learning, with real robot experiments demonstrating improvements over robot-only training.
We will release the resources needed to fabricate and operate these skins.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

Visuo-tactile and force-aware policy learning. A growing body of work suggests that combining vision with touch or force can improve precision and sample efficiency on contact-rich tasks, both at execution time and as a representation-learning signal [ 34 , 10 , 7 , 8 , 19 , 12 , 35 , 11 ] . Most visuo-tactile policies, however, rely on localized or sparse sensing. Work on multi-fingered hands [ 11 , 7 , 8 ] has used fingertip sensors [ 7 , 11 ] or a small set of force-sensing resistors on the palm and finger links [ 8 ] , while gripper-based systems use sparse magnetic patches on parallel-jaw grippers [ 9 ] , or dense arrays on soft parallel-jaw fingers [ 10 ] . A parallel line of work injects force or torque signals directly into vision-language-action models [ 13 , 14 , 35 ] or force-conditioned imitation learning [ 12 , 15 ] .
Most of these approaches are trained on robot data, which is costly to collect for dexterous hands. Methods that draw on human demonstrations do so with limited or heterogeneous sensing: [ 15 ] measures force at a single human fingertip, and FTP-1 [ 36 ] pretrains a generalist tactile policy on human and robot data from heterogeneous sensors, using sensor-specific encoders.
We build on FTP-1 with a tactile sensing interface that provides full-hand coverage and a shared taxel layout across human and robot hands, so that human and robot demonstrations can share a single tactile encoder without a separate cross-sensor alignment stage.

Tactile interfaces for dexterous manipulation. Tactile sensing for dexterous manipulation has advanced through both robot-mountable tactile skins and human-worn tactile gloves.
Robot skins use magnetic [ 20 , 21 , 9 , 22 ] and capacitive [ 23 ] sensing,
with coverage ranging from localized patches and fingertips to the full hand [ 24 ] . Human-worn systems such as STAG [ 25 ] , FlexGlove [ 27 ] or OpenTouch [ 31 ] provide full-hand tactile sensing, and FlexGlove additionally customizes sensor geometry to each user.
These systems, however, are designed for a single embodiment. Interfaces designed for both embodiments use mechanically matched structures [ 28 , 29 ] or identical sensors [ 30 , 26 ] , but they constrain the wearer to robot-specific hardware or provide coverage limited to the fingertips and palm.
SoTa instead fits a thin, flexible, and low-cost skin to each hand while preserving a shared 202-taxel layout across the fingertips, phalanges, and palm, so human and robot observations correspond by construction.
Table I surveys previously reported interfaces, their sensing coverage, and their support for human and robot embodiments.

Human-robot co-training for policy learning. Prior work incorporates human demonstrations either as action targets, using tracked or retargeted human motion [ 37 , 38 , 39 ] , or through auxiliary prediction objectives during co-training, such as predicting future frames [ 40 ] , future end-effector trajectories [ 41 ] , or 3D scene flow [ 42 ] .
Language prediction and cross-modal objectives also provide supervision for policy learning and the integration of additional sensing modalities [ 43 , 44 ] .
In visuo-tactile policy learning, prior work incorporates human demonstrations by aligning human and robot tactile representations using paired demonstrations [ 32 ] or automatically constructed pseudo-pairs [ 33 ] .
Unlike prior work, we combine full-hand tactile sensing with language-supervised
representation learning.
Our shared taxel layout allows human and robot observations to use a common tactile encoder, while task-phase labels provide supervision without requiring observation pairs across the two datasets.
Human demonstrations contribute to this auxiliary objective without motion retargeting or action labels.
Our experiments demonstrate improvements over robot-only training.

2026-10-05.title: World-Calibrated Proposal-to-Action Flow for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-05.authors: Jie He , Wei Li , Junwen Tong , Rui Shao , Wei-Shi Zheng , Liqiang Nie
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-05.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies generate action chunks by transporting samples from a task-agnostic isotropic Gaussian source. As this source is conditioned on neither recent execution nor predicted future evolution, (i) it discards the local continuity established by recently executed motion. (ii) Even when predictive world representations are introduced, they often only condition the transport dynamics rather than determine where generation starts, how far it may deviate, or along which action directions it may expand.
Building on this observation, we introduce ProAct , a world-calibrated proposal-to-action framework that makes the generative source itself predictable. (i) To preserve motion continuity, a lightweight Proposal Expert converts recent actions into a scene-aware hypothesis via one motion-anchored endpoint flow-matching step, initializing generation near the demonstrated action manifold. (ii) To jointly capture intended scene evolution and proposal–future compatibility, a prospective World Expert treats the hypothesis as a soft motion prior while predicting the task-consistent latent future. (iii) From this compatibility, the model calibrates a proposal-centered anisotropic source, where a bounded per-step extent controls the allowed deviation and a trace-normalized low-rank geometry under a condition-number budget allocates refinement over coupled translation, rotation, and gripper directions.
Compared with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , ProAct improves performance across simulation and real-world tasks while reducing denoising steps by 50%, inference latency by up to 25.8%, and increasing throughput by up to 34.8%.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models Black et al. (2024) ; Bjorck et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2026b) ; Luo et al. (2026) ; Shao et al. (2025) increasingly use diffusion Chi et al. (2025) or flow matching Lipman et al. (2022) to generate continuous robot actions, building on broader progress in fine-grained multimodal understanding and visual grounding Peng et al. (2026) ; Shao et al. (2024) ; Shao et al. (2023) ; Shao et al. (2019) . However, these generative decoders typically initialize each action chunk from a generic source distribution Intelligence et al. (2025) ; Zheng et al. (2026) , forcing the policy to repeatedly transport uninformed samples toward executable trajectories, as illustrated in the upper panel of Fig. 1 .
Such a generic source ignores readily available context that could inform where action generation should begin.
By making the source distribution itself contextually predictable, action generation can begin from a more informed region of the action space, yielding
a policy that is both more accurate and substantially cheaper to sample during closed-loop policy execution.

A generic isotropic source leaves two useful sources of information unexploited.
The first is recently executed motion . Although task-level behavior can be highly multimodal, physical motion often exhibits strong local regularity over short horizons, and recently executed, reliable actions are already available during closed-loop control Black et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026a) .
A naive strategy is to extrapolate this motion and reuse it for the next action chunk Jia et al. (2026) ; Zhan et al. (2026) . Yet such continuation becomes unreliable around contact, reorientation, gripper actuation, or task-phase transitions, where appropriate motion may deviate sharply from recent behavior Yang et al. (2026c) . Local continuity therefore indicates what is plausible from the recent past, but not necessarily what remains appropriate for the current scene and task. Recent motion should thus be treated as a proposal to be evaluated against the intended future, rather than as the action itself.

The second is predicted future evolution , which provides prospective evidence for calibrating such a proposal.
Prospective world modeling Zhao et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025) ; Tian et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026f) ; Zhu et al. (2026a) ; Li et al. (2026c) has increasingly been incorporated into VLA policies, but typically as auxiliary supervision or additional conditioning.
In these formulations, prospective information helps predict what should happen next, but is not explicitly used to calibrate an existing action hypothesis according to whether it remains appropriate for the anticipated task evolution.
The missing element is therefore an explicit interface between a candidate motion, prospective world reasoning, and generative refinement.

We build this missing interface around a propose–calibrate–refine principle and instantiate it as ProAct , a World-Calibrated Proposal-to-Action Flow framework. ProAct first constructs a scene-aware motion hypothesis, then uses prospective world reasoning to estimate the correction required to realize the intended future, and finally converts this calibration into the source distribution for flow-based action generation, as illustrated in the lower panel of Fig. 1 .

Specifically, (i) a lightweight Proposal Expert first converts recently executed actions into a scene-aware motion hypothesis. It extrapolates short-horizon motion and uses it to initialize the motion-anchored flow module, which grounds the proposal in the current VLM context through a single endpoint flow step. Rather than producing an executable action, this stage places generation near a plausible region of the demonstrated action manifold and provides a soft motion prior for subsequent reasoning. (ii) A prospective World Expert calibrates this proposal against the task-consistent future. The motion hypothesis is provided as contextual evidence for prospective reasoning, while the prediction target remains the demonstrated future encoded in the latent space of a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder Assran et al. (2025) .
Calibration readouts are further supervised by the residual between the demonstrated action and the proposal, forcing the shared world representation to encode both the task-consistent latent future and the proposal–future compatibility. (iii) The resulting calibration is finally expressed as a proposal-centered anisotropic source for action generation. A bounded per-step extent limits how far generation may deviate from the proposal, while trace-normalized low-rank geometry determines along which coupled action directions that correction should occur.
An Action Expert then transports samples from this calibrated source into executable action chunks using the base VLA’s original flow parameterization. Thus, ProAct changes where and how action generation begins while preserving the flexibility to depart from the proposal when needed.

Our primary contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate generative action prediction from a propose–calibrate–refine perspective, where recent motion provides a soft local hypothesis calibrated by task-consistent prospective reasoning, providing an interface between local motion continuity and future-aware action generation.

We introduce an asymmetric proposal-aware World Expert that uses motion to assist future prediction while anchoring the desired future independently of proposal correctness, and jointly predicts proposal-specific refinement extent and geometry at every horizon step.

We replace the isotropic Gaussian of flow-based VLAs with a world-calibrated, proposal-centered source while leaving their transport parameterization unchanged.

We validate ProAct across extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines while reducing denoising steps by up to 50%, demonstrating both superior effectiveness and inference efficiency.

2. We introduce an asymmetric proposal-aware World Expert that uses motion to assist future prediction while anchoring the desired future independently of proposal correctness, and jointly predicts proposal-specific refinement extent and geometry at every horizon step.

3. We replace the isotropic Gaussian of flow-based VLAs with a world-calibrated, proposal-centered source while leaving their transport parameterization unchanged.

4. We validate ProAct across extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines while reducing denoising steps by up to 50%, demonstrating both superior effectiveness and inference efficiency.

2026-10-05.title: Awomo-SimDataEngine: Agentic Simulation-ReadyWorld Generation
2026-10-05.authors: Awomo-PhysicalRSI Team , Danjiao Ma , Enhui Ma , Haohan Liu , Heng Jia , Hui Shan , Jianhua Xu , Jiahuan Zhang , Jiangdi Xu , Kaiwen Guo , Kaicheng Yu , Linwei Zhang , Liyang Jin , Maochun Luo , Pengyao Niu , Shiwen Li , Shuangyu Feng , Tong Zhang , Tianheng Wang , Xin Wang , Xiangru Huang , Yongqiang Huang , Zhaozhi Wang , Zijian Ma
2026-10-05.abstract:
Generating useful robot-training data requires more than visually plausible
scenes: objects must support interaction, placements must remain physically
valid, and tasks must admit repeatable execution. We present Awomo-SimDataEngine , an agentic system that connects asset and scene
generation to robot demonstration synthesis. Shared asset services provide
rigid and articulated objects, including structure-grounded part and joint
generation with ISArt. Scene generation supports two complementary routes:
Unravel reconstructs editable scenes from images, while SimForge builds
single-room and multi-room environments from text. A graph-native harness
coordinates construction, validation, and
bounded repair, routing failures to the responsible module while retaining
unaffected scene state. PolicyForge binds validated worlds to tasks and robot
embodiments to produce replayable demonstrations. Evaluations cover asset
geometry, scene quality, and downstream policy learning. On MuJoCo-based
LIBERO-Plus, co-training with Isaac Sim demonstrations improves the overall
success rate of a World-Action Model (WAM) from 77.17 % 77.17\% to 89.43 % 89.43\% . Goal and spatial
success improve by 31.66 31.66 and 6.25 6.25 percentage points, respectively.
These results support the utility of the generated data for cross-simulator
policy training, with more limited gains on long-horizon tasks.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Robot learning depends on demonstrations that cover varied objects,
environments, and manipulation goals. Collecting such coverage in the real
world is costly, while manually preparing each simulated environment limits
the scale and diversity of synthetic data. Generative models offer a way to
expand this training distribution, but their outputs must support interaction:
a plausible image or textured mesh can still hide invalid collision geometry,
inaccessible interiors, incorrect joints, unstable placements, or an
unreplayable initial state. These defects affect both whether demonstrations
can be collected and what policies learn from them.

Recent progress spans image-conditioned 3D assets, agentic scene construction,
and automated demonstration synthesis [ Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025a ; SAM 3D Team et al., 2025 ; Pfaff et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Ranawaka et al., 2026 ] .
Connecting these capabilities requires agreement on object identities,
coordinate frames, physical representations, task requirements, and validation
results. An asset replacement changes the geometry available for registration;
a revised scene changes the reset and interaction conditions seen by a
controller. An integrated system must preserve these dependencies and return
failures to the stage that can resolve them.

We introduce Awomo-SimDataEngine , an agentic system for constructing
simulation-ready worlds and converting them into robot demonstrations.
The system connects asset generation, scene generation, and demonstration
synthesis through a Graph-Native Harness for execution and repair.
Scene generation supports both visual references and language descriptions: Unravel reconstructs editable scenes from single-view images, whereas SimForge builds single-room and multi-room environments from text.
Both routes use shared asset services and produce worlds that can be checked,
edited, and bound to robot tasks. Figure 1 illustrates the shared execution framework and the image-driven route.

Scene construction begins with assets that are usable beyond rendering.
The asset module combines retrieval and generation with common geometry,
collision, and physical checks (Section 4 ). Articulated objects
add a structural requirement: their parts and joints must describe an
executable mechanism. ISArt addresses this through geometric–kinematic
planning, structure-conditioned part generation, and articulation binding.

The two scene-generation routes use these assets differently
(Section 5 ). Unravel progressively removes objects from a
reference image to expose occluded regions, then uses accumulated point-map
evidence to register and reassemble independently editable assets. SimForge
instead plans room geometry, object requirements, and spatial arrangements
from language, supporting both individual rooms and multi-room houses.
For both routes, plausible appearance
alone does not establish valid support, collision geometry, or articulation.

Construction failures need not be repaired where they are detected. A missing
asset calls for acquisition; an intersecting object calls for a placement
change; an incorrect joint may require revising the articulated asset.
The Graph-Native Harness (Section 6 ) makes these handoffs
explicit through shared state, validation evidence, bounded retries, and
checkpoints. It retains unaffected work and revalidates the dependencies of
each edit before construction proceeds.

PolicyForge then binds an accepted world to a task, robot embodiment,
and reset specification (Section 7 ). Scripted or
motion-planned teachers execute in Isaac Sim, producing synchronized images,
proprioception, and actions; successful validated episodes are retained for
training. Scene variants, object substitutions, and initial-state and language
augmentation diversify the resulting data. World validity, demonstration
success, and downstream policy performance remain distinct outcomes.

Module evaluations support the geometry and reconstruction methods: ISArt
achieves part-geometry CD 0.163 0.163 versus 0.268 0.268 for the combined
TRELLIS.2 + P3-SAM + X-Part baseline on 60 objects, while Unravel improves
blind human asset-fidelity scores from 4.9 4.9 to 8.6 8.6 on 160 objects.
These protocols are detailed in Sections 4.1 and 5.1.3 .
Text-driven scene quality is evaluated separately on 179 room prompts and
31 multi-room prompts using the SceneEval and SceneSmith protocols
(Section 5.2 ). These evaluations test complementary
properties rather than a single pooled quality score.
On the MuJoCo-based LIBERO-Plus benchmark, SimData-Ultra co-training increases
World-Action Model success from 77.17 % 77.17\% to 89.43 % 89.43\% when comparing each configuration’s best
evaluated checkpoint up to and including 13K steps, selected by overall
success, with gains of 31.66 31.66 and 6.25 6.25 percentage points in goal and
spatial generalization (Section 8 ). These results support the training utility of the
combined data-generation system across simulator boundaries; they do not
isolate each generator or augmentation’s contribution. The smaller
long-horizon gain motivates richer sequential task supervision.

This report makes four contributions:

Simulation-ready asset generation , including ISArt’s
structure-grounded articulated-object pipeline and shared candidate
validation, canonicalization, collision construction, and physical augmentation.

Complementary scene-generation routes : image-driven
reconstruction with Unravel and text-driven single-room and multi-room
construction with SimForge.

Integrated execution and demonstration synthesis : a
Graph-Native Harness coordinates attributed repair and acceptance, while
PolicyForge generates replayable demonstrations across scenes, tasks, and
robot embodiments.

Cross-simulator policy-learning evidence , showing a 12.26 12.26 -point overall gain on LIBERO-Plus at the best evaluated checkpoints
within a 13K-step budget,
with the largest improvement in goal generalization.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 3D assets and interactive environments

Hunyuan3D, TRELLIS, and SAM 3D generate geometry and appearance from visual
conditions [ Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025a ; Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025b ; Xiang et al., 2024 ; SAM 3D Team et al., 2025 ] .
Their outputs supply candidate assets for Awomo-SimDataEngine, which additionally checks
canonical orientation, measured extents, collision compatibility, and physical
attributes before simulator use. For articulated objects,
Section 4 introduces ISArt: structural planning conditions part
generation, and agentic binding and motion verification connect the parts to
an executable kinematic representation.

PartCrafter and OmniPart address part-level geometry generation, while
Articulate AnyMesh, Articulate-Anything, and SPARK estimate or reconstruct
articulated representations [ Lin et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Le et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ] .
ISArt connects explicit structural planning to a learned multi-part generator
and then refines articulation through simulation feedback. Its fixed-geometry
binding comparison separates joint estimation from the quality of generated
meshes; the part-generation comparison evaluates the latter independently.

HSSD-200, RoboCasa, and BEHAVIOR-1K provide reusable assets, scenes, or
household interaction settings [ Khanna et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024a ] . They
motivate the interaction requirements that generated assets must satisfy.
Awomo-SimDataEngine exposes retrieval and generation through a common asset lifecycle,
preserving source provenance separately from instance poses, articulation
states, and simulator-specific packaging.

## 2.2 Scene synthesis and single-view construction

ATISS and DiffuScene learn distributions over indoor object arrangements;
InstructScene, LayoutGPT, and PhyScene incorporate instructions, structured
relations, or physical constraints [ Paschalidou et al., 2021 ; Tang et al., 2023 ; Lin and Mu, 2024 ; Feng et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ] . These approaches
provide useful priors for scene composition. Awomo-SimDataEngine’s image-driven
path follows Unravel (Section 5 ), using object removal to expose
occluded regions and fixed-camera point evidence to guide reconstruction and
recomposition. Its execution graph records stage dependencies; removal order
provides local occlusion evidence rather than a global support or depth order.

Text2Room, GraphDreamer, DreamScene, AnyHome, WonderWorld, and MIDI explore text-,
graph-, or image-conditioned 3D scene construction [ Höllein et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Fu et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ] . Awomo-SimDataEngine uses
SimForge for text-driven single-room and multi-room construction, and Unravel
for single-image reconstruction. The latter retains object identities, masks,
point provenance, and registration evidence. Settling and visual audit check
the recomposed scene before packaging. This image-driven route does not imply
multi-view reconstruction or uniquely recoverable
metric geometry from an unconstrained image.

## 2.3 Agentic generation and execution harnesses

ReAct, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts, and Graph of Thoughts make tool use,
feedback, or structured reasoning explicit [ Yao et al., 2022 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2023 ; Besta et al., 2023 ] . Holodeck, SceneCraft,
SceneWeaver, SceneSmith, SAGE, and SceneCode connect language-model reasoning
to 3D scene tools or executable representations [ Yang et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025a ; Pfaff et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ] .

Awomo-SimDataEngine coordinates specialized modules through the execution contract in
Section 6 . Each repair records typed state, evidence, the
responsible module, affected workset, remaining budget, and checkpoint
decision. The contract spans ISArt articulation refinement, Unravel editing
and reconstruction, and world-owned PolicyForge feedback. Preserved state is
reused only when its input dependencies remain valid. These mechanisms support
recovery within a run; the policy experiments do not independently establish
harness efficiency or learning in the orchestrator.

## 2.4 Integrated worlds and policy-data synthesis

EmbodiedGen V2 connects simulation-ready assets, affordances, task-driven
worlds, editing, and simulator deployment [ Wang et al., 2026b ] . SimFoundry
reconstructs digital twins from video and generates object, scene, and task
cousins for policy learning and evaluation [ Ranawaka et al., 2026 ] . WorldComposer
also connects visual reconstruction and digital cousins to robot learning [ Lu et al., 2026 ] . These systems demonstrate the importance of linking
world representations to interaction and downstream training.

MimicGen expands demonstrations from a small set of human trajectories,
RoboMimic studies learning from offline demonstrations, and Diffusion Policy
models visuomotor actions through diffusion [ Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Mandlekar et al., 2021 ; Chi et al., 2023 ] . PolicyForge complements this work
by preparing worlds and task contracts for scripted or motion-planned
teachers, recording replayable resets and synchronized observations and
actions, and retaining successful demonstrations. Its contribution is the
generation and validation pipeline rather than a new policy optimizer.

SceneEval and RelScene evaluate semantic coherence and spatial relations [ Tam et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2024 ] . World-level checks and policy success answer
different questions. Section 8 evaluates whether Awomo-SimDataEngine
data improves a WAM policy across simulator boundaries; it does not rank
generators under a common scene benchmark or establish real-world transfer.
The system connects asset structure, image-grounded scene evidence, bounded
repair, and validated demonstration synthesis in one workflow.

2026-10-05.title: Less Decoder is More Encoder: Geometric Representation Learning from Novel View Synthesis
2026-10-05.authors: Keerthi Kaashyap , Dennis Anthony , Akshay Krishnan , Nhi Ngoc Nguyen , Jeremy Collins , James Hays , Shreyas Kousik , Animesh Garg
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
2026-10-05.abstract:
This paper examines the role of Novel View Synthesis (NVS) in geometric representation learning.
In principle, NVS should reason about 3D scene structure, thereby enabling transferable multi-view geometric representations. Yet, existing encoder-based NVS methods yield poor representations. This is not because of a lack of supervisory signal, but rather due to inconspicuous architectural choices: spatially expressive decoders that dilute representational capabilities of the scene encoder, and low-level pixel-space targets that hinder feature learning.
We present SNAP , a self-supervised encoder-decoder transformer that addresses both through a pose-conditioned local decoder and a latent-space reconstruction objective. SNAP is task agnostic, and we show that it is competitive with special-purpose geometry-supervised methods. SNAP also performs competitively against self-supervised representations across five tasks: visual localization, pose estimation, point correspondence, depth estimation, and robot manipulation.
Remarkably, SNAP ’s patch features exhibit emergent viewpoint invariance that approaches heavily supervised models despite lower compute and data budgets. Under camera shifts where standard 2D representations collapse, SNAP degrades more gracefully, revealing that restricting decoder expressivity actively prevents the suppression of transferable geometric structure. https://snap-nvs.github.io
2026-10-05.introduction:
Geometric understanding from images is a foundation of computer vision.
Methods like DUSt3R [ 1 ] , MASt3R [ 2 ] , and VGGT [ 3 ] demonstrate that transformers can produce rich, transferable geometric representations, when trained on large-scale annotated 3D data.
This supervision requirement is a fundamental bottleneck since dense 3D ground truth is expensive to collect at scale.

Novel View Synthesis (NVS) offers a compelling alternative [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
These models must reason about 3D scene structure to predict unseen viewpoints, providing a rich geometric supervision signal only from posed images, which are abundantly available across videos, robotics platforms, and structure-from-motion pipelines.
However, representations produced from feed-forward NVS methods transfer poorly to downstream geometric tasks.
We argue this poor transfer is not a signal failure, but rather an architectural failure, driven by two identifiable and independently addressable choices that dilute signal.

First , spatially expressive decoders tend to absorb the representational load of the task.
When a decoder has sufficient capacity to reconstruct a target view from any encoder output, the encoder is not pressured to maintain structured, locally discriminative features.
While the reconstruction task is solved, the latent representations are not geometrically grounded. Second , pixel-space reconstruction targets require modeling high-frequency aliasing statistics that are weakly related to 3D structure and semantics. Consequently, the reconstruction loss produces gradients that encourage the representation encoder to preserve fine-grained, image-specific statistics that are not directly informative about the underlying 3D structure or semantics.

We present SNAP , which addresses both failure axes with two targeted interventions. First, a pose-conditioned local decoder built on PRoPE [ 8 ] restricts the decoder’s receptive field via an explicit BlockNN mask applied to queried-view self-attention. This constraint forces the geometric structure to reside within the encoder’s scene representation rather than being an effect of the generative capacity of the decoder. Second, SNAP operates directly on frozen DINOv3 ViT-B patch features to provide a richer supervision signal than RGB reconstruction. This structured grounding is jointly aware of appearance, geometry, and semantics and produces higher quality representations.

Our main contributions are:

SNAP , a self-supervised multi-view spatial reasoning backbone that builds upon frozen 2D semantic latent spaces with an asymmetric NVS prediction objective, and latent feature targets to learn geometrically transferable representations without dense 3D supervision.

Mechanistic analyses isolating the independent impact of decoder expressivity and prediction space on geometric transfer, via receptive field sweeps and prediction space landscape experiments.

Empirical evaluation across five tasks matching or exceeding self-supervised baselines and competitive with geometry-supervised methods that require large-scale annotated 3D data.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

SNAP sits at the intersection of self-supervised representation learning, novel view synthesis, and geometric foundation models. Detailed discussions are provided in Appendix A .

Self-Supervised Representation Learning. Masked Image Modeling (MIM) has evolved from pixel-reconstruction (MAE [ 9 ] , SimMIM [ 10 ] ) toward latent-space prediction (I-JEPA [ 11 ] , V-JEPA [ 12 ] ). In multi-view regimes, CroCo [ 13 ] and Muskie [ 14 ] leverage cross-view completion to learn implicit 3D priors. SNAP extends this trajectory by utilizing frozen DINOv3 [ 15 ] features as opposed to pixel space targets used in Muskie [ 14 ] , which act as semantically structured latent distillation targets to provide a cleaner supervision signal for optimization.

Novel View Synthesis (NVS). Feed-forward NVS was established by architectures such as SRT [ 16 ] and RUST [ 17 ] , recently scaling to large-view models such as LVSM [ 4 ] , RayZer [ 6 ] , with contemporaneous works LagerNVS [ 18 ] and SVSM [ 7 ] continuing to extend the paradigm. However, most of these variants utilize expressive decoders that absorb the representational load of the task, leading to ungrounded latents. By constraining the decoder’s receptive field via a BlockNN mask, adopting PRoPE [ 8 ] , and targeting a latent feature space, SNAP ensures its representations prioritize 3D structural awareness over reconstruction statistics.

Geometry-Supervised Models. Recent foundation models, including DUSt3R [ 1 ] , MASt3R [ 2 ] , VGGT [ 3 ] , and D4RT [ 19 ] , achieve state-of-the-art performance but rely on massive 3D-annotated datasets. Similarly, π 3 \pi^{3} [ 20 ] and Depth Anything 3 [ 21 ] provide robust spatial priors via explicit 3D supervision. Conversely, SNAP approaches the geometric transferability of these models while remaining self-supervised and training on significantly less data and compute.

2026-10-05.title: UniIntervene++: An Adaptive Intervention Agent for Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Yudong Lin , Haoyuan Deng , Zhuoxuan Yuan , Zaijia Yang , Yuanjiang Xue , Ziwei Wang
2026-10-05.comment: Yudong Lin and Haoyuan Deng contributed equally. Ziwei Wang is the corresponding author. Code is available in our \href{ this https URL }{GitHub repository}
2026-10-05.abstract:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot policies to improve through physical interaction, but the assistance they require changes as their competence evolves. Existing intervention strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore become mismatched to the current policy. To address this, we propose UniIntervene++ , an adaptive intervention agent that learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, UniIntervene++ first formulates the evolving RL policy, trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process and learns their relative values online. Building on this, competence-adaptive intervention periodically probes the RL policy through unassisted execution, keeping control allocation responsive to its evolving capability. Finally, coupled experience learning allows assisted behaviors to improve the RL policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions. In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene, and when to return control as the RL policy improves.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of 89.67%, outperforming all baselines by at least 6 percentage points, while reducing human intervention to 0.77%, a relative reduction of at least 94.6% from the best baseline. Code is available in our GitHub repository .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot manipulation policies to
improve through physical interaction and adapt to contact dynamics, perception
errors, and task variation [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, real-world online RL remains costly:
rewards are often sparse, exploration can be unsafe or unproductive, and failed
rollouts consume robot time [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Human-in-the-loop RL (HiL-RL), such as HIL-SERL,
mitigates these issues through timely human corrections during online learning [ 7 ] . Yet current HiL-RL systems require a skilled operator to
continuously monitor training and repeatedly allocate control between autonomous
execution and assisted behavior, limiting real-world scalability [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

Recent work has begun to automate this role. AutoSERL reuses a single
demonstration to guide exploration and recover from predefined failure regions [ 11 ] , while UniIntervene detects sustained value degradation
and invokes a goal-conditioned recovery policy learned offline [ 12 ] . These methods provide useful automated assistance,
but the assistance required by the RL policy changes as its competence
evolves during online RL. Early in learning, intervention can prevent repetitive
failures and provide useful experience; later, excessive assistance can limit
the autonomous execution needed to further improve the RL policy [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Intervention
strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore
become mismatched to the current policy.

What is missing is an intervention agent that learns to allocate control
between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors as the task
policy improves online. This requires learning their relative values online
while keeping control allocation responsive to the policy’s evolving
competence. We therefore ask: Can an intervention agent learn a unified
control-allocation policy that adapts as the RL policy improves during
online RL?

To address this gap, we propose UniIntervene++ , an adaptive intervention agent that
learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous
assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, to compare autonomous
execution and different forms of assistance within a unified decision process, Unified Intervention Policy Learning places the evolving RL policy,
demonstration-guided trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy in
a shared decision space and learns their relative values online. To prevent
initially effective assistance from obscuring the RL policy’s evolving
competence, Competence-Adaptive Intervention , as illustrated in Fig. 1 , periodically probes the RL
policy through unassisted execution, providing direct evidence of its current
competence and enabling control allocation to progressively shift from
assistance-heavy to autonomy-heavy execution. Finally, to ensure that
intervention also contributes to improving the RL policy, Coupled Experience Learning uses assisted experience to train the task
policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions.
In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene,
and when to return control as the RL policy improves, without requiring a
separate offline intervention-learning stage. Across five sparse-reward
real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of
89.67%, exceeding the best baseline by 6 percentage points, while reducing
the human intervention rate to 0.77%. Its control allocation progressively
shifts toward the RL policy as autonomous competence improves.

The main contributions are:

We formulate online intervention as a unified control-allocation problem,
placing autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors in a shared
decision space and learning their relative values online.

We develop competence-adaptive intervention with coupled experience
learning, which keeps control allocation responsive to the RL policy’s
evolving competence while using assisted experience to improve the policy and
reshape subsequent intervention decisions.

Extensive real-world experiments across five manipulation tasks show that UniIntervene++ achieves 89.67% average success, outperforming the best baseline by
6 percentage points, while reducing the human intervention rate to 0.77%.

1. We formulate online intervention as a unified control-allocation problem,
placing autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors in a shared
decision space and learning their relative values online.

2. We develop competence-adaptive intervention with coupled experience
learning, which keeps control allocation responsive to the RL policy’s
evolving competence while using assisted experience to improve the policy and
reshape subsequent intervention decisions.

3. Extensive real-world experiments across five manipulation tasks show that UniIntervene++ achieves 89.67% average success, outperforming the best baseline by
6 percentage points, while reducing the human intervention rate to 0.77%.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning

Human guidance can make physical policy learning tractable by providing targeted interventions when autonomous exploration becomes unsafe or unproductive.
Interactive imitation learning established this data-collection principle:
DAgger queries expert actions on learner-induced states [ 16 ] ; HG-DAgger gives the supervisor control of the takeover
gate, whereas ThriftyDAgger formalizes intervention using novelty and risk [ 17 , 18 ] . For robot deployment, Sirius
treats takeovers as both corrective labels and evidence of human trust, then
reweights the collected experience for subsequent policy updates [ 19 ] . These supervised approaches mitigate covariate shift but
primarily optimize imitation of corrective behavior.

Reward-driven methods use intervention data beyond behavioral cloning. RLIF
turns the onset of an intervention into a negative reward and applies
off-policy RL, relaxing the assumption that corrective actions are
near-optimal [ 20 ] . In parallel, RLPD and SERL provide
sample-efficient off-policy learning that mixes prior data with online
interaction [ 21 , 22 ] . HIL-SERL combines this foundation
with human takeovers, storing corrective transitions in both demonstration and
online replay buffers [ 7 ] . E2HiL instead selects replay
samples by their estimated effect on policy entropy to use costly interventions
more efficiently [ 23 ] . Together, these systems show that
intervention can shape
where data are collected, which corrective actions are executed, and how the
resulting transitions influence learning. They nevertheless generally keep the
operator responsible for monitoring, intervention timing, and corrective
action generation. Our work retains human takeover as an external safety
backstop, but transfers intervention timing, corrective action selection, and
control return to an intervention agent that learns online together with the
RL policy.

## II-B Automated Intervention and Recovery

Robust execution is often obtained by pairing a nominal controller with a
localized fallback. Plan patching learns a model-free policy from
demonstrations only where an approximate planner’s transition model fails [ 24 ] , while manifold-return methods guide a policy from
out-of-distribution observations back toward its demonstration distribution [ 25 ] . In safe RL, Recovery RL and LS3 learn recovery
zones or safe sets from offline experience to constrain subsequent exploration [ 26 , 27 ] . MetaReSkill instead discovers
failure modes in simulation and uses model-predictive meta-reasoning to allocate
a limited training budget among failure-specific recovery policies [ 28 ] . Contact-mode transition models have also been used
to select among nominal skills and heuristically generated recoveries [ 29 ] .

RecoveryChaining learns a local model-free recovery policy in a hybrid action
space containing primitive actions and terminal nominal Options [ 30 ] . AutoSERL automates training-time recovery from
a single successful demonstration [ 11 ] . UniIntervene is the
closest value-based intervention formulation: it learns intervention behavior
offline and uses value degradation to trigger recovery [ 12 ] . Its learned values and supporting modules are fixed
before the target online learning process, however, and it does not formulate
control return as a decision that must adapt to the improving RL policy. UniIntervene++ moves the intervention learner into the online loop and learns entry,
corrective behavior, and exit from the same evolving value comparison.
