2026-10-05.title: Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration Curriculum for Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Juri Pfammatter , Kaixian Qu , Clemens Schwarke , Victor Klemm , Marco Hutter
2026-10-05.abstract:
Long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards pose an exploration bottleneck for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning: a policy started from the initial state rarely reaches the goal and receives no learning signal. Reference motions, hand-designed curricula, and shaped rewards supply this signal but require demonstrations or task-specific engineering; automatic start-state and goal curricula avoid this but typically expand from one side only, so the full distance to the target must be covered from that side.
We propose the Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration curriculum for Reinforcement learning (BVER), which expands from both ends at once. Inspired by bidirectional RRT planning, BVER grows start states outward from the goal and goals outward from the initial state distribution, biases both toward unexplored task space, and steers them toward each other, training one goal-conditioned policy on both.
On point-mass mazes, quadrupedal box climbing, and robot-arm ring-on-peg transfer, BVER learns faster than all compared reference-free curricula. On box climbing, it reaches 95% success on a 0.4 m 0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box in roughly 65% fewer iterations than the best of them, is the only one of them to learn to climb a 0.7 m 0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box, and yields a policy robust to start, goal, and yaw variation. Without a demonstration, it approaches the sample efficiency of reference-based curricula on the 0.4 m 0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box and on ring-on-peg transfer. Ablations show that expanding from both ends outperforms either direction alone.
Project website, videos, and code: https://bver-rl.github.io/
2026-10-05.introduction:
Many robotic tasks are naturally posed as reaching a goal: a quadruped that should climb onto a box is rewarded for standing on top of it, not for how it gets there. With such a sparse reward and a long horizon, a policy started from the initial state distribution rarely reaches the goal and thus receives no learning signal ( Florensa et al., 2017 ) : policy gradient methods such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) learn from the returns of the trajectories the policy currently generates, and a reward that none of them collects cannot guide it.

In robot control, the missing signal is typically supplied by terrain curricula with dense rewards ( Rudin et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2020 ) , reference motions ( Fuchioka et al., 2023 ) , hand-designed curricula ( Atanassov et al., 2025 ) , or curiosity rewards ( Schwarke et al., 2023 ) . These have enabled highly capable controllers but require a demonstration, task-specific engineering, or reward terms beyond the task objective.

Automatic curriculum learning replaces this design effort with intermediate tasks generated during training ( Narvekar et al., 2020 ; Portelas et al., 2020b ) . Start-state curricula begin closer to the goal, with start states taken from a reference trajectory ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Resnick et al., 2018 ) or from random walks outward from the goal ( Florensa et al., 2017 ) , and goal curricula keep the start fixed and propose intermediate goals ( Florensa et al., 2018 ; Ren et al., 2019 ; Cho et al., 2023 ) . Both expand from one end only: the frontier must cover the entire distance to the fixed end, and the policy trains on the target task from that side only.

Two mechanisms from sampling-based motion planning address this limitation. Rapidly-exploring random trees ( LaValle & Kuffner, 2001 , RRT;) extend the vertex nearest to a uniform sample of the space, so growth is biased toward large unexplored regions (the Voronoi bias), and RRT-Connect ( Kuffner & LaValle, 2000 ) grows one tree from the start and one from the goal and extends each toward the other until they meet. BVER (Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration curriculum for Reinforcement learning) transfers both to curriculum generation. It grows start states outward from the goal by random walks (the backwards expansion) and goals outward from the initial state distribution in the same way (the forwards expansion), connects the two sets, and trains a single goal-conditioned policy on both. Like reverse curriculum generation ( Florensa et al., 2017 , RC;) , BVER keeps only tasks of intermediate difficulty for the current policy, while its expansion covers the task space (Figure 2 ).

Our contributions are:

A bidirectional start–goal curriculum for sparse-reward, long-horizon goal-conditioned RL that generates both intermediate starts and goals, without reference motions, shaped rewards, or a hand-designed curriculum.

A bidirectional start–goal curriculum for sparse-reward, long-horizon goal-conditioned RL that generates both intermediate starts and goals, without reference motions, shaped rewards, or a hand-designed curriculum.

An expansion mechanism that carries the Voronoi bias of RRT and the connect step of RRT-Connect over to curriculum generation to propose feasible states as tasks.

Experiments showing that BVER learns fastest among the reference-free curricula on all six compared tasks, is the only one of them to learn to climb the 0.7 m 0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box, transfers to scanned terrains with the same hyperparameters, and outperforms either expansion direction alone.

1. A bidirectional start–goal curriculum for sparse-reward, long-horizon goal-conditioned RL that generates both intermediate starts and goals, without reference motions, shaped rewards, or a hand-designed curriculum.

2. An expansion mechanism that carries the Voronoi bias of RRT and the connect step of RRT-Connect over to curriculum generation to propose feasible states as tasks.

3. Experiments showing that BVER learns fastest among the reference-free curricula on all six compared tasks, is the only one of them to learn to climb the 0.7 m 0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box, transfers to scanned terrains with the same hyperparameters, and outperforms either expansion direction alone.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Automatic curriculum learning (ACL) adapts the training tasks to the learner ( Narvekar et al., 2020 ; Portelas et al., 2020b ) . Environment curricula sample generator parameters by learning progress ( Portelas et al., 2020a ) , replay levels by value loss ( Jiang et al., 2021 ) , generate regret-maximizing levels ( Dennis et al., 2020 ; Parker-Holder et al., 2022 ) , or widen domain randomization as performance improves ( Akkaya et al., 2019 ) ; reward curricula add intrinsic rewards such as RND ( Burda et al., 2019 ) , whose authors highlight global exploration as an important direction. BVER is complementary, changing only where episodes start and which goal they pursue.

Reverse curriculum generation ( Florensa et al., 2017 , RC;) grows start states outward from the goal by random-action rollouts and keeps those of intermediate difficulty, using resets but no demonstrations; BaRC ( Ivanovic et al., 2019 ) uses backward reachable sets of an approximate model instead. Demonstration-based methods reset to states of a reference trajectory ( Salimans & Chen, 2018 ; Nair et al., 2018 ) , sampled uniformly ( Peng et al., 2018 , RSI;) , moved backward on a schedule ( Resnick et al., 2018 , Backplay;) , or prioritized by success rate ( Tao et al., 2024 , RFCL;) . Go-Explore ( Ecoffet et al., 2021 ) and PBCS ( Matheron et al., 2020 ) return to rarely visited states from an archive and explore from there. Similarly, BVER seeds its random walks at stored states.

Goal curricula keep the initial state distribution and propose goals: GoalGAN ( Florensa et al., 2018 ) generates goals of intermediate difficulty; HGG ( Ren et al., 2019 ) and OUTPACE ( Cho et al., 2023 ) select achieved states by progress toward the target, and DISCOVER ( Diaz-Bone et al., 2025 ) by estimated achievability, novelty, and relevance; Skew-Fit ( Pong et al., 2020 ) and MEGA ( Pitis et al., 2020 ) select achieved states of low density; and C-Planning ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) commands waypoints between start and goal under a learned distance. VaPRL ( Sharma et al., 2021 ) and IBC ( Kim et al., 2023 ) build such curricula from replay-buffer states and, unlike BVER, need no resets. BVER builds on both lines of work, growing start states and goals toward each other and seeding them by Voronoi bias instead of visit counts or density.

A rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) ( LaValle & Kuffner, 2001 ) extends the vertex nearest to a random sample; vertices are thus selected in proportion to the area of their Voronoi regions, which biases the tree toward unexplored space ( Kuffner & LaValle, 2000 ) . RRT-Connect ( Kuffner & LaValle, 2000 ) grows trees from start and goal and connects them. R3L ( Morere et al., 2020 ) initializes a policy from RRT solutions, and SoRB ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ) searches a graph over replay-buffer states with a learned value function. Florensa et al. (2017) proposed combining start-state and goal generation as future work, citing RRT-Connect as the analogue; BVER follows this suggestion, growing a curriculum rather than a path.

Legged robots are mostly trained with dense rewards and terrain curricula ( Rudin et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2020 ) , with an inner-product reward for parkour ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , or with RSI on a trajectory-optimization reference ( Fuchioka et al., 2023 ) . Hand-designed curricula start jumps at random heights and upward velocities ( Atanassov et al., 2025 ) or grow obstacle dimensions and navigation distances with performance ( Hoeller et al., 2024 ) , and Schwarke et al. (2023) extend RND with a curiosity state for sparse-reward loco-manipulation. These methods yield highly capable controllers; BVER targets settings without such guidance.

2026-10-05.title: Native Action-Prior Learning from Videos for World Action Models
2026-10-05.authors: Zhaochong An , Fei Zhang , Menglin Jia , Duncan Frost , Zijian Zhou , Yikai Wang , Xudong Wang , Aditya Patel , Belinda Zeng , Tao Xiang , Serge Belongie , Amir Bar , Sen He
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.comment: Project Page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
World action models integrate future visual dynamics with robot action prediction, but their scalability remains limited by the need for action-annotated robot trajectories.
Observation-only videos contain rich evidence about interaction dynamics, but existing approaches typically use them either to pretrain visual representations that must later be adapted for control, or to infer latent actions that are subsequently grounded to robot commands.
We present NAVA-WAM , which introduces native action-prior learning by directly pretraining the action policy from observation-only videos, avoiding indirect representation-to-control transfer or a separate latent-action model.
Our training consists of two stages.
First, we pretrain on observation-only videos, where future-video flow-matching supervision over visual transitions is propagated through transition-structured joint attention to optimize the Action-DiT and learn action-relevant priors.
Second, we use action-labeled demonstrations to post-train the Action-DiT for robot control through joint video–action flow matching, while asymmetric attention decouples the visual branch from iterative action denoising and enables efficient action-only inference.
Extensive experiments show that NAVA-WAM consistently outperforms prior approaches under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, while demonstrating strong action-label efficiency and effective real-robot generalization.
These results establish native action-prior learning as an effective approach to directly pretrain action policies from observation-only videos, providing a scalable path beyond action-labeled robot data.
2026-10-05.introduction:
World action models (WAMs) ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026a ; Bi et al., 2026a ) incorporate future visual dynamics into action learning, with strong potential to improve policy generalization.
However, scaling WAMs remains challenging because they rely on action-annotated robot trajectories that are costly to collect and hard to standardize across embodiments.
In contrast, large-scale observation-only videos provide abundant information about physical interactions and state transitions without action labels.
The key challenge is therefore how to leverage such videos to learn priors that effectively improve action policy learning.

Existing approaches largely follow two paradigms for exploiting observation-only videos. Vision representation learning first learns visual or predictive representations from videos and then trains an action policy on top of them using action-labeled robot demonstrations ( Nair et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Assran et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) .
Because the learned video prior remains encoded in a vision-centric representation, its connection to executable actions is established only during downstream robot training, introducing an indirect representation-to-control transfer. Latent-action learning instead infers action-like variables from visual transitions and uses them as intermediate supervision for subsequent policy learning ( Schmidt and Jiang, 2024 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Bu et al., 2025b ; Bi et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ) .
While more action-oriented, this paradigm requires an additional latent-action modeling stage and relies on complex architectural or optimization constraints ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) to avoid shortcut solutions in which the latent action simply copies information from the target observation.
These constraints increase modeling complexity and can restrict the expressiveness of the latent-action space, thereby limiting the supervision provided to the policy and impairing its control learning.

These limitations motivate a simple question: Can observation-only videos directly optimize an action policy without relying on an intermediate interface? We answer this question with NAVA-WAM , which introduces native action-prior learning for world action models.
As illustrated in Fig. 1 , instead of first learning a separate visual representation or latent-action space and then using it in policy training, NAVA-WAM uses future-video prediction to directly pretrain the action policy.
This creates a direct learning path from scalable observation-only videos to the action policy, avoiding intermediate representation constraints and enabling more effective policy learning.

Specifically, NAVA-WAM adopts a joint Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture ( Liang et al., 2024 ) , comprising a Video-DiT and an Action-DiT that interact through joint attention while retaining modality-specific parameters.
During action-free pre-training, the Video-DiT is frozen and the Action-DiT is optimized solely through future-video flow-matching supervision.
Our transition-structured joint attention allows the Action-DiT to model visual transitions while participating in future-state prediction, enabling the video objective to directly optimize the action policy.
In this way, the Action-DiT learns action-relevant priors directly from visual transitions without requiring an intermediate interface.
During downstream post-training, we jointly optimize the video and action streams on action-labeled robot demonstrations through video–action flow matching, adapting the pretrained Action-DiT to embodiment-specific control.
We make cross-stream attention asymmetric to decouple the visual stream from the evolving action sample, allowing its representations to be cached and enabling efficient action-only inference without explicitly generating future videos.

We evaluate NAVA-WAM on the simulation benchmarks LIBERO/LIBERO-Plus ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Fei et al., 2025 ) and RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025a ) under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, demonstrating superior performance across both regimes.
We further deploy NAVA-WAM on a physical Franka FR3, achieving 93.3 % 93.3\% success across tabletop manipulation tasks, compared with 66.7 % 66.7\% for DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026c ) and 53.3 % 53.3\% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) .
Controlled experiments show that native action-prior learning consistently outperforms representation-based and latent-action-based approaches across action-label budgets, with larger gains in low-budget regimes.
Together, these results demonstrate that native action-prior learning can effectively leverage observation-only videos to learn action priors, improving generalization and action-label efficiency.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 World Action Models

Direct visuomotor policies learn observation-to-action mappings across tasks and embodiments ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Team et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , while vision–language–action (VLA) models further leverage semantic priors from large-scale vision–language pre-training ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024a ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Shin et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026f ; Yang et al., 2026a ) .
Their primary objective, however, remains conditional action prediction, leaving environment dynamics to be learned implicitly.
With recent advances in video modeling ( An et al., 2026a ; Qiao et al., 2026 ; An et al., 2026b ) , world action models (WAMs) instead explicitly couple action learning with predictive modeling of future visual evolution.
Existing WAMs can be broadly categorized into cascaded and joint architectures. Cascaded WAMs first extract predictive information from a video or world model and then use it to drive a separate action module ( Du et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024b ; Ko et al., 2024 ) .
Some methods explicitly generate future observations, visual subgoals, or motion cues before action prediction ( Bharadhwaj et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026d ; Li et al., 2026b ; Lou et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , while others condition policies on predictive intermediate representations without explicit pixel generation ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026b ) . Joint WAMs model future observations and actions within a shared architecture, enabling direct interaction between visual and action representations ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026a ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Bi et al., 2026b ) .
DreamZero and LingBot-VA ( Ye et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026a ) jointly perform future visual prediction and action generation during closed-loop control, whereas Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) retains future-video prediction as training-time supervision while performing action-only inference.
Dyna-2 ( Dyna Robotics, 2026 ) further shows that adding human videos through co-training improves cross-embodiment generalization. NAVA-WAM follows the joint WAM paradigm with action-only inference, while enabling the action-generating expert to be directly pretrained from observation-only videos.

## 2.2 Learning from Observation-Only Videos

Observation-only videos provide scalable supervision for physical interactions and state transitions without action annotations.
Existing robot learning approaches primarily leverage them through two paradigms. Vision representation learning learns visual or predictive representations from videos and uses them during downstream policy learning ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Nair et al., 2023 ; Goswami et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) .
VPP ( Hu et al., 2025 ) conditions policies on predictive video features, and Masquerade ( Lepert et al., 2025 ) learns visual representations through future robot-keypoint prediction.
V-JEPA 2 and JEPA-VLA ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Miao et al., 2026 ) use predictive video representations for planning and VLA learning.
Such approaches retain video-derived knowledge in visual representations whose connection to executable actions is established only during downstream policy training, resulting in an indirect representation-to-control transfer. Latent-action learning instead infers action-like variables from visual transitions as intermediate supervision for policy learning ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Nikulin et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025b ; Tharwat et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Wan et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026a ) .
LAPO ( Schmidt and Jiang, 2024 ) learns latent actions with a latent-to-action decoder, while LAPA ( Ye et al., 2025 ) pretrains a VLA through discrete latent-action prediction before grounding them to robot actions.
Motus ( Bi et al., 2026a ) incorporates optical-flow motion cues, while RepWAM and LingBot-VA 2.0 ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) learn transition-oriented action representations in semantic visual spaces.
However, these methods introduce an additional latent-action modeling stage and require architectural or optimization constraints to prevent shortcut solutions ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Chen et al., 2026a ) ,
which can constrain the learned latent-action space and the supervision it provides to the policy.
In contrast, NAVA-WAM introduces native action-prior learning to learn transition priors directly within the action policy, providing a direct path from scalable observation-only videos to action policy pre-training.

2026-10-05.title: Self-Repairing Recurrent Ensembles for Real-Time Recovery from Distribution Shift
2026-10-05.authors: Julian Lemmel , Pedro D. Wendel Garcia , Taisuke Kobayashi , Radu Grosu
2026-10-05.subjects: Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-05.abstract: Deploying a pretrained controller exposes it to conditions that are absent from its training data. Sensor drift, outright sensor failure and accumulating measurement noise all induce a distribution shift that can collapse an otherwise competent policy – typically at a point in time where no expert is available to supply corrective labels. We present a method that lets a policy recover from such shifts online and without supervision. Our controller is an ensemble of recurrent networks, each of which observes a randomly masked subset of the observation vector, and whose Gaussian outputs are combined through sequential Kalman fusion so that confident members dominate the consensus action. At deployment, we treat this consensus as a self-supervised label and fine-tune each member towards it, scaling each member’s contribution proportional to the complement of its squared Kalman gain. Gradients are computed using RFLO, an efficient and biologically plausible approximation of Real-Time Recurrent Learning, so that a parameter update follows every environment step and the policy reacts to a shift as it unfolds. On a range of simulated continuous control tasks, our approach recovers close to the original performance after a sensor shift, while ensembles that see the full observation are unable to recover. The same framework subsumes fully online interactive imitation learning: when an expert is present, the consensus label is replaced by the expert action and the identical update rule refines the policy during teleoperation.

2026-10-05.title: EmbPASS: Towards Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation
2026-10-05.authors: Pujun Guo , Yuanfan Zheng , Fei Teng , Mengfei Duan , Guoqiang Zhao , Yuheng Zhang , Kai Luo , Kailun Yang
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.abstract: Panoramic images provide a complete 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} field of view, enabling comprehensive scene understanding for embodied perception. However, heterogeneous embodied platforms exhibit substantial differences in observation viewpoints and spatial layouts, giving rise to cross-embodiment observation shifts that pose additional challenges to consistent and reliable panoramic perception, while systematic studies of this problem remain limited. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new task, termed Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation . Meanwhile, we establish EmbPASS , a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark spanning Vehicle , Drone , Wearable , and Quadruped platforms under a unified semantic taxonomy, providing a testbed for systematically studying cross-embodiment panoramic perception. We further propose EPONet , an open-vocabulary panoramic semantic segmentation network that integrates Relation-Aware Metric Adapter (RAMA) and Content-Adaptive Semantic Transfer (CAST) to enhance spatial modeling and semantic transfer under heterogeneous embodied observations. Extensive experiments show that EPONet achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS with 35.82 % 35.82\% mIoU, outperforming the strongest baseline by 1.10 % 1.10\% , while remaining competitive on existing panoramic segmentation benchmarks. The source code and EmbPASS benchmark will be made publicly available at https://github.com/guopj1/EmbPASS .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Environmental perception is fundamental to autonomous robots operating in complex and unconstrained real-world environments, where reliable scene understanding supports navigation, planning, and decision-making [ 1 , 2 ] . In recent years, panoramic vision has attracted increasing attention in robotic scene understanding due to its complete 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} Field of View (FoV) and more comprehensive environmental observations [ 3 , 4 ] . Despite the inherent projection distortions of panoramic imagery, panoramic scene understanding has continued to advance and has progressively expanded toward more open perception settings [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] .

However, systematic studies of panoramic semantic segmentation across heterogeneous embodied platforms remain relatively limited [ 5 , 6 , 8 , 9 ] .
In practical robotic deployments, differences in embodied platform configurations and sensor mounting conditions often result in distinct observation heights and viewpoints [ 10 , 11 ] , leading to substantial differences in panoramic appearance and spatial layout. Such differences give rise to cross-embodiment observation shifts, posing additional challenges to consistent and reliable panoramic perception. Meanwhile, acquiring dense panoramic annotations for each embodied platform is costly and becomes increasingly impractical as the diversity of embodied platforms continues to grow.

To enable panoramic scene understanding across diverse embodied platforms and address the above challenges, we introduce a new task, termed Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation . Accordingly, the model is trained only on pinhole images from a label-rich source domain and directly performs open-vocabulary semantic segmentation on panoramic images captured by unseen embodied platforms, without requiring target-platform annotations. As illustrated in Fig. (b), OPS [ 9 ] extends the FoV to 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} panoramic observations, while our task further considers heterogeneous embodied platforms to unlock platform diversity.

To systematically study this task, we construct EmbPASS , a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark for heterogeneous embodied platforms, as shown in Fig. (a). EmbPASS covers multiple representative platforms under a unified semantic taxonomy, providing a common testbed for evaluating cross-embodiment open panoramic segmentation. Compared with existing panoramic benchmarks [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , EmbPASS explicitly incorporates platform diversity, enabling systematic analysis of platform-dependent observation variations. EmbPASS further reveals clear platform-dependent differences in the spherical spatial organization of scene semantics. Since ERP projection distortion is inherently latitude-dependent, such semantic layout variations introduce additional geometric challenges for cross-embodiment panoramic perception.

Accordingly, we propose EPONet , an open-vocabulary panoramic semantic segmentation network for heterogeneous embodied platforms. To accommodate the diverse local distortion conditions encountered in heterogeneous embodied observations, we introduce Relation-Aware Metric Adapter (RAMA), which predicts metric parameters from content representations and directional neighborhood relations and uses them to constrain the sampling support, enabling structured spatial aggregation under diverse local geometric distortions. Meanwhile, to better exploit transferable pretrained semantics under varying observation conditions, we propose Content-Adaptive Semantic Transfer (CAST), which adaptively reorganizes and transfers intermediate CLIP [ 16 ] representations according to the current observation.

Extensive experiments on the established EmbPASS benchmark and existing panoramic segmentation benchmarks verify the effectiveness of EPONet. EPONet achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS, reaching 35.82 % 35.82\% mIoU and outperforming the strongest competing method by 1.10 % 1.10\% . It also remains competitive on the public Stanford2D3D [ 12 ] and DensePASS [ 15 ] benchmarks.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation and further establish EmbPASS , a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark for systematically studying this task.

We propose EPONet , a cross-embodiment open panoramic segmentation network that integrates RAMA and CAST for effective panoramic perception across heterogeneous embodied platforms.

Extensive experiments on EmbPASS and existing panoramic benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of EPONet, which achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS while remaining competitive on public panoramic benchmarks.

1. We introduce Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation and further establish EmbPASS , a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark for systematically studying this task.

2. We propose EPONet , a cross-embodiment open panoramic segmentation network that integrates RAMA and CAST for effective panoramic perception across heterogeneous embodied platforms.

3. Extensive experiments on EmbPASS and existing panoramic benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of EPONet, which achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS while remaining competitive on public panoramic benchmarks.

# II Related Work

## II-A Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation (OVSS) leverages vision-language models such as CLIP [ 16 ] to segment an open set of text-defined categories, but their image-level pre-training does not directly provide the spatial precision required for dense prediction. Existing training-based methods adapt vision-language models to dense prediction either by constructing and aggregating pixel-level image-text similarities [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] or by classifying category-agnostic mask proposals through region-text matching [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] .
Within the mask-based paradigm, SAN [ 24 ] attaches a lightweight side network to a frozen CLIP backbone and decouples mask proposal generation from CLIP-based region recognition.
Despite these advances, most OVSS methods are designed for and evaluated primarily on perspective images.

## II-B Panoramic Segmentation and Cross-Platform Perception

Panoramic semantic segmentation provides dense scene understanding over a complete 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} field of view [ 3 , 4 ] . Existing studies mitigate projection distortions through spherical geometry modeling [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] and distortion-aware spatial modeling [ 28 ] , while reducing reliance on panoramic annotations through unsupervised domain adaptation [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 15 , 29 , 30 ] and its multi-source and source-free extensions [ 31 , 32 ] .
Recent studies have also extended panoramic segmentation beyond conventional closed-set prediction to broader task settings [ 33 , 34 ] . In particular, OPS and subsequent work extend open-vocabulary segmentation to panoramic imagery, with models trained on FoV-restricted pinhole source images and directly evaluated on unseen panoramic domains [ 8 , 9 ] .

Meanwhile, cross-view and cross-platform perception have attracted increasing attention in robotic vision.
Existing studies transfer perceptual knowledge across substantially different viewpoints and platforms through cross-view adaptation and domain alignment [ 10 , 35 ] ; other works improve generalization across platforms and sensing configurations through geometric alignment and feature-level alignment, platform-aware modeling, and explicit modeling of camera configuration priors [ 11 , 36 , 37 ] .
Despite advances in both panoramic segmentation and cross-platform perception, open-vocabulary panoramic segmentation across heterogeneous embodied platforms remains largely unexplored.

## II-C Adaptive Spatial Sampling

Deformable convolutions adapt local sampling locations by learning spatially
varying offsets, thereby improving their ability to model complex geometric
variations [ 38 ] . Subsequent variants introduce modulation mechanisms [ 39 ] , grouped spatial aggregation [ 40 ] , and more efficient implementations [ 41 ] . In panoramic segmentation, distortion-aware spatial sampling has been explored through geometry-guided and deformable mechanisms to accommodate spatially non-uniform projection distortions [ 5 , 9 , 26 , 28 ] .
In contrast to deformable operators that directly predict pointwise sampling offsets, recent work parameterizes adaptive sampling through low-dimensional, signal-dependent local metrics, thereby constructing structured and content-adaptive sampling supports [ 42 ] .

2026-10-05.title: How to Find and Reuse Policies for Continuous Adaptation in Lifelong Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Saptarshi Nath , Inish M. D'Souza , Antonio Carta , Soheil Kolouri , Andrea Soltoggio
2026-10-05.comment: Code is available at this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: In lifelong reinforcement learning, retaining previously learned policies is not sufficient for effective transfer to a new task. Useful knowledge may be distributed across several prior policies, and its relevance may change as the learner acquires experience. One hypothesis is that task similarity can be effectively used in a continual learning setting to find and combine previously learned policies. To test it, Adaptive Mask Selection and Composition (AMSC) is designed to estimate similarity from online experience via non-parametric Wasserstein task embeddings from state-action-reward samples. The z-score-normalized sparsemax of the similarity scores are used to derive a variable-size support to periodically choose and weight policies to form a prior when learning a new task. On CT-graph and MiniGrid, AMSC achieves higher mean performance and forward transfer than the evaluated modular composition baselines while exhibiting no forgetting. Results on Continual World suggest that identifying relevant prior knowledge and determining its layer-specific composition may require additional layer-specific tuning. Ablations show that selecting relevant sources and determining how strongly to reuse them are central to these gains. Independently measured pairwise transfer is also positively associated with task-embedding similarity. These results indicate that task similarity can be an effective criterion to select and weight specific knowledge for reuse in lifelong reinforcement learning.

2026-10-05.title: CrowdOcc: Monocular Semantic Scene Completion for Quadruped Robots in Crowded Indoor Environments
2026-10-05.authors: Feiyang Chen , Jincheng Hu , Yiduo Chen , Jihao Li , Yue Liang , Bingzhao Gao , Yanjun Huang , Yuanjian Zhang
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.comment: . Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
2026-10-05.abstract: Monocular semantic scene completion (SSC) for quadruped robots remains underexplored in real crowded indoor environments, where human-scene occlusion disrupts static geometry and human occupancy predictions are often incomplete or spatially misplaced. We present CrowdOcc, an RGB-D dataset and monocular SSC framework for this setting. CrowdOcc contains 25.1K frames from 11 indoor scenes, with semantic occupancy annotations constructed through static-dynamic decoupling. Our framework combines: (i) Normal-Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) to complement depth-aware lifting with surface-normal cues for occlusion-robust geometry; and (ii) Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) to selectively model human-human and local human-scene relations in 3D. Our method achieves state-of-the-art SSC performance on CrowdOcc’s scene-disjoint test set, reaching 15.80 IoU, 11.40 mIoU, and 46.23 Human IoU, demonstrating generalization to unseen indoor scenes.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) predicts dense 3D occupancy and semantics from partial observations [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Monocular SSC further reduces the sensing requirement to a single RGB image, making it attractive for onboard perception on quadruped robots [ 8 ] . However, most existing SSC datasets are built around static indoor scenes or autonomous-driving settings, where the sensing viewpoint, scene dynamics, and occupancy distribution differ substantially from those encountered by quadruped robots in crowded indoor environments [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . In particular, existing datasets provide limited coverage of low-viewpoint observations with dense human presence and dynamic human occupancy. As summarized in Table I , this leaves real crowded indoor SSC for quadruped robots largely underexplored.

Crowded indoor scenes introduce two difficulties that are not well addressed by conventional monocular SSC pipelines. First, humans frequently occlude large portions of walls, floors, doors, and other static structures. The resulting incomplete observations weaken depth-based feature lifting and make the recovery of scene geometry less reliable [ 13 , 14 ] . Second, human occupancy remains difficult to recover reliably in crowded scenes. Partial observations and foreground-background ambiguity frequently lead to incomplete human geometry and erroneous spatial placement. These issues become more pronounced when the test environment differs from the training scenes, where scene-specific geometric priors no longer transfer reliably.

To address this difficulties, we introduce CrowdOcc, an RGB-D dataset for monocular SSC in real crowded indoor environments, together with a model tailored to scene geometry and human occupancy. CrowdOcc contains 25.1K frames collected from 11 independent indoor scenes using a quadruped robot. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , synchronized RGB-D, LiDAR, and IMU measurements are used for offline occupancy construction, while inference takes only a single RGB image. For scene geometry, we propose Normal-Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) module, which complements depth-based lifting with surface-normal cues and improves the representation of partially observed static structures. For human occupancy, we introduce Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) module, which selects human-related voxel candidates and explicitly models human-human and local human-scene interactions in 3D. We evaluate cross-scene generalization on test scenes excluded from both training and validation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art SSC performance under this protocol.

Our key contributions are:

Dataset. We introduce CrowdOcc, an RGB-D dataset for monocular SSC in real crowded indoor environments from a quadruped viewpoint, comprising 25.1K frames from 11 independent scenes, 8 occupied semantic categories, and 0.08 m voxels on a 50 × 60 × 96 50\times 60\times 96 grid.

Method. We propose NGSGF module and HCSI module to address the two main difficulties of crowded indoor SSC. NGSGF enhances static-scene geometry under human occlusion by coupling depth-based lifting with surface-normal cues, while HCSI refines human geometry and spatial placement through sparse human-centric 3D interaction.

Generalization. Extensive experiments on scene-disjoint test scenes show strong cross-scene generalization, with our method achieving state-of-the-art SSC performance on unseen indoor environments.

2026-10-05.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Monocular Semantic Scene Completion

Monocular SSC recovers dense 3D occupancy and semantics from a single RGB image [ 13 , 21 ] . MonoScene [ 8 ] established a representative image-to-voxel pipeline by lifting 2D features into a 3D volume and performing volumetric context reasoning. Subsequent methods improve either the lifting process or the resulting 3D representation [ 22 ] . VoxFormer [ 23 ] constructs depth-guided sparse voxel queries before dense completion, while NDC-Scene [ 24 ] performs feature projection in normalized device coordinates to reduce lifting ambiguity. ISO [ 9 ] further incorporates monocular depth into indoor SSC through depth-aware feature projection and multi-scale fusion. Recent approaches explore instance-level context, scene-adaptive decoding, Gaussian representations, and additional geometric priors to improve monocular occupancy prediction [ 25 , 14 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] .
Despite these advances, depth remains the dominant geometric cue for image-to-voxel lifting. Under heavy occlusion, depth alone provides limited information about local surface orientation and structural continuity. Our NGSGF complements depth-based lifting with surface-normal cues to improve static-scene geometry in crowded environments.

## II-B Human-Centric and Embodied Occupancy Perception

Vision-based occupancy prediction has been extensively studied in autonomous-driving settings [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] , with recent efforts extending it to embodied platforms. EmbodiedOcc [ 16 ] studies online occupancy prediction for vision-based robotic scene understanding, while EmbodiedOcc++ [ 34 ] further improves geometric modeling for robotic perception. OneOcc [ 12 ] considers SSC for legged robots using panoramic vision and develops platform-specific designs for gait-induced motion and omnidirectional sensing. Human-aware occupancy has also been explored for modeling human-scene spatial relations and dynamic agents [ 35 ] .
Existing instance-aware SSC methods model instance and scene context [ 25 , 36 ] . Our focus is targeted human-centric 3D reasoning to improve the completeness and spatial placement of human occupancy in crowded indoor scenes.

## II-C SSC Datasets and Occupancy Construction

Existing SSC datasets cover a wide range of sensing platforms and environments [ 37 ] . NYUv2 [ 15 ] and Occ-ScanNet [ 9 , 38 ] focus primarily on static indoor scenes, whereas SemanticKITTI [ 10 ] , SSCBench-KITTI-360 [ 17 , 18 ] , and Occ3D [ 11 , 19 ] are designed for autonomous-driving settings. WildOcc [ 20 ] extends occupancy prediction to off-road environments. More recent datasets consider embodied and panoramic perception: Human360Occ provides synthetic human-ego panoramic occupancy, while QuadOcc collects real panoramic data from a quadruped robot [ 12 ] . As summarized in Table I, none of these datasets jointly provide real crowded indoor scenes, low-viewpoint quadruped observations, and dynamic human occupancy.
Dense occupancy labels are commonly constructed by aggregating multi-frame observations. SurroundOcc [ 39 ] and OpenOccupancy [ 40 ] use temporal sensor accumulation to improve scene coverage, while Occ3D [ 11 ] additionally models visibility when defining occupied, free, and unobserved regions. Such aggregation is well suited to static geometry but is less reliable for dynamic objects. PointSSC [ 41 ] therefore separates static and dynamic components and registers dynamic observations across views. This assumption becomes problematic for humans, whose pose and shape vary continuously over time. CrowdOcc instead reconstructs the static scene from human-free sequences and derives human occupancy from synchronized current-frame observations, avoiding temporal accumulation of non-rigid human geometry.

2026-10-05.title: OmniAct3D: Leveraging Foundation Geometry and Evidence-Grounded Reasoning for Panoramic 3D Detection
2026-10-05.authors: Runtong Wu , Fei Teng , Di Wen , Guoqiang Zhao , Kunyu Peng , Kailun Yang
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.abstract: Accurate 3D detection is essential for mobile embodied agents, while Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) offer transferable visual and geometric priors. Yet existing VFM-based 3D detectors rely on narrow-view monocular images or discrete perspective views, limiting coherent surround perception; equirectangular projection (ERP) instead encodes a continuous 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} scene in a single image. Direct transfer remains difficult because ERP organizes geometry and visual information differently, making object-relevant cues hard to model, localize, and preserve. We propose OmniAct3D , a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP while preserving transferable VFM priors. To resolve geometric mismatch, the ERP-Ray Geometry Adapter ( ERGA-Ray ) models spherical viewing rays and periodic spatial structure. To localize evidence in scene-wide context, the Visual-Action Reasoning Chain ( VARC ) grounds each hypothesis in relevant panoramic evidence and converts it into a structured geometric action. To recover local cues lost under fixed token budgets, the Appearance-Guided Heading Expert (AGHE) re-encodes object regions at higher resolution for heading estimation. Experiments show that OmniAct3D improves over the previous best 3D detector by 2.96 2.96 NDS points on Spheriverse and over the unadapted VFM baseline by 24.87 24.87 mAP points on PanoMMOcc. With target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 95 95 – 98 % 98\% of the same-configuration mAP, indicating reusable object-level 3D reasoning across sensing configurations. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/FeiT-FeiTeng/OmniAct3D .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Accurate and robust 3D detection is essential for mobile embodied agents to understand and interact with the physical world.
From autonomous vehicles to mobile robots, agents must estimate the 3D locations, dimensions, and orientations of surrounding objects to support navigation, motion planning, and embodied decision-making [ 1 , 2 ] .

Recent VFM-based 3D detectors [ 5 , 6 ] leverage transferable visual and geometric priors for object-level 3D perception. Despite this progress, existing methods primarily follow two perspective-image paradigms. As shown in Fig. 1 ,
monocular methods [ 3 , 7 ] infer 3D boxes from a single perspective image but observe only a limited field of view;
Multi-view methods [ 8 , 9 ] extend the surrounding coverage using discrete perspective observations.
In contrast, equirectangular projection (ERP) encodes the surrounding spherical field of view within a single image, providing a unified and spatially continuous representation for coherent 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} perception [ 10 , 11 ] .

However, directly transferring perspective-trained VFM-based 3D detectors to ERP observations remains challenging because ERP organizes geometry and visual information differently from perspective imagery. This representation mismatch makes object-relevant cues difficult to model, localize, and preserve, giving rise to three challenges. First, the geometric priors of VFMs are learned predominantly from locally planar and non-periodic perspective imagery, whereas ERP exhibits spherical viewing directions, latitude-dependent distortion, and horizontal periodicity. Reusing these priors without adaptation therefore produces geometric representations misaligned with ERP structure, particularly at high latitudes and across the horizontal boundary. Second, although a single ERP image captures scene-wide context, the evidence relevant to each object occupies only a small portion of the panorama. Directly decoding 3D hypotheses from global features makes it difficult to localize and associate the supporting evidence for each object, especially when objects are small or occluded. Third, encoding an ultra-wide panorama under a fixed token budget compresses individual objects and discards fine-grained local appearance cues. The loss of features such as front–rear asymmetry impairs directed heading estimation.

To address these challenges, we propose OmniAct3D , a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP observations while preserving transferable VFM priors. To resolve the geometric mismatch, we introduce the ERP-Ray Geometry Adapter ( ERGA-Ray ), which models spherical viewing rays and ERP-aware spatial interactions to align pretrained foundation geometry with ERP-specific spherical and periodic structure. To localize object-relevant evidence in scene-wide context, we introduce the Visual-Action Reasoning Chain ( VARC ), which grounds each 3D hypothesis in relevant panoramic evidence and converts that evidence into a structured geometric action for object-level 3D reasoning. To recover local cues lost under a fixed token budget, we introduce the AGHE , which re-encodes object regions at higher resolution for directed heading estimation.

We evaluate OmniAct3D on Spheriverse [ 12 ] and PanoMMOcc [ 13 ] . On Spheriverse, OmniAct3D achieves 0.1887 / 0.1825 0.1887/0.1825 mAP/NDS, improving the previous best NDS by 2.96 2.96 points. On PanoMMOcc, it achieves 0.5897 / 0.4032 0.5897/0.4032 mAP/NDS and improves the unadapted VFM baseline by 24.87 24.87 mAP points. Moreover, with target-specific geometry adaptation via ERGA-Ray , VARC retains 95 % 95\% and 98 % 98\% of same-configuration mAP on Spheriverse and PanoMMOcc, respectively, indicating reusable object-level 3D reasoning across sensing configurations.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We propose OmniAct3D , a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP observations while preserving transferable VFM priors.

We introduce ERGA-Ray to align foundation geometry with ERP spherical and periodic structure.

We introduce VARC to ground 3D hypotheses in relevant panoramic evidence and convert that evidence into a structured geometric action, and AGHE to recover fine-grained local cues for directed heading estimation.

Experiments show that OmniAct3D improves NDS by 2.96 2.96 points over the previous best detector on Spheriverse and mAP by 24.87 24.87 points over the unadapted VFM baseline on PanoMMOcc; with target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 95 95 – 98 % 98\% of same-configuration mAP across sensing configurations.

1. We propose OmniAct3D , a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP observations while preserving transferable VFM priors.

2. We introduce ERGA-Ray to align foundation geometry with ERP spherical and periodic structure.

3. We introduce VARC to ground 3D hypotheses in relevant panoramic evidence and convert that evidence into a structured geometric action, and AGHE to recover fine-grained local cues for directed heading estimation.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Based 3D Object Detection

Vision-based 3D object detection estimates object locations, dimensions, and orientations from images. Monocular methods infer 3D states from a single perspective view using geometric constraints, depth estimation, or object-centric representations [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] .
Multi-view methods aggregate complementary observations through geometric projection, query-based aggregation, or BEV representations [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] , while temporal approaches further exploit cross-frame information [ 20 ] .
These methods are developed primarily for perspective imagery. Monocular systems have limited fields of view, whereas surround-view systems rely on multiple discrete camera views and cross-view integration. In contrast, our work studies object-level 3D detection directly from a panoramic representation for continuous 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} perception.

## II-B Omnidirectional Vision and ERP Perception

Equirectangular projection (ERP) represents a spherical field of view within a single image and naturally provides spatially continuous horizontal 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} coverage. ERP imagery has been studied for panoramic depth estimation, scene understanding, 3D detection, and omnidirectional occupancy prediction [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
However, ERP geometry differs fundamentally from perspective imaging due to latitude-dependent distortion, horizontal periodicity, and spherical viewing rays. Prior work addresses these properties through spherical convolutions and distortion sampling [ 25 , 26 ] , projection fusion [ 27 ] , and panoramic attention [ 28 ] . These works highlight the need for ERP-specific geometric modeling for coherent panoramic perception.

## II-C Foundation Models for Panoramic 3D Perception

Large-scale VFMs provide transferable priors for semantic and geometric perception. Visual models such as DINO [ 29 , 30 ] and SAM [ 31 , 32 ] learn reusable visual representations, while geometry foundation models such as UniDepth [ 33 ] , MoGe [ 34 ] , and VGGT [ 4 ] provide transferable priors for depth and 3D structure. We use the term VFM-based 3D detector for a 3D detector built on such pretrained models [ 6 , 35 , 36 , 37 ] .
Related work also develops camera-general geometry [ 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] .
Despite their transferability, adapting VFM-based 3D detection from perspective imagery to ERP remains challenging.
We address this perspective-to-ERP adaptation through ERP geometry alignment and evidence-grounded object-level 3D reasoning.

2026-10-05.title: RYOPO: Bringing End-to-End Category-Level Object Pose Estimation into Real Time
2026-10-05.authors: Hakjin Lee , Junghoon Seo , Jaehoon Sim
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Category-level object pose estimation predicts the rotation, translation, and metric size
of unseen instances within known categories.
Many accurate RGB-D methods rely on external instance segmentation and crop-based pose
estimation, introducing separate stages and object-dependent processing costs that hinder
real-time inference.
To bring accurate pose estimation into real time, we present RYOPO, an end-to-end trainable
query-based RGB-D set predictor. It jointly detects and segments objects and estimates their 9-DoF poses without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or a separately trained instance segmentor.
Shared image and scene encoding avoids repeated per-object crop encoding.
A query-conditioned geometry pathway associates observed 3D points and RGB features with
object queries and incorporates shared scene context.
Object-centric refinement uses the resulting point descriptors to update an explicit pose state
through pose-conditioned cross-attention and recurrent residual corrections.
On NOCS, RYOPO substantially improves on published RGB-D joint detection and pose estimation results.
It achieves competitive performance compared with two-stage methods
under all-object evaluation on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, while enabling
real-time full-frame pose estimation at 31.8 31.8 FPS on an RTX A6000.

2026-10-05.introduction:
Category-level object pose estimation predicts poses and metric sizes for unseen instances
within known categories, without test-instance CAD models [ 1 ] .
Common RGB-D pipelines use a separately trained instance segmentor to obtain object masks
and extract each object’s RGB crop and depth-derived point cloud for a per-object pose
network [ 2 , 3 ] .
This design adds an external segmentation stage and repeats crop encoding and pose
estimation for each detected instance, increasing inference cost with object count.
The resulting inference latency can limit closed-loop visual-servoing
performance [ 4 ] .
It can also reduce manipulation throughput by extending task cycles when perception
cannot be overlapped with robot motion [ 5 ] .

Joint methods already combine localization and pose prediction. CenterSnap [ 6 ] and ShAPO [ 7 ] use learned CAD-derived shape representations for RGB-D inference,
whereas YOPO [ 8 ] extends a detection transformer with parallel pose heads on
image-derived queries. We aim to extend the set-prediction formulation used by YOPO
to end-to-end RGB-D object pose estimation while achieving real-time inference.
The challenge is to gain accuracy from measured 3D geometry while keeping full-frame
computation within a real-time budget. This favors shared image and scene encoding over
independently encoding a crop for every object.

A straightforward RGB-D extension is to fuse encoded depth and RGB features before query decoding.
Early fusion makes depth available through shared features, but does not by itself specify
how each object’s measured 3D geometry should guide pose corrections.
In reference-box-based detection transformers such as DINO [ 9 ] , queries combine
content features with positional embeddings derived from 2D boxes. These spatial references
support image localization but do not explicitly represent 3D rotation, translation, or metric size.
We therefore investigate object-specific pose corrections guided by measured geometry and
the current pose estimate.

We present RYOPO ( R eal-Time YOPO ), a query-based RGB-D set-prediction framework for joint
detection, segmentation, and category-level object pose estimation. To the best of our
knowledge, RYOPO is the first end-to-end trainable query-based RGB-D set predictor for
category-level object pose estimation without explicit CAD-derived shape priors.
Built on the DETR-style EdgeCrafter architecture [ 10 ] , RYOPO
learns localization and pose estimation jointly, without a separately trained instance
segmentor or per-object crop encoder.

The key design couples object-associated geometry with an explicit pose state.
A query-conditioned geometry pathway associates measured 3D observations with object queries
and combines them with RGB appearance and shared scene context to update query content
and positional representations. Unlike YOPO’s parallel pose heads, object-centric refinement
combines object queries with current pose encodings for cross-attention to object
observations. Queries predict residual pose corrections; updated poses condition
further refinement without test-time optimization.

On NOCS, RYOPO substantially improves on published RGB-D joint detection and pose estimation
results. On REAL275 and HouseCat6D, performance is competitive with two-stage methods
under all-object evaluation. Our deployment achieves 31.8 31.8 FPS for full-frame pose estimation
on an RTX A6000 (Fig. 1 ).

Our main contributions are:

An end-to-end trainable RGB-D set predictor for joint detection, segmentation,
and object pose estimation without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or an external
instance segmentor.

An object-level depth integration method that associates observed 3D geometry with
DETR-style object queries, and a pose refinement method that combines query features
with the current pose state to attend to object observations and predict residual pose corrections.

Substantial gains over RGB-D joint methods on NOCS and competitive all-object
pose performance on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, with real-time pose inference.

1. An end-to-end trainable RGB-D set predictor for joint detection, segmentation,
and object pose estimation without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or an external
instance segmentor.

2. An object-level depth integration method that associates observed 3D geometry with
DETR-style object queries, and a pose refinement method that combines query features
with the current pose state to attend to object observations and predict residual pose corrections.

3. Substantial gains over RGB-D joint methods on NOCS and competitive all-object
pose performance on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, with real-time pose inference.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

Category-level object pose estimation. A central challenge is learning representations that generalize across
intra-category shape variation. NOCS [ 1 ] estimates pose and size by aligning
observed points with a shared canonical coordinate space.
SPD [ 11 ] and GCE-Pose [ 12 ] deform category shape priors, while
DPDN [ 13 ] combines prior deformation with direct pose regression.
Methods without explicit CAD-derived shape priors learn geometric
representations [ 14 , 15 ] , adaptive keypoints [ 2 ] , or features
guided by causal learning and knowledge distillation [ 3 ] .
AG-Pose and CleanPose use instance-level 3D models for NOCS training
supervision, requiring shape data in addition to pose annotations.
RYOPO constructs object-specific representations from predicted boxes and masks
within a joint predictor, without instance 3D models or explicit shape priors.

Joint object detection and pose estimation. Joint methods integrate object localization and pose estimation within a shared model.
CenterSnap [ 6 ] and ShAPO [ 7 ] jointly estimate RGB-D object poses
and reconstruct shapes using CAD-derived representations. ShAPO also uses test-time optimization.
FSD [ 16 ] also trains RGB-D detection and pose estimation end to end using center heatmaps.
It uses a frozen DeepSDF decoder pretrained on ShapeNet as a CAD-derived shape prior
for reconstruction and self-supervised learning.
YOPO [ 8 ] instead uses query-based set prediction for RGB-only pose estimation
without explicit shape supervision. Its decoder refines image-derived queries before
parallel heads predict pose.

This query-based formulation builds on DETR [ 17 ] and its
extensions [ 18 , 9 , 19 ] , while the
RT-DETR series [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] targets real-time detection.
Spatial encoding [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] and point–voxel cross-attention [ 27 ] also guide queries in 3 3 D detection. For efficient RGB-D pose estimation, we adopt
EdgeCrafter [ 10 ] as our detector foundation.
RYOPO extends this foundation by conditioning attention
to observed object geometry on an evolving 3D pose state.

Object- and scene-level feature fusion. RGB and point-cloud features provide complementary appearance and geometry cues.
For pose estimation, object-level fusion combines these cues within supplied object regions.
DenseFusion [ 28 ] uses dense feature fusion and iterative refinement for
instance-level pose estimation; SecondPose [ 29 ] fuses geometric and
pretrained semantic features for category-level prediction.

Scene-level image–point-cloud fusion extends integration to multi-object scenes through
early point/voxel feature augmentation [ 30 ] , query-mediated integration [ 31 , 32 ] ,
or feature exchange [ 33 ] . RYOPO combines shared image and scene encoding
with query-associated object observations, enabling object-specific pose refinement
within a joint set predictor.

2026-10-05.title: VIGOR: Zero-Shot Visual Generalization via Latent-Space Consistency in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Mingyu Park , Samyeul Noh , Hyun Myung , Donghwan Lee
2026-10-05.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) achieves strong sample efficiency by planning within learned latent dynamics, yet its performance degrades substantially under unseen visual distractions such as background variations, lighting changes, or camera shifts. Unlike model-free RL, where encoder perturbations affect only single-step predictions, MBRL suffers from a two-level vulnerability: visual distractions first push encoder outputs out of distribution, and these errors then compound through recursive latent rollouts over the planning horizon. We propose VI sual G eneralization via latent-space c O nsistency in model-based R L ( VIGOR ), a framework that enables zero-shot generalization to unseen visual distractions while retaining the sample efficiency of its MBRL backbone. VIGOR integrates three interdependent components: (i) asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation , which pairs weak-only and weak-to-strong latent views within a single batch; (ii) dynamics-level consistency , which enforces augmentation-invariant transition predictions through direct latent regression; and (iii) encoder-level stabilization , which prevents encoder drift under the cross-augmentation supervision imposed by dynamics-level consistency. Evaluations on the DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) and Robosuite show that VIGOR outperforms state-of-the-art model-free and model-based baselines, surpassing the second-best baseline by 3.4 % 3.4\% on DMC and 43.6 % 43.6\% on Robosuite. Ablations further show that VIGOR’s robustness is augmentation-agnostic: replacing the default augmentation with alternatives from distinct perturbation families preserves strong generalization, confirming that latent-space consistency, not the augmentation choice, drives robustness.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Visual reinforcement learning (visual RL) trains control policies directly from pixels, eliminating task-specific state estimation [ 26 , 25 , 45 , 44 ] . Despite success in locomotion and manipulation [ 8 , 23 , 17 ] , visual RL remains sensitive to unseen visual distractions: even minor shifts in backgrounds, lighting, or camera position can cause substantial policy degradation.

In model-free RL (MFRL), visual generalization has been addressed through data augmentation [ 16 , 20 ] , robust representation learning [ 18 , 4 , 48 ] , and stabilized value-function training [ 29 , 19 ] . Model-based RL (MBRL) offers superior sample efficiency by planning in learned latent dynamics [ 17 , 12 ] , but achieving visual generalization in MBRL is structurally more challenging. In MFRL, encoder perturbations affect only a single-step prediction. In MBRL, the problem is two-level: visual distractions first push encoder outputs out of the training distribution, and these out-of-distribution (OOD) latents are then recursively propagated by the dynamics model over a planning horizon H H , causing errors to compound across steps (Figure 1 ). This two-level vulnerability, which does not arise in MFRL, means that techniques effective for single-step robustness are insufficient when the encoder simultaneously serves a recursive dynamics model, Q-value networks, and a planner.

We propose VI sual G eneralization via latent-space c O nsistency in model-based R L ( VIGOR ), a framework that enables zero-shot generalization while retaining the sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone. VIGOR addresses the two-level vulnerability through three interdependent components: (i) asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation (AW), an asymmetric batch-splitting strategy that produces paired weak-only and weak-to-strong latents; (ii) dynamics-level consistency (DC), which enforces augmentation-invariant transition predictions by anchoring dynamics outputs to stable targets; and (iii) encoder-level stabilization (ES), which prevents the shared encoder from drifting under the cross-augmentation pressure imposed by DC.

We evaluate VIGOR on the DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) [ 40 ] and Robosuite [ 54 ] under the RL-ViGen zero-shot protocol [ 49 ] , covering seven visual distraction types—a substantially broader evaluation than the two types ( background-color , background-video ) typically considered in prior work [ 18 , 20 , 4 , 7 ] (Appendix D.3 ). VIGOR outperforms state-of-the-art MFRL and MBRL baselines, improving zero-shot generalization over the second-best baseline by 3.4 % 3.4\% on DMC and 43.6 % 43.6\% on Robosuite while retaining the sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone.
Ablation studies further reveal that naive transfer of MFRL strategies fails in MBRL: applying strong augmentation uniformly across the batch, without the asymmetric splitting of AW, achieves only 48 % 48\% of VIGOR’s performance on DMC (Section 4.3 ). Furthermore, VIGOR’s robustness is augmentation-agnostic: latent-space consistency, rather than any specific augmentation choice, drives generalization (Section 4.4 ; Appendix E.5 ).

Our contributions are:

Problem identification and analysis. We identify a two-level failure mode in MBRL: visual distractions first produce OOD encoder outputs, which then compound through recursive rollouts—a failure mode unique to recursive latent dynamics (Figure 1 ; Section 4.5 ).

Integrated framework for MBRL robustness. We propose VIGOR, which addresses this failure mode through three interdependent components (AW, DC, and ES) designed for the recursive world-model setting. We show that naive transfer of MFRL strategies fails in MBRL, that VIGOR’s integration is necessary, and that the resulting robustness is augmentation-agnostic (Sections 4.3 – 4.5 ; Appendix E.5 ).

State-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. VIGOR outperforms MFRL and MBRL baselines, surpassing the second-best baseline by 3.4 % 3.4\% on DMC and 43.6 % 43.6\% on Robosuite while preserving the strong sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone.

2. Integrated framework for MBRL robustness. We propose VIGOR, which addresses this failure mode through three interdependent components (AW, DC, and ES) designed for the recursive world-model setting. We show that naive transfer of MFRL strategies fails in MBRL, that VIGOR’s integration is necessary, and that the resulting robustness is augmentation-agnostic (Sections 4.3 – 4.5 ; Appendix E.5 ).

2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Visual Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

Latent-space MBRL learns compact world models for planning or imagination in latent space [ 6 , 10 , 12 , 14 , 17 ] . The Dreamer series adopts a decoder-based architecture that reconstructs pixel observations [ 9 , 11 , 12 ] , whereas TD-MPC uses a decoder-free architecture that plans without reconstruction [ 14 , 17 ] . Both families assume i.i.d. training and test distributions; in practice, unseen visual distractions push encoder outputs out of distribution, causing compounding rollout errors (Figure 1 ). VIGOR equips latent-space MBRL with three interdependent components (AW, DC, and ES) designed to mitigate this failure mode. An extended discussion of MBRL architectures and our backbone selection rationale is provided in Appendix F .

## 2.2 Visual Generalization in Model-Free Reinforcement Learning

MFRL approaches address visual robustness through data augmentation [ 16 , 20 , 37 ] , self-supervised representation learning [ 18 , 4 ] , and pretrained visual encoders [ 48 , 32 ] . These methods operate at the single-step level: the encoder maps observations directly to Q-values or policy outputs without recursive rollouts. In MBRL, by contrast, encoder perturbations propagate through multi-step latent rollouts and compound across the planning horizon, motivating VIGOR’s two-level design. A detailed survey is provided in Appendix G.1 .

## 2.3 Visual Generalization in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

Invariant MBRL methods [ 50 , 41 , 53 , 39 , 52 ] learn representations that discard task-irrelevant visual factors but typically require test-time adaptation . VIGOR targets the stricter zero-shot setting where no adaptation data are available.
Dr. G [ 7 ] is the most directly comparable prior work, as it explicitly targets zero-shot generalization in latent-space MBRL. It extends Dreamer [ 9 ] with dual contrastive objectives and an inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss. VIGOR differs in mechanism: rather than contrastive negatives and auxiliary supervision, it enforces dynamics-level consistency (DC) through direct latent regression, supported by asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation (AW) and encoder-level stabilization (ES). Built on TD-MPC2 [ 17 ] , VIGOR targets the same zero-shot setting through a fundamentally different inductive bias. A detailed survey is provided in Appendix G.2 .

2026-10-05.title: FUSEye: Training-Light Fisheye Detection with Overlapping Views and Zero-Initialized Adapters
2026-10-05.authors: Wenya Su , Kai Luo , Di Wen , Ruiping Liu , Yufan Chen , Junwei Zheng , Kunyu Peng , Kailun Yang
2026-10-05.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)
2026-10-05.comment: Source code will be available at this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: Fisheye cameras give mobile robots a single-sensor, low-cost view of their surroundings, yet the COCO-pretrained detectors that practitioners routinely reuse fail on them: strong radial distortion warps local image structure, while boundary compression shrinks objects to near-invisible sizes. Full fine-tuning closes much of the gap but requires abundant fisheye labels and compute. We present FUSEye, a training-light framework that turns a frozen-backbone COCO-pretrained extra-large YOLO26 detector (YOLO26-x) into a fisheye detector. FUSEye adds roughly 227 ​ k 227k new parameters while updating the inserted modules and the pretrained detection head. It addresses the transfer gap at three causally linked levels. At the input level, overlapping grid view generation and box remapping (GridViews) enlarge compressed boundary regions. At the feature level, zero-initialized residual adapters (Z-Adapters) correct distortion-induced feature misalignment. At the decision level, learned cross-projection agreement fusion (AgreeFusion) promotes low-confidence detections only when they are supported by consistent evidence across multiple views. On the WoodScape surround-view fisheye benchmark, FUSEye raises YOLO26-x from 0.148 0.148 to 0.266 0.266 mAP50 and retains 84.3 % 84.3\% fully fine-tuned accuracy. Moreover, randomly using only 25 % 25\% of the labeled training images, FUSEye achieves 0.2597 ± 0.0034 0.2597{\pm}0.0034 mAP50, retaining 97.6 % 97.6\% of its full-label performance. FUSEye also consistently improves YOLOv8-11 detectors, showing that the recipe is architecture-agnostic. Source code will be available at https://github.com/Su-wenya/FUSEye .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Fisheye cameras offer mobile robots a cost-effective wide-angle sensing solution: a single sensor captures a broad field of view, making fisheye cameras attractive for robot navigation and obstacle avoidance [ 1 , 2 ] .
Object detection is a fundamental perception task in these applications [ 3 ] .
Annotating fisheye datasets is labor-intensive, and prior work has adopted COCO-pretrained YOLO-family detectors as a starting point for adaptation [ 4 ] .
However, strong radial distortion causes spatially varying changes in object appearance and compresses objects near the image boundary, making features learned from perspective images less transferable to fisheye views [ 5 , 6 ] .
This limitation is particularly critical for mobile robots: pedestrians and obstacles entering the field of view may initially appear as small, strongly compressed boundary objects. Missing these early observations reduces the time available for braking or replanning.

This projection-induced domain shift poses a key challenge when adapting pretrained object detectors to fisheye imagery.
As illustrated in Figure , directly applying the COCO-pretrained extra-large YOLO26 model (YOLO26-x) to the mirror-view right (MVR) validation split of WoodScape [ 1 ] yields only 0.1480 0.1480 mAP 50 \mathrm{mAP}_{50} for car , person , and bus , while the complete cross-view fine-tuning reaches 0.3156 0.3156 .
Beyond boundary compression, training-light transfer involves two additional challenges.
Distorted object appearances can misalign the backbone features learned from perspective images, while overlapping crops used to recover peripheral objects can introduce duplicate and conflicting detection hypotheses.

Existing distortion-aware approaches involve different adaptation costs. Projection-aware kernel adaptation can require camera calibration [ 7 ] ; rectification networks introduce an additional preprocessing model [ 8 ] ; and deformable convolution methods modify the feature extractor and typically require full-model retraining [ 9 ] .
Generic parameter-efficient adapters reduce the number of updated parameters, but are not designed for the spatially non-uniform distortion of fisheye images [ 10 ] .
Slicing and multi-view inference enlarge small boundary objects, but conventional suppression or fusion treats redundant detections without explicitly considering whether they are supported across multiple projections [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Although these methods provide useful building blocks, their integration within a frozen-backbone fisheye adaptation framework remains less explored.
This observation motivates the central question of this work: can a COCO-pretrained detector be adapted to fisheye imagery without full-model fine-tuning, while jointly addressing input-level boundary compression, feature-level misalignment, and decision-level cross-view conflicts under a limited labeling and training budget?

We answer this question with FUSEye, a training-light framework, which views the transfer gap as a chain of three causally linked problems rather than a single capacity deficit.
At the input level, boundary objects are too compressed for the network input scale, so overlapping grid view generation and box remapping (GridViews) generate the full frame plus four overlapping patches and remap all boxes back to the original coordinates, requiring no calibration or dewarping.
At the feature level, radial distortion misaligns the features extracted by the shared backbone, so zero-initialized residual adapters (Z-Adapters) are inserted at three high-level backbone stages; the zero-initialized output projection keeps the pretrained model unchanged at the first step and then learns a residual correction for the fisheye domain with only 222,480 222{,}480 parameters on YOLO26-x.
At the decision level, multi-view inference produces duplicate and conflicting detections, so cross-projection agreement fusion (AgreeFusion) clusters per-view detections by class and intersection over union (IoU), re-scores multi-view clusters with a learned scorer of about 4,400 4{,}400 parameters, applies confidence-weighted box fusion, and preserves the baseline precision policy for single-view detections. GridViews supplies candidates for AgreeFusion, while Z-Adapters preserve initial per-view predictions. Each component can be ablated independently with the backbone frozen.

On the WoodScape MVR validation split, FUSEye improves YOLO26-x from 0.1480 0.1480 to 0.2661 0.2661 mAP50, retains 84.3 % 84.3\% of fully fine-tuned accuracy while training far fewer parameters, and preserves 97.6 % 97.6\% of its full-label performance when trained with only 25 % 25\% of the labels.
It also generalizes across YOLO families, improving mAP50 by 0.0580 0.0580 – 0.0829 0.0829 on the extra-large variants of YOLOv8, YOLOv10, and YOLO11 (YOLOv8-x, YOLOv10-x, and YOLO11-x) and the extended YOLOv9 variant (YOLOv9-e).
