2026-10-05.title: Toward Controlling Biology with Language:Offline Learning of Prompt-Conditioned Interventions for Cells, Organoids, and Biobots
2026-10-05.authors: Nam H. Le , Douglas Blackiston , Michael Levin , Josh Bongard
2026-10-05.subjects: Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.abstract:
Artificial intelligence increasingly serves as a natural-language interface to complex
technical systems, letting people accomplish sophisticated tasks by describing what they want
rather than specifying how to do it. Extending this interface to living systems is harder:
unlike code or images, a biological intervention has no closed-form linguistic meaning, and the
paired language-intervention-outcome data needed to learn such a mapping is expensive to
collect, since each example requires its own wet-lab experiment. One way around this is to
treat an existing archive of interventions and their already-observed outcomes as a fixed,
offline dataset, and use a vision-language model to judge, without any new experiments, whether
an archived outcome matches a natural-language description. But whether that judgment is
reliable enough to train a language-to-intervention mapping on – without new experiments and
without human validation – has remained unclear. Here we show that a natural-language
interface for a living organism – a xenobot, a synthetic multicellular construct with no
nervous system – can be learned entirely offline this way, using a vision-language model’s own
judgment as the sole training reward: an instruction is mapped to the intervention already on
record as producing the described behavior. This mapping generalizes to entirely new
instructions, evaluated against archive data withheld from training ( 80.0 % 80.0\% held-out accuracy
vs. a 66.7 % 66.7\% chance baseline, matching a network trained directly on ground-truth labels).
These results indicate that offline archives, combined with automated judgment, can substitute
for costly new experiments when learning to ground natural language in a living system’s own
recorded behavior – an intermediate step toward directing living matter with the same ease as
code, though whether these predicted interventions actually reproduce their intended behavior
on live, newly-stimulated cells remains to be tested.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Imagine a clinician or bioengineer simply describing what they want – calm this inflamed
tissue, direct these cells to close a wound, steer this synthetic biobot toward a target – and
having cells, organoids, or synthetic biobots ( Kriegman et al., 2021 ; Blackiston et al., 2021b ; Levin, 2021 ) carry out that intention directly, the way a
modern software system already responds to a natural-language request. Controlling living
systems this way is a long-standing goal across biology, medicine, and synthetic biology, yet
the interface remains fundamentally low-level: practitioners specify interventions parameter by
parameter, through trial and error informed by domain expertise. In other technical
domains, natural language has emerged as a high-level interface to complex systems: users
specify a goal – generate this code ( Fried et al., 2023 ) , design this molecule ( Bengio et al., 2021 ) , plan this trajectory ( Huang et al., 2022 ) – and a
learned model translates intent into low-level action. This raises a question central to
applied machine learning (ML): can a similar interface be learned for biological systems, mapping a
natural-language description of desired behavior to the physical intervention that elicits it?

Two properties make this hard. First, collecting paired (prompt, intervention, outcome) data
online is prohibitively expensive: each datum is a wet-lab experiment, ruling out approaches
that need a fresh experiment per prompt or per objective. Second, the objective space is
inherently multi-task and contains opposing goals – e.g. “stop” versus “accelerate” – and
a single policy trained across such goals is known to suffer objective interference, where the
gradient for one goal actively degrades another ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2018 ) , so naively
pooling all objectives into one unconstrained shared model is not a safe default either.
Together, these rule out the two most direct approaches: brute-forcing the mapping with enough
paired data, and training one policy across all objectives without accounting for how they
interact.

We address both properties by treating language-to-intervention as an offline learning problem.
Archives of intervention-outcome pairs already exist, collected for purposes other than
language-conditioned learning; we treat such an archive as a fixed dataset over which a policy
is trained without any new experiments. To supply a reward signal in the absence of labeled
prompt-outcome alignment, we use a pretrained VLM as a zero-shot scorer ( Rocamonde et al., 2023 ) , judging how well an archived outcome matches a natural-language
description, and check that judgment against independent, non-VLM ground truth rather than
trust it by assumption. The policy uses one output head per behavioral category over a shared
backbone.

This work makes three key contributions, each tested directly in
Section 4 rather than only asserted: (1) we demonstrate an archive-based
learning paradigm for language-to-intervention translation, using a vision-language model’s own
judgment as the reward in place of new experimental feedback; (2) we validate this approach
end-to-end, generalizing to entirely new instructions on archive data withheld from training at 80.0 % 80.0\% ground-truth accuracy, against a 66.7 % 66.7\% chance baseline; (3) we show this VLM-derived
reward is not redundant even with only two behaviors currently distinguished: replacing it with
a single fixed duration chosen directly from real velocity data trains to a comparable loss but
collapses held-out generalization to 59.1 % 59.1\% , below chance, while the VLM-fit reward reaches 80.0 % 80.0\% .
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Large language models serve as general-purpose interfaces to complex domains, generating
functional code ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , aiding molecular design ( Jumper et al., 2021 ) ,
and assisting scientific discovery ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , typically letting users specify
goals in language rather than low-level parameters. Biological control is harder: language has
no closed-form semantics for what an electrical stimulus should mean, and paired
(prompt, intervention, outcome) data is expensive to collect. Synthetic biology has produced
xenobots, living Xenopus laevis cell assemblies exhibiting coordinated motion ( Kriegman et al., 2021 ; Blackiston et al., 2021b ) , where targeted electrical or
optogenetic interventions elicit reproducible behavioral change ( Zajdel et al., 2020 ; Levin, 2021 ; Emiliani et al., 2022 ) , but control remains
manual, tuned parameter-by-parameter without a language interface.

Vision-language models can serve as zero-shot reward models ( Rocamonde et al., 2023 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , though rarely
validated against ground truth independent of the VLM itself – a gap we address directly.
Learning across opposing behavioral goals is a multi-task problem, for which task-specific heads
over a shared backbone are a standard remedy ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Ruder, 2017 ; Caruana, 1997 ) . Training from a fixed
archive with only terminal rewards places this work in the offline, contextual-bandit regime ( Levine et al., 2020 ; May et al., 2012 ) , for which derivative-free search such as CMA-ES ( Hansen and Ostermeier, 2001 ) is standard; we show the reward is in fact differentiable, so both
backpropagation and gradient-free search apply, and use their agreement to validate the optimum
found.

Two prior studies explore the underlying idea of prompt-to-intervention learning as a
proof-of-concept in simulated, artificial-life cells; we position this work explicitly against
the specific gaps each left open. Le et al. (2025) introduced a P2I network mapping a prompt embedding to a spatial vector
field steering simulated 2D cell collectives, scored by a VLM against a fixed one-word
vocabulary (e.g. “clustering” vs. “scattering”); the reward was treated as
non-differentiable by design, optimized only with ( 1 + 1 ) (1{+}1) -ES and a genetic algorithm, and the
paper flags gradient interference between opposing objectives as an open problem at multi-prompt
scale. Le et al. (2026) extends this, replacing the fixed vocabulary with a continuous,
free-form VLM score in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] – closer in spirit to the reward used here – but trained on a
single prompt (“form a cluster”), again assumed non-differentiability, and lists
gradient-trainable optimization and real-cell validation as explicit future work. This paper
answers both directly rather than by assumption: the VLM-derived reward is fit as a smooth,
differentiable function and trained by direct backpropagation, cross-validated against four
independent optimizers; we train and evaluate on 33 prompts
rather than one; and every experiment here is on a real, living, non-neural organism rather than
a physics simulation.

2026-10-05.abstract: Vision language model (VLM) agents can control robots through visual feedback and action primitives, but repeated model invocations and redundant observations incur substantial token overhead. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, an interactive code-execution framework that couples feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation: the agent composes classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action (VLA) policies into Python cells that perform conditional checks and local retries, returning only explicitly requested images and state feedback for replanning. Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, we compare PyRUA-Lean with a tool-calling baseline using the same GPT-6 Astra planner and underlying robot primitives. Under equal LLM-call budgets, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1% to 71.7%. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform robot manipulation by interpreting visual observations and robot state, then invoking motion, perception, and grasping primitives, including vision-language-action (VLA) policies [ 1 , 10 , 33 , 26 ] . Their efficiency depends partly on how these primitives are exposed to the planner. In a tool-calling interface, an operation that depends on a previous tool’s result generally requires another VLM invocation. Intermediate results also accumulate in the conversation and are processed in subsequent calls; in systems such as RPent [ 33 ] , motion primitives automatically return multiple camera images at the end of each step of execution. Tasks requiring repeated localization, motion, and recovery can therefore incur substantial inference overhead, even when individual primitives are reliable.

Executable code provides a way to reduce this overhead. A program can compose primitives, inspect their outputs, and execute conditional branches or retries before returning control to the VLM. Code-based robot control is well established: Code as Policies and ProgPrompt generate robot programs from language instructions [ 14 , 25 ] , while more recent systems incorporate execution feedback or refine programs across trials [ 9 , 16 ] . Outside robotics, code-based agent interfaces have also shown benefits in task completion and context efficiency [ 29 , 2 , 27 ] . These findings motivate our central question: how can a VLM agent compose robot primitives to reliably complete tasks while reducing token consumption through selective observation and context management?

We introduce PyRUA-Lean (Python for Lean Robot-Use Agents),
an interactive code-execution interface for feedback-driven
primitive composition and selective observation. The agent generates Python programs that compose robot primitives, check intermediate outcomes, and condition subsequent actions on execution feedback. Intermediate results remain available in a persistent program state, while only explicitly printed outputs and requested camera images are returned to the VLM. This allows the agent to handle intermediate execution steps without repeated model invocations and to control which observations enter its context.

PyRUA-Lean builds on RPent’s robot stacks and primitive implementations [ 33 ] . We compare it with RPent’s tool-calling agent under the same GPT-6 Astra planner, frozen VLA policies, evaluation task instances, and LLM-call budgets. Both agents operate without cross-episode memory. The comparison evaluates the interfaces as a whole, including their support for control flow, persistent program state, and observation delivery. Experiments cover 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365.

Our contributions can be summarized as:

An interactive interface for robot primitive composition. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, a Python execution interface built on RPent’s
robot stack. It supports feedback-driven primitive composition,
persistent program state, and selective observation delivery.

Comprehensive evaluation on three robot benchmarks. Across 700 simulated instances, PyRUA-Lean improves overall success
by approximately 14% relative to tool calling. On jointly solved
instances, it uses 49% fewer VLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens.

Analysis of efficiency gains and limitations. Traces and ablations identify fewer LLM calls as the main source of token savings, which persist without VLA policies or operating guides but diminish on VLA-dominated tasks, and illustrate geometric computation and scripted recovery.

2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLM-based robot control. Language models have been used to select robot skills, interpret execution feedback, and generate motion commands. SayCan grounds skill selection in language instructions and learned affordances [ 1 ] , while Inner Monologue incorporates environment feedback into planning [ 10 ] . More recent systems support finer-grained control: Show-Harness exposes discrete semantic actions to a VLM [ 8 ] , and GPT-6 Astra has been evaluated as an embodied policy that generates or corrects robot actions [ 26 ] . VLA models provide learned visuomotor capabilities for language-conditioned control [ 4 , 13 , 3 , 23 ] . Harness VLA integrates frozen VLA policies with analytic primitives through RPent, a memory-guided agent framework [ 33 ] . PyRUA-Lean builds on RPent’s robot stacks and primitive implementations, exposing these capabilities through an interactive Python interface. We compare this interface with RPent’s tool-calling interface using the same planner and underlying primitives, with cross-episode memory disabled in both agents.

Code-based robot control. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt generate executable robot programs from language instructions [ 14 , 25 ] , while VoxPoser generates code that constructs spatial value maps for motion planning [ 11 ] . Subsequent work explores execution feedback and program adaptation. CaP-X benchmarks coding agents across primitive abstraction levels and single- or multi-turn interaction modes [ 9 ] , and VLCP periodically regenerates a control function from updated observations within an episode [ 17 ] . Other systems accumulate reusable capabilities across trials: Voyager develops a code-based skill library in Minecraft [ 28 ] , ASPIRE refines robot programs and consolidates experience into reusable skills [ 16 ] , and RoboRSI converts established tool-use workflows into executable routines as part of a robot self-improvement system [ 19 ] . These studies establish program synthesis, feedback-driven execution, and skill reuse as complementary approaches to embodied control. Our focus is the success and inference cost of interactive code execution relative to tool calling over the same robot primitives, including VLA policies. We evaluate this comparison without cross-episode skill accumulation, while allowing state and code reuse within each episode.

Code-based interfaces for efficient agents. Research on general-purpose agents provides a broader motivation for this comparison. ReAct interleaves reasoning with environment interaction [ 32 ] , and Toolformer studies the use of external APIs by language models [ 24 ] . CodeAct shows that executable Python can improve agent performance relative to text or JSON action interfaces [ 29 ] , while SWE-agent demonstrates the importance of interface design for software-engineering agents [ 31 ] . More recent systems use code to compose tool calls and process intermediate results outside the model context, reducing the information returned to the VLM [ 2 , 27 ] . PyRUA-Lean applies these interface principles to robot manipulation, where observations are visual and primitive execution may fail. We measure task success together with LLM-call usage, input-token consumption, and inference cost, and analyze how programmatic composition and observation passing contribute to the gains.

2026-10-05.title: GlanceWAM: Sparse Test-Time Imagination for World-Action Models
2026-10-05.authors: Linhan Wang , Zijian An , Mingyuan Zhang , Chen Dai , Yi Xu , Can Cui , Jiayan Wang , Zichong Yang , Yinlin Chen , Lifeng Zhou , Chang-Tien Lu

2026-10-05.abstract:
Video generative models provide rich physical priors for robot learning, yet
existing world-action models (WAMs) face a fundamental trade-off: synchronous
video generation at control rate is latency-prohibitive, while abandoning
test-time visual imagination sacrifices task success.
We show that visual imagination achieves both real-time inference and
superior success rates when generated asynchronously off the critical path and consumed directly
in latent space.
We introduce GlanceWAM, which decouples imagination from control on a
single shared video DiT backbone: an asynchronous proposer glances ahead on a slow clock to imagine a single
lookahead frame seconds into the future in the background, while an action head decodes
action chunks at control rate ( 48 48 ms) purely in latent space without blocking. Enabled by a
non-interfering attention mask that isolates video representations and
staleness-robust horizon training that accommodates asynchronous lookahead
aging, GlanceWAM breaks the speed–success dilemma. Trained purely on demonstrations,
it attains 72.2 % 72.2\% on the 24-task RoboCasa kitchen benchmark (vs. 67.1 % 67.1\% for
synchronous Cosmos Policy) and 99.0 % 99.0\% on LIBERO while cutting per-chunk control latency 24 × 24\times relative to synchronous world-action models ( 48 48 ms on one A100). In single-arm and bimanual real-robot manipulation, it
achieves higher average success than π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} without any robot-data pretraining.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Video generative models capture rich physical priors over object dynamics, contact physics, and 3D scene evolution ( NVIDIA, 2025a ; Wan Team, 2025 ; SkyReels Team, 2025 ) , offering a promising foundation for autonomous robots to anticipate the consequences of their actions. In robot manipulation, world-action models (WAMs) leverage these predictive backbones through two distinct pathways: (i) representation shaping , where future-prediction losses enrich shared visual features, and (ii) visual foresight , where the model explicitly synthesizes future visual states to guide downstream policy execution ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . However, existing WAMs couple future prediction and action decoding synchronously at the control rate (Figure 1 a) ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ) . This tight coupling incurs two fundamental costs: prohibitive inference latency and myopic foresight. Over the short duration of an action chunk the scene barely changes, so predicting only that far ahead reduces world modeling to near-trivial reconstruction of the current observation.

To bypass this latency bottleneck, recent approaches advocate abandoning test-time visual imagination entirely, relegating video modeling purely to offline pretraining or feature regularization ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Cai et al., 2026 ) . While this strategy eliminates generative overhead during control, it discards explicit visual foresight—depriving downstream policies of the future visual destinations and spatial guidance needed for long-horizon manipulation. Conversely, architectures that retain visual foresight continue to couple dense future synthesis directly to high-frequency action chunks ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ) , remaining bounded by prohibitive diffusion latencies and near-static prediction horizons. Current world-action models are thus caught in a speed–success dilemma : either synthesize video synchronously at the control rate and forfeit real-time reactivity, or discard test-time imagination and forfeit the performance benefits of visual foresight.

In this paper, we show that this dilemma is not an intrinsic property of visual foresight, but an artifact of coupling imagination synchronously to high-frequency control chunks. Downstream policies do not require dense, frame-by-frame future video of the immediate milliseconds; they primarily need a distant spatial destination (“where to go”). We introduce GlanceWAM, a framework that decouples visual imagination from real-time control on a single shared video DiT backbone. GlanceWAM makes visual foresight fast through asynchronous execution off the critical path: the model glances ahead on a slow clock to generate a single lookahead frame seconds into the future ( H f ≈ 3 H_{f}\approx 3 s) in the background, completely isolating generative sampling latency from the high-frequency control loop. Crucially, the entire imagination-and-control loop operates purely in latent space without decoding to raw pixels, allowing the action head to decode short action chunks at the control rate ( 48 48 ms) in a single forward pass. This architecture is enabled by two key mechanisms: (i) a non-interfering attention mask (prefix-LM) that isolates video representations by preventing lookahead tokens from contaminating observation encodings, and (ii) staleness-robust horizon training that supervises the policy across varying time offsets ( u ∼ 𝒰 ( 0 , H f ] u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,H_{f}] ) to tolerate lookahead aging.

Trained purely on demonstrations, GlanceWAM establishes a new state-of-the-art among world-action models across both manipulation success rate and inference speed, resolving the speed–success dilemma in practice. On the 24-task RoboCasa kitchen benchmark ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) , GlanceWAM achieves 72.2 % 72.2\% success, outperforming both synchronous Cosmos Policy ( 67.1 % 67.1\% ) and imagination-free co-training ( 64.4 % 64.4\% ), while reaching 99.0 % 99.0\% on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . Concurrently, its action decoding executes in 48 48 ms per chunk on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU ( 24 × 24\times lower control-path latency than synchronous WAMs), operating comfortably within real-time control budgets. In single-arm and bimanual real-robot manipulation, GlanceWAM achieves higher average success than π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence, 2025 ) without any robot-data pretraining (§ 4.3 ). Systematic diagnostics further confirm that lookahead conditioning is causally load-bearing and remains robust under asynchronous execution delays, demonstrating that world-action models do not need to choose between speed and imagination—sparse, asynchronous visual foresight delivers both.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related work

World-action models. Generative video models capture expressive physical priors over scene dynamics, prompting diverse strategies to harness them for robot manipulation. Early “predict-then-act” paradigms synthesize dense multi-frame video rollouts and decode actions through inverse dynamics ( Du et al., 2023 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2026d ) , incurring severe generative latency on the critical control path. Recent world-action models (WAMs) tighten this integration: Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) co-denoises robot actions, single future observation frames, and value estimates within a unified diffusion sequence; LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026c ) , VideoVLA ( Shen et al., 2025 ) , and GigaWorld-Policy ( Ye et al., 2026 ) autoregressively interleave video and action tokens across matched intervals; and UWM ( UWM authors, 2025 ) jointly trains video and action diffusion. In these architectures, future prediction is tightly coupled to the action chunk horizon (e.g., 0.8 0.8 – 1.6 1.6 s), paying multi-step diffusion sampling overhead on every action chunk while predicting near-static short-horizon transitions. Conversely, purely auxiliary frameworks such as FLARE ( FLARE authors, 2025 ) leverage future prediction strictly as a representation learning objective without test-time foresight. GlanceWAM unifies both pathways: it decouples timescales to generate seconds-scale lookaheads ( H f ≈ 3 H_{f}\approx 3 s) on an amortized slow clock, while retaining real-time 48 48 ms action decoding purely in latent space. Concurrent works such as DeVA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026 ) explore alternative joint video–action denoising and compute-flexible architectures (detailed comparisons in Appendix A ).

Test-time imagination and efficiency. A recent line of inquiry questions whether world-action models require test-time visual imagination at all. Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) and AHA-WAM ( Cai et al., 2026 ) argue that future prediction is unnecessary during inference and can be relegated entirely to offline representation shaping. Both achieve this through causal attention masking, isolating observation token encodings so that future prediction tokens can be losslessly removed at test time. AHA-WAM further introduces observation-guided context routing and phase-offset training to refresh stale planner representations under temporal latency. Complementary acceleration efforts explore progressive distillation ( Akbari et al., 2026 ) , lightweight 1B architectures ( Li et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026e ) , persistent rolling memory ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , or predictive representation folding ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . While removing or distilling test-time generation mitigates sampling latency, amortizing world dynamics strictly into static weights deprives downstream policies of explicit visual targets. In this work, we demonstrate within a controlled, unified architecture that test-time visual foresight provides critical task guidance ( + 7.8 % +7.8\% on RoboCasa kitchen), and show that sparse asynchronous amortization removes the latency bottleneck without discarding imagination. Unlike prior WAMs that retain test-time imagination, GlanceWAM takes generation off the control path.

Visual lookaheads and foresight. Conditioning visuomotor policies on future visual targets has a rich foundation in hierarchical robot learning. Prior methods instantiate visual subgoals through image-editing models ( Black et al., 2024b ) , progress-filtered subgoal candidates ( Hatch & and others, 2025 ) , and dedicated high-level video planners refreshed every few seconds ( Physical Intelligence, 2026 ) . While GlanceWAM shares the principle of multi-second visual lookahead conditioning, it unifies the lookahead generator and policy backbone within a single video DiT rather than maintaining separate, disjoint models (e.g., BAGEL and π 0 \pi_{0} in Physical Intelligence (2026) ), ensuring that predictive world modeling directly shapes shared policy representations. On latency and representation grounds, an emerging line explores non-RGB and latent-space foresight: LaWAM ( Chen et al., 2026 ) and RepWAM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) propose predicting latent visual features or representation tokenizers rather than raw pixels; EgoWAM ( Li et al., 2026a ) , DreamWAM ( Yuan et al., 2026a ) , LiLa-WAM ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , and VLA-JEPA ( Sun et al., 2026 ) explore geometry, 3D flow, and joint-embedding predictive representations. However, in methods like LaWAM, subgoals are generated conditioned on the policy’s already-predicted actions, rendering the subgoal downstream of action selection. In contrast, GlanceWAM synthesizes action-independent lookahead latents seconds in advance to provide explicit spatial destinations (“where to go”) that guide subsequent action chunks directly in latent space.

2026-10-06.title: InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation
2026-10-06.authors: Yucheng Zhang , Sirui Xu , Jinhong Li , Liuyu Bian , Anatulya Nandi , Derek Zhang , Xiangchen Liu , Xueting Li , Umar Iqbal , Yu-Xiong Wang , Liang-Yan Gui
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR)
2026-10-06.comment: Project Page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Captured human-object interactions provide rich supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation, but they are sparse, heterogeneous, and not directly executable by robots. We introduce InterMimicGen, a self-evolving motion-imitation framework in which robot motion data and a tracking policy improve each other. First, we consolidate motion-captured human-object interaction datasets and retarget them into humanoid robot references while preserving whole-body coordination and dexterous hand-object relationships. This produces a large and diverse humanoid robot reference collection for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation. Second, we train a physics-based generalist tracker that executes these references in simulation on a humanoid with dexterous hands, covering a scale and diversity beyond prior humanoid tracking systems for loco-manipulation. Third, we close a data flywheel: each round makes small, task-preserving changes to where an interaction takes place and how the body performs it, fine-tunes the tracker on them, and keeps only the variants whose simulated execution completes the task, which seed the next round. With more iterations, these small edits compound into broader coverage around the sparse original demonstrations while preserving task semantics and motion quality. Experiments show contact-preserving retargeting across robot configurations, broad tracking with a single generalist policy, executable motions that keep growing over augmentation rounds, and transfer to real robots. InterMimicGen provides a unified path from heterogeneous human demonstrations to a continually expanding motion resource for humanoid robot learning.
2026-10-06.introduction:
The value of human demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation extends beyond reproducing the trajectories they record. Each demonstration captures one coordinated solution in a high-dimensional interaction space, but even a large motion-capture corpus provides sparse samples of this space rather than dense coverage of their feasible variations. Covering these variations therefore requires either a policy that can infer the physically feasible manifold from these sparse samples, or a data-generation process that enriches the data with coordinated, physically valid variations.

A natural route is to train a tracking policy by collecting more references, but any fixed set of references still leaves these variations uncovered. When we look back, generalist trackers already generalize well in locomotion ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , where a motion close to a demonstration usually remains feasible. Loco-manipulation is less forgiving. The robot must hold contact with an object while keeping its balance, so a small change in posture or object placement can break a grasp, push the hand into the object, or make the robot fall. As a result, a tracker that executes a demonstration may still fail on the same task where the trajectory is shifted by only a few centimeters (Sec. 4.4 ). Covering them therefore requires data that grows with the tracker rather than a fixed collection. We build this as a data flywheel , in which executable data and the tracker grow together.

To instantiate this flywheel, we introduce InterMimicGen , a self-evolving motion-imitation data engine that couples human-object interaction retargeting, large-scale motion imitation, and iterative data expansion. We first consolidate heterogeneous human-object motion-capture data (Figure 3 ) and retarget the interactions into humanoid robot references. Our retargeter keeps both long-horizon body-object relations and the finger contact that holds small objects: a whole-body solver shapes the grasp to follow the object’s geometry rather than captured finger poses alone, and a fine-grained cleanup then refines the contact at the millimeter scale. The result is a large and diverse robot reference collection for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation, as shown in Figure InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation . Physics-based trackers then execute these references in simulation on a humanoid robot with dexterous hands, and the same trackers later grow together with their reference data through iterative data expansion.

The goal of this expansion is not to invent new tasks; each human interaction becomes a seed for physically distinct realizations of the same semantic behavior, in the spirit of MimicGen ’s demonstration-driven data expansion ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) . We vary object and body motion through small edits around previously validated interactions, such as placing a box farther left or crouching more deeply. Each round fine-tunes the tracker on the current references and edited candidates, executes the candidates in simulation, and retains only rollouts that complete without failure. Drawing on InterMimic ’s insight that a policy can correct imperfect motion by learning from it ( Xu et al., 2025d ) , imitation repairs errors introduced by the edits. The successful rollouts then seed the next round. This feedback is the defining step of Inter Mimic Gen : corrected motions expand the reference set, and the expanded set enables the tracker to realize progressively larger variations.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we consolidate heterogeneous human-object interaction (HOI) data and retarget them into, to our knowledge, the most diverse humanoid robot reference collection (see Sec. 4.1 ) for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation. Second, using these references, we train a physics-based generalist tracker that realizes this repertoire on a target embodiment at a scale beyond prior humanoid tracking systems ( Weng et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026b ) for loco-manipulation. Third, we introduce a self-evolving augmentation-learning loop that expands this repertoire through coupled variations in object and whole-body motions, turning validated interactions into a growing resource for subsequent learning of whole-body controllers.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Human-object interaction data. Human-object and human-scene capture datasets provide complementary interaction references across whole-body grasping, object tracking, bimanual manipulation, and scene-level coordination ( Taheri et al., 2020 ; Bhatnagar et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Lv et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . These resources differ in object diversity, contact structure, and body and hand annotation, shaping the supervision available for imitation. Among them, InterAct ( Xu et al., 2025c ) consolidates heterogeneous interaction sources, while HiPHI ( Ji et al., 2026 ) adds extensive body-object capture. We combine their motion into a robot reference collection and expand physically executable coverage through retargeting and humanoid robot execution in simulation.

Whole-body and dexterous motion retargeting. Motion retargeting adapts demonstrations across morphologies using learned mappings or optimization objectives built from skeleton structure, contact cues, and geometric correspondences ( Villegas et al., 2018 ; Aberman et al., 2020 ; Villegas et al., 2021 ; Reda et al., 2023 ; Araújo et al., 2025 ; Cao et al., 2026a ) . For interaction, the relationships between body, object, hand, and scene must survive the change in embodiment rather than only the joint trajectory ( Kim et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Dexterous teleoperation and synthesis study high-quality hand or hand-arm transfer ( Handa et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) , but whole-body interaction also requires those contacts to remain consistent with locomotion and balance. Our retargeter therefore separates the problem into a coarse whole-body interaction solve and a local dense contact refinement, so hand motion is improved without disturbing the body-object motion.

Physics-based imitation and whole-body manipulation. Physics-based imitation began with example-guided control of individual skills ( Peng et al., 2018 ) and later scaled to shared controllers over diverse motion libraries ( Won et al., 2020 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . On physical humanoids, teleoperation and imitation enable whole-body control ( He et al., 2024 ; Ze et al., 2025 ) , while universal tracking policies and visuomotor extensions broaden the motion and sensing interfaces ( Yin et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2025 ) . Object-centric extensions couple body and object dynamics for grasping and dynamic skills ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Tessler et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025d ; Xu et al., 2026a ) , and then move to real-world humanoid loco-manipulation ( Weng et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Dao et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Kalaria et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2026 ) . Our work starts from reference tracking and extends it into a self-evolving data engine, with real deployment.

Demonstration augmentation and iterative generation. A demonstration can be reused beyond its recorded trajectory ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) : collected segments preserve task intent, while execution under adapted conditions becomes valid training data. Later systems extend this execution-validated reuse to bimanual dexterity ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , skill composition ( Garrett et al., 2024 ) , intervention-driven data collection ( Hoque et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , policy self-improvement ( Bousmalis et al., 2024 ) , and humanoid loco-manipulation ( Lin et al., 2026 ) . A related line in character and humanoid control scales policies through generated experience or closed-loop motion generation ( Xu et al., 2025a ; Debbad et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Our setting differs in both domain and mechanism: we expand dexterous and agile humanoid loco-manipulation from motion-capture references, and we self-evolve through motion imitation itself instead of a separate kinematic motion synthesizer, which is often brittle for object interaction.

2026-10-06.title: Recursive Video In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot
2026-10-06.authors: Wenrui Bao , Xinxin Liu , Bingxin Xu , Yuzhang Shang
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
2026-10-06.abstract: LLM agents that orchestrate frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies improve across episodes through text memory, which records what the agent did but not how the task is done. A demonstration video shows it, but fits poorly into an agent’s context. The full video slows every turn, fixed keyframes lose the contact detail that decides whether a grasp holds, and what the agent needs shifts from the task’s structure while planning to the frames around each contact. We introduce Recursive Video In-Context Learning ( RV-ICL ) , a training-free method that turns a demonstration into a hierarchy the agent navigates rather than a prompt it receives. The hierarchy is built from the sub-events of the demonstration, such as grasps and releases. Its levels grow finer, from keyframes of the whole task to phases, moments and short clips, and are exposed through read-only tools. The agent reads the coarse levels before planning. During execution it re-enters the hierarchy whenever a step needs more detail and loads only the clip of its current sub-goal. One demonstration per task is enough. Built on RPent, RV-ICL raises success from 92.6% to 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO and from 86.7% to 95.8% on LIBERO-Plus.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as the deliberative layer of robot systems. They decompose instructions, localise objects, and call learned visuomotor policies for the contact-rich steps they cannot perform analytically ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2022 ) . Recent agentic harnesses push this design further. HarnessVLA ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , released as the RPent framework, exposes a frozen VLA as one retryable primitive among a few analytic ones. A coding agent orchestrates them and improves across episodes through text memory : recipes, lessons and failure rules. Under distribution shift, this design outperforms end-to-end VLAs by a wide margin.

How far the agent can improve, however, is bounded by what text can record. The agent writes its memory from its own execution traces, so the memory describes its calls and their outcomes rather than the task itself. It can record that a grasp failed, but not what a successful execution looks like: which object is taken first, from which side the hand approaches, how high the object is lifted, when the gripper opens. Such knowledge is spatial and temporal, and it is hard to put into words.

What is hard to put into words is easy to show: a video of the task captures all of it, frame by frame. Such a video is also cheap to obtain. A human demonstration only requires recording a person actually performing the task, with no action labels or other annotation. Large models can learn from demonstrations placed in their context, in text ( Brown et al., 2020 ) and with interleaved images ( Alayrac et al., 2022 ) . This suggests letting the agent watch a demonstration of its task, much as a person watches a how-to video before trying something new.

But in what form should the video enter the agent’s memory? The obvious answers fail for three reasons. (i) Length. A demonstration spans hundreds of frames, and the agent re-reads its whole context at each of its tens to hundreds of turns. Long contexts also degrade how well models use their content ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . (ii) Resolution. A few keyframes are affordable, but they drop the frames around each contact, which decide whether a grasp holds or a placement registers. (iii) Timing. What the agent needs changes over the episode: the task’s structure before it acts, and the frames around a particular contact once it reaches that step. No fixed presentation of the video can satisfy all three constraints at once.

Since each moment of the episode calls for a different part of the demonstration, why not let the agent watch just that part, and only at that moment? Methods for long documents and long videos already take this route: instead of reading everything, the language model navigates a hierarchical index ( Sarthi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Packer et al., 2023 ) . We bring this idea to embodied agents, which decide from their own progress when to look closer: before a delicate contact, at the start of a new sub-goal, or after a step goes wrong.

We build such an index over a demonstration and call the method Recursive Video In-Context Learning ( RV-ICL ) . The index is a tree whose levels grow finer: event-driven keyframes of the whole task, the phases between sub-events, the moments around each sub-event, and short clips from any camera ( Figure 1 a). The agent reads the coarse levels before planning and does not collect clips up front. Whenever it needs more detail during execution, the agent re-enters the tree at the node of its current sub-goal and pulls only the relevant clip ( Figure 1 b). The demonstration is thus consulted recursively, at the level of detail and the moment the agent’s progress calls for.

RV-ICL requires no training, no change to the VLA, and one demonstration per base task. The hierarchy is built from the sub-events of the demonstration, the instants at which one sub-task ends and the next begins. The same construction therefore applies to any task that decomposes into sub-tasks. We make the following contributions:

We introduce video in-context learning to tool-using robot agents: their text memory cannot record what a successful execution looks like, but a demonstration video shows it frame by frame ( Section 3.1 ).

We propose Recursive Video In-Context Learning ( RV-ICL ), which lets the agent look only at the part of the demonstration its current step needs, by giving it recursive access to a hierarchy built from the demonstration’s sub-events ( Section 3 ).

On LIBERO-PRO, RV-ICL raises the success rate of HarnessVLA from 92.6% to 96.5%, above every baseline, and on LIBERO-Plus from 86.7% to 95.8% across seven kinds of perturbation. On the long LIBERO-10 tasks it gains up to 12 points, where keyframes or the whole video of the same demonstration gain at most 2 ( Section 5 ).

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 LLM agents for robot manipulation

Language models entered robotics as planners over pre-trained skills. SayCan ( Ahn et al., 2022 ) scores LLM proposals by learned affordances, ProgPrompt ( Singh et al., 2023 ) and Code as Policies ( Liang et al., 2023 ) write programs over perception and control APIs, and VoxPoser ( Huang et al., 2023 ) composes 3D value maps for a motion planner. Inner Monologue ( Huang et al., 2022 ) feeds execution feedback back to the planner, and Voyager ( Wang et al., 2023 ) accumulates a library of verified skills.

A recent line of agentic harnesses puts a coding agent in charge of a frozen VLA. HarnessVLA ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) exposes the VLA as a retryable primitive and learns its operating range from text memory; Robo-Harness K1 ( Li et al., 2026 ) augments such agents with perception; CaP-X ( Fu et al., 2026 ) benchmarks coding agents for manipulation; RATS ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) learns through play; and RAPID ( Liu et al., 2026 ) synthesises agent programs from demonstrations.

The knowledge these systems carry across episodes is textual or programmatic. RV-ICL keeps the harness unchanged and adds a visual record of how the task is performed, together with a protocol for consulting it.

## 2.2 Learning from demonstrations in context

In language models, a few demonstrations in the prompt suffice to specify a task ( Brown et al., 2020 ) , although models draw mostly on their format and label space rather than the exact input–label mapping ( Min et al., 2022 ) . Flamingo ( Alayrac et al., 2022 ) extends in-context learning to interleaved images.

In robotics, one-shot imitation has been learned by meta-learning from human videos ( Yu et al., 2018 ) and by video-conditioned policies ( Jain et al., 2024 ) . In-context imitation has been achieved by tokenising demonstrations as keypoints for an off-the-shelf LLM ( Di Palo and Johns, 2024 ) , by training a policy to continue interleaved demonstration trajectories ( Fu et al., 2024 ) , and by conditioning a VLA on structured demonstrations ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . When an LLM acts directly as the policy, one-shot demonstrations yield no aggregate gain ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) .

All of these present the demonstration once, as a prefix for the next actions. Our agent makes tens to hundreds of decisions per episode, so the question is not only whether to show a demonstration but which part, and when .

## 2.3 Recursion in language-model reasoning and retrieval

Recursion lets a bounded model handle inputs and problems that exceed its context. Recursive summarisation condenses a book into a tree of summaries read top-down ( Wu et al., 2021 ) , and RAPTOR ( Sarthi et al., 2024 ) retrieves from such a tree at the level of abstraction a question requires. For long videos, VideoAgent ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and VideoTree ( Wang et al., 2025 ) likewise inspect only the frames or branches a question needs.

Recursive decomposition splits a problem as needed. ADaPT ( Prasad et al., 2024 ) decomposes a sub-task further only when the executor fails on it, THREAD ( Schroeder et al., 2025 ) spawns child threads that return only what the parent needs, and Recursive Language Models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) call themselves over slices of a context too long to read at once. Tree of Thoughts ( Yao et al., 2023 ) searches over such trees of intermediate steps.

A related family decides when to fetch information. FLARE ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) retrieves when upcoming tokens are uncertain, and Self-RAG ( Asai et al., 2024 ) learns to request retrieval on demand. Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) and Self-Refine ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) feed the outcome of an attempt into the next one, and MemGPT ( Packer et al., 2023 ) pages information between a bounded context and external storage.

RV-ICL brings recursion to an embodied agent. The demonstration is a tree read at the level each decision requires, and the agent descends whenever its progress in the physical task calls for more detail: before a delicate contact, at a new sub-goal, or after a step goes wrong.

2026-10-06.title: AffordCraft: Scalable Construction of Task-Ready Simulation Assets from Single Images
2026-10-06.authors: Haoyun Yang , Xueyang Zhou , Ziyi Xie , Yongchao Chen
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.comment: . Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Robot learning in simulation depends on the objects the simulator offers.
Many tasks need objects with separate parts, joints that allow the required
motion, and physical properties that remain valid under contact. Existing methods recover this structure anew for every image: generative models predict parts and joints that mostly fail to settle or move in simulation, and general-purpose agents need a long session of model calls for each photograph. AffordCraft builds
such an asset from a single RGB image and a task instruction by retrieval
instead of generation: it locates the object and the part to operate,
selects a matching entry from a library of articulated assets, and fits it
to the image while keeping its parts and joints intact. Without any box or
mask marking the object, AffordCraft produces a physically valid asset for
1,703 of 2,000 photographs from 31 categories. Five generative methods pass
on at most 45% of the same photographs and, at the median, need 10 to 78
times our GPU time per valid asset. On 50 cluttered images, 162 of 237
annotated objects pass the same physical test after automatic detection.
Growing the library from 141 to 11,372 entries needs no change to the method
and raises category coverage from 46% to 100% and the share of selections
with the requested label from 18% to 51%. We also build manipulation
tasks from the constructed assets, both with single objects and in composed
scenes; policies trained on scripted demonstrations complete both kinds of
tasks from initial states unseen in training.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Simulation eliminates the hardware, operator time, and repeated resets required by experiments with real objects ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Ranawaka et al., 2026 ) . Its usefulness, however, is fundamentally limited by the quality of the assets it contains. Many everyday objects are articulated: cabinet doors rotate about hinges, drawers translate along rails, and storage bins slide within frames. To reproduce their behavior, a simulator must represent them as multiple rigid bodies connected by joints, equipped with appropriate collision geometry and physical parameters that remain stable under contact. Constructing such assets manually is labor-intensive and difficult to scale.

A mesh may visually resemble a cabinet while lacking any explicit representation of its door, hinge, or interior structure. Existing automatic methods typically recover this information independently for each input image, making the process both expensive and difficult to generalize. Generative models can infer geometry and articulation from photographs ( Cao et al., 2026b ; Cao et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , but their predictions often fail to produce physically valid assets: parts may not rest stably, contacts may be inconsistent, and articulated components may not move as intended (Table 1 ). General-purpose agents can construct functional assets through modeling tools ( Guo, 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) , yet doing so for a single photograph may require a lengthy sequence of model calls and substantial tool interaction.

Crucially, the articulation structures of everyday objects are highly repetitive. A drawer, for example, may slide along the same axis in both a desk and a filing cabinet. This observation suggests replacing open-ended reconstruction with retrieval and adaptation from a library of articulated, part-decomposed assets. Such libraries mitigate the cost of modeling and physical validation: each mechanism is constructed and verified once, then reused across many objects. Given an image, selecting and fitting a suitable library asset transforms single-view reconstruction from an unconstrained generation problem into a constrained matching problem over known mechanisms. The resulting system can therefore produce physically grounded simulation assets more efficiently, reliably, and consistently.

We present AffordCraft, which builds a task-ready simulation asset from one RGB
image and a task instruction (Figures 1 and 2 ). It locates the object and the part the task acts on
and determines the required motion, such as a rotation about a hinge. It then
retrieves library entries by category and visual similarity, and a multimodal
model checks which of them provide that motion at the right part, or abstains
if none does. Finally, it scales and places the chosen entry without changing
its parts or joints, and accepts the result only if it passes a physical test
in simulation. The image encoder and the multimodal model can be exchanged,
and the library grows by adding entries.

The result is a functional substitute, not a copy of the photographed object.
A cabinet of another color is usable as long as its door hinges where the task
requires. Assets that share a mechanism but differ in appearance also give
policy training the appearance variation of several objects, which a single
exact copy does not.

Our contributions are:

Structure built once and reused. Parts, joints, and physical
parameters are modeled and checked once, in the library; construction selects
among them instead of estimating them for every image. AffordCraft delivers a physically valid asset for 85% of 2,000 photographs, at a median
of 40 s per input on one RTX 5090 and 0.8 GPU-minutes per valid asset, while
generative methods reach at most 45% and need 8–63 GPU-minutes under the
same protocol and test (Table 1 ). Growing the library from 141 to
11,372 entries improves coverage and selection, and retrieval stays near
50 ms.

Task-conditioned construction under a physical gate. The
instruction fixes which part must move and how. A multimodal selector checks
each candidate against its recorded structure and rejects 1,093 of the 5,874
candidate attempts, adaptation keeps the selected bodies and joints, and an
asset is accepted only after it passes a physical test in simulation. Removing
the task condition costs 22 percentage points of correctly built assets,
removing the articulation adapter 40, and removing physical-feedback
reselection 11 (Table 2 ).

Large-scale evaluation. We evaluate on
2,000 photographs from 31 categories and on 50 cluttered images with 237
annotated objects, always from the full image with no box or mask. Seven
external methods are scored by the same test as ours, five of them on all
2,000 inputs: an asset counts only if it exports, carries valid inertia,
settles under gravity, rests on real support, and moves at the requested
part.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

PartNet and SAPIEN provide part-annotated, articulated objects for interactive
simulation ( Mo et al., 2019 ; Xiang et al., 2020 ) . Large object and scene
collections add appearance and layout at
scale ( Deitke et al., 2023b ; Deitke et al., 2023a ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2017 ) ,
but they lack the moving parts and joints that manipulation needs. Because
articulated assets are built by hand, another line of work recovers geometry
from images, with multi-view neural fields and surface
reconstruction ( Mildenhall et al., 2020 ; Müller et al., 2022 ; Kerbl et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Yariv et al., 2021 ; Barron et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ) or with feed-forward and generative models that use one or a few
views ( Yu et al., 2021 ; Hong et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Long et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Jun & Nichol, 2023 ; Nichol et al., 2022 ) .
These methods return a surface, not a mechanism. Part-level methods track
articulated poses and locate actionable
parts ( Weng et al., 2021 ; Mo et al., 2021 ; Geng et al., 2023 ) ;
Articulate-Anything infers articulation with a vision-language
model ( Le et al., 2025 ) ; and PhysX-Anything, PhysX-Omni, and PAct
generate geometry together with parts or physical
attributes ( Cao et al., 2026a ; Cao et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . None of
these routes produces, from one photograph and at scale, an asset whose parts
and joints a simulator can operate: generators return a surface or an
unverified guess of the joints, and part-level methods assume that the object
already exists as a mesh or a dataset entry. Section 4.2 measures this gap with one physical test. AffordCraft instead starts from the
requested interaction and selects a mechanism that the library already holds.

Embodied platforms and manipulation benchmarks come with fixed object
sets ( Brockman et al., 2016 ; Kolve et al., 2017 ; Savva et al., 2019 ; Szot et al., 2021 ; James et al., 2020 ; Yu et al., 2019 ; Mees et al., 2022 ; Mu et al., 2021 ; Gu et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Makoviychuk et al., 2021 ) ,
and SimFoundry assembles interchangeable components into scenes that preserve
affordances ( Ranawaka et al., 2026 ) . General multimodal agents can
already build interactive assets: GPT-6 Astra projects replay robot episodes
in simulation ( Guo, 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) . Such an
agent rediscovers the mechanism in a session of many model calls for every
photograph.
On our 200-input subset it produces a physically valid asset for 34.5% of the
inputs, at a median of 24 minutes and 2.90 USD of model calls per input
(Table 1 , Appendix A.9 ). In AffordCraft the structure is recorded once in the
library and reused by every query.

Much recent work on policy learning builds on interactive environments.
RoboTwin 2.0 generates demonstrations at scale, RoboDojo benchmarks generalist
policies, and MimicGen multiplies a few human demonstrations into
many ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) .
Policies from RT-1 and PaLM-E to OpenVLA, Octo, and Diffusion Policy learn
from such interactions and from open robot
datasets ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Driess et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2022 ; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) ,
and their transfer to hardware relies on randomized and offline
data ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) . All of them
depend on the available object set: a task can be demonstrated or scored only
if some object provides the required motion. AffordCraft supplies such objects as
the bodies, joints, and physical parameters that simulators accept, and
leaves the policy architecture open; Section 4.5 trains
policies on constructed assets.

2026-10-06.title: Physics Residual Dynamics and Reduced Order Whole-Body Planning for Obstacle Aware Human Robot Cloth CoTransportation
2026-10-06.authors: Moein Forouhar , Kosar Behnia , Anirvan Dutta , Hamid Sadeghian , Ville Kyrki , Sami Haddadin , Gokhan Alcan , Eckehard Steinbach
2026-10-06.abstract: Human–robot co-transportation of deformable objects requires predicting object deformation during motion, since obstacle clearance depends on both the grasp points and the unactuated interior. We present a hierarchical planning framework that combines a learned cloth model with a reduced-order whole-body model of a dual-arm mobile manipulator. A physics-residual conditional recurrent variational autoencoder (p-cRVAE) predicts the full cloth configuration from grasp-point observations by learning a residual correction to a computationally efficient linearized physics model, limiting error accumulation over 40-step planning horizon. The predicted cloth dynamics are embedded in a model predictive path integral (MPPI) planner using a reduced-order representation of a dual-arm mobile manipulator that preserves the non-holonomic base constraint and arm workspace limits. An MPC layer subsequently refines the sampled motion into smooth, executable references for whole-body control. The reduced-order formulation achieves tracking performance comparable to the full 17-DoF model while reducing computation time by approximately 80%. Across four co-transportation scenarios and two carrying speeds, the proposed framework maintains cloth-obstacle clearance where a corner-following baseline results in collisions, while whole-body refinement reduces final cloth deformation from 0.93 m to 0.28 m.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Human–robot co-transportation of deformable objects is an important capability for service robotics, with applications in handling textiles, bedding, and flexible loads that are difficult for a single agent to manipulate. By sharing the task, the human and robot can distribute the support of the object while guiding it toward the desired configuration. Unlike rigid objects, deformable objects change shape under gravity and variations in their boundary conditions. Consequently, for obstacle-aware transportation, collision avoidance based only on the grasping points and initial object shape is insufficient; the evolving shape must also be considered during planning. Developing a suitable predictive model is therefore challenging due to the high-dimensional, nonlinear, and coupled dynamics of deformable objects [ 1 ] .

Physics-based models provide a physically grounded approach to capturing deformation dynamics, but their computational cost makes them impractical for motion planning. Data-driven methods offer inexpensive surrogates, but require careful strategies to achieve reliable generalization [ 2 ] . This challenge is further complicated during execution, where only partial observations may be available. Although dense visual point clouds provide detailed surface information, occlusions and large deformations make reliable point correspondence and state estimation difficult [ 3 ] . A practical deformable object model should therefore combine physical grounding with computational efficiency while inferring the evolving full-object configuration from sparse observations that can be reliably obtained during transportation, ideally the grasped corner points.

Beyond object modeling, co-transportation requires a motion planner that accounts for the robot model to generate feasible trajectories while maintaining the desired object geometry and avoiding environmental obstacles. Addressing these requirements in a single high-fidelity optimization problem can be computationally demanding. Sampling-based predictive methods, such as model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, offer an attractive alternative by evaluating candidate action sequences through parallel rollouts without requiring derivatives of the dynamics or cost function, and are well-suited to high-dimensional search spaces. However, finite-sample variability can produce noisy action sequences, which are undesirable when smooth reference trajectories are required. Conversely, optimization-based methods provide trajectory refinement but become increasingly challenging as the planning dimensionality and nonlinearity grow.

Furthermore, effective co-transportation of large deformable objects benefits from a dual-arm robot with a mobile base: the two arms provide distributed support, while base mobility extends the workspace beyond the arms’ stationary reach. We study this problem on GARMI [ 4 ] , which has two torque-controlled, seven-degree-of-freedom arms and a velocity-controlled, nonholonomic differential-drive base. Thus the developed planner must coordinate arm and base motions while respecting joint, workspace, and nonholonomic constraints.

To address these challenges, we propose a hierarchical framework that combines a learned physics-residual dynamics
model with sampling- and optimization-based planning. The planning problem is deliberately divided between the
two paradigms to exploit their complementary strengths. An upper MPPI layer combines the deformable-object model
with a reduced-order robot model to efficiently explore candidate transportation motions while accounting for the
evolving cloth configuration, environmental obstacles, and robot constraints. A lower MPC layer then refines the resulting
trajectory into smooth and feasible task-space references for the robot’s whole-body controller.

The key contributions of this work include:

Physics-residual cloth dynamics (p-cRVAE): A deformable-object model combining a coarse physics-based model with a learned residual predictor to improve prediction accuracy and generalization beyond the training distribution, building on [ 5 ] .

Reduced-order whole-body robot model: A reduced-order representation of GARMI that captures the relevant arm and mobile-base workspaces and constraints, enabling efficient MPPI planning and MPC refinement.

Hierarchical planning: A sampling- and optimization-based architecture that jointly coordinates the deformable object, robot arms, and mobile base while generating smooth reference trajectories for real-time whole-body control.

1. Physics-residual cloth dynamics (p-cRVAE): A deformable-object model combining a coarse physics-based model with a learned residual predictor to improve prediction accuracy and generalization beyond the training distribution, building on [ 5 ] .

2. Reduced-order whole-body robot model: A reduced-order representation of GARMI that captures the relevant arm and mobile-base workspaces and constraints, enabling efficient MPPI planning and MPC refinement.

3. Hierarchical planning: A sampling- and optimization-based architecture that jointly coordinates the deformable object, robot arms, and mobile base while generating smooth reference trajectories for real-time whole-body control.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Human–robot collaborative transportation of deformable objects has largely
been approached without a representation of the object’s configuration.
Kruse et al. [ 6 ] keep a sheet taut through joint torque sensing
and add a depth camera that detects folds, reducing the cloth to a single
corrective direction. Nicola et al. [ 7 ] train a convolutional
network on segmented depth images to estimate the relative pose between the
robot’s grasp and the operator’s hands, assuming the material between the hands
to be rigid, and drive the robot to hold that pose near a rest configuration.
De Schepper et al. [ 8 ] track the operator’s skeleton
alongside force–torque measurements, inferring intention from human key points
rather than from the material. Sirintuna et al. [ 9 ] blend an
admittance reference with the operator’s hand velocity through an adaptive
index that summarises the object’s deformability in a single scalar, and apply
the same interface to a multi-robot team [ 10 ] . These methods do not
use a model of the deformable object within the control framework.

A separate line of work models the configuration of deformable objects directly.
Several approaches use dense visual observations, such as point clouds or RGB
images, to encode the object into a compact latent state and predict its future
motion, as in [ 11 , 12 ] . These models can
capture shape details such as wrinkles and curvature, but they require visual
observations of the deformable object during inference.
However, obtaining a continuous and unobstructed view of the
material can be difficult because of occlusions caused by the robot, the human,
or the object itself. Behnia et al. [ 5 ] avoid this requirement by
predicting the full configuration of a rope and fabric using only the measured
positions of their corner nodes. Their conditional recurrent variational
autoencoder (cRVAE) is used as the forward model of a receding-horizon controller for
obstacle-aware manipulation.

At the robot level, whole-body control coordinates arm and base motions to track
grasp-point trajectories while managing redundancy. For safe human–robot
interaction, impedance controllers are used for both
fixed-base [ 13 ] and mobile
manipulators [ 14 ] to enable compliant behavior during
physical interaction with the environment. For mobile robots with nonholonomic
constraints in the base, Iskandar et al. [ 15 ] first
derived the reduced-order dynamic model of the robot that is constraint-free
and then built the whole-body control framework upon it. For redundant robots,
task-priority control [ 16 ] organizes tasks hierarchically,
projecting lower-priority commands into the null space of higher-priority tasks
to avoid interference with their execution. Any remaining redundancy can be
exploited to accommodate additional control objectives [ 17 ] .
Alternatively, optimization-based approaches formulate the control framework as
an optimization problem that achieves multiple task objectives through weighted
cost functions [ 18 ] . In addition to task
execution, the controller must maintain the robot within its admissible
operating region. To this end, potential-based control terms have been developed
to incorporate safety-related objectives into whole-body
control [ 19 ] .

2026-10-06.title: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models
2026-10-06.authors: Xiaodong Wang , Tianle Li , Chuanxin Song , Junliang Xie , Zhanmi Zhong , Suiying Wu , Peixi Peng
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.comment: Code: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction. First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences. Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy. Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 further supports its applicability across robot datasets. Moreover, using our trained world model to initialize a vision-language-action model improves LIBERO success, suggesting its utility for downstream policy learning. GitHub : https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/SimForcing
2026-10-06.introduction:
Recent advances in large-scale video generation and world
foundation models ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ; Ali et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026a ) ,
have expanded the potential of learned visual dynamics
for embodied intelligence.
Beyond video synthesis, these models can generate training
experiences for robot policies ( Jang et al., 2025 ) and support the improvement of vision-language-action
(VLA) models through synthetic
rollouts ( Guo et al., 2026b ) .
Benchmarks such as WorldArena ( Shang et al., 2026 ) further assess their utility as data engines, policy
evaluators, and action planners.
Despite this progress, visually convincing predictions
do not necessarily ensure reliable physical interactions
or strong downstream performance ( Shang et al., 2026 ) .
For robotic manipulation, a key challenge remains:
learning precise responses to continuous action trajectories
while preserving realistic appearance and temporally
coherent scene dynamics.

Existing approaches address this problem through different
training paradigms, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .
One approach learns video prediction directly from real robot
videos and their associated actions such as
IRASim ( Zhu et al., 2025b ) and
Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026c ) .
This provides direct supervision for action-conditioned generation,
but learning precise action responses and complex visual dynamics
jointly from real videos remains challenging.
Another approach introduces an explicit visual structure.
For example, RoboDream ( Ye et al., 2026a ) anchors generation
to rendered robot motion and conditions on scene and object
priors. Such compositional inputs provide additional control,
while requiring the corresponding priors to be constructed
and supplied. Qwen-RobotWorld ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) also needs scene video as prior. However, the potential of simulation data to improve real-video prediction without additional priors remains
underexplored.

Simulation provides structured supervision for action-dependent motion, complementing the appearance and interaction diversity of real videos. Transferring this knowledge nevertheless presents two challenges. First, appearance differences complicate direct matching between simulated and real observations. Second, predicted simulation trajectories are imperfect; a real-domain model that relies too heavily on them may inherit their errors. These challenges motivate transferring motion knowledge through temporal differences in latent space to mitigate the influence of appearance differences, while controlling the model’s reliance on potentially inaccurate simulation predictions.

We present SimForcing , a novel world modeling framework that addresses these challenges through motion knowledge transfer and controllable simulation guidance. To transfer motion knowledge across domains with different appearances, we first train a mixture-of-transformers world model on synthetic rollouts with trajectory augmentation, learning action-dependent motion from diverse robot trajectories. The resulting model initializes the student and serves as a frozen teacher. Our key transfer mechanism is latent-motion distillation, which aligns temporal differences between adjacent teacher and student video latents rather than directly matching their appearances. This motion-focused supervision internalizes the teacher’s simulation-derived priors within the student, directly
enhancing its ability to predict real-world video dynamics. Joint flow-matching and motion-distillation objectives on paired simulated and real videos further develop prediction capabilities in both domains within the same student, without requiring additional scene or object decomposition.

To benefit from explicit simulation predictions without becoming overly dependent on their accuracy, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout. Injecting simulation latents into multiple video transformer blocks provides a motion reference throughout generation, while latent corruption and condition dropout train the student to handle imperfect or absent simulation guidance. At inference, we introduce a simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance (CFG) that combines predictions from branches with and without simulation latent input, balancing explicit simulation guidance with the student’s internalized motion priors. This design enables the model to exploit reliable simulation predictions while limiting the influence of inaccurate ones. The jointly trained student generates both the simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference.

Experiments on Bridge show that SimForcing outperforms
Ctrl-World, EnerVerse-AC, and a GeniWorld reimplementation
across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD, improving both reconstruction
fidelity and perceptual similarity.
It also achieves lower LPIPS than Cosmos-Predict2.5 with
substantially faster inference.
Evaluation on InternData-A1 supports its applicability across
robot datasets, while ablations demonstrate the complementary
benefits of motion distillation and simulation conditioning.
Beyond video prediction, initializing a downstream VLA with
the pretrained world-model experts improves average LIBERO
success from 82.6 % 82.6\% to 89.2 % 89.2\% under action-only training
relative to Wan DiT initialization, with gains also observed
in the other training settings. Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce SimForcing, a robot world model framework for transferring
motion knowledge from simulation to real-world video
prediction in latent space, internalizing simulation-derived
motion priors within the world model.

We propose a controllable mechanism for exploiting
simulation predictions while limiting overreliance on
inaccurate guidance. Our simulation-conditioning CFG scheme
combines this explicit guidance with the motion knowledge
internalized through distillation.

We outperform state-of-the-art methods on Bridge across
PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD, and demonstrate the framework’s
applicability to InternData-A1 dataset.
LIBERO experiments preliminarily validate the pretrained
video expert’s utility for policy learning.

1. We introduce SimForcing, a robot world model framework for transferring
motion knowledge from simulation to real-world video
prediction in latent space, internalizing simulation-derived
motion priors within the world model.

2. We propose a controllable mechanism for exploiting

inaccurate guidance. Our simulation-conditioning CFG scheme

3. We outperform state-of-the-art methods on Bridge across
