2. The Anchor Verifier, which grounds execution verification in the WAM’s own predicted future and executed actions, identifying when the scene no longer supports continuation.

3. The Anchor-Guided Recovery, which translates the alarmed anchor into a corrective instruction and strengthens instruction guidance, enabling a WAM to use its own predicted future as a recovery goal and return to a state from which the original task can continue.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 World Action Models and Future Prediction

WAMs integrate future prediction into robot control [ Shen et al., 2026 ] . Joint video–action models couple anticipated visual changes with robot actions in a single generative process [ Zhu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Ye et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2026 ] , whereas cascaded interfaces pass visual future states as explicit conditions to inverse dynamics models (IDMs) [ Du et al., 2023a ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Liang et al., 2025 ] . The role of prediction depends on the inference interface: Fast-WAM separates the benefit of video co-training from that of explicit future generation at test time [ Yuan et al., 2026 ] . Related efforts use video models as simulators or reward sources [ Yang et al., 2024 ; Escontrela et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2026 ] and diagnose whether generated futures follow the commanded actions [ Chen et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ] . We focus on WAMs whose predicted future states condition action generation and thus accompany the resulting actions.

In these interfaces, and in work on aligning visual features and instructions with action decoding [ Qiu et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026c ] , the predicted future is an input to action generation and plays no further role once the actions are produced. FFDC is the exception: it retains the prediction and compares it with incoming observations to judge whether the remaining actions can still be trusted, shortening execution or replanning when they cannot [ Wang et al., 2026b ] . Dense correspondence from long-range flow or all-pairs point tracking [ Wu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2026 ] could also relate the two frames, but it measures motion rather than task relevance. HarnessWAM also intervenes during WAM execution, but monitors subgoal completion rather than the prediction [ Gu et al., 2026 ] . Here, as in adaptive-horizon methods [ Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Nie et al., 2026 ] , the signal only decides whether to continue, and replanning starts from the deviated state.

## 2.2 Execution Verification and Recovery

Execution monitoring for learned policies draws on internal features, action consistency, and semantic progress [ Gu et al., 2025 ; Agia et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2023b ; Duan et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026c ] . Diagnostics for world models further expose inconsistency between imagination and execution, from rollouts that violate physical and causal consistency [ Chen et al., 2026b ] to actions that diverge from a correctly imagined future [ Li et al., 2026b ] . A detector, however, says only that something went wrong, not what state to return to.

Existing recovery methods obtain their target from outside the acting policy. Planner-level loops revise behavior from environmental feedback and constraint violations [ Huang et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ] , and test-time language correction takes the instruction from a human [ Liu et al., 2023c ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Shi et al., 2024 ] . Policy-level recovery for VLAs is learned from failure-and-recovery data [ Liu et al., 2023e ; Dai et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ] or inferred by an auxiliary predictive component, either a dynamics model [ Pan et al., 2026 ] or imagined states toward which recovery is directed [ Shin et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ] . Each obtains its objective at the cost of training or a second model, and none derives it from the plan the policy was executing. FAVOR takes the objective from that plan: the future the WAM predicted before acting is what recovery restores. Since a WAM accepts only an observation and an instruction, the VLM only translates this future into an instruction rather than estimating a target of its own. This translation step draws on VLM work in task-directed visual perception [ Yu et al., 2025 ] and spatial reasoning [ Zhang et al., 2026b ; Xiong et al., 2026 ] . However, formulating an appropriate corrective instruction does not ensure that the WAM will act on it.

In the WAM considered here, an IDM decodes actions from the predicted future, so the influence of a corrective instruction on execution depends largely on how it shapes future generation. Yet the WAM used here exhibits limited sensitivity to instruction changes, producing largely unchanged outputs across different instructions (Figure 1 ). On the policy side, prior work makes corrections effective by training on them [ Liu et al., 2023c ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Shi et al., 2024 ] or by aligning visual features and instructions with action decoding [ Qiu et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026c ] . On the generation side, classifier-free guidance strengthens a condition at inference time [ Ho & Salimans, 2022 ] , and controllable generation and editing steer diffusion models with visual conditions [ Tan et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Qin et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Wu et al., 2024a ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025a ] or instructions [ Yu et al., 2026 ] . FAVOR strengthens the instruction on the generation side at inference time: guidance makes it shape the generated future, and the IDM turns that future into recovery actions, without retraining.

2026-10-06.title: VLA-ZO: Fast Zeroth-Order Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-06.authors: Jaemin Kim , Jiahn Kim , Taesik Gong
2026-10-06.abstract: Adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models to deployment-time distribution shifts is important for reliable robotic operation, but conventional first-order adaptation can exceed the memory budget of inference-oriented deployment platforms. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a forward-only alternative with inference-level memory, but accurate gradient estimation requires many perturbation queries, making naive ZO prohibitively slow for large VLA models. We present VLA-ZO, a framework for fast ZO adaptation that exploits the structure of VLA computation. By confining adaptation to the action side, VLA-ZO keeps the expensive vision-language prefix frozen and reuses its conditioning states across perturbation queries and optimizer steps, while schedule-aware prefetching hides state-transfer overhead. On LIBERO camera-viewpoint shifts, VLA-ZO reduces end-to-end adaptation time by 25.59 × \times at q = 16 q=16 and 32.54 × \times at q = 64 q=64 relative to baseline ZO, while improving average task success from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% and 63.58%, respectively. These results show that making ZO faster can make larger query budgets practical, providing a promising path toward resource-efficient VLA adaptation on deployment platforms.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are emerging as a general interface for robotic control ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ) , but deploying a fixed policy is often insufficient in real-world environments.
Changes in camera viewpoint, appearance, and operating conditions shift the observation distribution away from that seen during training, causing VLA policies to degrade sharply under such shifts.
Specifically, the success rates of state-of-the-art VLAs collapse from 95 % 95\% to below 30 % 30\% under modest perturbations to camera pose and robot initial state ( Fei et al., 2025 ) .
Recent work has explored one-shot adaptation ( Li et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) , in which a VLA policy is adapted using a single demonstration from a target environment.
This setting enables data-efficient post-deployment adaptation to address these distribution shifts.

This adaptation, however, must run on the deployment platform itself, under a compute and memory budget provisioned for inference rather than training.
Conventional first-order adaptation fits this setting poorly (Figure 1(a) , left): backpropagation requires retaining intermediate activations that can otherwise be discarded during inference, substantially increasing memory requirements ( Cai et al., 2020 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) .
Even with gradient checkpointing enabled, this overhead grows with batch size: for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , first-order adaptation uses 20.27 GiB of peak memory at batch size 16 and 54.69 GiB at batch size 64, compared with the corresponding inference-level footprints of 12.74 GiB and 27.71 GiB for forward-only ZO. The relative gap therefore increases from 1.59 × 1.59\times to 1.97 × 1.97\times .
Moreover, gradient checkpointing trades memory for additional recomputation and does not remove the need for a backward-capable execution path.
These requirements make first-order adaptation difficult to accommodate in inference-oriented deployment stacks as VLA models scale.

This motivates zeroth-order (ZO) optimization as a natural alternative (Figure 1(a) , right), as it enables adaptation using only forward evaluations without backpropagation.
Rather than explicitly computing gradients through backpropagation, ZO methods estimate gradients by perturbing model parameters and comparing the resulting objective values using only forward evaluations ( Duchi et al., 2015 ; Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017 ; Malladi et al., 2023 ) .
By estimating parameter updates solely from forward evaluations, ZO avoids backpropagation and substantially reduces the memory requirements for adaptation, making it attractive for memory-constrained devices as well as deployment environments where backward execution is unavailable or undesirable.
Despite these advantages, the potential of ZO optimization for adapting VLA policies remains largely unexplored.

In this work, we first show that ZO optimization can effectively adapt VLA policies under deployment-time distribution shifts, but at a substantial runtime cost from repeated forward evaluations (Figure 1 ).
This trade-off is governed by the query budget q q , the number of random perturbation directions evaluated per optimization step, each as a ± \pm pair of forward passes.
A larger q q improves the gradient estimate, allowing adaptation quality to approach first-order performance while peak memory remains at the inference level.
The same knob, however, also determines the computational cost: every additional direction requires two more forward passes through the full model, causing adaptation time to grow with q q and quickly exceed that of first-order adaptation.
Because modern VLAs contain expensive vision and language components, naively applying ZO can therefore require hours of adaptation.
Thus, the main obstacle to practical ZO-based VLA adaptation is not whether it works, but whether it can run fast enough.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Recent work has increasingly studied data-efficient adaptation of pretrained VLA policies from limited target-domain supervision ( Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) .
At the extreme of this low-data regime, one-shot methods adapt a VLA policy
using only a single target-domain demonstration.
FTM and FLA enable such adaptation to novel camera viewpoints ( Li et al., 2026 ) , while DART addresses visual and embodiment shifts and
considers domain-level adaptation across tasks ( Kang et al., 2026 ) .
Our focus is complementary: rather than developing a new adaptation method,
we study how to reduce the computational cost of zeroth-order VLA adaptation
under deployment-time compute and memory constraints.

Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates gradients from perturbed forward
evaluations without backpropagation.
MeZO ( Malladi et al., 2023 ) enables LLM fine-tuning with approximately the memory footprint of
inference and reports performance comparable to backpropagation on several
language tasks.
Subsequent benchmarking examines how task alignment and optimizer design
affect ZO fine-tuning ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , while SubZero explores
low-rank perturbations in random subspaces ( Yu et al., 2025 ) .
For execution efficiency, MobiZO parallelizes perturbation evaluations through
Multi-Perturbed LoRA within existing inference engines ( Gao et al., 2025 ) .
In general deep-network training, DeepZero combines sparse coordinate-wise
gradient estimation with reuse of features preceding the perturbed layer
and forward parallelization ( Chen et al., 2024 ) .

2026-10-06.title: Encoded but Not in Control: Revealing the Grounding Gap in Vision-Language Robot Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Shaohan Jiang , Jiahang Cao , Qiduo He , Fengting Deng , Kun Wu , Jingkai Sun , Jiaxu Wang , Qiang Zhang , Qihao Zheng , Chunfeng Song , Ping Luo , Andrew F. Luo
2026-10-06.abstract:
Instruction following is central to language-conditioned robot policies: language should determine what to do when the same scene permits multiple valid actions. Yet successful execution alone cannot establish whether a policy follows the instruction or infers the task from the scene. We study this ambiguity through scene-preserving instruction interventions , using valid target substitutions, arbitrary nouns, and unrelated sentences while holding the scene fixed. We evaluate vision-language-action (VLA) policies and world-action models (WAMs) in simulation and in real-world experiments. Our analysis addresses three questions: (a) Does task success imply instruction following? When instructions request a different visible object, all evaluated policies predominantly approach and pick up the incorrect original target associated with the scene. (b) Is this failure caused by language insensitivity? Instruction perturbations affect task performance. A layerwise action lens shows intermediate action predictions respond to these perturbations. Linear probes accurately recover instructed targets, indicating modified instructions are encoded despite rarely determining target selection. (c) Why does encoded language fail to control action? Attention analysis indicates weak instruction-token contributions to action generation. Target-token attention can remain focused on the original object, revealing a mismatch between target encoding and visual grounding. UMAP and shared non-negative matrix factorization show target information remains accessible within representations increasingly organized by scene identity.
Our findings expose a grounding gap concealed by nominal success and provide a diagnostic framework. They further establish a concrete criterion for progress: policies should reliably follow valid changes in user intent, even when they conflict with scene-favored behavior.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Language-conditioned robot policies promise a natural interface for specifying what a robot should do in an environment. Recent VLAs ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) and WAMs ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) demonstrate strong performance across manipulation tasks, embodiments, and visual environments, commonly evaluated by task success under a given instruction and environment. However, task success alone does not establish that the instruction determined the behavior. In many robot datasets, a scene is repeatedly paired with one target object or task, so the scene alone may suffice to infer the demonstrated behavior without resolving the requested behavior. A policy can consequently achieve high success by exploiting scene–task correlations while its ability to follow language remains unclear.

Instruction following requires evidence that changing a valid instruction in a fixed scene redirects behavior toward the newly specified target. Evaluations using linguistic perturbations and modality ablations reveal brittleness and task-dependent language sensitivity in VLA policies ( Fei et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025b ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . More directly, LIBERO-CF and LangGap expose instruction-following failures under alternative feasible instructions in fixed scenes ( Fang et al., 2026 ; Hou & Zhao, 2026 ) , while InstructMove constructs scenes where language must distinguish among multiple feasible actions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Mechanistic analyses further find that prompt information can remain decodable despite limited behavioral use, with action generation relying strongly on visual inputs ( Grant et al., 2026 ) . Building on these findings, we use scene-preserving instruction interventions to investigate how target-selection failures relate to the encoding, visual grounding, and contribution of instruction information to action generation, linking behavioral failures to action-level responses and internal representations across VLA and world-action models.

Part I: Does nominal task success imply instruction following? We revisit this question across VLA and WAM policies, with additional real-world experiments. When a valid instruction requests another object in the same scene, the policies predominantly approach and manipulate the original target. We refer to this directional preference as a scene-conditioned behavioral prior . It reveals a failure that standard success rates cannot expose: a policy may successfully reproduce the expected behavior for a familiar scene without allowing language to determine which behavior it executes.

Part II: Is target-conflict failure caused by language insensitivity? This failure cannot be attributed simply to absent linguistic influence. Controlled instruction perturbations produce systematic, task-dependent changes in policy performance. A layerwise action lens shows that intermediate action predictions respond differently to target substitutions and random sentences, evidencing language sensitivity in action generation. Linear probes also recover target and scene identities from fine-tuned representations with high accuracy, so target information remains available despite incorrect object selection. Policies thus respond to language at behavioral and representational levels, yet the failure persists even when the modified instruction affects action predictions and its target remains encoded—motivating a closer look at how this information contributes to action selection.

Part III: If target information is encoded, why does it fail to control action? Attention contribution analysis shows instruction tokens contribute little to action generation relative to visual inputs, and target-token attention can stay fixed on the original object even after the instruction names a different target. UMAP reveals a shift from object-based to scene-based clustering after fine-tuning; shared non-negative matrix factorization likewise identifies transitions from object-dominated to scene-dominated components in both π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7. High target decodability thus coexists with limited instruction contribution, misaligned visual attention, and increased scene dependence, characterizing why encoded language does not reliably guide target selection.

We describe this dissociation as a representation-to-control grounding gap : linguistic information can be represented within a policy without reliably governing action selection. Our analyses distinguish sensitivity to language, accessibility of target information, and behavioral adherence to the instruction. These target-selection failures also extend to the evaluated world-action models, showing that visual prediction objectives alone do not ensure instruction following. Our findings motivate a stricter grounding criterion: a valid change in instruction should reliably select a different behavior within the same scene. We hope this work encourages evaluations that test such control directly and provides a diagnostic basis for investigating where encoded instructions fail to guide action. Ultimately, progress should be measured by how reliably robots act on the user’s current intent, even when it conflicts with familiar scene-task associations.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Language-conditioned robot policies. Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions.
Recent models such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} couple a pretrained
vision-language backbone with a dedicated action expert that generates
continuous action chunks through flow matching ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . GR00T N1 adopts a dual-system
architecture in which a vision-language module interprets visual
observations and language instructions, followed by a diffusion
transformer that generates continuous motor actions ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) .
World action models (WAMs) instead incorporate explicit visual-dynamics
modeling into policy learning. LingBot-VA adopts an autoregressive
diffusion framework that jointly learns future-frame prediction and
policy execution, using a shared latent space and a
Mixture-of-Transformers architecture to integrate visual and action
tokens ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Fast-WAM retains video co-training
during training but removes explicit future prediction at test time,
directly producing actions from the learned world representations ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . These complementary architectures motivate
our evaluation of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , GR00T N1.7, LingBot-VA, and FastWAM,
allowing us to examine whether instruction-grounding failures persist
across both VLA and world-action modeling paradigms.

Evaluating and improving instruction following. Recent studies investigate if task success reliably reflects language
grounding. LIBERO-PRO reports persistent behaviors under corrupted
instructions ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) , while LIBERO-Plus evaluates robustness
to linguistic, visual, and physical perturbations ( Fei et al., 2025 ) .
Multilingual evaluation further reveals step-dependent language
sensitivity ( Dong et al., 2026 ) . To test semantic control more directly,
LIBERO-CF and LangGap vary instructions within existing scene
layouts ( Fang et al., 2026 ; Hou & Zhao, 2026 ) , while InstructMove introduces
semantic distractors that require language-dependent action
selection ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Complementary methods strengthen
language conditioning through counterfactual language–action augmentation
in navigation ( Glossop et al., 2026 ) , Bayesian training
objectives ( Lian et al., 2026 ) , counterfactual action
guidance ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and instruction augmentation coupled with
guidance against a vision-only prior ( Zhan et al., 2026 ) .
Building on these studies, we connect behavior under scene-preserving
instruction interventions to internal policy representations. Target substitutions test semantic redirection, whereas arbitrary nouns
and random sentences diagnose language dependence without necessarily
specifying executable alternatives.

Language representations and behavioral influence. Probing studies distinguish decodable information from its use by a
model, emphasizing the need for controls when interpreting probe
accuracy ( Belinkov, 2022 ; Hewitt & Liang, 2019 ) .
In robotics, Lu et al. (2025) decode symbolic object and action
states from OpenVLA for monitoring within the cognitive architecture.
Using counterfactual prompts, activation injection, sparse autoencoders,
and probes, Grant et al. (2026) identify distinct VLM and action-expert
roles and report decodable prompt categories despite weak behavioral
sensitivity in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .
VLA-Trace combines representation analysis, attention knockouts, and
behavioral interventions to identify model-dependent control pathways
and limitations in fine-grained semantic following ( Shi et al., 2026 ) .
We build on these findings by pairing instruction interventions with
layer-wise analyses of target and scene information across VLA and WAM
policies, examining how instructed-target representations relate to
action selection when language and scene-associated behavior conflict.

2026-10-06.title: AUTOPILOT An Advanced Perception, Localization and Path Planning Techniques for Autonomous Vehicles Using YOLOv7 and MiDaS
2026-10-06.authors: Harshkumar Devmurari , Gautham Kuckian , Prajjwal Vishwakarma
2026-10-06.comment: Published in the 2023 International Conference on Advanced Computing Technologies and Applications (ICACTA), IEEE
2026-10-06.abstract: Self driving vehicles have emerged as a reliable technology that has the capability to transform transportation and mobility. The development of self driving cars requires significant advances in a number of areas, including perception, localization, decision making, and control. This research paper is based on the project implementation of the combination of object detection using YOLO (You Only Look Once), depth sensing using MiDaS for the localization and perception of obstacles, perspective transform, and decision making for path planning in self driving cars. The contemporary state of the technology for object detection, depth sensing, localization, and path planning evaluates the performance of the combined system through simulations and experiments. The results show that the combination of YOLO and MiDaS provides a new robust system for object detection and depth sensing. This research paper contributes to the advancement of self driving car technology and provides new and innovative approaches to the perception and localization of obstacles in the environment. Keywords: YOLO, MiDaS, perception, localization, decision making

2026-10-06.title: Towards Quadruped-Provided Localization and Active Tracking for Micro-UAVs
2026-10-06.authors: Alejandro Lorite Mora , Andrés Faíña
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted version (before peer review) of a paper accepted at CLAWAR 2026, Cranfield, UK, 14 to 16 September 2026. The published version, titled "Towards Quadruped-Provided Localization and Active Tracking for Nano-UAVs", will appear in the CLAWAR 2026 proceedings (Springer, Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems)
2026-10-06.abstract: Micro unmanned aerial vehicles (micro-UAVs) are small enough to reach confined spaces that larger robots cannot access, but too small to carry the sensing and computing power required for autonomous flight. We move the localization stack entirely off the aerial platform onto a quadruped robot with a 7-degree-of-freedom (DOF) arm, which supplies the micro-UAV (27 g bare, 42 g with fiducial markers) its full 6-DOF pose. A camera at the arm’s end-effector detects AprilTag fiducial markers on the drone and composes that observation with the quadruped’s own self-localization to place the drone in a shared map frame—so the ground robot localizes its partner, rather than only tracking it relative to the camera. The arm acts as an actively-controlled observer, repositioning to keep the drone in view as both robots move; the drone carries only an inertial measurement unit and fuses the external pose to fly commanded setpoints. In lab flights the external pose is accurate to 12–16 mm, enough to fly the drone autonomously within 2–5 cm of motion-capture-fed control. Having the quadruped actively follow the drone reduces the tracking error from 11.0 cm to 6.9 cm by holding the camera in the close range, where the markers are most accurate.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Traversing narrow passages and highly constrained environments generally necessitates the use of small robotic platforms. However, reducing the robot’s size also limits the payload capacity available for sensors, onboard computation, and communication systems. This trade-off is evident in current aerial inspection applications, which are predominantly performed using relatively large unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). These platforms can carry advanced sensing suites and powerful onboard processors, enabling autonomous navigation and operation in complex environments. Their large size, however, prevents them from accessing the confined or hazardous spaces that applications such as search-and-rescue missions and infrastructure inspection often require.

In contrast, micro-scale UAVs possess the agility and compact form factor required to access narrow and cluttered spaces that are inaccessible to larger platforms. Nevertheless, their limited payload capacity significantly restricts their sensing and computational capabilities, preventing fully autonomous navigation in such environments. As a result, micro-UAVs often rely on external infrastructure, offboard computation, or human assistance to safely traverse and operate within confined spaces.

A micro-UAV that cannot localize itself must obtain its pose either by adding onboard sensing or by receiving it from an external source. Scaling the payload up is the usual answer when a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) is unavailable, as in indoor drone flight [ 11 ] : visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) are the standard methods at the kilogram scale [ 17 , 7 , 19 ] , but they degrade in featureless or poorly-lit environments and cannot run on sub-30 g platforms, because the stereo or LiDAR sensors and the VIO/SLAM computation exceed the payload, computing power, and power a micro-UAV can carry. Micro-UAVs instead rely on lighter methods such as optical flow or learned visual navigation [ 16 ] , which also degrade where visual texture is weak, as it often is in the confined spaces micro-UAVs are meant to reach.

The other option is to receive the pose from an external source. Micro-UAVs commonly rely on external infrastructure for this. Motion capture (MOCAP) with Crazyswarm2 [ 9 ] provides centimeter accuracy but requires a pre-installed array of cameras. Ultra-wideband (UWB) localization, which estimates range from fixed radio anchors, shares the same pre-setup constraint. Fiducial markers are the standard low-cost option. AprilTag [ 15 ] is the most widely used, and its accuracy and failure modes are well characterized [ 12 ] . Recent open micro-UAV frameworks build on fiducial-marker localization for the same reason [ 6 ] ; but in all such work the observing sensor is fixed or rigidly mounted to the platform being localized. Repositioning the observer instead—moving it to keep the target in view—is an instance of active perception [ 2 ] and, at the control level, visual servoing [ 5 ] , but both classically serve the observer’s own task rather than sustaining the external localization of a separate, non-sensing robot.

A common alternative is to let a ground vehicle help localize the UAV, providing mapping and localization support. Such cooperative UAV and unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) teams have been studied for GNSS-denied navigation with complementary sensing across platforms. UWB cooperative localization [ 18 ] requires radios on both platforms. The most closely related work is by Akhihiero et al. [ 1 ] , where a UGV provides mapping, self-localization, and UAV state estimation in subterranean environments using UGV LiDAR and UWB, but the formulation requires either UAV or UGV to be stationary during state updates. Gross et al. [ 8 ] make similar architectural choices with UGV LiDAR plus stereo and IMU on the UAV. In all of these the UAV still carries its own localization sensors—stereo, inertial measurement unit (IMU), altimeter—and the ground robot only refines that estimate rather than replacing it. Despite the growing interest in cooperative robotic systems, the problem of enabling localization for sensing-constrained micro-UAVs through information provided by a ground robot remains insufficiently studied.

In our system the micro-UAV carries only an IMU, with no exteroceptive sensing and no way to localize itself, so the ground partner supplies its entire absolute 6-DOF pose while both robots move. The drone’s onboard extended Kalman filter (EKF) fuses that external pose with its IMU to follow position setpoints. A quadruped with a 7-DOF arm estimates the drone’s pose externally from observing AprilTags on the drone, with the arm acting as an actively-controlled perception platform that repositions to keep the drone in view. The estimate is produced in the quadruped’s map frame rather than only relative to the camera, so the ground robot localizes the drone rather than merely tracking it. That pose is ready for a mapping-and-planning module to consume; integrating that module is the natural next step and is not evaluated here.

Our contributions are (i) the integrated localization-and-tracking system—AprilTag-anchored external pose estimation with an actively-controlled arm—for a micro-UAV with no localization sensing, deployed end-to-end in the Robot Operating System (ROS 2); and (ii) preliminary validation of the approach in lab settings. The external estimate localizes the drone to 12–16 mm once a constant calibration bias is removed. This is accurate enough to fly the drone autonomously along commanded trajectories, within a few centimeters of motion-capture-fed control. Moreover, active arm tracking improves rather than degrades the pose, because it holds the drone in the close range where fiducial accuracy is higher, so the quadruped’s own motion helps rather than harms the estimate it provides.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 METHOD

## 2.1 System Overview

We use a quadruped robot with an arm that provides the perception capabilities for drone localization. All sensing, estimation, and control run on the quadruped, while the drone is only a thin actuator that executes setpoints.

The ground platform is a Boston Dynamics Spot [ 4 ] with the Spot Arm and a Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB Developer Kit (Fig. 1 ). It localizes itself from its five stereo RGBD cameras, a gray-scale camera pointing to the ground, and an IMU. The aerial platform is a Crazyflie 2.1+ (27 g bare, 92 × \times 92 × \times 29 mm) with no positioning sensors; it carries a custom chassis with four 36h11 AprilTags (58.5 × \times 58.5 mm) on its lateral faces for visibility from any azimuth, bringing the flight mass to 42 g. A Crazyradio PA (2.4 GHz, USB) plugged into the Jetson removes the need for a separate ground station. To report position accuracy we use an OptiTrack MOCAP system of eight PrimeX 13W cameras covering a 4 × \times 4 × \times 2.5 m volume; both robots carry reflective markers tracked by it.

All software runs in ROS 2 Humble [ 13 ] in an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker container deployed on the Jetson PC, with packages for the quadruped’s ROS 2 driver [ 3 ] , the micro-UAV control stack [ 9 ] , the AprilTag detector ( apriltag_ros ), and our integration code. Two paths run concurrently (Fig. 2 ): a perception path that fuses the quadruped’s sensors and the arm-mounted camera into the drone’s pose, and a command path that carries trajectory setpoints to the drone. The control system consumes a single composed transform, T map → drone T_{\text{map}\to\text{drone}} (section § 2.2 ). Because this pose is already expressed in the map frame, it is also what an on-board planner would need, so a mapping-and-planning module can be added later without changing the perception path.

## 2.2 Drone Localization in the Map Frame

The goal of this stage is to know where the drone is—its full 6-DOF pose, position and orientation—expressed in the same global map frame that Spot uses to navigate, so that the aerial and ground platforms share one coordinate system. Since the drone carries no positioning sensors, this pose is recovered entirely from the arm camera’s view of the on-board AprilTags together with Spot’s own self-localization. The estimate is assembled as a chain of coordinate transforms, each linking one frame to the next:

Fiducial detection. Detecting the drone’s AprilTags yields the camera-to-drone transform T cam → drone T_{\text{cam}\to\text{drone}} , the final two links of the chain in Eq. 1 . With markers on four lateral faces the camera sees one or two tags at a time. When more than one is visible we use the single strongest detection by decision-margin followed by Perspective-n-Point (PnP)-covariance trace, then compose with a static transform to obtain T cam → drone T_{\text{cam}\to\text{drone}} . This process runs on the CPU.

Pose stream and watchdog. The pipeline emits one map-frame pose per detection and does not extrapolate between detections, so during a detection gap it simply publishes nothing. Tolerance to short gaps instead comes from the drone’s onboard EKF, which coasts on its IMU until the next external pose arrives. A safety watchdog complements this: if the drone is airborne and no pose update arrives within a short timeout, it commands an immediate landing, so the drone is never left flying without a position estimate when it leaves the camera’s view.

## 2.3 Active Tracking

The quadruped’s arm acts as an actively-controlled perception platform, repositioning to keep the drone in the hand camera’s field of view. When the drone moves away from the center of the view, a new optimal camera position is calculated. Then, inverse kinematics (IK) is solved with the Spot Arm IK service to compute the required joint angles. The onboard locomotion controller handles foothold planning and dynamic balance. Finally, the quadruped walks and moves the arm simultaneously to re-center the drone in the image.

Let 𝐩 d \mathbf{p}_{\text{d}} be the predicted drone position at the next control step—estimated by fitting a velocity to the recent detections and extrapolating, which also lets the arm keep tracking briefly through a detection gap—and 𝐩 c \mathbf{p}_{\text{c}} the current hand-camera position. The controller maintains two conditions: the camera’s optical axis points at 𝐩 d \mathbf{p}_{\text{d}} , and the camera-to-drone distance ‖ 𝐩 d − 𝐩 c ‖ \|\mathbf{p}_{\text{d}}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{c}}\| is driven toward a fixed stand-off d offset ≈ 0.9 d_{\text{offset}}\approx 0.9 m. Larger distances remain usable—accuracy degrades only gradually with distance—so this is a preferred operating point rather than a hard limit, and it depends on the camera resolution, the AprilTag size and family, and lighting conditions. Algorithm 1 summarizes the control loop.

## 2.4 Experimental Setup

All experiments run in our indoor robotics lab within a 3 × 3 × 2 3\times 3\times 2 m working volume. Eight OptiTrack PrimeX 13W cameras, mounted around a 4 × 4 × 2.5 4\times 4\times 2.5 m volume and aimed inward, track this space and provide 6-DOF ground truth at 120 Hz. We use this ground truth in two ways: as the evaluation reference in every experiment, and—in selected runs (Experiment 2)—as the external pose source fed to the drone, so it can be compared head-to-head against the AprilTag estimate. Every run records the following data: fiducial detections, the composed T map → drone T_{\text{map}\to\text{drone}} pose, joint states, and the OptiTrack streams—together with a description of the run’s configuration (pose source, AprilTag backend, hand-camera resolution, and mocap-to-odom calibration).

2026-10-06.title: STC-MPM: Coupled Deformation, Progressive Damage, and Cut Formation in Soft-Tissue Cutting
2026-10-06.authors: Kewei Zuo , Jiahe Chen , Ziao Kuang , Junsheng Zhu , Etsuko Kobayashi
2026-10-06.abstract:
Cutting is a recurring operation in robotic automation, from food
preparation to surgical tissue resection. For highly compliant targets,
blade motion may deform or displace the material rather than advance
the intended cut, while progressive failure changes load transfer and
subsequent tool–tissue interaction. A computational description must
therefore connect cut formation to the evolving mechanical response,
rather than specifying the incision independently of material failure.
We present STC-MPM (Soft Tissue Cutting with the Material Point Method),
a framework that couples finite-strain deformation, history-driven
continuum damage, and configurable post-failure treatment. Damage
initiates only when a tensile-strain history
exceeds a material threshold within the blade process zone.
Progressive degradation changes stress transmission before the
post-failure policy is applied, while the remaining tissue continues
to deform, move, and interact with the tool. Numerical scalpel studies
using delayed particle deactivation follow this response through
insertion and withdrawal. Under identical
blade motion, reducing the damage-rate limit leaves the first recorded
damage time unchanged but delays and increases peak reaction force,
delays particle deactivation, and increases the fixed-cohort
displacement statistic at maximum insertion. The matched comparison
illustrates how post-initiation failure evolution alters subsequent
tool loading and recorded material motion. STC-MPM thus supports joint
analysis of cut formation and accompanying tissue response without a
pre-inserted cutting interface.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Cutting is a recurring operation in robotic automation,
from slicing fruits and vegetables in food preparation to surgical
tissue resection [ 4 , 16 , 1 ] .
These tasks require a robot to produce an intended material separation,
not merely execute a blade trajectory. When a workpiece is well
supported and its shape changes little, tool travel can approximate
cutting progress. That approximation becomes unreliable for highly
compliant or weakly constrained targets: the tool can compress, stretch,
or displace the material before separation occurs. In surgery, the
intended cut must also be achieved while preserving the surrounding
tissue [ 1 ] .

The central difficulty is the two-way coupling between cutting and
material response. Tool contact deforms the tissue and moves it
relative to the blade; progressive failure then reduces load-carrying
capacity and redistributes the loading. These changes alter subsequent
contact, deformation, and tissue motion. Blade advancement therefore
need not imply equivalent cut advancement, and the same tool trajectory
can produce different cutting and tissue-motion outcomes. Force alone
does not resolve this ambiguity. In automatic tissue traction, for
example, insufficient traction can impede cutting, whereas excessive
traction can cause unwanted splitting [ 3 ] . A lower
force is therefore not an unconditional improvement, and smaller tissue
motion does not necessarily imply that an equivalent cut has been
achieved.

Addressing this difficulty computationally requires deformation, load
transfer, progressive loss of load-carrying capacity, and cut formation
to participate in the same evolving interaction. Material properties,
support conditions, and instrument motion provide the context for
interpreting those responses. Cutting models have supported the
analysis of tool loads and motion in deformable
materials [ 4 ] , while differentiable simulation
has enabled parameter inference and motion
optimization [ 5 , 6 ] . Here, the aim is to
compare cut formation, local deformation, and region displacement
under controlled changes in the formulation or operating condition.
This requires obtaining tool loading and tissue response from the
same evolving body, rather than interpreting a force trace or final
incision in isolation.

Existing approaches make different assumptions about how a cut is
introduced. Geometric cutting algorithms can accommodate complex
cutting surfaces, but a separation rule based on the tool geometry does
not itself determine whether the material has reached a failure
condition [ 7 , 8 ] . Models constructed
around a prepared cutting interface provide a different route, but
restrict separation to the surface represented in that
construction [ 6 ] . Mechanical failure models already
exist for tissue insertion and cutting [ 9 , 4 ] ;
the issue is therefore not an absence of failure mechanics across the
field. Our focus is a formulation that carries the failure history with
the deforming material, drives post-failure treatment through that response, and
continues to compute the resulting tissue motion without a pre-inserted
cutting interface.

We present STC-MPM (Soft Tissue Cutting with the Material Point Method)
to address this coupled process. Damage is initiated within the blade
process zone only when the material strain history exceeds its
threshold. Progressive degradation changes stress transmission before
a distinct post-failure policy changes material activity or
particle–grid transfer compatibility. These changes enter the
subsequent mechanical update, allowing failure to
alter later tool loading and tissue movement. Cut formation, tool
reaction, and tissue movement are thus computed together, rather than
prescribing the tissue trajectory or the final cut independently.
The material point method provides the particle–grid representation
used to advance the body and retain its material
history [ 10 ] .

The main contribution is the STC-MPM formulation and its coupled
numerical realization for soft-tissue cutting. The numerical study
combines local damage-update checks with a representative scalpel
sequence, including withdrawal, and a matched failure-evolution
comparison. These studies examine tool loading, local failure, and
material-region motion together rather than treating a damage image or
final opening as a complete account of the interaction. Sections II and III review prior
work and background. Section IV presents STC-MPM,
followed by its numerical assessment.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Mechanical Failure Models

Cohesive-zone models (CZM) represent failure through a traction–separation
relation on an interface. They provide a direct description of crack
opening and interfacial work, as demonstrated in cohesive needle-insertion
models [ 9 ] . A pre-inserted cohesive surface limits
failure to the represented path, but this restriction does not apply to
all CZM formulations: adaptively introduced cohesive surfaces can permit
fracture along evolving paths [ 11 ] . The relevant
tradeoff is how the fracture interface is introduced and updated, rather
than whether interface-based models include failure mechanics.

Continuum damage mechanics (CDM) instead represents degradation within
material volumes through internal state variables [ 12 ] .
For the present problem, its main advantage is the ability to describe
loss of load-carrying capacity around a moving blade while the affected
material remains part of the deforming body. This makes pre-separation
stress redistribution and its influence on surrounding tissue explicit,
without embedding the future cut as an interface in the initial body.
However, volumetric degradation does not by itself create independent
crack faces. Local softening also requires control of its spatial scale;
crack-band approaches relate the softening energy density to a fracture
energy through a characteristic length [ 13 ] .

Phase-field fracture provides a gradient-regularized alternative closely
related to damage mechanics: an evolving field represents a diffuse
crack, with fracture energy and an internal length entering the governing
problem [ 14 ] . Finite-strain, anisotropic formulations
have been applied to soft biological tissue [ 15 ] .
These models offer capabilities beyond a local scalar damage law, but
also require spatial resolution of the regularized crack field. CDM,
CZM, and phase-field formulations therefore make different commitments
about degradation, localization, and crack representation; none is
universally preferable.

STC-MPM uses local, history-dependent volumetric damage to follow
progressive changes in tissue support, with post-failure topology
handled separately. This is a modeling choice for the coupled
cutting process, not a claim of a new general fracture theory. More
broadly, robotic cutting models already connect fracture toughness,
deformation, blade geometry, and motion [ 4 , 16 ] .
The distinction sought here concerns where failure is permitted, what
state drives its progression, and how that progression changes the
continuing mechanical response.

## II-B Computational Models for Soft-Material Cutting

Finite-element methods (FEM) provide a well-established setting for
nonlinear tissue deformation and instrument interaction. Cohesive FEM
has reproduced needle insertion into soft phantoms [ 9 ] ,
and inverse FEM has supported flexible-needle control in deforming
structures [ 17 ] . Extended FEM can represent complex
cutting surfaces without conforming remeshing by enriching the
displacement field [ 7 ] . Phase-field FEM offers a
different route, resolving diffuse cracks without explicitly tracking a
sharp interface [ 14 , 15 ] .

DiSECt combines finite-element deformation with virtual nodes and
springs across a preprocessed cutting surface. Knife contact forces
progressively weaken these springs, enabling differentiable parameter
inference and cutting-motion optimization [ 5 , 6 ] .
Its prepared fracture surface is a restriction of that particular
construction, not of FEM in general. A recent study by Moreno-Mateos and
Steinmann couples finite-strain bulk deformation with cohesive fracture,
adhesion, and friction, and compares the resulting soft-material cutting
response with experiments [ 18 ] . Thus, coupled
mechanical cutting is not exclusive to particle-based methods.

The difficulty for conventional continuous, mesh-conforming FEM is that
changing material connectivity and large distortion require additional
handling of the discretization. Remeshing, enrichment, cohesive-interface
updates, or a resolved diffuse crack field address different parts of
this difficulty. Recent adaptive phase-field work also targets the cost
of resolving evolving fracture zones in soft, nearly incompressible
materials [ 19 ] . The motivation for a particle–grid
representation is therefore to avoid advecting a permanently connected
material mesh through the cutting process, not an inability of FEM to
simulate fracture.

Meshfree representations have long supported fracture without a fixed
volumetric mesh; Pauly et al. combined point-based deformation with
explicit crack tracking [ 20 ] . MPM instead transports
material state on particles while solving momentum on a background
grid [ 10 ] ; APIC improves the velocity
transfer [ 21 ] . These are computational ingredients, not
constitutive failure criteria.

Mechanical failure also predates recent MPM cutting simulators. Ionescu
et al. modeled anisotropic soft-tissue failure by removing matrix or
fiber stress contributions after strain thresholds were
exceeded [ 22 ] . The phase-field branch of CD-MPM
couples continuum damage and dynamics [ 23 ] , while
AnisoMPM extends damage modeling to anisotropic
fracture [ 24 ] . Other phase-field MPM formulations address
anisotropic surface energy [ 25 ] and nearly
incompressible rubber-like solids [ 26 ] . MPM has also been
used specifically for needle–tissue interaction [ 27 ] .
These studies preclude a novelty claim based simply on combining MPM,
soft materials, and mechanical failure.

A separate line of work concerns numerical discontinuities. Compatible
particle-in-cell (CPIC) transfers permit geometry-defined cuts and rigid
coupling [ 28 ] ; CRESSim-MPM uses tool distance fields to
restrict incompatible transfers in surgical cutting and
suturing [ 8 ] . BladeMaster generates persistent particle-side
labels online in total-Lagrangian MPM, maintaining discontinuities after
withdrawal and supporting subsequent contact between cut
faces [ 29 ] . These developments address how material
regions remain kinematically distinct, which is different from specifying
a constitutive law for pre-separation degradation.

Not all recent MPM cutting models are geometry-only. CulinaryCut-VLAP
updates particle damage in a blade band using contact, approach-speed,
and downward-motion conditions, and reduces elastic moduli with
that damage [ 30 ] . Its driver differs from the tissue
strain-history threshold used here, but its damage-dependent stiffness
must be acknowledged. More generally, particle methods do not remove
all discretization difficulties: benchmarks identify challenges near
free surfaces and strong gradients [ 31 ] .

STC-MPM focuses on the coupling of blade-localized mechanical
initiation, history-driven stress degradation, and the subsequent
loading and motion of the remaining tissue. Unlike pre-inserted-interface
methods, its damage state resides in the moving material; unlike a
geometry-only cut rule, edge proximity alone is insufficient to cause
failure. Post-failure handling includes delayed particle deactivation
and an optional persistent side-compatible transfer treatment
(Section IV-D ). The archived scalpel comparison
evaluates the delayed-deactivation configuration.

2026-10-06.title: Arm-wise Compositional Generalization in Dual-Arm Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-06.authors: Zaibin Zhang , Binghao Ran , Yuhan Wu , Zhongbo Zhang , Yifan Wang , Junwei Jiang , Junlan Xiao , Wangcheng Shi , Li Kang , Yiran Qin , Zhenfei Yin , Lijun Wang , Huchuan Lu
2026-10-06.comment: Technical Report
2026-10-06.abstract: Generalization in multi-arm collaboration can be studied as composing familiar atomic skills in new ways across arms. However, existing evaluations offer limited insight into which training and architectural choices support this ability under different coordination requirements. We introduce ACG-Bench , a benchmark for Arm-wise Compositional Generalization that provides a common testbed for studying skill recomposition in dual-arm policies. It contains 23 task–condition pairs across 8 task families, with 6 in-domain conditions and 17 unseen compositions covering reordering, synchronization, their combination, and cross-task composition. All methods receive the same per-arm atomic prompts, and success requires achieving the task goal while satisfying physical milestones and specified order or timing constraints. Using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} as a common vision-language-action backbone, we compare representative data-augmentation and architectural strategies with shared source data and a common evaluation protocol. Our architectural study examines arm-token grouping, skill-specific LoRA adapters (SkillLoRA), and arm-wise attention (AWA), highlighting the complementarity of skill-conditioned parameters and attention structure. Combining these choices yields AE-VLA , which achieves 21.53% generalization success in simulation, compared with 2.94% for Single π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 3.06% for MA-VLA, and 5.53% for two independently controlled π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policies. On physical SO101 robots, AE-VLA reaches 39.00% mean success across five unseen conditions, compared with 10.00% for the strongest baseline. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing dual-arm policies that generalize beyond fixed training routines.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Dual-arm vision-language-action (VLA) models have made progress in learning manipulation tasks ( Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025a ) , but executing familiar tasks does not establish whether their component skills can be recombined.
The same placing skills may need to run in a different order or synchronize their completion, while skills learned in separate tasks may need to work together.
We call this ability Arm-wise Compositional Generalization (ACG), ie., reusing familiar arm-level skills under training-time unseen coordination requirements.
Such reuse offers a path beyond fixed collaboration routines without collecting demonstrations for every possible combination.

Existing benchmarks study skill transfer and composition through language grounding, skill chaining, and atomic-to-composite manipulation ( Mees et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Haresh et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , whereas dual-arm benchmarks mainly evaluate coordination patterns seen during training ( Mu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) .
Recent methods explore Arm Shuffle in MA-VLA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and arm-specific representations in TwinVLA ( Im et al., 2026 ) and SkillVLA ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) .
However, differences in backbones, datasets, and evaluation settings make their effects on compositional generalization difficult to isolate.
This motivates a controlled study: which training and architectural choices help familiar arm-level skills generalize to unseen compositions?

We introduce ACG-Bench , comprising 23 task–condition pairs across 8 task families: 6 in-domain conditions and 17 unseen compositions covering reordering , synchronization , Sync+Reorder , and cross-task composition .
All methods receive identical per-arm atomic prompts from a common phase scheduler, isolating execution of a supplied composition from skill planning.
Success requires both the task goal and compliance with physical milestones and specified event order or timing, rather than merely reaching the final state.

We first compare three execution baselines.
All three use the same pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) , source data, and evaluation protocol.
The first is the standard π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , where a single shared model jointly controls both arms.
The second is MA-VLA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which retains this shared-model setup.
It introduces Arm Shuffle during training to augment arm-role assignments.
The third is an independent-control baseline, which instead deploys a separate π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy for each arm.
Each policy produces actions only for its assigned arm.
These comparisons examine whether arm-role augmentation or independent control improves compositional execution over the standard shared policy.
Despite their different designs, all three baselines show limited generalization to unseen compositions.

Starting from the standard shared-model π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we then investigate three targeted architectural changes: arm-token grouping for arm-specific representations, skill-specific LoRA adapters (SkillLoRA) for skill-conditioned parameters, and arm-wise attention (AWA) for regulating cross-arm information flow.
Individual changes yield modest gains, whereas their combination, AE-VLA , achieves 21.53% generalization success in simulation and 39.00% mean success across five unseen conditions on physical SO101 robots, compared with the strongest baseline means of 5.53% and 10.00%, respectively.
These findings suggest that modest architectural changes can substantially improve arm-wise compositional generalization within a shared policy, building on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s pretrained capabilities.

Our contributions are threefold:

ACG-Bench: a benchmark for systematic evaluation of dual-arm skill recomposition across changes in order, synchronization, and cross-task combinations.

A unified empirical study: comparisons of representative augmentation-based and architectural strategies using a common π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone, source dataset, and execution protocol.

Design insights and AE-VLA: evidence of complementary benefits from skill-conditioned parameters and arm-wise attention, validated through their combined configuration in simulation and on physical robots.

1. ACG-Bench: a benchmark for systematic evaluation of dual-arm skill recomposition across changes in order, synchronization, and cross-task combinations.

2. A unified empirical study: comparisons of representative augmentation-based and architectural strategies using a common π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone, source dataset, and execution protocol.

3. Design insights and AE-VLA: evidence of complementary benefits from skill-conditioned parameters and arm-wise attention, validated through their combined configuration in simulation and on physical robots.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLA models map visual observations and language to robot actions, with recent
systems improving task, scene, and embodiment transfer through large robot
datasets, pretrained representations, and generative action
heads Brohan et al. (2022) ; Zitkovich et al. (2023) ; Team et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2024) ; Black et al. (2024) ; Pertsch et al. (2025) ; Intelligence et al. (2025a) ; Wen et al. (2025) .
Several systems support bimanual control NVIDIA et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2026) ,
and steerable policies study task composition through prompts or
subgoals Intelligence et al. (2026) . We focus on a different source of shift:
the local behaviors remain familiar, but the order or timing of skills across the two
arms changes. We study this shift on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .

Bimanual policies have been studied through joint action prediction,
cross-arm attention, and explicit coordination modules Grotz et al. (2024) ; Chernyadev et al. (2024) ; Lai et al. (2025) ; Glossop et al. (2025) .
ACG asks whether the learned coordination can support relations absent
from training. We test this with shared scene context and restricted
attention between local arm streams.

TwinVLA ( Im et al., 2026 ) represents shared and arm-specific inputs through
twin VLM streams with joint attention, sharing its visual encoder and action
head. SkillVLA ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) uses hierarchical skill decisions,
per-arm action generation, and adaptive communication for cooperative
behaviors. MA-VLA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) studies atomic instruction assignment
and arm-role permutation for compositional generalization.
We study the related ideas of per-arm token groups, skill-specific weights,
and attention access under one training and evaluation setup.
Appendix B.4 details the differences from
the complete prior systems.

Existing benchmarks evaluate generalization over objects, layouts, goals,
visual appearance, task sequences, and skill combinations James et al. (2020) ; Mees et al. (2022) ; Mu et al. (2021) ; Liu et al. (2023) ; Haresh et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) .
Recent bimanual and multi-robot suites expand task and scene
diversity Mu et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Qin et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2026b) .
ACG-Bench controls the low-level skill vocabulary and changes the arm-level
event graph itself. Its constraint-aware metric also rejects executions that
reach the final state through the wrong order or timing, making coordination
structure an explicit evaluation target.

2026-10-06.title: Controllable and Photorealistic Pedestrian Risky Motion Generation for End-to-End Driving Safety Evaluation
2026-10-06.authors: Siyuan Liu , Miao Li , Haibao Yu , Haohong Lin , Qing Zhou , Bingbing Nie , Ding Zhao
2026-10-06.comment: Website at this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving requires sensor-level safety-critical data, since raw observations are directly mapped to future trajectories [ 1 ] . However, high-risk vehicle-pedestrian interactions are rare in real-world driving logs. This motivates synthesizing vehicle-pedestrian conflict scenarios at the sensor-level to evaluate models under realistic deployment conditions [ 2 ] .

Existing approaches for safety-critical scenario generation follow trajectory-based or video-based paradigms. For trajectory-based methods, adversarial [ 3 ] methods often generate unnatural trajectories, and learning-based [ 4 ] methods suffer from data scarcity. Both of them lack multi-view video rendering. In contrast, video-based methods satisfy sensor-level requirements [ 5 , 6 ] , but lack behavioral controllability. Recent technical advances provide new ways to address these challenges. 3DGS converts driving logs into photorealistic scenes [ 7 ] , text-conditioned motion generation models enable fine-grained control [ 8 ] , and animatable avatars facilitate dynamic integration [ 9 ] . However, because existing motion datasets focus on daily tasks [ 10 ] , models trained on them fail to capture safety-critical pedestrian dynamics [ 11 ] . Bridging this gap requires constructing safety-critical pedestrian datasets to train generative models for controllable, photorealistic scene editing and end-to-end algorithms evaluation.

Our key insight is that safety-critical scenario generation requires hierarchical decomposition: macro-level collision paths governed by trajectory control, micro-level actions guided by joint dynamics, and sensor-level inputs realized via photorealistic rendering. To this end, we propose ControlPed, a three-stage framework comprising trajectory generation, motion synthesis, and photorealistic rendering. Trained on 422 real conflict trajectories and 857 hazardous human motion sequences (Fig. 1 a), ControlPed couples a conflict trajectory generator with a text-driven motion diffusion model (Fig. 1 b–c). A hard root constraint guarantees strict alignment between generated motions and target trajectories. Animatable avatars are subsequently composited into 3DGS scenes to render photorealistic camera videos (Fig. 1 d). Finally, these synthesized scenarios serve to evaluate seven end-to-end driving models, closing the loop from conflict synthesis to safety assessment (Fig. 1 e).

This work makes the following key contributions:

HazardPed Dataset: We present HazardPed , a safety-critical dataset that combines real conflict trajectories, HD maps, and human motions. It bridges the scarcity of risky interaction data, providing a prior for controllable pedestrian scenario generation.

ControlPed Generator: We propose ControlPed , a controllable scenario synthesis method that couples trajectory-level conflict generation with text-conditioned motion diffusion. It achieves sensor-level photorealism without sacrificing fine-grained pedestrian control.

Safety Evaluation Benchmark: We establish a photorealistic benchmark to evaluate autonomous driving safety. This benchmark enables third-party testing agencies and regulatory bodies to assess algorithm reliability before real-world deployment.

1. HazardPed Dataset: We present HazardPed , a safety-critical dataset that combines real conflict trajectories, HD maps, and human motions. It bridges the scarcity of risky interaction data, providing a prior for controllable pedestrian scenario generation.

2. ControlPed Generator: We propose ControlPed , a controllable scenario synthesis method that couples trajectory-level conflict generation with text-conditioned motion diffusion. It achieves sensor-level photorealism without sacrificing fine-grained pedestrian control.

3. Safety Evaluation Benchmark: We establish a photorealistic benchmark to evaluate autonomous driving safety. This benchmark enables third-party testing agencies and regulatory bodies to assess algorithm reliability before real-world deployment.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Safety-Critical Scenario Generation

Trajectory-based scenario generators synthesize hazardous interactions via behavior perturbation [ 3 , 12 ] or traffic priors [ 4 ] . However, their 2D bird’s-eye-view representations strip away key pedestrian dynamics essential for vision-based end-to-end models. Conversely, video-based approaches introduce sensor-level realism via asset insertion or pose-guided editing [ 5 , 6 ] , yet lack fine-grained trajectory or human control. Asset insertion struggles to enforce precise terminal collision states, while 2D pose editing lacks metric grounding, preventing control over real-world vehicle–pedestrian distances. Consequently, achieving joint controllability over macro trajectories and micro pedestrian motions in photorealistic rendering remains an open challenge.

## II-B Human Motion Generation and Datasets

Text-conditioned human motion generation models, built on diffusion architectures [ 8 , 11 ] , synthesize diverse motions from language but lack spatial grounding to specify coordinate dynamics. Although recent spatial control techniques incorporate trajectory or sparse joint constraints [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , their applicability remains bounded by the underlying training data. Standard motion benchmarks built on AMASS, HumanML3D, and BABEL focus almost exclusively on daily activities [ 16 ] . Consequently, critical conflict dynamics, such as abrupt dodging or freezing under imminent vehicle threat, remain remarkably scarce, hindering the generation of safety-critical scenarios.

## II-C Scenario Reconstruction and End-to-End Evaluation

3DGS enables photorealistic rendering and has been widely adopted in driving scenario reconstruction [ 17 ] . To handle dynamic objects, recent approaches decouple foreground actors from background modeling, allowing moving entities to be controlled independently [ 7 ] . Advances in pose-driven animatable avatars further free pedestrians from rigid log replaying, enabling the insertion of hazardous human behaviors into reconstructed scenes. For safety evaluation, existing paradigms face clear trade-offs: open-loop tests on passive logs lack reactivity, simulators exhibit a pronounced sim-to-real gap. Recently, reconstruction-based closed-loop simulations combine realism with interactivity by evaluating models on rendered real-world scenes [ 2 ] , yet they lack critical pedestrian-involved hazards. Therefore, injecting controllable pedestrian behaviors into photorealistic reconstructed scenes is essential for end-to-end safety evaluation.

2026-10-06.title: Talk, Render, Act: Integrating Social Gesture and Digital Face with Synchronized Speech for Conversational Humanoid Robot
2026-10-06.authors: Jin Jiang , Kun Li , Jiancong Ma , Shengcai Liao
2026-10-06.abstract: Expressive humanoid interaction requires speech, facial animation, and body gestures to form a coherent response. However, many full-body humanoid robots produce speech and gestures without a visually expressive face, while talking-face animation and robot gesture generation are typically developed separately. We present Talk, Render, Act (TRABot), an agent-based framework comprising specialized agents for motion-atom construction, dialogue generation, motion planning, and facial animation. First, to produce natural and semantically meaningful gestures, we construct Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms by segmenting long-form, G1-retargeted BEAT2 motion into units with natural gesture boundaries, human-verified communicative functions, and feasible trajectories. Second, to preserve semantic order and coordinate body motion with the spoken response, we introduce a Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner. Given an ordered semantic function sequence and an estimated response duration, the planner selects approved atoms to realize the longest feasible action sequence while accounting for transitions and neutral recovery. Finally, we deploy a Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration system on a physical G1 humanoid, combining streaming dialogue audio, audio-driven facial animation, and semantically planned body motion in a unified real-time interaction loop. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that TRAbot achieves the best overall performance among all compared conditions in terms of naturalness, expressiveness, and multimodal coherence.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Human face-to-face communication relies on the coordination of verbal and nonverbal behaviors. Speech conveys linguistic content, whereas facial movements and body gestures provide complementary cues for affective expression, emphasis, and deictic reference [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Consequently, expressive humanoid interaction requires speech, facial animation, and body motion to be coordinated semantically and temporally [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

Recent advances have substantially improved the individual components of embodied interaction. Speech-driven talking-face models generate articulatory and expressive facial motion from audio [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Social robots such as Furhat and Haru combine dialogue with expressive facial displays, gaze, or platform-specific physical behaviors [ 12 , 13 , 4 ] . These systems demonstrate the value of facial embodiment, but they do not provide the expressive motion of a full-body humanoid. Conversely, co-speech gesture methods generate semantically or rhythmically appropriate body motion for virtual agents and robots [ 2 , 6 ] . Recent work further enables streaming, semantically aligned gestures on physical humanoids [ 14 ] , but focuses on speech and body motion without a continuously animated talking face. Holistic animation methods jointly model facial and bodily behavior for digital humans, including real-time interactive generation [ 15 , 5 , 16 ] . Such systems operate in a shared virtual representation and do not address robot-specific motion feasibility or state-dependent execution. Taken together, these approaches leave the coordination of streaming speech, an audio-driven digital face, and semantically planned humanoid motion within a unified conversational system insufficiently explored.

A direct combination of existing components does not fully resolve this problem because facial and bodily behaviors involve different representations and time scales. Facial animation can be generated frame by frame from streaming audio. Humanoid body motion must instead be organized into semantically meaningful actions, validated for the target embodiment, connected from the current robot state, and composed within the duration of a spoken response. Dialogue generation operates at the level of communicative intent and reply duration, whereas motion execution requires concrete trajectories that satisfy these constraints. These differences motivate an agent-based architecture in which each agent performs a distinct generation or decision process and communicates through explicit semantic and temporal variables.

We present Talk, Render, Act (TRABot), an agent-based framework comprising one offline agent and three online agents. The offline Motion Atom Construction Agent transforms long-form, G1-retargeted BEAT2 motion [ 17 ] into Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms with natural gesture boundaries, human-verified communicative functions, and feasible trajectories. The resulting atoms provide inspectable and reusable robot actions while establishing a semantic interface between dialogue generation and motion planning.

During interaction, the Dialogue Agent generates a spoken reply together with an ordered function sequence and an estimated response duration. The Motion Planning Agent implements our Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner, which selects approved atoms to realize the longest feasible action sequence within the available response duration while accounting for transitions and neutral recovery. A state-aware executor recomputes each transition from the robot state reached during execution. In parallel, the Facial Animation Agent generates facial motion from the same streaming audio used for speech playback. The Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration system executes the resulting speech, facial animation, and body motion concurrently within a unified real-time interaction loop. This organization preserves the modality-specific processing required by facial rendering and robot execution while coordinating all three modalities through a shared spoken response.

The main contributions of this work are threefold.

We construct Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms by segmenting long-form, G1-retargeted BEAT2 motion into units with natural gesture boundaries, human-verified communicative functions, and feasible trajectories.

We introduce a Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner that maps an ordered function sequence and a response-duration estimate to the longest feasible action sequence while accounting for transitions, neutral recovery, and the current robot state.

We develop a Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration System that coordinates dialogue audio, audio-driven facial animation, and semantically planned humanoid motion through specialized agents in a unified real-time interaction loop.

1. We construct Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms by segmenting long-form, G1-retargeted BEAT2 motion into units with natural gesture boundaries, human-verified communicative functions, and feasible trajectories.

2. We introduce a Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner that maps an ordered function sequence and a response-duration estimate to the longest feasible action sequence while accounting for transitions, neutral recovery, and the current robot state.

3. We develop a Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration System that coordinates dialogue audio, audio-driven facial animation, and semantically planned humanoid motion through specialized agents in a unified real-time interaction loop.
