2026-10-06.title: Mulligan: Performance-Guided Data Collection for Efficient On-Robot Learning
2026-10-06.authors: Lars Ankile , Perry Dong , Rohan Bhowmik , Aneesh Muppidi , David D. Yuan , Shuran Song , Chelsea Finn
2026-10-06.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Learning from human demonstrations is a reliable way to teach robots new tasks, but the gains from each additional demonstration shrink as the policy improves. Continued improvement can instead come from supervised deployment, where an operator places the objects and intervenes when the policy fails.
We ask how to maximize improvement from a fixed budget of supervised episodes on high-precision manipulation tasks with wide ranges of object placements.
We observe that failures can concentrate in a small subset of initial states, so uniform collection spends much of the operator’s time on states the policy already handles. Mulligan makes the initial-state distribution a decision, starting each round’s episodes at observed failures and untried states. To further improve data efficiency, we augment interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all data, including failures that imitation discards.
Across three real-world tasks evaluated on 2,550 held-out, blinded episodes and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched collection budgets, and combined with value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+ Mulligan , improves final real-task success by 10–34 percentage points. With operator interventions, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes, remaining productive while the policy learns. Videos, code, and data are available at https://mulligan.page/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Human demonstrations are a popular starting point for teaching a robot a new manipulation task [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , but the returns on additional demonstrations often diminish as success rate improves, especially for tasks requiring high precision [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
A common next step is to collect corrections with a human in the loop (HiL), where an operator places the objects for each episode, takes control when the policy goes off track, and the corrections join the training set [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Recent systems show this reliably achieves high success rates on physical hardware [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , but every episode still costs operator time.
The cost is easier to bear in supervised deployment, where an operator already oversees the robot on real tasks and its rollouts arrive as a byproduct.
We study the batch-online form of this loop [ 17 ] , which retrains the policy only between rounds, and ask how to get the most improvement out of each supervised episode.

Several lines of work address parts of this question.
Interactive imitation learning trains any policy class by behavior cloning (BC) on the corrections but cannot learn from the failed rollouts that deployment yields as a byproduct [ 13 , 14 ] .
Real-world RL learns from every rollout, failures included, through a value function, but gathers those rollouts by exploring online on the hardware [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] and has shown its best results under narrow initial-state distributions [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] (ranges in Sec. K.3 ). In simulation, its learner [ 18 ] fails when the range widens, and human interventions [ 20 ] do not recover it ( Fig. 2 ).
Batch-online systems [ 17 ] combine corrections with a value function, training it on deployed rollouts as well, with a policy updated only between rounds and on the wide initial-state distributions of real deployment [ 15 , 16 ] .
The lines differ in policy class and learning update.
Recent work scales corrections and RL to vision-language-action (VLA) policies rather than asking how much improvement each supervised episode can provide.

Our key observation is that failures are often unevenly distributed across the initial-state space. E.g., in Mulligan : Performance-Guided Data Collection for Efficient On-Robot Learning (middle), 95% of a policy’s failures fall in 25% of the initial states even though its overall success rate is 86%.
Raising the success rate means correcting those failures where they happen.
Under uniform collection, the policy makes fewer mistakes as it improves, and the operator becomes increasingly passive.
Yet the operator who decides when to intervene also places the objects, so the initial-state distribution is a decision rather than a fixed part of the task, and can be made deliberately.
The choice is independent of the policy class and learning update, so it combines with any of the methods above.
The question is how to find those states without exhaustive search.

Mulligan finds them with the outcomes each round already produces, deciding which initial states the next round visits and what the operator records there ( Mulligan : Performance-Guided Data Collection for Efficient On-Robot Learning , right, and Sec. 3.1 ). The first round covers the initial-state space evenly and yields the first evidence of where the policy fails. Each later round balances retrying the initial states where the previous one failed with exploring the rest of the space for new failures. At a retried initial state, a correction begins where the policy went off track, so when the mistake is big, it teaches only recovery. Instead, the operator can record a full demonstration from the same initial state, a counterfactual demonstration that places the missing behavior in the policy’s support. Mulligan only decides what each round collects, so we evaluate it with two learners, imitation alone and imitation with a value function trained on all rollouts, failures included, that selects among the policy’s actions ( Sec. 3.2 ).

Our main contribution is Mulligan , a data-collection strategy for batch-online imitation and reinforcement learning that selects each round’s initial states from the policy’s observed performance and yields more improvement from the same supervised budget.
Across three real-world tasks ( Fig. 3 ), evaluated on 2,550 held-out, blinded episodes, and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched supervised collection budgets.
Combined with value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+ Mulligan improves final-round success on the real tasks by 10–34 percentage points over HG-DAgger [ 12 ] and completes more tasks per robot minute ( Sec. 4 ).
With an operator intervening, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes with no round below 90%, so learning does not come at the cost of task completion.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

We build on interactive imitation learning, which collects human corrections under the policy’s own state distribution and provides recovery supervision where the policy drifts [ 11 , 12 ] . This line has studied when the human should intervene, by expert judgment [ 12 ] or estimated uncertainty [ 28 , 29 ] , and has scaled collection to long-horizon bimanual manipulation with expressive policies [ 7 , 13 , 14 ] . Interventions also carry implicit reward signal [ 30 ] , and a second family combines human-in-the-loop collection with RL: RLIF [ 23 ] derives rewards from intervention signals, HiL-SERL [ 20 ] learns from corrections via RLPD [ 18 ] , and ConRFT [ 22 ] and EXPO-FT [ 19 , 24 ] extend this to finetuning VLAs. We similarly learn from the robot’s own rollouts as well as the corrections, but update the policy between rounds rather than online. Closest to our setting are RECAP [ 15 ] and LWD [ 16 ] , which improve VLAs over rounds of supervised deployment at scale. These recipes focus on the learning update, e.g., advantage-conditioned training on accumulated experience in RECAP. Mulligan instead decides where each round’s episodes begin and leaves the learning update unchanged. We evaluate it with imitation alone and with a value function trained on all rollouts, and it could be combined with either recipe.

Reinforcement learning has trained policies on physical robots since early policy search over motor skills [ 31 , 32 ] and end-to-end visuomotor learning from pixels [ 33 , 34 ] , and recent systems make on-robot training sample efficient [ 21 , 24 , 25 , 35 , 36 ] . These systems report their best results under centimeter-scale initial-state randomization [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] (ranges in Sec. K.3 ), where a few episodes reach every initial state. We study ranges wide enough that a round’s budget covers only part of the space, so the choice of where to start decides which states the operator supervises. A related line improves robots from their own experience in batches, without a human in the loop [ 37 , 38 , 39 ] , and Dong et al. [17] show that a Q-function with best-of- N N extraction improves policies in autonomous batch-online interaction. We adopt their value-learning and extraction design, since best-of- N N improves a generative policy without backpropagating through its sampling chain ( Sec. K.2 ), and add the operator’s corrections and counterfactual demonstrations to the value function’s training data. App. K extends this discussion to real-world RL systems and to RL finetuning of expressive policies.

Where episodes begin has been a design choice in RL since restart distributions were used to direct policy improvement [ 40 ] . Curricula move initial states toward intermediate difficulty, expanding outward from the goal [ 41 ] , generating goals of suitable difficulty [ 42 ] , resetting to states along demonstrations [ 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 ] or a guide policy’s rollouts [ 48 ] , or returning to stored states and replaying the levels with the highest learning potential alongside fresh ones [ 49 , 50 ] . Narvekar et al. [51] and Portelas et al. [52] survey the area. Hard-example mining concentrates training on what a model gets wrong within a fixed dataset [ 53 ] . For real robots, recent work chooses what to collect by which environmental factors to vary [ 54 ] , which failure conditions a model predicts [ 55 ] , where the policy is uncertain [ 56 ] , which failure states its executions reveal [ 57 , 58 ] , which perturbations to apply during a demonstration [ 59 ] , or in what order a human demonstrates [ 60 ] . Mulligan moves the initial-state choice to a supervised deployment, where the operator places each initial state, and mixes retried and fresh states as prioritized level replay does. Because the operator can complete the task from any state, collection is not limited to a band of intermediate difficulty and can go to the hardest states found so far, where a counterfactual demonstration records the missing behavior within the same round.

2026-10-06.title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collision-Free Locomotion of an Underactuated Biped
2026-10-06.authors: Jagannath Prasad Sahoo , Saurabh Kumar , Surya Prakash S.K. , Samiran Datta , Abhay Dwivedi , Amit Shukla
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-06.abstract:
A bipedal robot cannot deviate from its path to avoid an obstacle
without disturbing its balance, and this coupling is most severe on
underactuated platforms such as the biped considered here, which has
four actuated joints per leg and no hip or ankle roll. This paper presents
a Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) framework in which a
High-Level (HL) policy observes the robot pose, 36 raycast proximity
measurements, moving-obstacle states, and a receding-horizon local
goal, and outputs a body-velocity command ( v x , v y , ω yaw ) (v_{x},v_{y},\omega_{\text{yaw}}) every ten control steps, while a
velocity-conditioned Low-Level (LL) policy tracks each command
through PD-controlled joint targets. Both policies are trained
jointly with Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). Because the converged gait is
task-agnostic, it is frozen and driven by classical planners over the
same command interface, yielding three controlled baselines,
SAC+A ⋆ , SAC+RRT ⋆ , and SAC+APF. Across 100 evaluation
trials per method in randomized PyBullet environments, the proposed
method reaches the goal in 98.0% of static and 88.0% of dynamic
trials, against at most 78.0% and 68.0% for the planner hybrids,
with path lengths within 4% of the A ⋆ reference, and
ablations confirm that each observation channel and reward term
contributes materially to this performance. This present project information and videos are available at HRL-Biped .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Obstacle-aware walking remains an open problem for three compounding
reasons. A biped is underactuated, so its floating base cannot be
commanded directly and every avoidance maneuver perturbs balance.
Its velocity set is gait-limited and asymmetric, since a biped
needs several steps to change speed or heading, and on our platform
the absence of roll joints further restricts lateral motion. Moving
obstacles demand anticipation, since by the time proximity alone
signals danger a walking robot may no longer have time to step
aside.

Existing approaches occupy two extremes (Fig. 1 ).
Flat end-to-end RL policies map observations directly to joint
targets [ 1 ] , train slowly, generalize poorly to unseen
layouts, and must relearn locomotion whenever the task changes.
Decoupled pipelines instead track a geometrically planned path with
an independent gait controller [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] ,
ignoring balance coupling and, for global planners, moving
obstacles. Neither extreme addresses all three difficulties at
once, which motivates separating navigation from gait generation
without severing the feedback between them.

Given an underactuated biped with eight actuated leg joints, a
known static occupancy map, and moving obstacles whose trajectories
are unknown in advance, the controller must reach a goal at least
6.0 m away without collision or fall, sensing static geometry
through proximity measurements and moving obstacles through their
relative position and velocity, while generating joint-level
actions at 50 Hz.

We solve this with a two-level hierarchy in which both levels are
learned and trained jointly. A lightweight planning layer computes
a global path on the known static map and extracts a
receding-horizon local goal. The high-level (HL) policy decides
where to go next, emitting a body-velocity command 𝐮 = ( v x , v y , ω yaw ) \mathbf{u}=(v_{x},v_{y},\omega_{\text{yaw}}) from the robot pose,
raycast distances, moving-obstacle states, and the local goal. The
low-level (LL) policy decides how to walk, converting each command
into leg-joint targets and executing it for H = 10 H=10 consecutive
control steps before the HL policy is queried again. This
abstraction shortens the effective navigation horizon tenfold, and
joint training lets the gait adapt to the command distribution the
navigation layer actually issues. Because the converged LL policy
is a pure velocity-conditioned gait skill, it can be frozen and
driven by classical planners over the same interface, which we
exploit to build three controlled baselines, SAC+A ⋆ ,
SAC+RRT ⋆ , and SAC+APF, in which only the command generator
differs.

The contributions of this work are as follows.

A jointly trained two-level HRL framework in which an HL SAC
policy outputs body-velocity commands from pose, raycast,
dynamic-obstacle, and local-goal observations, and a
velocity-conditioned LL SAC policy executes each command for ten
control steps.

An HL observation and reward design covering both static
layouts and moving obstacles, including a time-to-collision (TTC)
term inducing anticipatory avoidance.

A controlled benchmark against SAC+A ⋆ ,
SAC+RRT ⋆ , and SAC+APF hybrids driving the identical frozen
gait, isolating the navigation layer’s contribution.

An ablation over HL observation channels and reward
components quantifying their effect on success, collision, and
failure rates.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Obstacle avoidance began with classical planning. Global methods
such as A ⋆ [ 2 ] and
RRT ⋆ [ 3 ] compute near-optimal paths on a
known map, and reactive methods such as artificial potential
fields [ 4 ] and the dynamic window
approach [ 5 ] respond to sensed obstacles online. These
assume a base that executes commanded velocities faithfully, the
reactive ones suffer local minima and oscillation, and applied to a
biped they decouple avoidance from balance. CLF-CBF quadratic
programs [ 6 ] restore real-time safety guarantees
but still treat the gait as a separate tracking problem.

Reinforcement learning then removed the need for hand-designed
reactive rules, maturing first on wheeled robots for mapless
navigation [ 7 ] , goal-driven
exploration [ 8 ] , and crowd
navigation [ 9 ] . In parallel, model-free RL
produced robust legged locomotion, including periodic-reward gaits
on Cassie [ 10 ] , transformer-based humanoid
locomotion [ 11 ] , footstep-conditioned
walking [ 12 ] , and massively parallel training for
quadrupeds [ 13 , 14 ] . In our own prior work we
trained multi-skill locomotion for the same underactuated platform
using waypoint-based reward shaping [ 15 ] . The two
lines rarely meet: navigation policies assume a statically stable
base, locomotion policies do not avoid obstacles, and the one
flat-RL attempt at bipedal avoidance [ 1 ] is limited to
fixed, known obstacle positions.

Hierarchical RL bridges the two. Temporal abstraction via
options [ 16 ] and goal-conditioned hierarchies
such as HIRO [ 17 ] showed that a coarse-timescale
high-level policy simplifies long-horizon tasks.
DeepLoco [ 18 ] learned a footstep-level planner
over a stepping controller, hierarchical commands have been used
for quadruped navigation [ 19 ] , and recent
bipedal social navigation adopts a related
decomposition [ 20 ] . Our work targets an underactuated
biped without roll joints, combines raycasts with explicit
dynamic-obstacle states at the HL, trains both levels jointly, and
benchmarks the learned HL against classical planners driving the
identical learned gait, which prior HRL locomotion studies do not.

2026-10-06.title: Dual-Rate Force-Image Control with Model-Based Orientation Limits for Robotic Ultrasound
2026-10-06.authors: Tyler Foster , Qiang Zhang , A B M Tahidul Haque , Anh Thu Nguyen
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-06.comment: gigures, conference
2026-10-06.abstract: Robotic ultrasound couples a high-rate contact-force loop with slower, delayed image feedback, so image-guided ultrasound probe rotation can perturb contact force before the resulting image response is observed. We derive a closed-form orientation-rate limit that bounds the modeled rotation-induced estimated-force excursion over a finite horizon while accounting for disturbance rejection by the fast force loop. The limit depends on local contact stiffness, force-loop gains, a conservative rotation-to-force gain bound, the excursion budget, and the prediction horizon. We implement this model in a dual-rate controller with timestamp-based delay reconstruction and joint-torque-based force estimation, and evaluate it on a curved gelatin phantom using paired controller comparisons and component ablations. Relative to unconstrained image guidance, the proposed rate-limited controller reduced first-second root-mean-square (RMS) estimated-force error by 0.40 N while increasing cue-convergence time by 0.94 s. A fixed rate cap near the analytically predicted ceiling produced no resolvable difference in force error and converged 0.32 s faster, indicating that the principal practical value of the model is the rate-design rule rather than online prediction. Delay reconstruction had no resolvable effect at the tested latency. A single-subject popliteal scan demonstrated feasibility, although the image cue was noise-limited on heterogeneous tissue.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Brightness mode (B-mode) ultrasound provides real-time, radiation-free imaging at comparatively low cost, but its image quality depends strongly on how the probe interacts with tissue. A sonographer continuously coordinates probe position, orientation, and contact force while responding to surface geometry, tissue compliance, and the image itself; robotic ultrasound is therefore a coupled sensing-and-control problem rather than a trajectory-following task. Reviews accordingly identify scan-path generation, probe–tissue force regulation, and image-quality or orientation optimization as the central components of autonomous systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and recent surveys [ 4 , 5 ] note open gaps, among them that orientation-related interaction forces are often simplified and that real-time image feedback is still rarely integrated into online scan optimization [ 5 ] .

Image features extracted directly from ultrasound can close the robot-positioning loop [ 6 ] , and visual servoing on ultrasound confidence has been used to improve image quality through probe orientation [ 7 ] .
Interaction-force information [ 8 , 9 ] and probe-mounted distance sensing [ 10 ] have been used to estimate the local surface normal and regulate orientation, explicit force/moment control improves interaction under heterogeneous contact [ 11 ] , ultrasound feedback has enabled autonomous screening of tubular structures [ 12 ] , and image-quality estimates have been used to adapt the commanded force [ 13 , 14 ] . Image and force sensing are therefore established as complementary. Learning-based methods have extended autonomy to navigation, compliant scanning, and complete clinical workflows [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , including policies trained under explicit force constraints [ 18 ] ; this work instead keeps a physically structured force loop and uses the image only as a measured cue.

A control issue that is less explicitly addressed is the multirate dynamic coupling between force regulation and image-guided probe correction. Robot state and wrench estimates update at high rates, whereas B-mode images are acquired, transferred, and processed at much lower rates and with non-negligible latency. The difficulty is more fundamental than asynchronous sensing alone, because the two loops are coupled through the contact. An orientation correction computed from an image changes probe indentation, the contact moment, and consequently the normal force before a new image becomes available. Conversely, a fast force regulator reacts to the normal displacement induced by the orientation update and can partially oppose the intended correction. Dual-loop approaches have demonstrated image-dependent force adaptation and robust force tracking [ 14 ] , Li et al. [ 19 ] incorporate trajectory-dependent feedforward and delay compensation for contact-force tracking, and Qian et al. [ 20 ] combine image guidance with biomechanics-informed force measurement. These approaches do not treat the image-guided orientation loop and the high-rate force loop as a delayed multirate system whose cross-coupling is predicted and used in the controller.

This paper treats that coupling as the control problem. We propose a dual-rate orientation controller in which the slow image-guided loop accounts for both its own latency and its effect on the fast contact loop: the image cue is reconstructed to the present instant from the frame’s capture timestamp; the force excursion that a candidate correction would produce is predicted from a conservative bound on the rotation-to-force gain; and the prediction credits the fast loop with the portion of that excursion it will reject within the prediction horizon. This credit separates the method from a one-step safety filter, which must assume the excursion persists and therefore admits a lower rotation rate. While the correction demand is saturated, the constraint reduces to a ceiling on the rotation rate that depends only on the contact stiffness, the force-loop gains, the gain bound, the force budget, and the prediction horizon, so it can be evaluated before image-guided correction begins, once the local stiffness and a valid upper bound on rotation-to-force gain have been established.
The platform has no force/torque sensor ; contact force is estimated from joint torques. This raises the force noise floor and introduces model-dependent bias, so the force margins the controller must respect are small relative to the estimate’s error. The contributions are:

a closed-form design rule for the maximum image-guided orientation rate that limits the modeled rotation-induced force excursion over a finite horizon while accounting for force-loop rejection;

a closed-form design rule for the maximum image-guided orientation rate that limits the modeled rotation-induced force excursion over a finite horizon while accounting for force-loop rejection;

a paired hardware evaluation on a curved phantom against force-only, newest-frame, and fixed-rate-cap baselines, with ablations isolating the constraint, the fast-loop credit, delay reconstruction, and online sensitivity estimation, showing that the ceiling sets the trade-off between cue-convergence time and force error, and that a fixed cap near the predicted rate matches the online constraint in force error; and

a single-subject popliteal scan testing feasibility on living tissue.

2026-10-06.title: Transporting Unsecured Stacked Payloads with a Quadrupedal Robot via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-06.authors: Nobuo Namura , Masayuki Hiromoto , Kento Uemura , Hironobu Sasaki , Kanata Suzuki
2026-10-06.abstract:
Transporting unsecured payloads with legged robots over uneven terrain requires balancing locomotion performance and payload stability, since aggressive motion can destabilize the payload even when the robot remains stable.
We study quadrupedal transportation of unsecured stacked boxes on an edgeless torso-mounted board without dedicated payload sensors or active carrier mechanisms.
To address this trade-off, we propose Payload-Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement learning for Transportation (PAMORT).
PAMORT trains a multi-objective base policy conditioned on a preference vector that weights locomotion and payload-stability reward groups, then trains a weight adjuster on the frozen policy to adapt this preference online from proprioception.
In simulation, PAMORT achieves comparable or better overall transportation success than a corresponding single-objective baseline across different payload configurations, including an unseen three-box stack, despite training only with two boxes.
Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 demonstrate zero-shot transfer to slopes and steps at or beyond the training difficulty, with mean success rates of 0.850 for PAMORT and 0.675 for the baseline across eight tasks.
These results demonstrate robust unsecured-payload transportation with online adaptation of the locomotion–payload trade-off from proprioceptive information.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Recent advances in reinforcement learning have enabled quadrupedal robots to traverse challenging terrain, including stairs, slopes, and rough ground. As locomotion becomes more robust, practical tasks beyond mobility itself are becoming increasingly important. One such task is payload transportation, for which legged robots are particularly attractive in environments where wheeled platforms cannot easily operate.

Conventional robotic transportation often mechanically secures the payload to the robot or constrains it using sidewalls, containers, or other fixtures. Such approaches are effective for reliable transport, but they may require payload-specific fastening, loading, and unloading procedures or dedicated carrier structures. In applications such as warehouses or construction sites, however, it can be useful to temporarily transport boxes, tools, or materials without securing each item individually. Rather than replacing mechanically secured transportation, this work aims to complement it with a more flexible capability that does not rely on payload-specific fixation. We therefore consider the task shown in Fig. 1 , where a quadruped carries unsecured stacked boxes on a flat carrier while traversing uneven terrain.

Transporting unsecured payloads introduces challenges beyond locomotion with rigidly attached loads. Even when the robot itself remains stable, acceleration, body motion, and terrain-induced impacts can cause the payloads to slide, become misaligned, or fall. Payload stabilization therefore requires state-dependent whole-body motions and cannot, in general, be reduced to simply keeping the torso level. Designing such coupled behaviors manually is difficult, making reinforcement learning well suited to this problem. At the same time, the task exhibits an inherent trade-off between locomotion performance and payload stability. Aggressive velocity tracking can increase payload motion, whereas prioritizing payload stability can lead to overly conservative locomotion and reduced traversal performance.

To address this trade-off, we propose Payload-Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement learning for Transportation (PAMORT), a framework that adapts the balance between locomotion performance and payload stability online. PAMORT builds on TAR [ 1 ] , a learning-based locomotion framework using privileged teacher representations and a proprioceptive student encoder for terrain adaptation. We extend TAR to a multi-objective (MO) base policy that separates the reward into move and payload groups and conditions a single policy on their objective weights, enabling behaviors from conservative payload preservation to aggressive locomotion. A weight adjuster is then trained on the frozen MO base policy to adapt these weights online from the robot state. PAMORT therefore adjusts the locomotion–payload trade-off without dedicated payload sensors, manipulators, or active carrier mechanisms. We also introduce a preference-aware terrain curriculum to facilitate learning across different objective balances.

In simulation, the MO base policy represents different move – payload trade-offs within a single policy, and PAMORT achieves higher overall transportation success than the task-adapted TAR baseline (TAR*) across diverse uneven terrains. Its advantage is also retained when the number of payloads differs from the two-payload training configuration. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 further demonstrate that unsecured stacked payloads can be transported over uneven terrain, while preserving the performance advantage of PAMORT observed in simulation.

The main contributions of this work are:

We study uneven-terrain transportation of unsecured stacked payloads and demonstrate that the task can be performed using only the quadruped’s standard proprioceptive sensing and leg degrees of freedom, without dedicated payload sensors, manipulators, or active carrier mechanisms.

We propose PAMORT, a payload-adaptive multi-objective reinforcement learning framework that combines a preference-conditioned MO base policy with an online weight adjuster to explicitly manage the trade-off between locomotion performance and payload stability, supported by a preference-aware terrain curriculum for effective training across the preference space.

Through simulation and real-world experiments, we show that PAMORT represents multiple locomotion–payload trade-offs within a single policy and improves transportation performance over the TAR* baseline while generalizing to payload configurations different from those used during training.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Payload Transportation with Legged Robots

Many studies on payload transportation with legged robots assume that the payload is rigidly attached to the robot or mechanically constrained using carriers, containers, or high-friction interfaces [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . In these settings, the main challenge is typically to maintain robust locomotion under changes in total mass, center of mass, or inertial properties. Mechanical constraint is effective for reliable transportation, although it may require payload-specific fastening, loading procedures, or dedicated carrier structures.

Other works have considered unsecured or dynamically moving payloads. Ball-on-plate stabilization has been studied with legged robots [ 7 ] , while quadruped-mounted manipulators have been used for active payload stabilization [ 8 ] . LocoTouch [ 9 ] uses tactile sensing to directly observe payload–carrier interaction during locomotion. Dynamic loads moving inside containers have also been investigated [ 5 , 6 ] , and SteadyTray considers stabilization of objects carried by a humanoid robot [ 10 ] . These studies show that unstable payloads can be handled through mechanical constraint, direct sensing, or additional actuation.

Compared with a single unsecured object, stacked payloads introduce not only motion relative to the carrier but also inter-payload displacement and toppling, making them a compact but challenging case of unsecured transportation. However, uneven-terrain transportation of such payloads by a quadruped without dedicated payload sensing or additional stabilization hardware remains underexplored. Our work focuses on this setting using only standard proprioception and leg actuation.

## II-B Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning

Conventional reinforcement learning typically combines multiple criteria into a single scalar reward using fixed weights and optimizes a policy for one predefined objective balance. Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), in contrast, explicitly represents multiple objectives and their trade-offs, and has been studied through approaches such as learning sets of Pareto-optimal policies [ 11 , 12 ] .

Preference-conditioned MORL instead incorporates an objective-weight or preference vector into a single policy, allowing different trade-offs to be selected after training by varying the preference input [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . This formulation is particularly attractive for robot control, where priorities such as speed, stability, safety, and energy efficiency may conflict and change with the operating condition. Related conditioning schemes have also been explored in continuous control and locomotion to generate diverse behaviors from a single policy [ 16 , 17 ] .

More recent work has further considered adapting preferences online rather than selecting them manually. AMOR [ 18 ] , for example, learns a high-level policy that dynamically adjusts the objective weights of a frozen preference-conditioned controller for character motion tracking, enabling the behavior to adapt to changing task requirements.

Our work follows this direction but considers unsecured payload transportation, where locomotion performance and payload stability must be balanced under partial observability. The objective weights are adapted online without direct observation of the payload state.

2026-10-06.title: What the Guard Misses, the Robot Executes: Implied Harm in VLA Instructions
2026-10-06.authors: Sripad Karne , Arjun Balaji
2026-10-06.comment: Under review at the SPAIS 2026 workshop (CoRL 2026)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) act on instructions without being able to refuse, so screening
harmful requests falls to monitors. We test whether these monitors catch ordinary robot tasks requested
for harmful reasons, holding the task fixed while varying only how explicitly the intent is
stated. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} completes the task at every level of explicitness, as often as for harmless
controls. Text guards flag nearly every blunt request but
few implied ones: up to 95% of implied-harm runs end with the task done and no flag raised, and up to
90% even after recalibrating on robot instructions. Monitoring the model’s activations does not close
this gap. Linear probes separate harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly in the base
language and vision-language models, but this separation weakens after robot training in two model families, most for implied harm.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Robot foundation models now take open-ended language instructions and act on them in the physical
world [ 14 , 2 ] . Unlike a chat model, the vision-language-action models (VLAs) we study
cannot refuse: they output only actions. Checks on harmful requests therefore sit mostly outside the policy [ 21 ] , for
example in a guard that screens the instruction, a planner or judge above it [ 20 ] , a
filter on its actions, or a monitor that reads its activations. We study two that
act before the robot moves: text guards, which read the instruction, and activation probes, which read
the model’s internal representation of it.

The hardest requests to screen are ordinary acts done for harmful reasons. Turning on a stove is
harmless until the purpose is to burn someone. In language models, safety monitors
catch overtly harmful requests and miss subtler ones [ 11 ] . We ask whether the same
holds when the request drives a robot. We find that the robot ignores the purpose entirely, and the
guards notice it only when it is stated bluntly.

We test two VLAs, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 2 ] and OpenVLA-OFT [ 13 ] , on five kitchen tasks from
LIBERO-Goal [ 15 ] , attaching a harmful reason to each, such as putting cream cheese in a bowl
to make a dog sick. Each reason is phrased three ways: with the harm implied (L1, indirect), stated as fact (L2, direct), or announced outright (L3, blunt). Each is paired with a harmless control of similar length.
The task never changes; only the wording does. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} completes the task at every level as often
as it does for the controls. OFT seems safer, but it is not: it fails every request that includes a reason, harmful
or not, because it cannot handle the extra sentence. Neither robot responds to the harm, so any check has to come from outside the policy, such as a text
guard that screens the instruction.

Looking at the text guards Llama Guard 3, WildGuard and Qwen3Guard, we find they respond to wording,
not harm. They catch nearly every blunt request but few indirect or direct ones, even though human
annotators recognize the intent in most of them. When the harm is only implied, up to 95% of harmful runs end with the task done and no
flag raised. Inside the model, the harm signal appears to weaken with robot training. A linear probe separates harmful from harmless
instructions almost perfectly in the base language and vision-language models, but loses much of this
after robot training, most of all when the harm is only implied. We make three contributions:

A controlled intent test for VLAs. The act, objects and scene stay fixed while only the
stated purpose and its explicitness vary, and guards and probes run on the same instructions.

What the guard misses, the robot executes. As when monitoring chat models, guards catch
mostly blunt harm, and the robot carries out the harmful requests they miss.

Robot training erodes the harm signal. In two model families, harmful intent is easy to read from the model before robot training and harder after it, extending the known loss of
vision-language knowledge in VLAs [ 8 ] to safety-relevant content.

2. What the guard misses, the robot executes. As when monitoring chat models, guards catch

2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

ASIMOV [ 22 ] tests whether models
judge robot scenarios as safe, without executing them. Closest to us, HazardArena [ 4 ] runs VLAs on matched safe and unsafe tasks with the same motor act and finds they execute both. There, the harm comes from what an object is used for; in ours, it comes only from the stated reason.

Off-the-shelf text guards miss most jailbreak prompts against
LLM-based robots [ 17 ] , in part because guards rely on surface
keywords [ 23 ] . In language models, monitors likewise mostly catch requests
whose harm is explicit [ 11 ] . We test whether this gap carries over to robots, where
a missed request is executed.

VLAs are brittle to paraphrased instructions [ 12 ] and can ignore
the instruction altogether [ 5 ] . Robot training also erodes the vision-language knowledge
they inherit [ 8 ] , and probes have so far looked inside VLAs mainly for motion
and state features [ 9 , 3 ] . Less is known about whether harmful intent survives robot training, which determines whether a monitor
reading the VLA’s activations can catch what text guards miss.

2026-10-06.title: Dynamics-Aware Adaptive Corridors with Feasibility-Perturbed Trust-Region SQP for Certified Nonholonomic Motion Planning
2026-10-06.authors: Yang Shi
2026-10-06.abstract: Optimisation-based parking planners usually impose collision constraints only at the time samples, so a vehicle corner can cut an obstacle between samples, and no executable trajectory exists until the solver converges. We present a planner for car-like vehicles with reverse gear in which every iterate of the optimisation phase satisfies the discretised dynamics exactly and keeps the whole vehicle rectangle clear of obstacles between the samples. Each time interval receives one convex corridor that holds all vehicle corners at both ends and is shrunk by a sweep margin bounding how far the corner paths leave their chords. Separating half-planes give the corridors a direction out of obstacles when the initial guess is in collision; later, heading-aligned boxes are grown from the speed, curvature and step of the current iterate and rebuilt after accepted steps. A feasibility-perturbed trust-region sequential quadratic programming method projects each step onto the dynamics by feedback and verifies it exactly; the cost decreases monotonically, and once the corridors stop changing, limit points are Karush–Kuhn–Tucker points of the corridor-constrained problem or violate a constraint qualification. On 820 benchmark cases the planner succeeds in 818 without penetration (797 from the first initial guess), none of the 7103 evaluated optimisation-phase iterates is unusable, and it succeeds in 96.5% of the cases when 99% of the initial guesses intersect an obstacle. Its manoeuvres take 0.7% longer in the median than those of a similarly certified exact-collision baseline. The guarantees hold for the planning model, not for a physical vehicle.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Parking lots, loading bays and narrow passages force a car-like vehicle to plan close to obstacles, often with several changes between forward and reverse gear. Most planners for these scenes work in two stages [ 1 , 2 ] : a search-based front end such as Hybrid A* [ 3 ] finds a coarse path, and a numerical optimal-control back end turns it into a trajectory that respects the vehicle dynamics. The back end discretises time and imposes the collision constraints at the samples. Between two samples a corner of the vehicle moves along an arc that the constraints do not see, and a minimum-time objective drives the trajectory against the obstacles, where such an arc can cut an obstacle vertex. In our benchmark of 820 cases, the exact dual formulation OBCA with a minimum distance of 0.10 m returns 76 trajectories that penetrate an obstacle between samples (Section VI-B ).

The two main families of back ends pay for their collision model in different ways. Exact formulations [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] give nonconvex nonlinear programs whose size grows with the number of obstacles; they hold at the samples only, and an interrupted solve does not in general return an executable trajectory. Corridor formulations [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] replace the obstacles by convex sets around the front-end path and obtain linear constraints, but the sets are built from geometry around a reference that the front end supplies, so the back end inherits the quality of that reference. When we perturb the front-end path so that 99% of the warm starts intersect an obstacle, our re-implementation of a safe-travel-corridor planner, solved by IPOPT, succeeds in 14.1% of the cases (Section VI-H ).

Sequential convex programming (SCP) and trust-region methods, which solve the back end as a sequence of convex subproblems, split according to what their iterates satisfy. Penalty methods such as SCvx [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , applied to parking by Boyali and Thompson [ 13 ] , carry violations of the dynamics and of the constraints until the penalty vanishes. Feasible-set methods such as CFS [ 14 ] keep the iterates feasible at the samples but exclude nonlinear dynamics, and their vehicle version SLiFS [ 15 ] penalises the dynamics again. STO [ 16 ] rebuilds its corridors at every SQP iteration without keeping the iterates feasible, and the anytime optimiser of Chen et al. [ 17 ] repeats complete nonlinear solves until a time limit. Among the planners in Table I , none certifies inter-sample collision avoidance of every iterate while its convex sets change. That property is what a planner needs if it is to be stopped early: the last iterate is then a trajectory the vehicle can execute, not an intermediate point of an optimisation.

We provide this property with two components. DA-ASC builds one convex corridor per interval from the current iterate, holding all four corners of the vehicle rectangle at both ends of the interval, and shrinks it by a sweep margin that bounds how far the RK4 motion can leave the chord. FP-SQP solves a restricted quadratic subproblem inside these corridors, projects the step onto the dynamics by time-varying LQR feedback, verifies the result exactly and accepts it by a trust-region ratio test. Our earlier work used line-search and trust-region SCP with pseudospectral discretisation for longitudinal on-ramp merging [ 18 , 19 ] and for entry trajectories [ 20 ] , with slack variables and ℓ 1 \ell_{1} merit functions and without obstacle geometry; the present planner keeps its iterates feasible instead. The contributions are as follows.

A shared convex corridor per interval with a sweep margin that certifies collision avoidance of the whole vehicle rectangle between the samples, along the motion of each interval, not only of its corners at the samples (Proposition 1 , Corollary 1 ).

Corridors of two kinds: separating-hyperplane (SH) polygons, which give the feasibility-restoration phase (Phase I) a direction out of the obstacles when the warm start is in collision, and heading-aligned DA-ASC boxes for the optimisation phase (Phase II), grown with targets from the speed, curvature and step of the current iterate and rebuilt only after accepted steps, finitely often (Section IV-B , Lemmas 1 and 2 ).

FP-SQP, an adaptation of the feasibility-perturbed trust-region SQP of Wright and Tenny [ 21 ] to corridors that change: every Phase-II iterate satisfies the RK4 dynamics and its interval motions are collision-free, the cost decreases monotonically without a penalty weight, and once the corridors stop changing every limit point is a KKT point of the corridor-constrained problem or violates the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) (Theorem 1 ).

Certified anytime behaviour and linear per-iteration cost: none of the 7103 Phase-II iterates evaluated on 139 cases is unusable, and the subproblem is an optimal-control-structured quadratic program whose cost per iteration grows linearly with the horizon (Sections VI-D and VI-E ).

OBCA-CT, a variant of OBCA that shares one separating hyperplane per interval and adds the sweep margin, which makes the exact dual formulation certifiable between samples and serves as the strongest baseline (Proposition 3 ).

An evaluation on 820 cases against six baselines, all re-implemented with the same front end, vehicle model and independent collision check, including warm starts in collision and a closed-loop simulation that shows how the clearance buffer and an input margin are chosen for execution (Section VI ).

Section II reviews related work, Section III states the problem, Section IV describes the planner, Section V gives its properties, Section VI reports the experiments, and Section VII discusses the limitations.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Collision Formulations and Inter-Sample Safety

Exact collision formulations constrain the full vehicle shape against every nearby obstacle. OBCA [ 4 ] writes the distance between two polytopes through dual variables and makes the constraint smooth; H-OBCA [ 5 ] warm-starts it from Hybrid A* [ 3 ] , and TDR-OBCA [ 23 ] adds temporal and dual-variable warm starts and reformulates the problem. Li and Shao [ 6 ] use a polygon-area test instead. All of these impose the constraint at the samples of the discretised problem, and the number of constraints grows with the number of obstacles. With the step lengths that minimum-time parking produces, a corner can cross an obstacle vertex between two samples: in our benchmark, OBCA with d min = 0.10 d_{\min}=0.10 m returns 76 penetrating trajectories in 820 cases (Section VI-B ).

Three ideas address the gap between samples. Embodied Footprints [ 22 ] enlarge the footprint by buffers that depend on speed and curvature and optimise the buffers with the trajectory; the analysis assumes forward driving and states that reverse driving is symmetric. Allamaa et al. [ 24 ] bound the collocation polynomial of an orthogonal-collocation transcription by a convex envelope, so that point constraints hold along the whole interval. Swept-volume methods [ 25 ] constrain the region swept by the body directly. Our sweep margin belongs to the first group, with a different mechanism: the four corners at both ends of an interval lie in one convex corridor, so the chord of every corner path lies in it as well, and only the arc-to-chord deviation of the RK4 motion remains to be bounded (Proposition 1 ). The margin is a smooth function of the state and the time scale, so the subproblem stays a quadratic program; the same argument applied to one separating hyperplane per interval gives the certified variant OBCA-CT (Proposition 3 ), which we use as the strongest baseline.

## II-B Corridor Construction

Corridor methods replace the obstacles by a convex set around a reference, which turns the collision constraint into linear inequalities. The safe travel corridors of Li et al. [ 7 ] cover the vehicle by two discs, dilate the obstacles by the disc radius, and give each disc centre an axis-aligned box per sample, grown around the front-end path once. LIOM [ 8 ] keeps the disc-and-box model but rebuilds the boxes from each intermediate solution, softening the dynamics by a penalty so that each intermediate problem has only box constraints; in its hardware test, 0.01 m is added to the disc radius to absorb small tracking errors. Liu et al. [ 26 ] combine corridor constraints with parking-slot matching, and TPCKC [ 9 ] adds vertex-to-polytope constraints only for the obstacles that the current solution hits. Schäfer et al. [ 27 ] derive driving corridors from reachable sets on structured roads. STO [ 16 ] , the closest method in structure, grows a polygon around each reference point by GJK-accelerated ellipse shrinking and expansion and rebuilds it at every SQP iteration, including across gear shifts. None of these corridor planners claims that its iterates are usable before convergence.

In robotics, safe flight corridors [ 28 ] , IRIS [ 29 ] and FIRI [ 30 ] build large convex polytopes around ellipsoids; FIRI calls a region manageable when it contains a prescribed seed set, and our Lemma 1 uses the term in that sense. Linear safe corridors [ 31 ] give a quadrotor swarm continuous-time safety through the convex-hull property of Bernstein polynomials, and SFC-constrained SCP has been applied to fixed-wing aircraft [ 32 ] . The SH polygon of Section IV is simpler than these regions: it intersects a heading-aligned box with one supporting half-plane per nearby obstacle and does no ellipsoid inflation. We use it because, when the vehicle overlaps an obstacle, the normal of that half-plane points out of the obstacle, which gives Phase I a descent direction from warm starts that are in collision.

## II-C Sequential Convex Programming and Trust-Region Convergence

Sequential convex programming methods differ in whether their iterates are feasible. SCvx [ 10 , 11 ] relaxes the linearised dynamics by a virtual control with an exact penalty and proves convergence to a stationary point; Luo et al. [ 12 ] identified errors in the original convergence proof and re-established convergence under stricter assumptions, and we refer to SCvx convergence in that form. GuSTO [ 33 , 34 ] updates the trust region and the penalty weight jointly and shows convergence in continuous time, and continuous-time SCvx [ 35 ] enforces path constraints between nodes through an integrated exterior penalty. Boyali and Thompson [ 13 ] applied successive convexification to parking. In all penalty-based methods an iterate may violate the dynamics or the constraints until the penalty vanishes, so interrupting them yields no usable trajectory; our SCvx baseline also needs its penalty weight tuned (Section VI-A ).

Feasible methods keep the constraints satisfied along the way. CFS [ 14 ] solves a sequence of problems on a convex feasible set around the current iterate and converges to a (weak) local optimum, but its assumptions exclude equality constraints and therefore nonlinear dynamics; SLiFS [ 15 ] brings the idea to vehicles with discs and handles the nonlinear dynamics by an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty and a trust region. Sequential convex restriction [ 36 ] keeps racing trajectories feasible by restricting the track to convex polygons. Feasible SQP in nonlinear programming [ 37 , 38 ] tilts the search direction into the feasible set; the feasibility-perturbed trust-region SQP of Wright and Tenny [ 21 , 39 ] instead perturbs each step back to feasibility and proves global convergence under a restriction of the subproblem. We adapt the latter, with Hauser’s projection operator [ 40 ] as the perturbation, and extend its analysis to corridors that change after accepted steps.

“Trust region” also has other meanings in vehicle planning. Chen et al. [ 17 ] use a trust region to select the obstacles that enter the constraints, and their anytime loop repeats complete nonlinear solves until a time limit; Bu et al. [ 41 ] adapt a trust region around local terrain approximations; for spacecraft, Bernardini et al. [ 42 ] make the radius state-dependent. Jaitly et al. [ 43 ] express ellipsoidal corridors as projections of orthogonal trust regions. Among the planners in Table I , none certifies inter-sample collision avoidance of every iterate while its convex sets change.

2026-10-06.title: DASH: A da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid Robots as an Accessible Platform for Surgical Robotics Research
2026-10-06.authors: Sara Wickenhiser , Junrong Zhou , Zekai Liang , Lizzie Peiros , Michael C. Yip
2026-10-06.abstract: Robotic minimally invasive surgery offers well-documented clinical benefits, but the cost and infrastructure requirements of purpose-built platforms limit access in rural and lower-resourced facilities. Recent work has teleoperated general-purpose robots for laparoscopic tasks and in vivo procedures, but relied on handheld instruments coupled through passive linkages rather than native robotic actuation. Instead, we adapt da Vinci Classic and Xi instruments onto general-purpose robots that can integrate in clinical workflows. We present DASH, a da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid platforms, consisting of two types of adapters that require no modification to the instruments themselves. Each adapter is compatible with many robotic platform load capacities, engages the instrument’s native latch, and wirelessly identifies inserted tools to load instrument-specific kinematics and coupling matrices. Teleoperated experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DASH and its benefits for enabling research access to surgical robotic platforms.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Minimally Invasive Surgery (MIS) offers patients smaller incisions, faster recovery times, and lower surgical risk compared to traditional open procedures [ 1 ] . Today, the gold standard for robotic MIS is purpose-built surgical robotic platforms, such as the da Vinci Surgical System, which has been widely adopted across major hospitals worldwide. Although these highly specialized platforms have demonstrated exceptional performance and achieved widespread clinical adoption, most existing operating rooms were designed for manual operation, causing modern robotic platforms to require extra coordination for equipment positioning [ 2 ] . Typical surgical platforms have large physical footprints with dedicated infrastructure requirements [ 3 ] , limiting their accessibility, particularly in resource-constrained settings where an entire suite dedicated to one platform may be infeasible.

The core challenge lies not in the surgical procedure itself, but in the infrastructure required to perform it. Recently, general-purpose robotic platforms have been explored as a potential pathway towards more accessible laparoscopic surgery. Humanoid robots [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] offer unique advanta
ges with their human-like morphology, allowing them to operate within existing surgical infrastructure and workflows. Furthermore, general purpose humanoid robots have recently emerged as viable platforms for laparoscopic surgery [ 7 ] , including teleoperated in vivo procedures [ 8 ] . Together, these studies highlight the potential of general-purpose humanoid systems to broaden access to high-quality surgical care. Beyond surgical settings, humanoid robots have been applied to support patient interaction [ 9 ] , bedside assistance [ 10 ] , and hospital logistics [ 11 ] . Using a versatile platform such as a humanoid robot can reduce the overall infrastructural requirement for robotic surgery, potentially decreasing the need for a dedicated operating suite for robotic surgical platforms. A platform that can contribute across multiple clinical workflows, rather than serving a single purpose, may improve resource utilization while reducing capital, storage, and operational demands, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

Enabling humanoid robots and serial-link platforms to use general surgical robotic end effectors, such as the da Vinci surgical tools, facilitates robotic platforms to have full actuated control over position and orientation of surgical instruments. This integration makes general-purpose robotic platforms more versatile and easier for healthcare systems to incorporate into existing workflows, helping address workforce shortages. This work introduces two separate adapters, one designed for the Classic and one for the Xi da Vinci surgical instruments, allowing these instruments to be transferred from the da Vinci platform onto smaller, more versatile robotic systems.

DASH utilizes the latching mechanism on board the tool itself, wirelessly identifies the inserted tools, adapts to its coupling matrix, and fits on both robotic humanoid and serial-link platforms, distinguishing it from existing surgical adapters. Intraoperative instrument exchange is a routine and important aspect of any surgical operation. Previous adapters, including MOPS [ 12 ] , enable the use of da Vinci surgical tools for research but do not support wireless identification or automatic adaptation for different instruments, nor do they leverage the native latching mechanisms of Classic and Xi tools. In contrast, our platform places particular emphasis on compatibility with humanoid robots, positioning DASH as a step toward a general humanoid surgical assistant that can be deployed in hospitals.

Both DASH adapters support tool interchangeability, allowing multiple surgical instruments to be swapped in and out while preserving the procedural versatility required across different surgical tasks. By decoupling the high precision instruments from the proprietary system, the infrastructure burden of offering robotic minimally invasive surgery is reduced. In this work, our contributions are threefold:

The design and fabrication of separate da Vinci Classic and Xi tool adapters compatible with serial-link and humanoid platforms

A wireless tool-identification pipeline that loads instrument-specific kinematics and calibration on insertion

Extensive quantitative evaluations of DASH have been conducted on a humanoid platform against the previously developed humanoid laparoscopic system [ 8 ] , demonstrating substantial improvements in both operational responsiveness and RCM control precision.

# II Related Works

## II-A Conventional systems for surgical robotics research

The Da Vinci Surgical System drastically advanced MIS, increasing precision, lowering recovery times, reducing surgeon fatigue [ 1 ] , and standardizing readily available MIS tools. The Da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) [ 13 ] is often used in research labs to continue advancing surgical robotics [ 14 ] . The dVRK can perform tasks like cutting [ 15 ] , suturing [ 16 ] [ 17 ] , removing debris [ 18 ] , and cauterizing [ 19 ] . The tools the dVRK uses are readily available, making these tools accessible and standardized. The ease of access motivates the need for adapters such as DASH that enable other robotic platforms to use highly precise surgical equipment.

Johnson & Johnson recently released a more compact surgical platform called OTTAVA [ 20 ] . This surgical platform is integrated to the operating table, making it more compact and transportable. DASH was designed to enable humanoid robots to bring this level of precision to surgical settings, with the added benefit of having potential to be even more versatile than a standalone surgical platform.

## II-B Humanoid robots

Humanoid robots are versatile and have been shown to assist with critical aspects of human medical assessments [ 21 ] . Beyond this, humanoid robots have also been shown to succeed with manual handheld laparoscopic tools in teleoperated in-vivo surgeries [ 8 ] . While impressive, this work can be expanded by replacing the handheld laparoscopic tools with surgical tools that can be controlled completely through actuation, like the da Vinci surgical tools. Additionally, humanoid robots have been used as assistants in a cadaveric sphenoidectomy [ 22 ] .

## II-C Serial-link robots

Serial-link robots such as the Franka Emika Panda robot are used throughout hospitals for various medical tasks including MIS. An example of one such platform is the Mazor X, which was shown to reduce postoperative hospital stays by almost 34% [ 23 ] .

There are many types of laparoscopic MIS tool mounts, enabling robots, like humanoid and serial manipulators, to perform surgical tasks [ 21 ] . Other platforms utilize the tools end-effector to ’swap’ between tool tips rather than changing out the whole instrument [ 24 ] . Few platforms exist that enable the swapping of whole tools, but one such platform is MOPS [ 12 ] . While MOPS enables the swapping of tools, it fails to wirelessly identify which tool is inserted and adapt to its kinematic constraints, a crucial step for seamless operational use.

2026-10-06.title: Bilinear Flow Policy: Distributional Extrapolation for Goal-Conditioned Visuomotor Imitation
2026-10-06.authors: Wonsuhk Jung , Sundhar Vinodh Sangeetha , Chen Xu , Abhishek Gupta , Masha Itkina , Shreyas Kousik , Haruki Nishimura
2026-10-06.abstract:
Goal-conditioned imitation learning (GCIL) with flow matching is a promising framework that can represent multimodal behaviors while adapting to diverse, user-specified goals, yet often fails when goals lie outside the demonstration support.
To extrapolate to such unseen goals without collapsing multimodality—a problem we call distributional extrapolation —we introduce Bilinear Flow Policy ( BFP ),
a generative visuomotor policy that combines transductive retrieval with a bilinear conditional flow.
Given an unseen observation-goal pair, BFP retrieves an “anchor” training example and transductively reformulates the unseen pair as this familiar anchor plus a residual term.
For this decomposition to guide action prediction, the residual must compactly encode how the current observation-goal pair differs from the anchor, and the anchor must be chosen so that this difference is predictive of the corresponding action distribution.
BFP achieves this with pretrained visual features and a novel learned anchor-selection algorithm.
The novel bilinear flow then models how the anchor and the residual jointly determine the multimodal action distribution. We prove that, for bilinear flow under suitable assumptions, action distribution error at unseen goals is bounded by the in-distribution flow-matching error up to problem-dependent factors.
Across five manipulation tasks in simulation, BFP achieves 2.63 × 2.63\times the out-of-distribution success rate of a
GCIL policy and 1.36 × 1.36\times that of the strongest extrapolation-targeted baseline.
On two real-world tasks, BFP improves over GCIL by 32 % 32\% .
Finally, our theory yields practical, pre-deployment diagnostics for predicting which trained policies will extrapolate well and to which unseen goals.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Goal-conditioned imitation learning (GCIL) is a promising framework to learn versatile visuomotor behavior: a single policy can adapt to diverse, user-specified goals at deployment ( Ding et al., 2019 ; Park et al., 2025 ) .
Conditional flow matching further makes this framework expressive by modeling multimodal distributions of actions, allowing the policy to represent multiple behavior modes to achieve the same goal ( Reuss et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2024 ) .
Nevertheless, deployment may require the policy to act toward unseen goals, where it encounters observation–goal pairs not seen during training.
Standard GCIL policies, including generative variants, can become unreliable on such unseen inputs ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Urain et al., 2024 ) .
This motivates distributional extrapolation : extending goal-conditioned behavior to unseen goals while preserving multimodality.

One natural route to extrapolation is to identify how behavior should change as the policy input (i.e., current observation and goal) changes, then reuse the same rule to infer behavior for a new input by comparing it with a training example ( Ousherovitch & Wang, 2026 ) .
When this relation is known, it can be encoded directly into the policy; for instance, the behavior should remain invariant to task-irrelevant perceptual perturbations ( Zhu et al., 2023b ) , transform equivariantly under known geometric changes ( Wang et al., 2024a ) , or be composed of reusable policy components ( Mishra et al., 2023 ) .
These methods generalize by encoding a particular, known deployment shift as an inductive bias.
They are effective when this prescribed relation matches the nature of the shift, but require the relevant task-specific semantics or transformation laws to be specified a priori.

When the underlying observation-goal-action relation is unknown, an attractive alternative is to learn it from comparisons among demonstrations.
Bilinear transduction ( Netanyahu et al., 2023 ) achieves this by decomposing an observation-goal condition x x into an “anchor” training example a a and a residual δ = x − a \delta=x-a , then constrains the predictor to a low-rank interaction between features of the two factors.
Thus, rather than specifying a task-specific transformation explicitly, the model learns from the data how the anchor and the residual jointly determine behaviors within a generic low-rank relationship.
This reparameterization converts an out-of-support query into a potentially unseen combination of individually familiar factors; under low-rank, coverage, and conditioning assumptions, prediction error at unsupported queries is provably bounded by the training error ( Shah et al., 2020 ; Simchowitz et al., 2023 ) .
Existing robotic instantiations, however, are state-based and deterministic, leaving open how to construct this decomposition from visuomotor demonstrations and how to extrapolate a multimodal action distribution.

In this work, we ask whether this relational formulation can support generative goal-conditioned visuomotor policies.
We introduce Bilinear Flow Policy (BFP), which extrapolates to unseen goals by transductively relating novel observation-goal conditions to demonstrated examples in the training data. BFP applies bilinear transduction to a conditional flow field, extending relational extrapolation from deterministic actions to multimodal action distributions. It also combines a compact visual representation with a learned anchor policy to find generalizable relations in visuomotor settings.

We also derive an end-to-end distributional extrapolation bound that relates in-distribution flow-matching error to the Wasserstein error of the generated action distribution at unseen goals.
The bound’s training-error and coverage terms further motivate two pre-deployment diagnostics: held-out flow loss for selecting among trained policies, and anchor–residual coverage for identifying unseen-goal queries on which a selected policy is likely to remain reliable.

We evaluate BFP on five goal-conditioned visuomotor manipulation tasks across three simulation benchmarks.
On the simulation tasks, BFP achieves 79 % 79\% average out-of-distribution (OOD) success ( 2.63 × 2.63\times that of matched GCIL and 1.36 × 1.36\times that of the strongest extrapolation-targeted baseline) while retaining comparable in-distribution performance, across 4,200 rollouts.
On the two real-world robotics tasks, BFP improves over the matched GCIL baseline by 32 percentage points on average.

In summary, our contributions are threefold.

We introduce BFP , a generative goal-conditioned visuomotor imitation policy learning framework that extrapolates to unseen goals preserving behavior multimodality.

We derive an end-to-end bound relating in-distribution flow error to unseen-goal action-distribution error.
The theorem motivates practical pre-deployment diagnostics for selecting trained policies and assessing their reliability on specific unseen goals.

Across controlled multimodal regression, five simulated manipulation tasks, and two real-world tasks, BFP substantially improves OOD performance over matched generative GCIL and extrapolation-targeted baselines.

1. We introduce BFP , a generative goal-conditioned visuomotor imitation policy learning framework that extrapolates to unseen goals preserving behavior multimodality.

2. We derive an end-to-end bound relating in-distribution flow error to unseen-goal action-distribution error.
The theorem motivates practical pre-deployment diagnostics for selecting trained policies and assessing their reliability on specific unseen goals.

3. Across controlled multimodal regression, five simulated manipulation tasks, and two real-world tasks, BFP substantially improves OOD performance over matched generative GCIL and extrapolation-targeted baselines.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

We first situate our work within the generalization regimes studied in goal-conditioned policies.
We then categorize extrapolation methods by how they map changes in policy inputs into behavior changes and reuse that rule beyond training support.
Prior work either hand-crafts this rule or use demonstration data to learn it. BFP follows the latter approach.

Generalization Regimes of Goal-Conditioned Policies. Goal-conditioned policies use a single policy across many desired outcomes ( Gupta et al., 2019 ; Park et al., 2025 ) , while generative variants model multimodal action distributions for a given goal ( Reuss et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2024 ) .
Their generalization beyond training state–goal combinations has been studied under two distinct regimes.
In stitching , where both the state and goal have been seen during training, but not together, the policy must recombine familiar transitions or trajectory segments to connect them ( Lawson et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) .
Another studies unseen-goal generalization , where the desired goal itself lies outside the training support and pursuing it requires the policy to act at out-of-distribution state–goal inputs ( Hong et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) .
We study this regime in generative visuomotor imitation, where policies must generalize from visual inputs while preserving multimodal behavior.

Hand-crafted Extrapolation Rules. Some approaches extrapolate through hand-specified rules for how behavior changes with the policy input ( Urain et al., 2024 ) .
Representation-based methods seek invariance to task-irrelevant variation by reducing observations to task-relevant objects, regions, keypoints, or geometry ( Zhu et al., 2023b ; Manuelli et al., 2019 ; Zhu et al., 2023a ) .
Equivariant policies prescribe how known scene transformations should transform actions or action distributions ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Funk et al., 2024 ) .
Compositional methods define reusable factors (e.g., skills, objectives, or sensor modalities) and prescribe how they may be recombined ( Mishra et al., 2023 ; Urain et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024b ) .
Their representations and components may be learned, but the rule is fixed a priori; this is effective when relevant structure is known, but restrictive otherwise.
We instead study settings where this rule is not obvious and must be inferred from demonstrations.

Learning Extrapolation Rules from Demonstrations. When no rule is known a priori , some prior works learn it by predicting a desired action from training examples and residuals that quantify the input change from each example to the query. DARP ( Pfeifer et al., 2026 ) instantiates this locally by retrieving the k k nearest examples, predicting from each example and its residual, and aggregating the results.
Bilinear transduction (BT) ( Netanyahu et al., 2023 ) instead assumes that a suitable anchor and compact residual induce a low-rank action-prediction problem, and uses a bilinear model to predict actions for unseen anchor–residual combinations.
Subsequent work extends this principle to offline RL and task-level extrapolation ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ousherovitch & Wang, 2026 ) .
Robotic applications, however, have considered state inputs, where residuals are directly defined in compact coordinates and anchors are chosen using task-specific heuristics.
We study whether the same principle extends to generative visuomotor imitation, where defining a compact residual, selecting an anchor that exposes the low-rank relation, and preserving multiple valid actions are all nontrivial.
