2026-10-06.title: Human-in-the-Loop Neuro-Symbolic Drift Anticipation for Reliable Visual SLAM
2026-10-06.authors: Junhyun Nam , Wonse Jo
2026-10-06.comment: IFAC conference paper; 5 figures
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper introduces Hybrid DeepSEE (HDS), a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) neuro-symbolic framework for proactive drift anticipation in Visual SLAM (V-SLAM). While data-driven models offer predictive power, their “black-box” nature often yields physically inconsistent outputs in out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. To address this, HDS integrates neural drift risk estimation with symbolic constraint reasoning. By utilizing a Large Language Model (LLM) as a reasoning bridge, the framework translates qualitative human context into interpretable symbolic constraints. Building upon this architecture, we propose a superior drift anticipation framework that ensures enhanced reliability and consistency in Visual SLAM
2026-10-06.introduction:
Reliable state estimation is a fundamental requirement for the safe deployment of autonomous mobile robots in mission-critical domains such as industrial automation and defense operations. In such systems, localization accuracy directly affects feedback control performance, trajectory tracking stability, and overall operational safety ( Kelly and Sukhatme, 2009 ) . Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (V-SLAM) has become a widely adopted solution due to its ability to extract rich environmental information using low-cost cameras ( Cadena et al., 2016 ) .

Real-world V-SLAM systems, despite their advantages, experience cumulative drift, which refers to the accumulated errors in pose estimation while driving ( Cadena et al., 2016 ) . As a result, there is a divergence between the estimated and true trajectories.
From a control perspective, the estimation degradation can propagate through the feedback loop, leading to performance deterioration or potential instability ( Radisavljevic-Gajic, 2024 ) . Drift is particularly pronounced in challenging environments characterized by repetitive textures, abrupt illumination changes, and low-feature regions, where measurement reliability is significantly reduced ( Savinykh et al., 2022 ) .

In safety-critical domains, such as nuclear maintenance, defense operations, and human-robot collaboration, estimation failures can lead to catastrophic consequences including human casualties or severe environmental damage. In these high-stakes contexts, even minor SLAM drift transcends simple positioning errors, potentially triggering abrupt trajectory deviations that propagate into the control loop ( Cadena et al., 2016 ) . Therefore, it is essential not only to correct errors after they occur but to anticipate degradation before significant drift compromises the system. Early awareness of drift risk enables proactive supervisory actions—such as motion regulation or re-localization triggers—thereby preserving closed-loop reliability and operational integrity without relying solely on post-hoc, reactive correction ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) .

To address this need, we propose a conceptual Neuro-Symbolic Drift Anticipation Framework that introduces a constraint-aware supervisory layer above a conventional V-SLAM estimator using Human-in-the-Loop approach. It monitors drift risk and evaluates consistency under predefined constraints without altering the estimated pose. This supervisory evaluation aims to prevent physically implausible or high-risk estimation conditions.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

Designing a proactive supervisory framework for anticipating drift risk in V-SLAM-based state estimation.

Proposing a constraint-aware Human-in-the-Loop regulation mechanism that encodes expert geometric and kinematic knowledge through a language-mediated interface, enabling adaptive drift-risk control under explicitly defined safety constraints.

1. Designing a proactive supervisory framework for anticipating drift risk in V-SLAM-based state estimation.

2. Proposing a constraint-aware Human-in-the-Loop regulation mechanism that encodes expert geometric and kinematic knowledge through a language-mediated interface, enabling adaptive drift-risk control under explicitly defined safety constraints.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Geometric Visual SLAM

Classical visual SLAM systems rely on geometric consistency, feature matching, and nonlinear optimization to estimate camera trajectories. Representative systems such as ORB-SLAM3 ( Campos et al., 2021 ) utilized feature-based tracking, local bundle adjustment, and loop closure detection to refine pose estimates. These approaches achieve high accuracy in structured and well-textured environments through principled optimization over pose graphs.

However, geometric SLAM systems are fundamentally reactive: accumulated drift is corrected only after sufficient loop evidence is detected. In large-scale exploration or non-revisitable trajectories, loop closure cannot be guaranteed, leading to persistent divergence. Furthermore, feature-based methods degrade significantly in challenging environments—such as low-texture regions or areas with illumination volatility—where reliable feature correspondences become sparse or ambiguous.

Conventional mitigation strategies primarily rely on loop closure detection, which compensates accumulated errors after revisiting previously mapped locations ( Ho and Newman, 2006 ) . Although effective in structured environments, loop closure mechanisms are inherently reactive and provide no guarantee of bounded estimation performance during large-scale exploration or high-speed maneuvers ( Cadena et al., 2016 ) . In safety-critical systems, it is insufficient to only rely on the traditional loop closure mechanisms due to safety.

## 2.2 Learning-Based Drift and Error Estimation

Recent advances have incorporated deep learning into SLAM pipelines to improve robustness and error awareness. In particular, SEESys–the state-of-the-art online extension of the DeepSEE ( Hu et al., 2023 ) framework–introduced an edge-assisted architecture that achieves real-time pose error estimation with an average end-to-end latency of 37.3 ms ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . By leveraging an attention-based multi-modality model (TimeSformer), SEESys demonstrates the feasibility of delivering instantaneous quality-of-service (QoS) metrics for mobile robots and AR devices.

However, despite their real-time capabilities, recent approaches that integrate deep neural networks (DNNs) into V-SLAM pipelines to enhance perceptual robustness remain fundamentally data-driven black-box systems. While these methods can produce numerically plausible motion estimates, they lack mechanisms to formally enforce geometric or kinematic consistency. As a result, physically inadmissible trajectories may emerge, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) environments, where such inconsistencies can arise unpredictably and introduce additional risk into downstream control processes ( Radisavljevic-Gajic, 2024 ) . Furthermore, although systems such as SEESys provide auditory feedback to human operators, they do not offer explainable reasoning nor enable dynamic injection of contextual constraints into the inference loop.

## 2.3 Neuro-Symbolic and Constraint-Aware Learning

Neuro-symbolic learning aims to integrate data-driven perception with symbolic reasoning to overcome the limitations of black-box models. Logical Neural Networks (LNNs) enable differentiable reasoning under explicitly defined logical rules, offering improved interpretability and consistency. However, their application to proactive drift anticipation in robotic localization remains largely unexplored.

In contrast to prior work, our framework integrates neural drift risk estimation with symbolic constraint enforcement under a Human-in-the-Loop paradigm. By leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) as a reasoning bridge to encode expert-defined constraints, we enable a Hybrid DeepSEE (HDS) approach that aligns learned representations with formal safety and kinematic principles.

2026-10-06.title: Demonstration-Calibrated Port-Hamiltonian Retuning for Manipulation Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Yulong Yang , Fan Wu , Christine Allen-Blanchette , Amit Chakraborty
2026-10-06.abstract: Diffusion and VLA policies for manipulation are often deployed through downstream impedance controllers. The stiffness and damping gains of these controllers affect task success, yet are commonly inherited from data collection rather than selected for the deployed policy. Although empirical gain sweeps can improve performance, they require repeated evaluation rollouts. We introduce PHRetune, an offline method that derives controller gains for a frozen policy without evaluation rollouts or gain search. Our approach learns a port-Hamiltonian model from demonstrations to estimate the effort and energy associated with the policy’s predicted actions. The policy is applied to recorded demonstration observations, and its predictions are assessed against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. From this comparison, we derive a single gain scale in closed form, adjusting the downstream controller while preserving the policy and its action representation. The gains are fixed before evaluation, without requiring a prior manipulator model, task rewards, policy retraining, or additional runtime computation. Across LIBERO suites, PHRetune improves Diffusion Policy success by up to 9.4 percentage points, with the derived gains achieving the highest observed success rates in empirical gain sweeps. On all four real-world manipulation tasks, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline. The same procedure improves success with SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT on every task, while reducing acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones.
2026-10-06.introduction:
The behavior of a learned manipulation policy depends not only on its predicted actions, but also on the controller that executes them.
Diffusion and vision-language-action (VLA) policies often command end-effector targets through a downstream impedance or operational-space controller [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
The controller’s stiffness and damping therefore shape how policy predictions are realized as motion and interaction forces [ 4 , 5 ] .
Yet these gains are commonly inherited from teleoperated data collection or simulator defaults rather than selected for the deployed policy [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] .
Recent studies show that this choice materially affects policy learning and execution, and that more compliant settings can improve task success [ 9 , 10 ] .

Prior work addresses this issue either by incorporating compliance into policy learning or by tuning the downstream controller.
Variable-impedance actions, explicit compliance predictions, and learning from intent–execution mismatch modify the action representation or training procedure rather than retuning the controller of an unchanged policy [ 11 , 12 , 10 ] .
Controller-side approaches instead optimize tracking through a dynamics model, prescribe stiffness from demonstration variability, or search directly over evaluation rollouts [ 13 , 14 , 9 ] .
These approaches respectively rely on a model-based tracking objective, omit the deployed policy’s predictions, or require execution feedback to select gains.
Our goal is to derive a fixed gain tailored to a frozen policy using its task demonstrations, without requiring a prior manipulator model, policy retraining, or gain-selection rollouts.

We introduce PHRetune (pronounced “free-tune"), an offline method that derives controller gains for a frozen policy from its existing task demonstrations, without additional robot interaction for gain selection.
A port-Hamiltonian formulation relates action attenuation and controller softening through their effects on the energy supplied by policy-generated setpoints [ 4 , 15 ] .
Under a linear impedance model, this relationship provides a closed-form map from admissible action scalings to controller gains.
We determine this action scaling using a surrogate fitted to demonstration transitions, assessing the policy’s predictions on recorded observations against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets.
Gain selection therefore remains blind to evaluation outcomes, requiring neither gain search nor additional robot or simulator rollouts.
The resulting controller gains are fixed before evaluation, leaving the policy, action representation, and inference procedure unchanged and introducing no additional runtime overhead.

Across three LIBERO suites, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline.
The gains derived before evaluation also achieve the highest observed success rates in empirical gain sweeps.
These improvements extend to four real-world manipulation tasks, where PHRetuned Diffusion Policy again outperforms the nominal policy and all evaluated baselines on every task.
Applying the same procedure to SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT improves success on every task, with motion evaluations showing reduced acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Visuomotor manipulation policies, including diffusion policies and VLA models, commonly predict joint- or end-effector targets that are executed by lower-level controllers [ 16 , 1 , 2 , 17 ] .
Their closed-loop behavior therefore depends on controller gains, although benchmark environments typically treat these gains as fixed parameters rather than quantities selected for the deployed policy [ 18 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 19 , 20 ] .

One line of work incorporates compliance into policy learning. VICES jointly commands Cartesian motion and impedance [ 11 ] , while related methods learn variable-impedance profiles from task experience or demonstrations [ 21 , 22 ] .
Adaptive Compliance Policy predicts compliance alongside diffusion-generated motion [ 12 ] , and Mind the Gap learns implicit impedance from intent–execution mismatch [ 10 ] .
These approaches modify the action representation or training procedure to learn compliant behavior, rather than retuning the downstream controller of an unchanged policy.

A complementary line tunes the downstream controller.
DiffTune differentiates a tracking objective through a dynamics model [ 13 ] , while demonstration-based rules map motion variability to stiffness [ 14 ] .
Tune-to-Learn empirically evaluates how controller gains affect policy learning and execution, demonstrating that gain selection can substantially alter task performance [ 9 ] .
These approaches select gains through tracking objectives, demonstration statistics, or evaluation rollouts.
PHRetune instead uses a demonstration-calibrated energy model to assess the frozen policy’s predictions on recorded observations against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets.
This assessment determines a fixed gain scale while preserving the policy, its action representation, and the controller structure.
Gain selection therefore requires no policy retraining nor robot or simulator rollouts.

Impedance control specifies the dynamic relationship between motion and interaction force around a virtual equilibrium [ 4 ] , while operational-space control formulates motion and force control directly in task coordinates [ 5 ] .
When a learned policy commands this equilibrium, its setpoint updates can supply energy to the controlled system rather than serving solely as kinematic targets. Port-Hamiltonian modeling describes this interaction through stored energy, dissipation, and power-conjugate ports [ 15 ] .
Under the linear impedance model considered here, spring effort and setpoint velocity form a power-conjugate pair.
This representation provides a common basis for relating action attenuation and controller softening through their effects on the energy associated with setpoints.

These foundations also underpin energy-shaping and passivity-based control.
Interconnection and damping assignment passivity-based control (IDA-PBC) shapes the closed-loop storage and dissipation structure through feedback synthesis [ 23 ] , whereas energy-tank methods regulate energy exchange during online variations in stiffness or interaction [ 24 , 25 ] .
PHRetune addresses a different design problem.
It neither synthesizes a new feedback law nor enforces a runtime energy budget, but uses a demonstration-calibrated energetic model to derive fixed gains for an existing impedance controller before deployment.
The port-Hamiltonian formulation thus supports an offline retuning rule tailored to a frozen policy, with gain selection remaining blind to evaluation outcomes.

2026-10-06.authors: Yi Zhao , Sebastian Scherer
2026-10-06.comment: . Project website (code and videos): this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Training-free acceleration of a diffusion policy is accepted when an internal similarity signal
reports that the shortcut changed nothing. We price every monitor a control loop can afford in
closed-loop success rather than feature distance, over 114 114 accelerator configurations and four
policy families: two accelerators each clear their own gate’s bar and log every reuse as certified,
while on one task one finishes every episode and the other none. A monitor is two
designs, not one — the statistic it reads, and what it does when that statistic fires.
Published gates re-arm after every rejection, and under that response even an oracle handed
every forward pass and the exact local action error loses twenty points; absorbing
the same statistic costs one point, and most of its speed. What makes a response that never
forgets affordable is a statistic that rarely fires, and what it must measure is deviation from
the policy the accelerator replaced — which a chunked policy has already paid for, its last
plan not yet expired and free to read. Guarding every call this way cuts per-call compute by 1.55 1.55 – 3.09 × 3.09\times , where any reference-requiring check at the same coverage would have to
stop accelerating altogether. On three of our four families the schedule alone already holds
the pre-stated ± 2 \pm 2 -point margin. What the monitor is measurably worth shows in three places:
on the fourth family, where it rescues the candidate selection landed on; on four configurations
it did not select; and on a contact-rich fifth family, chosen where the schedule was expected to
fail and run after every design choice was frozen, where no unmonitored arm at its speed holds
the margin and the monitored one does.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Diffusion policies spend most of their inference budget recomputing what changed little since
the previous control call; training-free accelerators exploit that by caching features,
skipping denoising steps or reusing action chunks.

Knowing when a shortcut is admissible is the unsolved half, and the field’s answer is to let
the accelerator watch itself: compare a cached quantity against a freshly computed one and
reuse while they agree. Closed-loop success is reported for the setting that ships, but the rule deciding
each reuse is argued in feature space, a weak predictor of closed loop [ 1 ] . Validated
in closed loop instead, the outcome is not a matter of degree: a cross-call cache in our sweep
drives LIBERO-10 success from 97 % 97\% to 6 % 6\% (Fig. 1 ) while certifying every
one of the 161,000 161{,}000 reuses it logs across all its episodes.

Rather than report one failure we measured the whole design space. Section III prices
every monitor a control loop can afford, over 114 114 configurations from four policy families,
and the map is strongly negative: at a matched acceptance rate an exogenous gate does not beat
discarding forwards at random, and an oracle handed every forward pass and the exact deviation still
loses twenty points. What failed there is the response , not the signal, and the

2026-10-06.title: FreeSpeed: Training-Free Speed Control for Generative Robot Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Yuxuan Hu , Shilin Shan , Qiheng Wang , Jinghan Yang , Junqiao Fan , Hao Wan , Jianfei Yang
2026-10-06.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Online control of execution speed is essential for deploying robot policies in real-world scenarios, as robots may need to speed up under time constraints or slow down to facilitate human interaction and improve safety. However, imitation-learned policies inherit the execution speed of their demonstrations, and test-time speed modification can introduce unrecoverable out-of-distribution observations, reducing task success. We observe that the directional inconsistency of action chunks reflects task-phase criticality, indicating how aggressively action step lengths can be modified while preserving task success. Based on this observation, we introduce FreeSpeed , a training-free module that post-processes action chunks from pretrained policies. FreeSpeed resamples each predicted chunk at the requested rate, then uses directional inconsistency between adjacent actions as the primary signal for rescaling. This signal adaptively determines how closely the execution speed can approach the requested speed, allowing flexible speed adjustment within the evaluated limits without compromising task success. Across three policy families and 50 simulated tasks, FreeSpeed supports online speed changes, with realized execution rates spanning 0.22 × 0.22\times to 2.53 × 2.53\times among settings that preserve per-task success. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, FreeSpeed achieves an average success rate of 94.0 94.0 %, matching the frozen policy’s 93.8 93.8 %, while realizing execution rates from 0.38 × 0.38\times to 1.97 × 1.97\times .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Modulating execution speed online matters when robots operate across changing
tasks and deployment conditions.
Fast motion improves efficiency in repetitive manipulation ( Zeng et al., 2020 ) , whereas slow motion can be essential for safe and comfortable human–robot interaction in shared workspaces ( Lachner et al., 2021 ; Hostettler et al., 2025 ) , particularly as robots are increasingly deployed in diverse human-centered tasks ( Fan et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026b ; Hu et al., 2026c ) . Within a single manipulation task, a robot may need to move quickly during routine phases, such as object transport, and slow down during phases that require precision, such as object placement and grasping ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . A deployed policy should therefore accept speed requests during execution rather than operate at a single pace fixed during training.

Imitation-based policies learn the execution speed implicitly from demonstrations ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and they do not normally expose the speed control interface. Despite the impressive speed-modification performance of existing methods ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Nam et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Hu et al., 2026a ; Jing et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , almost all require a training process closely tied to task-specific data augmentation. This process typically involves specifying speed factors, post-processing collected demonstrations, and then fine-tuning or retraining a policy in a speed-informed manner. This dependence can limit the methods’ adaptability to unseen scenarios, making speed control feasible but difficult to generalize.

Therefore, it is necessary to explore training-free, model-independent speed control that can transfer directly across tasks and pretrained models. A straightforward approach is to downsample or upsample the predicted action chunk at test time. At a fixed command frequency, combining or skipping action steps accelerates execution by reducing the number of executable steps, while interpolation slows execution by adding intermediate steps. Despite its simplicity, this approach changes step lengths, which can induce out-of-distribution (OOD) observations ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Arachchige et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Nam et al., 2025 ) and cause subsequent trajectory predictions to drift ( Ross et al., 2011 ) (Section 5.5 ). This is particularly risky during task phases that require precision, such as grasping and placing, where execution errors at critical steps can cause the entire task to fail.

To this end, we identify directional inconsistency as a test-time indicator of task-phase criticality. In the studied tasks, inconsistency tends to be high during critical phases and low otherwise. Adjusting action step lengths according to this signal helps preserve task success while allowing more aggressive speed changes during less critical phases. Building on this insight, we introduce FreeSpeed, a training-free, plug-and-play module for frozen action-chunking policies. FreeSpeed also builds on action resampling but adapts the command step length according to the directional consistency of the predicted action chunk. It pushes execution speed toward its limit when consecutive action directions remain consistent and gradually shifts execution back toward the original speed as inconsistency increases. It uses only the policy’s predicted motion and requires no policy updates, additional data, or a learned scheduler. The same interface accepts both fixed and time-varying rate commands. The contributions of this work are as follows.

We use adjacent-action cosine inconsistency as a training-free proxy for phase criticality and show in Section 5.5 that adapting step-length rescaling to this signal keeps the frozen policy’s observations close to the training distribution under both acceleration and deceleration.

# 2 Related Work

Existing methods differ in which components are modified to enable speed control. They can be broadly grouped into three approaches: (1) incorporating speed variation into policy learning; (2) adapting both policy learning and the execution framework; and (3) training auxiliary speed-control modules while keeping the base policy frozen.

The first group modifies the policy through demonstration retiming ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Jing et al., 2026 ) , rate-aware objectives or architectures ( Hu et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or speed-augmented pretraining followed by RL fine-tuning ( Nam et al., 2025 ) . These methods primarily target faster execution, with limited attention to deceleration or user control. TempoVLA ( Jing et al., 2026 ) supports user-specified rates but requires training to enable this capability.

The second group combines policy adaptation with precise tracking. SAIL and RACE process collected demonstrations, use reached states as action prediction targets, and combine execution retiming with high-gain control ( Arachchige et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . SAIL’s ablation indicates that high-gain control contributes substantially to its acceleration gains. Building on this approach, Yang et al. (2026) further learn faster-than-demonstration execution from human-modulated rollouts.

The third group freezes the base policy and trains an external speed controller. SpeedTuning trains a speed policy online via reinforcement learning ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) , whereas SuP trains a downsampling scheduler offline using a learned world model ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Both require additional training and select execution rates autonomously rather than follow user-specified rates.

In contrast, FreeSpeed adjusts a frozen policy’s output toward rates specified by the user in real time, supporting both acceleration and deceleration. It requires no post-processing of training data, no speed-informed retraining, and no change to the low-level control law or controller gains. Table 1 summarizes these capabilities and compares FreeSpeed with the aforementioned methods.

2026-10-06.title: End-to-End Safe Social Navigation via Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning and Probabilistic Perception
2026-10-06.authors: Tommaso Van Der Meer Andrea Garulli , Antonio Giannitrapani , Renato Quartullo , Alberto Vaglio , Alexandre Alahi
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: Autonomous social navigation requires balancing efficiency, physical safety, and social compliance. Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods provide a viable and effective solution but often rely on unrealistic assumptions, such as the knowledge of humans’ position and velocity. In this paper, we introduce JESSI (JAX-based E2E Safe Social Interpretable navigation), a lightweight end-to-end RL framework that maps raw LiDAR scans directly to kinematically feasible control commands. JESSI enhances safety via Dirichlet-parameterized continuous action spaces and deterministic bounding, while an integrated attention-based perception module extracts probabilistic human states for interpretable, socially aware decision-making. Through extensive simulations and real-world deployment on a differential-drive robot, we demonstrate that jointly optimizing the RL policy with a supervised perception signal in a multi-task paradigm enhances social behavior. Ultimately, JESSI is able to balance high navigation success rates and superior social behaviors compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
2026-10-06.introduction:
The deployment of autonomous mobile robots in unstructured, human-populated environments has seen tremendous progress in recent years. Navigating effectively in these scenarios is a challenging task. It requires a delicate balance between navigation efficiency, strict physical safety (e.g., avoiding collisions with walls and pedestrians), and adherence to unwritten social norms (e.g., maintaining comfortable distances) [ 1 , 2 ] . While classical model-based planning algorithms have long been the standard, they often struggle to capture the complex, interactive nature of crowd dynamics [ 3 ] . Consequently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm, allowing robots to learn sophisticated navigation policies directly from the interaction with the environment.

Despite achieving impressive results in simulated environments, state-of-the-art RL and model-based social navigation approaches often rely on strong, and sometimes unrealistic, assumptions that inhibit their real-world applicability:

Perfect state observability : many top-performing algorithms assume the availability of the exact state of all surrounding humans (e.g., precise positions and velocities) at any given time [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . In reality, onboard perception is limited by sensor noise, limited fields of view, and severe occlusions.

Omission of static obstacles : several foundational social navigation policies focus exclusively on human-robot interaction, omitting static obstacles from their formulation or training environments [ 4 , 5 ] . This renders them inapplicable in typical, cluttered indoor spaces.

Humans as generic obstacles : conversely, navigation methods designed to operate directly from raw sensor data or classical dynamics often treat humans merely as moving geometric shapes [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . By lacking an explicit semantic understanding of human presence, these methods produce navigation policies that are highly optimized for collision avoidance but exhibit poor social behavior.

Kinematic infeasibility : many continuous-action RL algorithms generate commands that do not intrinsically respect the kinematic of the robot, relying instead on artificial a-posteriori velocity clipping which can destabilize learning and execution [ 13 , 14 ] .

In the broader context of autonomous driving, recent breakthroughs have demonstrated that purely reactive End-to-End (E2E) systems, which directly map sensor inputs to control commands, often suffer from poor sample efficiency and lack of interpretability [ 15 ] . To overcome this, the community adopted multi-task learning paradigms, demonstrating that jointly optimizing auxiliary perception tasks alongside the primary planning objective significantly enhances the overall navigation performance [ 16 , 17 ] .

Inspired by these advancements, we introduce JESSI ( JAX-based E2E Safe Social Interpretable navigation ). JESSI is a novel reinforcement learning framework designed to bring the benefits of multi-task E2E learning into the realm of safe social navigation. An overview of the proposed method is shown in Fig. 1 . Its core design principles are:

End-to-end : breaking away from the assumption of perfect state observability, our architecture cascades a perception network and an actor-critic policy to compute control actions directly from raw LiDAR scans. Bypassing the need for an external oracle to provide humans’ positions and velocities, the system natively handles real-world sensor noise, limited fields of view, occlusions, and also considers static obstacles for motion planning. Moreover, the network is agnostic to the specific LiDAR setting implemented.

Safety : to ensure physical safety and strictly respect the kinematic constraints of a differential-drive robot, JESSI maps the continuous action space using Dirichlet distributions [ 18 ] . This is coupled with a deterministic bounding mechanism [ 8 ] that prevents actions leading to collisions with static obstacles.

Social compliance : unlike standard raw-sensor end-to-end methods, JESSI explicitly models human presence. The perception module extracts spatial and velocity estimates of surrounding pedestrians from the LiDAR stack. By feeding this structured information into the policy’s scene attention layer, the robot is intrinsically encouraged to learn socially compliant behaviors.

Interpretability : JESSI does not implement a purely black-box network but uses an intermediate representation layer. The perception module explicitly outputs confidence scores and bivariate Gaussian distributions representing the states of visible humans. This not only grounds the RL policy on a physically meaningful latent space but also provides useful insight into the robot decisions. However, differently from pure modular pipelines, the overall architecture maintains full differentiability, allowing for different training paradigms to be employed.

Efficiency : despite integrating a dedicated perception module, JESSI features a deliberately lightweight neural architecture. Implemented using the JAX library [ 19 ] , it leverages hardware-accelerated vectorization and just-in-time (JIT) compilation. This combination of compact architecture and JAX compilation enables efficient inference, making the policy suitable for real-time deployment on embedded systems.

The primary contribution of this work is a hybrid navigation framework that combines the strengths of end-to-end and modular architectures. This structure provides the explicit interpretability of modular pipelines while preserving total differentiability for joint optimization. In addition, the adoption of Dirichlet distributions, together with a deterministic action space bounding algorithm introduces a rigorous safety layer that ensures kinematic feasibility and collision avoidance at the control level.

The paper is organized as follows: Sec. II presents the considered robot kinematic model and the proposed method, Sec. III showcases the simulated environment employed and the simulation experiments performed against various baselines. Sec. IV introduces the experiments carried out in the real world on two different robotic platforms, and Sec. V draws some conclusions giving useful insights on the proposed algorithm.

The core of the proposed approach is an integrated neural network including a perception module and an actor-critic policy, designed to process raw sensory data and output safe navigation commands. The overall architecture is detailed in Fig. 3 .

2026-10-06.title: When to Switch: Reliable Action-Chunk Extension for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-06.authors: Seonghoon Yu , Dongwon Kim , HyungRok Jung , Yoonjae Baek , Byung-kwan Lee , Suha Kwak , Jeany Son
2026-10-06.comment: Pre-print
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models serve as unified policies for robotic manipulation,
yet their expensive inference forces robots to pause between policy calls,
resulting in stop-and-go execution that interrupts smooth motion and prolongs task completion.
Extending the action chunk reduces policy calls and hence these pauses,
but predicting farther into the future makes long-chunk execution unreliable.
To understand where this unreliability arises,
we analyze action errors within long chunks and find that they concentrate around transitions
between manipulation subskills, growing sharply with chunk length.
This suggests the importance of transition timing , i.e. , when to switch subskills within a chunk.
Motivated by this observation,
we introduce RACE ( R eliable A ction- C hunk E xtension),
a framework that predicts the transition timing from an auxiliary one-step denoising pass
and conditions action generation on it.
By learning and conditioning on transition timing,
RACE reduces errors at subskill transitions and enables reliable execution of longer action chunks.
Across simulation benchmarks, RACE outperforms fine-tuning at the same chunk length;
with 2 × 2\times longer chunks, it surpasses recent state-of-the-art and efficient VLAs in success rate,
and with 4 × 4\times longer chunks, it remains competitive.
On a real robot, RACE uses 4 × 4\times longer chunks,
which reduces the idle time caused by stop-and-go execution by about 5 × 5\times ,
while achieving a higher success rate than fine-tuning with the same chunk length.
Code and a real-robot demo are available on Github .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) ,
such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and GR00T ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) ,
serve as unified policies for diverse robotic manipulation tasks by generating actions on top of large-scale vision-language models.
However, their large scale makes each policy inference computationally expensive.
Consequently, the robot often finishes executing its current actions before the next ones are ready,
forcing repeated pauses between policy calls that disrupt continuous robot operation, i.e. , stop-and-go execution ( Black et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) .
Over hundreds of control steps, these pauses accumulate into idle time ,
which prolongs task completion and interrupts smooth robot motion,
hindering the real-world deployment of VLAs.

Action chunking ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ) mitigates these pauses by predicting multiple consecutive actions per policy call,
keeping the robot in motion longer between policy inferences.
Extending this chunk ( Wang et al., 2026c ) further reduces the number of policy calls and the time lost to these pauses,
making robot execution more continuous.
Moderately longer chunks even improve task success,
which has been attributed to temporal consistency ( Liu et al., 2025a ) or implicit ensembling ( Lazzati et al., 2026 ) .
Pushing the chunk further, however, forces the policy to predict farther into the future
and to execute longer without intermediate feedback ( i.e. , open-loop execution).
Beyond a certain length, this makes execution unreliable and success rates decline ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Liang et al., 2026 ) (Fig. 1 ).

To better understand why long-chunk execution becomes unreliable, we examine how action errors are distributed within a chunk.
Besides the gradual error growth expected from open-loop execution,
we also observe pronounced error spikes around transition points ,
the steps at which the robot switches from one manipulation subskill ( e.g. , approaching, grasping, or lifting) to the next (Fig. 2(a) ).
Since demonstrations do not annotate subskills,
we detect these points as abrupt changes in action dynamics using PELT ( Killick et al., 2012 ) , following prior work ( Jia et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) (Appendix A ).
The error spikes at these transition points grow substantially with chunk length (Fig. 2(b) ; measured as in Appendix E.4 ).
As the chunk grows longer,
the policy must anticipate these subskill switches farther in advance without intermediate feedback,
making these switches increasingly difficult to predict.
This suggests that transition timing , i.e. , when to switch subskills within a chunk,
is an important challenge in long-chunk execution.

Motivated by this observation, we introduce RACE
( R eliable A ction- C hunk E xtension),
a framework that enables VLAs to reliably execute longer action chunks
by learning to predict transition timing and conditioning action generation on it.
Learning to predict transition timing makes the action expert aware of upcoming transitions,
and conditioning on the predicted timing further informs every denoising step of where transitions are expected within the chunk,
together reducing errors around transitions.
To achieve this, RACE proceeds in two stages:
1) Transition-timing Prediction via One-step Denoising ,
which estimates a transition-timing prior from an auxiliary one-step denoising pass and the cached VLM features,
supervised by transition labels automatically extracted from demonstrations;
and 2) Transition-conditioned Action Generation , which injects the prior into every denoising step
through token-wise modulation of the action expert, with learnable gates controlling its strength per step.
Since error spikes appear at transitions at every chunk length (Fig. 2(b) ),
RACE reduces these errors across chunk lengths (Fig. 2(c) ),
improving task success not only for longer chunks but at each chunk length (Fig. 1 ).

In our experiments, RACE outperforms fine-tuning at the same chunk length on manipulation benchmarks;
with 2 × 2\times longer chunks, it achieves higher success rates than recent state-of-the-art VLAs and efficient VLA approaches,
and with 4 × 4\times longer chunks, it remains competitive with them.
On a real robot, using 4 × 4\times longer chunks reduces idle time by about 5 × 5\times ,
and RACE achieves a higher success rate than fine-tuning with the same chunk length.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify transitions between manipulation subskills
as where action errors concentrate when extending action chunks,
suggesting the importance of transition timing within a chunk.

We introduce RACE, a framework for R eliable A ction- C hunk E xtension
that learns to predict transition timing from an auxiliary one-step denoising pass, making the action expert transition-aware,
and conditions generation on it via token-wise modulation with per-step learnable gates.

Experiments show that RACE achieves higher success rates than recent state-of-the-art and efficient VLA approaches
with 2 × 2\times longer action chunks and remains competitive with 4 × 4\times longer chunks,
and enables longer chunks that reduce idle time on a real robot.

# 2 Related Work

VLAs adapt pretrained vision-language models to robot control using diverse robot demonstrations ( Wang et al., 2026d ) .
Early models such as RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) and OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) generate discrete action tokens autoregressively,
while later models predict continuous action chunks
through parallel decoding ( Kim et al., 2025 ) or flow-matching action experts ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) .
RACE reduces the pauses caused by their inference latency by making longer action chunks reliable.

Action chunking ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) predicts multiple future actions per policy call,
but later actions in a longer chunk become unreliable without new observations. Adaptive chunking methods ( Liang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Feng et al., 2026a ) therefore execute only the reliable prefix of each chunk.
PACE ( Nie et al., 2026 ) shortens execution around transitions detected from low-speed valleys,
whereas RACE makes those actions reliable so that the whole chunk can be executed.
Closest to our work, PolicyTrim ( Wang et al., 2026c ) extends the chunk through reinforcement learning at a substantial training cost,
whereas RACE requires only lightweight post-training of the action expert (Appendix B.7 ). Asynchronous execution ( Black et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) hides inference latency by generating the next chunk during execution,
but some idle time remains when inference takes longer than executing a chunk;
longer chunks can further reduce it (Sec. 4.5 ), so RACE is complementary to asynchronous execution.

Another line of work reduces the cost of each policy call by pruning visual tokens ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026b ) or reusing computation across consecutive calls ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) .
These methods leave the number of policy calls unchanged, whereas RACE reduces it; the two are orthogonal and can be combined.

Demonstrations are often decomposed into subskills,
through either change-point detection on action trajectories ( Killick et al., 2012 ; Jia et al., 2024 ) or manual stage annotation ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Buamanee et al., 2026 ) .
Prior work injects this structure into the policy
as a prediction target, by predicting the goal state of each subskill ( Jia et al., 2024 ) ;
as an input, by conditioning on the inferred stage or within-subtask progress ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Buamanee et al., 2026 ) ;
or as an auxiliary output, by generating a progress sequence jointly with actions ( Liu et al., 2026a ) .
RACE instead supervises the action expert to predict the transition timing within each chunk,
encouraging transition-aware action representations,
and further conditions action generation on the predicted timing.

2026-10-06.title: Virtual model control for compliant reaching under uncertainties
2026-10-06.authors: Yi Zhang , Daniel Larby , Fumiya Iida , Fulvio Forni
2026-10-06.abstract: Virtual Model Control (VMC) is an approach to design a controller for force-controlled robots in complex uncertain environments. While this method was primarily investigated for legged robot locomotion in the past, it can be more generally applicable to other types of robotic systems. This paper investigates the VMC framework for reaching tasks in a force-controlled robotic arm. We propose six different approaches to designing virtual models in order to achieve reaching tasks in environments with obstacles and uncertainties. A force-controlled 8 degree-of-freedom humanoid robot was used to validate the proposed approach in the real world. We conducted three experiments to test the performance of VMC controllers in terms of predictability, sensitivity to external force, and adaptability against known and unknown obstacles. Experimental analyses show that, even though the proposed approach needs to sacrifice accuracy and trajectory optimality, it enables us to design complex reaching motions under uncertainties, in an intuitive and extendable manner.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Safe planning and control of robotic arms for reaching tasks in uncertain cluttered environment are still unsolved problems.
The fundamental issue lies in the inability of traditional motion control and planning methods to negotiate in real time with real-world scenarios, which are inherently unstructured and where object shapes and obstacle locations are only partially known.
In fact, the remarkable speed and accuracy of our best industrial robots require a well-known and restricted factory floor environment.

The conventional solutions typically employ an interplay of complex sensing, state estimation, planning, and feedback control, but most of them require complex and computationally expensive sensing and planning processes, which lack interact-ability to accommodate uncertainties.
Furthermore, the best planning methods such as Probabilistic Road Map (PRM) [ 1 ] , Rapidly Exploring Random Tree (RRT) [ 2 ] , Potential field (PF) [ 3 ] are then often realised through inverse kinematics and joint-space high-gain PID control. This makes the robot stiff to guarantee accurate tracking, at the cost of low sensitivity to external perturbations, such as unknown obstacles.
As a result, conventional solutions show limitations in cluttered environments, characterized by inaccurate information.

This paper advocates for methods that integrate motion planning and motion control to handle uncertainties in a safe way. Ideally, we want to take advantage of the available information on the environment and also offer a certain degree of compliant motion for real-time adaptation to unexpected scenarios.
We propose the use of virtual model control [ 4 ] for the safe, intuitive, and tractable approach to plan and control reaching tasks for articulated robotic arms.
In virtual model control, the robot behavior emerges from the interaction between the mechanics of the robot interconnected with designed ‘virtual’ mechanism, given by a collection of springs and dampers organized in a suitable geometry.
Eventually, this ‘embodied’ controller is simulated in a computer and realized through current/torque commands to the actuators.
The virtual mechanism pulls the robot behavior into specific patterns, leaving a certain degree of sensitivity to the interaction with the environment.
The robot steers in the direction defined by the total energy of the system, shaped by virtual mechanisms and environment. Therefore, trajectory planning and motion control are integrated.

Our hypothesis is that virtual model control offers a practical solution to the challenge of safe motion planning and control, by negotiating between various task specifications in complex environments.
Specifically, this paper proposes six distinctive ways to design virtual models for the purpose of reaching in uncertain cluttered environment, illustrated in Fig. 1 . Simple reaching is the most intuitive motion planning approach.
It shows similarities with PD control and impedance control in end effector space [ 5 , 6 ] . Geometric , moving-reference , and force-driven
reaching extend motion planning with additional features, leading to
a higher degree of accuracy and design flexibility. Obstacle and multi-obstacles avoidance consider how to reach the target location while avoiding known obstacles.

We highlight two key features of virtual model control:
(i) predictability of (controlled) behavior and
(ii) its intuitive design .
Virtual model control makes the action of the controller explicit.
The resulting control algorithms are predictable because they correspond to a mechanical interaction driven by physics. By inspecting the virtual mechanisms and the environment where the robot operates, we have an expectation of the intended motion, which makes the controller easier to understand and debug. Furthermore, given the planning requirements, the design of the controller is as simple as placing virtual components and tuning their parameters. This allows one to tailor the design of the controller to the specific features of the task.
Through suitable tuning of the (virtual) mechanical parameters, the robot remains compliant.
The force exerted when a reaching cannot be achieved is controlled by the virtual stiffness of virtual mechanical springs. That is, virtual model control trades motion accuracy for controlled sensitivity to the interaction with the environment. The controlled robot also enjoys the benefits of passivity [ 7 ] , i.e. stability and robustness, and controlled impedance [ 8 ] .

The paper is organized as follows. The virtual model control approach is discussed in Section II through examples. The robot platform and implementation details are provided in Section III .
The experiments are discussed in Section IV :
(i) unperturbed reaching,
(ii) reaching with known obstacles, and
(iii) reaching with unknown obstacles. Further discussions and conclusions are provided in Section V .

2026-10-06.title: Benchmarking Generative Trajectory Models for Active-Inference Control
2026-10-06.authors: Yulin Li , Mohsen A. Jafari , Andrea Matta
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted at the 7th International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI 2026). including appendix and references; 4 figures. Code: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Learning from trajectory demonstrations offers a route to active-inference control of complex systems whose dynamics are difficult to model explicitly. We introduce generative active-inference control (GenAIF), in which one generative trajectory model learns from demonstrations and measured action interventions to supply a goal-conditioned policy distribution and a state-to-observation likelihood mapping. From this control design, we derive three model requirements: (i) useful action proposals, (ii) accurate prediction under imposed actions, and (iii) probabilistic observation evidence for belief updating and expected information gain. We benchmark diffusion, autoregressive Transformers, conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs), and flow matching in a MuJoCo manipulation task with multiple physical conditions. Diffusion delivers the strongest control across the tested dynamics, while CVAE combines comparable short-horizon prediction with much faster inference. Correct conditioning is decisive, and trajectory reuse offers further computational savings. With the same frozen models, a hidden-dynamics experiment demonstrates prompt belief adaptation after an unannounced tilt change; subsequent instability identifies sustained inference as a remaining challenge. These findings support the use of shared generative trajectory models to connect action proposal, controlled prediction, and observation evidence within GenAIF.
2026-10-06.introduction:
People learn how to act by trying, observing, and adjusting. Watching someone learn a movement can help us adapt to the same unfamiliar physical dynamics [ 1 ] . Active Inference (AIF) offers an elegant account of how organisms bring perception and action together: an internal generative model connects hidden causes to sensory observations, and perception updates beliefs by minimizing variational free energy (VFE), an upper bound on sensory surprise [ 2 , 3 ] . Action selection looks ahead through expected free energy (EFE), combining preferences for useful, safe outcomes with the information that an action is expected to reveal [ 5 , 6 ] .

Our goal is a general framework that learns how a complex system behaves and how to control it from trajectory demonstrations. It should accommodate prior knowledge of system structure and hidden dynamics when available, and eventually learn their structure, form, and range when such knowledge is limited or absent.

Realizing this goal is computationally demanding: the controller must predict uncertain consequences while searching continuous action sequences [ 7 , 8 ] . Learned proposals can concentrate a finite EFE-evaluation budget on useful futures. We first explored this route in autonomous parking, combining diffusion-generated strategies with AIF evaluation and observation-driven adjustment [ 21 ] . Although the approach generalized to new parking settings, its design was tailored to that task. This experience led us to ask how much of the active-inference loop a single learned trajectory model could support.

Can a single learned generative trajectory model provide both a proposal distribution over policies and action-conditioned predictions of future observations sufficient for belief updating and expected-free-energy evaluation in active inference?

We propose generative active-inference control (GenAIF) around this shared model of action–observation trajectories. The same learned parameters support candidate generation and prediction under supplied actions; predictive evidence then supports belief updates about hidden operating conditions. The controller uses these operations to alternate between observing, updating its belief, and selecting actions according to task preferences and expected information gain. We learn the model offline from demonstrations supplemented with measured action interventions. At this stage, the hidden variables and their possible values are specified.

This design leaves a concrete model-selection problem. Which capabilities must a trajectory generator provide, and which generative families can provide them together at a useful computational cost? We identify three requirements: actionable trajectory proposals, accurate prediction of observations under externally imposed actions, and predictive evidence that can distinguish hidden conditions using actual observations. A plausible generated trajectory does not by itself establish the latter two capabilities. These requirements give us a way to test our framework’s learned component and offer other researchers practical criteria for combining AIF with generative trajectory models.

We design two groups of experiments in a custom MuJoCo ball-pushing environment to evaluate diffusion, autoregressive Transformers, conditional VAEs, and flow matching. The first benchmarks the required model capabilities and computational cost across different physical conditions. The second uses the same trained models to track a hidden dynamics change from replayed actions and observations, testing whether their predictive evidence remains reliable over time. At the tested settings, diffusion gives the strongest direct control, while CVAE provides similar short-horizon position prediction at lower cost. Reuse reduces computation with model-dependent effects on control. All four models initially identify the dynamics change but fail to sustain confidence; belief-guided action selection remains open.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) we propose GenAIF, in which a single model learned from trajectory demonstrations supplies a goal-conditioned policy distribution and a state-to-observation likelihood mapping; (2) we develop a MuJoCo environment and benchmark to evaluate the capabilities required of this shared model; and (3) we compare four generative model families in performance and computational cost, and demonstrate belief updating under changing hidden dynamics through a replay-based experiment.

2026-10-06.title: Dataset-Free Compliant Humanoid Loco-Manipulation with Dynamic Online Posture
2026-10-06.authors: Seungho Yeom , Zhenyu Wu , Jaeyoung Huh , Diego Williams , Yuheng Zhi , Soofiyan Atar , Michael Yip
2026-10-06.abstract:
Most humanoid loco-manipulation controllers require human motion data to learn whole-body coordination and posture, leaving policies reliant on external sources to provide this data. We present OCLO (Online-posture Compliant LOco-manipulation), a humanoid loco-manipulation system trained without human motion data and commanded only through two end-effector targets. Because these targets do not uniquely determine whole-body posture, OCLO generates pelvis height and torso orientation online using an analytic reachability prior, further refined through policy-in-the-loop sampling with a task-agnostic cost. OCLO also learns whole-body compliance by displacing end-effector references according to measured forces through a spring-damper model, encouraging the legs, waist, and pelvis to yield to external loads.
In simulation, using the reachability prior leads to a 77.8% success rate in acquiring the commanded reference, a vast improvement over the 37.8% success rate accomplished without the prior.
Further, refinement reduces end-effector orientation error across all evaluated tasks. The same posture module improves a pretrained SONIC controller on four of five tasks. Without compliance training, policies tend to lose balance under disturbances rather than sacrifice tracking. On a Unitree G1, OCLO maintains balance under end-effector disturbances that cause its ablations to fail and performs seven loco-manipulation tasks, including crouched walking and picking up a box from a low surface. Project website: oclo-humanoid.github.io
2026-10-06.introduction:
A humanoid that manipulates while standing must decide not only where its hands should go, but also how the rest of the body should support them. Manipulation intent can come from many sources: an operator can stream hand poses, a script can specify geometric trajectories, or a learned policy can output end-effector targets from perception and language. These interfaces specify the hands, but not the related requirements for the rest of the body, for example, how low the pelvis should sit, how far the torso should lean, or how posture should change under contact.

Most humanoid loco-manipulation controllers resolve this ambiguity through human motion priors [ 22 , 1 , 16 ] . A human motion prior provides both posture and whole-body coordination, but requires motion data and often leaves posture tied to an external source, such as head or chest tracking [ 22 , 2 ] or a posture generator learned from human motion [ 19 ] . Most compliant humanoid controllers also learn from human motion, and their posture still comes from a reference motion or an upstream root command [ 12 , 11 , 13 ] . Controllers trained without human data instead expose posture as an explicit operator command [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , and planners that do choose posture optimize a task-specific objective [ 20 , 21 , 24 ] . Without such a source, low or extended end-effector targets can become difficult to reach from a fixed nominal stance.

We present an approach to loco-manipulation that does not require obtaining posture from human motion, an external command, or a task-specific planner. To this end we separate posture generation from physical support. The control policy is responsible for maintaining balance under interaction, while the posture itself must be generated online from the end-effector targets available at deployment. This separation is important because the problem is not purely geometric: the upstream source specifies where the hands should go, but only the robot experiences the payloads and contact forces that affect balance. The generated posture must therefore make the targets reachable while allowing the controller to remain stable under interaction.

We realize this separation with OCLO ( O nline-posture C ompliant LO co-manipulation),
a humanoid loco-manipulation system with four main components. First, all training commands, including end-effector targets, interaction forces, and locomotion commands, are procedurally sampled. Second, OCLO realizes whole-body compliance through force-displaced EE references and a lower-body policy trained to accommodate the resulting motion: measured end-effector forces displace the commanded references through a spring-damper model, and the body is trained to yield to that displacement. Third, posture is generated online by an analytic reachability prior over pelvis height and torso orientation, and can be refined by policy-in-the-loop sampling that evaluates candidate postures using the frozen controller without any task-specific cost. Finally, we demonstrate the resulting system on a Unitree G1 using two hand controllers alone, with no explicit pelvis or torso command.

The two-end-effector interface is intended to separate upper-body intent from lower-body support. In this work we demonstrate the interface through teleoperation; learned upstream policies are left to future work (Sec. V ).

Our experiments isolate the contribution of each component. In simulation, the analytic prior substantially improves reference acquisition compared with policy-in-the-loop sampling alone, while refinement reduces end-effector orientation error across all evaluated tasks. The same posture module also improves a pretrained SONIC controller [ 1 ] . Policies trained without randomized end-effector targets and force perturbations are substantially less robust to disturbances, particularly those applied through the arms. On a Unitree G1, OCLO withstands end-effector disturbances that its ablations cannot and performs seven loco-manipulation tasks, including crouched walking, low-object pickup, cart manipulation, and full-height board interaction, all without explicit posture commands (Fig. Dataset-Free Compliant Humanoid Loco-Manipulation with Dynamic Online Posture ).

Overall, the key technical contributions of this paper are:

Human-motion-free compliant whole-body training. As in prior procedurally trained controllers [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , all training commands are sampled and no human motion data is used. We add compliance to this setting. Sampled end-effector forces displace the commanded references through a spring-damper model whose randomized parameters the policy observes, and the legs, waist, and pelvis are rewarded for tracking the displaced references, so the robot learns to yield to external loads through coordinated whole-body motion. On a Unitree G1, the resulting system performs seven loco-manipulation tasks using only two hand controllers and remains stable under end-effector disturbances that cause its ablations to fail.

Online posture generation from two end-effector targets. We introduce an analytic reachability prior over pelvis height and torso orientation, followed by optional policy-in-the-loop posture refinement using the frozen controller. The prior guides the search toward postures that make both end-effectors reachable, while refinement evaluates candidate postures using a task-agnostic cost over stability, compliance, and effort, with no task reward or task-specific value function as used in prior posture planners [ 20 , 21 ] . The reachability prior enables reliable online posture generation, while policy-in-the-loop refinement improves end-effector orientation accuracy. The same posture-generation module also improves a controller pretrained on human motion.

# II Related Work

OCLO has four properties. It is trained without human motion data, compliance is trained into its policy, its posture is chosen online, and it performs loco-manipulation on a physical humanoid. Table I positions prior systems along these
four axes. Among the compared systems, OCLO is the only one marked positively on all four.

Learning from human motion. Most humanoid loco-manipulation controllers are trained as motion trackers from human data. OmniH2O [ 22 ] , SONIC [ 1 ] , GMT [ 16 ] , ExBody [ 15 ] , and ResMimic [ 17 ] follow this paradigm, while Mobile-TeleVision [ 2 ] and AMO [ 19 ] retain human-motion priors for upper-body or posture generation. HOMIE [ 3 ] , HugWBC [ 4 ] , and ULC [ 5 ] avoid human data through procedural training, but posture remains an explicit command and none trains whole-body compliance. We compare against pretrained SONIC [ 1 ] and also apply our posture module to its controller.

Posture as an external command. Existing systems typically obtain posture from an external source: the operator in HOMIE [ 3 ] and HugWBC [ 4 ] , a hand-derived intermediate command in AMO [ 19 ] , a root-height input in FALCON [ 8 ] and CEER [ 13 ] , or a higher-level agent in Walk These Ways [ 18 ] . Other unified controllers retain the stance learned beneath task-frame EE targets [ 6 , 7 ] . Closer to our setting, R2S2 [ 20 ] trains task-specific planners that select body height and torso bend over a frozen, human-motion-free skill space. In contrast, OCLO generates posture online from the EE targets alone, with no task-specific objective, and trains the whole body to yield under interaction loads.

Compliance and sampling-based refinement. Our compliance formulation follows impedance control [ 28 , 29 ] through force-dependent reference displacement, as used in related form by FACET [ 10 ] and GentleHumanoid [ 11 ] . Prior humanoid systems incorporate force through critic-only signals [ 8 ] , motion-derived compliance [ 12 , 11 ] , or explicit arm control modes [ 9 ] ; FACET [ 10 ] and Zhi et al. [ 14 ] train force-aware policies without human data but do not demonstrate humanoid loco-manipulation. CEER [ 13 ] is the closest interface to ours. Its G1 policy, distilled from a teacher trained on human motion, tracks compliant end-effector and root-pose commands with fixed impedance gains and no force observation at deployment, and its upstream source must supply the root pose, including height. Sampling-based planners can add online decisions above learned controllers without retraining [ 26 , 25 ] . Most closely, Sumo [ 24 ] searches a pretrained policy’s command space, including torso posture, toward task-specific goals in simulation. Ego-VCP [ 21 ] runs CEM above a frozen controller on a Unitree G1, choosing end-effector positions and body height through a learned world model and a task-specific value function. OCLO instead searches only the posture interface with a task-agnostic cost, refining a closed-form prior that can also run onboard alone.

2026-10-06.title: Learning Coordinated Visuomotor Box-Pushing from Solo Demonstrations
2026-10-06.authors: Ryusei Matsumoto , Mei Kinjo , Yoko Sasaki , Keisuke Okumura
2026-10-06.comment: . Accepted for presentation at the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Multi-robot imitation learning, particularly in settings where visuomotor policies are deployed in a communication-free, onboard decentralised style, represents an attractive paradigm.
However, its realisation remains insufficiently understood, largely due to the difficulty of collecting collective demonstrations, since a single operator cannot control many robots simultaneously.
Meanwhile, unlike coupled collaborative manipulation, many coordinated tasks achieve system-wide efficiency primarily through minimising inter-robot interference.
This structure motivates us to study whether data collected by a teleoperated single-robot can be leveraged for large-scale coordinated box-pushing as a testbed.
We systematically investigate dataset creation strategies and lightweight policy architectures.
In particular, experiments with up to 40 robots highlight the difficulty of acquiring effective coordination solely through passive observation of other operating robots, revealing a concrete bottleneck for multi-robot research.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Robotic learning from human demonstrations has become a powerful paradigm for acquiring capable visuomotor policies, ranging from autonomous driving to dexterous manipulation [ 8 , 10 , 6 ] .
However, extending imitation learning to the multi-robot domain remains substantially more challenging.
This is because, in addition to multi-robot-specific challenges such as task decomposition [ 15 ] and interaction modelling [ 16 ] , learning coordinated multi-robot policies suffers from the difficulty of collecting high-quality demonstration data for collective motions.

More concretely, a closer look at modern robotic learning systems reveals that teleoperation has become the dominant paradigm for collecting high-quality robot demonstrations [ 14 ] .
Although a human operator may be able to control a small number of robots simultaneously, obtaining demonstrations for large-scale collective behaviours rapidly becomes impractical due to the increasing cognitive and operational burden.
One possible solution is to employ multiple expert operators to jointly generate demonstrations; however, such an approach scales poorly as the number of robots increases.
Consequently, scalable multi-robot imitation learning has remained underdeveloped.

While a few recent studies have explored multi-robot imitation learning [ 30 , 25 ] , they typically rely on external infrastructure such as motion capture systems for globally consistent state estimation, limiting real-world deployment.
In contrast, modern single-robot systems increasingly achieve robust operation using only onboard sensing and computation [ 27 , 20 ] .
In a similar spirit, we argue that multi-robot coordination should likewise be achievable using compact onboard visuomotor policies that directly map pixels to actions under resource constraints.
Communication-free and fully decentralised approaches are further attractive for scalable deployment, avoiding bottlenecks such as latency, packet loss, and communication infrastructure dependencies.

These observations motivate the development of onboard, communication-free visuomotor policies for scalable multi-robot coordination learned from solo demonstrations .
We use “solo demonstrations” to mean demonstrations in which only a single robot is directly controlled by a human and only that robot’s observation-action pairs are recorded, even when other robots are present as static or autonomous context.
Our central question is then how such policies can be effectively attained.
Focusing on a coordinated box-pushing task in which multiple mobile robots collect scattered objects into a designated region to clean up a workspace ( Fig. 1 ), this study aims to provide empirical insights into the aforementioned challenge using large-scale deployments.

We specifically chose this task because it goes beyond mere multi-robot navigation while remaining closely connected to practical multi-robot applications such as collective construction [ 34 ] .
Although prior works have explored vision-based multi-robot tasks such as collision avoidance [ 45 ] and flocking [ 21 , 32 ] , our setting differs substantially in both task complexity with physical interaction and system scale, up to 40 robots.
Through this setup, our contribution is a systematic real-robot study of what kinds of solo demonstrations actually induce effective coordination, revealing a nuanced picture.
Surprisingly, data collected with static peer robots provides a strong and data-efficient signal, outperforming data collected among actively moving policy-controlled robots.
However, throughput does not scale linearly with robot count, suggesting that dynamic-agent data collection remains an unresolved bottleneck.
These findings highlight scalable multi-robot learning as a worthwhile open challenge.

# 2 Problem Setting

The task setup is illustrated in Fig. 1 .
A team of differential-drive robots [ 43 ] collects boxes (28 in the experiments) scattered throughout the white-walled workspace and transports them to a target bin located at the centre.
The bin is marked by a tower with coloured blocks for visual recognition, and the robots dispose of the collected boxes by dropping them into a hole at the base of the bin.
The workspace layout is available in the appendix.
Each robot operates solely on a Raspberry Pi running ROS 2, without GPU acceleration, and is equipped with a front-facing camera that provides ego-centric observations with a field of view of 120 ° 120\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} .
At each control step ( 5 Hz 5\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} ), robots receive RGB image observations and output velocity commands.
Crucially, the robots operate in a communication-free, onboard decentralised manner, without relying on external infrastructure such as localisation systems.
The markers mounted on top of the robots are used solely for measuring task completion progress.

We refer to this task as “coordinated” box pushing to deliberately distinguish it from “collaborative” counterparts (e.g., [ 33 , 41 , 13 ] ), which require tightly coupled problem solving that cannot be accomplished by a single robot alone.
Coordinated tasks can be completed by a single robot, while deploying multiple robots can improve task throughput through concurrent operation [ 35 ] .
Yet, inter-robot interference can significantly degrade performance.
For example, in our setup, robots may collide head-on and become stuck, steal boxes being transported by other robots, or even push other robots into the disposal hole; all of which were observed in practice.
In particular, the densely populated workspace often leads to congestion, making such coordination failures ubiquitous.
This distinction between coordinated and collaborative settings is fundamental to this study, as it enables us to train multi-robot policies from solo demonstrations.
