2026-10-06.title: Robust Surgical Robotic Instrument Tracking via Sequential Multi-Cue Fusion and Sim-to-Real Self-Training
2026-10-06.authors: Hanyang Hu , Zekai Liang , Florian Richter , Michael C. Yip
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Efficient and robust tracking of surgical robotic instruments is important for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery, yet remains challenging due to the complexity of surgical scenes and the unconventional geometry of surgical instruments.
Keypoint-based approaches are efficient, but their performance depends on reliable feature detection. Improving these detectors with real-world supervision is difficult because accurate real-world annotations are costly to obtain at scale. To address this limitation, we introduce a tracker-guided self-training framework that adapts a model pretrained on synthetic images to unlabeled real-world videos. Given measured robot joint states, an uncertainty-aware EKF recursively corrects the instrument pose and the observable joint angles by comparing projected model features with detected keypoints, shaft boundaries, and mask-derived cues. An RTS smoother subsequently refines the resulting trajectory, which is projected into pseudo-labels for fine-tuning the feature detector without laborious pose annotations. Experiments on real-world videos demonstrate consistent improvements from self-training across all evaluated keypoint metrics, and the resulting model outperforms prior approaches in both accuracy and runtime. The code and data will be released upon publication.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RMIS) has gained increasing attention for improving surgical safety and efficiency while reducing surgeon fatigue. Accurate, low-latency estimation of articulated instrument pose relative to the endoscopic camera is a fundamental perception capability in RMIS. Reliable pose feedback supports downstream tasks including visual servoing [ 1 ] , augmented-reality guidance [ 2 ] , and autonomous tissue manipulation [ 3 ] .

Modern approaches to markerless surgical robotic instrument pose estimation generally follow one of two paradigms: keypoint detection with PnP-based pose reconstruction [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , or instrument segmentation followed by iterative render-and-match optimization [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Given the computational complexity of rendering-based optimization methods, keypoint-based pose estimation methods are generally better suited to real-time robot control due to their fast inference speed. However, their accuracy depends heavily on reliable visual feature detection, which is prone to suboptimal endoscopic imaging conditions.

Compared with general robotics, the scarcity of accurately annotated real-world data makes improving feature detection robustness for surgical robots particularly challenging.
Prior work has explored synthetic data generation with photorealistic rendering to alleviate the scarcity of annotated real-world data [ 5 , 7 ] . Although these approaches have demonstrated promising feasibility and performance gains, a substantial sim-to-real gap remains. Synthetic data alone is often insufficient to achieve the robustness required for reliable deployment in real-world applications.

To address the scarcity of annotated real-world data in surgical robotics, we present a self-training framework for surgical instrument pose reconstruction that enables
sim-to-real transfer
using unlabeled real-world images. During adaptation, a distribution-aware Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) [ 12 ] , followed by a Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother [ 13 ] , aggregates observations across unlabeled real-world trajectories to obtain robust and temporally consistent pose estimates. These estimates are then projected back into the image space to generate pseudo-labels, which provide supervision for adapting the model to the target domain without requiring ground-truth annotations (Fig. 1 ).

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A self-training framework that leverages unlabeled real-world images to improve the accuracy and robustness of surgical robotic instrument feature detection.

An efficient, distribution-aware EKF that fuses complementary keypoints, shaft edges, and mask-derived observations for robust instrument pose tracking.

A pose-to-feature pseudo-labeling strategy that converts smoothed trajectories into feature annotations with consistency-based sample weighting.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Accurate tracking of articulated surgical instruments is challenging due to partial visibility, cable-driven kinematic errors, and limited endoscopic image quality. Earlier approaches relied on external sensing or fiducial markers [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] , or explicit modeling of transmission errors [ 18 ] and calibrating the remote center of motion (RCM) [ 19 ] , whereas recent markerless methods estimate instrument pose from visual observations using either feature-based or rendering-based approaches. Among feature-based methods, [ 4 ] model camera-to-robot calibration and kinematic errors as a lumped error transform, which they track using visual landmarks and shaft boundary observations. [ 6 ] extend this framework with learned shaft edge detection and pixel-based probabilistic observation models, while [ 7 ] introduce unified keypoint and edge detection together with an efficient geometry-based pose solver. EKFs have also been used to fuse visual observations with robot kinematics for instrument tracking and online hand-eye calibration [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] . On the other hand, rendering-based methods exploit dense instrument shape information by comparing rendered silhouettes with instrument segmentation through iterative optimization [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . [ 8 ] optimize instrument pose through differentiable rendering and demonstrate improved robustness over PnP-based methods, while [ 10 ] achieve real-time tracking using evolutionary optimization and batch rendering. However, rendering-based methods remain computationally demanding and are sensitive to incomplete or noisy segmentation caused by occlusion and complex surgical scenes.

Outside surgical robotics, self-supervised learning and self-training have been explored to adapt pose estimation models using unlabeled real-world data. CtRNet [ 24 , 25 ] uses differentiable pose estimation and rendering for self-supervision to improve segmentation and keypoint detection on unlabeled real-world images. More closely related to tracker-supported self-training, [ 26 ] fuse object pose predictions with robot odometry in a pose graph to generate temporally consistent pseudo-labels. [ 27 ] use an adaptive unscented Kalman filter to refine spacecraft pose estimates for online self-training.
These works demonstrate how geometric and temporal consistency can provide supervision for pose learning without laborious data annotation.
However, these approaches have not been adapted to RMIS, where partial visibility of the instrument, suboptimal endoscopic imaging conditions, and complex tissue backgrounds make both feature detection and pose tracking substantially less reliable.

2026-10-06.title: FLEX-WAM: Flexible Block-Causal World-Action Models for Long-Horizon Imagination and Planning
2026-10-06.authors: R. Khorrambakht , Joseph Amigo , Félix Lebel , Leon Seetoo , Jean Ponce , Zhenzhen Li , Ludovic Righetti
2026-10-06.abstract: World–action models (WAMs) promise a unified model that predicts action-conditioned futures, generates feasible actions, and supports planning in imagination. However, existing joint video–action models often use computationally heavy, fixed-horizon backbones ill-suited to streaming inference and stable long-horizon open-loop rollouts. We introduce FLEX-WAM, a Flexible and Efficient Block-Causal World–Action Model for unified simulation and policy inference. FLEX-WAM supports variable-length contexts and non-causal prediction horizons, as well as infinite autoregressive generation frame by frame or block by block. Its block-causal, KV-cacheable architecture combines axial attention and blockwise diffusion forcing to enable efficient real-time rollout and deployment-time latency–throughput tradeoffs without retraining. Joint training can nevertheless produce plausible futures that weakly respond to commanded actions. We address this failure mode by balancing state and action flow-matching gradient contributions across the state–action diffusion-noise grid and regulating world-model sampling using Forward-Dynamics (FD) elasticity , an efficient training-time proxy for action responsiveness. Across simulated and real-world datasets, FLEX-WAM achieves superior multi-step prediction quality and latency while producing stable joint state–action rollouts for thousands of steps. As a joint action proposer and simulator within MCTS, it solves long-horizon PushT and all five OGBench Puzzle-4x4 tasks entirely in imagination. On a bimanual OpenArm-based robot, a single checkpoint jointly serves as a play policy and expected-outcome predictor, enabling real-time identification and collection of model–reality mismatches for future self-improvement.

2026-10-06.title: Social Navigation for Tour-guide Robot
2026-10-06.authors: Vikram Shree , Jose Nino
2026-10-06.comment: . Accepted at the 5th Workshop on Social Robot Navigation, IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: We propose a force-based model for social navigation of a tour-guide robot. Social forces due to various factors like obstacles, user position and heading, have been accounted for in the model. We claim that each one of these forces makes the robot more sociable to the user and we design an experimental setup for evaluation. In the experiment, the user follows an autonomous robot to a destination in a known map, while undertaking a few simple sub-tasks in the middle, which serve as distractions. For each participant, we run several rounds of the experiment, each with different forces and a shortest path, A*-search baseline model. Using per-round subjective indicators, we propose to study the effect of our force model on constructs such as: follow-ability, perceived safety, and perceived intelligence.
2026-10-06.introduction:
In this work, we present a social force model for a tour-guide robot and conduct experiments to study its effect on human’s perception about the robot. As the globe is becoming more connected, cities around the world are attracting more tourists every year. As a result, more people are exploring public spaces like museums, parks and shopping malls. Often, these huge public spaces are clumsy and time consuming to navigate through, especially for elderly people. This motivates the development of a tour-guide robot, which helps the tourists in navigating to their destinations, thus, making the tour more fulfilling and productive.

To be a successful tour-guide robot, it needs to properly follow the expectations of tourists, thus adding social constraints on robot’s behavior. For example, it is reasonable for a tourist to expect that the robot moves at a safe speed, so that they can follow it without rushing through the scene. Thus, traditional shortest path planning approaches need to be adapted in this scenario to account for social constraints imposed by the user. In this work, we are interested in evaluating the benefits of following social constraints from a human’s perspective.

The main focus of social navigation research in the past years has been to help the robot stay farther away from humans in crowded environments; however, there is little work in the case when the robot has to guide a human to a destination. In scenarios, where the robot has to simply reach a destination, the humans are treated as obstacles and thus, there is a penalty associated with coming too close to the humans. In contrast, a tour-guide robot needs to stay close to the tourist, so that they do not get lost in the crowd. Furthermore, it should move in a manner that makes it easier for the tourist to follow. These challenges motivate our social force model where the robot is acting as the leader and is tasked to guide the tourist to their destination, in a friendly manner. Fig. 1 shows schematic of a social tour-guide robot, helping out a user to navigate safely to the goal location, while following social constraints.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Robot Navigation in Presence of Humans

Social constraints first entered into navigation with a promise of keeping safe distance between the robot and humans [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Bellarbi et al. [ 1 ] established social rules that allow the robot to navigate smoothly and socially in indoor environments. Ramon-Vigo et al. [ 2 ] leveraged inverse reinforcement learning to transfer skills of human navigation behavior to a robot. Perez-Higueras et al. [ 3 ] take a cost-based optimization route where a social cost map is learned from expert demonstrations. However, these works do not address the challenges that arise when the robot is leading a human, which is necessary for a tour-guide robot.

Few researchers have studied the problem of human interaction with guide robots [ 4 , 5 ] . Shen et al. [ 4 ] explored the “object approaching” behavior for guide robots in a museum. Azenkot et al. [ 5 ] introduced multiple modes of guidance for blind people. However, these works focused on human-robot communication, and social navigation constraints were ignored.

## II-B Social Force Model

Researchers first proposed to add pseudo forces onto the robot to mimic socially acceptable behavior [ 6 , 7 ] . One of the earliest works on social forces is by Helbing et al. [ 6 ] where the authors added social forces owing to the presence of humans and intermediate goals in the environment. Zhang et al. [ 7 ] incorporate attractive and repulsive forces for the robot to address two social constraints: speed control to stay close to the user and maintaining safe distance from obstacles in the environment. However, they fail to evaluate the effect of those forces through human experiments and surveys.

Our work extends the existing social force model for tour-guide robot, developed by Zhang et al. [ 7 ] , by adding additional force due to the limited field of view of the human.
In addition to adapting the speed and maintaining safe distance from obstacles, we add attractive force in order to impel the robot to stay close to the heading direction of the user. Furthermore, to establish the utility of the force model, we evaluate the effect of each force on the user through rigorous human-participant studies.

2026-10-06.title: EvoMem-VLA: State-Evolution Memory for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
2026-10-06.authors: Yuheng Na , Zhide Zhong , Junjie He , Junfeng Li , Haodong Yan , Jiaan Wang , Jiaguan Zhu , Yangyang Zheng , Tianyu Huang , Haoang Li
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on current observations and lose task-relevant evidence once it leaves view, limiting performance on long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. Existing efforts incorporate compressed historical features or sparse visual keyframes. However, isolated snapshots can leave the policy uncertain about what changed during past interactions and which action should follow. To overcome this limitation, we propose EvoMem-VLA, which constructs state-evolution memory by explicitly encoding and retaining observed changes between historical states. These change representations preserve evidence of interaction outcomes, allowing the policy to track task progress beyond isolated snapshots. Specifically, we introduce conditional delta tokenization to encode ordered frame pairs into directional, source-conditioned delta tokens, each associated with its corresponding state evidence. A shared VLM backbone supports task-adaptive routing: normal long-horizon tasks follow a direct action route, whereas multi-stage tasks use a subtask route that generates an executable subtask as an additional input for action generation. With a single jointly trained policy for each simulation benchmark, EvoMem-VLA achieves success rates of 80.7% on RMBench, 82.0% on RoboMME and 83.8% across four real-world tasks spanning two robot embodiments. These results represent substantial improvements over the previous state of the art in all three evaluation settings.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained visual and semantic knowledge to robot control, enabling increasingly general instruction following and manipulation across tasks ( Brohan and others, 2023 ; Kim and others, 2024 ; Black and others, 2024 ; Zheng and others, 2025a ) . However, their performance remains limited on long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. This is because a policy conditioned only on the current observation and instruction lacks access to past events that determine future actions ( Koo and others, 2026 ; Shi and others, 2026 ; Yang and others, 2026a ) . As a result, the policy may lose track of task progress and generate an incorrect action.

Recently, there have been efforts to augment VLAs with historical memory. Existing approaches represent history using discrete state features ( Koo and others, 2026 ; Shi and others, 2026 ; Li and others, 2023 ) or sparse visual keyframes ( Yang and others, 2026a ; Chen and others, 2026b ; Sridhar et al., 2026 ) . However, task-relevant changes often remain implicit in the stored history (Figure 1 (a)). Long-horizon control requires the policy to relate remembered states to changes during task execution. Without an explicit representation of these changes, the policy must extract them from sparse state evidence when determining task progress and selecting the next action. This motivates a memory representation that retains both what was observed and how it changed relative to an earlier observation.

To address this limitation, we propose EvoMem-VLA, a state-evolution memory paradigm that explicitly encodes and retains observed interaction changes between sparse historical observations (Figure 1 (b)). By linking change representations to corresponding visual states, this memory preserves evidence of interaction changes. Therefore, compared with VLAs that rely on discrete state memory, our policy can distinguish interaction processes that discrete history alone leaves ambiguous and use explicit change evidence to generate the appropriate next action. We instantiate this paradigm as a unified VLA with multi-scale state-evolution memory and task-adaptive routing. Specifically, to explicitly represent the visual change from the source frame to the target frame, we introduce conditional delta tokenization ( Kerssies and others, 2026 ) to encode ordered frame pairs sampled from recent observations and selected keyframes into delta tokens. We then construct state-evolution memory by arranging these delta tokens alongside the initial frame, recent historical frames, and selected keyframes ( Yang and others, 2026a ) in temporal order. Next, the state-evolution memory is fed into a shared VLM backbone together with the task instruction and current observation. Additionally, the VLM backbone supports task-adaptive routing: for normal long-horizon tasks without multi-stage planning, it predicts actions directly; for multi-stage tasks, it first generates an executable subtask and then appends it to the original input context to guide action generation ( Yang and others, 2026b ) .

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose EvoMem-VLA, a state-evolution memory paradigm that explicitly retains observed interaction changes alongside historical states. This enables policies to use remembered change evidence for action generation rather than infer what happened from sparse historical states alone.

We propose EvoMem-VLA, a state-evolution memory paradigm that explicitly retains observed interaction changes alongside historical states. This enables policies to use remembered change evidence for action generation rather than infer what happened from sparse historical states alone.

We develop a unified VLA that organizes conditional delta tokens with initial, recent, and keyframe observations into multi-scale state-evolution memory. Its shared VLM backbone supports task-adaptive routing for direct action prediction or action generation conditioned on an executable subtask.

EvoMem-VLA achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 80.7% on RMBench ( Chen and others, 2026a ) , 82.0% on RoboMME ( Dai et al., 2026 ) , and 83.8% across four real-world tasks on two robot embodiments. We use one jointly trained policy per simulation benchmark, with RMBench ablations further validating the contribution of conditional delta tokenization.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language representations to language-conditioned robot control ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Shukor et al., 2025 ) . RT-2 and OpenVLA formulate action generation as autoregressive prediction over discretized action tokens ( Brohan and others, 2023 ; Kim and others, 2024 ) . More recent approaches introduce continuous or hybrid action generation ( Kim et al., 2025 ) : π 0 \pi_{0} uses a flow-matching action expert ( Black and others, 2024 ) , CogACT and DexVLA condition diffusion-based action experts on VLM features ( Li et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2025 ) , and HybridVLA combines autoregressive prediction with diffusion action generation ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . X-VLA studies policy scaling across heterogeneous robot embodiments ( Zheng and others, 2025a ) . Despite advances in action representation and policy scaling, these models do not inherently maintain a persistent record of task execution. When earlier evidence leaves the observation window, a policy may lose track of what it has observed or completed, even when this history is needed to disambiguate visually similar states requiring different actions.

History-aware policies address this limitation by retaining or transforming past observations ( Zhang and others, 2025 ; Ni and others, 2025 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Torne et al., 2026 ) . RoboFlamingo compresses temporal vision-language features into an LSTM policy state ( Li and others, 2023 ) , while TraceVLA overlays tracked point trajectories on current images as visual motion prompts ( Zheng and others, 2025b ) . HAMLET encodes observations as temporally discriminative moment tokens and aggregates them through a lightweight causal memory module ( Koo and others, 2026 ) . MemoryVLA maintains perceptual and cognitive representations in long-term memory and retrieves relevant entries for action prediction ( Shi and others, 2026 ) . EventVLA retains the initial observation and a recent history window alongside event-triggered keyframes in bounded memory ( Yang and others, 2026a ) . MemER uses a high-level policy to select and consolidate keyframes, predict the current language subtask, and delegate execution to a separate low-level controller ( Sridhar et al., 2026 ) . Complementary approaches use language and reasoning to guide action generation ( Zawalski and others, 2024 ; Belkhale et al., 2024 ; Huang and others, 2025 ) : on multi-subtask data, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} predicts a semantic subtask before generating the corresponding action chunk ( Physical Intelligence and others, 2025 ) , while WLA-0 jointly learns textual-subtask prediction, future-state prediction, and action synthesis ( Yang and others, 2026b ) . These methods provide remembered states, motion cues, and subtask context through distinct interfaces. However, the cited state-oriented memories lack dedicated inter-state change representations, while TraceVLA’s short-window motion traces are not integrated with sparse long-term state evidence. MemER provides history to its high-level policy, but its controller receives only the predicted subtask, current images, and robot state. In contrast, EvoMem-VLA organizes multi-scale visual states and learned inter-state changes in state-evolution memory shared by subtask and action prediction. Tasks without textual-subtask supervision retain a direct action route through the same VLA policy.

2026-10-06.title: RMMBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robotic Mobile Manipulation
2026-10-06.authors: Huapeng Li , Fuxiang Feng , Jinqiu Fan , Shuo Yang , Fengjiao Chen , Xuezhi Cao , Ran Song , Wei Zhang
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted to the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), November 9-12, 2026, Austin, TX, USA
2026-10-06.abstract: Although the advancement of vision-language models (VLMs) has endowed robots with enhanced environmental understanding and task reasoning, a comprehensive evaluation methodology is important to advance the integration of VLMs in robotic navigation and manipulation. However, current benchmarks lack a comprehensive method to evaluate diverse robotic tasks, and evaluation metrics remain relatively constrained, making it difficult to assess the embodied capabilities of VLMs in a thorough and fine-grained manner. To address this issue, we propose RMMBench, an evaluation benchmark that requires robots to understand language instructions and perform long-horizon tasks in continuous spaces. RMMBench seamlessly integrates high- and low-level embodied tasks into a unified framework, constructing a "navigation-manipulation" task suite comprising 70 canonical task scenarios that range from localized manipulation to long-horizon composite navigation. The results reveal that leading VLMs still face major challenges in spatial localization when performing mobile manipulation tasks, and also highlight the necessity of enhancing the spatial perception capability of robots during long-horizon interactions. 2026-10-06.title: TUCO: Curating Simulation Demonstrations for Sim-to-Real Robot Policy Co-Training
2026-10-06.authors: Ning Zhu , Mengfei Zhao , Yikai Tang , Zhangyujie Sun , Peihao Li , Dongyue Ni , Jindou Jia , Jianfei Yang
2026-10-06.abstract:
Simulation demonstrations can supplement scarce real-world data for robot policy co-training.
However, the value of using data curation to actively select these demonstrations for sim-to-real co-training remains underexplored. Existing curation methods also lack a unified criterion for measuring trajectory-level utility and set-level coverage from closed-loop target behavior. To address these gaps, we present the first systematic study of data curation for sim-to-real robot policy co-training and propose T rajectory-level U tility and set-level C overage O ptimization ( TUCO ). TUCO uses influence functions to trace how each source demonstration affects target-domain scoring rollouts.
Our key insight is that these effects can be decomposed into an overall contribution to target return and variation across rollouts, providing a common closed-loop basis for measuring trajectory utility and set coverage. We further propose a performance-aligned subset optimizer that combines these measures in a unified curation objective to reduce redundancy and select complementary demonstrations. Extensive experiments on RoboMimic and OmniReset establish the value of active simulation data curation for sim-to-real policy co-training and show that TUCO achieves state-of-the-art performance across single-simulator, sim-to-sim, and sim-to-real settings.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Imitation learning is essential for robot manipulation, but the amount of available training data is limited by the cost of real-world teleoperation ( Mandlekar et al., 2022 ; Belkhale et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2025a ; Saxena et al., 2025 ; Jia et al., 2026a ; Jia et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) .
Automated data generation in simulation offers a scalable alternative ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Hou et al., 2026 ) , motivating sim-to-real co-training that combines abundant simulation demonstrations from a source domain with limited real demonstrations from the target
deployment domain ( Maddukuri et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ) . However, domain shifts make source demonstrations differ in their utility to the target policy, while large source pools may include redundant or simulation-specific behaviors. Directly using the full pool can therefore increase training costs and introduce negative transfer ( Dass et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . This raises a central but unaddressed question for sim-to-real co-training: which simulation demonstrations should be selected to improve target-domain policy performance?

Robot data curation aims to improve policy performance by constructing training subsets that exclude unhelpful or redundant demonstrations, with existing methods broadly falling into three groups. (1) Quality-based approaches filter noisy demonstrations using data statistics and execution cues ( Belkhale et al., 2023 ; Hejna et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Sojib et al., 2026 ) . They offer efficient offline selection but provide no direct link to closed-loop performance ( Bedi, 2026 ) . (2) Utility-based approaches estimate downstream value from target similarity, validation loss, or policy behavior ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2023 ; Memmel et al., 2025 ; Dass et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Influence Function -based methods are highly promising since they can estimate how reweighting a training example changes the learned model and a downstream metric ( Koh & Liang, 2017 ) . CUPID ( Agia et al., 2025 ) applies influence functions to closed-loop evaluation by aggregating each demonstration’s effects across policy rollouts with their returns.
Although the resulting scalar utility connects data selection to target performance, independent ranking does not account for relationships within the selected subset and can select redundant demonstrations while overlooking complementary ones. (3) Diversity-based approaches explicitly model these relationships to reduce redundancy and improve coverage ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Sirigiri et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2024 ) , but their criteria typically measure
differences in representation space without grounding them in closed-loop target behavior. Under
domain shift, such differences may reflect simulator-specific variation that offers little support for target-policy execution. These limitations yield another important question: How can trajectory-level utility and set-level coverage be jointly optimized in closed-loop performance?

Our key observation is that the influence of a demonstration across closed-loop target-policy rollouts can be explicitly decomposed into two signals: an overall contribution to target return and the remaining variation across rollouts, providing a common closed-loop basis for measuring trajectory-level utility and set-level coverage. The overall contribution indicates how much a demonstration supports target performance, while relationships among the remaining components reveal redundancy and complementarity across demonstrations. However, since variation across rollouts alone does not imply a positive contribution to target performance, subset selection should retain demonstrations whose effects align with target success and favor candidates that add new closed-loop support beyond the current subset.

Beyond these methodological limitations, existing data curation research has a limited evaluation scope. Most studies focus on single-domain settings or transfer between simulators, or among real-world datasets ( Du et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2025b ; Memmel et al., 2025 ; Hejna et al., 2025a ; Dass et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , leaving sim-to-real policy co-training underexplored. Meanwhile, sim-to-real co-training studies primarily examine mixing ratios and training strategies ( Maddukuri et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) , with limited attention to which simulation demonstrations best support real-world policy learning. We aim to extend data curation from single-simulator and sim-to-sim settings to sim-to-real co-training through a unified protocol. Within this
broader evaluation, we explore whether actively selecting simulation demonstrations improves real-world policy performance when the numbers of source and target demonstrations are held fixed.

To our knowledge, we conduct the first systematic study of simulation data curation for sim-to-real robot policy co-training and introduce T rajectory-level U tility and set-level C overage O ptimization ( TUCO ), a novel set-level curation framework grounded in target-policy closed-loop behavior. First, we present a closed-loop influence decomposition that separates each
demonstration’s overall contribution to target return from its variation across target-domain scoring rollouts, providing a common basis for measuring trajectory-level utility and set-level coverage. Second, we introduce a performance-aligned subset optimizer that combines both measures in a unified curation objective. It favors demonstrations that support target success and complement the current subset, reducing redundancy during selection. We establish a unified evaluation protocol on RoboMimic ( Mandlekar et al., 2022 ) and OmniReset ( Yin et al., 2026 ) spanning single-simulator, sim-to-sim, and sim-to-real settings and show that TUCO achieves state-of-the-art curation performance. More importantly,
we show that active simulation data curation improves sim-to-real policy co-training: TUCO improves over full-pool co-training by 65.0, 35.0, and 80.0 percentage points ( pp \mathrm{pp} ) across the three real-world tasks and outperforms random selection with the same numbers of source and target demonstrations.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Data Curation for Robot Learning. Existing approaches assess demonstrations through quality, utility, or diversity. Quality-based methods use
statistical dependence ( Hejna et al., 2025b ) and execution cues ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Sojib et al., 2026 ) to estimate demonstration quality. Utility-based methods condition selection on target-data similarity ( Du et al., 2023 ; Memmel et al., 2025 ) or estimated training contributions ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Dass et al., 2026 ) , with influence functions relating these contributions to
imitation loss ( Lee et al., 2026 ) and closed-loop return ( Agia et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Diversity-based
methods construct subsets through deduplication and trajectory diversity ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Sirigiri et al., 2026 ) or distribution matching ( Feng et al., 2025 ) .

Cross-Domain Robot Co-Training. Simulation data generation ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) supports co-training with limited
real demonstrations. Composition-oriented studies examine simulation scale and mixing ratios ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Maddukuri et al., 2025 ) , while alignment methods improve source-target compatibility through observation-action alignment ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) and visual
invariance ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Complementary approaches regulate source contributions through learned
mixture weights ( Hejna et al., 2025a ; Sima et al., 2026 ) and training schedules ( Wei et al., 2026 ) .

2026-10-06.title: Optimal Control with Learned Critics under Unmodeled State Dependencies
2026-10-06.authors: Philipp Schoch , Markus Ryll
2026-10-06.comment: Keywords: Model Predictive Control, Model-Based Reinforcement Learning, iLQR, Value Function Approximation. Presented at 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin TX, USA
2026-10-06.abstract: Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides a structured and constraint-aware mechanism for decision-making, but its reliance on optimization-friendly analytical dynamics models limits its use in tasks with contacts and other hard-to-model state dependencies. Model-free reinforcement learning avoids explicit modeling assumptions but typically requires large amounts of interaction data. We present a learning-based MPC framework that combines the data efficiency and structure of local model-based planning with learned components that compensate for incomplete dynamics and finite-horizon myopia. The method augments a nominal analytical model with a residual dynamics network that learns missing state-dependent effects from data and combines the resulting planner with a learned action-value critic that injects long-horizon MDP structure into the local iLQR optimization. To make this practical at reinforcement-learning scale, we develop a GPU-accelerated batched iLQR solver that evaluates learned dynamics and critic networks inside the optimal-control loop and solves thousands of trajectory-optimization problems in parallel. The complete system is integrated into a robotics simulator, enabling scalable model-based reinforcement learning under incomplete dynamics. Experiments on biased and incompletely modeled control tasks show that the approach improves closed-loop control performance while preserving the model-based structure needed for efficient constrained trajectory optimization.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Computing optimal control policies for agents acting in stochastic environments is a central challenge in sequential decision making.
Formally, this amounts to solving a Markov Decision Process (MDP) [ 17 ] : finding a policy that maximizes expected cumulative reward over potentially infinite horizons.
The field has produced a rich landscape of approaches, broadly organized into trajectory optimization, model-free reinforcement learning (RL), and model-based reinforcement learning methods [ 13 ] .

Model Predictive Control (MPC) performs trajectory optimization in a receding-horizon fashion, enabling precise control and explicit satisfaction of state and input constraints. However, MPC requires an optimization-friendly analytical dynamics model, often difficult or impossible to derive for systems involving contacts or other highly nonlinear effects, and breaks down if relevant state variables remain unmodeled. Contact-rich tasks are a representative case, because making and breaking contact introduces discontinuous phase boundaries over which gradient information can become uninformative [ 16 ] , while classical multi-phase or mixed-integer formulations lead to large nonlinear programs that are brittle and rarely compatible with real-time replanning [ 7 ] .
A second limitation is the finite horizon itself. MPC applies a finite-horizon surrogate to an infinite-horizon MDP, so a horizon that is too short can make the controller greedy, trap it in local minima, or prevent task completion when intermediate subgoals must be reached before the final objective becomes attainable [ 6 ] .
A third limitation is that standard MPC formulations operate on explicit state variables and analytical models, making it nontrivial to use high-dimensional sensor observations such as rgb or depth images directly inside the planner.

Model-free RL sidesteps these limitations: learned policies are cheap at inference and can consume high-dimensional observations.
However, model-free methods are notoriously sample-inefficient, scale poorly with state-space dimensionality, and struggle with long-horizon tasks where reward-sparsity impedes exploration [ 17 , 1 ] .

Model-based RL promises to combine the data efficiency of planning with the flexibility of learning [ 13 ] .
A compelling paradigm in this space is to use MPC as a critic: the planner provides a structured, locally accurate estimate of the action-value function, which can be used to bootstrap a global Q Q -approximator which after training supplies long-horizon guidance back to the MPC, allowing even to correct for mismatches in the dynamics model. [ 3 ] demonstrates this in the setting of gradient-free sampling-based control.
A key remaining challenge is that MPC critics still require an accurate dynamics model, a requirement that fails whenever relevant state variables lack a tractable analytical description, e.g. object contact dynamics in manipulation.

In this work, we develop a learning-augmented constrained MPC framework that embeds two learned components directly into the planner. A residual dynamics model augments the nominal analytical model and exposes otherwise unmodeled state dependencies to optimization, while a learned critic injects global MDP information into the finite-horizon objective to reduce myopia and improve guidance under multi-phase cost-structure; unlike in sampling-based MPC [ 3 ] , the critic enters the Riccati recursion through its first- and second-order derivatives. Following the DDP formulation, we realize this approach with a GPU-accelerated batched ALM-iLQR solver that integrates both learned components inside the optimal-control loop and scales to thousands of parallel environments, enabling efficient model-based reinforcement learning.

Core contributions: (i) a constrained MPC formulation that combines residual dynamics learning with a learned critic, and (ii) a learning-based DDP-style solver that makes this formulation practical for model-based reinforcement-learning, scaling to thousands of parallel environments.

2026-10-06.title: VAMPS: Visual and Motor Policies from Sampling-Based Planning
2026-10-06.authors: Mohamed Yassine Kabouri , Pietro Noah Crestaz , Quang-Nam Nguyen , Qilong Cheng , Ludovic Righetti , Nicolas Mansard
2026-10-06.abstract: Learning robot policies directly on physical systems remains difficult because data collection is costly and policy exploration can be unsafe. We introduce Visual and Motor Policies from Sampling-Based Planning (VAMPS), a framework that uses Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control to train reusable policies without human demonstrations. VAMPS supports two training modes. For one-step proprioceptive policies, it operates iteratively in simulation: the policy warm-starts MPPI, and the refined trajectories provide new supervision as the policy changes. A learned terminal value improves short-horizon planning, while an Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) critic guides the policy update. Iterative refinement outperforms training once on frozen MPPI data, and we transfer the learned locomotion policy to a Unitree Go2. For visuomotor policies, VAMPS operates directly from real-robot data. MPPI uses task-specific state estimates to plan and execute trajectories while recording RGB and sensor observations on a Flexiv Rizon 10S. Action Chunking with Transformers predicts action chunks, reducing the effective prediction horizon, and is trained offline on this fixed dataset. We demonstrate visuomotor pick-and-place and force-aware whiteboard erasing. In the latter task, the policy additionally observes the measured 6 6 -D wrench and desired normal force. These results show that VAMPS can learn policies either in simulation followed by hardware transfer or directly from autonomously collected real-robot data.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Learning directly on physical robots, through interaction and sensor feedback, remains a major challenge, despite being the most direct route to acquiring effective sensorimotor behaviors. This is especially compelling for contact-rich robotics, including pick-and-place manipulation, force-regulated interaction, and quadruped locomotion. Current learning methods do not yet solve this problem at scale: they typically rely on human demonstrations or move exploration to simulation before transferring the resulting policy to hardware. This work takes a step toward methods that can autonomously and efficiently collect sensorimotor experience on robots and turn it into better policies.

This objective has been pursued through three main routes. Imitation learning methods such as Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [ 35 ] and Diffusion Policy [ 5 ] clone human teleoperation and learn rich behaviors. Their bottleneck is data: demonstrations are expensive, performance is bounded by the operator, and cloning a fixed dataset leads to compounding errors [ 27 ] . DAgger [ 27 ] corrects those states by querying an expert policy on states visited by the learned policy. Reinforcement learning [ 12 ] needs no demonstration, but it has to explore, and exploration is a bottleneck on contact-rich tasks with short episodes [ 21 ] . Trajectory Optimization (TO) [ 34 , 13 ] , in contrast, optimizes individual rollouts for a given cost. While gradient-based TO relies on derivatives that are challenging to compute in contact-rich tasks, sampling-based planners [ 31 ] handle non-smooth contact dynamics and run in parallel on GPUs [ 32 ] . Yet their search space scales exponentially with the planning horizon [ 7 ] .
They are commonly used in receding horizon, which requires online replanning and does not directly produce a reusable policy.

The complementarity between trajectory optimization and policy learning has long been recognized, notably by Guided Policy Search (GPS) [ 17 ] and subsequent optimizer-policy coupling methods [ 23 , 19 ] . This perspective combines the precision of model-based optimization with the fast execution of a learned controller, while avoiding direct exploration by the learned policy. We build on this principle and use MPPI as a behavior generator from a model and a task cost.

In this work, we introduce Visual and Motor Policies from Sampling-Based Planning (VAMPS), a framework that distills trajectories generated by MPPI into reusable robot policies without human demonstrations or simulator gradients. MPPI plans with a model, a task cost and task-specific state estimates, while the learned policy maps the observations available at deployment directly to actions. VAMPS supports two training modes that share this planner-to-policy principle.

VAMPS-Iterative trains a one-step proprioceptive policy in simulation. Small prediction errors can move such a policy away from the states in a fixed training dataset and compound over time [ 27 ] . The policy therefore repeatedly warm-starts MPPI, which refines its behavior and provides new supervision as the policy evolves. This loop does not require simulator gradients. A learned terminal value improves short-horizon planning, while an IQL [ 15 ] critic guides the policy update through Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) [ 25 ] . We train the policy in simulation and transfer it to a real robot.

VAMPS-Batch uses MPPI to autonomously collect a real-robot dataset and train a visuomotor policy from it. MPPI uses task-specific state estimates to plan and execute trajectories on the robot while RGB images, robot sensors and actions are recorded. ACT [ 35 ] predicts action chunks, reducing the effective prediction horizon. For the tasks considered here, we collect the MPPI episodes once, freeze the dataset and train ACT offline. At deployment, ACT maps images and robot sensors directly to action chunks and does not use the task-specific state estimates.

Our contributions are threefold. (1) We introduce V isual a nd M otor P olicies from S ampling-Based Planning ( VAMPS ), a framework that uses MPPI to train reusable policies either in simulation or directly from real-robot data. (2) VAMPS-Iterative trains one-step proprioceptive policies. We show that iterative refinement outperforms training once on frozen MPPI data, a simple behavioral-cloning coupling between MPPI and the policy is sufficient, and a learned terminal value improves short-horizon planning. We transfer the resulting locomotion policy to a Unitree Go2. (3) VAMPS-Batch uses MPPI to autonomously collect a fixed real-robot dataset without human demonstrations and trains chunked ACT policies on it. We demonstrate this mode on pick-and-place and force-aware whiteboard erasing with a Flexiv Rizon 10S.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

GPS [ 17 ] and its visuomotor extension [ 16 ] pioneered the idea of using local TO controllers to supervise policy learning. In the same cycle of ideas, [ 23 ] formalized the TO-policy coupling via ADMM to enforce agreement between them. [ 19 ] later used augmented-Lagrangian updates and sensitivity information to improve this coupling. CACTO-SL instead combines TO with actor-critic learning and uses the policy to warm-start the optimizer [ 1 ] . More recently, [ 11 ] trained diffusion policies to warm-start gradient-based TO. Their method alternates policy learning and trajectory refinement, and uses the feedback gains returned by the optimizer in the training loss. These methods rely mainly on gradient-based TO and differentiable dynamics.

PI 2 GPS [ 4 ] replaces the gradient-based local optimizer with the derivative-free PI 2 algorithm. However, it initializes the local policies from kinesthetic demonstrations and pretrains its visual features on a pose-prediction task. This work studies how to scale the GPS idea using modern tools from derivative-free optimization [ 14 ] , offline RL [ 18 ] and imitation learning [ 35 ] . VAMPS-Iterative uses GPU-parallel MPPI in receding horizon. It requires a model and a task cost but does not require simulator derivatives, feedback gains or a human warm start. The policy repeatedly warm-starts MPPI, which refines its behavior and provides new supervision. To improve short-horizon planning, we introduce a learned terminal value trained on the planner transitions. To filter the planner actions, we train an IQL critic [ 15 ] on MPPI trajectories and policy rollouts, and use its advantage in AWR [ 25 ] to give more weight to high-advantage actions.

Visuomotor imitation methods such as ACT [ 35 ] and Diffusion Policy [ 5 ] predict sequences of actions from visual observations. Action-sequence prediction reduces the effective prediction horizon and limits the accumulation of one-step errors. These methods are commonly trained from human demonstrations. VAMPS-Batch instead uses MPPI to collect real-robot RGB, sensor and action episodes, and trains ACT on the resulting fixed dataset. Task-specific state estimates guide MPPI during data collection but are not provided to the deployed policy. For force-aware erasing, MPPI records RGB images, the measured wrench and the desired normal force, and ACT learns a force-conditioned policy from these episodes. We deploy the proprioceptive policy learned by VAMPS-Iterative on a Unitree Go2 and the visuomotor policies learned by VAMPS-Batch on a Flexiv Rizon 10S.

2026-10-06.title: CoDance: Learning Reactive and Compliant Human-Humanoid Interaction from Video
2026-10-06.authors: Zhuoqun Chen , Shucheng Jia , Boyuan Chen
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-06.comment: Project website: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Partnered human-humanoid interaction couples locomotion with continuous physical contact. A humanoid needs to coordinate with a person’s motion while responding to interaction forces and maintaining stable and natural movement. We present CoDance , a framework for learning reactive and compliant human-humanoid interaction from video. We study partnered dancing as a challenging instantiation, where a humanoid coordinates its footsteps with a moving partner and maintains continuous two-hand contact. Given a single video of two human dancers, CoDance retargets their motions into a robot reference and a moving partner. We introduce a multi-link compliance augmentation that transforms the kinematic demonstration into force-aware training data by adapting the robot reference under structured forces at both hands. Policies trained on this data follow the observed partner while preserving the demonstrated locomotion style and responding compliantly to physical interaction. In simulation, the policies adapt their footsteps to changes in the partner and reproduce approximately 80% of the wrist displacement encoded by the augmented demonstrations. On a physical humanoid, CoDance enables sustained two-hand dancing with a human partner including repeated transitions between forward and backward motions.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Humanoid robots are increasingly capable of reproducing dynamic and expressive human motion through advances in motion imitation, retargeting, and reinforcement learning [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, most learned humanoid behaviors remain focused on the robot in isolation, tracking a motion reference or following a locomotion command while treating external contact primarily as a disturbance. Physical interaction with a person poses a unique challenge. When two partners walk, carry, guide, or dance together, their motions are continuously coupled through both observation and contact. The robot needs to adapt its motion to the partner and accommodate interaction forces while preserving balance and the natural movement.

We study this problem through partnered dancing, a demanding form of sustained physical human-humanoid interaction. The robot coordinates its footsteps with a moving partner while preserving the demonstrated locomotion style and maintaining continuous two-hand contact. Differences in timing, position, and body geometry therefore need to be accommodated through compliant motion. This creates a direct conflict with conventional motion imitation, where deviations from the reference are treated as tracking errors. Recent compliant tracking methods [ 4 ] address physical perturbations during motion imitation, but partnered interaction also requires the robot to adapt its locomotion to another person while continuously responding to physical contact.

We introduce CoDance, a framework for learning reactive and compliant human-humanoid interaction from a single video of two people dancing ( Fig. 2 ). CoDance reconstructs and separately retargets the two dancers, using one as the robot reference and the other as a moving partner during training. The policy observes sparse partner keypoints and coordinates its footsteps directly with the partner’s motion, without relying on a prescribed velocity or trajectory. At deployment, the simulated partner is replaced by a real person whose corresponding keypoints are measured from a small set of motion-capture markers.

A central challenge is that video provides motion without the interaction forces. We address this with a multi-link compliance augmentation that transforms the kinematic demonstration into force-aware training data. Structured interaction events apply forces at one or both hands, with coupled displacements and force directions informed by the partner’s motion. Each event adapts the robot reference according to the sampled force and commanded stiffness, encoding how the robot should respond to physical interaction while preserving the demonstrated motion. Temporal reversal, force-free samples, and clip chaining further expand a short demonstration into long-horizon interaction trajectories. Our final data can support different locomotion objectives while sharing the same partner-following and compliance objectives.

We evaluate each component of CoDance in simulation and deploy the learned policy on a physical humanoid. Changing or removing the partner observation shows that the policy uses the observed human motion to adapt its footsteps. Under interaction forces, the learned policy reproduces approximately 80% of the wrist displacement encoded by the augmented demonstrations, compared with about 20% for a stiff tracking baseline. The demonstrated locomotion style can be learned through either adversarial imitation or reference tracking, while removing the locomotion objective substantially degrades the resulting motion. Clip chaining further enables transitions between forward and backward motions. # II Related Work

## II-A Partnered Dancing and Human-Humanoid Interaction

Physical robot dancing has been studied for more than two decades. Ms DanceR [ 5 ] follows a human partner through force sensing on an omnidirectional base. Model-based humanoids have performed box-step dances by adapting their steps to contact forces [ 6 ] or leading through compliant arm motion [ 7 ] . Recent learning-based methods generate dance motion on legged robots [ 8 ] , interactive motions between two humanoids [ 9 ] , and hand-holding dances under velocity commands [ 1 ] . Learned humanoids have also coordinated with people for object carrying [ 10 , 11 ] and acquired interaction skills from human videos or paired human demonstrations [ 12 , 13 ] . CoDance studies a different setting where a humanoid learns the locomotion style from paired human video, follows an observed human partner, and maintains compliant two-hand contact.

## II-B Whole-Body Motion Imitation for Humanoids

Physics-based character control learns natural motion through reference tracking [ 14 ] or adversarial objectives [ 3 , 15 ] . These approaches have transferred to physical humanoids for expressive whole-body control [ 1 , 2 ] , teleoperation [ 16 , 17 ] , and diverse motion tracking [ 18 ] . These methods primarily consider single-agent motion, where tracking objectives keep the robot close to its reference. Physical interaction introduces contact forces that can require motion away from this reference. In CoDance, the locomotion objective preserves the demonstrated lower-body motion while the upper body adapts to interaction with the partner.

## II-C Compliant Control and Motion Tracking

Impedance and admittance control regulate robot motion under physical contact [ 19 ] . Learned controllers extend these ideas to legged robots through impedance-reference tracking [ 20 ] , joint position-force control [ 21 ] , and compliant task-space control for humanoid loco-manipulation [ 22 ] . For humanoid motion tracking, SoftMimic [ 4 ] augments references with inverse-kinematics solutions under sampled forces, while GentleHumanoid [ 23 ] learns upper-body compliance using guiding forces and human motion. Our augmentation takes one step further to target sustained partnered locomotion. Force events act on one or both wrists with coupled displacements and directions informed by the partner’s motion, producing force-aware references for compliant two-hand interaction during partner following.

2026-10-06.title: Safe Ergodic Control for Multi-Robot Systems via Quadratic Programming
2026-10-06.authors: Yo Toyomoto , Mohamed Elobaid , Bryce L. Ferguson , Alberto Quattrini Li , Shinkyu Park
2026-10-06.abstract: Ergodic control drives robots to spend time in each region in proportion to a spatial distribution of interest, making it well suited for dense spatiotemporal environmental monitoring. Existing safe ergodic controllers rely on offline trajectory optimization or hierarchical architectures, which limit real-time applicability and decouple the ergodicity objective from the safety constraint. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based controller that treats ergodicity and safety jointly. We first introduce a Gaussian-kernel ergodic metric that, unlike the classical indicator-based metric, is time differentiable. This allows the exponential decay of the metric to be imposed as a time-varying control barrier function (CBF) constraint, relaxed by a slack variable, alongside hard CBF constraints for region containment and inter-robot collision avoidance. We establish that the resulting QP remains feasible from any safe initial configuration and that, up to the slack term, the ergodic metric decays exponentially. Simulations show improved performance over baseline methods, and experiments with three aerial vehicles validate the work on real hardware.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Employing multiple mobile sensors, such as underwater robots and aerial vehicles with onboard sensors, yields far denser spatiotemporal data over a vast field than manual sampling [ 1 ] . A key challenge, however, lies in operating these robots efficiently; in particular, adapting their motion to an area of interest is critical to monitoring performance (e.g., through assigning a probability density function as in search and rescue scenarios [ 2 ] , or mimicking heat maps corresponding to industrial inspection).
In this context, coverage path planning has been widely studied, seeking the shortest path that covers the field [ 3 , 4 ] . Coverage control has also been applied to distribute multiple robots such that their stationary spatial distribution matches the area of interest [ 5 , 6 ] . However, neither approach directly optimizes the time history of the robots’ positions to match the spatial distribution required for monitoring the area.

Ergodic control instead matches the robots’ trajectories to the target spatial distribution.
Mathew and Mezić proposed in [ 7 ] an ergodic metric that quantifies the discrepancy between the fraction of time the robots spend in each region and the target distribution. Because this metric is difficult to use directly in controller design, they proposed the spectral multiscale coverage (SMC) method, which approximates both distributions using Fourier series and derives a closed-form control input that minimizes the discrepancy between their Fourier coefficients. Fourier series-based ergodic control has since been widely studied [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , and alternative approximations of the ergodic metric, e.g., using heat equations [ 16 ] , kernel functions [ 17 ] , sample-based kernel embedding [ 18 ] and optimization methods, e.g., learning methods [ 19 ] , and flow matching methods [ 20 ] , have been explored. However, none of these methods guarantee safety, such as collision avoidance between robots. Several studies incorporate safety constraints in ergodic trajectory optimization [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] , but, to the best of our knowledge, all of them are executed offline or rely on a long optimization horizon, which makes them difficult to adapt online. Hierarchical approaches that run SMC in an upper layer and a control barrier function (CBF)-based safety filter in a lower layer have also been proposed [ 24 , 25 ] . This hierarchical structure, however, cannot guarantee decay of the ergodic metric as the safety filter may degrade ergodicity convergence.

This paper presents a single-layer quadratic programming (QP)-based controller that decreases the ergodic metric while ensuring safety. To this end, we first define an ergodic metric using a Gaussian kernel which renders the metric time differentiable. This metric definition also differs from [ 17 ] in that we apply the Gaussian filter to all terms of Equation (23) in [ 17 ] , which more accurately captures the similarity of the trajectory to the target distribution. This property allows us to design the controller with a constraint-driven approach [ 26 ] , which can be executed online in real time from the current state. Specifically, the decay rate of the ergodic metric is imposed as a constraint that is affine in the control input, structured as a time-varying CBF [ 27 ] , so that additional safety-critical constraints can be added as CBFs by construction.
Unlike hierarchical approaches [ 24 , 25 ] , the control input is optimized by considering the ergodic-metric decay and the safety constraints simultaneously.
Simulations compare the decay of the ergodic metric under the proposed controller against the SMC and hierarchical SMC-CBF methods, and experiments with multiple Crazyflies, as shown in Figure 1 , validate the controller design.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Notations are introduced below. Section II introduces a novel ergodic metric using a Gaussian kernel, and the control problem is formulated. Section III presents a controller design based on a CBF-based QP approach. Section IV validates the controller through simulations across various scenarios against baseline methods, and further experimental results with Crazyflies are presented. Section V concludes the paper and discusses directions for future work.

2026-10-06.title: Vela: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models with Adaptive Action Curve Parametrization
2026-10-06.authors: Yifan Li , Jiaxu Wang , Dongming Wu , Yicheng Jiang , Ryan Ji , Xiangyu Yue , Yanwei Fu
2026-10-06.abstract:
Most vision-language-action models represent future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, tying temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise representation wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision required for contact-rich manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce Vela, a vision-language-action foundation model that represents future robot behavior as continuous trajectories. Vela combines a compact spline-based action representation with motion-dependent temporal support and a shared action interface for heterogeneous embodiments, allowing a fixed output budget to adapt its temporal resolution across motions.
We pretrain Vela on large-scale multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate it on LIBERO-X, EBench, and two real-world long-horizon tasks, egg-cake cooking and potato shredding, obtaining promising results across simulation and physical manipulation.
These results highlight the potential of continuous action representations as a foundation for future embodied foundation models.
Project page and more results: https://clementine24.github.io/Vela/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models are rapidly scaling to larger datasets, broader task distributions, and more diverse robot embodiments ( Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Yet most VLAs still represent future motion as a fixed-length sequence of actions sampled on a predetermined temporal grid. This pointwise interface assigns separate prediction capacity to highly correlated neighboring actions and couples the output budget to both prediction horizon and temporal resolution: representing a longer future requires more action points, while a fixed budget forces coarser sampling. Conversely, spreading the same budget over a long horizon can remove the local precision needed for contact-rich manipulation. Because temporal continuity is learned implicitly, execution also relies on a predefined sampling grid. These limitations reflect a mismatch between current VLA representations and the objects they control: robot actions are not isolated points but samples from continuous motions.

A trajectory-level representation provides a more natural action space. Instead of predicting every temporal sample, a policy can predict a compact set of parameters that defines a continuous trajectory and query that trajectory at the desired temporal locations. This representation compresses correlated actions, exposes temporal continuity, and decouples trajectory geometry from the time span over which it is executed. The same fixed parameter budget can therefore describe a long, smooth motion or a short, finely resolved one, while supporting different control frequencies. Splines provide a practical realization of this idea: a small set of control points specifies a continuous curve that can be evaluated on arbitrary temporal grids.

Trajectory-level representations have a long history in robotics, including dynamical and probabilistic movement primitives ( Ijspeert et al., 2013 ; Paraschos et al., 2013 ) . Recent learning-based policies have explored dynamical-system parameterizations ( Bahl et al., 2020 ) , differentiable trajectory optimization ( Wan et al., 2024 ) , and geometric curve representations ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Spline-based policies have further studied compact action tokenization, asynchronous execution, and temporal rescaling ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . These studies show the value of structured motion representations, but they mainly focus on task-specific policies, individual robot platforms, or downstream action tokenization and execution. Whether trajectory-level action modeling can serve as the output space for foundation-scale VLA pretraining across large, heterogeneous robot datasets remains largely unexplored.

To address this gap, we build a VLA that learns future motion in trajectory space and make this representation trainable at foundation scale. A shared cross-embodiment action interface and scalable supervision procedure allow the same model to absorb heterogeneous robot corpora. We further make the temporal span of each prediction motion-dependent: with a fixed number of spline control points, each demonstrated motion is assigned a sample-specific horizon by selecting the longest span that adequately represents it under a noise-aware criterion. Smooth motions can therefore use longer spans, whereas motions with rapid local variation can use shorter spans without changing the output budget. We train this framework on large multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate its transfer to downstream manipulation tasks.

Our main contributions are:

We show how trajectory-space action modeling can be scaled to VLA pretraining through a shared cross-embodiment action interface and a training procedure designed for large heterogeneous robot corpora.

We introduce motion-dependent horizon adaptation, selecting for each demonstrated motion the longest temporal span that a fixed spline budget can represent under a noise-aware criterion.

We evaluate the framework with controlled comparisons, downstream manipulation benchmarks, and ablations, showing improvements from trajectory-space modeling, large-scale pretraining, and horizon adaptation, particularly under contact-rich, long-horizon, and distribution-shifted tasks.

1. We show how trajectory-space action modeling can be scaled to VLA pretraining through a shared cross-embodiment action interface and a training procedure designed for large heterogeneous robot corpora.

2. We introduce motion-dependent horizon adaptation, selecting for each demonstrated motion the longest temporal span that a fixed spline budget can represent under a noise-aware criterion.

3. We evaluate the framework with controlled comparisons, downstream manipulation benchmarks, and ablations, showing improvements from trajectory-space modeling, large-scale pretraining, and horizon adaptation, particularly under contact-rich, long-horizon, and distribution-shifted tasks.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action Foundation Models. Extensive research on vision-language models has advanced cross-modal alignment and downstream visual reasoning ( Li et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) .
Building on this progress, vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models scale robot learning across heterogeneous tasks, data, and embodiments by coupling pretrained vision-language representations ( Beyer et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) with generalist action policies ( Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) . Recent systems further improve cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization through heterogeneous co-training, embodiment alignment, and predictive supervision ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Cai et al., 2026a ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ) ; related robot-control work also studies structured visual representations ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Yet the low-level motion interface of modern chunk-based VLAs remains largely organized around fixed-resolution sequences of sampled future actions.
Recent work begins to relax this temporal rigidity: MoH ( Jing et al., 2025 ) models multiple prediction horizons, while AutoHorizon ( Wang et al., 2026b ) and AAC ( Liang et al., 2026 ) use attention patterns and action entropy to determine execution lengths. These methods still operate on sampled action sequences.
In contrast, Vela makes temporal support part of the action representation itself, using a fixed set of control points to parameterize continuous trajectories with motion-adaptive future spans.

Spline-Based Robot Policies. Structured representations of robot motion have long been studied through dynamical and probabilistic movement primitives ( Ijspeert et al., 2013 ; Paraschos et al., 2013 ) . Recent work incorporates splines into learned policies for efficient action tokenization ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , asynchronous execution Yang et al. (2026) , and structured action generation across policy backbones Tian et al. (2026) . B-spline Policy Han et al. (2026) accelerates visuomotor policies through adaptive spline fitting and temporal rescaling. These works primarily study splines as policy-level representations, tokenizers, or execution interfaces. To our knowledge, Vela is the first VLA foundation model established in trajectory space through large-scale pretraining on multi-embodiment robot data. Our framework is designed to support this scaling: a unified action interface accommodates heterogeneous embodiments, while a noise-calibrated horizon procedure constructs spline targets on the fly. Together, Vela constructs consistent trajectory targets from heterogeneous datasets, investigates spline trajectories as the output space of a foundation model.
