2026-10-06.title: A Unified Dynamics Framework for Reinforcement Learning and Classical Control of a Six-DOF Pipeline-Tracking ROV in NVIDIA Isaac Sim
2026-10-06.authors: Cheng Siong Chin , M. Venkateshkumar , Jianhua Zhang
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-06.abstract: Reinforcement learning controllers for underwater vehicles are usually trained against one physics representation and, when a live simulator or hardware is available, deployed against another, so reported tracking performance does not always describe what the controller will do once it leaves the training environment. This paper reports a pipeline-tracking control architecture for a six-degree-of-freedom remotely operated vehicle (ROV) in which a single Universal Scene Description (USD) scene supplies the real BlueROV2-Heavy mass, added-mass, damping, buoyancy, and eight-thruster allocation parameters to both halves of the system: a vectorized NumPy implementation of Fossen’s marine-craft equations, and an interactive NVIDIA Isaac Sim deployment in which the identical equations are applied as forces to a PhysX rigid body at every physics step. The Coriolis-centripetal coupling term C( ν \nu ) ν \nu is included as the primary dynamics model in both branches, and a controlled ablation restricted to proximal policy optimization (PPO) and trust region policy optimization (TRPO) shows that including the term does not destabilize either algorithm and modestly improves tracking accuracy, an approximately 19 percent reduction in standoff root-mean-square error for TRPO. Five reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO, soft actor-critic (SAC), twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3), deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), and TRPO, are trained against an identical environment, reward, and 30-episode randomized evaluation harness through a checkpoint-compatibility layer that lets any trained policy be scored by the same evaluation code. The same shared-dynamics pipeline is extended with six classical and model-based control baselines, proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, sliding-mode control, fuzzy logic control, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), each driven by the identical guidance geometry and thruster-allocation map as the learned policies, so that any performance difference reflects the control law itself. Under Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization achieve the strongest combination of a 100 percent success rate and competitive-to-best tracking accuracy; PID, fuzzy logic control, and the ANFIS surrogate also reach 100 percent success with somewhat looser tracking; DDPG and TD3 each show a specific, explainable failure mode rather than a general weakness of off-policy learning; and classical, model-based control remains a strong, competitive, low-cost baseline against the best learned policies on this task.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Subsea pipelines carry oil, gas, and slurry across seabeds that divers and tethered inspection vehicles cannot reach cheaply or safely, and the standard inspection task for a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) is to fly a fixed standoff distance above the pipeline while avoiding rock outcrops and the seafloor itself [ 1 ] . The six coupled degrees of freedom of an underwater vehicle, surge, sway, heave, roll, pitch, and yaw, make the task difficult to hand-code, since damping, added mass, Coriolis-centripetal coupling, and buoyancy interact nonlinearly with vehicle attitude [ 2 ] . Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an alternative to hand-tuned controllers: a policy trained against a physics model learns the coupling directly from reward signal rather than from a linearized approximation of it, and recent work reports reinforcement-learning controllers [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] that track paths, hold depth, and dock autonomous underwater vehicles under disturbances that defeat a fixed-gain proportional-integral-derivative loop.

Most of this work is validated inside the same simulator used for training, with a single algorithm, and rarely against a classical or model-based controller built from the same dynamics model. A policy is trained and evaluated against one instance of a dynamics model, sometimes with domain randomization applied to the model’s own parameters, and the paper reports how that policy performed inside the training loop [ 6 , 7 ] . Whether the same policy behaves identically once handed to a different physics engine, whether a reported result generalizes across the family of algorithms used for continuous control, and whether a learned policy actually outperforms a well-tuned classical controller given the same dynamics model and guidance geometry, are typically left open [ 8 ] . NVIDIA Isaac Sim narrows the first question for many robot classes by pairing a GPU-accelerated PhysX engine with a Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graph that serves as a single source of truth for a robot’s geometry and physical parameters [ 9 , 10 ] , and a recent underwater-specific extension, MarineGym, adapts Isaac Sim’s physics backbone to marine hydrodynamics at high simulation throughput [ 11 ] . A worked architecture in which the same, Coriolis-coupled equations of motion, read from one parameter set, drive a vectorized trainer, an interactive deployment scene, and a shared bank of classical baselines alike, has not been reported for a pipeline-tracking task.

This paper builds a USD scene encoding a 6-DOF ROV’s mass, added mass, linear and quadratic damping, buoyancy, and eight-thruster allocation matrix as scene attributes, parsed by two independent code paths: a NumPy-vectorized implementation of Fossen’s marine-craft dynamics [ 2 ] , with the Coriolis-centripetal coupling term C( ν \nu ) ν \nu included as part of the default governing equation, integrated with a fixed-step fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme across 64 parallel environments; and an interactive Isaac Sim deployment in which a controller reads the live PhysX pose and velocity of the rigid body at every physics step, computes the identical Coriolis, damping, thruster, and buoyancy terms, and applies them as a body-frame force and torque, letting PhysX integrate the vehicle in place of a second Runge-Kutta solver. A controlled ablation, restricted to two of the five compared reinforcement-learning algorithms, shows that including this term is safe and modestly beneficial, motivating its use as the primary model throughout rather than as a simplification to be engineered around. Against this Coriolis-inclusive architecture, five reinforcement learning algorithms are derived, trained, and evaluated: PPO [ 12 ] with generalized advantage estimation [ 13 ] , SAC [ 14 ] , TD3 [ 15 ] , DDPG [ 16 ] , and TRPO [ 17 ] , scored through a single checkpoint-compatibility layer built around PPO’s own evaluation code; and six classical and model-based controllers, PID, sliding-mode control, fuzzy logic control, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system, are added as baselines under the identical guidance geometry and thruster-allocation map, so that any performance difference reflects the control law rather than the task setup. Sections III through V present the shared architecture, dynamics, and RL environment; Sections VI and VII derive the five reinforcement-learning algorithms; Section VIII presents the six classical and model-based baselines; Section IX describes the Isaac Sim deployment; Sections X and XI give the evaluation protocol and the resulting comparison; Section XII discusses the comparison and its limitations.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Guidance and control for underwater vehicles

Line-of-sight guidance coupled with proportional-integral-derivative or sliding-mode control remains the reference approach for autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) path following; a recent survey documents three decades of refinements to the guidance law, from constant look-ahead distance to adaptive and time-varying variants that cope with current disturbances [ 1 ] . These methods are computationally cheap and well understood, but each new disturbance model or actuator constraint typically requires a new stability proof, and the resulting controllers do not adapt online to dynamics they were not designed against.

## II-B Reinforcement learning for underwater tracking and following

Deep deterministic policy gradient and its twin-delayed variant have been used for AUV path following and depth tracking under current disturbance, with reported reductions in cross-track error of up to two-thirds relative to a PID baseline once a recurrent state encoder and a learnable guidance parameter are added [ 4 ] . Proximal policy optimization has been used for three-degree-of-freedom motion planning without a prior disturbance model [ 8 ] , and soft actor-critic variants, sometimes combined with a long short-term memory encoder, produce adaptive trajectory-tracking controllers for underwater vehicles [ 18 , 19 ] . Obstacle-aware extensions add a real-time avoidance term to the reward or the action space, closer to the pipeline-tracking task addressed here, since a policy that only tracks a centerline still routes around fixed and moving obstacles [ 20 ] . Across this literature, a learned policy generalizes across current strength and payload changes that would require re-derivation of a classical controller; the recurring gap is that a policy is validated inside the dynamics model it was trained against, with sim-to-real or sim-to-sim transfer left as future work [ 3 , 5 ] , that a single algorithm is typically reported per task, and that a classical baseline built from the same dynamics model is rarely reported alongside the learned policy.

## II-C Off-policy and trust-region continuous control

DDPG combines a deterministic policy with an actor-critic architecture and a replay buffer, extending value-based deep reinforcement learning to continuous action spaces, and is sensitive to function-approximation error in its single critic and to exploration-noise scale [ 16 ] . TD3 addresses this with twin critics under clipped double-Q learning, delayed policy updates, and target-policy smoothing noise, reporting more stable learning than DDPG on standard continuous-control benchmarks [ 15 ] . SAC frames the objective as maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, adding an entropy bonus to the reward and automatically tuning the temperature coefficient against a target entropy [ 14 ] . TRPO constrains each policy update to a trust region bounded by the Kullback-Leibler divergence between successive policies, computed via a conjugate-gradient approximation to the natural gradient and enforced with a backtracking line search, and is the on-policy predecessor PPO’s clipped surrogate objective was designed to approximate more cheaply [ 17 ] . Comparisons spanning all of these families against one environment, reward, and evaluation code are less common than single-algorithm reports, which motivates the comparison undertaken here.

## II-D Simulation platforms and the sim-to-real gap

Purpose-built underwater simulators such as HoloOcean and UNav-Sim provide photorealistic rendering and sensor models for AUV research but were not designed for the throughput population-based reinforcement learning needs [ 21 , 22 ] . General-purpose GPU-accelerated simulators built for terrestrial and aerial robots, most visibly Isaac Gym and its successor Isaac Sim, solved the throughput problem by vectorizing physics and observation computation on the GPU [ 9 , 23 ] . Isaac Sim’s Universal Scene Description graph lets a single scene file describe a robot’s geometry, sensors, and physical parameters once, consumed by rendering, physics, and any downstream training or deployment script that opens the same file [ 10 ] . MarineGym extends Isaac Sim’s PhysX backbone with a hydrodynamic plugin for underwater vehicles and a domain-randomization toolkit aimed at narrowing the sim-to-real gap [ 11 ] . Domain randomization itself, varying physical parameters during training so a policy does not overfit to one simulator instance, was established for manipulation and has since been applied to marine vehicles directly [ 24 , 25 ] .

## II-E The Omniverse, Isaac Sim, and Isaac Lab simulation stack

Three related but distinct layers of NVIDIA’s robotics-simulation stack (see Figure 1) are referred to throughout this paper and are worth separating explicitly. Omniverse is the underlying platform and engine: it provides the core 3D graphics, physics, and simulation infrastructure, together with the USD-based scene representation of Section III-A, on which higher-level tools are built. Isaac Sim is the robotics simulation environment built on Omniverse, supplying the virtual world, robots, sensors, physics, and robotics-specific tooling, including a ROS 2 bridge, needed to construct and test a vehicle such as the ROV modelled here. Isaac Lab is a further, reinforcement-learning-oriented framework built around Isaac Sim, providing a vectorized training environment and tooling for running many parallel simulation instances against a single policy-optimization loop [ 26 ] . An engine, in this sense, is the software infrastructure that performs the underlying computation, rendering, collision and force calculation, and standardized scene representation, so that applications built on top of it do not have to develop these capabilities from scratch, in the same sense that a car’s engine supplies motive power a driver does not directly interact with.

A generic Isaac-centred workflow for this class of problem proceeds in four stages: building and validating a vehicle model and its hydrodynamic behaviour inside Isaac Sim’s GUI and visual debugging tools; defining a reinforcement-learning task in Isaac Lab by specifying observations (vehicle pose, velocity, and target waypoint), actions (thruster commands), and a reward (reaching the target while minimizing energy consumption); training a control policy with many parallel environment instances running under Isaac Lab; and deploying the trained policy back into Isaac Sim for visual evaluation, optionally bridged to ROS 2 for robotics-system integration. Figure 2 illustrates this pipeline in the general case, including an optional connection to a physical vehicle.

The architecture reported in this paper (Section III onward) follows the Isaac Sim half of this stack directly: the ROV model and its hydrodynamics are built and validated as a USD scene, and the trained policy is deployed and evaluated visually inside Isaac Sim, with an equivalent ROS 2 bridge available but not exercised. Training itself, however, is carried out by a purpose-written, NumPy-vectorized implementation of the same Fossen dynamics described in Section IV, so that the same five algorithms of Sections VI and VII, and the six classical baselines of Section VIII, can be trained, implemented, and compared at a wall-clock cost of minutes rather than hours on the hardware. Nevertheless, the same environment definition would transfer to an Isaac-Lab-based training loop with observations, actions, and reward specified as above.

2026-10-06.title: DiVeR: Decision-Critical Verifier Learning for VLA Test-Time Scaling
2026-10-06.authors: Seongheon Park , Heecheol Kim , Shulin Tian , Lilika Makabe , Namiko Saito , Katsushi Ikeuchi , Sharon Li , Yasuyuki Matsushita
2026-10-06.abstract:
Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data.
Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time.
Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory.
At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes.
To address this, we propose DiVeR , which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction.
Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.
Videos are available at: Project Page .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Kim et al., 2024 , Black et al., 2024 , Intelligence et al., 2025b , Intelligence et al., 2025a , Bjorck et al., 2025 ) learn generalist robot policies from large-scale multimodal demonstrations, but further scaling remains limited by the high cost of robotic data collection ( Ma et al., 2026 ) .
Test-Time Scaling (TTS) 1 1 1 We use test-time scaling to denote parallel scaling via repeated sampling and ranking multiple action candidates, rather than sequential scaling via extended rollouts or iterative refinement ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) . ( Snell et al., 2024 , Jang et al., 2026 , Kwok et al., 2025 ) offers a complementary route to improving VLA performance without collecting new demonstrations or retraining the base policy. Rather than executing a single sampled action, a pretrained VLA can be viewed as a stochastic generator that proposes multiple candidate action chunks at each decision step. Since this distribution may contain both successful and unsuccessful continuations, a verifier can rank the candidates and select the one most likely to make task progress. This naturally leads to verifier-guided Best-of- N (BoN) sampling, a generator–verifier framework that converts additional inference-time computation into better action selection.

A practical approach to verifier learning is to train lightweight classification-based verifiers ( Yang et al., 2025 , Tsao et al., 2026 , Attarian et al., 2026 ) from trajectory-level success and failure outcomes, avoiding costly step-level supervision ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and the inference overhead of external VLM-based judges ( Liang et al., 2026 , Kwok et al., 2025 , Kwok et al., 2026a ) .
However, existing approaches propagate each trajectory outcome uniformly across all visited states or state–action pairs, implicitly treating them as equally informative for candidate discrimination.
This assumption can be problematic in long horizon robotic execution, where the informativeness of trajectory-level supervision for candidate discrimination can vary substantially across states.

Our key observation is that not all states are equally consequential for action selection .
As illustrated in Figure 1 (a), at states such as free-space motion or post-grasp transport, sampled action candidates remain highly similar. We refer to these as routine states , where candidate selection is relatively inconsequential and provides limited signal for learning to discriminate among actions.
In contrast, at decision-critical states , such as pre-grasp or pre-placement alignment, plausible candidates diverge more strongly, and small differences in action choice can substantially affect downstream outcomes. Figure 1 (b) further shows that such high-criticality states are sparse and temporally localized rather than uniformly distributed throughout a trajectory.
This pattern echoes findings in language generation, where only a sparse subset of high-entropy minority tokens can lead to divergent continuations and steer generation toward distinct downstream trajectories ( Wang et al., 2025 ) .
Together, these observations suggest that uniformly weighting all visited states can dilute the supervision signal from the relatively few states where accurate candidate discrimination matters most.

In this paper, we introduce DiVeR , a D ecision-cr i ticality-weighted VeR ifier for VLA test-time scaling that focuses learning on states where action selection matters most.
Our key idea is to estimate decision criticality from disagreement among plausible actions under the frozen VLA policy. At each visited state, we sample multiple action candidates and measure the dispersion of their action-expert representations. Low dispersion characterizes routine states where the policy proposes similar behaviors, whereas high dispersion identifies states where plausible actions diverge and candidate selection can substantially affect downstream outcomes.
This provides a practical proxy for decision criticality without requiring step-level supervision or additional environment interaction. DiVeR uses this signal to reweight the verifier objective, concentrating trajectory-level supervision on states where accurate candidate discrimination is most consequential.

We evaluate DiVeR on two simulated manipulation benchmarks and a real-world robotic platform using π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .
Across policies and environments, DiVeR improves task success by up to +13.6% over single sample inference and +3.4% over the strongest baseline.
Notably, DiVeR also surpasses the VLM-based verifier by +4.6% success rate while reducing verifier inference latency by over 𝟕𝟎𝟎 × \mathbf{700\times} .
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of focusing verifier learning on the sparse states where candidate differences matter most.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify a limitation of uniform verifier training, showing that routine states dominate trajectories while providing limited signal for candidate discrimination, whereas sparse decision-critical states are more consequential for action selection.

We propose DiVeR , a novel decision-criticality-weighted verifier that uses action-expert representation variance as a practical proxy for decision criticality and places greater emphasis on states with stronger candidate disagreement.

We validate DiVeR across simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in task success through more effective verifier-guided Best-of- N N action selection, with negligible verifier overhead at inference.

# Related Works

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models learn generalist robot policies by fine-tuning pretrained vision-language backbones on large-scale robot demonstration data ( Ma et al., 2026 , Kim et al., 2024 , Bjorck et al., 2025 , Black et al., 2024 , Barreiros et al., 2025 ) .
Recent approaches
further improve these policies along several complementary directions,
including geometry-aware representations that enhance 3D spatial understanding ( Qu et al., 2025 , Li et al., 2026 ) , memory mechanisms for long-horizon tasks ( Shi et al., 2026 , Torne et al., 2026 , Sridhar et al., 2026 ) , and world models that capture
environment dynamics ( Ye et al., 2026 , Cen et al., 2025 , Gao et al., 2026 ) . While effective, these directions
strengthen the policy itself and thus require additional data collection,
architectural modification, or retraining. In contrast, we treat the
pretrained VLA as a frozen stochastic action generator and improve its
execution purely at inference time, making our approach complementary to
these advances.

Test-time Scaling in LLMs improves performance by allocating additional computation at inference time rather than through further training, e.g., via repeated sampling with majority voting ( Wang et al., 2023 , Brown et al., 2024 , Kang et al., 2025 ) or verifier-guided Best-of- N selection with outcome- and process-level reward models ( Snell et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2025 , Oh et al., 2026a , Kang et al., 2026 ) .
Recent studies further suggest that not all generation steps are equally consequential: a small subset of high-entropy forking tokens can act as branching points that steer reasoning toward different continuations, while many low-entropy tokens largely follow an already determined trajectory ( Bigelow et al., 2025 , Wang et al., 2025 , Al-Khalili et al., 2026 ) .
Focusing supervision on these forking tokens can therefore yield disproportionate gains, suggesting that the value of supervision may vary across a trajectory.
We study an analogous non-uniformity in robotic control through decision-critical states , where candidate action selection can have substantially different downstream consequences.
Accordingly, we focus verifier learning on these sparse states rather than treating all states uniformly.

Test-time Scaling in VLAs. Motivated by advances in LLM test-time scaling, recent works have adopted
generate-then-verify paradigms for robotic control.
For example, (1) VLM-based verifiers score candidate actions
with large vision-language models ( Kwok et al., 2025 , Kwok et al., 2026b , Dai et al., 2025 , Liang et al., 2026 , Duan et al., 2025 ) , but
their inference cost and deployment overhead hinder real-time control;
(2) Verifier-free methods instead rely on the policy’s internal signals, such
as distributional confidence or candidate density ( Jang et al., 2026 , Rosasco et al., 2025 , Choi et al., 2026 ) ,
yet these signals are not grounded in task outcomes;
(3) Classification-based verifiers ( Yang et al., 2025 , Attarian et al., 2026 , Tsao et al., 2026 ) offer a lightweight alternative by learning from trajectory-level outcomes, but weight all visited states uniformly.
Our approach instead accounts for the non-uniform importance of states by
estimating decision criticality from action-expert representation variance and
placing greater training emphasis on states where candidate actions diverge
and selection is most consequential.

2026-10-06.title: RobotUse: Allocating Computation, Context, and Decisions
2026-10-06.authors: Junhoo Lee (1), Injun Baek (2), Seungyeon Kim (2), Suhyun Jeon (2), Minkyu Kim (2), Baekseung Kim (2), Nojun Kwak (2) ((1) KAIST, (2) Seoul National University)
2026-10-06.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Robot agents must connect their intended actions to observed outcomes while retaining the context needed to revise their choices over repeated attempts. Existing interfaces often leave these choices inside predefined tools or require agents to manage detailed execution code and its growing history. We introduce RobotUse, a robot agent harness that organizes computation, context, and decisions around specifying and revising physical actions. Agents visually select targets and poses, while the backend handles geometry, motion planning, and control. Subagents retain detailed interactions within each subgoal and return the information needed for subsequent decisions. Continual harnessing lets agents learn from execution by updating a persistent playbook. On RoboLab, RobotUse achieves 45% task success, outperforming CaP-X by 6.7 percentage points while maintaining compact decision contexts and reducing reliance on predefined action abstractions. Furthermore, we show that RobotUse learns from real-world execution despite imperfect feedback and transfers what it learns to subsequent tasks. Project page is available at https://robotuse-team.github.io/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Everyday actions give concrete form to simple intentions: a door opened just enough to pass through, a dial turned until the sound is right. These intentions guide what to change, by how much, and when to adjust, without requiring every movement to be consciously specified.

General-purpose agent design requires deciding which responsibilities belong to model reasoning and which should be delegated. A model’s ability to perform a computation does not mean that the computation should be performed through model inference. Programs can process information outside the active context, while subagents can conduct detailed interactions and return the results needed for subsequent decisions ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Bengre & Curme, 2026 ) . Recent agent harnesses organize computation and context to support long-horizon, multi-step work and retain experience across interactions ( Karten et al., 2026a ; Karten et al., 2026b ) . The design question is how to allocate computation and context so that the model retains the decisions that matter without repeatedly re-deriving the backend computations needed to realize them.

However, physical action requires coordinating high-dimensional, continuous motion under geometric and contact constraints. Even a simple goal entails choices about position, orientation, and approach that must change with the scene and observed outcomes. Code-based policies express these choices through programs over perception and control tools ( Liang et al., 2023 ) , leaving the agent to connect physical intentions and failures to execution logic. On the other hand, high-level skills delegate execution but can conceal choices needed for adjustment ( Ahn et al., 2023 ) . Experience can improve programs and skills ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , yet accumulating abstractions can make the connection between internal decisions and physical outcomes harder to inspect and repair. A robot harness must therefore delegate execution complexity while retaining the context needed to interpret outcomes and guide subsequent actions.

We propose RobotUse, an intent-based agent harness that organizes computation, context, and decisions around specifying and revising physical intent (Fig. 1 ). The main agent maintains task intent in language and delegates subgoals and constraints to a general-purpose subagent. The subagent grounds this intent in visual observations by selecting and refining task-relevant targets, positions, and orientations. The backend translates these visually specified choices into executable motion through perception, geometric computation, motion planning, and control. Detailed observation, selection, and recovery histories remain in the subagent’s local context, while outcomes, current state, and unresolved constraints return to the main agent to guide subsequent intent and delegation. A playbook guides decomposition and delegation, and accumulates experiential guidance about what worked, under which conditions, and what to try differently. Continual harnessing updates this guidance while keeping the execution backend fixed, allowing experience to change subsequent decisions without rewriting robot control code.

Our evaluation compares task completion, inference cost, token usage, and execution time on RoboLab. We examine dependence on the provided grasp tool and track task completion across successive harness revisions. Across successive playbook refinements, accumulated experience improves task performance. Together, these studies examine how the reasoning demands of robot manipulation depend on the responsibilities assigned to the model and how execution experience can improve the guidance governing those responsibilities.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Agent harnesses organize the computation and information through which a language model acts.
ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions and observations to revise plans during interaction ( Yao et al., 2023 ) .
SWE-agent studies how the design of an agent’s tools and environmental feedback shapes its behavior and performance ( Yang et al., 2024 ) .
Recursive Language Models treat long inputs as an external environment that the model can inspect programmatically and decompose through recursive calls ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) .
Prime Agent extends this approach with persistent execution, recursive subagent sessions, and retained histories, allowing the model to construct strategies while the harness manages execution and state ( Karten et al., 2026a ) .
Deep Agents similarly uses delegation to isolate detailed work from the supervisor’s context, with context inheritance available when a subagent needs to continue prior work ( Bengre & Curme, 2026 ) .
Reflexion retains verbal feedback in episodic memory to improve decisions in subsequent trials ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) .
Continual Harness updates prompts, subagents, skills, and memory from execution trajectories ( Karten et al., 2026b ) .
Our work brings this allocation of computation and context to physical action.
We study the boundary at which geometric execution can be delegated while task-relevant choices remain accessible to the agent, and local interaction histories can be separated while preserving the information needed for subsequent decisions.
Experience is retained as playbook guidance over this interface with the execution backend held fixed.

Vision-language-action models map images and instructions to robot actions, as in RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) , OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2025b ) ; we include π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) as a representative baseline.
Early language-model robot agents separate decisions about what to do from the motor skills that carry them out.
SayCan grounds skill selection in language relevance and affordance estimates ( Ahn et al., 2023 ) , while Inner Monologue uses environmental feedback to revise task plans ( Huang et al., 2023 ) .
PIVOT exposes continuous action choices to vision-language models by rendering candidate actions on images and refining them through iterative visual selection ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) .
Research has also expanded the agent’s responsibility to constructing and improving executable behavior.
Code as Policies generates programs that compose perception and control APIs ( Liang et al., 2023 ) .
ASPIRE diagnoses failures from multimodal execution traces, repairs control programs, and accumulates validated improvements in a reusable skill library ( Lu et al., 2026 ) .
GaP constructs graphs of perception, planning, and control modules and refines their structure and parameters through simulation rehearsal ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches support flexible behavior by making executable programs and skill compositions objects of generation and revision.
Inspired by the earlier separation of decision-making and execution, we develop a harness that retains concrete physical choices at the agent interface while delegating their geometric realization to the backend.
Subgoal interactions remain in local contexts, and experience accumulates as guidance about which choices worked and how to adjust them, without modifying the underlying execution code.

2026-10-06.title: Nudge Before You Push: Physics-Aware Navigation via Tactile Probing
2026-10-06.authors: Xianyao Li , Fang Xu , Ruitong Tian , Bowen Sun , Xiao Hu , Yang Ye , Jing Du
2026-10-06.abstract: Visually identical containers can conceal loads that require different handling decisions. We present TANav , which uses a brief nudge to measure push resistance for navigation under a site-defined handling boundary. TacPhys reads the force sequence, with optional RGB-D and kinematics, into a mass estimate for push authorization. A repeated-patrol planner weighs probe and route costs, requests a second contact when useful, and reuses observations across visits. In simulation, TacPhys approaches a resistance-only Bayes reference and reduces missed pushes from 28.7% to 5.5% relative to peak-force thresholding at comparable low-risk operating points. In repeated-patrol simulation, TANav recovers 90% of the oracle’s path saving, more than halves human interventions relative to always-detour, and reduces boundary violations from 4.3% to 2.9% relative to RGB-D-only probing. On a quadruped manipulator with a Hall-array fingertip, offline zero-shot MAE is 0.28–1.07 kg on containers up to 2.82 kg. Force-rise calibration at 3 kg gives 93.5% pooled offline accuracy (86.4% on non-cube episodes); a separate raw-peak rule gives 15 of 20 correct online decisions on unseen boxes.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Industrial patrol robots revisit routes that may change between inspection cycles [ 15 , 7 ] . We consider staging areas where temporarily placed cartons or totes can obstruct familiar paths. Box-like containers can conceal different payloads behind similar exteriors, while accessible, approximately planar sides allow repeatable probing from complementary directions. Before moving an unfamiliar box, a person nudges it to feel resistance. TANav turns this intuition into a mass estimate that informs the route-clearing decision.

The decision also differs from mechanical movability. Navigation among movable obstacles (NAMO) uses movability or manipulation cost inferred from attempts or appearance [ 16 , 9 ] . A site instead permits clearing light containers and reserves heavier loads for operators, even if both are movable. The decision thus compares mass with a site-defined boundary auditable against known loads.

TANav separates contact interpretation, push authorization, and route choice (Fig. 1 ). A gripper-mounted fingertip records nudge resistance; TacPhys reads force sequences into mass for comparison with the site boundary. The planner checks eligibility before comparing push and detour costs, requests useful additional contacts, and reuses observations across visits to amortize probing. Hardware tests assess offline mass transfer and calibrated force decisions; patrol evaluation is simulated.

The mass estimate also parameterizes simulated patrol cost. Auxiliary center-of-mass (CoM) classes describe load distribution and support analysis of the information provided by the probe.

The nudge supplies evidence for authorization. The tested try-push and appearance-prior policies reach similar autonomy but authorize 55.5% of heavy containers in simulated patrol. RGB-D observations during the nudge leave 4.3% violations, force sequences 2.9%, and two-contact agreement 1.0%. Caching observations amortizes contact cost across visits. Force sequences improve decision trade-offs over scalar summaries, with similar gains across encoders. Offline hardware tests show zero-shot transfer on light containers and deferral through contact agreement; online decisions use site calibration.

Our contributions are:

A formulation of load-dependent navigation with a diagnostic probe, an explicit authorization boundary in mass units, and TacPhys , a learned sequence reader that estimates mass from push resistance.

A repeated-patrol decision scheme that weighs contact and route costs, selectively acquires a second probe, and reuses observations across visits.

A simulation-to-hardware evaluation across two tactile front ends, covering a resistance-only reference, offline mass transfer, site-calibrated online decisions, and simulated patrol efficiency and authorization errors.

An identifiability analysis of the probe: an orthogonal second contact improves both mass and CoM estimates, and contact onset is a key protocol variable for CoM transfer to hardware.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

NAMO extends geometric planning by allowing a robot to rearrange obstacles [ 16 ] , including under incomplete knowledge of movability [ 22 , 9 ] . Subsequent methods infer affordances, manipulation cost, or movability from observations [ 20 , 26 , 21 ] . Mobile manipulators also combine navigation with learned pushing control and interaction-state estimation [ 4 , 23 ] ; tactile skins support negotiation of obstacles during contact [ 1 ] . We study a diagnostic contact before route clearing, using its response to evaluate an authorization boundary and comparing readers under the same planner in simulation.

Interactive perception uses actions to reveal properties that passive sensing cannot resolve [ 5 ] . Inertial estimation can use manipulator excitation [ 2 ] , tactile in-hand interaction [ 17 ] , or non-prehensile pushing [ 6 , 12 ] . Pushing mechanics and experimental datasets show how friction and contact geometry affect the response [ 11 , 10 , 24 ] . Optical tactile sensors provide deformation measurements [ 8 , 25 ] , with calibrated force regressors supporting push-based weighing [ 14 ] ; magnetic arrays provide local loading measurements [ 18 , 3 ] . We use a force sequence as the simulation–hardware interface and assess the information needed for a navigation decision.

2026-10-06.title: PreAct-Nav: Agentic Reasoning Before Action for Urban Navigation
2026-10-06.authors: Jing Xie , Shouwei Ruan , Yubin Wang , Yuxiang Zhang , Junwei Yang , Songchang Jin , Dianxi Shi
2026-10-06.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Urban navigation requires embodied agents to reach a destination described in language through a sequence of local movements ( Mei et al., 2026b ) . The agent sees only part of its surroundings, while the route may extend beyond several intersections and turns. A locally feasible movement is therefore not necessarily useful for reaching the destination. As an example, the route in Figure 1 first requires approaching a crossing before continuing toward the goal. Thus, reliable navigation in such environment requires connecting such intermediate steps to the long-horizon goal while anticipating how local actions may affect subsequent progress.

Recent language and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled navigation agents to reason explicitly about instructions, observations, and possible actions ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Long et al., 2024 ; Ruan et al., 2026 ) . Rather than directly executing a policy prediction, these agents use reasoning to assess where to move next. EvoNav ( Dai et al., 2026 ) further incorporates historical experience and future thoughts by retrieving past experience and predicting subsequent actions and landmarks. These advances establish reasoning over experience as a practical way to improve navigation decisions.

Despite this progress, connecting local reasoning to long-horizon navigation remains challenging in two respects. First , historical context records past observations and actions, but provides limited guidance for subsequent movements toward the long-horizon goal. Local decisions may therefore be reasonable in isolation yet inconsistent across steps. Second , reasoning about future actions and landmarks in language does not provide visual evidence of what a proposed movement might reveal. A passage that appears plausible from the current view may remain occluded or fail to lead toward the intended route. These limitations make it difficult to determine whether a locally plausible action will support progress toward the destination.

In this paper, we propose PreAct-Nav , a training-free agentic reasoning harness that equips frozen navigation policies with anticipatory reasoning. Our central idea is to maintain medium-horizon subgoals to guide local decisions, evaluate proposed actions using predicted visual outcomes before execution, and update navigation memory using execution feedback. A shared VLM reasoner uses the current subgoal, relevant experience, and visual predictions to decide whether to retain or revise the proposed action. This reasoning loop connects action evaluation and revision before execution with memory updates afterward, without updating model weights.

Specifically, the PreAct-Nav harness organizes a VLM reasoner and two callable tools into a four-stage reasoning loop (Figure 2 ). During Action Preview , the reasoner reads Navigation Memory , which maintains the current subgoal and relevant experience across decisions. If the available evidence is insufficient, it queries the Predictive Sandbox , which uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views for the proposed movement ( Bar et al., 2025 ) . During Action Review , the reasoner uses predicted visual cues to assess whether the proposed action makes progress toward the current subgoal. It retains a supported action or revises a contradicted one; a revised action returns to preview and review within a fixed reasoning budget. In Action Execute , the agent follows the accepted movement. Finally, Memory Update compares the expected cues with the next real observation, records the outcome, and updates subgoal progress for the next decision. By coordinating context, tool use, and execution feedback, the harness maintains medium-horizon guidance across local actions: prediction guides revision, and real feedback updates memory.

We evaluate PreAct-Nav on UrbanNav with three navigation policies and two VLM reasoners. Our method achieves relative improvements of 6.71% in success rate (SR) and 4.19% in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the benchmark’s original policy. Experiments with other policies and reasoners further assess its applicability beyond a single backbone. Component ablations and analyses of individual decisions examine the roles of memory and prediction, with larger prediction gains on longer routes and routes with more turns. In summary, our contributions are:

❶We introduce PreAct-Nav, a training-free navigation harness that reviews and revises policy actions using memory and visual prediction before execution.

❷We develop Navigation Memory to maintain medium-horizon subgoals alongside observed experience and update their progress through execution feedback.

❸We expose an action-conditioned world model as a Predictive Sandbox, providing future visual cues for action reasoning under the current subgoal.

❹We evaluate the harness across navigation policies and VLM reasoners, with component ablations and analyses of memory, prediction, and navigation difficulty.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-and-language navigation grounds instructions in observed scenes, from navigation graphs to continuous environments ( Anderson et al., 2018b ; Krantz et al., 2020 ) . Learned policies translate observations and goals into local movements ( Mei et al., 2026b ; Sridhar et al., 2024 ; Hirose et al., 2026 ) , while CityWalker learns urban navigation from web videos ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . LM-Nav composes pretrained models without fine-tuning ( Shah et al., 2023 ) , while CompassNav supervises feasible-action decisions ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Explicit reasoning supports instruction interpretation ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Qiao et al., 2025 ) , multi-expert assessment ( Long et al., 2024 ) , and retrieved experience with future thoughts ( Dai et al., 2026 ) . ReAct and Inner Monologue interleave reasoning with feedback ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023 ) , while Toolformer learns when and how to call tools ( Schick et al., 2023 ) . Our frozen reasoner coordinates memory and prediction through a harness to review and revise movements before execution.

Memory enables agents to reuse experience without encoding every interaction in model weights. Reflexion stores verbal reflections ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , REMem retrieves temporally grounded events ( Shu et al., 2026 ) , and M3-Agent builds multimodal episodic and semantic memories ( Long et al., 2026 ) . Agentic Context Engineering incrementally updates contextual playbooks using execution feedback ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . In navigation, DUET combines a growing topological map with local observations ( Chen et al., 2022 ) , and PanoNav retains exploration history to avoid repeated local deadlocks ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . Our Navigation Memory couples observed experience with an active medium-horizon subgoal that provides shared context for action review and revision. Execution feedback updates its objective and progress cues, so memory tracks both past outcomes and the current purpose of navigation.

Video generation provides a visual representation of future plans: UniPi generates goal-conditioned videos and extracts control actions from them ( Du et al., 2023 ) . Action-conditioned world models instead predict observations for a specified movement. Navigation World Models use such predictions to plan paths or rank proposed trajectories ( Bar et al., 2025 ) , while Cosmos Policy fine-tunes video models for visuomotor control and planning ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . In computer-use agents, R-WoM grounds language-model simulations in retrieved tutorials ( Mei et al., 2026a ) . Access to a world model, however, does not ensure effective use of its predictions ( Qian et al., 2026 ) . Our focus is how visual prediction informs navigation reasoning. The Predictive Sandbox exposes the world model as a callable tool; the VLM interprets predicted visual cues against the current subgoal to retain or revise a movement. Real observations subsequently establish progress and update memory, linking predictive reasoning to execution feedback.

2026-10-06.title: $R^2$-WAM: Repair-and-Reject Post-Training for World Action Models
2026-10-06.authors: Ruiyan Xu , Haisheng Su , Sixu Lin , Zhaokun Yue , Chengming Hu , Xin Jin , Guiliang Liu
2026-10-06.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) emerge as a promising foundation for policy refinement by predicting the consequences of sampled actions.
However, visually plausible predictions can mislead policy refinement if they fail to reflect the input actions.
To address this mismatch, we introduce R 2 R^{2} -WAM , a two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework that first improves the consistency of predicted futures with input actions, then uses these futures to select inferior action samples for negative fine-tuning.
The repair stage grounds imagination in observed robot behavior through a kinematic alignment score that measures agreement between predicted and demonstrated motion, enabling the predicted video to faithfully reflect its input actions.
Using the repaired video model, the rejection stage compares imagined outcomes of sampled and demonstrated actions, selectively applying negative fine-tuning to samples whose predicted task progress falls below the demonstrated reference by a prescribed margin.
Together, the two stages extend video prediction from representation learning to consequence-based policy refinement without additional environment interaction or changes to the inference procedure. R 2 R^{2} -WAM achieves 93.8% average success on RoboTwin 2.0
across clean and randomized settings.
On the long-horizon real-world Fold Shirt task, it achieves
87.5% average success, compared with 0% for Fast-WAM.
2026-10-06.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising approach to robotic control by guiding action generation with predicted visual outcomes.
Existing WAMs typically learn to predict video and actions jointly in pixel or latent space ( Ye et al., 2026b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) , thereby grounding action generation in predicted scene dynamics.
Beyond direct robot control, recent studies have explored using action-conditioned world models as simulators to predict the consequences of candidate actions and provide feedback for policy improvement ( Guo et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ) .
This is particularly useful when demonstrations provide limited coverage of execution errors and collecting physical trials is costly ( Chandra et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) .

A key prerequisite for effective policy post-training with a world model is that it faithfully predicts how the environment changes in response to actions.
Although modern video generation models can produce visually plausible predictions ( Wan et al., 2025 ) , they do not necessarily preserve physical properties such as kinematics and dynamics.
Consequently, generated videos may appear realistic while failing to reflect the supplied actions ( Yang et al., 2026b ) .
Evaluating actions with such predictions can mistake video model errors for policy failures, causing the policy to learn from outcomes its actions would not produce ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) .

To reduce mismatch between imagined and actual consequences, prior methods ground generated videos in robot motion using inverse dynamics ( Wang et al., 2026 ) or extracted 3D flow ( Dharmarajan et al., 2025 ) .
These methods rely on auxiliary components to obtain motion feedback, but do not ensure that the video faithfully follows a supplied action.
Recent methods improve imagined feedback by fine-tuning world models on real policy rollouts ( Guo et al., 2026a ) , updating the model as the policy evolves from task-critical keyframes ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , or training on diverse actions with supervision ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
These methods improve action grounding, but leave open how observed demonstration outcomes can identify unreliable predictions before they are used to evaluate sampled policy actions.

To fill this gap, we propose repairing the video expert using observed consequences of demonstrated actions, then using the repaired expert to reject sampled actions with inferior predicted task progress (Figure 1 ).
To this end, we introduce R 2 R^{2} -WAM , a two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework comprising predictive repair and action rejection (Figure 2 ), comprising the following modules:

1) Predictive repair turns each demonstration into a test of action fidelity: given the same observation and action, the video expert generates a future that can be compared with what the robot actually did.
A kinematic alignment score measures whether the generated robot motion follows the observed motion and selects predictions with substantial discrepancies for negative fine-tuning.
This stage improves the video expert before its imagined consequences are used to judge sampled policy actions, reducing the risk that prediction errors become misleading training signals.

2) Action rejection uses the repaired video expert to judge what sampled actions are likely to achieve.
With the expert frozen, we predict futures for sampled and demonstrated actions from the same initial observation, then compare their task progress using STEAM ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .
Sampled actions whose predicted progress falls below the demonstrated reference by a prescribed margin are selected for negative fine-tuning, while demonstrations remain the positive targets.
This directs policy updates toward actions with evidence of inferior consequences.

Together, the two stages turn video prediction into feedback for
policy post-training without additional environment interaction or
changes to the inference procedure.
We conduct an extensive empirical study across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks
and two real-world manipulation tasks, evaluating action fidelity,
negative-selection accuracy, and downstream policy success. R 2 R^{2} -WAM improves average success over action-conditioned Fast-WAM
by 3.3 percentage points in simulation and raises average success
on the long-horizon real-world Fold Shirt task from 0% with
Fast-WAM to 87.5%.

# 2 Related Work

World action models couple future prediction with action generation
through joint diffusion modeling of video and
actions ( Ye et al., 2026b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) ,
causal modeling ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and latent action
representations ( Bi et al., 2026 ) . WorldScape Policy
2.0 ( Su et al., 2026 ) extends this framework with memory and multimodal
conditioning. Predictions can also guide control through visual
representations ( Hu et al., 2024 ) or explicit motion plans:
RoboFlow4D ( Lin et al., 2026a ) predicts multi-frame 3D motion to condition
action generation. Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) couples video and action
experts through shared attention, using video prediction to learn world
representations without generating future videos at deployment.
We build on Fast-WAM to use predicted consequences
for policy post-training.

RECAP ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) refines policies through
advantage-conditioned learning from experience.
World-model-based approaches use synthetic rollouts and predicted
consequences for policy fine-tuning ( Guo et al., 2026b ) ,
advantage estimation ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , and preference
optimization ( Hung et al., 2025 ) .
To improve the reliability of imagined feedback,
VLAW ( Guo et al., 2026a ) adapts its world model using real rollouts,
while WoVR ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) regulates imagined rollouts and
co-evolves the world model and policy.
Our approach uses observed demonstration futures to repair
action-inconsistent predictions without additional environment
interaction. The repaired video expert then guides selective
negative fine-tuning of actions whose predicted progress falls
below the demonstrated reference.

2026-10-06.title: GJK-CBF: Control Barrier Functions for Convex Rigid Body Collision Avoidance on SE(3)
2026-10-06.authors: Yi-Hsuan Chen , Shuo Liu , Wei Xiao , Michael Otte , Calin Belta

2026-10-06.abstract: Collision avoidance among convex bodies is a fundamental problem in robotics. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide a practical framework for real-time safety filtering due to their computational efficiency. For general convex bodies, exact separation measures, such as distance or scaling factor, are typically computed through optimization. Existing CBF formulations often obtain the required gradient via differentiable optimization (diffOpt), adding computational overhead. In contrast, we leverage the Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi (GJK) algorithm to obtain the current witness pair—the pair of points realizing the minimum distance or penetration depth—and formulate a CBF, termed GJK-CBF , whose gradient is constructed directly from the relative rigid-body motion of the witness pair, without resorting to diffOpt . This formulation applies to both 2D and 3D environments across a broad class of convex body pairs, provided that at least one in each one-to-one interaction is strictly convex. The proposed GJK-CBF is validated in various scenarios, including multi-robot position swapping in both 2D and 3D, navigation through a vertical slit in 3D, and its applicability to manipulators. The results demonstrate collision-free motion across all scenarios while reducing the conservativeness introduced by geometric approximations, particularly in narrow environments. A video of all simulations is available at https://youtu.be/eDvscHhGIj0 .
2026-10-06.introduction:
One of the key difficulties in robotic navigation is to simultaneously satisfy system kinematic/dynamic constraints, safety requirements, and actuation limits. The problem is further complicated when collision avoidance must explicitly account for the geometry of both the ego robot and nearby robots/obstacles. For each pair of bodies, referred to as a collision pair, the separation distance depends on their relative configuration, i.e., position and orientation, and is nontrivial to evaluate and differentiate. The notion of configuration obstacles [ 1 ] was proposed to account for robot geometry via Minkowski operations and has been widely used in motion planning [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . While the same geometric representation underlies classical collision-detection algorithms such as Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi (GJK) [ 5 ] and the Expanding Polytope Algorithm (EPA) [ 6 ] to characterize distance proximity, these methods are not designed for safety control synthesis.

Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) [ 8 ] , on the other hand, provide a systematic approach to synthesizing safe controllers. CBF safety constraints can be implemented on-the-fly, either jointly with Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs) [ 9 ] or as minimally invasive safety filters to simultaneously address safety and stabilization objectives.
Several CBF formulations have been developed for collision avoidance, and we focus only on those that explicitly account for the geometries of both bodies. Optimization-based approaches solve an optimization problem to compute a measure of separation,
such as a scaling factor [ 10 ] , minimum distance [ 11 , 12 ] , smooth distance approximation [ 13 ] , or exact Signed Distance (SD) [ 14 ] . This measure is then used to define a CBF, and its gradient is obtained through differentiable optimization (diffOpt) [ 15 ] . A similar workflow has also been applied to uncertain obstacles [ 16 ] using constrained convex generators. In contrast, optimization-free approaches construct CBFs based on polytope vertices [ 17 ] , supporting hyperplanes for ellipsoids [ 7 ] and polytopes [ 18 ] , or Bernstein-polynomial SD fields [ 19 ] . Such approaches are computationally efficient, but generally rely on surrogate distance measures.

These two classes of methods appear to suggest a trade-off between geometric exactness and computational efficiency.
However, although the SD sensitivity in our previous work [ 14 ] was derived through diffOpt, the resulting gradient expression was independent of the sensitivity of the optimizer but depended only on the optimizer itself, i.e., the witness pair (the pair of points realizing minimum distance when separated or penetration depth when intersecting).
Motivated by this, we propose GJK-CBF 1 1 1 Although the name suggests the use of GJK, the formulation only requires a witness pair, which may also be obtained via optimization. , a CBF framework that retains the exact distance and obtains its gradient directly from the (instantaneous) witness pair without diffOpt (Fig. 1 ).

Related witness-pair-based distance gradients have appeared in earlier studies [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Proximity queries like GJK have been incorporated into real-time CBF safety filters, while obtaining their gradients through diffOpt with randomized smoothing [ 25 ] or a Schur-complement acceleration [ 26 ] .
Another related work is [ 7 ] , which designs CBFs using rotating supporting hyperplanes and derives a closed-form gradient by exploiting the special algebraic structure of ellipsoids, but does not directly generalize to other geometries.
The most closely related work to our approach is [ 27 ] , which formulates the distance-based CBF directly on S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) , but does not provide an explicit form for the distance gradient.

To the best of our knowledge, existing approaches do not provide a CBF formulation with an explicit expression for the exact distance gradient for general convex rigid bodies. To address this gap, we develop GJK-CBF , in which, once a witness pair is given, the exact distance is immediately determined, and its gradient can be obtained accordingly. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

The proposed GJK-CBF is geometry-agnostic within the class of convex rigid bodies and applies in both 2D and 3D workspaces, provided that at least one body in each collision pair is strictly convex (Def. 3 ) .

We derive an explicit expression for the distance gradient on S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) solely from the witness pair without diffOpt, enabling optimization-based distance solvers to be replaced by GJK proximity queries. We also provide equivalent Euler-angle and quaternion representations.

We show that the proposed CBF framework can be implemented in a decentralized fashion, assuming that the information associated with each collision pair is accessible to the corresponding robots.

We validate our method across different 2D/3D scenarios and compare it
with the supporting-hyperplane-CBF [ 7 ] , showing that our method is less conservative while remaining collision-free.

2026-10-06.title: Tackling Sim-to-Real Mismatch Through Sampling-Based Disturbance Observers: From Analytical Models to Learned World Models
2026-10-06.authors: Tianqi Zhu , Jun Yang , Jianliang Mao , Cong Li , Shihua Li
2026-10-06.comment: . Project website: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Robotic controllers increasingly rely on analytical models, simulators, cost-query interfaces, and learned world models. However, physical deployment can deviate from nominal assumptions, and additional disturbances may arise even when the model itself is accurate. In control systems, disturbance observers (DOB) are widely used to estimate such unmeasured effects from nominal models and measured feedback. Classical DOB formulations are generally built around explicit plant models. This paper develops the sampling-based disturbance observer (SDOB), extending the DOB principle to a broader range of models, including simulators and learned world models, through state-rollout or cost-query interfaces. SDOB separates two observable channels: state-effect disturbances, for which the feedback state differs from its prediction, and cost disturbances, for which the same query state receives different costs as the perceived environment changes. Diverse simulation and real-robot experiments across traditional and learned models demonstrate the effectiveness of SDOB in compensating for sim-to-real mismatch and improving control performance.
2026-10-06.introduction:
From early model-based control to modern robotics built on simulators and learned models, deployment has always involved discrepancies between simulator models and physical plant. In classical systems, these discrepancies appear as parameter uncertainty, unmodeled dynamics, and external disturbances ( Ohnishi et al., 1996 ; Chen et al., 2016 ) ; in contemporary robotics, the same problem is often discussed as the sim-to-real gap ( OpenAI et al., 2020 ; Jaquier et al., 2025 ) . Such discrepancies can degrade tracking performance and closed-loop stability. If a disturbance is measurable, feedforward compensation can often reduce its influence. In practice, the relevant disturbances are often unmeasured or entangled with model uncertainty. Classical DOB formulations estimate these effects in systems described by explicit plant or low-dimensional state-space models ( Ohnishi et al., 1996 ; Chen et al., 2016 ; Sariyildiz et al., 2020 ) . Conventional MPC operates within the same model-based setting, optimizing behavior over a finite horizon using explicit dynamics and constraints ( Garcia et al., 1989 ; Mayne et al., 2000 ; Ostafew et al., 2016 ) . DOB estimates can therefore be incorporated into its prediction and optimization loop, for example by correcting output predictions ( Yang et al., 2015 ) .

However, modern robotic systems increasingly use sampling-based MPC when the dynamics or costs are highly nonlinear, nonsmooth, or accessible only through simulators. Sampling-based MPC evaluates candidate action sequences through forward rollouts. Methods such as model predictive path integral control (MPPI) ( Williams et al., 2018a ; Carius et al., 2022 ; Koptev et al., 2024 ) and the cross-entropy method (CEM) ( Rubinstein, 1997 ; Kobilarov, 2012 ; Pinneri et al., 2021 ) rank these candidates using scalar trajectory costs. Because they require only forward rollouts and scalar costs, these methods can use nonlinear simulators without analytic derivatives. At the same time, rollout evaluation has expanded beyond analytical dynamics to perception-derived cost maps and signed-distance fields ( Hornung et al., 2013 ; Oleynikova et al., 2017 ; Zucker et al., 2013 ) , while world models ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ) learn action-conditioned latent dynamics for prediction and planning. This flexibility allows MPC to use a broader range of models, but it also makes disturbance estimation less direct. The resulting interfaces may provide neither an invertible plant representation nor a clearly defined input-equivalent disturbance channel. Unmodeled effects are therefore revealed through deviations in the feedback state or changes in the costs assigned to queried states, for example after contact, perception updates, or obstacle motion. The controller observes these effects only after executing an action and receiving feedback. Taken together, these changes leave a mismatch between the information required by classical DOB formulations and the interfaces exposed by modern predictive models.

To address this interface mismatch, we present SDOB as a framework for feedback-based disturbance compensation in analytical models, simulators, and learned predictors exposed through rollout or cost-query interfaces. We refer to each member of this family as a modern model. The state channel fits feedback transitions within a task-defined disturbance parameterization, while the cost channel models local transport of environment-dependent costs. Together, these channels specify how observed mismatch enters subsequent rollout and cost evaluation. SDOB therefore targets locally persistent, task-relevant mismatch rather than complete identification of the sim-to-real gap. The main contributions are:

A new interface-level disturbance representation is introduced for modern models. Unlike conventional DOB formulations that primarily describe disturbances through plant dynamics and state evolution, SDOB separates observable deployment mismatch into two complementary channels: a state-effect disturbance that alters rollout states and a cost disturbance that changes costs at fixed query states. This extends disturbance observation to environment-dependent cost evaluation.

Based on this representation, SDOB introduces a next-generation approach to disturbance observation that operates through forward rollouts and cost queries. Unlike classical DOB designs built on explicit transfer functions or state-space equations, SDOB does not require access to the analytical expressions of the underlying model. It estimates both disturbance channels online and incorporates their effects into future state propagation and cost evaluation, without plant inversion or model retraining.

The framework is extensively validated across diverse simulation environments and real-robot platforms, spanning analytical-model disturbance compensation, moving-obstacle navigation, latent and visual world-model planning, mobile-robot navigation, dual-arm obstacle avoidance, and humanoid dual-arm manipulation with PointWorld, demonstrating its applicability across different model classes and robotic tasks.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the classical DOB formulation used as a reference. Section 4 presents SDOB, including its deployment-oriented interpretation, two disturbance channels, and compensation interfaces. Section 5 reports the simulation and real-robot experiments. Section 6 concludes the article and discusses its limitations and future directions.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 DOB-Based Control

Classical DOB-based control estimates input disturbances from a nominal plant, commonly through an inverse model and low pass filtering, to improve motion control robustness ( Ohnishi et al., 1996 ; Shim and Jo, 2009 ; Sariyildiz et al., 2020 ; Park and Back, 2024 ) . Nonlinear DOB formulations extend this principle to robotic dynamical systems ( Chen et al., 2000a ; Chen et al., 2000b ; Mohammadi et al., 2013 ; Chen et al., 2016 ) . Active disturbance rejection control (ADRC) and extended state observer (ESO) methods likewise estimate lumped uncertainty in feedback loops ( Han, 2009 ; Gao, 2003 ) , while DOB-enhanced predictive control incorporates disturbance estimates into prediction and optimization ( Yang et al., 2015 ) . Many classical DOB formulations assume an explicit plant model and a predefined disturbance channel. These assumptions are difficult to retain when control operates on images, latent or object centric states, or rollout distributions available only through forward simulation and cost evaluation.

## 2.2 Sampling-Based MPC

Sampling-based MPC optimizes candidate action sequences through forward rollouts and ranks, weights, or refits them using trajectory costs ( Theodorou et al., 2010 ; Williams et al., 2015 ; Williams et al., 2018a ; Pinneri et al., 2021 ) . Requiring only simulated futures and scalar costs makes it suitable for nonlinear, nonsmooth, and black box models. Tube-MPPI uses MPPI to generate a nominal trajectory and an ancillary tracking controller to keep the actual state within a tube around that trajectory ( Williams et al., 2018b ) . Robust model predictive path integral control (RMPPI) extends this architecture with augmented rollouts of the nominal and actual dynamics, tracking-aware importance sampling, and safety logic for nominal-state propagation ( Gandhi et al., 2021 ) . Parameter uncertainty can be incorporated directly into path integral control ( Abraham et al., 2020 ) , while Shield-MPPI integrates control barrier functions for safety ( Yin et al., 2023 ) .

## 2.3 Dynamic Environment Estimation and Cost Prediction

Planning in dynamic environments requires anticipating how environmental motion changes collision risks and trajectory costs. Dynamic occupancy grids estimate occupancy and motion ( Nuss et al., 2018 ) , while Occupancy Flow Fields jointly predict their future evolution ( Mahjourian et al., 2022 ) . ImplicitO supports continuous occupancy and flow queries at selected locations, avoiding dense scene prediction ( Agro et al., 2023 ) . To evaluate candidate trajectories, neural motion planners learn spatiotemporal cost volumes ( Zeng et al., 2019 ) , while QuAD queries predicted occupancy at planning-relevant locations ( Biswas et al., 2024 ) . These methods primarily focus on predicting occupancy or planning costs, with less emphasis on treating cost changes at fixed query states as a distinct disturbance channel for online estimation and compensation.

## 2.4 Sim-to-Real Adaptation

Sim-to-real adaptation takes a complementary approach by changing the training distribution, system model, or simulator. Domain randomization broadens the training variation ( Tobin et al., 2017 ) , system identification calibrates the dynamics ( Tan et al., 2018 ) , and feedback driven simulator adaptation updates the simulator from real experience ( Chebotar et al., 2019 ) . Adaptation methods can align latent representations under unknown target appearances ( Yoneda et al., 2022 ) , while ManiDreams propagates perceptual, parametric, and structural uncertainty through task specific predictive models ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Such methods adapt the simulator, representation, policy, or predictive state, but remain tied to variations represented during training or adaptation. Greater simulator fidelity also does not guarantee that method rankings or task outcomes transfer to hardware ( Kadian et al., 2020 ) , particularly when learned states do not map directly to physical variables.

## 2.5 World Models for Prediction and Planning

World models learn action conditioned representations for imagined futures, from early latent models ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ) to PlaNet ( Hafner et al., 2019 ) , Dreamer ( Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) , and TD-MPC2 ( Hansen et al., 2024 ) . Learned dynamics for manipulation ( Ai et al., 2025 ) , broader predictive architectures ( LeCun, 2022 ) , V-JEPA ( Bardes et al., 2024 ) , and PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) extend this direction toward feature level and 3D action conditioned representations. These models improve prediction, but nominal replanning does not usually preserve recurring execution mismatch as an explicit disturbance. Actuator bias, contact mismatch, object drift, and environmental change can therefore reappear as rollout error at every control cycle.

These developments motivate extending disturbance observation to a broader range of predictive models. To establish the conceptual basis for this extension, the next section revisits the basic principle of classical DOBs.
