2026-10-06.title: ExStereo: Lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action Models to 3D with Explicit Stereo Representations
2026-10-06.authors: I-Chun Arthur Liu , Jason Chen , Gaurav S. Sukhatme , Daniel Seita
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract: Three-dimensional perception is critical for robotic manipulation, particularly for high-precision tasks, as recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB observations is inherently ill-posed. However, many Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely solely on RGB observations for perception. Leveraging recent advances in foundation models for stereo matching, we introduce ExStereo, a stereo module that augments pre-trained 2D VLAs with 3D perception. ExStereo reconstructs scene geometry from stereo image pairs and renders multi-view observations as an explicit stereo representation for stereo feature extraction. The action tokens from the action expert selectively attend to the resulting stereo tokens through our proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, enabling the policy to generate robot actions conditioned on 3D scene information. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage before task-specific post-training, using a self-supervised learning objective on large-scale stereo data. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two publicly available VLAs, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and SmolVLA, and evaluate them in simulation and on a real-world bimanual PiPER platform. Across both settings, VLAs fine-tuned with ExStereo consistently outperform baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of stereo perception for robotic manipulation. Our anonymous project website is available at https://exstereo-vla.github.io/ExStereo/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , demonstrating impressive visuomotor capabilities. By building on large-scale pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [ 4 , 5 ] , these policies learn from semantic priors, acquire diverse skills from demonstrations, and generalize across objects and instructions. However, most VLA models operate on monocular RGB observations processed through pre-trained 2D vision encoders to extract features for downstream action generation. Operating on 2D visual tokens, these policies lack precise depth and geometric information. While effective in controlled settings, real-world interactions often require accurate spatial relationships and object locations, as well as robustness to occlusions and visual variations.

Recent work has explored injecting 3D structure into VLAs [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , achieving strong performance on 3D manipulation tasks. However, these methods depend on RGB-D sensors, which require precise calibration and are sensitive to sensor noise. Meanwhile, StereoVLA [ 10 ] and StereoPolicy [ 11 ] leverage stereo image pairs to obtain implicit stereo features for policy learning. StereoVLA requires training its VLA from scratch, while StereoPolicy provides only modest improvements to pre-trained VLAs. In this work, we show how effectively leveraging explicit stereo representations can equip 2D VLAs with metric 3D perception and substantially improve their performance.

We propose lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action models to 3D with Ex plicit Stereo Representations (ExStereo), a stereo module that equips pre-trained, off-the-shelf VLAs with 3D spatial perception. It takes a stereo image pair as input and employs a pre-trained stereo foundation model [ 12 ] to obtain a disparity map. Using the camera intrinsics and stereo baseline, the disparity map is transformed into a metric depth map and 3D point cloud. The point cloud is rendered from four orthogonal viewpoints (Top, Front, Left, and Right) using z-buffering. The four views are then tiled horizontally to form a multi-view observation, which is fed into a Vision Transformer (ViT) [ 5 ] to obtain stereo tokens. The stereo tokens are utilized for action generation through the proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, where the action tokens serve as queries and the stereo tokens serve as keys and values. This allows the action tokens to selectively attend to relevant 3D visual features without modifying the large prefix token sequence or the weights of VLMs, enabling pre-trained robot policies to efficiently integrate the stereo module during post-training. See Figure 1 for an overview.

To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage with a masked autoencoding objective prior to post-training. During mid-training, patches of the multi-view observation are randomly masked, and the VLA is trained on a large-scale stereo dataset to reconstruct the missing patches while learning to extract relevant visual features for action generation from incomplete observations. During post-training, the stereo module is frozen to prevent overfitting to task-specific demonstrations.
We evaluate ExStereo on ten simulated RoboTwin [ 13 ] tasks and three real-world tasks using a bimanual AgileX PiPER platform. ExStereo improves the average simulation success rate of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} from 51.2% to 76.4% and its real-world success rate from 16/60 to 50/60 trials, while also outperforming point-cloud and implicit-stereo baselines.

The contributions of this paper are:

We propose ExStereo, a novel stereo module that lifts any 2D VLA to 3D for fast adaptation without requiring additional pre-training of the base policy.

We demonstrate that explicit stereo representations, when used appropriately, yield stronger downstream manipulation performance than implicit representations.

Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show that VLAs equipped with ExStereo greatly improve upon the performance of their base VLAs while outperforming other strong baselines.

1. We propose ExStereo, a novel stereo module that lifts any 2D VLA to 3D for fast adaptation without requiring additional pre-training of the base policy.

2. We demonstrate that explicit stereo representations, when used appropriately, yield stronger downstream manipulation performance than implicit representations.

3. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show that VLAs equipped with ExStereo greatly improve upon the performance of their base VLAs while outperforming other strong baselines.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, also commonly referred to as robotic foundation models, fine-tune pretrained VLMs to output robot actions, such as end-effector pose deltas or joint targets, by training on large-scale teleoperation data [ 14 ] . Representative systems include RT-2, OpenVLA [ 1 ] , SmolVLA [ 15 ] , and the π \pi family [ 16 , 2 , 17 , 18 ] . We refer the reader to [ 19 , 20 ] for surveys.
Early VLAs discretized actions into tokens and predicted them autoregressively [ 21 , 1 ] , whereas recent policies attach a dedicated action expert trained with diffusion or flow matching to produce smooth, high-frequency action chunks [ 16 , 2 , 15 ] .

Camera configurations have broadened in parallel, from a single third-person view to wrist-mounted cameras and to multi-camera rigs that observe the workspace from several sides [ 2 ] . Across these variants, each view is still processed by a monocular 2D encoder so metric scale and inter-object spatial relations must be inferred from appearance. Prior work has addressed these limitations by incorporating depth sensors [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , such as RGB-D cameras. However, these sensors often degrade on transparent [ 24 ] and reflective surfaces and are sensitive to sensor noise, calibration errors, and point cloud artifacts, making high-quality 3D reconstruction challenging. Beyond these hardware limitations, visual representations remain a key bottleneck. Existing 2D vision backbones [ 4 , 25 , 26 ] generalize well across diverse visual domains but lack explicit 3D structure. In contrast, 3D vision backbones directly capture geometry from point clouds [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] , but tend to underperform their 2D counterparts due to the scarcity of large-scale 3D training data.

These limitations motivate a 3D perception approach that preserves the scalability and representational strengths of 2D vision while providing explicit geometric information. Stereo setups are common on robot platforms and can recover such geometry from binocular disparity, yet the second image is rarely exploited by the policy. ExStereo builds on this observation and equips pre-trained VLAs with an explicit 3D representation computed from a stereo pair.

## II-B Stereo Vision in Computer Vision

Stereo matching recovers metric depth by estimating disparity between a rectified left–right
image pair without active depth sensors. Previous classical methods build a cost volume and refine
disparity with 3D convolutions or recurrent updates [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] .
More recently, the field has moved toward stereo foundation models that generalize zero-shot
across domains by transferring priors from monocular depth models. FoundationStereo [ 34 ] establishes this direction through large-scale pretraining, and later work improves robustness
on transparent, reflective, and textureless surfaces where depth sensors
fail [ 35 , 36 ] . Fast-FoundationStereo [ 12 ] distills these models for near real-time inference. We leverage it in ExStereo to obtain an explicit 3D representation.

## II-C Stereo Vision in Robotics

Stereo cameras recover depth from binocular disparity, making them more reliable for transparent, specular, and textureless objects, where conventional depth sensors often struggle. Prior work has applied stereo vision to challenging materials such as glass [ 24 , 37 ] , as well as to stereo-based grasping and tracking [ 38 ] . More recently, StereoPolicy [ 11 ] and StereoVLA [ 10 ] extract features from stereo modules, which we characterize as implicit representations (see Section IV-A for details), and combine them with language or RGB image features as inputs to a VLM for policy learning. In contrast, we use a stereo module to construct an explicit 3D representation of the scene and feed the corresponding tokens directly into the action expert for policy learning.

2026-10-06.title: Distributed Cascade Force Control of Soft-Tactile-Based Multi-robot System for Object Transportation
2026-10-06.authors: Duy Anh Nguyen , Nhat Minh Dinh Le , Nhan Huu Nguyen , Pham Duy Hung , Van Anh Ho , Trung Dung Ngo
2026-10-06.comment: . Published in the 2024 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)
2026-10-06.abstract: In this paper, we present a d istributed c ascade f orce c ontrol system (DCFC) for multiple robots with the aim of pushing a rigid object towards a desired moving target without their inter-robot communication. These mobile robots are equipped with 360-degree vision-based soft tactile sensors utilized to determine contact location and resultant impact force. By investigating the dynamics of moving rigid objects on the flat, we proposed a distributed cascade control. The inner loop control incorporates contact force and positioning, ensuring the robots’ pushing contact and application of the desired force to the object. The outer loop control coordinates the robots to push the object in a desired direction without inter-robot communication, regardless of the unknown object mass. The stability and convergence of the system are verified using the Lyapunov stability theory. We also conducted simulation and real-word experiments to validate the performance of the proposed control method, and the experimental results showcase the successful coordination of multiple robots in pushing an object towards a moving desired direction.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Collective object transportation by multiple robots can be employed in many practical applications, such as smart warehouses, construction sites, and search and rescue missions. To achieve collaborative tasks, a distributed control system for consensus decision-making among the robots conducted at the individual level based on local information and interactions with neighbouring robots is required. The advantages of a distributed control system for multi-robot systems are known as scalability, robustness, and adaptability when deployed in dynamic and uncertain environments. This allows the robotic system to handle the complexity of a given task and the number of robots required for the task, such as heavy object transportation, inspired by the ants as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

Research on object transportation by multi-robot systems is roughly categorized into two groups named pushing and grasping . In general, the pushing method involves exerting force on an object through physical contact but physical attachment, while the grasping approach requires a physical connection between the robot and the transported object. In general, pushing is more challenging than grasping because no additional gripping tool is needed while the dynamics of rigid objects are critically required.

The primitive strategy for multiple mobile robots to transport an object involves controlling robots’ velocity and/or formation while dealing with forces between the object, robots, and the surface as disturbances. Inspired by collective behaviours in social insects in [ 1 ] , the authors proposed simple group behaviour-based algorithms for pushing a box forward without communication. These algorithms were extended by employing sensors to detect the goal, allowing the robots to relocate around and push the object when the goal was detected [ 2 ] . Further studies analyzed the stagnation recovery based on ants’ behavior and tested the box-pushing algorithm by tracking changing goals with different types of boxes [ 3 , 4 ] . However, these kinetic strategies have limitations as they did not account for the physical interaction between the object and the surface, which plays a critical role in object transportation, especially across various terrains or slopes [ 5 ] . Uncontrollable forces between the object and the robots can exceed safety limits and harm both the robots and the object, particularly fragile ones. These methods may lead to inaccuracy in task performance as they do not incorporate rigid-body object dynamics to represent object behaviour.

Recent studies addressed the above-mentioned problems by considering object dynamics and robot forces . Grasping techniques with controllable exerted force provided greater control freedom for robots to push or pull objects with the motion of local objects measured by each robot as implicit information for force coordination [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . In [ 6 ] , it was proved that all the robots’ contact forces converged to a leader force direction, resulting in a force-amplifying effect. An extension of this work considered both force and torque consensus [ 7 ] , as well as steering the leader’s force to navigate the system in narrow spaces [ 8 ] . In other directions, decentralized adaptive control leveraged the theory of adaptive control method to estimate system parameters and manipulate the object simultaneously [ 9 , 10 ] . The desired object states, such as linear and angular velocity and desired trajectories, were achieved and proved through the Lyapunov stability theory. Within the scope of pushing methods, some researchers proposed collective transportation strategies based on occlusion, where robots only pushed the object when their vision of the goal was obscured [ 11 ] , [ 12 ] . Maintaining continuous pushing on the object while transporting it towards the desired direction is always challenging with pushing methods. In [ 13 ] , object transportation was performed by employing explicit force control of two pushing robots while cluster space control for the formation and relative positioning was maintained through continuous intercommunication.

This paper introduces a distributed cascade control system for multiple soft-tactile-based robots specialized in transporting rectangle-shaped objects without communication. Using the soft tactile sensors developed in our previous work [ 14 ] , real-time tactile information on each robot is obtained from physical interaction within a multi-agent robotic system and with the surroundings. The proposed control strategy enables the robots to exert pushing forces while maintaining constant contact with the object. The proposed approach demonstrates adaptability and versatility in cascade distributed control for soft-tactile-based robot systems, accommodating various object masses and dealing with moving in the desired direction.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II overviews rigid-body object dynamics and introduces our mobile robot platform. Section III outlines the problem and objectives. Section IV examines our proposed DCFC and includes proof of its stability. Section V presents the results and the discussion of both simulation and real-world experiments. Finally, the conclusions are presented in Section VI.

2026-10-06.title: Learning Task and Motion Plans from Real Demonstrations with Hybrid Flow Matching
2026-10-06.authors: Zuleika Redondo Garcia , Andreu Matoses Gimenez , Javier Alonso-Mora
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires a task plan and the motion that executes it. Generative planners trained on demonstration produce both in one pass, requiring neither a symbolic domain nor search. To date, however, they have relied on thousands of scripted demonstrations of fixed-base arms and executed open loop.
This paper presents a hybrid flow matching planner: a single network generates the symbolic plan with masked discrete flow matching and the motion trajectory with continuous flow matching. Unlike prior generative planners, we aim to learn from a much smaller set of demonstrations and to execute the plan in closed loop. Two properties of the data compensate for the small dataset.
A demonstration resumed from any of its intermediate actions is itself a demonstration, which multiplies the training samples and enables replanning after every action. Objects of the same kind are interchangeable, which turns demonstrations of one goal into demonstrations of every permuted goal. Our base implementation produces valid plans on 68% of held-out scenes; a training and generation scheme for the discrete plan raises this to 76%, and replanning after every action raises the task completion rate from 40% to 53% in a kinematic simulation.
The planner matches the task completion rate of motion-only flow matching policies while additionally providing the symbolic plan, and it outperforms previous hybrid diffusion formulations on both task completion and plan validity. We validate the planner on a real mobile manipulator.
Videos and project page: andreumatoses.github.io/research/hybrid-flow-planning
2026-10-06.introduction:
Mobile manipulation tasks such as tidying a room or assembling a structure require a robot to decide what to do and how to move. To stack three cubes on a target table (Fig. 1 ), a robot has to choose which cube to pick first, from which side of which table, in which position to place it. It also has to produce the base and arm motion for each choice. The two levels depend on each other: a cube can only be reached from certain sides of a table, and a covered cube cannot be picked. Task and motion planning (TAMP) produces both the action sequence and the motion that realizes it while keeping them consistent [ 1 ] .

Classical TAMP methods search over symbolic action sequences and call a motion planner to check each candidate [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . They need a hand-written model of the task: predicates, action operators, and samplers for continuous parameters such as grasps and base placements. The search is also expensive, which limits replanning when the scene changes. Learning can guide the search [ 6 , 7 ] or distill planner solutions into policies [ 8 ] , but both still depend on the planner and its model.

Generative models trained on demonstrations take a different route. The task knowledge enters through the demonstrations, so no planning domain is written by hand. A plan then costs one generation pass with a fixed number of network evaluations instead of a search over candidate plans. Diffusion and flow matching policies capture the multimodal distribution of demonstrated motion and generate whole trajectories [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . On long tasks with several distinct decisions, however, the model blends different behaviors and the trajectory commits to none of them. Høeg et al. [ 13 ] address this with a discrete and a continuous diffusion process in one network that generate a symbolic plan together with the trajectory, and show that the joint generation outperforms trajectory-only generation.

The space of task and motion plans is combinatorial, as each possible action sequence must be grounded in the geometry of the scene. Prior joint symbolic and continuous generative planners have therefore relied on hundreds to thousands of demonstrations per task, often generated by scripted experts on fixed-base manipulators and executed open loop [ 13 ] .
For real mobile manipulators, however, demonstrations are typically collected through teleoperation and cannot be generated at that scale. This limited coverage raises three challenges:
generalization to unseen scenes and plans, generation of variable-length symbolic plans, and error accumulation during open-loop execution.

We address these challenges with a hybrid flow matching planner for mobile manipulation trained on about one hundred real demonstrations. Given an observation of the scene, a single network simultaneously generates a discrete symbolic plan and the continuous trajectories of both the mobile base and the end effector.
To improve data efficiency, we augment each demonstration with its suffixes, the remaining plan and trajectory after each of its actions, which also enables the planner to replan after every action. We also exploit object interchangeability through object permutations, a consistent renaming of the objects in plan and observation, to obtain goal-conditioned demonstrations.
We further constrain the generated plans to well-formed action sequences, adapt training to variable-length plans, and automatically balance the discrete and continuous losses.

We evaluate the method on a mobile manipulator building a three-cube tower from 109 teleoperated demonstrations. Generated plans are validated with a symbolic model, executed in kinematic simulation, and evaluated on the real robot. We compare against motion-only flow matching and the hybrid diffusion planner of Høeg et al. [ 13 ] , and ablate the proposed components.

The contributions of this paper are:

A hybrid flow matching planner that jointly generates the symbolic plan and the motion of a mobile manipulator, with a training and generation scheme that improves symbolic plan validity and task completion.

Two augmentations that exploit the structure of task and motion demonstrations, which allow replanning after every action and goal conditioning without new demonstrations (Section IV-D ).

An evaluation on real demonstrations against motion-only flow matching and hybrid diffusion [ 13 ] , with ablations and a deployment on the real robot (Section V ).

1. A hybrid flow matching planner that jointly generates the symbolic plan and the motion of a mobile manipulator, with a training and generation scheme that improves symbolic plan validity and task completion.

2. Two augmentations that exploit the structure of task and motion demonstrations, which allow replanning after every action and goal conditioning without new demonstrations (Section IV-D ).

3. An evaluation on real demonstrations against motion-only flow matching and hybrid diffusion [ 13 ] , with ablations and a deployment on the real robot (Section V ).
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Task and motion planning (TAMP) integrates symbolic task planning with geometric reasoning to ensure that high-level action sequences are physically feasible [ 1 ] . Existing approaches couple these levels in different ways. Hierarchical methods progressively interleave task and motion planning [ 2 ] , while planner-independent frameworks allow symbolic planners to invoke black-box geometric samplers [ 3 , 5 , 14 ] . Logic-geometric programming instead optimizes the action sequence and its associated motion jointly [ 4 ] . Learning has also been used to guide the planning process, for example by ranking candidate refinements [ 6 ] or predicting promising action sequences before geometric verification [ 7 ] . Other work distills planner-generated solutions into visuomotor policies [ 8 ] . These approaches generally retain an explicit planning model, either during execution or when generating training data. In contrast, we consider learning symbolic plans and their associated motions directly from teleoperated demonstrations.

Diffusion models generate multimodal trajectories from demonstrations, for planning [ 9 , 15 ] and for visuomotor control [ 10 ] . Flow matching trains the same class of models with a regression objective and supports sampling in only a few integration steps [ 11 ] ; it has since been adopted for robot policies [ 16 , 12 ] . For long-horizon tasks, however, task structure is often provided separately. Generative skill chaining composes diffusion models according to a given skill sequence [ 17 ] , SkillDiffuser learns discrete skill abstractions from language instructions [ 18 ] , and LTLDoG constrains sampling with temporal logic [ 19 ] . Inside classical TAMP, diffusion models have served as samplers for continuous parameters [ 20 , 21 ] , while language models can provide high-level plans that are subsequently grounded by a diffusion model [ 22 ] . In these approaches, the symbolic task structure is provided, inferred, or planned separately from the continuous motion. Our planner instead generates both jointly.

Discrete diffusion and flow models generate token sequences by progressively unmasking an initially masked sequence [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . Campbell et al. [ 27 ] combine such a masked discrete flow with a continuous flow to co-design protein sequences and structures, while Diffusion Forcing assigns individual noise levels to tokens so that a single model can support both full-sequence and next-token generation [ 28 ] . Closest to our work, Høeg et al. [ 13 ] jointly generate a symbolic plan and continuous trajectory using discrete and continuous diffusion processes within a single transformer, with independent noise levels for the two modalities. On simulated and real tabletop tasks, the joint generation outperforms trajectory-only diffusion. Our work builds on this hybrid formulation, replacing diffusion with flow matching and studying the more data-limited setting of teleoperated mobile-manipulation demonstrations.

Relabeling and symmetry provide complementary ways to reuse demonstrations without collecting additional data. Hindsight experience replay relabels trajectories according to achieved goals [ 29 ] , while equivariant policies incorporate scene symmetries into the policy architecture [ 30 ] . Receding-horizon execution similarly improves robustness by repeatedly replanning over fixed-length action chunks [ 31 , 10 ] . This strategy has also been applied to real mobile manipulation using relatively small per-task demonstration sets supplemented by co-training data [ 32 ] . Our work exploits object interchangeability for symbolic relabeling and performs replanning at symbolic action boundaries rather than at a fixed temporal horizon.

2026-10-06.title: Flow Policies as Actions of Skill-Level World Models: Learned and Symbolic Abstractions for Long-Horizon Planning
2026-10-06.authors: Andreu Matoses Gimenez , Andrei-Carlo Papuc , Chris Pek , Javier Alonso-Mora
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Latent world models enable robots to plan by predicting the consequences of actions.
Planning long tasks with control-rate actions requires many prediction steps, which enlarges the search space and accumulates error.
Skill-level actions shorten these sequences, but a symbolic skill vocabulary requires domain knowledge and labeled demonstrations.
We construct skill-level actions from the inputs of a flow-matching policy trained on demonstrations segmented into complete skills.
The policy maps a noise seed and an observation, optionally with a code or label, to a complete skill execution, so one execution is one world-model transition.
On this mechanism we propose four action abstractions with increasing task knowledge: a compressed seed, two discrete codes learned from the demonstrations, and a symbolic label.
We evaluate them with a common world-model training procedure and planning framework on simulated block rearrangement tasks that require up to 14 sequential skills.
The symbolic label succeeds in over 90% of the tasks that require up to six skills and degrades beyond.
Without any label, an object-centric learned code matches it on single-skill tasks and retains half to three quarters of its success on tasks of two to five skills.
Ablations attribute much of the label’s advantage to its planner knowing which actions are applicable, rather than to the label itself.
Beyond six skills the search, not the world model, limits success.
Project page: andreumatoses.github.io/research/flow-skill-wm
2026-10-06.introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation tasks, such as rearranging block towers, require sequences of skills whose outcomes determine which actions can follow.
Planning directly over motor commands involves many prediction steps and a large search space.
Task-and-motion planning addresses this difficulty by combining high-level actions, such as moving or stacking a block, with motion planning [ 1 ] .
These high-level actions, called symbolic operators, describe what an action does and when it can be performed.
For example, moving a block requires that no other block rests on it.
Specifying these actions and rules requires domain knowledge.

Latent world models offer a learned way to predict the consequences of candidate actions.
They allow a planner to evaluate action sequences in a compact, learned representation of the scene before executing them [ 2 , 3 ] .
The choice of action abstraction determines the temporal scale of these predictions: motor commands describe individual control steps, whereas skills describe complete behaviors.
A central question is how to construct skill-level actions that a world model can predict and a robot can execute.

We investigate this question using flow-matching policies trained on demonstrations of complete skills [ 4 ] .
A flow policy generates a sequence of motor commands from the current observation and a sampled noise input, called a seed .
It can also receive a code or label that specifies the intended behavior.
The planner selects these inputs, while the policy generates the motion.
We treat each complete policy execution as one world-model transition between settled scenes, where the robot and objects are at rest (Fig. 1 ).

Within this framework, we compare four action abstractions: a compressed seed of the policy; a discrete code learned from the scenes before and after a demonstrated skill; an object-centric learned code describing which object moves and where it goes; and a hand-written symbolic label specifying the skill, object, and target.
Each abstraction provides inputs from which the policy generates the robot’s motion.
All four use demonstrations divided into complete skills, but the first three do not require demonstrations to be annotated with symbolic action labels.

Planning also requires deciding which actions to consider at each step.
The abstractions differ in how these candidates are selected.
The symbolic label uses hand-written rules, called preconditions , to determine which actions can be performed, and effects to describe how they change the scene.
The learned-code abstractions instead use learned models to estimate which actions can be performed and their effects.
We therefore ask how both the action abstraction and the selection of candidate actions affect planning as the required number of skills increases.
We study these factors in a simulated block rearrangement problem using a shared policy architecture, world-model training procedure, and planning framework.

transition corresponds to a complete flow-policy execution

Four action abstractions spanning compressed seeds,
learned codes, and symbolic labels, evaluated on block
rearrangement tasks of increasing difficulty
(§ IV , § V ).

Ablations and diagnostics examining how candidate action

planning success (§ V ).

# II Related Work

World models and temporal abstraction. Latent world models support control by predicting the consequences of candidate actions in a learned representation of the scene [ 5 , 6 ] .
TD-MPC2 combines short model rollouts with a learned value estimate of the final rollout state [ 7 ] .
Others extend the horizon by predicting the effects of longer actions: CAVIN separates high-level effects from low-level motion generation [ 8 ] , and HWM learns world models at multiple temporal scales, compressing sequences of primitive actions into latent actions and using predicted subgoals to guide lower-level planning [ 9 ] .
We instead set the prediction timescale through a flow policy trained on demonstrations of complete skills: one policy execution is one world-model transition, and the policy itself produces the underlying motor commands.
Planning thus operates over skills rather than control steps, reducing the number of predictions required for long-horizon tasks.

Generative policies and planning. Diffusion and flow policies can represent multiple behaviors for the same observation [ 10 , 4 , 11 ] , and Diffuser uses a generative trajectory model directly for planning [ 12 ] .
DSRL shows that the input noise of a frozen diffusion or flow policy controls its behavior, and uses reinforcement learning to select it [ 13 ] .
DiWA fine-tunes diffusion policies with reinforcement learning on experience imagined by a learned world model [ 14 ] .
We likewise keep the policy fixed, but search over its inputs with a separate world model at planning time.
These inputs form an executable action abstraction: the planner selects a seed and, where applicable, a code or label, and the policy turns them into a complete skill.
The challenge is to represent these inputs in a form that supports both reliable execution and prediction of their effects.

Learned and symbolic action abstractions. Genie, LAPO, and LAPA infer latent actions from changes between observations without action annotations [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Our learned codes also capture changes between observations, but a flow policy trained on demonstrated motor commands executes the corresponding skills.
This removes the need for symbolic action labels, though demonstrations must still be segmented into complete skills.
Task-and-motion planning uses symbolic operators that describe actions and their preconditions [ 1 ] ; such symbols can also be learned from given skills [ 18 ] .

Building on these ideas, we seek an action abstraction that lets a world model predict the effects of complete skills and a robot execute them.
We study four such abstractions, combining learned codes and symbolic structure, to identify what supports long-horizon planning and what continues to limit it.

2026-10-06.title: PatternDex: Learning Interaction Patterns to Guide Reinforcement Learning of Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Objects
2026-10-06.authors: David Minkwan Kim , Runfa Blark Li , Beckham Po-Ju Lee , Nikolay Atanasov , Truong Nguyen
2026-10-06.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: In this paper, we develop a method that enables bimanual dexterous hands to manipulate articulated objects with a high success rate without suffering from an embodiment gap. We observe that the correlation between hand motions and object motions is dictated by the object rather than the hands and can be learned from human-object demonstrations. Based on this observation, we propose PatternDex, a method that learns this correlation and represents it as a token sequence, which we call an interaction pattern. From this pattern, PatternDex estimates the wrist motions and contact points that fit the target robot, and then trains a reinforcement learning policy that exploits these estimates as guidance. Since the guidance fits the target embodiment, the policy explores only the actions that the target robot can execute and thus achieves high success rates. PatternDex also requires only simple fine-tuning to train a new robot, since it can reuse the learned interaction pattern. We evaluate PatternDex with bimanual dexterous hands on human demonstrations from the ARCTIC dataset. PatternDex achieves, on average, a 92.8% success rate with Allegro hands, while the state-of-the-art baseline achieves 52.2%. Also, it achieves success rates above 70% with three other robot hands after fine-tuning alone. Furthermore, we verify that the learned policy transfers well to a real-world task of opening a microwave. Videos and additional results are available at https://patterndex.github.io/PatternDex/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation of articulated objects, such as opening a microwave door or a laptop lid, is a challenging problem because it requires coordinating and synchronizing high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) hands.
Successful approaches for these tasks adopt imitation learning, which trains a reinforcement learning policy to reproduce the motions observed in human demonstrations [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
A straightforward method is to train a policy with robot execution data collected through teleoperation, where a human operator controls the robot hands directly [ 1 , 2 ] . However, collecting teleoperation data is expensive and time-consuming.
Another approach is to use kinematic retargeting that maps the human finger joints to the robot finger joints [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , but this method becomes unreliable when the embodiment gap between the human and the robot hands is large.
A more recent approach [ 7 ] observes that the human wrist motion is less sensitive to the embodiment gap than the finger motion, so it imitates only the human wrist motion and learns the finger actions with reinforcement learning.
However, this method addresses the embodiment gap with respect to the fingers but not with respect to the hand size and structure. When the robot wrist is placed at the human wrist pose, a larger robot hand exceeds the manipulation workspace, and a smaller hand fails to reach the object. Thus, imitating the human wrist alone is still insufficient to eliminate the embodiment gap.

We observe that in articulated manipulation tasks, the correlation between the hand and object motions is dictated by the desired object trajectory, rather than the hands. The key idea of our work is to learn this relationship and to represent it as a sequence of tokens in a latent space. We refer to such a sequence as an interaction pattern . Since the interaction pattern depends on the object rather than the hands, it is agnostic to the hand embodiment and can be mapped not only to human hands but also to various robot hands.
We develop a model that learns the interaction Pattern from human-object demonstrations and decodes it into training guidance for a reinforcement learning (RL) policy to achieve Dex terous manipulation of articulated objects. We refer to our method as PatternDex . By encoding an interaction pattern and combining it with a robot hand description, PatternDex estimates wrist motions and contact points that fit the target robot hand and uses them as guidance to drive the policy’s actions.
Fig. gives an overview of PatternDex, where the interaction pattern is learned from human demonstrations and reproduced with bimanual dexterous robot hands in simulation and the real world. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

We learn a latent representation of bimanual object manipulation in the form of a token sequence, which we call an interaction pattern. This representation captures the hand-object correlation dictated by the desired object trajectory and is agnostic to specific hand embodiments.

We design a guidance predictor that combines an interaction pattern with a robot hand description to predict the wrist motions and contact points for the desired manipulation task. Since the interaction pattern transfers across robot hands, the predictor is trained once and needs only simple fine-tuning for a new robot hand.

We train an RL policy with the wrist motions and contact points from the predictor as guidance. Since the guidance fits the target robot hand, the policy learns actions within the robot’s capabilities rather than imitating human motions that are not feasible for the robot. As a result, our guided policy achieves higher success rates than policies trained directly from human hand motions.

# II RELATED WORK

Dexterous Manipulation with Imitation Learning. Reinforcement learning has solved dexterous manipulation tasks by designing a reward that specifies what to achieve in each task [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] or by using a pretrained controller that moves the fingers so that the policy only gives high-level commands [ 11 ] . However, such methods are hard to design manually for long-horizon tasks such as manipulating an articulated object. Many works therefore learn a policy by imitating human hand-object demonstrations, which show how the human hand moves and where it touches the object [ 4 , 5 , 3 , 6 , 7 ] . ManipTrans [ 4 ] and DexMachina [ 5 ] kinematically retarget the human hand motion by matching a fixed set of keypoints on the human hand with the corresponding keypoints on the robot hand. ReGRIND [ 3 ] and TopoRetarget [ 6 ] formulate retargeting as an interaction-mesh optimization that preserves the spatial relationship between the hand and the object. Since these methods map each human finger to a robot finger, the retargeted motion becomes infeasible when a robot hand such as the large four-fingered Allegro hand follows the motion of the smaller five-fingered human hand. ObjDex [ 7 ] avoids this finger mapping by using only the human wrist trajectory as a reference, but the robot wrist is still placed at the human wrist pose. Therefore, a robot hand of a different size either exceeds the manipulation workspace or fails to reach the object.
In contrast, we solve this problem by estimating wrist motions that fit the robot embodiment instead of using the human wrists directly. We further add contact points estimated for the same embodiment, so the policy is guided on where the wrist should go and what the fingers should touch.

Hand-Object Motion Correlation. A line of work in computer graphics generates human hand motion from object motion. OMOMO [ 12 ] takes object motion alone and predicts where the hands should be to achieve it, and then generates a body pose from the predicted hands. CAMS [ 13 ] uses the object shape and a sequence of object poses to predict the hand pose for each frame in a space defined with respect to the object and the contact. Both works show that a consistent correlation exists between object motion and the hand motion that achieves it, and that this correlation can be learned from human motion data. However, these methods generate the motion of human hands and have not been applied to a robot hand of a different embodiment. Accordingly, we learn this correlation as an embodiment-independent token sequence and apply it to robot hands by decoding the wrist motions and contact points for a given target hand.

2026-10-06.title: DNPush: Distributed Nonparallel Pushing Force Control of Multi-Robot Systems for Object Transportation
2026-10-06.authors: Duy Anh Nguyen , Pham Duy Hung , Trung Dung Ngo
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
2026-10-06.abstract: This letter proposes DNPush, a Distributed Nonparallel Pushing force controller for cooperative object transport without inter-robot communication. Each robot uses local force measurements, a preassigned force weight, and a locally expressed desired transport direction, without requiring an object model, contact locations, a CoM estimate, or moment arm magnitudes online. DNPush regulates nonparallel force magnitudes from local force direction misalignments through a reciprocal-sine law. Under the stated contact conditions, Lyapunov analysis with LaSalle’s invariance principle proves convergence to a unique rotational equilibrium, where perpendicular force contributions cancel and the net torque from normal forces is zero. Object velocity converges to the desired transport direction, and suitable contact regions exist for convex polygons. Simulations isolate the reciprocal-sine scaling mechanism, five-robot coordination, and active rotational damping. Hardware experiments with soft tactile differential-drive robots achieve a velocity direction error of 0.61 ∘ ± 0.79 ∘ 0.61^{\circ}\pm 0.79^{\circ} over five trials with a fixed transport direction and demonstrate object transport through waypoints with three robots.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Cooperative pushing mobile robots move objects through direct body contact, unlike grasping , which relies on mechanical attachment, or caging , which maintains geometric enclosure [ 1 ] . Each robot pushes the object at a contact location, which determines the direction of the applied force and its rotational effect about the object CoM [ 2 , 3 ] .

For a given set of contact locations, the pushing forces must be coordinated to achieve the desired object motion. A centralized controller can allocate the force magnitudes using global information about the object geometry and pushing directions. However, global information may be limited, and reliable inter-robot communication cannot always be assumed [ 4 ] . Distributed control reduces this dependence by allowing each robot to regulate its own pushing force using local information. The challenge is to design local control laws so that the resulting pushing forces collectively produce the desired object motion [ 4 , 1 ] . A previous distributed force controller [ 5 ] considered parallel pushing on a common object edge. It used the local force direction misalignment Δ i \Delta_{i} to rotate the object until the common pushing direction aligned with the desired transport direction, without inter-robot communication.

This method is limited to a common pushing direction and does not directly extend to nonparallel pushing. Nonparallel contacts remove the common straight edge requirement and allow robots to push on different or curved boundary regions with different rotational effects about the object CoM. However, reducing each local force direction misalignment no longer guarantees that the resultant pushing force aligns with the desired transport direction. DNPush instead uses Δ i \Delta_{i} to scale each pushing force magnitude, allowing the nonparallel forces to coordinate their resultant while stabilizing object rotation without inter-robot communication, as summarized in Fig. 1 .

The main contribution of this work is DNPush, a distributed controller for nonparallel pushing that achieves coordinated force allocation without inter-robot communication or moment arm magnitudes in the online controller. At equilibrium, the resulting force allocation balances both the perpendicular force contributions and the net torque from the normal forces. Under the stated contact conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of this equilibrium and use a Lyapunov analysis with LaSalle’s invariance principle to prove asymptotic rotational convergence, followed by alignment of the normal force resultant and convergence of the transport direction. Simulations isolate the reciprocal-sine scaling mechanism in a two-robot comparison, demonstrate coordinated force allocation with five robots, and characterize the role of rotational damping. Hardware experiments validate the controller on tactile-based mobile robots.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Cooperative object transport using multi-robot systems is commonly grouped by transport strategies, categorized as caging, grasping, and pushing [ 1 ] . Caging methods surround the object and maintain geometric containment during transport [ 6 , 7 ] . Caging requires the robots to maintain a coordinated enclosing configuration around the object throughout transport. Grasping methods physically attach the robots to the object, allowing them to transmit forces and torques in multiple directions. Several distributed controllers exploit these fixed connections to regulate shared object motion under limited inter-robot communication or uncertain object parameters [ 8 , 9 ] . This bidirectional interaction supports coordinated translation and rotation, but requires secure mechanical attachments and suitable grasp points.

Using pushing forces for object transport avoids the above-mentioned requirements, but each robot is restricted to unilateral contact forces. Classical manipulation research established the mechanics and controllability of planar pushing [ 2 , 3 ] . Earlier behavior- and occlusion-based methods used simple local rules to coordinate cooperative pushing without explicit communication [ 10 ] , but did not directly regulate the magnitudes of multiple nonparallel contact forces. Recent cooperative pushing studies have increasingly considered contact configuration and pushing planning. Contact locations have been optimized to improve the achievable object wrench under frictional constraints [ 11 ] . In [ 12 ] , hybrid optimization methods have also been developed to generate and switch among their associated pushing forces for multi-robot transport in complex environments. Force- and tactile feedback methods have been developed for robust pushing under uncertain object properties, and contact changes [ 13 , 14 ] while tactile SLAM methods estimate object shape and pose online during planar pushing [ 15 ] . Most of these works address contact selection, pushing mode planning, globally coordinated force allocation, or reactive manipulation under uncertain interactions. DNPush instead considers a fixed nonparallel contact configuration and addresses how several robots coordinate their pushing force magnitudes using only local tactile feedback and no inter-robot communication.

The most related work is the previous study of Distributed Cascade Force Control (DCFC) for soft tactile multi-robot object transport [ 5 ] . DCFC used local tactile force regulation and established rotational convergence without inter-robot communication. However, it required parallel pushing forces applied at contacts on a common straight object edge. This requirement restricts its application to objects with a sufficiently long straight boundary segment that accommodates multiple robots. DNPush overcomes this limitation by allowing nonparallel boundary contacts of pushing forces on the transported object and changing the role of force direction misalignment. Instead of reducing the misalignment to zero, DNPush uses it to set the local force magnitude, balancing the force components perpendicular to the desired direction, and creating a restoring torque under the ordered opposite moment condition.

2026-10-06.title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
2026-10-06.authors: Sribalaji C. Anand , George J. Pappas
2026-10-06.comment: Under review
2026-10-06.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team’s own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary’s reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary’s bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Multi-robot systems increasingly delegate planning, negotiation, and trust assessment to LLM agents [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . This raises a security question that the control community is well positioned to answer: when one agent in the team is compromised, how much can it degrade mission performance before its behavior becomes detectable, and which properties of the communication network determine that degradation?

Two literatures address adjacent versions of this question and both miss its central feature. Security studies of multi-agent LLMs consider ungrounded tasks (consensus on a scalar [ 4 , 5 ] , robustness of a shared answer under faulty agents [ 6 ] or similar tasks [ 7 ] ) in which agents exchange and filter messages but cannot check a claim against the world, so a persuasive lie is unfalsifiable. Classical resilient consensus and estimation ( r r -robustness, W-MSR [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] ) share this assumption: agents filter received values , and there is no notion of verifying a value. In a grounded robotic task, by contrast, the physical world is a ground-truth oracle. We study a basic task of this kind: a multi-robot survey where a team measures the value of every cell in a region and pools the measurements into a shared map. A robot can re-measure a cell its neighbor reported and compare, but every re-measurement consumes budget that would otherwise advance the survey, so verification cannot be applied everywhere.

We argue that this verification cost [ 11 ] , together with the graph structure, governs a compromised agent’s reach. The resulting question, how much damage an adversary can inflict while remaining within what an honest agent would produce, is exactly what system-theoretic security [ 12 , 13 ] is built to answer: the adversary is constrained not by an energy bound but by stealth with respect to a stated detector, and impact is characterized as a function of the detector, the system, and the adversary’s access. We bring this system-theoretic security framework to a multi-robot LLM survey team. Our contributions are:

Formulation. A model of a survey team whose robots share a map by gossip over a communication graph and can re-measure each other’s reports at a cost, in which a compromised robot is a stealthy adversary limited by the team’s detectors (Sections II – III ).

Verification bound. Proposition 1 bounds from below the probability that the compromised robot’s reports are verified, using the node degrees of the communication graph and the verification budget.

Damage bound. Using Proposition 1 , Proposition 2 bounds from above the error of any stealthy attack, as the value of a linear program over the adversary’s bias distributions. Its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage; below a critical verification level the worst attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, rather than many small ones. Under a record deadline it also yields an exact verification-parity rule (Corollary 2 ).

Experiments. Tests of both bounds with LLM-driven honest robots, measuring where the LLM agents differ from the assumptions behind the bounds, so that the role of the LLM is quantified rather than assumed (Section VI ).

2026-10-06.title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
2026-10-06.authors: Haonan Chen , Feiyang Wu , Yuxiang Ma , Mustafa Mete , Pengfei Ye , Junxuan Shen , Cheng Zhu , Aurora Ruggeri , Kelvin Cheung , Jiayuan Mao , Edward Adelson , Jiajun Wu , Robert D. Howe , Yilun Du
2026-10-06.abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action–force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Controlling interaction forces is important for contact-rich manipulation,
where excessive or insufficient force can damage objects or cause task
failure. This is particularly important when grasping soft objects (e.g.,
fruits, soft packages), handling deformable objects, or performing precise
insertion [ 1 , 2 ] . Existing robotic systems obtain such
feedback using wrist-mounted force/torque sensors [ 3 ] ,
flexible printed circuit board (FPCB)-based tactile
sensors [ 4 , 5 ] , or optical tactile
sensors such as GelSight Mini [ 6 ] . However, these sensing solutions introduce hardware and integration overhead and can require changes to the manipulator’s form factor and mechanical structure. Commercial six-axis
force/torque sensors from manufacturers such as ATI and Bota can cost several
thousand dollars per unit, excluding robot-specific mounting hardware and
system integration [ 7 , 8 ] . FPCB-based
tactile sensors often require custom fabrication, wiring, and calibration,
while optical tactile sensors require embedded cameras, illumination, and
compliant sensing surfaces that may wear under repeated contact. These
limitations motivate a natural question: Can a robot estimate force directly
from visual observations and use these estimates to guide contact-rich
manipulation?

In this work, we investigate learning force-aware manipulation using visual
observations of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. As illustrated in
Fig. 1 , contact forces produce visible deformation in the
gripper, providing visual cues for force estimation. Prior studies have
explored this relationship through simulation-based force prediction and
experimental analysis of Fin Ray deformation [ 9 , 10 ] . The gripper is
inexpensive and can be fabricated by 3D printing with TPU. We train a visual
force estimator to infer force from wrist-camera images of the gripper
during contact.

To use visual force estimates for manipulation, we first train a visual
force estimator on calibration data and use it to label task demonstrations.
We then train an action–force proposal policy on these demonstrations to
jointly generate candidate actions and the associated forces values from the demonstration distribution. At test time, the policy jointly samples multiple action–force candidates. We execute the action associated with the force value closest to a task-specific target derived from the demonstration force estimates. We evaluate the method on berry picking,
empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results
show that visual force estimates can guide action selection for contact-rich
manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce a visual force estimation method that infers force from the visible deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper.

We develop an action–force proposal policy and an inference-time selection procedure that uses target forces from demonstrations to guide action selection.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on four contact-rich manipulation tasks (berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion) without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

1. We introduce a visual force estimation method that infers force from the visible deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper.

2. We develop an action–force proposal policy and an inference-time selection procedure that uses target forces from demonstrations to guide action selection.

3. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on four contact-rich manipulation tasks (berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion) without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A Hardware-Based Force and Tactile Sensing

Dedicated force and tactile sensors obtain contact information through
several sensing mechanisms. Force-torque sensors provide accurate measurements
but require mounting, wiring, and calibration, while piezoelectric tactile
sensors capture high-frequency stimuli [ 11 ] . Optical tactile
sensors instead image a compliant sensing surface [ 12 ] .
GelSight recovers contact geometry and force-related signals [ 13 , 14 ] ,
with subsequent designs exploring compact integration and biomimetic
structures [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Related approaches reconstruct contact geometry and estimate forces from
tactile images [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] , while
GelSight Fin Ray variants integrate optical tactile sensing into compliant
fingers [ 21 , 22 ] . Another direction observes the
gripper structure itself. De Barrie et al. [ 9 ] use
finite-element simulation data to train a model that predicts contact forces
and stress distributions from finger deformation images. Kitamura et al. [ 10 ] relate camera-observed finger deformation to contact forces measured by 16
sensors embedded in the grasped object. Stuhne et al. [ 23 ] introduce SofIA, which uses a depth camera to observe the state of its
compliant fingers. Forces for Free estimates contact force from visual
observations of a tendon-driven underactuated hand optimized for force
observability [ 24 ] . Building on visual observation of
compliant structures, our work uses estimated forces to label demonstrations
and train a policy whose generated force values guide action selection.

## II-B Force and Tactile Feedback for Robotic Manipulation

Force and tactile information support both contact perception and manipulation
control. For perception, prior work uses touch to assess and improve
grasps [ 25 , 1 , 3 ] , estimate object
pose from contact [ 26 ] , and track object shape and pose
during manipulation [ 27 ] . These contact cues also
support grasp adjustment, sliding, pivoting, and rolling [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] .
Policies combining vision and touch extend these capabilities to learned
manipulation and in-hand rotation [ 31 , 2 ] , with
further work incorporating audio [ 32 ] or adapting vision-only
policies to force/torque sensing [ 33 ] .
For control, tactile feedback supports cable following and needle
threading [ 34 , 35 ] , while tactile-informed dynamics
support predictive control for packing [ 36 ] . Hierarchical
and reactive approaches integrate contact feedback into broader manipulation
systems [ 37 , 38 , 39 ] . Other methods
explicitly learn force or compliance control: RETAF separates tactile
grasp-force control from arm pose prediction [ 40 ] , Adaptive
Compliance Policy learns variable compliance from demonstrations [ 41 ] ,
and UMI-FT uses force-labeled demonstrations collected with a handheld
interface to learn motion, grasp force, and stiffness [ 42 ] .
Our method uses visual force estimates as training labels and policy-generated
forces for inference-time action selection, without dedicated contact-sensing
hardware at deployment.

## II-C Test-Time Searching

Prior work has explored inference-time search over sampled robot actions using learned interaction models [ 43 ] and diffusion-based planning [ 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 ] .
Frozen generative robot policies can be improved at test time by ranking action samples with auxiliary objectives. Value-Guided Policy Steering (V-GPS) [ 48 ] ranks policy samples using an offline-learned value function. Bidirectional Decoding [ 49 ] selects action chunks using consistency with previous decisions and contrast among future plans. Generative Predictive Control (GPC) [ 50 ] ranks and refines policy samples using a learned world model. DynaGuide [ 51 ] guides generative policies with learned dynamics, VLS [ 52 ] uses VLM-based trajectory rewards, and TouchGuide [ 53 ] steers pretrained generative visuomotor policies [ 54 , 55 ] by using a tactile-informed Contact Physical Model to refine early visual-policy samples toward physically feasible contact. Our method uses visual force estimates to label demonstrations for policy training. At test time, the policy jointly generates candidate actions and force values. We select the action whose policy-generated force is closest to the target. The visual force estimator does not score candidates at test time.

2026-10-06.title: Emergent Underactuation in Fully Actuated Multirotors by Minimizing a Homogeneous Allocation Cost
2026-10-06.authors: Antonio Franchi , Barbara Bazzana
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-06.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-06.introduction:
Conventional parallel-axis multirotors generate force along one
body-fixed direction and must reorient it to accelerate laterally.
Fully actuated multirotors remove this structural coupling by generating
a complete body wrench independently of attitude, enabling independent
pose control and physical interaction [ 1 , 2 ] . Representative architectures use
bidirectional spatial thrust arrangements [ 3 , 4 ] , unidirectional tilted
propellers [ 5 ] , active tilting mechanisms [ 6 , 7 ] , or reconfigurable structures [ 8 , 9 ] . This actuation freedom is
particularly valuable in aerial manipulation and contact inspection,
where force application cannot generally be subordinated to attitude
motion [ 10 , 11 ] .

In these platforms the control-allocation layer distributes a requested wrench among the
available actuators. Redundant actuation supports constraints, failure
accommodation, and secondary optimization [ 12 , 13 ] . For multirotors, allocation geometry
determines force–moment coupling and failure tolerance [ 14 ] , while optimal allocation for prescribed
wrenches has also been considered [ 15 ] . Standard
homogeneous costs include norms and power laws, notably the
minimum-norm cost underlying pseudoinverse allocation.

A different redundancy problem arises when position is prescribed and attitude
remains free. Position determines the required world-frame force,
whereas attitude selects its body-frame direction. The directionally
nonuniform actuation of the platform therefore assigns different infimal allocation
costs to attitudes realizing the same translation.

This work shows that minimizing a positively homogeneous allocation cost selects
underactuated-like behavior on a fully actuated multirotor. Aligning any
fixed minimizing direction with the required world-frame force confines
the body force to a fixed one-dimensional subspace without transverse
components. Full actuation remains valuable when disturbances or motion
changes modify the required-force direction: transverse authority
generates the new force immediately while reorientation recovers
minimum-cost alignment. Thus, nominal efficiency favors
underactuated-like motion, while full actuation supports tracking
resilience.

The main contributions of this study are:

a fiberwise infimal-cost formulation showing that positively homogeneous
allocation costs induce force-magnitude-independent minimizing
directions;

a characterization of the minimum-cost attitude family, emergent
underactuation, and the exact optimality-gap ordering of full-pose
trajectories realizing the same position motion; and

a parallel-thrust lower bound and disturbance-response
interpretation clarifying the efficiency and tracking roles of
underactuated and fully actuated force generation.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2  Related Work

Multirotor modeling and control have developed from platform-specific
dynamic models and near-hover stabilization [ 16 , 17 ] toward nonlinear and geometric
control on SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) and SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) [ 18 , 19 ] . Differential flatness and
polynomial trajectory generation have enabled dynamically feasible and
aggressive flight [ 20 , 21 ] , while
efficient motion primitives and aerodynamic feedforward have extended
these capabilities to online planning and high-speed tracking [ 22 , 23 ] . These approaches exploit the
underactuated structure of conventional parallel-thrust multirotors, for
which translation determines a preferred thrust direction and attitude
orients that direction in space.

Aerospace flight-control research emphasizes robustness, control
effectiveness, handling qualities, and integrated vehicle–controller
design. Incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion provides high-performance
attitude control with online adaptation of control effectiveness [ 24 ] , and its combination with structured robust control
supports disturbance rejection and full-pose tracking of redundantly actuated
multirotors [ 25 ] . Multirotor co-design
has addressed robust performance, handling qualities, and motor failures
jointly [ 26 ] , whereas bidirectional fixed-pitch
propulsion has been studied through unified modeling, nonlinear control,
and control allocation [ 27 ] . These developments show how
actuation design and feedback control jointly determine the usable
wrench authority of a multirotor.

A complementary research line changes the actuation geometry itself.
Tilted, vectored, bidirectional, and reconfigurable rotor arrangements
provide complete or configuration-dependent wrench authority [ 1 , 28 , 3 , 5 , 4 , 6 , 29 , 7 , 30 , 8 , 9 ] .
Allocation-based classifications clarify how rotor number, placement,
orientation, and tilting mechanisms determine attainable wrenches and
platform capabilities [ 14 , 31 , 2 ] . At the control level, intrinsic tracking on
homogeneous Riemannian manifolds provides a unified treatment of fully
actuated mechanical systems that includes omnidirectional aerial robots [ 32 ] . This literature mainly exploits full actuation for
independent pose tracking, enhanced wrench generation, or
configuration-specific objectives. This work instead investigates which
attitude is selected when only translation is prescribed and allocation
cost determines the use of the remaining actuation freedom.

Redundant actuation and fault tolerance provide a further connection
between vehicle geometry and allocation. General control-allocation
methods distribute commanded inputs while accommodating actuator
constraints and secondary objectives [ 12 , 13 ] .
For multirotors, allocation has been studied through force–moment
coupling, control authority, failure tolerance, and energy-aware wrench
realization [ 14 , 15 , 33 ] .
Relaxed-hover solutions show how attitude and residual rotor authority
can sustain flight after severe actuator loss [ 34 ] , while controllability analyses characterize the
authority retained under rotor degradation and failure [ 35 ] . These studies assess or optimize allocation for a
specified wrench, failure condition, or operating regime. The
redundancy considered here additionally includes the attitude freedom
that maps one prescribed world-frame force into different body-frame
allocation demands.

This distinction is especially relevant to aerial manipulation and
physical interaction. Early aerial manipulators combined multirotors
with robotic mechanisms and interaction controllers [ 36 , 37 ] . Compliance and impact-absorbing
mechanisms subsequently improved contact robustness [ 38 ] , while conventional underactuated platforms were
shown capable of applying sustained forces through coordinated attitude
and contact control [ 39 ] . Fully actuated platforms
permit contact force and vehicle orientation to be regulated more
independently, as demonstrated for omnidirectional contact inspection [ 40 , 11 ] . Reviews of aerial
manipulation and multirotor physical interaction document the resulting
diversity of platforms, mechanisms, controllers, and tasks [ 10 , 41 , 42 ] .

Across these research directions, actuation geometry is commonly
evaluated through wrench feasibility, tracking performance, robustness,
or the cost of realizing a prescribed wrench. The question considered
here is different: for a prescribed position motion and free attitude,
which full-pose realization minimizes allocation cost? The fiberwise
formulation shows that positive homogeneity makes the minimizing
directions independent of force magnitude and can select a fixed
body-force direction, thereby recovering an underactuated-like nominal
realization from a fully actuated architecture.
