2026-10-06.title: Test-Time Training as Residual Memory for Robot Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Haoxuan Wang , Gengyu Zhang , Ramana Rao Kompella , Gaowen Liu , Yan Yan
2026-10-06.comment: Project page at this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Memory is essential for long-horizon robotic manipulation, where successful actions may depend on past events that are no longer recoverable from the current observation. As episodes grow longer, however, retaining the full history becomes increasingly costly, creating a fundamental scalability challenge for memory-augmented policies.
Existing approaches address this challenge by either storing selected past observations in a bounded memory bank or compressing interaction history into a fixed-size parametric state through Test-Time Training (TTT).
Yet these formulations do not explicitly distinguish between historical information that can already be recovered from the policy’s current context and information that must persist beyond it.
We introduce TTT-RM , which repurposes TTT as Residual Memory , using fast weights not to generically compress history but to complement a bounded memory bank by preserving task-relevant historical information that cannot be recovered from the policy’s current context.
Concretely, TTT-RM learns a history decoder that reconstructs historical representations from the current observation and retrieved memory.
The resulting reconstruction residual captures what this context fails to explain and serves as the learning target for TTT. The TTT slow weights are optimized against this residual target so that online fast-weight updates learn to encode complementary historical information over time. The fast-weight state is then queried to produce a residual memory representation that conditions action generation.
Extensive experiments on memory-intensive simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show that TTT-RM consistently improves across multiple memory designs, outperforms diverse baselines, and supports sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation is often partially observable, such that the current observation alone may not contain all information needed to determine the next action ( 13 ; 7 ) . An object may become occluded after being moved, an instruction may need to be recalled long after it is issued, or the next action may depend on which subgoals have already been completed and on the outcomes of earlier actions. Consequently, task-relevant information is distributed across the interaction history, requiring the policy to integrate past evidence to recover the latent task state. Effective policies therefore require memory mechanisms that preserve relevant historical information for history-dependent action prediction.

Yet many state-of-the-art robot foundation models ( 12 ; 15 ; 9 ; 11 ; 31 ) condition action prediction primarily on the current observation or a limited temporal context. While sufficient for local visuomotor reasoning, this limited context becomes inadequate when task-relevant information originates much earlier in the episode. Recent work addresses this limitation through two prominent memory designs. The first store selected multimodal observations as individually retrievable records in a bounded memory bank ( 22 ; 21 ; 30 ) , which we collectively refer to as Explicit Memory (EM) . EM preserves event-specific information and allows the policy to revisit past observations when needed. Its coverage, however, is constrained by the bank capacity, so relevant events may be omitted or evicted as the interaction history grows. Increasing the bank capacity can improve coverage but incurs additional storage and retrieval costs.

Test-Time Training (TTT) offers an alternative memory mechanism by encoding interaction history into fast weights that are updated online as new observations arrive ( 10 ; 8 ) . Unlike EM, which allocates storage to individually retained records, TTT continually integrates history into this fixed-size memory state. This fixed memory footprint avoids increasing storage with the amount of retained history, but shifts the challenge to determining what information should occupy its limited representational capacity. EM and TTT therefore provide complementary forms of persistence, with the former preserving individually retrievable events and the latter compressing history into its internal weights. Given TTT’s limited representational capacity, our key insight is to specialize its fast weights for task-relevant historical information that remains unrecoverable from the policy’s existing context, rather than using them as a generic history compressor.

We therefore introduce TTT-RM , a framework that augments robot policies equipped with Explicit Memory by repurposing TTT as Residual Memory to preserve task-relevant history that cannot be recovered from the policy’s current observation and retrieved memory. During training, a history decoder reconstructs historical representations from this context, and the resulting reconstruction residual captures what remains unexplained. This residual supervises the TTT slow weights so that online fast-weight updates learn to encode complementary historical information over the course of an episode. The fast-weight state is then queried to produce a Residual Memory representation, which is combined with retrieved memory to condition action generation. TTT-RM reuses the visual stream already processed by the Explicit Memory module, requiring no additional encoder or VLM forward passes. At inference time, the history decoder is discarded, while the fast-weight state is updated at every policy call and reset at the start of each episode.

TTT-RM is compatible with multiple Explicit Memory designs, making it a modular extension to existing history-dependent robot policies. Across multiple memory-intensive simulation benchmarks, TTT-RM consistently outperforms diverse baselines, demonstrating robust gains across different task settings. On real-world manipulation tasks, it improves task progress by 10% to 26.5% and supports sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage long-horizon stowing task.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2.  Related Work

## 2.1.  Explicit Memory for Robot Learning

A growing line of work augments robot policies with Explicit Memory, storing selected history as retrievable records. Existing methods differ in what they retain and how they organize it. MemER ( 22 ) retains task-relevant keyframes from prior robot experience. MemoryVLA ( 21 ) instead maintains a perceptual-cognitive memory bank spanning visual details and higher-level semantic information. EventVLA ( 29 ) stores visual anchors and sparse task-critical events, whereas Mem-0 ( 5 ) retains keyframes around subtask completion to support memory-conditioned planning and execution.
Other approaches organize history across representations or temporal scales. MemoryWAM ( 30 ) integrates recent frames, event-boundary anchors, and compact gist tokens. MEM ( 25 ) combines video-based short-term memory with text-based long-term memory, and DiM-WAM ( 26 ) maintains bounded banks of complementary historical event tokens. LaMem-VLA ( 17 ) accesses separate short- and long-term memory stores before encoding selected evidence into latent memory tokens. Together, these methods extend the policy’s effective temporal context through explicit storage and retrieval, but the information available at each decision point remains bounded by the memory budget and the records selected for retention.

## 2.2.  Test-Time Training and Fast-Weight Memory

Test-Time Training (TTT) was originally introduced as an adaptation paradigm in which model parameters are optimized on unlabeled test samples using a self-supervised objective ( 24 ) . Building on the broader idea of fast-weight models ( 20 ; 2 ; 19 ) , which encode past information through dynamically updated parameters, recent work has extended TTT to sequence modeling by treating fast weights as a recurrent memory state updated online as new inputs arrive ( 23 ; 4 ; 3 ) .
Beyond language modeling, related test-time optimization has also been explored for novel view synthesis and autoregressive video generation ( 32 ) . In robot learning, TTT has recently been adopted as a memory mechanism for history-dependent control. RoboTTT ( 10 ) integrates TTT layers into robot policies to compress interaction history into recurrent fast-weight states. WAM-TTT ( 8 ) instead meta-trains an adaptive memory that is updated from unlabeled human videos at deployment. Our work builds on this memory interpretation of TTT, but fundamentally changes what the fast-weight state is trained to preserve. Rather than generically compressing interaction history, TTT-RM specializes the fast-weight state to preserve residual information that is not recoverable from the current observation and retrieved memory.

2026-10-06.title: RoboIRS: Inference-Time Internal Representation Steering for Generalist Robot Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Jiuzhou Lei , Chang Liu , Dayou Li , Zhiyuan Zhang , Xiao Liang , Yu She , Zhiwen Fan , Minghui Zheng
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability.
To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters.
On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, RoboIRS improves the average success rate from 44.4% to 66.2%, outperforming alternative inference-time intervention baselines while adding little inference time.
We further validate RoboIRS on real-robot manipulation using the same π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy and demonstrate its applicability to a world-action model Cosmos Policy, where the average success rate improves from 35.4% to 55.4%.
These results show that directly steering internal robot-policy representations can improve the performance of robot policies at inference time. Project website is available at https://rollingoat.github.io/roboirs/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have recently emerged as promising architectures for robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language-conditioned task understanding, and action generation with future prediction in a unified policy. However, their performance often degrades on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, such as unseen scenes, novel object layouts, and new object appearances [ 1 , 2 ] . Importantly, this degradation does not necessarily imply complete incapability: a policy may still succeed on a subset of these OOD tasks, albeit at a lower success rate. This suggests that the policy may retain some of the internal computations required for successful execution even when its behavior becomes unreliable.

A similar phenomenon has already been observed in LLMs, which may produce both truthful and untruthful responses despite being queried under similar conditions.
This inconsistency suggests that the model may already contain internal representations associated with the desired behavior, even when they are not reliably expressed in its outputs [ 3 ] .
Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability and activation steering for large language models provides evidence that internal representations can be causally manipulated to alter model behavior.
Here, internal representations refer to intermediate output that encode information during model computation; in transformer-based models, these may include residual-stream activations passed between layers, as well as activations associated with individual neurons, attention heads, or other localized model components [ 4 ] .
Prior work has shown that high-level behaviors such as truthfulness, refusal, sentiment, and task execution can be localized in hidden representations and modified through activation-space interventions. Li et al. [ 3 ] steer LLMs toward truthful answers by intervening on truth-related activations, while Turner et al. [ 5 ] and Rimsky et al. [ 6 ] show that contrastive activation directions can control generation behavior without retraining the model. Zou et al. [ 7 ] frame such methods as representation engineering, where internal activations are treated as controllable objects for modifying model behavior.

Motivated by the findings in LLM, can we similarly steer the internal representations of a robot policy at inference time to improve its performance on OOD tasks?
Recent work has already extended mechanistic interpretability to vision-language-action (VLA) models. Grant et al. [ 8 ] and Swann et al. [ 9 ] use sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable residual-stream features associated with robot behaviors, but do not demonstrate how these features can improve downstream policy performance. Häon et al. [ 10 ] and Buurmeijer et al. [ 11 ] go further by intervening on internal representations to steer behaviors such as motion speed and end-effector height; however, their evaluations are limited to a small set of predefined behavioral attributes rather than general task performance. Hong et al. [ 12 ] instead use an LQR controller to steer the diffusion transformer’s hidden activations such that the resulting activations lead to robust robot behaviors and require constructed contrastive residual-stream pairs from matched nominal and perturbed observations to provide target activation levels.

In this work, we aim to improve the performance of a frozen robot policy under distribution shift through inference-time steering of its internal representations.
Rather than retraining the policy, we use these outcome-labeled activations to identify representations associated with successful and failed rollouts and intervene on the policy at inference time using a steering vector.
The goal is to bias an already capable but unreliable policy toward internal states that are more predictive of successful action selection.
Inspired by [ 3 ] , we first train a linear classifier to classify the internal representations and then use the classifier weight as steering vectors to change the internal representations such that the predicted actions are more favorable of successful rollouts.
We evaluate the proposed approach on two representative robot policies: the vision-language-action model π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 13 ] and the world-action model Cosmos Policy [ 14 ] .
We conduct experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings to assess whether inference-time internal representation steering improves task success rates under distribution shift.

The main contributions of this work are as follows.

We propose RoboIRS, which adapts the internal representation-steering paradigm from LLMs to robot policies and enables inference-time intervention on frozen policies using steering vectors derived from the internal representations of successful and failed rollouts.

We conduct simulation and real-robot experiments showing that RoboIRS improves the average SR of a fully trained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy under distribution shift from 44.4 % 44.4\% to 66.2 % 66.2\% , outperforms alternative inference-time intervention baselines, improves real-robot manipulation performance, and is also effective on Cosmos Policy despite its different training recipe and model architecture, increasing the average SR from 35.4 % 35.4\% to 55.4 % 55.4\% .

2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Mechanistic Interpretability and Steering in LLMs

Mechanistic interpretability increasingly studies how high-level concepts are represented in neural activations and whether these representations can be causally manipulated [ 4 , 15 ] .
Many intervention methods build on the observation that properties such as truthfulness and sentiment can be represented by linear directions or low-dimensional subspaces [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
Activation-steering methods exploit this structure by constructing directions from contrastive examples or demonstrations and injecting them into hidden states to control behavior without retraining [ 5 , 6 , 19 , 20 ] .
Such interventions have been applied to truthfulness, hallucination, and refusal behavior [ 3 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] .

## II-B Mechanistic Interpretability and Internal Representation Steering of Robot Policy Models

Recent robotics work has begun to apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to characterize the internal representations of VLA policies, with several studies further showing that the discovered features can serve as causal handles for behavior steering.
Khan et al. [ 24 ] use sparse autoencoders to identify action-related latent directions from contrastive action pairs and show that these directions can be manipulated to steer VLA action outputs without retraining.
Grant et al. [ 8 ] conduct a cross-architecture mechanistic study using activation injection, sparse autoencoders, and linear probes to analyze how visual, language, and action-generation pathways contribute to VLA behavior.
Swann et al. [ 9 ] use sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable features in VLA hidden states, distinguishing transferable motion primitives from episode-specific memorization, and causally validate selected features through steering experiments.

Several VLA papers move from feature discovery to explicit control of robot behaviors.
Buurmeijer et al. [ 11 ] formalize feature observability and controllability in VLA models and use lightweight linear interventions to steer encoded features during closed-loop execution.
Häon et al. [ 10 ] identify sparse semantic directions in transformer activations and use those directions to control policy behavior without retraining.
Mitra et al. [ 25 ] identify task-relevant attention heads and selectively update them, framing policy adaptation as targeted modification of relevant internal mechanisms.
COAST [ 26 ] constructs success- and failure-associated conceptor from rollout hidden states to steer VLA activations toward success-critical representations at inference time.
COAST is evaluated on imperfect policies, such as early fine-tuning checkpoints, using tasks drawn from the original benchmark distribution, whereas RoboIRS focuses on recovering the performance of fully trained frozen policies under unseen task perturbations.
Hong et al. [ 12 ] take a control-based approach to representation steering, constructing contrastive directions from paired nominal and perturbed inputs and using them to define robustness-relevant latent feature subspaces and target feature setpoints.
RoboIRS instead derives its intervention directly from successful and failed rollouts without requiring matched nominal and perturbed observation pairs.

## II-C Inference-Time Intervention of Robot Policies

Another line of work improves robot policies at inference time through action selection or generative guidance.
V-GPS [ 27 ] samples actions from a frozen policy and re-ranks them with an offline-RL value function, while RoboMonkey [ 28 ] , MG-Select [ 29 ] , and RoVer [ 30 ] select or refine VLA action candidates using learned verifiers, intrinsic confidence, or process rewards.
Related methods intervene directly during action generation: value-guided diffusion [ 31 ] biases diffusion trajectories with value gradients. Guided Action Flow [ 32 ] keeps the VLA frozen and uses gradients from a critic trained on successful and failed rollouts to steer flow-matching action generation toward higher-return actions.
PPGuide [ 33 ] trains a performance predictor and uses its guidance signal to steer pretrained diffusion policies away from predicted failure modes during inference.

2026-10-06.title: PerturBot: Breaking Shortcut Priors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Perturbative Training
2026-10-06.authors: Mingyu Liu , Chonghao Sima , Tianjian Feng , Hanqing Wang , Cong Chen , Hao Chen , Chunhua Shen
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract: A vision–language–action (VLA) policy can complete complex tasks while ignoring the evidence that should determine its actions. An object held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target. Language and action show the same pattern: a familiar noun can trigger the operation it was paired with in training even after the verb changes, and a gripper that closed on nothing may lift anyway. We call these dependencies modality shortcuts : regularities in successful demonstrations make visual, lexical, or motor cues sufficient to predict expert actions without the task evidence needed for the underlying decision. More demonstrations of the same kind can raise task success while leaving these shortcuts intact. We propose Perturbot , which makes task-relevant evidence easier to use and shortcuts insufficient on their own: it applies task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, enriches instructions with decision-relevant captions, and adds random and failed trajectory segments relabeled with the behavior they contain. It complements scaling by changing what is scaled, and leaves inference unchanged. Moreover, we propose GroundFscore , an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. Task success rate shows whether a policy improves, while GroundFscore reveals whether the policy scales healthily, relying on task evidence rather than shortcuts. Together, Perturbot and GroundFscore provide a training-and-evaluation framework for disentangling VLA decisions from shortcut priors while preserving responsiveness to task-relevant evidence.
2026-10-06.introduction:
“Success is a lousy teacher.”

Vision–language–action (VLA) policies can now perform complex manipulation
tasks ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ) , yet a
simple change in view can still divert them ( Figure 1 ). An object
held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target; changing “pick
up the bowl” to “push the bowl” may still elicit a grasp; and a gripper that
closes on nothing may lift anyway. Task success cannot
tell whether the policy uses the scene, instruction, and observed outcome to
decide what to do, or merely replays an action when a familiar cue appears.

We call such dependencies modality shortcuts , a multimodal instance of shortcut
learning ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) closely related to causal confusion in
imitation learning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ; Wen et al., 2020 ) . A modality shortcut
is not an unimportant input but an easily decoded cue that stands in for the
evidence a decision requires. Such cues arise from the regularity of successful
demonstrations: the target dominates the wrist view as the expert reaches for
it, each object name may be paired with a single operation, and gripper closure
is reliably followed by a lift. Behavior cloning rewards agreement with the
demonstrated action, not the evidence used to predict it, so nothing in the
objective stops the policy from relying on the cue.

This matters for scaling. Larger and more diverse demonstration corpora are
central to generalist robot learning ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2023 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) , but if new
trajectories preserve the same correlations, the shortcut rule and the intended
rule keep prescribing the same actions, and more data cannot distinguish them.
Higher success on familiar tasks then need not mean more reliable target
selection, instruction following, or outcome assessment: the policy grows more
proficient where shortcut and evidence agree yet stays brittle where they
disagree, which makes modality shortcuts a bottleneck for scaling.

Addressing this requires changing what the training data demand, not weakening
an input modality: the evidence a correct decision needs should be easier to
use, and shortcuts should be insufficient on their own ( Section 3.1 ). Perturbot does so with three training-time data interventions and no extra model or
forward pass at deployment: task-preserving wrist-view perturbations add
plausible distractors without changing the target or invalidating the recorded
action; decision-relevant captions make object attributes, spatial relations,
and requested operations explicit, each supported by the recorded behavior; and
caption-grounded trajectory expansion adds random-motion and failed-execution
segments relabeled with the behavior they contain, which add behavioral support
rather than recovery skills, since relabeling cannot create an unrecorded
correction. Perturbot thus
changes what is scaled: as data grow, it expands not only repetitions of
familiar behavior but also the range of decisions that depend on the scene,
instruction, and observed outcome.

Whether scaling achieves this cannot be read from task success: when shortcut
and evidence agree, policies relying on either can succeed, and robustness to
distractors can come from simply ignoring vision. We therefore propose GroundFscore , an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on
modality shortcuts. It pairs each input with edits that should leave the action
unchanged, such as an off-path distractor, and edits that should change it in a
known way, such as naming a different object; a high score requires both, so
ignoring an input does not help. Because it needs no robot rollouts, GroundFscore can be computed for every checkpoint as data grow: task success shows whether a
policy improves, and GroundFscore whether it improves for the right reason.

With a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone, we evaluate all eight component combinations on 50
real-robot General PnP cases and cover broader skills in RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025b ) ; ablations test whether success and evidence use rise
together as data grow and whether GroundFscore predicts online failures. Our
contributions are threefold:

We identify modality shortcuts in VLA learning , unifying salience capture , noun lock-in , and motor inertia , and explain why scaling demonstrations that preserve
these correlations need not remove them.

We identify modality shortcuts in VLA learning , unifying salience capture , noun lock-in , and motor inertia , and explain why scaling demonstrations that preserve
these correlations need not remove them.

We propose Perturbot , three independently ablatable data
interventions that keep action supervision valid, change what is scaled, and
leave inference unchanged.

We introduce GroundFscore , an offline score that, unlike task
success, indicates whether a policy scales healthily and cannot be raised by
ignoring useful evidence.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Scaling VLA policies. Vision–language–action (VLA) policies map observations and instructions to
actions; they are trained on large robot datasets and often initialized from
pretrained vision–language models ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) .
Their progress has followed the growth of demonstration data across tasks and
embodiments ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2023 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Walke et al., 2023 ) and
studies of how data diversity and composition shape transfer ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Hejna et al., 2024 ; Zha et al., 2025 ) , while evaluation has
expanded from nominal simulation benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Mees et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2024 ) to perturbed scenes and
instructions ( Fei et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
Success alone cannot show whether a policy improves by using task evidence or by
using a shortcut more consistently. GroundFscore measures shortcut reliance
offline; unlike action sensitivity to task-preserving perturbations, which has
been used to select demonstrations ( D’urso et al., 2026 ) , it also requires the
action to change when task-relevant evidence changes.

Shortcut learning. Neural networks often rely on features that are predictive in training but fail
under distribution shift, as studied under shortcut learning, simplicity bias,
and dataset bias ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ; Shah et al., 2020 ; Torralba and Efros, 2011 ) .
Visual question answering models can answer from language priors without
grounding the evidence in the image ( Goyal et al., 2017 ; Agrawal et al., 2018 ; Cadène et al., 2019 ) , and in imitation
learning, causal confusion and the copycat problem show that matching expert
actions need not identify the evidence that should control behavior ( de Haan et al., 2019 ; Wen et al., 2020 ; Park et al., 2021 ) . Recent VLA studies find
that policies can underuse language or let vision override instructions ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Lian et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) , and diagnose or
regularize how modalities are used ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . These
accounts usually examine one modality at a time; we tie each shortcut to the
decision it affects and trace all three to the regularity of successful
demonstrations.

Data interventions for robust policies. Data-centric methods improve robustness by varying appearance through
augmentation and domain randomization ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Laskin et al., 2020 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2023 ) ,
synthesizing or counterfactually editing demonstrations ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Ameperosa et al., 2025 ) , enriching or relabeling
instructions ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Glossop et al., 2025 ) , and widening behavioral
coverage with corrective, perturbed, or unstructured data ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Laskey et al., 2017 ; Lynch et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) . Perturbative
training has likewise reduced language-prior hallucinations in
vision–language models ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . Each of these
interventions is typically designed for one axis of variation, such as
appearance, geometry, language, or coverage; Perturbot instead targets the cue
that substitutes for evidence in a given decision, while keeping every action
label valid and leaving inference unchanged.

2026-10-06.title: An End-to-End Framework for Modelling Pneumatic Soft Robots Based on Differentiable Finite Element Methods
2026-10-06.authors: Shaohong Zhong , Yao Yao , Perla Maiolino , Ingmar Posner
2026-10-06.comment: Published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
2026-10-06.abstract: Soft robots present significant modelling challenges due to their non-linearity, complex dynamics and potentially intricate geometries. These difficulties in accurate system identification and dynamics modelling limit their applications in precise robotics tasks. Prior modelling approaches typically suffer from trade-offs in accuracy, computational efficiency, or speed. The differentiable finite element method (FEM) offers a promising balance between these desiderata for soft robot modelling, and enables the use of gradients for efficient calibration and trajectory optimisation. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end differentiable FEM-based framework designed to streamline modelling and system identification for pneumatic soft robots, enabling the generation of reliable models for downstream tasks. The framework automates the conversion of computer-aided designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes that accurately represent the robot’s geometry and actuation mechanism. By integrating easily acquired point cloud data with differentiable FEM, the framework achieves precise identification of material and dynamic actuation parameters using a minimal experimental setup. Additionally, the differentiable nature of the model facilitates trajectory optimisation by leveraging gradients from robot dynamics and contact interactions. We validate the framework by modelling a complex bellow-shaped pneumatic soft robot and demonstrate its efficacy in real-world motion planning tasks. Experimental results indicate high modelling accuracy, with a maximum positional error of less than 3 mm, and successful application in tasks such as path following and grasping.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Soft robots hold significant promise for achieving a high degree of adaptability and robustness, enabling safe manipulation of unknown objects and operation in unstructured environments [ 1 , 2 ] . By exploiting innovative designs and smart materials, soft robots can embody physical intelligence, allowing them to effectively respond to dynamic environmental challenges and uncertainties [ 3 , 4 ] . Within this domain, pneumatic actuators play a key role and are widely used for their lightweight design, high power-to-weight ratio, and simple manufacturing [ 5 ] .

For soft robots to reliably perform precise tasks, efficient and accurate models are required. However, modelling them is challenging due to material nonlinearities, complex dynamics, and intricate geometries [ 1 , 2 , 6 ] . These challenges are particularly pronounced in contact-rich scenarios, where robot dynamics couples with the environment [ 7 ] . These factors result in behaviours that are difficult to predict or computationally expensive to simulate without simplifying assumptions about geometry and deformation in prior analytical, numerical, or learning-based approaches [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

Compounding the challenges in dynamics modelling, the system identification process for soft robots, which is required for accurate modelling, also presents significant challenges. Past approaches are often laborious, requiring extensive human effort to design and tailor experimental setups for individual robots, and potentially require a substantial amount of data for calibration [ 1 , 2 , 10 ] . These challenges collectively hinder effective modelling of soft robots and limit their full potential in robotics tasks.

The differentiable finite element method (FEM) has emerged as an accurate and efficient approach for modelling soft robots [ 11 ] . By employing spatial discretisation, FEM numerically represents soft robots as a collection of interacting volumetric mesh elements, effectively capturing their nonlinear behaviours [ 8 ] . The method also enables direct gradient computation with respect to model parameters and control inputs, facilitating parameter estimation through real-world observations and other downstream tasks [ 8 , 9 , 12 ] .

In this work, we propose an end-to-end framework for efficient model creation and system identification for pneumatic soft robots using differentiable FEM, demonstrated on a complex bellow-shaped pneumatic actuator. An overview is in Fig. 1 . To minimise manual efforts in model creation, we introduce a generation method that directly converts CAD models to volumetric meshes via voxelisation. For model calibration, inspired by [ 13 ] , we leverage point cloud data from RGB-D cameras and perform gradient-based optimisation of material and dynamic actuation parameters using GPU-accelerated differentiable simulation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of the model through a series of downstream real-world motion planning tasks.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II LITERATURE REVIEW

## II-A Soft Robot Modelling

Soft robot modelling approaches can be broadly classified into three categories. The first involves analytical models that rely on simplified assumptions about geometry and deformation, such as Piecewise Constant Curvature [ 7 , 14 , 15 ] . While these models offer rapid predictions, they fall short in capturing complex geometries and material nonlinearities, thus sacrificing modelling accuracy. The second approach, data-driven methods, harness machine learning techniques to model and control soft robots [ 16 , 17 ] or deformable objects [ 18 , 19 ] . Despite their potential, these approaches lack physics-based models, and require substantial data and computational resources for training robot-specific models, limiting their generalisation. The third approach includes models based on discretised continuum mechanics, such as the Finite Element Method (FEM), widely applied for their detailed and accurate representation of soft robots’ actuation and geometry [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . FEM delivers accurate results, yet its substantial computational requirements pose challenges for integration into downstream robotics tasks.

## II-B Differentiable FEM for Soft Robot Modelling

Differentiable FEM promises to achieve improved balance between accuracy, efficiency, and speed [ 11 ] . It has already proved effective in system identification for soft robots. Dubied et al. [ 8 ] used differentiable FEM to estimate material parameters for three elemental soft robot configurations, employing an alternative muscle model for actuation alongside simplified geometries. Du et al. [ 9 ] also leveraged differentiable FEM combined with a hydrodynamic model, aiming at obtaining model parameters for controlling a soft underwater robot. Their approach also incorporated an alternative elastic energy model to simulate robot actuation. However, the reliance on oversimplified models in both attempts necessitates additional manual efforts for robot-specific model adaptations. Additional efforts are sometimes also required for bridging the sim-to-real gap [ 27 ] . Zhang et al. [ 12 ] addressed these limitations by generating tetrahedral meshes that accurately conform to the robot’s actuation and geometry. However, this approach is limited to the relatively simple design of the robot. Meanwhile, Ménager [ 28 ] et al. proposed a condensed dynamics model for trajectory optimisation for soft robots, yet only demonstrated in simulation for simple trajectories. In addition, a majority of these prior approaches require dedicated motion capture setups. They also demonstrate limited exploration in leveraging the model for downstream tasks, likely due to computational intractability. These limitations considerably constrain the utility of these prior differentiable FEM approaches for soft robots beyond modelling. Our proposed framework promises to address these drawbacks and generate models for complex soft robots without oversimplified geometry or actuation mechanism. Building on top of [ 13 ] , we leverage point cloud observations as dense signals for system identification of a complex actuated pneumatic robot, requiring a minimal setup. Our physics-based approach also removes the need for a residual model compared to [ 27 ] , increasing generalisability and utility for downstream tasks.

2026-10-06.title: Exploiting Hierarchical Controller Structure in Contextual Parameter Learning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-06.authors: Sebastian Hirt , Lukas Theiner , Jan Peters , Rolf Findeisen
2026-10-06.abstract:
Hierarchical control architectures are widely used to decompose complex control problems into interacting control levels and are particularly important in robotics, where planning, whole-body motion, and lower-level control must be coordinated across different levels of abstraction and time scales. Their overall closed-loop performance, however, depends strongly on parameters distributed across the hierarchy, such that tuning controllers on different levels independently may neglect relevant cross-layer interactions. We propose a contextual Bayesian optimization framework for joint parameter learning in hierarchical control systems. Rather than modeling closed-loop performance only as a scalar black-box function, we retain separate observations of task performance, realization quality, and control effort. A correlated multi-output Gaussian process models these performance components, while their known aggregation into the overall closed-loop objective is evaluated analytically. The formulation exploits three complementary consequences of hierarchical control: informative performance quantities exposed by the hierarchy, coupling between parameters of different controller levels, and variations of these relations with operating conditions. We evaluate the approach for humanoid loco-manipulation, jointly tuning a centroidal predictive controller and a whole-body controller for physical box pushing under varying box mass.
The proposed method achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during both training and adaptation among the considered baselines.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Complex control systems are frequently organized in hierarchical
architectures, with individual layers operating at different levels
of abstraction and time scales [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Such architectures are important in applications ranging from chemical
process control to aerospace systems and robotics.
More broadly, hierarchical and distributed control provide means
of managing complexity in interconnected cyberphysical
systems [ 4 ] .
In robotics specifically, high-level planning, dynamic motion generation,
whole-body coordination, and lower-level control must often be
combined to realize complex physical behaviors. Humanoid and legged robots provide prominent examples: reduced-order models are commonly used to plan motion and contact interactions, while lower-level (whole-body) controllers realize these plans on the full articulated system subject to dynamics, contact, and actuation constraints [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Similar hierarchical structures also arise in cascaded process control, trajectory tracking, and other multi-layer feedback systems.

While hierarchical decomposition makes complex online control problems tractable, it introduces a corresponding parameter-learning problem across interacting controller levels. The practical performance of each level depends not only on its own parameters, but also on how its outputs are interpreted and realized by the remaining hierarchy. Closed-loop parameter learning provides a means of adapting these parameters directly based on measured system performance [ 8 , 9 ] . Bayesian optimization (BO) is particularly suitable for this setting because it
targets expensive black-box objectives with a limited number of closed-loop
evaluations [ 10 ] . Beyond treating controller tuning as a generic black-box optimization problem, incorporating available prior knowledge and problem structure can improve learning efficiency. Such information has, for example, been exploited to guide preferential learning of individualized controller parameters [ 11 ] , while intermediate closed-loop observations can provide additional information beyond a single aggregate performance value [ 12 ] . These results motivate the systematic exploitation of information that is already available from the control problem and its closed-loop execution.

A key observation underlying this work is that hierarchical decomposition of
the online control problem does not generally imply a separable
parameter-learning problem. Upper-level controllers generate plans or
references that become demands on lower controller levels, while their
realization feeds back through the physical system and affects subsequent
upper-level decisions. Closed-loop performance therefore depends jointly on
parameters distributed across the hierarchy. At the same time, the hierarchy
exposes informative quantities describing task execution, realization of
internally generated references, and control effort. Importantly, these cross-layer relations can themselves change with the
operating condition, since variations in the plant, environment, or task can
alter the closed-loop dynamics and thereby how demands and limitations
propagate through the controller hierarchy.
Hierarchical control thus provides three
closely related sources of structure for parameter learning: informative
performance components, cross-layer parameter coupling, and
context-dependent interactions. These motivate hierarchy-informed performance
modeling, cross-layer joint parameter learning, and context-dependent transfer
and adaptation, respectively.
Fig. 1 summarizes these three elements and their
interaction within the proposed framework.

Existing work addresses individual aspects of this problem. Joint
parameter tuning across interacting controller levels has been studied for
cascaded and hierarchical control architectures [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , including robotic whole-body and locomotion
controllers [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . For example work on exoskeleton control similarly
showed the relevance of jointly learning parameters across controller
levels [ 19 ] . Separately, composite and gray-box BO
exploit intermediate quantities or known problem structure instead of modeling
the complete objective as a single black box [ 20 , 21 ] , while contextual BO has
been used to transfer controller-tuning information across changing operating
conditions [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] .
Related contextual policy-search approaches learn humanoid walking-controller
parameters that generalize across desired walking speeds [ 26 ] .

We combine these ideas in a common contextual surrogate over the parameters
of all controller levels. Within the composite-BO formulation, the modeled
outputs are hierarchy-derived task, realization, and effort quantities with
known linear aggregation. Compared with scalar contextual BO, we retain these
component observations and their statistical dependence. For hierarchical
controller tuning, this complements joint parameter optimization with a shared
component-level model across operating conditions. This also distinguishes the
present approach from our previous hierarchical surrogate [ 27 ] , which learns parameter-dependent
closed-loop dynamics. Here, we directly model informative episode-level
performance quantities, avoiding the need to identify and roll out a surrogate
of the complete closed-loop dynamics.

These three aspects arise from the same hierarchical closed-loop structure and
are therefore addressed within a single learning framework. We propose a
unified contextual Bayesian optimization framework for hierarchical controller
tuning that combines three complementary elements:
1) hierarchy-informed performance modeling : we retain and jointly model
task performance, realization quality, and control effort instead of learning
only their scalar aggregate,
2) cross-layer joint parameter learning : we optimize parameters across
interacting controller levels jointly, thereby retaining cross-layer
dependencies, and
3) context-dependent transfer and adaptation : we condition the same
performance model on measurable operating conditions that affect the system
dynamics and, consequently, the interaction between controller levels. This
enables information sharing across related dynamical conditions and adaptation
to previously unseen operating conditions. Accordingly, the deployment goal is
to recommend parameters for the observed operating context, rather than one
controller that is fixed across all conditions.

We evaluate the framework for humanoid loco-manipulation using two-handed box pushing with a Unitree R1. A centroidal predictive controller generates motion and contact-wrench references that are realized by an inverse-dynamics whole-body controller, while box mass acts as the operating context.

In the following, Section II introduces the control and learning
fundamentals. Section III presents the proposed hierarchy-aware contextual parameter-learning framework. Section IV applies the method to hierarchical humanoid loco-manipulation control. We conclude in Section V .

2026-10-06.title: ForeAct3D: Policy-Grounded Future World Modeling for VLA Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Zhe Tao , Feiran Wang , Gaowen Liu , Ramana Rao Kompella$ , Yan Yan
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract: Robots need to anticipate how their actions will change the world, since manipulation success hinges on the resulting contacts and object motions. However, existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that predict future observations from shared features leave the forecast decoupled from the actions the policy will actually execute, and impose no physical constraints on how the scene may evolve. We introduce ForeAct3D, a framework for policy-grounded future world modeling within VLA policies. Learnable geometric queries decode depth, semantic segmentation, and camera pose from the policy representation into current and future semantic 3D scene states, and the future queries are conditioned on the policy-generated action chunk to ground the forecast in the planned interaction. A physical-consistency closure relates the two states through background staticity and instance-level rigidity, and anchors the wrist-camera pose to end-effector kinematics. These objectives shape the shared representation used for action generation during training, and no future prediction is required at inference. Without robot pretraining, ForeAct3D achieves 98.3% average success on LIBERO and an average task length of 3.73 on CALVIN, outperforming its base policy on every suite. Ablations show that semantic 3D supervision, physical consistency, and action conditioning each improve manipulation performance, and that action conditioning substantially improves future object localization. Real-world experiments on spatial placement, object insertion, and sequential manipulation further raise average success from 6.7% to 37.8% over the base policy. The project page and code are available at https://github.com/anthonytao80-crypto/ForeAct3D.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Future world modeling aims to predict how a physical scene will evolve under robot actions. This capability matters for manipulation because the same intended action can succeed or fail depending on contact: a push may slide an object toward its target or tip it over, and an insertion may seat or jam. Anticipating such outcomes requires reasoning about both the current observation and the planned action, since the resulting transitions involve contact, changing occlusions, and object motion ( Zhen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Robots therefore need a mechanism that represents the physical world, models its transitions under robot actions, and predicts the resulting future states subject to physical constraints ( LeCun and others, 2022 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) .

Existing approaches to future world modeling for robotic manipulation broadly follow two directions. The first models future observations with action-conditioned video generation ( Zhu et al., 2025a ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025b ) . Such models capture how appearance evolves under actions, but represent the future in image space, leaving the underlying 3D structure and physical constraints implicit. The second extends Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) with auxiliary objectives that predict future observations or features from the policy representation ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) . We adopt the VLA setting because future-state supervision shapes the representation used for action generation while retaining direct action inference without test-time rollouts.

Achieving physically consistent future world modeling within a VLA policy poses three challenges. First, constructing a task-relevant state requires recovering 3D geometry from policy features and separating objects, the robot, and the background, so that the predicted state exposes the spatial configuration relevant to manipulation. Second, constraining state transitions requires current and future predictions to jointly satisfy physical constraints: viewpoint changes must be reconciled with a static environment, and moving objects must preserve rigid geometry. Predicting each state independently does not enforce these relationships. Third, grounding the future in action requires predicting the scene changes induced by the robot’s chosen action, since the same scene can evolve differently under different actions. Addressing these challenges calls for a structured state, physical constraints across time, and explicit conditioning on the policy’s planned interaction.

To close this gap, we introduce ForeAct3D , an action-conditioned semantic 3D world modeling framework integrated into VLA policies. As illustrated in Figure 1 , ForeAct3D constructs current and future scene states from the representation used for action generation. Learnable geometric queries decode depth, three-class semantic masks, and camera pose, jointly capturing scene geometry and its partition into object, robot, and background regions. During training, a physical-consistency closure relates the two states through background staticity, instance-level rigidity, and end-effector kinematics. Future queries additionally receive the policy-generated action chunk, grounding the predicted transition in the planned interaction. Together, these components train the shared VLA representation to encode a semantic 3D scene and its physically constrained evolution over the action horizon, while retaining direct action inference during deployment.

We evaluate ForeAct3D on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and CALVIN ( Mees et al., 2022 ) , achieving 98.3% average success and an average task length of 3.73 without robot pretraining. We further assess the predicted states through geometry, segmentation, and localization metrics, and examine the contributions of structured 3D prediction, physical consistency, and action conditioning through ablations. Real-world experiments on spatial placement, insertion, and sequential manipulation tasks confirm these gains on physical hardware. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce ForeAct3D, a framework for policy-grounded future world modeling within VLA policies that reconstructs current semantic 3D states and predicts future states conditioned on policy-generated actions.

We formulate physical-consistency regularization that relates current and future geometry through background staticity and instance rigidity, while grounding wrist-camera pose in end-effector kinematics.

We demonstrate improved policy performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world tasks, with component ablations assessing policy gains and prediction ablations showing the benefit of action conditioning for future object localization.

# 2 Related Work

Action-Conditioned Video Models. Action-conditioned video models predict future visual observations from the current scene and robot actions ( Finn et al., 2016 ; Finn and Levine, 2017 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025a ; Cen et al., 2025 ) . Approaches include autoregressive prediction over visual and action tokens ( Wu et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2025 ) and diffusion-based generation with frame-level action conditioning ( Rigter et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2025b ) . More recently, multi-view prediction and memory mechanisms have improved temporal consistency and enabled policy evaluation within generated rollouts ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . These advances strengthen action controllability and visual coherence, but video prediction alone does not guarantee that the underlying 3D state evolves subject to explicit physical constraints. For manipulation, this distinction matters because visually plausible predictions may still be geometrically inconsistent across views or fail to preserve object structure during an interaction. This motivates predicting scene geometry directly and constraining its evolution through physical relationships between current and future states.

Future World Modeling within VLA Policies. Another line of work integrates future prediction into VLA policies through auxiliary supervision of features shared with action generation. Prediction targets include latent features ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) and visual or geometric observations ( Wu et al., 2024a ; Zhen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Qian et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These objectives encourage anticipation but leave two gaps. First, future prediction alone does not enforce a physically coherent transition from the current scene. Second, shared features alone do not specify which planned action a predicted future corresponds to, motivating explicit action conditioning. ForeAct3D addresses both by jointly predicting current and future semantic 3D states, coupling them through physical-consistency constraints, and conditioning future queries on the policy-generated action chunk. Together, these components supervise structured scene evolution under the planned interaction within the representation used for action generation.

2026-10-06.title: RiskFly: Frustum-Aligned Spatio-Temporal Risk Fields for One-Stage Agile Flight in Dynamic Clutter
2026-10-06.authors: Luxia Ai , Haopeng Chen , Yuchao Mei , Guohao Zhang , Wenbing Tao
2026-10-06.abstract: Agile flight in unknown, cluttered, and dynamic environments requires a planner that knows where and when danger will appear, not only that a trajectory is dangerous. One-stage learning-based planners trained with differentiable privileged costs are fast and expert-free, but the only signal reaching their encoder is a scalar trajectory cost with no spatial or temporal structure, so avoidance degrades into late reactive maneuvers. We present RiskFly, a one-stage planner that predicts risk in the same space in which it acts. A dual-stream observation pairs a short depth sequence with a frustum-aligned inverted spherical range-map sequence, whose angular cells match the end-state proposals one to one. An auxiliary head regresses a frustum-aligned spatio-temporal risk field, supervised by a privileged closest-point-of-approach (CPA) target. This self-predicted field is queried differentiably along the instantiated quintic trajectory at its own arrival times, and also enters the training objective, so representation supervision and planning gradients meet in a single space. Privileged signals are discarded at deployment, and the planner runs map-free from onboard depth and proprioception. Extensive simulation and zero-shot real-world flights on resource-constrained platforms show higher success rates at comparable end-to-end latency.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Autonomous navigation is an essential capability for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) [ 1 ] . Limited onboard computation and low-fidelity sensing make high-speed collision-free flight in cluttered and dynamic environments demanding [ 2 ] , since the vehicle must decide continuously under motion blur, a narrow field of view (FoV), and frequent occlusions [ 3 ] . Classical modular pipelines of perception, mapping, planning, and control remain interpretable [ 4 , 5 ] . However, their detection and prediction modules add latency and accumulate error precisely when the reaction window is shortest [ 6 , 7 ] . Learning-based planners instead unify perception and planning in a single network, and infer actions directly from raw observations [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .

Among these, the one-stage paradigm [ 8 ] is attractive for embedded deployment. The FoV is partitioned into a frustum grid, a network regresses one scored terminal-state proposal per cell, and a feasible polynomial trajectory follows in closed form. Because the trajectory is an analytic differentiable function of the network output, the policy can be trained without expert demonstrations, using a physically grounded cost from privileged simulation geometry, and the natural extension to dynamic scenes feeds a short depth sequence to a temporal encoder and adds a dynamic-avoidance cost derived from ground-truth actor states.

This design, however, leaves two structural gaps. First, the supervision is spatially blind. A dynamic cost evaluated on the instantiated trajectory is a scalar, so the encoder learns that some trajectory was risky, but not which FoV direction or which future instant caused the penalty; when the shared representation is not motion aware, these gradients are attributed to static structure. Second, the observation is not aligned with the decision space: raw depth measures range along the optical axis and is distorted toward the periphery, whereas the planner reasons on an angular frustum grid, so the network must absorb this mapping implicitly, which wastes capacity and widens the sim-to-real gap.

A third gap concerns when safety is evaluated. Existing risk representations are either instantaneous clearances [ 12 ] or a time-collapsed azimuthal vector [ 13 ] , yet a trajectory reaches a given bearing at a specific time t k t_{k} , and that is where its safety should be queried. Spatio-temporal planners exploit this observation [ 14 , 15 ] , but one-stage learned planners have not internalized it.

We therefore propose RiskFly, a one-stage planner that predicts risk in the same space in which it acts. Following [ 13 ] , we build an inverted spherical range map from depth, align it to the frustum grid of the planner, and use it as one of two parallel streams alongside the raw depth sequence, combining an explicit geometry-consistent representation with dense implicit appearance cues. An auxiliary head regresses a frustum-aligned spatio-temporal risk field supervised by a privileged closest-point-of-approach (CPA) target, and this self-predicted field is queried along the instantiated trajectory at its own arrival times, so that representation supervision and planning gradients act on one shared field. All privileged quantities are training-only, and at inference the planner is map-free and detection-free.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a dual-stream observation for one-stage dynamic planning, pairing a short depth sequence with a frustum-aligned inverted spherical range-map sequence, so that the perceptual representation, the end-state proposals, and the risk prediction live on one angular grid.

We propose a frustum-aligned spatio-temporal risk field supervised by a privileged CPA-based target. An arrival-time differentiable coupling then injects the self-predicted field into the trajectory objective and into proposal scoring.

We validate the system on simulation benchmarks spanning static and dynamic density gradients and on zero-shot real-world deployment, with ablations isolating the three components.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Object-Aware Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance

Traditional UAV navigation in dynamic environments relies on explicit obstacle-motion models [ 6 ] . Hybrid representations model dynamic obstacles as geometric primitives while voxelizing the static scene, and an adaptive potential field can be driven from a spherical obstacle map [ 12 ] . Spatio-temporal formulations instead model time-varying occupancy directly: risk-aware corridors grow from particle-based dynamic maps [ 15 ] , while SPOT searches a space-time graph so that collision checking happens when the vehicle actually arrives [ 14 ] . At the control level, model predictive control (MPC) handles perception uncertainty and kinodynamic constraints, from intent prediction [ 16 ] and perception-enhanced control [ 17 ] to online covariance adaptation [ 7 , 18 ] .

These pipelines are interpretable, but depend on precise state estimation of every moving object: detection, association, and filtering form a serial dependency whose latency and error grow with occlusion and obstacle count, which forces conservative speeds and motivates methods that reason about motion from raw sensing.

## II-B Learning-Based Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance

Perception-to-action policies reduce decision latency by mapping observations directly to trajectory parameters. Early planners extract geometric cues from single-frame depth: YOPO [ 8 ] regresses frustum-conditioned end states with guidance learning, inverse reinforcement learning achieves agile flight in static clutter [ 19 ] , and mapless MPC with dual KD-trees keeps an optimizer in the loop without a map [ 20 ] . Such snapshot-based policies generalize poorly to dynamic scenes, because ego-motion-induced depth variation masks true obstacle motion.

Recent work therefore injects temporal information: aggregating historical range scans into a compact angular map captures obstacle kinematics [ 9 ] , a point-flow representation makes relative motion explicit [ 10 ] , and RL on point clouds achieves low-latency control [ 21 ] . Others retain an explicit detector with a safety shield [ 11 ] , learn a continuous dynamic distance map [ 22 ] , or address multi-modality with conditional diffusion [ 23 ] . Most are nevertheless shaped by aggregated scalar rewards, and internalize late reactive evasions rather than anticipatory detours. A risk-guided reinforcement-learning planner supervises a spatio-temporal encoder with a privileged CPA risk map [ 13 ] , but the risk is compressed into an azimuthal vector and detached before the actor, so no gradient links risk to the executed motion.

## II-C Field Representations and Differentiable Guidance

A complementary line of work rewrites discrete planning decisions as continuous scalar fields whose gradients are consumed directly by an optimizer. Time-of-arrival geodesic fields replace Euclidean goal attraction so that guidance flows around occluders [ 24 ] , cloth simulation fields delineate traversable space from a depth matrix [ 25 ] , and optical-flow fields serve as the policy input and encode the approach rate [ 26 , 27 ] . These work because a dense differentiable signal is a far richer training target than a scalar, but they are defined over space alone.

We take this step. RiskFly keeps the expert-free differentiable one-stage paradigm of [ 8 ] , adopts the explicit range-map abstraction of [ 13 ] but aligns it to the planning frustum, and turns the privileged risk signal into a spatio-temporal field queried at the arrival times of the trajectory.

2026-10-06.title: Leveraging Cost-effective Robotics for K-12 STEM Education through Water Quality Monitoring Tasks
2026-10-06.authors: Rishi Mukherjee , Andrew Ruiz , Travis Henderson , Resha Tejpaul , Kris Simonson , David Mulla , Brian McNeil , Nikolaos Papanikolopoulos , Junaed Sattar
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted to ICRA 2026
2026-10-06.abstract:
Engaging K-12 students in authentic scientific research remains a significant challenge, particularly at the intersection of environmental science and robotics.
We introduce the Jar Jar ROV, a low-cost, open-source Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) platform designed for citizen science-based water quality monitoring by middle school students.
This paper presents the design of the platform and the results of a large-scale deployment with over 100 100 students across a US state who built, programmed, and deployed the ROVs in local lakes.
The educational framework yielded high student engagement in hands-on activities, with ROV construction earning a perfect average score from mentors.
From a scientific standpoint, the program successfully established a grassroots monitoring network, generating nearly eleven thousand validated measurements of temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, and turbidity.
However, our evaluation identified a critical “engagement gap,” with student interest declining sharply during more complex tasks such as electronics assembly and data uploading.
This paper contributes both a validated, scalable model for integrating robotics into environmental education and a clear, data-driven roadmap for future improvements.
These enhancements focus on lowering technical barriers and creating a more intuitive link between data collection and scientific discovery, addressing a key challenge in empowering the next generation of citizen scientists.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Sustaining the health of our freshwater ecosystems requires widespread, consistent water quality monitoring, yet traditional methods are often too costly and resource-intensive for broad deployment [ 1 ] . Many public access water bodies, such as rivers and lakes, contain pollutants and pathogens that can be harmful to humans, including bacteria like E. coli, chemical contaminants from agricultural runoff, and heavy metals from industrial sources [ 2 ] [ 3 ] . Beyond health concerns, other properties such as water clarity, temperature, dissolved oxygen levels, and pH are useful to know beforehand when planning underwater activities such as diving, swimming, or recreational boating. These parameters also serve as critical indicators of aquatic ecosystem health, affecting fish populations, plant growth, and overall biodiversity.
Concurrently, there are national imperatives to foster STEM engagement among K-12 students, particularly in the critical middle school years when interest in science and technology can either flourish or wane.
While many educational initiatives exist, they often struggle to connect abstract concepts to tangible, real-world impact, leaving students disengaged. The challenge lies in simultaneously gathering vital environmental data and inspiring the next generation of scientists and engineers.

In this paper, we argue that educational robotics offers a powerful and compelling solution to bridge this gap.
A hands-on, purpose-driven robotics project can transform the abstract principles of engineering and environmental science into an exciting, goal-oriented mission.
For a middle school student [ 4 ] , the challenge is no longer just to learn about pH levels or sensor calibration in a classroom; it is to build and command a robot to explore the unseen world in their local lake.
This shift in perspective is profound: the robot becomes the educational conduit – a tangible vehicle that carries concepts of engineering, programming, and design directly into the service of scientific inquiry and environmental stewardship.

By empowering students to build and deploy their own Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs), we are not merely teaching them technical skills.
We are initiating them into the practice of citizen science [ 5 ] , where their work contributes to a larger, authentic scientific endeavor.
This approach addresses two fundamental challenges in STEM education: it provides a compelling “why” for learning difficult subjects and demonstrates that science is not just a body of knowledge, but an active, participatory process of discovery.
The data they collect is no longer a set of numbers in a textbook; it is a direct measurement of the health of their own community’s environment.

We thus present the Jar Jar ROV (Fig. 1 ), a low-cost, open-source underwater robotics platform explicitly designed to serve this dual mission.
This novel ROV is at a much lower price point than most commercially available platforms, less complex to operate, and more configurable than consumer-grade devices ( e.g. , [ 6 ] [ 7 ] ).
Such properties significantly lower the barriers of entry to robotics and underwater robotics as a whole, for citizen scientists and K-12 robotics enthusiasts.
We detail the development of the ROV and an accompanying curriculum, and report on a large-scale deployment with over 100 100 students across a US state.
Our findings demonstrate the immense potential of this model to generate both high levels of student engagement and a scientifically valuable dataset of freshwater quality.
Furthermore, we analyze the key challenges encountered, offering a data-driven perspective on how to refine this approach to support K-12 citizen science at scale better.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Educational Robotics

Educational Robotics has long been seen as an effective way to engage students in computational thinking, problem-solving, and STEM concepts [ 8 ] .
Previous research indicates that robots can motivate young people to explore computer science and engineering, with case studies demonstrating their use in introductory programming courses [ 9 ] .
Also, remotely accessible robotics platforms have been suggested to broaden research and learning opportunities at larger scales [ 10 ] .
Systematic reviews support these findings, showing that physical educational robots help develop skills like sequencing, debugging, and collaboration in young learners [ 11 ] .
Building on this foundation, researchers have examined educational robots as autonomous systems that emphasize design, performance, and interaction.
Comprehensive reviews have covered their effectiveness, motivation, and inclusion in robotics education [ 12 ] , while recent work illustrates how educational robots are evolving from classroom tools to platforms for innovation and citizen science [ 13 ] .
Quantitative reviews demonstrate moderate positive impacts of educational robots on student performance, though results differ based on instructional methods [ 14 ] , emphasizing the crucial roles of pedagogy (the manner of instruction delivery) and robot embodiment in influencing educational outcomes [ 15 ] .
Large-scale programs such as FIRST® Robotics Competition (FRC) have shown significant positive impacts on students’ STEM career choices and skills, with longitudinal studies demonstrating that participants are substantially more likely to major in engineering or computer science [ 16 ] [ 17 ] .
However, the high cost, competitive focus, and steep learning curve create barriers to entry, highlighting the need for more accessible, curriculum-focused initiatives that prioritize scientific inquiry over competition.

## 2.2 Citizen Science Initiatives

Citizen science offers possibilities to lower the barriers to entry for educational robotics, by allowing members with little expertise to participate in large-scale research through collaboration with high-expertise peers.
Technology-mediated citizen science projects have demonstrated success in strengthening global scientific infrastructure through distributed environmental monitoring, where volunteers use accessible technologies like Geo-Wiki and analyze data that would be infeasible for experts to gather alone [ 5 ] [ 18 ] .
The integration of mechatronics into citizen science has enabled new forms of participatory sensing through low-cost mobile surface vehicles for environmental monitoring [ 5 ] and community-based monitoring initiatives that engage local stakeholders in data collection [ 19 ] [ 20 ] .
Participatory science methods for water quality, combining volunteer-collected samples with remote sensing data, have proven effective in monitoring vulnerable near-shore habitats [ 21 ] .
However, these initiatives often rely on pre-built platforms or simple data collection tools, offering limited opportunities for participants to engage with the engineering and design process itself.

## 2.3 Citizen Science & Underwater Robotics

Recent advancements in underwater robotics reveal a gap  in the low-cost, low barrier to entry ROV space. Commercial ROVs like the Chasing Dory (below $1000) and Geneinno Titan ($1000+) [ 6 ] [ 7 ] exist, but they are not open-source or easily adaptable without domain-specific expertise. Open-source options such as the LoCO AUV and OpenROV require even more domain-specific expertise [ 22 ] [ 23 ] to build and operate, as well as support from maintainers in the case of issues.
While some projects have developed low-cost underwater platforms for education, they often lack direct connection to citizen science applications [ 23 ] .
Existing water quality monitoring systems employ multiple methods; e.g. , a community-based data collection approach, satellite-based data collection to measure water clarity [ 24 ] , or manual sample collection [ 25 ] .
These disparate approaches can result in sparse area coverage and many missing samples.
While some of these programs successfully engage volunteers in data collection, they face significant limitations in terms of the scope and precision of the measurements.
They provide platforms for submitting data, but no clear guidelines on how to gather it.
Additional inter-site challenges include a lack of cumulative temperature data, absent pH measurements, unreliable turbidity assessments (subjective Secchi disk readings rather than quantitative sensors), and unmonitored dissolved oxygen content as seen in [ 25 ] [ 26 ] .

The Jar Jar ROV project addresses these gaps by combining educational robotics with participatory citizen science through environmental monitoring, offering a solution that serves both as a cheap learning tool and a functional instrument for scientific contribution, filling the critical gap between high-cost/high-expertise systems and low-cost/low-functionality educational kits.
This kit provides a two-fold benefit: (1) it allows volunteer citizen scientists to easily deploy their existing equipment with minor modifications, and (2) it leverages the scale of participatory science by operating as a yearly program where middle school youth gather data from local lakes across the state.
