2026-10-06.title: Online Target-less Radar-LiDAR-Camera Extrinsic Calibration via Joint Optimization
2026-10-06.authors: Gunhee Shin , Yunsoo Kim , Chanhyuk Lee , Wanhee Kim , Minwoo Lee , Sungwoo Han , Jeongwoo Woo , Hyuntai Chin , Minha Park , Hyun Myung
2026-10-06.comment: . Accepted to the International Conference on Control, Automation and Systems (ICCAS 2026)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Fusing radar, LiDAR, and camera enables robust perception in diverse and adverse conditions, but the fusion performance critically depends on accurate extrinsic calibration among the three sensors.
In this paper, we address the problem of online target-less extrinsic calibration for the radar-LiDAR-camera system.
Existing target-less methods are mostly designed for a single sensor pair, and composing the pairwise results does not guarantee consistency across the three sensors.
Moreover, the sparse and noisy radar measurements make the radar-involving pairs unreliable.
To tackle these challenges, we propose a joint calibration framework that constructs residuals for each sensor pair and optimizes the extrinsics of all pairs together to minimize the overall residual.
Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive radar noise filter that rejects spurious radar returns using a range-dependent margin, and a correspondence accumulation strategy that aggregates sparse radar correspondences over frames.
We validate our method on an in-house radar-LiDAR-camera dataset covering diverse urban environments, where it reduces calibration errors across all sensor pairs over a state-of-the-art camera-LiDAR baseline.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Multiple modalities have been actively explored in recent robotics research, especially for perception and localization tasks.
Among various modalities, camera, LiDAR, and radar are commonly used due to their complementary characteristics.
Cameras provide rich texture and color information but are sensitive to lighting and weather conditions [ 1 , 2 ] .
LiDARs offer accurate 3D geometric information even in low-light conditions, but may degrade in geometrically degenerate environments such as long tunnels or featureless open roads [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
Radars, in contrast, remain robust under adverse weather conditions such as fog and rain where other sensors tend to degrade, and can directly estimate velocity, although they typically produce noisy measurements and have lower resolution [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] .

By fusing data from these sensors, systems can achieve more robust and reliable performance in diverse environments [ 1 , 3 , 4 ] .
However, to ensure fusion performance, several considerations must be carefully addressed, including appropriate sensor placement, extrinsic calibration, and temporal synchronization [ 1 , 9 ] .
When these considerations are not properly handled, the fused system can even perform worse than a single-sensor system.
Among these considerations, extrinsic calibration, which estimates the 6-DoF relative transformation between sensors so that their measurements share a common coordinate frame, is particularly critical [ 10 , 11 ] .

Extrinsic calibration methods can be widely categorized into target-based and target-less approaches.
Target-based approaches rely on hand-crafted calibration targets, such as checkerboards or AprilTags, with known geometry.
They yield reliable correspondences and high accuracy, but require dedicated targets and a controlled environment, which limits their flexibility [ 10 ] .
On the other hand, target-less approaches exploit natural features in the environment, such as planes or edges.
They are flexible and applicable to diverse environments, but tend to be less accurate and more dependent on the surrounding environment, which limits their reliability [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .

Owing to this flexibility, target-less calibration is widely used for online re-calibration in real-world deployments, especially for autonomous vehicles and field robots traversing unstructured environments, where aggressive motion and external impacts can shift the sensor alignment.
However, most existing methods focus on individual sensor pairs, such as camera-LiDAR [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] , LiDAR-radar [ 6 ] , camera-radar [ 7 , 18 ] , and camera-GNSS/INS [ 19 ] .
When operating a radar-LiDAR-camera system with such pairwise tools, calibrating each pair independently increases system complexity and yields mutually inconsistent extrinsic estimates.
Joint calibration of all three sensors is therefore needed, yet few works have addressed this problem.
To the best of our knowledge, the only existing approach [ 11 ] still requires a specially designed target.

In this paper, we address online target-less extrinsic calibration for radar, LiDAR, and camera sensors.
We propose a joint calibration framework that constructs residuals for each sensor pair and optimizes the extrinsics of all pairs together to minimize the overall residual.
In addition, we introduce two complementary mechanisms to handle the sparsity and noise of radar measurements that can destabilize the joint optimization: an adaptive noise filter that rejects spurious radar returns, and a correspondence accumulation strategy that aggregates radar correspondences across frames.
We validate our method on an in-house radar-LiDAR-camera dataset covering diverse urban environments, where it reduces calibration errors across all sensor pairs over a state-of-the-art camera-LiDAR baseline, with the radar-camera rotation error reduced by approximately 65%.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

## 2.1 Pairwise Target-less Extrinsic Calibration

Camera-LiDAR calibration is the most actively studied pairwise problem.
Conventional methods extract geometric features such as planes or edges from the scene and align them across modalities by minimizing photometric or geometric residuals [ 12 , 14 ] .
Galibr [ 13 ] instead used the ground plane [ 20 ] to estimate the extrinsics without relying on explicit feature correspondences, reducing the dependence on local feature quality.
While effective in feature-rich scenes, these methods are sensitive to the density of features and require careful parameter tuning across environments.

Learning-based methods estimate the extrinsics directly from raw images and point clouds using neural networks.
LCCNet [ 15 ] introduced an end-to-end network with iterative pose refinement, and CMRNext [ 16 ] and Ou et al. [ 17 ] improved generalization through cross-modal feature matching and iterative pose updates.
While these methods generalize well across scenes, they require large multi-modal datasets for training and do not naturally extend to other sensor pairs such as those involving radar.

Calibration involving radar is less explored, mainly because the sparsity and noise of radar measurements make direct correspondences difficult [ 8 ] .
Heng [ 6 ] calibrated LiDAR and radar by matching their ego-motion estimates, avoiding the need for per-frame point association.
For camera-radar calibration, Schöller et al. [ 18 ] matched radar reflectivity patterns to image edges, and Cheng et al. [ 7 ] estimated the extrinsics online using vehicle motion and scene-level priors.
However, these methods focus on a single radar-related pair and cannot be directly extended to a three-sensor system that includes camera, LiDAR, and radar.

## 2.2 Joint Multi-sensor Extrinsic Calibration

Joint calibration of camera, LiDAR, and radar has received little attention.
Domhof et al. [ 11 ] addressed the problem with a single target that all three sensors can detect, and estimated the extrinsics from per-modality detections through a joint optimization that keeps the three sensor pairs consistent.
While effective in controlled settings, the specially designed target restricts the method to an offline setup.
We instead propose an online target-less joint calibration framework that constructs residuals for each sensor pair from natural features, and optimizes the extrinsics of all pairs together to minimize the overall residual.

2026-10-06.title: NM-LIO: Multiple LiDAR-Inertial Odometry Addressing LiDAR Measurement Noise Discrepancy
2026-10-06.authors: Gunhee Shin , Seungjae Lee , Minho Oh , Dongkyu Lee , Jaeyoung Lee , Youngwoo Seo , Hyun Myung
2026-10-06.comment: . Published in the International Conference on Robot Intelligence Technology and Applications (RiTA 2024)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Multiple LiDAR-inertial odometry methods have been widely applied in robotic applications owing to their enhanced accuracy and reliability.
However, adopting multiple LiDAR systems can be challenging due to the discrepancies in measurement noise across different LiDARs.
Existing methods have typically overlooked the noise discrepancies, which can significantly affect accuracy.
In this paper, we propose Noise-aware Multiple LiDAR-Inertial Odometry (NM-LIO) that addresses the noise discrepancies.
We integrate a noise model to quantify the measurement noise of each LiDAR.
Additionally, we estimate the uncertainty of the residuals based on the measurement noise, allowing the measurement model to capture the noise discrepancies.
Our proposed method is evaluated on a public multiple LiDAR dataset and compared with state-of-the-art methods.
The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately estimate the odometry in various environments by accounting for the noise discrepancies.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [ 1 ] using 3D LiDAR sensors has been actively applied in robotic applications owing to their accuracy and reliability [ 2 ] , [ 3 ] .
Despite significant advancements in LiDAR-based SLAM methods [ 4 ] , traditional single LiDAR systems are susceptible to perspective limitations, particularly due to limited field of view (FOV) and occlusion.

To address this issue, multiple LiDAR systems have recently attracted research interest [ 5 ] , [ 6 ] , [ 7 ] .
However, adopting multiple LiDAR systems can be challenging due to the discrepancies in measurement noise across different LiDARs.
Different LiDARs will have different measurement noises, which arises from the variations in manufacturers or scanning patterns [ 8 ] .
Existing methods have typically overlooked the noise discrepancies, treating the measurement noise as homogeneous, which can significantly affect accuracy.

To tackle the challenge above, we propose Noise-aware Multiple LiDAR-Inertial Odometry (NM-LIO) that addresses the noise discrepancies.
We integrate a noise model to quantify the measurement noise of each LiDAR.
Additionally, we estimate the uncertainty of the residuals based on the measurement noise during the state update process, allowing the measurement model to capture the noise discrepancies.
We evaluate the proposed method on a public multiple LiDAR dataset [ 9 ] and compare it with state-of-the-art methods.
The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately estimate the odometry in various environments by accounting for the noise discrepancies.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
In Section 2 , we provide a review of related works.
In Section 3 , we describe an overview of our proposed multiple LiDAR-inertial odometry system and the details of each key process.
The experimental results are presented in Section 4 followed by the conclusions in Section 5 .
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Fast-LIO [ 10 ] and Fast-LIO2 [ 11 ] are tightly-coupled iterated error state Kalman filter (IESKF)-based LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) systems that serve as foundational frameworks for numerous LIO systems.
Fast-LIO enhances computational efficiency by introducing a novel Kalman gain formula that reduces the computation complexity from the dimension of the measurements to the dimension of the state.
Additionally, Fast-LIO2 introduces an efficient incremental kd-tree data structure that enables dynamic insertion and rebalancing.
Several related works have incorporated advanced techniques such as adaptive downsampling [ 4 ] and efficient local map management [ 12 ] to improve the accuracy and robustness of the odometry.

Due to the limited FOV and occlusion of single LiDAR, multiple LiDAR systems have recently attracted research interest.
M-LOAM [ 5 ] proposes a sliding window-based multiple LiDAR odometry that simultaneously estimates poses and calibration parameters.
It computes the point-wise uncertainty by composing the state covariance and the extrinsic covariance.
MA-LIO [ 7 ] addresses the discrepancies in terms of temporal and spatial factors inherent in multiple LiDAR systems.
It mitigates these discrepancies by employing B-spline interpolation as an alternative for linear interpolation and accurately transferring points among LiDARs.
Additionally, it propagates point-wise uncertainty throughout the motion compensation process, assigning uncertainty caused by the motion to each point.
However, existing methods treat the measurement noise of each LiDAR as homogeneous, neglecting the discrepancies that can significantly affect the accuracy.

Several recent single LIO systems have addressed the measurement noise.
VoxelMap [ 13 ] incorporates the noise model from [ 8 ] , which estimates the noise based on uncertainties in both bearing direction and range measurements, to improve the robustness of odometry.
It composes measurement noise with pose uncertainty to represent point uncertainty, which is then propagated to the plane parameters, enabling a probabilistic representation of the environment.
LOG-LIO2 [ 14 ] further extends this approach by introducing a novel point uncertainty model that considers both measurement noise [ 8 ] and surface characteristics.
In our work, we utilize the measurement noise model from [ 8 ] to quantify the measurement noise for each LiDAR.
Additionally, by estimating the uncertainty of the residuals based on the measurement noise, we can capture the noise discrepancies across different LiDARs.

2026-10-06.title: DreamFormer: Dream Imitation with a Transformer World Model for Language-Conditioned Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-06.authors: Mostafa Kotb , Cornelius Weber , Muhammad Burhan Hafez , Stefan Wermter
2026-10-06.comment: submitted to IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems (TCDS)
2026-10-06.abstract: We introduce DreamFormer , a model-based agent that acquires language-conditioned, multi-task skills by imitating expert demonstrations within the latent imagination of a learned world model. DreamFormer first learns a task-agnostic Transformer world model from unstructured play data, then acquires task-specific behaviors by optimizing an intrinsic reward that aligns agent-generated rollouts with expert demonstrations in latent space. Since the policy is trained on-policy inside imagination, it is exposed to its own errors during training, mitigating the covariate shift inherent to offline behavioral cloning. To make long-horizon imagination affordable, DreamFormer encodes a high-resolution multi-view robotic observation into a single input token, avoiding both spatial downsampling and the multi-token representations used by prior Transformer world models. On the long-horizon CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer outperforms LUMOS, the comparable model-based agent, on single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs 2.34 average tasks completed per chain of five) while keeping imagination rollouts tractable. Against HULC, the behavior cloning baseline, it nearly doubles performance on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (1.30 vs 0.67), indicating that dynamics learned by the world model transfer more readily than a directly cloned policy. This is consistent with the role attributed to internal models in biological agents, where a model of environment dynamics supports behavior in situations not previously encountered.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Afoundational hallmark of human and animal intelligence is the ability to
construct rich internal representations of external reality—referred to as world
models —that enable biological agents to mentally simulate alternative scenarios, predict
future dynamics, and formulate optimal decisions prior to physical execution [ 1 ] .
Inspired by this mechanism, world models [ 2 ] have emerged as a promising
framework for enhancing the decision-making and predictive capabilities of embodied agents, offering a pathway toward more general and robust intelligent behavior [ 3 ] . Such models are used either to learn behavior inside their own imagination [ 4 , 5 ] or to plan at runtime [ 6 , 7 ] . Despite recent advances, learning world models that transfer across diverse downstream tasks remains an open challenge.

The difficulty in learning broad-purpose world models stems primarily from two methodological bottlenecks. First, in online learning paradigms, the model is continuously updated using data collected by an active policy. This creates a closed-loop exploration bias that inextricably entangles the learned transition dynamics with the specific task being solved. Second, joint reward modeling forces the dynamics model to learn representations optimized for a singular, task-specific reward signal. This tightly couples the latent space to one objective, restricting the model’s utility for downstream policy learning or real-time planning. Consequently, these paradigms inherently yield task-specific world models, significantly hindering knowledge transfer across diverse tasks.

We argue that constructing broad-purpose world models necessitates a shift toward offline learning from diverse offline datasets and task-agnostic (i.e., reward-free) training [ 8 ] . Once established, these models can serve as versatile foundations, used either to learn downstream task-specific behaviors or to optimize plans to reach a specified goal at runtime.

Motivated by this principle, we introduce DreamFormer , a model-based agent that first
learns a task-agnostic world model from unstructured play data, and subsequently
acquires task-specific behaviors entirely in the imagination of the
learned latent space. DreamFormer builds upon the Dream Imitation paradigm
(Section II-A ) introduced in DITTO [ 9 ] , which defines an intrinsic reward
encouraging the alignment between imagined policy rollouts and expert trajectories directly in the
model’s latent space; optimizing this reward by reinforcement learning induces imitation without
requiring access to expert actions. DITTO, however, validates the paradigm only in single-task settings, training a separate world model for each task without evaluating transfer across tasks. LUMOS [ 10 ] extends it to language-conditioned multi-task robotic manipulation, but adopts the DreamerV2 [ 4 ] world model in its standard configuration, which was developed for 64 × 64 64\times 64 resolution inputs and therefore requires aggressive spatial downsampling of high-resolution robotic observations.

At the architectural level, DreamFormer employs an autoregressive, GPT-style Transformer [ 11 ] , motivated by the proven superiority of Transformers over traditional recurrent dynamics models [ 7 ] . However, a critical bottleneck in deploying these architectures for visual control is tokenizing image observations. Conventional tokenizers, such as ViT [ 12 ] or VQ-VAE [ 13 ] , encode a single image into tens or hundreds of tokens. Over extended imagined rollouts, this growth in sequence length inflates both the memory footprint of the key–value cache and the cost of self-attention, which scales quadratically in the number of tokens attended over.

To mitigate this, prior approaches [ 14 , 15 ] have utilized a categorical variational autoencoder (VAE) [ 4 ] to encode each image into a single discrete token. However, this configuration was developed for low-resolution inputs such as Atari and does not extend to high-resolution
robotics without downsampling [ 10 ] . DreamFormer alleviates this constraint by scaling the categorical VAE: replacing the shallow convolutional encoder with a ResNet-18 backbone and expanding the capacity of the categorical latent space. It encodes full-resolution multi-view observations into a single input token, so that sequence length grows only with the imagination horizon and is independent of input resolution, keeping the memory and attention cost of imagination rollouts bounded by the horizon alone.

The primary contributions of this work are as follows:

A Broad-Purpose World Modeling Framework: We introduce DreamFormer , a model-based robotic agent that leverages offline datasets to learn a task-agnostic Transformer world model. By decoupling dynamics learning from singular reward objectives, the model builds versatile representations suitable for transfer across downstream tasks.

Low-Cost Long-Horizon Rollouts: We scale the categorical VAE with a ResNet-18 backbone and an expanded latent space, encoding full-resolution multi-view observations at one Transformer token per timestep. The sequence length of an imagined rollout therefore depends only on the horizon, bounding both the key–value cache and the quadratic cost of self-attention.

Language-Conditioned Multi-Task Transfer: We extend the Dream Imitation paradigm to train a language-conditioned multi-task policy entirely within the model’s latent space. On the CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer nearly doubles the performance of the model-free baseline on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment and outperforms the model-based baseline on single-environment evaluation.

# II Background

## II-A Dream Imitation

Dream Imitation is an imitation learning algorithm proposed in DITTO [ 9 ] that leverages learned world models to reformulate offline imitation learning as online reinforcement learning within the world model latent space. First, the expert trajectories are mapped into the model latent space; then, an imitation policy is unrolled starting from an arbitrary expert state in the model latent space. Finally, an intrinsic reward r t i ​ n ​ t r_{t}^{int} is defined to encourage the alignment of the unrolled policy latent states s t π s_{t}^{\pi} with expert latent states s t E s_{t}^{E} across multiple time steps:

This specific intrinsic formulation—a modified dot product—was empirically shown to outperform standard L2 and cosine similarity metrics by encouraging similarity without requiring exact matches [ 9 ] . Furthermore, unlike standard behavioral cloning, optimizing this intrinsic reward via reinforcement learning allows the agent to actively explore alternative trajectories within the simulated environment. By learning the policy ’online’ inside the world model’s imagination, Dream Imitation effectively mitigates the compounding errors and covariate shift typically associated with offline methods [ 16 ] . DITTO validates this paradigm in single-task settings, training a separate recurrent world model for each Atari game. DreamFormer extends it to language-conditioned robotic manipulation, training a task-agnostic Transformer world model.

## II-B Unstructured Play Data and Latent Planning

Learning from Play (LfP) [ 17 ] leverages unstructured, exploratory interaction data—often collected as humans freely manipulate the environment without predefined goals. Such data is diverse and unlabeled, capturing a wide range of behaviors. However, imitation learning from unstructured play data faces a multimodality problem [ 17 ] , where multiple valid high-level behaviors can connect the same current state s c s_{c} and goal state s g s_{g} . To address this challenge, Play-LMP [ 17 ] introduces a planning module that encodes the diverse behaviors linking the same ( s c , s g ) (s_{c},s_{g}) pair into a unified latent representation within a latent plan space. The planning module comprises two stochastic encoders: (1) a plan recognizer , which maps an entire sequence into a latent plan, and (2) a plan proposer , which infers a latent plan conditioned on the current and goal states. During inference, the policy is conditioned jointly on the current state, the goal state, and the inferred latent plan to resolve behavioral ambiguity.

2026-10-06.title: WasserMan: Benchmark for Underwater Manipulation Policy Learning
2026-10-06.authors: Danil Belov , Artem Erkhov , Sergei Parsegov , Pavel Osinenko
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Underwater manipulation couples visual decisions, contact forces and a
thruster-controlled floating base. We introduce WasserMan, to our
knowledge the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of
floating-base underwater contact manipulation. It provides ten expert-solvable
tasks, two vehicle–arm platforms, a bimanual configuration and underwater dynamics.
Nine tasks have learned-policy evaluations. We compare ACT, diffusion policies
(DP) and behavioral cloning on six tasks, with three training runs and equal
sampled-window budgets. Pretrained SmolVLA adds evaluations on three tasks.
In the tested settings, removing integral action can prevent completion,
while changing action interfaces can reduce learned-policy success despite
successful expert replay. Currents produce task-dependent changes in completion
and actuation effort. Versioned tasks,
demonstrations and per-episode evidence support a protocol separating
expert feasibility, learned completion and execution effort.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Underwater manipulation couples arm motion, contact and a thruster-controlled
floating base [ 1 ] . Intervention platforms [ 2 ] , valve turning
under currents [ 3 ] and dual-arm control [ 4 ] study this
coupling. A learning benchmark must distinguish an infeasible command interface
from a learned policy that fails to produce useful commands.

WasserMan formalizes this distinction. To our knowledge, it is the
first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base
underwater contact manipulation. Its ten-task catalogue spans panel interaction,
object collection, connector insertion and shipwreck intervention. The main
learning protocol covers PressButton, RotateValve, OpenHatch, CollectShell,
PushSlider and PullLever. Separately versioned ACT/DP evaluations cover
HotStab, CabinRecovery and CargoRelease, giving nine tasks with learned-policy results.
Wall Toss adds an expert delivery scenario. Two native vehicle–arm systems
and a custom twin-arm configuration support platform and bimanual comparisons.

We make three contributions. First, we provide extensible task contracts,
physical experts, floating-base platforms, distributable procedural
assets, demonstrations and fixed evaluation cohorts. Second, we report ACT, DP
and chunked-BC results on six tasks, with three independent training runs per
configuration. Third, a diagnostic protocol links expert replay to policy
evaluation and interventions on controllers, action interfaces and currents.
Contact, mechanism progress and vehicle response reveal differences hidden by success alone.

2026-10-06.title: Reachability-Guided Sequential Quadratic Programming-Guarded Model Predictive Path Integral for Safe Nonlinear Predictive Control
2026-10-06.authors: Alexandre Didier , Jason J. Choi , Namhoon Cho , Claire J. Tomlin , Melanie N. Zeilinger
2026-10-06.abstract: Safe robot control often requires combining long-horizon performance optimization with hard state and input constraints, but existing approaches tend to address this tradeoff partially. Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) methods such as model predictive path integral (MPPI) are effective in handling nonlinear and nonconvex environments, yet their finite-sample rollouts and unconstrained weighted-average update can return an unsafe control. Deterministic nonlinear MPC can explicitly incorporate constraints, but its real-time safety and performance depends strongly on warm starts and local convergence. Hamilton–Jacobi reachability (HJR) provides rigorous safety certificates, but offline value-function computation remains practical only for reduced-order models. We propose ReSQ-MPPI, a reachability-informed generation–refinement architecture that combines these complementary strengths. An HJR value function computed offline for a reduced-order model guides online MPPI sampling toward safe, promising trajectory candidates. The MPPI solution is then refined by a small number of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations in a full-order MPC problem. A key observation is that the standard MPPI inference step is an unconstrained weighted least-squares problem; ReSQ-MPPI replaces it with a constrained MPC refinement that recovers the MPPI update when it is feasible and minimally modifies it otherwise. Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing environments demonstrate that ReSQ-MPPI improves safety and performance over standalone MPPI, MPC, and reachability-filtered sampling-based control baselines.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Model predictive control (MPC) has become a powerful framework for solving complex decision-making problems in robotics, including whole-body control and locomotion [ 1 ] , mobile manipulation [ 2 ] , and autonomous driving [ 3 ] . A key advantage of MPC is its ability to naturally incorporate safety requirements, such as collision avoidance and actuator limits, as constraints within the optimization problem, making it well suited for safety-critical robotic applications. However, one of the crucial challenges with MPC for systems with complex dynamics is the complexity of nonlinear optimization that it entails inherently to be solved online.

Optimization-based methods , particularly those based on sequential quadratic programming (SQP), have emerged as promising approaches for efficiently solving nonlinear MPC problems [ 4 , 5 ] . However, these methods remain susceptible to infeasibility and rely heavily on a good initialization to achieve rapid convergence. In practice, the optimization is typically warm-started using the solution from the previous control loop. When the solver fails to find a feasible solution within the limited number of optimization iterations in real-time, the resulting control input may violate safety constraints and compromise system safety.

On the other hand, sampling-based MPC has emerged as an effective framework for approximately solving nonlinear optimization problems. Model predictive path integral (MPPI) and other variational inference MPC frameworks pose optimal control as a variational inference of the distribution of optimal control trajectories [ 6 ] . While these methods can effectively handle complex nonlinear dynamics and constraints within the finite prediction horizon, they lack principled mechanisms for ensuring long-term safety, such as recursive feasibility guarantees. Furthermore, as the system dimensionality increases and the feasible region becomes increasingly complex and nonconvex, a finite set of sampled trajectories may fail to contain any feasible solution. Finally, another key limitation of sampling-based MPC for safety is that, although individual sampled trajectories may each satisfy the safety constraints, the final control solution obtained by aggregating these samples can still violate safety during the inference step [ 7 ] .

Another school of control methods for safety assurance is to employ safety certificate functions [ 8 ] , typically computed offline. These methods verify a control invariant set and subsequently synthesize an online feedback controller that guarantees the system remains within this set, thereby satisfying the prescribed safety constraints. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability (HJR) [ 9 ] and control barrier functions (CBFs) [ 10 ] are prominent methodologies for designing safety certificates. However, both approaches suffer from poor scalability with respect to system dimensionality and the complexity of the dynamics, making them most suitable for reduced-order models. For high-dimensional, full-order robotic systems, safety is often achieved through robust formulations and layered control architectures [ 11 ] ; however, this approach inherently entails additional conservatism in the resulting closed-loop system due to margins addressing model errors.

Motivated by the limitations of existing approaches, this work proposes a new safe MPC framework, ReSQ-MPPI, that combines three key components: (1) an offline-computed HJR safety certificate based on a reduced-order model, (2) an MPPI that generates an initial solution candidate by sampling trajectories guided by the safety certificate, and (3) a small number of SQP iterations that refine the candidate solution to satisfy the constraints of the full-order system dynamics.

Our key observation is that the inference step in MPPI, which aggregates sampled control sequences into a single control solution, is an unconstrained weighted least-squares optimization. Consequently, even if all sampled trajectories individually satisfy the safety constraints, the aggregated solution is not guaranteed to remain safe. Previous works [ 12 , 7 ] address this issue by introducing a post-processing safety filter that projects the aggregated control onto the safe set. In contrast, our key idea is to unify control aggregation and safety enforcement into a single optimization problem. Specifically, we formulate the inference step as a constrained weighted least-squares problem within the SQP framework of nonlinear MPC.
Below, we detail how the proposed framework overcomes the individual limitations of existing SQP-based MPC, MPPI, and safety certificate methods.

ReSQ-MPPI vs. SQP & Sampling-based MPC: HJR-guided MPPI generates an initial solution that closely approximates the long-horizon optimal solution while accounting for safety. This warm start substantially improves the convergence and robustness of SQP. Unlike conventional MPPI, the proposed SQP formulation incorporates safety constraints directly into the control aggregation step, ensuring that the final control solution satisfies the desired safety requirements. Furthermore, the control sequence refined by SQP is used as the nominal input sequence for the MPPI at the next sampling instant, establishing a bidirectional coupling between MPPI sampling and SQP refinement. This interconnection significantly reduces the likelihood that either MPPI fails to sample a feasible trajectory or SQP fails to converge to a feasible solution within the limited number of optimization iterations.

ReSQ-MPPI vs. HJR: While conventional numerical HJR cannot be applied to higher-dimensional systems without neural network approximations, MPPI and MPC can impose hard safety constraints based on full-order dynamics.

MPC has long been regarded as one of the principal frameworks for safety due to its ability to explicitly incorporate state and input constraints into the online optimization. In classical MPC, safety is typically established through recursive feasibility , ensuring that the optimization problem remains feasible at every sampling time by designing terminal constraint sets that are control invariant. However, constructing such terminal sets is often challenging, particularly for complex nonlinear systems and safety constraints. Moreover, the resulting nonlinear optimization can be computationally demanding and may fail to converge to a feasible solution in real-time. Predictive safety filters (PSF) [ 13 ] have extended MPC to a supervisory safety layer that minimally modifies a nominal controller while maintaining safety through recursive feasibility. More recently, sampling-based MPC methods such as MPPI have emerged as alternatives for optimization-based MPC and PSF for safety [ 7 , 14 ] . Nevertheless, because these methods rely on a finite set of sampled trajectories, they generally lack formal recursive feasibility guarantees [ 12 ] . Consequently, when feasible trajectories are not sampled or the final aggregated control input does not preserve feasibility, long-term safety is not ensured.

To improve the safety of sampling-based MPC, various approaches are proposed which integrate safety certificates into the trajectory sampling process. The methods in [ 15 , 12 , 16 ] integrate CBFs with MPPI; however, the employed CBFs are typically simple distance-based functions that do not certify control invariance. The work of [ 7 ] integrates HJR least-restrictive safety filtering with MPPI. However, the approach is limited to low-dimensional system models because of the poor scalability of HJR. To improve scalability, recent methods have proposed usage of learning-based certificates, including neural CBFs [ 17 ] and neural approximations of HJR value functions [ 14 ] . While these approaches can be applied to higher-dimensional systems, formally verifying the safety guarantees of learned certificates remains an open challenge [ 18 ] . More recently, [ 19 ] uses CBFs to encourage safety during the training of a generative model that produces the proposal distribution for MPPI.

Specifically, for each sampled input sequence 𝒖 k j \bm{u}_{k}^{j} , at time step i i , if the state at the next time step x i + 1 | k j x_{i+1|k}^{j} is not within 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , we override u i | k j u_{i|k}^{j} with the safe optimal control input u s ​ ( x i | k j ) u_{\mathrm{s}}(x_{i|k}^{j}) , making sure that the trajectory stays within the maximal invariant set.

The main limitation of this approach is the poor scalability of the computation of the HJR value function V V . Due to the curse of dimensionality [ 9 ] , we can only use a reduced-order model of f f for its computation, which results in errors in the computed maximal safe set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and the safe controller u s u_{\mathrm{s}} . Thus, the safety for the full-order system is compromised with this approach itself, as we will see in our results.

## II-E Model Predictive Control

Another receding horizon approach to approximate ( 3 ) is model predictive control (MPC), see [ 4 ] for an overview. In contrast to MPPI, which proposes a sampling-based solution approach to ( 4 ), MPC leverages numerical optimization in order to solve constrained optimization problems of the form

In order to solve ( 7 ) online in real-time, we consider sequential quadratic programming (SQP) approaches such as described in [ 23 ] . SQP is an iterative optimization approach where the problem ( 7 ) is approximated as a quadratic program at the current solution iterate 𝒙 ¯ j | k \bar{\bm{x}}_{j|k} and 𝒖 ¯ j | k \bar{\bm{u}}_{j|k} . The solution of the quadratic program provides the next update step, until the iterates converge to a local KKT point.

Due to the local quadratic approximations, the solution quality of SQP solvers heavily depends on the initial warmstart of the solution iterates 𝒙 ¯ 0 | k \bar{\bm{x}}_{0|k} and 𝒖 ¯ 0 | k \bar{\bm{u}}_{0|k} . For MPC methods, the initial iterates are typically a time shifted solution obtained at the previous time step k − 1 k-1 . This can result in closed-loop solutions which are stuck in local optima for non-convex problems and may often fail to find feasible solutions. In this work, we aim to leverage the exploration capabilities of MPPI samples to resolve local optima issues.

2026-10-06.title: AgenticTactileVLA: Contact-Guided Execution-Time Supervision for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation without VLA Retraining
2026-10-06.authors: Elizaveta Semenyakina , Ivan Snegirev , Mikhail Kiselev , Miguel Altamirano Cabrera , Artem Lykov , Hajira Amjad , Dzmitry Tsetserukou
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation
strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects
compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual
feedback degrades under closure occlusion. AgenticTactileVLA is presented as an
execution-time supervisor that shifts part of object-specific adaptation from
prediction to physical interaction. A fixed VLA provides the approach and hand
targets; the supervisor decides whether to remain transparent, refine finger
flexion, retain or release the corrected configuration, return control to the
VLA for retry, or select a compliant hand-control regime. It uses
finger-position and motor-effort feedback as proprioceptive contact evidence
and requires neither tactile sensors nor VLA retraining. On a Unitree G1 with
a BrainCo Revo2 hand, a randomized matched-block evaluation on five objects
held out from VLA training yields 61.3% completion for the base VLA, 72.0%
for unconditional close-to-stall control, and 84.0% for the supervisor under
a shared budget; the gain is positive on every object and persists under
moderate pose perturbations. Ablations show the gain is not explained by
extended closure alone, and that selective triggering reduces correction
episodes by 65.7% with no detected change in completion. A retention audit
shows acceptance predicts retention in 88.9% of held-out cases, while
compliant objects expose conservative false rejection. A thin-walled-cup
study demonstrates contextual routing to compliant control, matching an
always-compliant reference. These results suggest that contact-guided execution-time adaptation can improve the object-level generalization of a fixed VLA to held-out objects by adapting physical realization without object-specific retraining.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A central challenge in robot learning is to generalize manipulation policies
to new objects while maintaining reliable physical execution. For
vision-language-action (VLA) models, this is particularly important in
contact-rich manipulation. Objects compatible with the same broad grasp
strategy may differ in geometry and compliance, changing the finger contacts
and interaction conditions required for successful execution. A VLA may
therefore generate a suitable approach yet still leave fingers without
sufficient support, produce an unsuitable terminal hand configuration, or
over-compress a fragile object. Such failures are difficult to resolve visually
during closure, when the hand increasingly occludes the contact region.

Many objects can be handled using a limited repertoire of broad grasp
strategies [ 1 , 2 ] , while their physical realization
may still require object-specific finger contacts and interaction effort. This
motivates reusing a fixed policy while adapting these physical details during
execution rather than through object-specific retraining.

We investigate a division of responsibility in which the VLA provides the
transferable manipulation strategy, while an execution-time supervisor adapts
its physical realization to the encountered object
(Fig. 1 ). The supervisor can modify finger flexion and gate
progression of the VLA-generated body reference, but does not replace the VLA
approach policy or learn a residual action model. Prior work has explored
tactile-conditioned VLA adaptation [ 3 , 4 ] and execution
monitoring and recovery [ 5 , 6 ] . Our work lies at their intersection
and asks: Can execution-time physical adaptation improve the realization
of a fixed VLA policy on objects outside its training set without
object-specific retraining?

AgenticTactileVLA augments a fixed VLA with a stateful execution supervisor.
At the terminal phase of nominal closure, it evaluates proprioceptive support
evidence. If support is sufficient, execution remains transparent to the
policy. Otherwise, body-reference progression is paused while whole-body
stabilization remains active, and unsupported fingers are corrected
independently. An accepted correction is retained; a rejected correction
releases the hand override and returns control to the VLA for subsequent
policy-generated retry.

A key principle is selective intervention : the supervisor acts only when
the policy-proposed closure is not sufficiently realized physically. To
separate this effect from simply closing farther or longer, we compare against
unconditional close-to-stall control under the same execution budget and use
component ablations to examine selectivity, effort-assisted stopping, and
verdict-dependent release.

Geometric correction alone is insufficient when the interaction regime must
also change. Fragile objects may deform before proprioceptive resistance is
large enough for reactive correction. AgenticTactileVLA therefore also selects
between nominal position control and a predefined compliant mode before
closure. Explicit handling cues can request compliant interaction, while a
vision-language model (VLM) can select between the two modes from image and
task context. The VLM selects only the interaction mode and does not generate
controller parameters or material estimates.

We use the term agentic to denote this bounded, stateful supervision:
deciding whether to remain transparent or intervene, adapting individual
finger references, accepting or releasing the corrected grasp, returning
control to the VLA for retry, and selecting the interaction regime. This distinguishes the layer from low-level reflexes by enabling high-level decision-making based on multimodal context. The
framework uses finger position and motor-effort signals as device-specific
proprioceptive evidence and requires neither additional tactile sensors nor
object-specific VLA retraining.

The main contributions of this work are:

A contact-guided execution-time supervisor for a fixed VLA, combining
selective intervention, bounded per-finger correction, grasp acceptance or
release, and policy-mediated retry.

A proprioceptive execution mechanism using finger position and
motor-effort feedback without additional tactile hardware, together with
language- or vision-conditioned selection between nominal and compliant
interaction modes.

Real-hardware evaluation on a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand under
matched execution budgets, including unconditional close-to-stall control,
component ablations, pose perturbations, retention diagnostics, and
fragile-object interaction tests.

The intended scope is adaptation of feasible policy-generated manipulation
strategies, not recovery from arbitrary incompatible approach errors.
Within this scope, we view execution-time physical adaptation as a step toward
more scalable object-level generalization of fixed VLA policies, reducing the
need for object-specific retraining while preserving the policy’s reusable
manipulation strategy.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Contact Sensing from Motor Feedback

Motor feedback can reveal physical robot–object interaction without dedicated
tactile sensors. Current as Touch [ 7 ] , Transferring Contact,
Not Just Motion [ 8 ] , and Pseudo-Tactile [ 9 ] use actuator or gripper signals for contact-aware
manipulation.

AgenticTactileVLA uses finger positions and motor-effort signals as
device-specific evidence of interaction resistance rather than calibrated
contact force. This evidence determines whether the nominal closure provides
sufficient support and, when necessary, guides local finger correction and
grasp acceptance or release.

## II-B Tactile Feedback for VLA Adaptation

Tactile feedback complements vision when physical interaction is difficult to
infer from images alone. VLA-Touch [ 3 ] combines a frozen VLA with
semantic tactile feedback and learned action refinement. TLA [ 10 ] and
VTLA [ 11 ] incorporate tactile observations into action generation,
while UniTacVLA [ 4 ] predicts contact changes to refine action
chunks. RoboTacDex [ 12 ] provides multimodal data for
visual–tactile dexterous humanoid manipulation.

In contrast, AgenticTactileVLA does not train a tactile-conditioned VLA or a
learned residual policy. Adaptation is placed in an external, nonlearned
execution layer while the VLA remains fixed. The supervisor stays transparent
when the policy-generated closure already provides sufficient support and
intervenes only when physical correction is required.

## II-C Execution Supervision and Interaction Control

Execution supervision connects predicted actions with observed consequences.
PLanAR [ 5 ] verifies expected effects and replans after deviations,
VoLo [ 6 ] combines monitoring with recovery, and VLAs Fail Differently [ 13 ] analyzes failure structure in motor-command sequences.

This work brings supervision to the closure-to-motion transition in dexterous
manipulation. The supervisor determines whether the physical realization of
the VLA action is sufficient, whether individual fingers should be corrected,
whether the resulting grasp should be retained or released, and whether
control should return to the VLA for another approach. A separate
interaction-mode layer selects between nominal position control and
current-limited compliant control before closure.

AgenticTactileVLA thus combines selective intervention, contact-guided finger
adaptation, grasp acceptance or release, policy-mediated retry, and contextual
interaction-mode selection within a single execution-time layer over a fixed
VLA policy.

2026-10-06.title: Frame-Level Temporal Alignment for Human-to-Robot Visual Adaptation
2026-10-06.authors: Xizhe Zhang , Jingfeng Zhang , Zirun Zhou , Hong Jia
2026-10-06.abstract: Transferring visual representations pretrained on human videos to robot manipulation requires learning reliable correspondences between human and robot demonstrations. However, paired demonstrations can differ in execution rate and in the proportion of non-key frames that do not directly reflect task progress. Frames at the same relative timestamp may therefore represent different task stages, which can cause correspondence learning to fail. To address these issues, we propose Frame-Level Temporal Alignment ( FLTA ), a framework that uses two temporal priors to adapt visual encoders pretrained on human videos for robot manipulation. It learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations, allowing frames at different relative temporal positions to match. A global progress prior combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target. A local temporal order prior penalizes backward transitions while allowing stays and varying forward rates to accommodate execution-rate differences. With ResNet-50 and ViT encoders, our method achieves relative improvements of 46.93 % 46.93\% and 65.96 % 65.96\% , respectively, over the best baselines in average simulation success rates and achieves higher task success rates on real-world manipulation tasks. These results also suggest that effective human–robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Our project page is available at https://rtx5090ultra.github.io/FLTA-Project-Page/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-based robotic manipulation relies on visual representations that capture task-relevant state information for action prediction. Learning such representations solely from robot demonstrations is challenging because robot data are costly to collect and often cover a limited range of tasks. Human videos provide a scalable, complementary source of interaction data, as they are relatively inexpensive to obtain, widely available, and rich in object manipulation experience ( Grauman et al., 2022 ; Bahl et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Srirama et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Pretraining on human videos can encode these experiences into transferable, task-relevant visual representations that support downstream policy learning and generalization beyond task-specific robot demonstrations ( Nair et al., 2023 ; Radosavovic et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) .

However, differences in movement capabilities and appearance between humans and robots create a substantial domain gap between human videos and robot observations ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Ben-David et al., 2006 ; Ganin et al., 2016 ) . As such, visual representations need to distinguish task progress because the downstream policy selects its next action based on the current observation ( Nair et al., 2023 ; Srirama et al., 2024 ) .
HRAlign ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , the state-of-the-art solution, uses paired human-robot videos for video-level contrastive alignment, learning shared task semantics to reduce this domain gap. However, frames sampled from paired human and robot videos may show different task stages despite sharing the same task instruction. Aligning their aggregated video representations does not explicitly establish which human and robot frames correspond to similar task progress.

This distinction is apparent for paired datasets such as RH20T ( Fang et al., 2024 ) , which provides human and robot demonstrations of the same task. As shown in Figure 1 , these videos exhibit two temporal differences. First, the videos contain different proportions of non-key frames, which do not directly reflect task progress. As a result, the action starts at different relative positions in the two videos. Second, execution-rate mismatch changes the duration of each task stage. Frames sampled at the same relative time may show different task progress. Statistics across tasks and video pairs are provided in Appendix A.1 . For example, sampled human non-key frames and robot key frames may contribute to a video-level positive pair. The aggregated video representations are pulled together even though the sampled frames show different task progress. Such stage mismatch may reduce the strength of the alignment signal used to learn task-progress representations, making it harder for downstream policies to select appropriate actions.

To address these issues, we propose a frame-level temporal alignment framework that adapts pretrained visual encoders using paired human and robot videos, without frame-level correspondence annotations. As shown in Figure 1 , we guide correspondence learning with the inductive bias that human and robot demonstrations generally progress toward task completion over time ( Hadji et al., 2021 ; Zakka et al., 2022 ) . First, we introduce a global progress prior D D that combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target between human and robot frames. It allows each frame to match multiple candidate frames while penalizing large differences in normalized temporal position, rather than requiring same-position matches. Second, we introduce a local temporal order prior Q Q to guide the order of matches for consecutive sampled frames.
As time progresses from the current human frame to the next sampled human frame, Q Q encourages the corresponding robot match to stay or move forward by penalizing backward transitions.
This encourages temporal order while allowing for execution-rate differences. During adaptation, we update only the affine parameters of normalization layers, a restricted parameterization previously used for domain adaptation ( Wang et al., 2021 ) . This restricts the parameter search space during adaptation, with the aim of improving the visual representations for downstream robotic manipulation.

On AGNOSTOS ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , our method achieves a 48.27 % 48.27\% relative improvement in average success rate over HRAlign with R3M-RN50 ( Nair et al., 2023 ) initialization. With D4R-ViT ( Dasari et al., 2023 ) initialization, it achieves a 65.96 % 65.96\% relative improvement over HRP ( Srirama et al., 2024 ) . With D4R-ViT initialization, it also improves success rates on all four real-world manipulation tasks compared with the Frozen and HRP baselines. Our experiments further show that effective human–robot adaptation does not require a large number of trainable parameters. Updating only 53.1K normalization-affine parameters achieves higher success rates than the late-adapter variant, despite using approximately 29.8 × 29.8\times fewer trainable parameters. Adaptation only takes approximately 13 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, without multi-GPU training. These results suggest that effective human–robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected.

2026-10-06.title: Human Behavior-Informed Crash Scenario Generation with Real-World Crash Priors for Autonomous Vehicle Safety Evaluation
2026-10-06.authors: Mingxing Peng , Xusen Guo , Long Chen , Xintao Yan , Siyu Teng , Jun Ma
2026-10-06.abstract: Reliable safety evaluation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) is essential to improving road safety, yet it depends critically on realistic simulation of rare crashes. Existing crash scenario generation methods can increase collision occurrence, but often fail to realistically reproduce how crashes evolve before impact or the distribution of crash types observed in the real world. Here, we present CrashSim, a human behavior-informed crash scenario generation framework that uses real-world crash priors to guide generative multi-agent traffic simulation for more reliable AV safety evaluation. These priors capture how real-world crashes evolve before impact and how different crash types are distributed, allowing limited crash data to guide realistic and scalable scenario generation across naturalistic driving contexts. We evaluate CrashSim against competing methods, showing that it more closely reproduces real-world pre-impact behavior, collision dynamics, collision geometry and crash-type distributions. We further use CrashSim to construct nuCrash dataset, containing over 4,000 crash and near-crash scenarios. Closed-loop evaluation of five AV planners shows that nuCrash more effectively exposes differences in planner safety capabilities than nuScenes. An LLM-assisted evaluation agent further analyzes planner failures to provide capability-level diagnoses and targeted improvement guidance. Together, CrashSim enables realistic and scalable crash generation for more informative AV safety evaluation. Keywords : Crash Scenario Generation; AV Safety Evaluation; Generative AI; Large Language Models; Diffusion Models

2026-10-06.title: TacOT: Learning Contact-Rich Dexterous Manipulation from Human Demonstrations via Tactile-Guided Optimal Transport
2026-10-06.authors: Xingting Li , Yifan Han , Zijian Lin , Wei Hou , Chuqiao Lyu , Shoujie Li , Wenbo Ding
2026-10-06.abstract:
Learning contact-rich dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations
provides a scalable source of interaction data, yet transferring such
skills to robots remains challenging due to unreliable human–robot
correspondence. Existing human-to-robot transfer methods typically
rely on visual appearance or motion similarity, which may associate
similar motions with different contact states and force patterns.
Tactile dynamics provide interaction-aware cues to distinguish
manipulation processes with similar motions but different contact states.
We introduce tactile-guided optimal transport (TacOT),
a framework for human-to-robot contact-rich manipulation. TacOT leverages action–tactile dynamic
time warping to identify human–robot demonstration correspondences with
consistent interaction dynamics and uses these correspondences to guide
soft optimal transport alignment in a shared policy representation space.
This enables human demonstrations to provide contact-rich supervision for
robot policy learning without requiring predefined frame-level
human–robot pairing.
Across four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, TacOT improves
closed-loop success rates over action-guided OT by up to 17 points on in-distribution tasks and 20 points under targeted human-to-robot out-of-distribution transfer. Further analyses show that
tactile-guided correspondence selects demonstration pairs with more
consistent contact dynamics and produces latent representations that
better reflect interaction-state evolution.
These results demonstrate that tactile dynamics provide an effective
semantic signal for establishing reliable human-to-robot correspondence
in contact-rich dexterous manipulation.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Learning contact-rich skills with dexterous robot hands remains
constrained by the scarcity of robot demonstrations. Collecting
multi-finger interactions on physical robots is slow, labor-intensive,
and difficult to scale across objects, scenes, and contact conditions.
Automated demonstration generation and visuo-tactile pretraining
improve data efficiency [ 1 , 2 ] , while large
multi-embodiment datasets broaden the coverage of robot
learning [ 3 ] . Yet dexterous manipulation remains
underrepresented because its critical variations lie not only in
appearance and motion, but also in how contact is established,
maintained, and released.

Human demonstrations offer a scalable source of this missing
interaction diversity. Wearable and in-the-wild systems can capture
natural hand motion, visual observations, and contact signals across
diverse manipulation behaviors [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
However, leveraging human data raises a fundamental correspondence
question: which human interactions provide meaningful supervision
for robot behavior despite differences in embodiment?
Existing approaches commonly rely on visual similarity or
end-effector motion [ 8 , 9 ] . These cues are
insufficient for contact-rich dexterous manipulation: similar wrist
motions can correspond to free-space motion, contact establishment,
or forceful interaction, while morphologically different human and
robot motions may realize the same physical behavior.
Consequently, demonstrations can appear aligned in vision or
kinematics while differing substantially in finger contacts
and force distributions.

We therefore cast human-to-robot imitation as identifying
interaction-consistent behavior rather than merely closing
appearance- or motion-domain gaps. The relevant unit of
correspondence is a temporally extended action–contact pattern,
not an individual visually similar frame. Tactile trajectories
disambiguate interaction phases that vision and kinematics leave
uncertain. Here, tactile information serves not only as a policy
observation but also as a supervision signal for matching human
and robot demonstrations with consistent interaction dynamics.
Although prior work has demonstrated the value of touch for
policy conditioning, tactile representation learning, and
cross-sensor transfer [ 7 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] ,
using joint action–tactile dynamics to establish human–robot behavioral correspondence remains underexplored.

The same interaction may exhibit temporal variations between human and robot demonstrations, and multiple human segments may correspond to similar robot behaviors. Therefore, effective correspondence requires flexible alignment beyond frame-wise matching. Dynamic time warping (DTW) addresses the temporal requirement through order-preserving sequence alignment [ 15 ] . To support soft correspondence, we adopt entropy-regularized optimal transport (OT), which couples human and robot policy representations without predefined one-to-one pairing [ 16 , 17 ] . The key challenge is to define a transport cost that reflects interaction compatibility between human and robot behaviors. We use joint action–tactile dynamics to guide this cost, favoring correspondences consistent in both motion and contact.

We present tactile-guided optimal transport ( TacOT ),
a framework for contact-rich human-to-robot manipulation.
TacOT combines DTW distances computed separately over action
and tactile trajectories to identify interaction-consistent
human–robot demonstration pairs. These pairs guide OT by
reducing their latent transport costs, favoring compatible
interactions while retaining soft coupling across all pairs.
Optimized jointly with a multimodal flow-matching objective,
this alignment allows contact-rich human demonstrations to
supervise a shared policy space anchored by robot data.
Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate human-to-robot imitation for contact-rich
dexterous manipulation as an interaction-consistent correspondence
learning problem, using joint action–tactile dynamics to guide
soft optimal transport alignment.

We develop a matched-sensing human–robot platform and
a multimodal flow-matching policy for joint learning from
visual, motion, and tactile demonstration data from human and robot systems.

We evaluate TacOT on four real-world dexterous manipulation
tasks. Compared with action-guided OT, TacOT improves success rates by up to 17 percentage points in-distribution and 20 percentage points under targeted human-to-robot transfer.

# II RELATED WORK

Dexterous Imitation Learning. Dexterous imitation learning models high-dimensional, contact-rich hand–object interactions across tasks and embodiments. Video-based methods derive robot-executable supervision through physics-aware policy learning or hand–object reconstruction and retargeting [ 18 , 19 ] . Being-H0, VITRA, and Being-H0.5 scale dexterous VLA pretraining through hand-motion modeling and action representations shared across human and robot embodiments [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] , while DexHiL incorporates coordinated arm–hand interventions for policy adaptation [ 23 ] . These methods broaden supervision beyond robot teleoperation, but transferring human manipulation skills still requires alignment between human and robot representations and often robot-specific adaptation data.

Tactile Representation and Transfer. Recent work learns tactile representations transferable across sensors, objects, and tasks. Self-supervised methods extract reusable tactile features [ 10 ] , while multi-sensor approaches learn representations across heterogeneous visuo-tactile platforms [ 24 , 12 ] . MimicTouch incorporates human tactile demonstrations into contact-rich robot learning [ 7 ] , and UniTacHand learns shared representations for human-to-robot tactile transfer [ 14 ] . These studies emphasize tactile representation learning and transfer; TacOT additionally uses tactile trajectories to guide human–robot demonstration matching during policy learning.

Learning from Human Demonstrations. MimicPlay learns long-horizon robot behaviors from human play data [ 5 ] , while EgoMimic co-trains human and robot demonstrations through visual and action-space alignment [ 8 ] . EgoBridge constructs pseudo-pairs from end-effector trajectories to guide optimal-transport alignment between human and robot representations for robots with two-finger grippers [ 9 ] . However, similar motions can involve different contact states in dexterous manipulation. TacOT therefore combines end-effector motion, hand actions, and tactile evolution to identify correspondences consistent in both motion and contact dynamics.

2026-10-06.title: Asynchronous Tracking, Optical Communication and 3D Motion Capture using Event-based Sensors
2026-10-06.authors: Ziwei Wang , Angus Apps , Holly Battisson , Iain Guilliard , Timothy Molloy , Robert Mahony
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Inter-robot communication is a key enabling technology in cooperative robotics applications.
While wireless communication is ubiquitous, simple, and effective, it has inherent limitations: the receiving robot cannot easily localise the source of an incoming signal, clock synchronisation is challenging, and signals are broadcast to all nearby devices rather than targeted recipients.
Optical communication provides a complementary channel that is inherently directional and spatially localised, directly addressing these limitations.
Event cameras are bio-inspired dynamic vision sensors that respond to changes in image intensity with high temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and low latency, making them well-suited as receivers for high-rate optical communication in cooperative robotic systems.
In this paper, we propose the Asynchronous Tracking and Optical Communication (ATOC) system, which integrates LED smart-beacon modulation, event-based detection, optical tracking, and event-data demodulation in a single pipeline.
By simultaneously tracking and demodulating multiple LED smart beacons, ATOC transforms a conventional visual marker into a robust communication channel suitable for a wide range of high-impact robotics applications.
We validate ATOC in a suite of laboratory studies and two ‘applications’: a smart-city demonstration and a 3D motion-capture system.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Visual tracking of stationary and moving beacons or markers is an enabling technology across a wide range of robotics applications, including warehouse and logistics systems, cooperative automotive leader-follower systems, distributed robotic networks, visual motion capture, etc .
In most existing systems, beacons are distinguished either by their appearance, such as ArUco markers, colour patterns, or barcodes, or by active (visible or ultraviolet) light, identified through colour, geometric arrangement, or flicker signals.
While such markers can be recognised, they cannot communicate: they convey nothing beyond their own identity.
This is an increasingly important limitation in distributed robotics, such as cooperative driving, smart cities, and formation or swarm control, where agents must continually exchange identity and state information.
Beacons that can be tracked and also transmit data are especially valuable where radio-frequency (RF) communication is unreliable or impractical due to interference, multipath, background noise, bandwidth saturation, intentional signal jamming, or in challenging transmission environments, such as underwater.
Optical Camera Communication (OCC) is a popular alternative for short-range, line-of-sight wireless communication.
Lightweight OCC channels are relatively easy and cheap to integrate into existing robotic systems [ 1 ] .
Beyond the communication channel itself, OCC also provides a cost- and power-efficient method for localisation, an important consideration in cooperative robotics applications.
Existing OCC systems typically rely on traditional CMOS or CCD cameras to capture the modulated blinking of LED transmitters.
The maximum data rate achievable with standard off-the-shelf frame-based cameras is low, at most 100 to 250 bits per second (bps) [ 2 ] , and most systems report rates well below this.
Higher data rates can be achieved with advanced high-speed cameras or more sophisticated transmitter-receiver setups that allow image sensors to capture down-sampled high-frequency information [ 3 ] .
However, these systems demand substantial computational resources or dedicated physical infrastructure [ 4 ] .
Furthermore, the short exposure times of high-speed cameras require brighter LED transmitters, reducing beacon power efficiency and limiting their effective range.

In contrast to traditional frame-based cameras that accumulate irradiance for all pixels within the exposure time, event cameras continuously monitor the logarithmic light intensity at each pixel independently, generating events only when brightness changes exceed a predefined threshold.
This architecture provides microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range (over 120 dB), reduced motion blur, and lower power consumption.
These characteristics make event cameras ideal for integration into existing sensor suites [ 5 ] , capable of detecting high-frequency modulated light from smart beacons for high-speed, low-latency communication between autonomous robots.

In this paper, we propose the Asynchronous Tracking and Optical Communication (ATOC) system, which integrates LED smart beacons emitting a modulated optical signal that is tracked, demodulated, and decoded by asynchronous event processing.
The high temporal resolution and sensitivity of event cameras enables high baud rate communication (relative to existing OCC systems) along with accurate high-speed tracking of the visual beacon.
We exploit the flickering nature of the beacon to detect candidate beacons as event-blobs in the data stream [ 6 ] , and then track beacons using the AEB (Asynchronous Event Blob) tracker [ 7 ] .
Events associated with each tracked beacon are processed using a modified event-based high-pass filter [ 8 ] to reconstruct the transmitted intensity signal asynchronously.
An onset detection algorithm then extracts the binary bitstream, automatically synchronises with the start delimiter, and decodes the transmitted message.
We transmit ASCII-encoded messages using Modified Frequency Modulation (MFM) line coding, with an extended Hamming code for error correction and a dedicated start delimiter for framing and synchronisation.
The communication pipeline is designed to be simple, robust and computationally efficient.

We validate ATOC through a series of indoor and outdoor experiments that encompass both controlled performance evaluation and real-world robotic applications.
A spinning-disk experiment characterises communication accuracy under varying transmission rates and image-plane velocities, demonstrating error-free transmission at 12.5 kb/s for motion up to 3.5 kpx/s and at 11.11 kb/s for motion up to 9.2 kpx/s.
The system also detects and validates newly visible beacons within 5 ms.
In an outdoor bicycle experiment, ATOC decodes 138 ASCII characters during a single 327 ms observation, demonstrating its potential for smart-city applications.
Finally, we use ATOC to achieve 3D visual motion capture and demonstrate this by capturing a musician playing a quebecois fiddle tune.
In the two-camera setup, a packet counter in the transmitted message allows global temporal synchronisation of independent event cameras with a precision of 4.54 μ \mu s, enabling 3D reconstruction with a precision of 2 mm at approximately 4 kHz.
The resulting track quality matches or exceeds state-of-the-art motion capture systems at a fraction of the complexity, requiring no central synchronisation hardware and no cabling between cameras.
The total hardware cost, including event cameras and inexpensive LED beacons, makes this potentially one of the simplest and highest-performance visual motion capture systems possible with current technology.

In summary:

We propose the Asynchronous Tracking and Optical Communication (ATOC) system that integrates visual beacon detection and tracking with broadcast optical camera communication, and demonstrate its capability for high-rate data communication in real-world experiments.

We develop a robust event-based optical communications pipeline, including message encoding, beacon detection and tracking, signal onset and start-delimiter detection, synchronisation, and bit error correction.

We validate ATOC through quantitative characterisation across a range of transmission rates and image-plane speeds, and through two real-world applications: a smart-city deployment and a wireless 3D motion-capture system in which a packet counter broadcast by each beacon synchronises multiple uncabled event cameras for high-rate 3D reconstruction.

The beacon PCB designs and all code developed will be provided as open source resources when the paper is published.

1. We propose the Asynchronous Tracking and Optical Communication (ATOC) system that integrates visual beacon detection and tracking with broadcast optical camera communication, and demonstrate its capability for high-rate data communication in real-world experiments.

2. We develop a robust event-based optical communications pipeline, including message encoding, beacon detection and tracking, signal onset and start-delimiter detection, synchronisation, and bit error correction.

3. We validate ATOC through quantitative characterisation across a range of transmission rates and image-plane speeds, and through two real-world applications: a smart-city deployment and a wireless 3D motion-capture system in which a packet counter broadcast by each beacon synchronises multiple uncabled event cameras for high-rate 3D reconstruction.
