# II Related Work

There is an established literature in Optical Camera Communication (OCC) exploiting LED light modulation [ 2 ] .
Different keying technologies investigated include under-sampled frequency shift on-off keying (UFSOOK) [ 9 ] , camera multiple frequency shift keying (CM-FSK) [ 10 , 11 ] , pulse width modulation/pulse position modulation (PWM/PPM) [ 12 , 13 ] , spatial-2-phase-shift keying (S2-PSK) [ 14 ] , camera on-off keying (C-OOK) [ 15 ] , etc .
There are also several established standards ( e . g ., IEEE 802.15.7) for short-range optical wireless communications [ 2 ] .
Usually, to capture the high-frequency LED blinking signal, a high-speed camera is required, up to 1000 fps [ 16 , 17 ] .
Lower frame rate CMOS cameras with the selective capturing strategy [ 18 ] , such as under-sampled modulation [ 19 ] or other custom-built systems [ 20 , 21 ] have also been investigated.
LiFi technology offers much higher speed and lower latency, but requires strict alignment of photodiodes, dedicated hardware, and faces challenges including poor robustness to motion, limited transmission distance (typically 1–10 m indoors), and difficulty in handling multiple sources.

In the robotics field, researchers have recognised the potential of event cameras to create low-cost optical communication channels for embedded and robotic systems.
Wang et al. [ 22 ] demonstrated effective, lossless transmission at 500 bps in full sunlight at a distance of 100 m.
Subsequent research has introduced improved algorithms and processing pipelines, leading to enhanced tracking and communication performance [ 23 , 24 ] .
Recent work has also explored parallel transmission channels using digital micro-mirror devices (DMDs) [ 25 ] and 2D dynamic markers [ 26 , 27 ] to further increase transmission rates.
Joubert et al. [ 1 ] characterised an event camera LED setup for event-based imagers applied to modulated light signal detection.
Some preliminary results were also obtained by Perez-Ramirez et al. [ 28 ] where events were first accumulated into synchronous frames.
They then proposed a start frame delimiter (SFD) and symbol design derived from the Composite Waveform, and showed some Bit Error Rate (BER) results for the transmission of 2-byte packets.
Soga et al. [ 29 ] proposed an algorithm for OCC using LED bars, where clusters are uniquely identified using Walsh-Hadamard code pilot sequences.
Tofighi et al. [ 30 ] assigned different pulse patterns to codewords in a static look-up table.
Although the number of pulses is assigned such that the most common codewords use fewer pulses, the transmission rate remains variable depending on the message.

A key requirement for embedded and robotic system optical communications is the ability to track the source of transmission.
General event-based tracking algorithms have an extensive literature including pose estimation and close-range tracking [ 31 ] , with applications in multi-agent unmanned aerial vehicles [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] and autonomous underwater vehicle systems [ 35 , 36 ] .
Tracking fast blinking LED markers is a natural specialisation of the general algorithms.
Censi et al. [ 37 ] proposed a pose tracking algorithm using four infrared LED markers with different blinking frequencies which are distinguishable by event cameras.
They accumulated triggered events in short time windows and tracked the pose of a drone fitted with LED markers using a particle filter.
Instead of the traditional CMOS cameras, Chen et al. [ 38 ] used an event camera in their visible light positioning system with multi-LEDs, which largely reduced the computational cost and latency.
They estimated different frequencies of LED markers based on the time intervals between positive-negative transitions at a pixel and then tracked LED markers with their GM-PHD filter, resulting in an accuracy of 3 cm when the distance between LEDs and camera is less than 1 m.
More recently, monocular systems have employed LED beacons flashing at distinct frequencies, mounted on agile quadrotors [ 39 ] or on rigid boards [ 40 ] , to enable real-time, PnP-based motion capture.

Combining tracking and optical communications is a natural next step for embedded and robotic systems.
Soga et al. [ 41 ] extended their OCC work [ 29 ] to perform real-time tracking and communication from multiple LED bars.
Our early work on smart visual beacon systems [ 22 ] already had a tracking module that has been extended to manage asynchronous detection, tracking, and track management of small blob-like objects, enabling high-speed, real-time tracking of LED beacons [ 7 , 42 ] .
The present paper extends our preliminary work [ 22 , 42 ] to improve the communications protocols and exploit the multi-target detection and tracking capability.

2026-10-06.title: Real-Time Conformal-Seeded Hybrid Inverse Kinematics for Offset Redundant Manipulators
2026-10-06.authors: Duc Cuong Vu , Van Tung Nguyen , Duc Hai Nguyen , Manh Cuong Nguyen , Vu Trung Tran , Minh Nhat Vu
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper presents a conformal-seeded hybrid strategy for solving inverse kinematics of offset, redundant 7-DoF robot arms of the humanoid class. Analytical inverse kinematics (AIK) provides closed-form solutions with very low computational cost. However, for offset kinematic structures, the exact closed-form solution is generally unavailable, and practical AIK must rely on an approximate or simplified kinematic model. In contrast, numerical inverse kinematics (NIK) can achieve high-precision solutions on the full kinematic model. However, its convergence is highly sensitive to initialization. To overcome these limitations, we propose a two-stage hybrid inverse kinematics framework with conformal-calibrated seed selection . First, an approximate analytical model efficiently enumerates a finite set of candidate joint solutions. Second, we rank these candidates using a lightweight learned predictor of post-refinement difficulty , wrapped by split-conformal prediction into a calibrated upper bound that serves as the selection score . The best-ranked seed is then refined using a Levenberg-Marquardt solver on the full kinematic model. The proposed method combines fast candidate generation, learned seed ranking with a calibrated difficulty bound , and accurate numerical refinement, achieving real-time performance of less than 40 µ ​ s 40\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} and a success rate of 100 % 100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in our evaluation on reachable targets. We validate the approach through large-scale stochastic simulation across the workspace and experimental demonstrations with motion planning on a humanoid robot arm. Demonstration videos are available at https://youtu.be/aeiBmw1XRbw.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Modern robotic systems increasingly require inverse kinematics (IK) solvers that are both computationally efficient and robust across diverse kinematic structures. Applications such as industrial manipulation [ 1 ] , trajectory optimization [ 2 ] , trajectory planning [ 3 ] , require reliable real-time IK computation under redundancy, joint limits, and complex workspace constraints. These requirements become particularly challenging for robots with high degrees of freedom or nontrivial kinematic structures, where conventional IK methods may exhibit unstable convergence behavior or insufficient real-time reliability. This work targets offset 7-DoF redundant arms of the spherical-shoulder, offset-wrist class widely adopted in humanoid and dual-arm platforms, for which exact closed-form IK is unavailable and purely numerical solving is initialization-sensitive; the humanoid arm studied throughout serves as the representative instance.

Analytical approach: For robots with relatively simple kinematic structures [ 4 ] , certain classes of manipulators [ 5 ] , or well-structured redundant manipulators with favorable kinematic properties [ 6 ] , closed-form Analytical Inverse Kinematics (AIK) solutions can be derived. By exploiting geometric relationships and kinematic symmetries, AIK provides exact solutions with extremely low computational cost and strong numerical stability , making them particularly attractive for real-time control and industrial applications. However, AIK is limited [ 7 ] when considering manipulators with high degrees of freedom, kinematic redundancy, or calibrated systems with kinematic parameter offsets . Explicit analytical solutions are derived from an ideal kinematic chain model; practical factors such as mechanical tolerances, assembly errors, or calibration updates modify the robot description (DH parameters or URDF model), rendering the analytical solution inaccurate or even invalid.

Numerical approach : To overcome these limitations, Numerical Inverse Kinematics (NIK) methods have been widely adopted [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] ,
in which the IK problem is typically formulated as a nonlinear optimization problem accounting for joint limits, motion smoothness, manipulability, etc. [ 11 ] . A major advantage of numerical methods lies in their generality and flexibility , which can operate with many types of robots [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , requiring only the forward kinematics to formulate the optimization problem. Despite their flexibility, NIK methods suffer from several limitations, particularly regarding initial guess selection and computational time . A poor initial guess may cause the solver to become trapped in local minima or near kinematic singularities [ 15 ] .
In addition, iterative numerical solvers often exhibit unpredictable computational times on the order of milliseconds [ 7 ] .

Hybrid approach: Regarding hybrid approaches, the survey in [ 16 ] shows that several studies have attempted to combine analytical and numerical IK methods. For example, [ 17 ] employs Particle Swarm Optimization to estimate the elbow orientation; however, the execution time remains on the millisecond scale and the positioning accuracy is still limited. In [ 18 , 19 ] , the authors analytically compute the wrist and shoulder joint configurations, followed by an iterative method to solve the elbow configuration. Although this approach achieves relatively fast execution, it still depends heavily on the initial guess, requires a spherical wrist structure, and exhibits large errors near workspace boundaries. Furthermore, in [ 20 ] , the authors partially derive analytical solutions for the wrist joints while solving the remaining joints using the Newton–Raphson method. A common limitation of these approaches is that they mainly focus on reducing the dimensionality of the numerical optimization problem, while the initialization process for iterative refinement still relies on heuristic or random strategies. Consequently, the optimization process may still become trapped in local minima or require a large number of iterations for convergence.

In this study, motivated by the speed and robustness of analytical approaches, together with the generality and flexibility of iterative methods, we adopt a H ybrid I nverse K inematics (HIK) paradigm that leverages the complementary strengths of both. In a typical HIK framework, an approximate AIK (quasi-analytical IK) solution is first used to generate candidate initial seeds, which are selected and subsequently refined by an iterative numerical solver such as the Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) algorithm. By leveraging analytical initialization, HIK methods can significantly improve convergence robustness compared to purely numerical approaches.

However, a key limitation of existing HIK methods is that joint configuration selection mechanisms ( seed selection ) often rely on heuristic criteria, such as minimum joint displacement or maximum manipulability, which do not explicitly account for the convergence behavior of the numerical solver and may therefore lead to suboptimal performance. To address this challenge, this study proposes an additional seed-selection mechanism integrated into the HIK framework, called C onformal- S eeded H ybrid I nverse K inematics (CS-HIK) , that systematically identifies analytical seeds most compatible with the subsequent numerical refinement process (shown in Fig. 1 ). The proposed approach leverages conformal prediction to evaluate the reliability of candidate solutions and select seeds that are more likely to converge successfully during numerical optimization. As a result, the method aims to maximize the convergence success rate while maintaining real-time computational performance across the entire robot workspace. The framework addresses pose-only IK queries, the prevailing industrial setting in which the solver itself resolves the redundancy; the arm angle is nevertheless exposed as an explicit input of the analytical stage (Section III-A), so a higher-level planner may command it, e.g. for obstacle avoidance or posture optimization.

The proposed quasi-AIK, executed within sub- μ ​ s \mu\mathrm{s} time, requires only a few LM iterations for convergence, addressing the limitations of both AIK ( offset, post-calibrated robots ) and NIK ( initialization sensitivity and computational cost ).

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A novel Conformal-Seeded Hybrid Inverse Kinematics (CS-HIK) framework, whose core contribution is a learned seed-selection mechanism: a lightweight predictor of post-Levenberg–Marquardt refinement difficulty ranks the quasi-AIK candidate seeds, and split-conformal prediction wraps it into a calibrated, distribution-free upper bound that serves as the selection score. This score identifies reliable initializations for LM refinement on the full kinematic model, yielding fast and robust IK performance with joint-limit awareness.

Extensive evaluation and benchmarking, including full-workspace Monte-Carlo analysis, comparisons with representative inverse kinematics methods for an example humanoid robot arm, and real-time experimental validation, demonstrating improved robustness, accuracy, and computational efficiency.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the kinematic model and constraints of the redundant manipulator under consideration. Section III introduces the proposed CS-HIK framework, including the derivation of the approximate analytical IK and the conformal seed selection strategy. Section IV reports simulation, benchmarks, and experimental results. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

A novel Conformal-Seeded Hybrid Inverse Kinematics (CS-HIK) framework, whose core contribution is a learned seed-selection mechanism: a lightweight predictor of post-Levenberg–Marquardt refinement difficulty ranks the quasi-AIK candidate seeds, and split-conformal prediction wraps it into a calibrated, distribution-free upper bound that serves as the selection score. This score identifies reliable initializations for LM refinement on the full kinematic model, yielding fast and robust IK performance with joint-limit awareness.

2. Extensive evaluation and benchmarking, including full-workspace Monte-Carlo analysis, comparisons with representative inverse kinematics methods for an example humanoid robot arm, and real-time experimental validation, demonstrating improved robustness, accuracy, and computational efficiency.

2026-10-06.title: Grounded in Time: A Multi-Source Dataset and Benchmark for Temporal Grounding in Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-06.authors: Yi Wang , Yang Yang , Guangqi Xu , Sumin Lin , Ning Kang , Pengxiang Lu , Xiaotong Chen , Zeyu Xue , Ping Deng , Xing Liu , Chenguang Yang , Zhenyu Lu
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires inferring task-relevant states from past interactions when the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the appropriate action. Despite progress in benchmarking memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models, application-oriented tasks requiring history-dependent semantic inference remain underrepresented. We introduce GiT (Grounded in Time), a dataset and benchmark for grounding manipulation decisions in past events across biolaboratory, household, and industrial scenarios. It includes real-robot and Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) style demonstrations covering 18 bimanual tasks, together with simulation data and a ManiSkill-based evaluation suite covering nine tasks. Fine-grained subtask annotations and annotated counterfactual task pairs, in which similar current observations require different actions depending on prior events, support policy learning and targeted evaluation of history use. Evaluations of representative end-to-end VLA models in simulation and on selected real-world tasks reveal substantial room for improvement in history-dependent manipulation. The dataset and benchmark are available at the project page .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have strengthened visual understanding and instruction following [ 5 ] . Building on these advances, vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated generalizable manipulation across tasks and environments [ 6 ] , including long-horizon household activities [ 7 , 8 ] . In such long-horizon settings, current observations may be insufficient for action planning, motivating memory-augmented policies that support spatial recall, action sequencing, and task-progress tracking [ 9 , 10 ] . Within this broader effort to leverage interaction history, we focus on a specific capability crucial for following history-dependent instructions: associating past interaction events with objects and task-relevant states in the current scene to determine appropriate actions. For example, when several bowls look alike, executing “Put the bowl I just used back in the cupboard” requires identifying the target from interaction history rather than appearance alone. This capability is particularly relevant to household assistance and collaborative assembly, where actions by humans or other robots can determine the referents and requirements of subsequent instructions.

Existing robotic memory-centric benchmarks, such as [ 3 , 4 ] focus on in-episode state tracking, primarily assessing memory through abstract, purpose-built manipulation tasks. While useful for isolating specific memory skills, these settings offer limited coverage of everyday workflows in which prior interactions determine the meaning of subsequent instructions. In such workflows, a new request may refer to interactions completed before it was issued, including those performed by humans or other robots. When the current observation provides insufficient evidence to identify the intended objects or task-relevant states, the robot must interpret these earlier events and link them to the current scene. We term this capability pre-episode semantic grounding : grounding a current instruction in scene objects and task-relevant states using interactions completed before the current task episode begins.

To support pre-episode semantic grounding , we introduce Grounded in Time (GiT) , a multi-source dataset and benchmark for history-dependent bimanual manipulation in biolaboratory, household, and industrial settings. The GiT dataset combines simulated trajectories from ManiSkill3 [ 11 ] , real-robot demonstrations collected through virtual reality (VR) teleoperation, and human demonstrations collected with a sensorized handheld gripper inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [ 12 ] . It comprises over 4,680 episodes across 18 tasks, totaling more than 3.3 million steps and more than 30 hours of interaction. Each sample pairs a pre-episode interaction video with a manipulation instruction and execution trajectory.

Both the training and test splits include annotated counterfactual A–B pairs with matched scenes at the start of the current task but different pre-episode histories and required actions. The GiT benchmark uses the test-set pairs to assess whether policies ground current instructions in the relevant prior interactions.

Our main contributions are as follows:

A multi-source dataset. We introduce the GiT dataset, linking pre-episode interaction histories to subsequent bimanual manipulation across three application domains.

A semi-automated annotation pipeline. We develop a pipeline for hierarchical trajectory and segment level annotation, covering 180 subtask categories.

A benchmark and empirical evaluations. We establish the GiT benchmark and evaluate selected end-to-end VLA policies, revealing limitations in history-dependent manipulation. We complement these evaluations with small-scale real-robot experiments.

# II Related Work

## II-A Datasets for Robotic Learning

Robotic manipulation datasets have expanded the coverage of tasks, environments, and embodiments available for policy learning. Simulation-based resources such as RLBench [ 13 ] and LIBERO [ 14 ] provide diverse tasks with generated or human-collected demonstrations. In the real world, BridgeData V2 [ 15 ] and DROID [ 16 ] broaden skill and scene coverage, while Open X-Embodiment [ 17 ] and RoboMIND [ 18 ] support learning across robotic embodiments. Human demonstrations provide another source of supervision: RH20T [ 19 ] pairs human videos with robot executions, and UMI [ 12 ] enables manipulation data collection using handheld grippers. Domain-specific efforts such as AutoBio [ 20 ] and LabUtopia [ 21 ] target biology-laboratory automation with high-fidelity simulation of fluid handling, instrument interfaces, and chemically meaningful interactions, emphasizing precise protocol execution rather than memory-dependent instruction grounding. These resources primarily support learning how to execute specified tasks across diverse conditions. However, greater trajectory diversity and access to demonstration videos do not by themselves ensure supervision for interpreting requests whose referents depend on earlier interactions. The GiT dataset targets the challenges by linking pre-episode interaction videos to subsequent instructions and execution trajectories, with counterfactual A–B pair annotations in both training and test splits.

## II-B Memory‑centric benchmarks for robotic manipulation

Robotic manipulation benchmarks evaluate different aspects of task execution. Table I summarizes a comparison of representative robotic manipulation benchmarks along key dimensions. BEHAVIOR-1K [ 1 ] emphasizes realistic, long-horizon everyday activities, while RoboEval [ 2 ] assesses bimanual execution quality through fine-grained behavioral metrics. However, task realism and execution quality alone do not isolate the need for historical information. To evaluate history dependence more directly, RMBench [ 4 ] organizes manipulation tasks by memory complexity, whereas RoboMME [ 3 ] evaluates counting, object permanence, reference resolution, and motion imitation, including tasks that identify manipulation targets from prior videos. These controlled tasks help isolate specific memory skills, but success on such tests alone does not establish reliable grounding of history-dependent instructions in practical workflows. Compared with prior benchmarks, our benchmark uniquely targets the pre‑episode memory capability. It requires policies to reason over completed historical episodes for decision‑making, rather than maintaining and updating continuous task states within ongoing interactions. Moreover, our benchmark complements previous efforts by focusing on pre-episode semantic grounding in application-oriented biolaboratory, household, and industrial tasks.

2026-10-06.title: ROOT: Discovering Rewards for User-Specified Embodied Behaviors
2026-10-06.authors: Eren Sadikoglu , Aditya Taparia , Xinyuan Liu , Ransalu Senanayake
2026-10-06.abstract: Reinforcement learning for embodied control remains constrained by the difficulty of reward specification. Although recent large language model (LLM)-based methods can synthesize reward functions from natural-language descriptions, they often fail to capture subtle behavioral properties that humans care about, such as natural gait, posture, and movement style. This limitation arises because many desired behaviors are easier to recognize visually than to encode in a reward function. We introduce Reward Optimization via Observable Trees (ROOT), a framework for discovering reward functions that align learned policies with user-specified embodied behaviors. Rather than relying solely on scalar training statistics, ROOT casts reward design as an observation-guided search over a persistent experiment tree that stores reward programs, trained policies, and rollout observations, together with behavioral insights distilled by a video-language model, to diagnose behavioral failures and guide subsequent reward refinements. We evaluate ROOT on seven tasks across four embodiments: simulated Hopper, HalfCheetah, Ant, Unitree Go2, and as well as the real-world Unitree Go2. ROOT produces behaviors that better align with user intent than those generated by existing LLM-based reward-generation methods, achieving up to 86.8% locomotion-completeness accuracy and improving Vid-LLM behavioral alignment from 3.56/5 to 4.14/5 , a 16.5% improvement over baselines. Human evaluations further support these results, with ROOT preferred in 51–63% of pairwise comparisons.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled increasingly capable robotic behaviors in recent years [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Learning these behaviors depends on reward functions that translate the desired task into a training objective. This translation is relatively straightforward when the objective is well-defined and directly measurable, such as reaching a target position or maintaining a desired speed. However, reward design becomes more challenging when the desired behavior also involves qualitative properties, such as posture, limb coordination, and movement style. For example, asking a quadruped to trot forward requires both forward motion and coordinated leg movements in a recognizable trotting motion. Such properties are often easier to recognize visually than to specify through hand-crafted reward terms.

To reduce this burden of manual reward engineering, recent methods such as Eureka [ 5 ] and Text2Reward [ 6 ] use large language models (LLMs) to generate executable reward programs from natural-language instructions and environment descriptions. These approaches automate reward design across diverse control tasks. However, generated rewards may not fully
capture the requested behavioral properties, allowing policies to earn high returns while deviating from the user’s intent. A quadruped instructed to trot forward, for instance, may learn to propel itself using its front legs while dragging its hind legs, earning a high reward for forward motion without exhibiting the alternating diagonal leg coordination that defines a trot. We refer to this mismatch between the user’s intended behavior and the learned policy’s behavior as the behavioral gap . Because scalar training statistics alone may not reveal this gap, recent methods incorporate visual feedback to guide reward refinement [ 7 , 8 ] . Yet identifying a behavioral failure is only part of the refinement process, this feedback must also inform which past reward to revisit and what modification to test next.

To that end, we present Reward Optimization via Observable Trees ( ROOT ), which organizes reward discovery as an observation-guided search over a persistent tree of experience (Fig. 1 ). Each experience connects a reward program and its trained policy with rollout observations, scalar diagnostics, and distilled behavioral insights, while branches represent alternative reward refinements. A multi-agent reasoning framework uses this accumulated evidence to diagnose failures, revisit promising rewards, and propose targeted refinements that address the behavioral gap. Across seven tasks on four simulated embodiments (Hopper, HalfCheetah, Ant, and Unitree Go2), with additional validation on a physical Go2, ROOT produces policies that better align with user intent and are preferred by human evaluators over existing LLM-based reward-design baselines. Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate reward discovery as a search over an observable “experience tree” that stores reward programs, trained policies, rollout observations, scalar diagnostics, hypotheses, and behavioral insights, allowing subsequent generation to build on past experience.

We formulate reward discovery as a search over an observable “experience tree” that stores reward programs, trained policies, rollout observations, scalar diagnostics, hypotheses, and behavioral insights, allowing subsequent generation to build on past experience.

We introduce ROOT , a multi-agent framework which use past evidence from the experience tree to diagnose failures, revisit promising rewards, and propose targeted refinements.

We demonstrate that ROOT improves alignment with user intent over existing reward-design baselines across multiple embodied tasks, and show how past experience contributes to these improvements.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Reward design remains a major bottleneck in embodied RL, with 92% of practitioners relying on manual reward tuning and 89% reporting sub-optimal rewards [ 9 ] . LLMs facilitate reward design by translating task descriptions into reward signals [ 10 ] , structured specifications [ 11 ] , or executable code [ 6 ] . EUREKA [ 5 ] refines sampled reward programs using training statistics and optional human feedback, while REvolve [ 12 ] and CARD [ 13 ] explore evolutionary refinement and trajectory-preference evaluation. Auto MC-Reward [ 14 ] separates reward generation, code critique, and trajectory analysis to guide revisions. More structured approaches include R* [ 15 ] , which evolves modular reward structures and learns their parameters from trajectory preferences, and ORSO [ 16 ] , which interleaves reward selection with policy optimization. These approaches automate reward synthesis and refinement, motivating further study of how experimental feedback should guide subsequent reward-design decisions.

Reflexion [ 17 ] retains textual reflections in episodic memory to guide subsequent trials. In reward design, RF-Agent [ 18 ] formulates reward optimization as Monte Carlo tree search, storing reward programs and training feedback in tree nodes and using scalar task evaluations, self-verification, and tree statistics to guide selection and expansion. ROOT emphasizes behavioral evidence in this process: each experiment links a refinement plan to the resulting policy behavior, while parent–child
relationships preserve the reference reward. Its reasoning procedure uses these records to jointly select an earlier reward to revisit and a modification to test, informed by alternative refinements and observed
regressions across branches. We investigate how access to accumulated experimental
evidence and visual feedback contributes to reward discovery.

A separate line of work uses vision language models (VLMs) to provide behavioral supervision through several mechanisms. VLM-RMs [ 19 ] derive rewards from image–text alignment, RL-VLM-F [ 20 ] learns reward models from visual preferences, and VLM-CaR [ 21 ] generates executable rewards to reduce repeated VLM inference. Related preference-based approaches include LAPP [ 22 ] , which learns from LLM preferences over state–action trajectories, and ReWiND [ 23 ] , which learns language-conditioned rewards from demonstrations and adapts policies without additional task demonstrations. Closest to ROOT, ELEMENTAL [ 7 ] combines visual demonstrations, generated reward features, inverse reinforcement learning, and iterative self-reflection. VIRAL [ 8 ] refines reward code using training statistics and optional human or video-language-model feedback. ROOT uses visual critique of its own trained-policy rollouts as experimental evidence, without requiring task demonstrations. These assessments remain linked to the corresponding reward refinements and inform subsequent search decisions.

2026-10-06.title: Attention-Based Surface Representation Learning for Robot State Prediction and Open-Ended Surface Classification
2026-10-06.authors: Oleg Kushnarev , Alexander Belyaev
2026-10-06.abstract: For ground robots operating in outdoor environments, understanding the properties of the underlying terrain is essential for ensuring reliable operation. In most perception-based studies, this problem is formulated as categorical classification with a fixed number of classes defined during training. We propose an approach that enables new surface classes to be added as trainable vectors, which can subsequently be used to address higher-level tasks. By employing a learning paradigm based on predicting the robot's next state in time and using attention blocks, we improved classification accuracy to 98.56% on the Belyaev-Kushnarev dataset and 94.8% on BorealTC.

2026-10-06.title: Humanoid Rickshaw Pulling: Whole-Body Locomotion under Coupled Wheeled Loads
2026-10-06.authors: Yangzhi Yang , Xiansheng Lin , Zhaoming Xie , Xiaobin Xiong
2026-10-06.abstract: Humanoid robots could transport payloads substantially heavier than themselves by pulling passive wheeled vehicles instead of carrying the load. This capability, however, creates a coupled locomotion problem: the robot must maintain persistent upper-body contact while adapting to unknown, configuration-dependent forces arising from the payload, vehicle, and terrain. We present a whole-body control framework for humanoid rickshaw pulling that tracks commanded vehicle motion while preserving balance and stable grasps under uncertain load dynamics. During training, a privileged teacher exploits vehicle states, interaction forces, and load properties. Its actions and latent are distilled into a history-conditioned student that implicitly infers coupled dynamics from proprioceptive responses, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. Comparisons with No History and Only History baselines show that the resulting policy achieves accurate vehicle tracking while reducing vehicle oscillation, torso tilt, and actuation cost. Behavioral analysis shows that Unitree G1 propels the rickshaw and generates gait-synchronized whole-body reactions that stabilize its lateral and roll motions. Moreover, pulling redistributes joint effort and yields a lower robot-normalized cost-of-transport proxy than unloaded walking over most tested load–speed conditions. On hardware, a single policy performs starting, sustained pulling, turning, and stopping with both rigid payloads and human passengers, handling a loaded rickshaw mass of up to 115 kg without load-specific retuning. These results demonstrate robust heavy-load transportation through coordinated and persistent humanoid–vehicle interaction.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Humanoid robots are expected to transport people, tools, and goods in human-centered environments. Directly carrying a payload places substantial demands on joint torques, structural strength, and balance. Pulling a passive wheeled vehicle offers an alternative: the wheels bear much of the payload weight, while the robot supplies propulsion and steering through sustained physical contact. This arrangement may enable transport of loads substantially heavier than the robot itself. We study humanoid rickshaw pulling as a representative task in which whole-body locomotion must control a coupled wheeled load.

The central challenge is to regulate vehicle motion while maintaining humanoid balance and persistent bimanual contact. Forces transmitted through the handles couple the vehicle’s motion to the robot’s arms and torso. These forces depend on payload mass and distribution, wheel–ground interaction, and the relative robot–vehicle configuration. Nonholonomic rolling constraints further shape the forces required for propulsion and turning. The controller must coordinate stepping, posture, and arm motion across starting, sustained pulling, turning, and stopping. During deployment, this coordination must be achieved without direct observations of vehicle state, interaction forces, or load parameters.

Recent advances in reinforcement learning have enabled robust sim-to-real locomotion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Whole-body control methods extend these capabilities to object transportation, sequential contacts, and sustained dynamic interaction [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Humanoid interaction with passive wheeled systems has also been explored through model-based loaded-cart transportation [ 12 , 13 ] and learning-based approaches to agile object pushing and pulling [ 14 , 15 ] . Building on these developments, we focus on sustained rickshaw pulling across different load configurations. The robot must maintain stable, command-responsive locomotion while coordinating propulsion and steering through persistent handle contacts and adapting to load- and condition-dependent vehicle dynamics.

Randomizing physical parameters during training can improve policy robustness to dynamics variations and facilitate sim-to-real transfer [ 16 , 1 ] . In humanoid rickshaw pulling, similar instantaneous humanoid observations can correspond to different vehicle states and load parameters, and may require different control responses. Observation histories provide cues about the coupled dynamics by capturing the humanoid’s response to previous actions. Prior work combines dynamics randomization with memory-based policies to support implicit dynamics inference [ 16 ] , while legged-locomotion systems use proprioceptive histories for adaptation under varying physical conditions [ 3 , 17 , 5 ] . Privileged learning and asymmetric actor–critic training additionally exploit simulator-only information to guide policy learning [ 18 ] . These complementary ideas motivate privileged supervision of a control-relevant representation of humanoid–vehicle interaction that can be inferred from onboard observation history during deployment.

We develop a whole-body controller using privileged teacher–student learning. The teacher uses vehicle states, interaction forces, and load properties to guide action and latent distillation into a student using onboard observation history. We then jointly fine-tune the student encoder and action head to refine control with the inferred representation. Training spans randomized vehicle, payload, and terrain conditions, while policy comparisons examine the roles of observation history, privileged training, and arm coordination.

Beyond reliable pulling, we investigate how persistent interaction with a wheeled load changes humanoid motion and actuation demands. Handle reactions influence the robot’s balance. We examine this interaction through gait-resolved handle forces, centroidal motion, and joint-effort redistribution. Positive mechanical work and squared-torque proxies characterize actuation demands across load–speed conditions, with walking comparisons identifying where pulling reduces the robot-normalized squared-torque proxy.

The main contributions of this work are:

A whole-body learning framework for humanoid rickshaw pulling that coordinates vehicle-motion tracking, balance, and persistent bimanual contact. Privileged teacher–student training transfers vehicle, interaction, and load information into a deployable controller using onboard observation history, without direct vehicle-state, contact-force, or load-parameter measurements.

An empirical characterization of humanoid–rickshaw interaction that identifies load-dependent joint-effort redistribution and gait-synchronized handle reactions consistent with damping-like effects on lateral and roll motion. The analysis identifies conditions under which pulling yields a lower robot-normalized squared-torque proxy than the evaluated walking baseline.

Real-world validation of a single policy with robot and human passengers at loaded-rickshaw masses of 60–115 kg. Without load-specific retuning, the policy executes starting, sustained pulling, and stopping, with the heaviest loaded rickshaw approximately 3.15 times the robot’s mass.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A History-Based Locomotion Adaptation

Observation–action history provides information about unobserved dynamics for locomotion adaptation [ 3 , 5 ] . RMA conditions a base policy on privileged environmental properties encoded as a latent, which an adaptation module estimates from history during deployment [ 17 ] . A-RMA subsequently fine-tunes the policy with the adaptation module fixed to accommodate estimation errors in bipedal locomotion [ 19 ] . History-conditioned transformers provide another route, learning action selection from observation–action sequences through reinforcement learning [ 5 ] . These approaches distinguish the use of history from the training procedure that shapes its representation.

## II-B Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation

Whole-body loco-manipulation coordinates locomotion, balance, and object interaction through a common control objective. Unified MPC explicitly couples robot and object dynamics in multi-contact optimization [ 9 ] . Learning-based methods realize box pickup and carrying on Digit [ 7 ] , while WoCoCo organizes diverse humanoid tasks through sequential contact stages [ 8 ] . COLA learns proprioception-only human–humanoid collaborative carrying [ 20 ] . FALCON jointly trains lower-body locomotion and upper-body position control with adaptive force compensation, including real-world cart pulling [ 10 ] . HMC combines position, impedance, and hybrid force–position control
for contact-rich humanoid manipulation [ 21 ] .These studies establish complementary approaches to coordinating body motion and contact forces.

## II-C Humanoid Interaction with Passive Wheeled Systems

Passive wheeled objects have independent motion constrained by wheel–ground contact, making their dynamics part of the interaction task. Rioux and Suleiman combine load-dependent motion primitives, whole-body control, and navigation for loaded-cart transport, including suppression of transmitted oscillations [ 13 ] . HUSKY exploits skateboard tilt–steering coupling to coordinate pushing, steering, and contact transitions [ 22 ] . HAIC infers object dynamics from proprioceptive history and demonstrates agile cart pushing and pulling under varying loads [ 14 ] . Building on these studies, we investigate sustained bimanual rickshaw pulling through simulation analyses and real-world evaluation across load configurations.

2026-10-06.title: Continual Humanoid Motion Learning
2026-10-06.authors: Zhewen He , Hao Huang , Geeta Chandra Raju Bethala , Chong Yu , Tao Chen , Anthony Tzes , Yi Fang
2026-10-06.abstract: Humanoid whole-body controllers can now track a diverse set of dynamic motions, but they are typically trained offline and then frozen, so teaching such a controller a new skill tends to erode the skills it already mastered. We study continual learning for humanoid whole-body motion , where a single controller must acquire skills from a sequential task stream without revisiting past data. We introduce Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN , a progressive neural network (PNN) policy that prevents catastrophic forgetting by construction while reusing knowledge across skills through lightweight low-rank adaptation. A two-level motion-similarity measure, built from dynamic time warping aggregated by optimal transport, decides which prior skill to build on and how much new capacity to allocate, yielding strong forward transfer and large efficiency gains. Across six sequentially learned skill categories, our similarity-guided LoRA policy attains the best forward transfer ( 0.125 0.125 vs. 0.079 0.079 ) and the highest average accuracy among all methods, while saving up to 94.5 % 94.5\% of trainable parameters and 40.8 % 40.8\% of training time. The resulting controller reaches 96.13 % 96.13\% sim-to-sim transfer and is deployed on a physical Unitree G1. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/continual-humanoid-learning-35D3 .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Whole-body control underpins humanoid behavior: robust locomotion requires coordinating the legs, torso, and arms to manage balance and momentum while supporting task-relevant motion. Driven by learning-based motion tracking with sim-to-real pipelines that exploit large-scale human motion, a single policy can track or generalize across a broad repertoire of agile whole-body skills Cheng et al. (2024) ; He et al. (2025a) ; Radosavovic et al. (2024) ; Luo et al. (2024) ; Han et al. (2025) . Yet such policies are trained offline and deployed as essentially static controllers, making it hard to incrementally acquire new motions. The obvious workaround—fine-tuning on the new motion set—triggers catastrophic forgetting, often causing severe regressions on previously mastered behaviors Wang et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2024) . This contrasts sharply with human learning, where new skills are added while old ones are retained. Continual learning (CL) explicitly targets this stability–plasticity dilemma and is well studied in computer vision and natural language processing Shi et al. (2025a) , but in robotics it remains under-explored and is demonstrated mostly in manipulation and navigation rather than legged whole-body control Mendonca et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2024) . To our knowledge, continual learning for humanoid whole-body motion has not been systematically studied. Such continual acquisition can also extend generalist controllers Luo et al. (2025) , offering a practical route toward an ever-growing generalist.

We therefore target this gap: enabling one policy to sequentially acquire whole-body skills (Fig. 1 ) with strong transfer at low cost. Building on Progressive Neural Networks (PNN) Rusu et al. (2016) , we instantiate a frozen sub-network per task, which isolates prior competencies and makes zero forgetting a structural guarantee rather than something we must optimize for. The challenge, and our focus, is to make this expansion reuse knowledge across skills while staying parameter- and computation-efficient. We grow each new sub-network with parameter-efficient LoRA adapters Hu et al. (2022) instead of training it from scratch, and we guide expansion with a two-level motion-similarity measure that selects the most related prior skill to inherit from and sets each adapter’s capacity from the expected transfer. Across a continual suite of six skill categories, this yields the best forward transfer among strong baselines, while cutting trainable parameters and training time substantially, with zero forgetting by design.

We formulate and benchmark continual humanoid whole-body motion learning , providing the first pipeline for continually acquiring humanoid whole-body skills, together with adapted multi-motion and standard-CL baselines under a unified protocol.

We propose Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN , in which a motion-similarity measure drives inheritance from the most related prior skill and adaptive expansion, making continual learning both parameter- and computation-efficient.

Our method delivers the strongest forward transfer and large efficiency gains (up to 94.5 % 94.5\% fewer trainable parameters and 40.8 % 40.8\% less training time) with zero catastrophic forgetting, validated through sim-to-sim transfer and real-robot deployment on a Unitree G1.

2026-10-06.related_work:
Learning-based control has rapidly expanded the repertoire of humanoid whole-body skills, from real-world RL locomotion driven by proprioceptive history Radosavovic et al. (2024) and expressive upper-/lower-body coordination Cheng et al. (2024) to unified controllers that expose fine-grained command spaces Xue et al. (2025) . A particularly active direction is whole-body motion tracking , where a single policy imitates large libraries of reference motions He et al. (2025a) ; Han et al. (2025) and, more recently, scales to generalist controllers that track thousands of clips Luo et al. (2025) . Despite this progress, such controllers are typically trained offline and then deployed as fixed models: incorporating a new skill requires retraining or fine-tuning, which degrades previously mastered behaviors—in stark contrast to how humans accumulate skills over time.

Continual (or lifelong) learning studies how an agent can incrementally acquire tasks from a non-stationary stream while balancing the stability–plasticity trade-off and mitigating catastrophic forgetting Wang et al. (2024) . Classical strategies fall into three families: regularizing important weights ( e.g . , EWC Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) ), parameter isolation via pruning or masking ( e.g . , PackNet Mallya and Lazebnik (2018) ), and dynamic architecture growth such as Progressive Neural Networks Rusu et al. (2016) ; more recent work adapts large foundation models with lightweight low-rank modules to limit interference Luo et al. (2026) . In robotics, continual learning has been explored mainly for manipulation and mobile platforms— e.g . , continually improving mobile manipulation Mendonca et al. (2025) , growing skill libraries through unsupervised discovery Wan et al. (2024) , online neurogenesis for lifelong legged control Srisuchinnawong and Manoonpong (2025) , self-evolving VLA skill spaces with expert routing Wu et al. (2025) , and language-augmented skill composition Meng et al. (2025) . To the best of our knowledge, continual learning has not been investigated for humanoid whole-body motion. We address this gap with Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN , a progressive policy that continually acquires humanoid whole-body skills with zero forgetting and strong, low-cost transfer.

2026-10-06.title: Bi-manual Stabilization of the Cervical Spine for Safe Physical Human-Robot Interaction in Rolling Maneuvers
2026-10-06.authors: Elizabeth Peiros , Moira Bohley , Lucas Yager , Derek Chen , Rebecca Fellbaum , Chris D'Ambrosia , Ananya Rao , Xiao Liang , Michael C. Yip
2026-10-06.abstract:
The neck, specifically the cervical spine, is a highly fragile and mobile part of the body with a high risk of catastrophic injury. Whether someone is injured on a battlefield, in a natural disaster, or in an athletic event, great care is always taken with the cervical spine when transporting, rolling, or moving the patient. In this work, we present an algorithm and adaptations for bi-manual robots to stabilize the cervical spine during rolling maneuvers.
We investigate techniques to maximize grip strength within safety bounds and present a control approach for proper neck rotation.
We found that with our approach, a bi-manual robot is capable of achieving human-level performance in maintaining target rotational alignments. The axial alignment for the robot with prediction was within .21°of human novices.
2026-10-06.introduction:
The neck, specifically the cervical spine, is a highly fragile and mobile part of the body with a high risk of catastrophic injury in major events. It is a focal point when there is ever consideration for spinal injury or head injury: car crashes, falls, collisions in sports, explosions. In field medicine, it is a major consideration during patient transport and maneuvering. Robots have been used in practice to lift patients [ 1 , 2 ] or reposition limbs [ 3 ] , but have not yet been used for a delicate and important role such as cervical spine repositioning and stabilization.

Patient transfers and extractions are common across multiple domains. Military corpsmen and wilderness medicine experts are trained to perform these tasks with minimal personnel and equipment, while nurses, EMTs, and other first responders are trained to use equipment and work with large teams to perform these transfers [ 4 ] . A common requirement across all transfers is a focus on the head and neck to stabilize injury, maintain an airway, and organize cables, pumps, or central lines during transfer [ 4 ] .

In regard to stabilizing strategy, the rigid spinal collar, which is made of plastic and placed around the neck to restrict all cervical spine motion during transport, is likely what comes to mind. However, despite their prevalence, these are not considered best practice. Current practice has moved away from rigid collars because research shows that they can increase intracranial pressure and blood circulation [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Evidence also suggests that rigid collars can increase the risk of hypoxia by reducing airflow to the lungs [ 9 ] .

A rigid collar is nonetheless used when personnel and time are limited, as military corpsmen experience when evacuating a wounded warrior from active combat. 2026-10-06.title: Autoware in Construction: Gap Analysis and LiDAR Perception Toward Off-Road Autonomous Driving
2026-10-06.authors: Yu Otsuki , Teja Emmey , Sena Matsushita , Akiro Harada , Takeshi Miura
2026-10-06.comment: 2026 IROS 5th Workshop on Future of Construction
2026-10-06.abstract: Autoware is an open-source autonomous driving software platform widely adopted by researchers and industry developers. Originally developed primarily for public-road applications, including passenger vehicles, taxis, and buses, Autoware is increasingly being extended to off-road environments such as construction and agricultural sites. Construction sites, however, differ fundamentally from public roads and challenge many assumptions underlying conventional autonomous driving systems. They are characterized by unstructured terrain, airborne dust, continuously evolving site conditions, and construction-specific objects. This paper presents lessons learned from ongoing efforts to extend an Autoware-based autonomous driving system to large dump trucks operating at construction sites. We identify gaps between public-road and off-road construction applications across the sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules of the Autoware stack. We then discuss potential solutions for addressing these gaps, with particular emphasis on ongoing LiDAR-based perception pipeline development and findings from field testing. Finally, we propose a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomous driving for construction vehicles.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Autoware is a modular, open-source autonomous driving software stack that has supported research and development across a wide range of applications, including passenger vehicles, buses, taxis, delivery vehicles, industrial vehicles, and racing cars. Originally implemented on ROS 1 [ 1 ] and since migrated to ROS 2, its architecture integrates sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, control, and vehicle-interface components (Fig. 1 ). This modularity allows individual components to be replaced or extended for each operational design domain (ODD).

Construction sites represent a substantially different ODD from public roads. Construction environments introduce rough terrain, airborne dust, continuously changing site geometry, feature-poor environments, construction-specific objects, and coordinated operations among heterogeneous machines [ 3 ] . These conditions challenge several assumptions embedded in public-road autonomous driving systems and require adaptations throughout the Autoware stack. Recently, the Autoware Foundation has initiated an off-road pilot encompassing mining, racing, and planetary applications [ 4 ] .

As part of our effort to extend Autoware to construction environments, we are integrating the Autoware software stack into a large construction dump truck, as shown in the center of Fig. 2 . The vehicle has been retrofitted with LiDAR, camera, GNSS, and IMU sensors, onboard computers, and an electronic control unit interface.

Based on this ongoing development effort, this paper makes three contributions. First, it presents a module-level gap analysis between the existing Autoware architecture, which was developed primarily for public-road autonomy, and the requirements of off-road autonomy in construction environments. Second, it distills lessons learned from the development and field testing of a LiDAR-based perception pipeline for construction sites. Third, it discusses a roadmap toward end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving for construction vehicles.

2026-10-06.title: Terrain-Dependent Intra-Cycle Leg Timing for Effective Locomotion on Granular Slopes
2026-10-06.authors: Long Zhao , Xingjue Liao , Feifei Qian
2026-10-06.abstract: Legged locomotion on inclined granular terrain depends sensitively on terrain properties and robot gait. Yet, the effect of gait timing on locomotor performance remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how intra-cycle leg timing affects the upslope locomotion of a hexapedal robot on granular surfaces inclined from 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} to 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} . We find that appropriately selected slow phase timing substantially improves locomotion relative to constant-angular-velocity actuation, while the optimal slow-phase center shifts toward smaller leg angles. In contrast to previous findings on level granular terrain, our single-leg force measurements show that this shift cannot be explained by the angular location of peak normal force. Instead, changing the slow-phase center reshapes the temporal combination of normal and shear forces generated by the phase-shifted tripod groups. Comparison of the reconstructed force profiles indicates that effective propulsion occurs when propulsive shear force coincides with sufficient terrain-generated normal support. A force-based model that combines granular resistive force theory with this propulsion criterion reproduces the observed dependence of locomotor performance and optimal gait timing on surface inclination, providing a framework for selecting optimal gait timing in challenging deformable environments.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Recent advances in mechanical design, sensing, control, and autonomy have substantially improved the mobility and versatility of legged robots [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . These advances have expanded their potential for applications including industrial inspection and search and rescue [ 1 , 5 ] , as well as planetary exploration [ 6 , 7 ] . Despite this progress, robust locomotion over deformable terrain remains challenging. Loose granular substrates can yield and rearrange under loading, leading to substantial leg penetration and slip [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . These effects become more severe on granular slopes, where reduced shear resistance and increasing downslope loading can promote backward slip and eventually locomotion failure [ 7 , 11 ] . On inclined granular terrain, increasing surface inclination alters the internal stress state of the substrate, reducing the available shear resistance and promoting downslope yielding and slip; insufficient terrain support can also lead to excessive sinkage and unstable leg–terrain contact [ 12 , 7 , 11 ] . These effects reduce locomotion robustness and can ultimately lead to slope-dependent locomotion failure [ 13 , 11 ] .

Robophysics studies have demonstrated that understanding terrain–robot interactions can enable relatively simple strategies for improving locomotion on granular slopes [ 14 ] . For example, it was found that sidewinding robots can increase shear resistance forces and reduce slip on granular slopes by increasing the length of the body in contact with the substrate as inclination increases [ 12 ] . Similarly, for bipedal locomotion, slope-dependent adjustment of step length and center-of-mass height has been shown to improve climbing success [ 13 ] , while recent work has demonstrated that foot-driven terrain manipulation through cleated foot design can further improve locomotion on steep granular slopes [ 15 ] . More recent work has further identified reduced shear resistance, delayed leg anchoring, and increased backward slip as important mechanisms underlying locomotion degradation and failure on granular slopes [ 11 ] .

While these studies demonstrate the importance of adapting robot–terrain interactions to surface inclination, they have largely focused on contact geometry, body posture, or foot design. The role of intra-cycle leg timing and coordination between multiple legs on granular slopes remains less well understood. On level granular terrain, it was found that locomotor performance is strongly influenced by limb kinematics and interaction speed [ 8 , 16 ] . In particular, Buehler-clock timing – the placement of slow leg rotation phase within each gait cycle – can strongly influence robot speed by changing how the slow phase overlaps with the force-generating portion of the leg trajectory [ 16 ] . Granular resistive force theory further provides a means of predicting the net force on complex intruders by integrating local resistive stresses over their surfaces [ 17 ] . However, it remains unclear how the optimal Buehler-clock timing changes with surface inclination and whether the performance of an alternating-tripod gait can be explained from isolated single-leg forces or instead depends on the temporal combination of forces generated by the two phase-shifted tripod groups.

In this study, we investigate how Buehler-clock timing governs the upslope locomotion of a hexapedal robot on granular surfaces. We systematically vary the center of the slow phase across four surface inclinations and show that the optimal timing shifts toward earlier leg angles as inclination increases. Single-leg force measurements demonstrate that this shift cannot be explained by a corresponding shift in the angle of peak normal force. We then reconstruct the combined normal and shear forces generated by the two phase-shifted tripod groups and show that gait timing controls when propulsive shear force coincides with sufficient normal support. By relating these force relationships to robot displacement on inclined granular media, we reveal the mechanism governing locomotion performance on granular slopes, and develop a predictive model that reproduces the dependence of locomotor performance and optimal gait timing on surface inclination and robot parameters, providing a basis for terrain-aware gait and robot-design optimization.

# 2 Materials and Methods

## 2.1 Robotic Platform and Gait

A small RHex-type [ 18 ] robot (Fig. 1 a) was used to investigate locomotion on level and inclined granular surfaces [ 18 ] . The robot body measured 22 cm in length and 10 cm in width, with a total mass of 1.5 kg. It was equipped with six C-shaped rotary legs, each with a radius, R R , of 3 cm, a width of 0.8 cm, and an arc span of 225 ∘ 225^{\circ} . The angular positions of the robot legs, ϕ \phi , were controlled using a microcontroller (Arduino Uno), and actuated by servo motors (Dynamixel XL330). The motor axles were mounted at a hip height, h h , of 2 cm, measured vertically from the bottom of the body (Fig. 1 d).

During all locomotion experiments, the robot used an alternating tripod gait [ 18 ] in which the six legs were divided into two groups, as color-coded in Fig. 1 a. The three legs within each group moved synchronously, while the two groups moved with a phase offset of half a gait cycle. The alternating tripod gait was biologically inspired by insect locomotion [ 19 , 20 ] and has been widely used in studies of legged-robot locomotion on granular media [ 8 , 10 , 11 ] .

The periodic rotary motion of each leg was generated using a Buehler clock [ 18 ] . Instead of rotating at a uniform angular velocity, each leg rotated slowly with angular speed ω s \omega_{s} through a prescribed angular interval and rapidly with angular speed ω f \omega_{f} through the remainder of the cycle, producing the piecewise-linear relationship between ϕ \phi and normalized time t / T t/T shown in Fig. 1 c. The orange shaded slow interval (referred to as the slow phase hereafter) could be fully defined using the Buehler clock timing parameters, including its angular range ϕ s \phi_{s} , duty factor d c d_{c} , and angular center ϕ 0 \phi_{0} .

## 2.2 Robot Locomotion Experiments

Robot locomotion experiments were conducted in a 127 cm × \times 65 cm tiltable fluidized bed [ 21 , 22 ] , as illustrated in Fig. 1 e. The fluidized bed was filled with 300 ​ µ ​ m 300~\mathrm{\text{\textmu}m} -diameter glass beads (Grainger) to a depth of 10 cm. This depth was selected to minimize boundary effects [ 23 ] on the interaction between the robot legs and the granular substrate. Glass beads are widely used as a model granular substrate [ 9 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 11 ] , as they produce qualitatively similar rheology with sand, while their uniform size and simple geometry facilitate the preparation of repeatable packing states [ 27 ] .

Three motion-capture cameras (OptiTrack Prime 13W) were installed around the fluidized bed to record the three-dimensional position (Fig. 1 e, x x -fore-aft, y y -lateral, z z -surface normal) of the robot at 240 frames per second. An additional video camera was positioned beside the sand bed to record side-view video of each trial at 30 frames per second.

Before each trial, air was passed upward through the base of the sand bed to fluidize the glass beads and reset the compaction and level of the substrate. The airflow was then gradually ramped down to zero, allowing the particles to settle into a flat, loosely packed state [ 8 , 21 ] . The sand bed was then tilted to the prescribed inclination, θ \theta (Fig. 1 e). Subsequently, the robot was placed at a fixed initial position with its longitudinal axis aligned with the upslope direction (Fig. 1 e, x x -axis).

Using this data collection protocol, we performed two sets of experiments to evaluate the effect of Buehler-clock timing on robot locomotion performance: (1) Buehler-clock actuation with a systematically varied slow-phase center, to determine how slow-phase timing affects locomotion and identify the optimal timing at each inclination, and (2) constant-angular-velocity actuation as a baseline to evaluate the benefit of nonuniform leg rotation speed. Both sets of experiments were conducted at surface inclinations of θ = 0 ∘ \theta=0^{\circ} , 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} , 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} , and 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} .

For the Buehler-clock experiments, the slow-phase center was initially varied from ϕ 0 = 140 ∘ \phi_{0}=140^{\circ} to 190 ∘ 190^{\circ} in increments of 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} . Additional values were tested near the high-displacement region to refine the resolution: ϕ 0 = 165 ∘ \phi_{0}=165^{\circ} and 175 ∘ 175^{\circ} at θ = 0 ∘ \theta=0^{\circ} , 165 ∘ 165^{\circ} at θ = 5 ∘ \theta=5^{\circ} , 155 ∘ 155^{\circ} and 165 ∘ 165^{\circ} at θ = 10 ∘ \theta=10^{\circ} , and 145 ∘ 145^{\circ} , 155 ∘ 155^{\circ} , and 165 ∘ 165^{\circ} at θ = 15 ∘ \theta=15^{\circ} . Each tested condition was repeated three times. For all trials, the gait period was fixed at T = π ​ s T=\pi~\mathrm{s} , with a phase offset of 0.5 ​ T 0.5T between the two alternating leg groups (Fig. 1 c, blue and red). The slow-phase angular range was fixed at ϕ s = 48.7 ∘ \phi_{s}=48.7^{\circ} , and the slow phase occupied half of the gait period, corresponding to a duty factor of d c = 0.5 d_{c}=0.5 .

For the constant-angular-velocity experiments, each leg rotated at ω = 114.6 ∘ , s − 1 \omega=114.6^{\circ},\mathrm{s^{-1}} ( 2 ​ rad , s − 1 2~\mathrm{rad,s^{-1}} ). This angular velocity gives the same gait period, T = π ​ s T=\pi~\mathrm{s} , and the same average angular velocity as the Buehler-clock gait, allowing the effect of intra-cycle velocity modulation to be evaluated relative to a constant-velocity baseline.

For all trials, the robot completed 10 gait cycles, and the displacement between its positions in the initial and final motion-capture frames was used to quantify locomotion performance and compare the effects of surface inclination, slow-phase center, and actuation strategy.

## 2.3 Single-Leg Force-Profile Measurements

To understand how the robot legs interacted with the granular substrate during locomotion, we conducted single-leg force-profile measurements. A C-shaped leg driven by a servo motor was mounted at a fixed height above the granular surface, whereas a six-axis force–torque sensor (ATI, Nano25) measured the granular resistive force exerted on the leg (Fig. 1 b). Measurements were conducted at inclination angles of θ = 0 ∘ \theta=0^{\circ} , 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} , 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} , and 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} , corresponding to the same inclinations used in the locomotion experiments. Before each measurement, the granular bed was prepared using the same fluidization and settling procedure as in the robot locomotion experiments. After the sand bed reached the prescribed inclination, the force sensor was biased to zero before the leg began rotating, thereby removing the static gravitational contribution of the leg and mounting assembly from the measured forces.

Two sets of force-profile measurements were conducted. In the first set, the leg was driven directly using the complete Buehler-clock trajectory employed in the robot locomotion experiments. In the second set, the leg was rotated at the constant angular velocities ω s \omega_{s} and ω f \omega_{f} , corresponding to the slow and fast phases of the Buehler-clock gait, respectively. During each trial, the synchronized force components (Fig. 1 b, F x F_{x} , and F z F_{z} ) and leg angular position ϕ \phi were recorded.
